question: This craft makes cloth by interlacing lengthwise threads with crosswise threads, while a loom holds the lengthwise threads in place. What is the craft called?
In weaving traditions among Ghana’s Asante and Ewe communities, narrow woven strips are sewn together to create a prestige cloth worn for important occasions. What is this cloth called?
Unlike dance performed primarily for entertainment, this practice is carried out as part of worship, rites, or communal ceremonies. What is this kind of dance called?

In Māori tradition, this forceful group performance combines chanting, rhythmic foot stamping, and emphatic gestures. New Zealand’s national rugby team is well known for performing this form of ritual dance before matches; what is it called?

Inside Vatican City's Apostolic Palace, this chapel has a ceiling of nine Genesis scenes by Michelangelo, including the image of God reaching toward Adam. Cardinals also gather here to elect a pope. What is the chapel's name?
The Sistine Chapel is named for this 15th-century pope, who restored the earlier Cappella Magna between 1477 and 1480. Which pontiff's patronage is commemorated in the chapel's name?
Born in 1811 in what is now Hungary, this Romantic composer became a famed touring pianist and wrote the B-minor Piano Sonata and the Transcendental Études. Who was he?

Franz Liszt’s touring performances in the 1830s and 1840s provoked an unusually intense public frenzy, with admirers crowding his concerts and avidly seeking keepsakes. What term was coined for this phenomenon?
Before his concert career, Franz Liszt studied piano with a Viennese pedagogue who had been a pupil of Beethoven and later wrote the influential School of Velocity. Who was this teacher?

This single-reed woodwind has a nearly cylindrical bore and a flared bell, and its most common form is the B-flat soprano instrument. Its lowest register is named after an earlier single-reed instrument. What instrument is it?
The clarinet’s development is generally credited to this German instrument maker around 1700. He adapted the earlier single-reed chalumeau by adding a register key.

A clarinet launches the opening of this George Gershwin composition for solo piano and jazz band with a famous rising glissando. The work premiered in 1924 at a concert titled “An Experiment in Modern Music.”
Mozart wrote his A-major concerto for clarinet for this virtuoso, whose playing inspired several of the composer’s late works. The same musician was also the dedicatee of Mozart’s Clarinet Quintet.

An artist can create this kind of image by looking in a mirror, and the result may serve as both a likeness and a statement about identity or artistic authorship. What is this kind of artwork or practice called?
The 1433 panel Portrait of a Man in a Turban is sometimes proposed as the earliest known panel self-portrait. Which Early Netherlandish painter made it?
Which Dutch Golden Age artist became especially famous for making an unusually large body of self-portraits in both paintings and prints, revisiting his face across many stages of his life?
This 1939 self-portrait shows the artist twice, in contrasting dresses, with exposed hearts joined by a blood vessel. What is this Mexican painter’s work called?

One self-portrait by Norman Rockwell, made for a 1960 Saturday Evening Post cover, shows the artist seated at an easel consulting a mirror, with reproductions of famous artists’ self-images pinned beside the canvas. What is this work called?

This military aviator serves in a navy rather than an air force and may fly fixed-wing aircraft from a carrier or helicopters from ships. Missions can include combat, reconnaissance, anti-submarine warfare, transport, and search and rescue. What is this occupation?

A Navy pilot may take off from and land aboard this large warship, whose flight deck lets naval aircraft operate far from land. Its role in World War II helped reduce the dominance of battleships. What is this vessel?
This compact, one-handed cutting tool has a short handle and a blade set perpendicular to it, making it useful for splitting kindling and chopping small pieces of wood. What is this tool called?

During the American temperance movement, which activist became notorious for entering saloons and using a hatchet to smash liquor containers and furnishings? Her raids in Kansas around 1900 made her a nationally known figure.

The FDA lists lipstick, foundation, blush, eyeliner, and mascara as examples of products in this broad cosmetic practice. In ancient Egypt, men and women used it for appearance and other purposes. What is this practice called?
In ancient Egyptian makeup, this eye cosmetic was worn by both men and women and was thought to protect against glare and harmful influences. What was it called?
This social ceremony publicly marks two people entering marriage, often through spoken vows and symbolic customs. A reception may follow the ceremony. What is this celebration called?
At many weddings, this circular piece of jewelry is exchanged or presented as a symbol of commitment and is commonly worn on a finger. What is this object called?
In many Jewish weddings, the couple stands beneath a temporary canopy supported by poles, often representing the home they will build together. What is the traditional name for this structure?
Which color occupies the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum, next to orange and opposite violet? In additive RGB light, it is one of the three primary colors.

In Renaissance Europe, brilliant red garments could be dyed with an imported colorant made from scale insects that feed on prickly-pear cacti in Mexico. What insect-derived dye was prized for producing vivid crimson shades?
Red became a prominent political symbol of communism and socialism. Which 20th-century union of republics used a red flag bearing a gold hammer and sickle before dissolving in 1991?

Red is often associated with anger and danger, while a particular shade was tested as a possible calming color in a 1979 experiment at Seattle’s Naval Correctional Facility. What shade was the subject of that experiment?

Louisiana has 64 of these county-equivalent primary civil subdivisions, a usage rooted in French colonial and Catholic ecclesiastical administration. What is the natural name Louisiana gives one of them?

Louisiana’s parish system includes a group of parishes east of the Mississippi River, including East Baton Rouge and Tangipahoa, in an area that was once part of a Spanish colonial province. What is this region called?

Quito’s former Mariscal Sucre site in the city center closed in 2013 and was converted into a public park. Chicago’s Midway and O’Hare are still-operating examples of what kind of facility, built for aircraft arrivals, departures, and servicing?

Among the airports serving Illinois’s largest city, which one is a major Southwest Airlines base, lies southwest of the city center, and was renamed for a decisive 1942 U.S. naval victory in the Pacific?

Opened in 1869 after a decade of construction, this sea-level passage across northeastern Egypt links Port Said on the Mediterranean with the Red Sea near its southern end. What waterway lets ships travel between Europe and the Indian Ocean without rounding Africa?

On July 26, 1956, Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser announced that Egypt would take control of the company operating the Suez Canal. The ensuing armed confrontation involved Egypt, Israel, Britain, and France; what international crisis followed?

This northern Manhattan neighborhood was formally organized as a Dutch village in 1658 and named after a city in the Netherlands. Its central and western sections became a major center of African American cultural life in the 1920s and 1930s. What neighborhood is it?
What early-20th-century population movement brought large numbers of African American residents from the South to Harlem and other northern cities?
A landmark on West 125th Street in Harlem, this theater became famous for its Amateur Night, where a young Ella Fitzgerald won in 1934. What venue is it?
This South Asian island country lies southeast of India in the Indian Ocean and became a republic in 1972 after having been called Ceylon. What is its current natural name?
Named for an 18th-century governor of Madras, this shallow strait separates Sri Lanka from Tamil Nadu in southeastern India. What is the waterway called?

Sri Lanka’s Parliament meets in this city southeast of Colombo, designated as the country’s legislative capital. Colombo remains the island’s largest city and its principal executive and judicial center; name the legislative capital.

This shallow gulf lies between Sri Lanka’s western coast and southeastern India, and its islands and coral reefs are protected by a major marine biosphere reserve on the Indian side. Identify this body of water.
Named from a Greek expression meaning “between rivers,” this historical region of West Asia was home to Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia, and Assyria. What is this region?
Mesopotamia’s eastern major river rises in the mountains of eastern Turkey and flows south through Iraq. It joins the Euphrates near Al-Qurnah; what is its name?
This major river of Mesopotamia rises in Turkey, then flows through Syria and Iraq before joining the Tigris. Which river is it?
Much of Mesopotamia lies within this modern country, whose capital is Baghdad. What is the country?
The Tigris and Euphrates rivers, which define Mesopotamia, ultimately drain toward this body of water at the region’s southeastern edge. What is it called?

In Franz Kafka’s 1922 short story, a performer sits in a cage while rotating watchers observe him, and his promoter ends each public display after forty days despite his wish to continue. What is the deliberate abstention from food at the center of this performance called?

In Franz Kafka’s story about public fasting, a performer is neglected near the animal cages after joining a circus and explains that he had never found food he liked. The story’s German title is “Ein Hungerkünstler”; what is its English title?

Which 17th-century French neoclassical dramatist wrote the tragedies *Andromaque* and *Britannicus*? Elected to the Académie française in 1673, he became one of the defining playwrights of French classical drama.
Jean Racine’s 1677 tragedy follows a queen of Athens who confesses a forbidden passion for her stepson Hippolytus while her husband, Theseus, is believed dead. What is the title of this play?
A. A. Milne’s 1926 collection follows a teddy bear whose honey-seeking plan involves a balloon and a bees’ nest. What is the name by which this character is commonly known?
The Hundred Acre Wood setting associated with Winnie-the-Pooh was inspired by walks A. A. Milne took with his son in this real area of Sussex. What is the name of this forest?

In Mary Shelley’s novel, this ambitious Swiss student studies at Ingolstadt and investigates the decay of living things before discovering how to animate a being. After the deaths of people close to him, he pursues his creation into the Arctic, where Robert Walton’s expedition finds him.

In Mary Shelley’s novel, which explorer writes letters to his sister, Margaret Saville, describing his voyage toward the North Pole? His crew rescues Victor Frankenstein while he is pursuing his creation across the ice.

Victor Frankenstein’s boyhood friend from Geneva is devoted to literature and travels to Ingolstadt to join him. After nursing Victor through a fever, he is murdered by the being Victor created during their travels in Ireland. Who is this character?

This memoir recounts a Jewish teenager’s experiences alongside his father in Auschwitz and Buchenwald during 1944–1945. It is the first volume of a trilogy completed by Dawn and Day; what is the memoir’s title?

Night recounts a Jewish teenager’s deportation from Sighet and imprisonment with his father in Nazi concentration camps. Which Romanian-born writer, later awarded the 1986 Nobel Peace Prize, wrote the memoir?
Night opens in a Nazi-established ghetto in this Transylvanian town, where Moishe the Beadle’s warnings about deportation were ignored. What town was Wiesel’s home before the family was sent away?
In Night, Wiesel’s father dies in this camp in January 1945, and the U.S. Army liberates it that April. What camp near Weimar is the memoir’s final major setting?

This English Romantic poet wrote the sonnet “On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer” and the odes “To a Nightingale” and “On a Grecian Urn.” His medievalist ballad “La Belle Dame sans Merci” later influenced the Pre-Raphaelite movement; who was he?
John Keats addresses a “light-winged Dryad of the trees” in this ode, then imagines the bird’s song continuing after his own death. The poem ends by asking, “Do I wake or sleep?” Name the poem.
In this poem by John Keats, an ancient vessel is addressed as a “bride of quietness” and a “Sylvan historian.” Its closing lines declare, “Beauty is truth, truth beauty”; name the poem.

John Keats wrote a sonnet about sitting down to reread this Shakespearean tragedy. Its aging king divides his kingdom among his daughters, then banishes Cordelia when she will not compete in flattery; name the play.
In this John Keats ballad, a knight recounts meeting a mysterious woman with wild eyes, being taken to her cave, and dreaming of pale kings and princes who warn him. What is the title?
What is the name of the quantity written “n choose k” that counts the k-item subsets of a set of n distinct items and equals n!/[k!(n − k)!] when 0 ≤ k ≤ n?
Binomial coefficients form a triangular array whose outer edges contain 1s and whose interior entries are each the sum of the two entries directly above them. What is this array called?
For a binary operation, swapping the two operands leaves the result unchanged, as in a + b = b + a for real numbers. What is this property, which matrix multiplication generally does not have?

Commutativity generally fails for matrix multiplication, but one special square matrix leaves any compatible matrix unchanged when multiplied on either side. What is this special matrix, analogous to the number 1 for ordinary multiplication?

What is the name for a finite algebraic expression made from coefficients and variables using addition and multiplication, where every variable is raised only to a nonnegative integer power? Constants are allowed as well.
For a polynomial such as 4x⁶ − x² + 9, the greatest exponent among its terms is 6. What is the name of the measure given by that greatest exponent?

Unlike checking many individual examples, what kind of deductive argument establishes a mathematical claim for all possible cases by deriving it from accepted assumptions, definitions, and rules of inference?

In a mathematical proof of a statement about positive integers, one common method verifies a starting case and then shows that truth at one integer guarantees truth at the next. What is this method called?
In discussions of mathematical proof and intuitionistic logic, what principle states that for any proposition P, either P or not P must hold?

For an acute angle in a right triangle, this trigonometric function is the ratio of the adjacent leg to the hypotenuse. On a circle of radius one, it also gives the horizontal coordinate associated with the angle. What is the function?

In any triangle, the cosine function supplies the angle-dependent term in the relation c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, where C is the angle between sides a and b. What theorem uses this relation to find the third side from two sides and their included angle?
The reciprocal of the cosine function is another standard trigonometric function, and it is undefined wherever cosine is zero. What is this reciprocal function called?

For an angle θ, the cosine function gives the horizontal coordinate of the point reached by rotating from (1, 0) through θ on a circle with radius one. What geometric locus extends the right-triangle definition to arbitrary real angles?
For every circle, this constant is the quotient of its circumference and diameter. Its decimal expansion begins 3.141592 and neither terminates nor repeats; what is the constant?
Around 250 BCE, this Syracusan mathematician developed a polygonal method for bounding Pi, repeatedly doubling the number of sides until he reached a 96-sided polygon. Who was he?
A celebrated equation connects Pi, the imaginary unit, and the base of natural logarithms, with the exponential expression e^(iPi) equal to -1. What is this identity commonly called?

In dimensional analysis, what theorem named for an American engineer says that physical relationships can be expressed using dimensionless groups? These groups are conventionally labeled with lowercase Greek pi, distinguishing this use from the circle constant.
This 17th-century infinite product is formed from fractions involving consecutive even and odd integers, and its limit equals half of Pi. What is this classical product called?

In a 2011 insurance commercial titled “State of Unrest,” a man calls an agent at 3 a.m., and his wife takes the phone to ask what the agent is wearing; the reply is, “Uh, khakis.” What recurring character, originally portrayed by an employee of the insurer, is on the other end of the call?

In 2020, State Farm reimagined Jake from State Farm for a new generation of commercials, replacing original actor Jake Stone with this actor. He appears as the character in a red shirt and khakis and has shared ads with celebrities including Aaron Rodgers and Paul Rudd; who is he?

This Cuban-Spanish actress played a nurse whose involuntary vomiting whenever she lies complicates the mystery in *Knives Out*, and later portrayed Marilyn Monroe in *Blonde*. She also played CIA agent Paloma in *No Time to Die*; who is she?

In *Knives Out*, Ana de Armas plays a compassionate nurse whose inability to lie without vomiting becomes a key detail in the investigation of mystery novelist Harlan Thrombey’s death. What is the character’s name?

In Marvel stories, this character begins as Captain America’s close ally during World War II and later returns as a brainwashed Soviet operative with a cybernetic arm. In the MCU, Wakandans call him the White Wolf, a name distinct from the comics character Hunter. Who is he?

After the presumed-dead Bucky Barnes is recovered and conditioned by Soviet handlers, he is sent on covert missions with a cybernetic arm and eventually confronts Captain America. What codename does he use in this identity?

This short-form video platform lets users create and share vertical clips with music, effects, and other audio. It became known worldwide for viral dance trends and is operated by a company founded in China.

On TikTok, what personalized discovery feed recommends videos based on signals such as what a user watches, likes, and shares? It appears as a tab separate from the feed showing posts by followed accounts.
TikTok’s parent company also operates Douyin, the short-video service tailored to mainland China. What is the name of the Beijing-based technology firm founded in 2012 by Zhang Yiming?

This Mojang sandbox game first appeared in public alpha in 2009 and formally launched for personal computers in November 2011. Its procedurally generated worlds are made of three-dimensional blocks that players can gather, craft with, and build from; what game is it?

In Minecraft, this green hostile creature sneaks toward players and explodes when it gets close. Its distinctive shape reportedly originated when a developer mixed up the height and width values of a pig model; what creature is it?

Minecraft players can enter this lava-dominated underworld through a portal made with obsidian. It is separate from the End, the realm of floating islands where the Ender Dragon awaits; what dimension is it?
In Minecraft, this material lets players create circuits, logic gates, switches, and automated contraptions. What is the name of this resource used to power mechanical devices?

Which indigenous Tibetan religion is traditionally traced to the ancient kingdom of Zhangzhung and to the teacher Tonpa Shenrab, whose historicity is uncertain? Though it predates Tibetan Buddhism, its living institutional tradition took shape around the 10th and 11th centuries as Buddhism spread in Tibet.
In Bön, some teachings are said to have been hidden and later brought to light as revealed treasures. What is the traditional title for a person who discovers and reveals such teachings?

In Algonquian oral traditions, this supernatural being is associated with winter and a hunger for human flesh that cannot be satisfied. Some accounts describe a person transformed into this malevolent figure, whose appetite only grows.

The Wendigo appears in traditions among communities including the Cree, Ojibwe, and Innu, whose ancestral languages are related across parts of the Great Lakes and northeastern North America. What Indigenous language family connects these peoples?
In Norse mythology, this fortified realm is the home of the Æsir and contains Odin’s hall, Valhalla. A rainbow bridge links it to Midgard, the world of humans; what is this realm called?

In Norse cosmology, this rainbow bridge connects Asgard with Midgard, the realm of humans. Heimdall watches over this route between the divine stronghold and the human world; what is the bridge called?

A shepherd and harpist in the Hebrew Bible, this figure became the second king of Israel after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. He is also traditionally credited with defeating a Philistine giant and establishing a royal dynasty.
In the biblical account of David’s rise to fame, this Philistine champion challenged the Israelite army near the Valley of Elah. David defeated him with a sling and a stone.
David captured this Jebusite stronghold and made it the capital of the united Kingdom of Israel. He later brought the Ark of the Covenant there.

This Jewish festival commemorates the Maccabean recovery of Jerusalem and the rededication of the Second Temple. Observed for eight nights, it is associated with lights, fried foods, and games played with a spinning top.
During Hanukkah, one extra light is used to kindle the eight ceremonial lights and is not counted among them. What is the traditional name for this attendant light?
During Hanukkah, children often play a game using a four-sided spinning top marked with Hebrew letters that abbreviate the phrase “A great miracle happened there.” What is this top called?
Hanukkah begins on the 25th day of this Hebrew calendar month and is the only Jewish holiday that begins in it and concludes in Tevet. Which month is it?
This Greek hero was the son of Zeus and Alcmene and became renowned for completing a set of twelve labors, including defeating the Nemean Lion and capturing Cerberus. What is his natural Greek name?
Heracles was ordered to perform the Twelve Labors by this cousin, a king of Mycenae and Tiryns. Who was the king?
Heracles’s final labor was to capture this three-headed hound, which guarded the entrance to the Greek underworld. What was the hound’s name?
After Heracles ascended to Olympus, he married this goddess associated with youth. Who was she?
In one account of Heracles’s death, a poisoned garment caused him unbearable agony, and he built a funeral pyre on this mountain. What mountain was it?

Scientists use this term for the condition that distinguishes biological organisms from nonliving matter. It is known to occur on Earth, but no instance has yet been detected beyond our planet. What is this phenomenon?

In estimates of intelligent life beyond Earth, what equation starts with the rate of star formation and multiplies factors such as the fractions of stars with planets, habitable worlds, and civilizations capable of communication? It was formulated at a 1961 meeting in Green Bank, West Virginia, to estimate detectable civilizations in the Milky Way.
In solution chemistry, what name is given to properties that depend on the concentration of dissolved particles rather than on the particles’ chemical identities?

When a nonvolatile solute is dissolved in a solvent, the solvent must reach a higher temperature before it boils; for dilute solutions, the size of this change depends on molality and the number of dissolved particles. Which colligative property describes this effect?
What is the simplest one-carbon alcohol, a colorless, flammable liquid used as an industrial solvent and fuel? Its toxic metabolism can cause severe damage to vision.
In industrial chemistry, methanol is oxidized to this simplest aldehyde, which is used to make adhesive resins for products such as particleboard and laminate flooring. What compound is it?

On Mars, this immense shield volcano rises about 21.3 kilometers and is the tallest planetary mountain currently known in the Solar System. It is part of the Tharsis region and is the youngest of Mars’s large volcanoes. What is it?
Late-19th-century astronomers catalogued Olympus Mons as a bright albedo feature before its mountainous nature was confirmed by spacecraft. What name did they give this feature?
Olympus Mons began forming during which Martian geologic period, before eruptions continued into the Amazonian?

This group of warm-blooded vertebrates is distinguished by feathers, beaks, and hard-shelled eggs. Its living members evolved from theropod dinosaurs, making them the only dinosaurs alive today. What is this group?
In zoology, the scientific study of birds includes investigating their anatomy, classification, behavior, and evolution. What is this field called?

A famous Late Jurassic fossil from Solnhofen preserves feathers alongside teeth and a long bony tail. In discussions of birds’ evolutionary history, what early avialan is often cited as a link between non-avian dinosaurs and later forms?
Birds produce vocal sounds with a specialized organ near the base of the trachea, where it divides into the bronchi. What is this sound-producing organ called?

This calculated atomic property describes how strongly an atom draws the shared electrons in a chemical bond toward itself. It helps estimate bond polarity, and familiar numerical treatments include scales based on bond energies or effective nuclear charge. What is this property?

Electronegativity became associated with a dimensionless scale introduced in 1932, whose values were inferred from bond energies within a valence-bond framework. Which American chemist proposed that scale and later became famous for advocating high-dose vitamin C?

On the Pauling electronegativity scale, one element has the maximum listed value of 3.98, while caesium is at the low end with a value of 0.79. Which element holds the maximum, represented by the symbol F?

Electronegativity can be assigned using a scale whose defining estimate is the mean of an atom’s first ionization energy and electron affinity. Named for the theoretical chemist who introduced this approach, what is this scale called?
Electronegativity describes an atom’s pull on shared bonding electrons; chemistry also has a contrasting term for the tendency to give up valence electrons. What is that contrasting property called?

First published in the United States in 1876, this library classification system arranges materials in ten main classes, each subdivided into divisions and sections. Its decimal notation allows increasingly specific subjects to receive more detailed numbers. What is the system called?
In Dewey Decimal Classification, a complete call number combines a subject class number with a book number. What common form of the book number represents the author?

In a 1942 philosophical essay, Albert Camus examines whether life is worth living and develops his account of the conflict between human longing for meaning and an indifferent universe. What is the essay’s title?

In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus uses this term for the clash between people’s longing for an intelligible purpose and a universe that offers no satisfying answer. He treats recognizing this tension, rather than escaping it through suicide or religious faith, as a central philosophical task. What is the term?

What philosophical movement, rooted in the writings of Kierkegaard and Nietzsche and later associated with Sartre and de Beauvoir in France, begins with concrete human experience and examines freedom, responsibility, choice, and the search for meaning?
Within existentialism, what principle associated with Sartre holds that people are not born with a complete, fixed nature but shape who they are through their choices and actions?

What is the name of the macroeconomic curve that depicts a short-run inverse association between inflation and unemployment? It is used to consider the tension between price stability and very low unemployment, though later theory challenged the idea of a lasting tradeoff.

In 1967, this economist argued alongside Edmund Phelps that the tradeoff represented by the Phillips curve applies only in the short run. He also correctly predicted the stagflation of the 1970s. Who was he?
Which New Zealand-born economist’s study of British wage inflation and unemployment gave the Phillips curve its name? He was also an engineer and later taught at the London School of Economics.
These speech sounds are produced with little or no narrowing of the vocal tract, unlike consonants, and they usually form the center of a syllable. What are they called?

In phonological descriptions, vowels commonly occupy the central structural position in a syllable, while consonants may form an onset before it or a coda after it. What is this syllabic position called?
Some vowels glide from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable; the sound in the English word “toy” is a familiar example. What is this kind of vowel sound called?

Unlike ordinary spelling, this standardized system assigns symbols to speech sounds across languages. Linguists use it to record precise vowel pronunciations as well as consonants; what is its full name?

Born in Trier in 1818, this German philosopher and economist developed influential analyses of capitalism and class conflict. He later collaborated with Friedrich Engels on a revolutionary political pamphlet.
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published this 1848 political pamphlet as a program for revolution. It describes class struggle and ends with a call for workers of the world to unite.
Karl Marx’s major critique of political economy was published in three volumes between 1867 and 1894. Its first volume analyzes commodities and includes his discussion of commodity fetishism.
In Karl Marx’s account of capitalism, this class owns no means of production and earns wages by selling its labor power. He contrasted it with the bourgeoisie, which controls productive property.

Karl Marx developed this approach to understanding social change, which explains how the ways people produce and distribute goods shape institutions and political ideas. It places conflict between economic classes at the center of transformations across societies over time.

What term describes someone who competes in sports requiring strength, speed, power, or endurance, whether professionally or as an amateur? In A. E. Housman’s elegy about a celebrated young race winner, the person carried shoulder-high is an example of this.

Which English poet wrote an elegy in which a victorious athlete is carried shoulder-high, first after winning his town a race and later in death? The poem contrasts the runner’s brief fame with the fact that he will not live to see his record surpassed.

After winning three NCAA titles at UCLA under coach John Wooden, this center became the NBA’s all-time leading scorer before LeBron James passed him and became famous for his signature skyhook. He led the Milwaukee Bucks to their first NBA championship in 1971; who was he?

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar joined this Wisconsin franchise as a rookie and led it, alongside Oscar Robertson, to its first NBA title in 1971. The same team won its second championship in 2021 behind Giannis Antetokounmpo; what is the franchise?

In standard chess, this special move combines a king’s two-square movement toward one of its own rooks with that rook’s relocation to the square the king crossed. It is legal only if the king and chosen rook have not moved, the path is clear, and the king does not pass through or end on an attacked square.
In castling, what notation identifies the version in which the king moves toward the rook on the a-file rather than toward the rook on the h-file?

In singles or doubles, competitors use strung rackets to send a felt-covered ball across a net on a rectangular court, and a point ends when one player cannot make a valid return. The sport’s four annual majors are the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open. What sport is this?
In professional tennis, what ball-tracking technology was introduced for electronic review and player challenges in 2006, allowing officials to visualize a shot’s trajectory and landing location?
Which tennis major is played on red clay at Stade Roland-Garros in Paris and is the clay-court event in the four-tournament Grand Slam calendar?

Players in this fantasy game create characters with classes, form adventuring parties, and rely on a referee to narrate the world and portray nonplayer characters. First published by TSR in 1974, it uses polyhedral dice to resolve exploration and combat; what is the game called?

One of the two creators of Dungeons & Dragons developed the game from miniature wargaming with Dave Arneson and worked at TSR in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. His young daughter is often credited with helping settle the game’s title; who was this designer?
In Dungeons & Dragons, this rules framework was established with the 2000 third edition and became the basis for a wider system of tabletop games. What is the framework called?
Dungeons & Dragons grew out of miniature wargaming, and its first rules drew on a variation of a 1971 medieval miniatures game with fantasy elements. What was that predecessor game?

What is the name of the 1947 New Mexico episode in which a rancher found debris, Army Air Forces personnel briefly announced a “flying disc,” and the announcement was retracted within a day? The recovered material was later attributed to equipment from a secret balloon program, but the episode became a lasting UFO legend.

In later official explanations of the Roswell UFO incident, what secret program was identified as the source of the debris? It used trains of linked balloons and equipment to detect Soviet nuclear tests, with operations based near Alamogordo Army Air Field.
Which Massachusetts governor became the Democratic nominee for president in 1988? His campaign was remembered for a tank photo-op and advertisements criticizing the state’s prison furlough program.

During the 1988 presidential campaign, which convicted murderer became the focus of advertisements attacking Michael Dukakis over Massachusetts’ prison furlough program? He had escaped while on furlough and committed violent crimes in Maryland.

Which 1846 emigrant wagon-train expedition, led in part by James Reed, left Illinois for California, took a purported shortcut across the Great Salt Lake region, and became trapped by winter snow in the Sierra Nevada?

The Donner Party chose a route promoted in a guidebook as a faster way to California. It crossed the Great Salt Lake region, where difficult terrain and delays helped leave emigrants short on supplies; what was this route called?

While Congress met in Washington to count Electoral College votes from the 2020 election, a crowd of Donald Trump supporters forced its way into the building where lawmakers were meeting, interrupting certification of Joe Biden’s victory. Lawmakers reconvened and completed the count the following morning. What event is described?
answer: January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol

question: During the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol, this Capitol Police officer retreated up a staircase while drawing rioters away from the Senate chamber. Video of his actions later became widely known. Who was the officer?

During the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol, this Air Force veteran was fatally shot by a Capitol Police officer as she tried to climb through a broken window in a door leading to the Speaker’s Lobby. What was her name?

What name is given to the violent 1854–59 struggle in a western U.S. territory and neighboring Missouri, where proslavery and antislavery settlers battled over whether slavery would be permitted there? Disputed elections, rival governments, and raids made this conflict a prelude to the Civil War.

During Bleeding Kansas, this 1854 federal law organized two new territories west of Missouri and Iowa and let settlers decide whether slavery would be allowed through popular sovereignty. It overturned the Missouri Compromise’s prohibition on slavery north of 36°30′ in the region.

During Bleeding Kansas, proslavery forces attacked this antislavery town in May 1856, destroying its Free State Hotel and the presses of two antislavery newspapers. The assault was followed days later by John Brown’s retaliatory killings at Pottawatomie Creek.
During Bleeding Kansas, this abolitionist led the 1856 killings of proslavery settlers near Pottawatomie Creek. Three years later, he led a raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry.

On a morning in 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers used four commercial airliners in a coordinated assault: two struck Manhattan skyscrapers, one hit the U.S. Defense Department’s headquarters, and another crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers resisted. Which American painter and illustrator made more than 300 covers for The Saturday Evening Post, beginning with his first in 1916? During World War II, he also turned President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s ideals into four everyday-life paintings that helped promote a national war-bond campaign.

The 1990 Voyager 1 image known as the Pale Blue Dot was taken after this astronomer and science writer urged NASA to turn the spacecraft’s camera back toward Earth. He later made the photograph central to a 1994 book about humanity’s place in the cosmos; who was he?
This early jazz pianist and composer claimed to have invented jazz during recorded conversations with folklorist Alan Lomax. He led the Red Hot Peppers and composed “King Porter Stomp”; who was he?

During Library of Congress recordings with Jelly Roll Morton, which New Orleans trumpeter disputed his views on scat singing and discussed the making of “Heebie Jeebies”? This Hot Five leader later recorded “What a Wonderful World.”

This German-language opera is the fourth and final work in Richard Wagner’s Ring cycle, with a prologue and three acts. In its finale, Brünnhilde rides onto Siegfried’s funeral pyre as the Rhine rises and Valhalla burns. What is this opera, whose title is commonly translated as “Twilight of the Gods”?
In Götterdämmerung, this son of Alberich schemes to make Siegfried forget Brünnhilde and later kills him while pursuing the ring. What is his name?

What colossal copper monument, given by France to the United States, stands on an island at the entrance to New York Harbor? Its classical figure holds a torch and a tablet bearing the date of American independence in Roman numerals.

For the Statue of Liberty, which French sculptor designed the colossal figure and proposed it as a gift celebrating American independence and French-American friendship? His design was built in France before being shipped to New York in sections.

What German Expressionist art movement was founded in Dresden in 1905 by artists including Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Fritz Bleyl, Erich Heckel, and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff? Emil Nolde later became associated with this group.
A member of Die Brücke created this 1915 self-portrait in which he appears in military uniform beside a severed hand, symbolizing the threat war posed to his artistic future. What is the title?
A composer can rearrange the order of the notes in an interval or chord while retaining the same underlying notes. What is this process called?
In musical inversion of a C-major triad, the notes remain C, E, and G, but E is placed in the bass with the other chord tones above it. What is the name of this specific triad position?

After beginning his career as a commercial illustrator in New York, this artist used silkscreen printing to repeat images drawn from advertising, consumer products, and celebrity photographs. His studio became a gathering place for artists and musicians, and he also made experimental films such as the silent, eight-hour view of the Empire State Building. Name this leading American Pop artist.

Andy Warhol based a famous repeated portrait on a publicity photograph of an actress from the 1953 film Niagara. In his 1962 diptych, 25 brightly colored images of her face sit beside 25 black-and-white versions that grow increasingly faint. Which actress is depicted?

Andy Warhol’s New York studio became a meeting place for artists, poets, musicians, drag performers, and wealthy patrons. Its best-known early location, on East 47th Street, had walls covered in silver foil and paint; what name was given to the studio?

In 1962, Andy Warhol exhibited a group of 32 canvases, each depicting a different variety of the same familiar canned food. The repeated red-and-white packaging made the work a landmark example of his interest in mass-produced consumer goods; what is the series called?

Andy Warhol managed this New York rock band and featured it in his multimedia events known as the Exploding Plastic Inevitable. The band’s 1967 debut album had a cover designed by Warhol featuring a peelable yellow banana. Name the band.

This American roots genre is known for ensembles featuring banjo, fiddle, mandolin, guitar, and upright bass. Bill Monroe helped popularize it, and Earl Scruggs became a defining banjo player in its early development. What is the genre?

In bluegrass music, which North Carolina-born banjo player joined Bill Monroe’s Blue Grass Boys in 1945? He became famous for a three-finger picking style and later formed the Foggy Mountain Boys with Lester Flatt.
A Belgian-born Manouche guitarist and composer helped pioneer jazz manouche. After a fire left two fingers of his left hand unusable, he adapted his technique and continued performing. Who was he?

In 1934, Django Reinhardt teamed up with this violinist to form the Quintette du Hot Club de France, a group known for its distinctive lineup of three guitars, violin, and double bass. Who was the violinist?

Born near Anamosa, Iowa, this American Regionalist painter became nationally prominent with a 1930 painting of a stern man holding a pitchfork beside a woman in front of a house. He also created a satirical 1932 canvas contrasting stiffly posed members of a patriotic hereditary society with a dramatic Revolutionary War scene. Name this artist.

In Grant Wood’s 1930 painting, a man holding a pitchfork stands beside a woman in front of a house. The models were Wood’s dentist and his sister Nan, and he said the figures represented a father and daughter. What is the title of the painting?
At Giverny, Monet repeatedly painted a crossing over his lily pond, and in London he also made views of structures spanning the Thames. What recurring subject connects these works?

Among Bridges in Claude Monet's Paintings, one London series shows the same Thames crossing beneath shifting fog and light. Monet painted these views around 1900 from rooms at the Savoy Hotel; which bridge is depicted?

This set of orchestral suites by a Baroque composer was associated with a royal barge journey along the Thames. One of its best-known movements is the lively D-major “Alla Hornpipe”; what is the work called?
The Water Music was composed for a royal barge journey on the Thames under this German-born composer, who also wrote Messiah and the coronation anthem Zadok the Priest. Who was he?

This English painter and designer joined the Pre-Raphaelite circle after meeting Dante Gabriel Rossetti at Oxford, and later created designs for Morris & Co. His paintings include *The Golden Stairs* and *The Beguiling of Merlin*; who was he?
Edward Burne-Jones helped revive a medieval craft used to decorate church windows, and one of his designs depicts St Cecilia playing a handheld organ. What form of decorative art is this?
This French Romantic composer wrote the operas *Manon*, *Werther*, and *Thaïs*. The last includes a famous violin intermezzo often performed on its own. Who was the composer?
Jules Massenet’s opera *Thaïs* includes an orchestral intermezzo featuring a prominent solo violin, often performed independently. By what short title is this piece commonly known?

This large-scale vocal form combines soloists, chorus, and orchestra to present a dramatic story, often drawn from religious or biblical subjects. Unlike opera, it is generally performed without theatrical staging; Handel’s *Messiah* is a famous example. What is this form?
Which composer wrote the oratorio *Messiah*, first performed in Dublin in 1742, including its famous “Hallelujah” chorus?

Richard Wagner wrote both the music and the libretto for this German-language sequence of four myth-based music dramas over roughly 26 years, completing it in 1874. Its first complete staging opened the inaugural Bayreuth Festival in 1876. What is the cycle’s natural German title?

Wagner described Der Ring des Nibelungen with a German term that presents it as a unified theatrical undertaking, not merely four unrelated operas. Meaning “stage festival play,” the term reflects a structure of three performance days preceded by a preliminary evening. What term did he use?
At the first complete presentation of Der Ring des Nibelungen in 1876, this opera opened the preliminary evening at Bayreuth. Its title refers to the gold of the Rhine. Which opera was it?

In a symphony orchestra, this is the largest and lowest-pitched standard bowed string instrument, typically tuned E1–A1–D2–G2 and sounding an octave below written pitch. It can play bowed orchestral lines or provide a plucked pulse and a regularly moving low line in jazz; what instrument is it?
In a passage for the double bass, a score may direct the player to set aside the bow and pull and release each string with a finger to produce plucked notes. What is this playing technique called?

Which immense oval amphitheater in Rome began construction under Vespasian in 72 CE and was dedicated by Titus in 80 CE? Its tiered arcades and arena hosted gladiatorial contests, animal hunts, and public executions.

Beneath the arena floor of the Colosseum, a network of corridors housed animal cages and connected to mechanical lifts that brought animals and scenery into view. What is the established name for this underground complex?
An Alabama-born composer, bandleader, and music publisher is often called the “Father of the Blues.” He wrote “Beale Street Blues” and “St. Louis Blues”; who was he?
W. C. Handy’s 1914 composition combines a twelve-bar verse with a contrasting section influenced by habanera rhythm. It became one of his most enduring standards; what is the title?

Which Swedish operatic soprano became internationally famous in the nineteenth century and was nicknamed the “Swedish Nightingale”? Her 1850 American tour, promoted by P. T. Barnum, helped make her a household name.

Which Danish author wrote the fairy tale “The Nightingale,” often associated with Jenny Lind because the Swedish soprano was known as the “Swedish Nightingale”? He also wrote “The Snow Queen” and “The Emperor’s New Clothes.”

Born in Dublin, this British painter became known for psychologically intense, distorted human figures. His 1944 triptych depicting three figures at the base of a crucifixion became one of his best-known early works; who was he?
In 1944, Francis Bacon exhibited a triptych of three anguished, biomorphic forms against an orange ground, a work that helped establish his reputation. What is the title of this painting?
answer: Three Studies for Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion

question: A string quartet is layered with sampled speech and sounds recorded on rail journeys in this 1988 minimalist composition. Its three sections juxtapose American travel before the war, European journeys during it, and the postwar period; what is the work called?
Different Trains was written for and recorded by a San Francisco-based group of four musicians founded in 1973 by violinist David Harrington. What is the ensemble's name?

This Mexican muralist painted *Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in Alameda Park*, which depicts historical figures including Porfirio Díaz and Francisco Madero. He also created a controversial Rockefeller Center mural that was destroyed after he included Vladimir Lenin. Who was this artist?
Diego Rivera painted this fresco for the lobby of 30 Rockefeller Plaza, where his depiction of Vladimir Lenin led Nelson Rockefeller to order the work destroyed. What was the mural called?
In music, what term names performers who use their voices to perform lyrics, melodies, or other musical material? In popular performance settings, they often use handheld microphones.
Vocalists such as Ella Fitzgerald have used this improvisational technique, producing nonsense syllables rather than lyrics over a melody. What is this technique called?

This Osage-American ballerina became the first major American prima ballerina of American Indian descent. She was especially celebrated for her performances in works choreographed by George Balanchine. Who was she?

Maria Tallchief rose to prominence dancing the title role in George Balanchine’s 1949 staging of *The Firebird*. Which Russian-born composer wrote the ballet’s score, first performed in Paris in 1910?

Which fourth-century BCE Greek sculptor is celebrated for the statue of Hermes carrying the infant Dionysus and for the famed Aphrodite of Knidos? His work helped establish a more naturalistic, sensuous style in classical sculpture.
The nude Aphrodite created by Praxiteles became a celebrated attraction at a sanctuary in this ancient Carian port city on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor. What was the city’s name?

This side-blown woodwind family spans the historical traverso and the modern C concert instrument. Its members range from the piccolo to alto and bass versions and appear in orchestras, bands, and chamber ensembles. What is this family called?

Within the Western transverse flute family, this compact relative sounds an octave above the standard C instrument and is often assigned brilliant, high-register orchestral lines. Which instrument is it?

In the history of the Western transverse flute, what name identifies its Baroque wooden predecessor, typically fitted with one key and later supplanted in much concert practice by the Boehm-system instrument?
In a dance studio, what horizontal handrail do performers hold for support while warming up and practicing controlled exercises before moving to the center of the room?

During exercises at the ballet barre, dancers may use this numbered stance, counted fifth in the standard sequence of five. It places one turned-out foot crossed in front of the other, and a spring from a demi-plié into relevé from this stance is called a sous-sus.

This Edo-period Japanese artist began working as a child and continued refining his style until his death at age 88. He worked in painting, book illustration, and ukiyo-e woodblock printing, and is especially known for a famous image of a cresting wave.

Katsushika Hokusai made this woodblock print with a towering, curling blue crest, three boats carrying fishermen, and a small mountain in the distance. It became the best-known image in his landscape series devoted to views of that mountain.

Katsushika Hokusai depicted this 3,776-meter volcano from many viewpoints in a celebrated print series, and it appears in the distance behind the boats in his most famous wave print. What is the name of this highest mountain in Japan?

In this landscape print from Katsushika Hokusai’s views of Mount Fuji, the mountain’s broad slopes appear brick-red beneath a band of blue sky, with clouds gathering near the summit. Identify the print.

Prints by Katsushika Hokusai helped fuel a late-19th-century European fascination with Japanese art and design, influencing painters such as Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh. What is this cultural trend commonly called?

This satirical musical, subtitled “A Musical Vaudeville,” premiered on Broadway in 1975 and follows Roxie Hart and Velma Kelly, rival defendants who turn their murder trials into a contest for fame. Its score includes “All That Jazz” and “Razzle Dazzle”; what is the show’s title?
In Chicago, which director and choreographer co-wrote the book with Fred Ebb and shaped the original production’s vaudeville staging? He also choreographed the musical Sweet Charity.
Born in Brooklyn in 1917, he was billed as “Traps the Drum Wonder” as a child before leading a celebrated jazz big band. Which musician was renowned for his speed and extended solos?

Buddy Rich’s virtuosic jazz performances centered on a percussion setup typically comprising a snare, a bass component, and cymbals. Players of this instrument often choose between traditional and matched grips; what is it called?

Diego Velázquez painted a nude woman seen from behind, with Cupid holding a mirror toward her face. Which title is commonly used for this canvas, which Mary Richardson attacked with a meat cleaver in 1914?
During a 1914 protest at London's National Gallery, a British suffragette struck the Rokeby Venus repeatedly with a meat cleaver. What was her name?
What is the name for a religious song of praise or devotion, especially one sung in Christian worship? Such songs are often composed for communal singing and may close with “amen.”

Which hymn has lyrics by John Newton, an Anglican clergyman and former slave trader, and was first published in 1779 in the collection *Olney Hymns*? The melody now commonly associated with it is called “New Britain.”

What is the name for the practice of writing, drawing, or painting on walls and other surfaces, often in public view and without the property owner’s permission? It includes both ancient inscriptions and elaborate modern street-art pieces.
Graffiti survives on the walls of this Roman city, which was buried by Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. Its ruins include the House of the Faun and one of the largest amphitheaters in the Roman world.

This anonymous British graffiti artist became widely known after a framed artwork of a girl reaching toward a red heart-shaped balloon began shredding itself just after it sold at auction in 2018. What is the artist’s name?

This New York artist painted the 1986 public mural Crack is Wack to warn about crack cocaine. His graffiti-inspired style often featured bold outlined figures with radiating lines around them; who was he?

Created in 1939 shortly after its artist’s divorce from muralist Diego Rivera, this double self-portrait shows two seated versions of the same woman holding hands, with an exposed artery connecting their hearts. What is the painting called?
The Two Fridas was painted in 1939, the year Frida Kahlo divorced this Mexican muralist, who created the Detroit Industry fresco cycle. Who was he?

Born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia in 1915, this jazz singer received the nickname Lady Day from saxophonist Lester Young. She became known for her expressive phrasing and recordings including “God Bless the Child.” Who was she?

Billie Holiday’s 1939 recording of this song made it a landmark protest against lynching. Its lyrics contrast the scent of magnolia with burning flesh and depict bodies hanging from a tree. What song is it?
Born in Modena and celebrated for his ringing high Cs, which Italian tenor became one of opera’s most recognizable performers? His final performance was the aria “Nessun dorma.”
Luciano Pavarotti joined Plácido Domingo and José Carreras in a celebrated operatic trio that brought opera to audiences around the world. What was the trio known as?

Unlike a freestanding statue, this sculptural method keeps its forms attached to a background. The forms may rise slightly above the surface or be carved into it, as in a variety associated with ancient Egyptian art. What is this technique?

In Egyptian relief sculpture, what variant places the carved forms below the surrounding stone surface instead of raising them above it? Its recessed contours can catch strong daylight and create shadows along the carved edges.

This orchestral work by Edward Elgar presents a theme followed by fourteen contrasting sections, each associated with one of his friends. Its best-known section is a tribute to music publisher Augustus Jaeger. What is the work?
In the Enigma Variations, the ninth variation honors a close friend of Elgar’s who worked as a music publisher and encouraged him during periods of self-doubt. What was this friend’s name?

Covering the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, this monumental fresco by Michelangelo depicts Christ’s return as the dead rise, with some figures ascending toward heaven and others descending toward damnation. What is the title of this Renaissance painting?
In The Last Judgment, the artist included a self-portrait as the flayed skin held by St. Bartholomew. Which Renaissance master painted this fresco?
What aesthetic concept names a quality associated with admiration and pleasure? John Keats famously links it to truth in the closing lines of “Ode on a Grecian Urn.”
Which English Romantic poet ends “Ode on a Grecian Urn” by equating beauty with truth?

Which Indian percussion instrument consists of two tuned hand drums: a smaller treble drum and a larger bass drum? The smaller drum is commonly called the dayan, while the larger one is called the bayan.
Within a tabla pair, what is the name of the larger bass drum, usually played with the left hand? A player can bend its pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its drumhead.

This vast collaborative textile artwork commemorates people who died during a devastating epidemic, with individual panels often made by family members and friends. It was first displayed on the National Mall in 1987; what is the work called?

The AIDS Memorial Quilt was conceived by this San Francisco activist after he saw placards honoring people who had died of AIDS at a 1985 march. He helped organize the project’s first display on the National Mall in 1987; who was he?

Commissioned by Pericles in the fifth century BCE and designed by Ictinus and Callicrates, this temple was built on the Acropolis in Athens as a sanctuary for the city’s patron goddess. What is its natural name?

Several metopes, pedimental figures, and a sculpted frieze were removed from the Parthenon and taken to Britain in the early 1800s under the direction of the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire. What collective name is commonly given to these sculptures?

This composition has a title expressed as a duration, and its three movements are signaled by the opening and closing of a piano lid rather than by played notes. At its 1952 premiere in Woodstock, New York, sounds from the audience and surroundings became what listeners heard.

The composer of 4′33″ also used chance procedures inspired by the I Ching and wrote Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano, whose strings were altered with inserted objects. Who was this American composer, a longtime collaborator of choreographer Merce Cunningham?

Born in Tacoma in 1941, this American artist studied interior design at the University of Washington before making blown glass the focus of monumental sculptures and installations. After co-founding a Washington glassmaking center in 1971, he became known for series such as Seaforms and Persians. Who is he?
Dale Chihuly received a Fulbright Fellowship in 1968 and subsequently worked at this Venetian glass factory, where he observed a team-based approach to glassblowing. Name the company.
In jazz, performers may improvise melodies with nonsense syllables, shaping them rhythmically instead of relying on conventional lyrics. What is this vocal technique called?
A celebrated practitioner of scat singing, this American vocalist was born in Newport News, Virginia, and recorded the 1959 album *Porgy and Bess* with Louis Armstrong. Who is she?

On the chromatic scale, this pitch lies one semitone above A and one semitone below B natural. It is the tonal center of the major key whose key signature contains exactly two accidentals. What pitch is it?
The major key centered on B-flat has two flats in its key signature. Besides B-flat itself, which pitch is the other flat, following the standard order of flats?
This Rococo oil painting shows a woman in a suspended garden seat as a hidden admirer watches from the bushes. A putto gestures for silence while her shoe flies through the air; what is this work?
The Swing is a celebrated Rococo garden scene featuring a woman on a swing and a hidden lover. Which French painter created this painting?

A stage biography follows a Founding Father’s rise, political rivalries, and duel with Aaron Burr, using a score that blends hip-hop, R&B, and Broadway styles. What musical, created by Lin-Manuel Miranda, tells this story?

Hamilton was inspired by a biography of Alexander Hamilton written by a historian known for detailed accounts of prominent American figures. Who wrote the book that served as the musical’s source material?
What is the name for a designed family of letterforms used in communication, whose styles may include both serif and sans-serif forms?
At the Bauhaus in 1925, Herbert Bayer designed a geometric typeface with lowercase letters only as part of a proposed alphabet intended for use across languages. What was this typeface called?

Before printed books became widespread, scribes and artists produced these hand-copied volumes with decorated initials, miniature scenes, and marginal figures; gold or other metallic foil often enriched their pages. What is the natural name for this kind of book?

Among illuminated manuscripts, which Insular Gospel book, created around the late eighth or early ninth century, is famed for its intricately ornamented Chi-Rho page and is preserved at Trinity College Dublin?
Beethoven’s late work in B-flat major has four expansive movements, including a searching Adagio sostenuto and a famously demanding fugue finale. What is this work commonly known as?

Piano Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major, Op. 106 was dedicated to Beethoven’s aristocratic pupil and longtime patron, a Habsburg royal also associated with the composer’s Op. 97 piano trio. Who was the dedicatee?
It has a hollow wooden body, usually four strings tuned in perfect fifths, and is the highest-pitched standard member of its instrument family. What small bowed instrument is described?

A Genoa-born virtuoso composed a set of 24 caprices for violin, with the final caprice later inspiring works by Liszt and Rachmaninoff. Which 19th-century performer was renowned for his dazzling technique on the instrument?

A score may direct violinists to stop drawing the bow and pluck the strings with a finger; this instruction is often contrasted with arco, which calls for bowing. What Italian musical term names the plucked technique?
The 1716 “Messiah” violin, now held by Oxford’s Ashmolean Museum, is a celebrated surviving example of this Cremonese maker’s work. Which luthier crafted it?

This architectural style is one of three canonical forms of ancient Greek architecture, alongside Doric and Ionic. Its capitals are more elaborately ornamented than those of the other two styles. Which style is it?

In Vitruvius’s account of the Corinthian order, a Greek craftsman supposedly took inspiration from a basket on a young woman’s grave, around which foliage had grown. Which sculptor is credited with turning that sight into the design for the order’s distinctive capital?

This Florentine-born High Renaissance artist worked as a sculptor, painter, architect, and poet. His marble Pietà and David, along with frescoes in a Vatican chapel, made him one of the era’s defining figures. Who was he?
Michelangelo carved this over-life-size marble nude for Florence; the biblical youth is shown before his battle with Goliath, holding a sling over his shoulder. What is the sculpture called?
Michelangelo signed this marble group on the sash across Mary’s chest; it portrays the Virgin holding the dead Christ and was completed in 1499 for a French cardinal. What is this work called?

Michelangelo painted scenes from Genesis across the ceiling of this chapel in the Apostolic Palace, including the image of God reaching toward Adam. The Last Judgment occupies its altar wall; name the chapel.
At age 71, Michelangelo took charge of the architecture of this Vatican City church, reshaping its western end and contributing to the design of its famous dome. Name the church.

Rossini’s final opera premiered in Paris in 1829, with a French libretto adapted from Friedrich Schiller’s play. Its story includes Governor Gesler forcing a Swiss archer to shoot an apple from his son Jemmy’s head. What is the opera’s English title?

The composer of William Tell also wrote The Barber of Seville and La Cenerentola. This Italian composer’s final opera features an overture that ends with the famous “March of the Swiss Soldiers.” Who was the composer?

Born in Salzburg in 1756, this Austrian prodigy performed for European courts as a young child and later composed in nearly every major musical genre of his era. His final years in Vienna produced operas, piano concertos, and a Requiem left unfinished at his death. Who was this composer?

Mozart composed this opera with librettist Emanuel Schikaneder, whose plot follows Prince Tamino and bird-catcher Papageno as they seek Pamina. Its Queen of the Night sings a famous coloratura aria, while Sarastro leads a temple community. What is the opera?

Among Mozart's large orchestral works, this one is catalogued as No. 41 and is in C major; its finale is famous for weaving several themes together in counterpoint. Its nickname alludes to the king of the Roman gods. What work is it?

Mozart was born in this Austrian city in 1756, which was then the seat of an archbishopric. Today, the city is also known for its hilltop fortress and an annual festival devoted to classical music. What is the city?

Mozart wrote this 1791 work for Anton Stadler, a virtuoso whose instrument was specially modified to extend its low register; its Köchel catalogue number is 622. It was among Mozart’s final completed works for soloist and orchestra. What is it?

This German composer wrote both the words and music for his mature stage works, made extensive use of leitmotifs, and composed Tristan und Isolde as well as a four-opera cycle based on Norse and Germanic legends. Who was he?

Richard Wagner envisioned opera as a unified work combining poetry, music, visual design, and drama rather than a sequence of separate musical numbers. What German term names this ideal of a “total work of art”?

Richard Wagner had this theater built in a Bavarian town specifically for his artistic vision. Its specially designed auditorium and concealed orchestra pit hosted the first complete performance of his Ring cycle in 1876. What is the theater called?
What is the name of Franz Schubert’s 24-song cycle setting poems by a single German poet? It opens with “Gute Nacht” and concludes with “Der Leiermann.”
The texts of Winterreise come from a sequence of poems by this German writer, who also wrote the poems Schubert set in Die schöne Müllerin. Who was the poet?

Francisco Goya painted this series of fourteen dark, often grotesque works directly onto the walls of his home, the Quinta del Sordo. It includes scenes such as Saturn Devouring His Son and Witches’ Sabbath. What is the series called?

The Black Paintings were painted directly onto the walls of the Quinta del Sordo by this deaf Spanish artist. He also created The Disasters of War and the portrait The Third of May 1808. Who was the artist?
Ludwig van Beethoven wrote this five-movement orchestral work to evoke rural life and the experience of nature, including a scene beside flowing water and a sudden storm. What is its formal name?
answer: Symphony No. 6 in F major, Op. 68

question: In Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6 in F major, Op. 68, one movement features imitations of a nightingale, quail, and cuckoo near its close. What is the descriptive title of this movement?

This Egyptian queen was a prominent figure of the Amarna Period and appears in artworks with her husband and their children. A celebrated painted limestone bust of her, wearing a tall blue crown, is displayed in Berlin. Who is she?

Nefertiti is often depicted beside this pharaoh, her husband, in scenes devoted to the sun disk Aten. He shifted Egypt’s religious focus toward Aten and founded a new capital at Akhetaten. Who was this ruler?

What is the musical term for a brief, light instrumental composition, often written for piano but also composed for other ensembles? Beethoven’s Für Elise is a well-known example of this kind of piece.
György Ligeti’s Six Bagatelles for wind quintet drew six selected and rearranged movements from an earlier piano cycle. What is the title of that source cycle?

An exposed steel lattice wraps this 80,000-seat Olympic venue, whose design was developed by a Swiss architecture firm with Chinese collaborators. It served as the principal venue for the 2008 Summer Olympics and hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2022 Winter Olympics; what is its official English name?

The design of Beijing National Stadium was led by a Basel-based Swiss architecture practice that also designed the conversion of London’s Tate Modern. Which architectural firm was responsible for the stadium’s design?

This installation fills a gallery with hanging scrolls and bound volumes covered in invented characters that resemble Chinese writing but cannot be read. Created in the late 1980s and early 1990s, it turns meaningless text into an immersive environment. What is the work?

The artist behind Book from the Sky invented and carved thousands of pseudo-Chinese characters for its printed pages, making the text look familiar while remaining unreadable. Which Chinese contemporary artist created the installation?

Born in Vienna in 1825, this Austrian composer and violinist made his professional debut leading an orchestra of 24 musicians in 1844. After his father’s death, he took over his father’s orchestra and became internationally renowned for Viennese waltzes, including a celebrated 1867 work known as the Blue Danube. Who was this composer?

One stage work by Johann Strauss II premiered at Vienna’s Theater an der Wien in 1874. Its plot features disguises, a masked ball, and a prank aimed at embarrassing Gabriel von Eisenstein; what is the name of this operetta?

Which large brass instrument uses a cup-shaped mouthpiece and valves to produce the lowest notes in a typical orchestra’s brass section? Its broad, coiled tubing and prominent bell are also familiar in concert and marching bands.
Which forward-facing-bell instrument, a marching-band version of the tuba, is designed to wrap around the player’s shoulders? Its design is associated with bandmaster John Philip Sousa.

A French Romantic composer wrote an opera based on Prosper Mérimée’s novella about a fiercely independent woman whose relationship with a soldier ends in her murder. The same composer also wrote an opera about two pearl divers who love the same priestess. Who was this composer?
Georges Bizet wrote an opera set on Ceylon in which Nadir and Zurga, both in love with Leïla, sing the duet “Au fond du temple saint.” What is the title of this opera?

Born in Alton, Illinois, in 1926, this trumpeter made his professional debut with Charlie Parker’s bebop quintet and later led recordings that reshaped several styles of jazz. Who was the musician behind Kind of Blue and Birth of the Cool?
Miles Davis built his distinctive sound on this high-register brass instrument, played by buzzing the lips into a mouthpiece. What three-valved instrument was it?

Miles Davis recorded this landmark 1959 album with musicians including John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, and Bill Evans. Its opening track is “So What,” followed by “Freddie Freeloader.” What is the album’s title?
Miles Davis worked with arranger Gil Evans on this 1960 orchestral jazz album, which features an adaptation of the second movement of Joaquín Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez. What album is it?

This German composer became a leading figure in 18th-century operatic reform, pressing for more direct dramatic expression and less ornamental vocal display. His 1762 Vienna opera Orfeo ed Euridice helped exemplify that approach.
In Christoph Willibald Gluck’s 1762 opera Orfeo ed Euridice, what serene, solo-flute-led ballet passage accompanies Orpheus as he moves through the Elysian Fields?

This 16th-century Netherlandish painter filled village scenes with carefully observed peasants, proverbs, and winter landscapes. His works include a crowded panel illustrating dozens of sayings and a snowy scene of hunters returning to a village; who was this artist?

In Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s 1568 painting, six men with impaired sight move along a country path, with the leader already falling into a ditch and the others following. Now held at Naples’ Capodimonte Museum, what is this work called?

Aaron Copland completed this 1948 work on commission from a celebrated swing-era bandleader; after a lyrical opening movement, it moves through a solo cadenza into a jazz-inflected finale. Which work is it?

The Clarinet Concerto was commissioned by this swing-era bandleader, who premiered it with the NBC Symphony Orchestra under Fritz Reiner in 1950. His big band popularized the 1937 recording of “Sing, Sing, Sing.” Who was the musician?

Completed in 1939, this painting depicts an American socialite at the top of a New York skyscraper, falling, and lying on the ground below. Clare Boothe Luce commissioned the work but was horrified by its finished depiction. What is the painting’s title?

The Suicide of Dorothy Hale was painted by a Mexican artist known for self-portraits, including one featuring a thorn necklace and a hummingbird. She was also married to muralist Diego Rivera. Who was the artist?
Developed in ballroom culture, this dance style turns poses associated with fashion photography into a performance, using angular lines and stylized hand movements. What is this dance style called?
Voguing emerged from the ballroom scene of this New York City neighborhood, whose Apollo Theater became a landmark venue for Black performers. Which neighborhood is it?

What international avant-garde movement took shape in Zurich in 1916 around a cabaret founded during World War I? Its artists and writers challenged established cultural values through chance, collage, absurdist performances, and deliberately anti-art works.
Within Dadaism’s early Zurich circle, which German writer co-founded the Cabaret Voltaire with Emmy Hennings in 1916 and performed “Karawane,” a sound poem made largely from invented syllables?

Which 1959 album by the bassist-composer who led the Jazz Workshop includes “Better Git It in Your Soul,” “Jelly Roll,” and an elegy for tenor saxophonist Lester Young? It also features “Open Letter to Duke,” a tribute to Duke Ellington.
On Mingus Ah Um, the elegy “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat” honors a tenor saxophonist known for his relaxed phrasing and his work with Count Basie’s orchestra. Which musician is memorialized by the piece?

This art transforms paper into recognizable figures, geometric constructions, and abstract forms through folding, traditionally without cutting or gluing. Its iconic creations include cranes. What is this art called?
In modern origami, this Japanese artist helped establish a system for diagramming folds and developed wet-folding, a technique that gives paper figures rounded, sculptural forms. Who was he?

This Spanish artist trained under his father beginning at age seven, later spent most of his adult life in France, and helped develop Cubism with Georges Braque. He also painted a stark 1937 anti-war canvas responding to the bombing of a Basque town. Who was he?

Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque helped establish this movement, whose fractured forms combine geometric shapes with multiple viewpoints rather than presenting an object from a single perspective. What is this movement called?

Pablo Picasso made this large 1937 monochrome anti-war canvas after the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War; its imagery includes a screaming horse, a bull, and a grieving mother. What is the painting’s title?

In this 1907 proto-Cubist canvas, Pablo Picasso arranged five angular nude women in a brothel scene, with some faces rendered like African masks. The title refers to a street in Barcelona. What is this painting?

Pablo Picasso’s paintings from this 1901–1904 phase often use a restricted cool-toned palette and portray isolated, melancholy figures; the period followed the suicide of his friend Carlos Casagemas. What is this phase of his career called?

Developing in Japan during the early 17th century, this theatrical form blends dramatic acting, dance, and music in highly stylized performances. Elaborate costumes, striking makeup, and conventions such as dramatic held poses are among its hallmarks. What is this form of theater?
Which Japanese theatrical tradition uses large puppets operated by three-person teams, accompanied by shamisen music and joruri narration? It developed partly before and influenced Kabuki.
Erik Satie’s Gymnopédies, Maurice Ravel’s Boléro, and Claude Debussy’s La Mer and “Clair de Lune” are landmarks of a French concert tradition. What is this national tradition called?

Within French classical music, which composer wrote the orchestral triptych inspired by the sea that premiered in Paris in 1905, with movements titled “From Dawn to Noon on the Sea,” “Play of the Waves,” and “Dialogue of the Wind and the Sea”?

Its opening motif consists of three repeated Gs followed by a lower E-flat, set in a short-short-short-long rhythm that the composer develops throughout the work. Completed in March 1808, this C-minor orchestral work was first performed at a Vienna concert that December alongside the composer’s sixth numbered work in the same genre. What is its natural title?
In discussions of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, which biographer is associated with the doubtful account that Beethoven described the opening motif as “fate knocking at the door”?

Joseph Haydn composed this orchestral work for his first London visit, and it became famous for a startling fortissimo in the slow movement after a quiet repeated theme. It is the second of his twelve London symphonies; what is its standard numbered title?
In Symphony No. 94 in G major, the famous interruption occurs in the second movement, whose pace is indicated by an Italian term meaning a walking tempo. What is the movement’s tempo designation?

Jane Taylor’s poem, published in 1806 in *Rhymes for the Nursery*, supplied the familiar lyrics to this traditional English-language children’s song. Its melody is shared with the alphabet song and the French tune “Ah! vous dirai-je, maman.” What is the song?
The familiar lyrics of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star were adapted from her poem “The Star,” published in the 1806 collection *Rhymes for the Nursery*. Who was this English poet?
