This 1434 oil-on-oak panel depicts a full-length couple in a richly furnished interior. A small convex mirror on the rear wall reflects two additional figures and extends the apparent space of the scene. What is this Jan van Eyck painting called?
The Arnolfini Portrait is built up with thin, translucent oil layers that create luminous colors and finely rendered textures. Which Early Netherlandish painter signed and dated it 1434?

The Arnolfini Portrait has prompted competing interpretations of the couple’s gesture, mirror, and witnesses. Which art historian famously proposed that the scene records a marriage-related legal agreement, an interpretation that remains debated?

In this dramatic Schubert lied, one singer shifts among the narrator, a father, his frightened child, and a supernatural rider. A relentless triplet figure in the piano evokes a horse galloping through the night, and the song concludes with the child dead in his father’s arms. What is the title of the work?
The text set by Schubert in Erlkönig comes from a ballad first published in 1782. Its author also wrote Faust and The Sorrows of Young Werther; who was this German writer?

This Florentine Early Renaissance painter established his own workshop by 1470 and later traveled to Rome to paint frescoes in the Sistine Chapel. He is especially known for mythological works including *Primavera* and *The Birth of Venus*. Who was he?

In this painting by Sandro Botticelli, the goddess stands on a giant scallop shell as wind figures propel her toward the shore of Cyprus. A woman waits on the shore with a flower-patterned cloak; what is the painting’s title?
Born in Rohrau in 1732, this Austrian composer spent much of his career serving the Esterházy family and wrote more than 100 symphonies. Which composer is described?
Joseph Haydn’s younger brother also became a composer and spent much of his career serving the prince-archbishops of Salzburg. What was his name?
Joseph Haydn directed music for the Esterházy princes at a remote Hungarian country residence near Fertőd, later developed by Prince Nikolaus into a lavish estate. What was it called?
Joseph Haydn composed this oratorio using a libretto based on Genesis and Milton’s Paradise Lost. The work premiered in Vienna in 1798; what is its title?
Joseph Haydn’s Op. 33 includes six works for an ensemble made up of two violins, a viola, and a cello. What is the standard name for this ensemble?

In medieval Europe, these fortified residences could combine a central keep with curtain walls, a portcullis, and a moat. Early examples sometimes stood on an artificial mound beside an enclosed courtyard; what are these structures called?
Among the Loire Valley castles, which Renaissance royal residence is known for its double-helix staircase, designed so people can ascend and descend without crossing paths?
This sacred musical form sets the texts of the Western Christian Eucharistic liturgy. Its customary cycle includes the Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, and Agnus Dei; what is it called?
A special form of Mass takes its name from the opening word of its Introit and is associated with services for the dead. What is this type of Mass called?
Raven Chacon became the first Native American composer to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music with this work in 2022. What is the title of this Mass?
Born in Eisenach in 1685, this German late-Baroque musician became Thomaskantor in Leipzig in 1723 and composed a vast body of cantatas, fugues, and keyboard works. Who was this composer?

Bach dedicated a set of six works for orchestra to a Prussian nobleman, and each uses a distinctive combination of soloists and orchestra. The fifth features violin, flute, and harpsichord together as soloists. What is the collection called?
In Bach’s keyboard set associated with Count Hermann Karl von Keyserlingk, an aria is followed by 30 numbered sections, with every third section written as a canon. What is this work commonly called?

Bach’s posthumous reputation grew after a landmark 1829 Berlin performance of the St. Matthew Passion helped spark his nineteenth-century revival. Which young composer organized and conducted that performance?
From 1723, Bach held a senior musical post at Leipzig’s St. Thomas School, while directing music for four Lutheran city churches. What was the German title of his position?

In a traditional wind instrument, a player squeezes an air-filled bag to supply a steady stream of air while a separate tube carries the tune. What is the continuously sounding pipe that holds an unvarying pitch beneath that melody called?
While a Bagpipe drone holds a steady accompaniment, which part of the instrument does the player finger to produce the changing melody notes?

This roof form spans an interior with a curved surface, often hemispherical but sometimes octagonal or onion-shaped. Florence Cathedral’s version has two shells, while the Pantheon’s has a central oculus; what is this architectural form called?

The dome of this Roman building was constructed under Hadrian between 118 and 125 CE. Its concrete ceiling has five rings of sunken panels, and a circular opening at its center lets in daylight; which building is it?

In botanical art, this structure is often the central subject of a close-up painting, with petals, stamens, and carpels shown in vivid detail. Alfred Stieglitz famously interpreted Georgia O’Keeffe’s enlarged paintings of it as resembling parts of the human body. What is this subject?

Which American painter, who was married to photographer Alfred Stieglitz, created *Black Iris III* and *Oriental Poppies* among her many flower paintings? Her enlarged floral images became closely associated with modernist close-up painting.

Artists arrange fruit, flowers, vessels, books, and other inanimate objects as their principal subjects, using light and composition to explore their surfaces and relationships. What visual-art genre became an independent specialty in the Netherlands in the early 1600s?

In 17th-century Dutch still-life painting, artists sometimes arranged skulls, extinguished candles, hourglasses, and wilting flowers to suggest that life and earthly pleasures are fleeting. What is the name for this symbolic type of composition?
Before a performance, musicians may adjust pegs or other sound-producing parts until an instrument’s pitches match a chosen reference pitch or system. What is this practice called?
In instrumental tuning, musicians can strike a small metal device with two prongs to produce a steady reference pitch, often A4 at 440 hertz. What is this device called?

Renaissance sculptor Donatello made monumental examples for Cardinal Rainaldo Brancacci and Antipope John XXIII, often combining a burial effigy with an elaborate architectural setting. What category of burial monument includes mausoleums and sepulchres?

Among Renaissance tombs, Donatello and Michelozzo’s monument for Antipope John XXIII stands inside a historic octagonal structure opposite Florence Cathedral, long used for Christian initiation. What is the name of that structure?
In this jazz style, the left hand alternates between low bass notes and chords while the right hand plays melodies and improvisations. What is this style called?
In histories of Stride Piano, this Harlem-born pianist is often called the “Father of Stride.” He composed “Carolina Shout,” a demanding piano solo that became a touchstone for the style; who was he?

What late-Renaissance style is known for elongated figures, artificial poses, intricate compositions, and strikingly unusual arrangements of space? It developed in European art after the High Renaissance.
A Venetian painter associated with Mannerism portrayed the origin of the Milky Way by showing the infant Heracles nursing at Hera’s breast, with milk scattering into stars. Who painted this scene?

What reusable template masks parts of a surface while allowing paint through selected openings to form a predetermined image or sign? It can be used to reproduce the same design across multiple surfaces.
Which French street artist used the stencil technique in Paris in the 1980s, creating images of rats and life-size figures? He is often cited as an influence on Banksy.

What term describes the perceived pitch distance between two notes, whether they sound together in harmony or one after another in a melody? A major third from C to E and a perfect fifth from C to G are examples.
A musical interval spanning eight diatonic scale steps and doubling the frequency of its lower note is exemplified by C4 to C5. What is this interval called?
In classical dance, this category consists of airborne movements in which both feet leave the floor. Pas de chat and grand jeté are examples; what is the category called?
Among ballet jumps, which named traveling leap takes off from one foot and lands on the other, with the dancer’s legs often stretched into a wide split while airborne?
This vividly colored Orthodox church stands on Moscow’s Red Square. Commissioned to commemorate the Russian conquest of Kazan, what is the building’s name?
The ruler who commissioned Saint Basil’s Cathedral after the conquest of Kazan was crowned Russia’s first tsar in 1547. What was this 16th-century ruler’s name?

What drawing implement has a graphite-and-clay core enclosed in wood, with different proportions of the two materials determining how hard or soft its marks are? Its medium hardness grade is commonly marked #2.
In pencil drawing, what technique creates shading or texture with separate dots rather than overlapping lines, making areas appear darker as the dots become denser?

In Gothic church façades, this large circular opening is divided by radiating stone tracery and is often filled with stained glass. At Amiens, the north-transept example is organized around a five-pointed star and 15 petal-like forms. What is this architectural feature?

The west rose window at this French Gothic landmark depicts the Apocalypse and the Last Judgment, while its north rose features the Virgin Mary, kings of Judah, and prophets. Which landmark has these distinct rose-window programs?

This Kansas City-born alto saxophonist became a central architect of bebop alongside Dizzy Gillespie and was widely known by the nickname “Bird.” He recorded landmark pieces including “Ko-Ko” and “Ornithology.” Who was he?

Charlie Parker’s celebrated bebop collaborator was a trumpeter whose puffed cheeks and bell bent sharply upward became signature features. He co-wrote “A Night in Tunisia” and helped bring Afro-Cuban jazz to wider audiences with “Manteca.” Who was this musician?

Conceived by Jerome Robbins, this 1957 musical sets a Romeo-and-Juliet romance amid a feud between the Jets and Sharks in a Manhattan neighborhood. Its score is by Leonard Bernstein, its lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, and its book by Arthur Laurents; name this work.

In the original 1957 Broadway production of West Side Story, this artist both directed and choreographed the show, having also conceived the musical. His staging made its extended dance sequences central to the storytelling; who was he?

In West Side Story, this musical number contrasts Anita’s praise of New York with Rosalia’s preference for Puerto Rico. Sung by members of the Sharks, it presents their differing views of life on the island and in the United States; name the song.

William Le Baron Jenney's 1885 Home Insurance Building in Chicago is often cited as an early example of a tall building whose metal frame supported its exterior walls. What term describes this very tall, multi-story building type, commonly used for offices, homes, and hotels?
Designed by Adrian Smith and opened in 2010, this Dubai skyscraper reaches 828 meters, including its spire, and is the world's tallest building. What is its name?

This Mexican painter returned to art while recovering from a bus accident at age 18, which left her with lifelong pain. She became famous for autobiographical self-portraits that combine Mexican folk imagery with explorations of identity and physical suffering; who was she?
Frida Kahlo married this fellow Mexican artist in 1929; their stormy relationship included a divorce followed by a remarriage in 1940. Who was the muralist she married?

Frida Kahlo spent much of her life in her family home in Coyoacán, a vivid blue house that now operates as a museum devoted to her life and work. By what well-known Spanish nickname is the house known?

Frida Kahlo’s work with this title was acquired by the Louvre after her 1939 Paris exhibition, becoming the first work by a 20th-century Mexican artist to enter the museum’s collection. What is the title of this small self-portrait, whose image is enclosed by a richly ornamented border?
In Frida Kahlo’s 1944 self-portrait, she wears a metal orthopedic corset and nails are embedded across her exposed body, with a barren landscape behind her. What is the title of this painting?

In classical architecture, this vertical support typically rises from a base through a shaft to a capital, which receives the entablature above. What is this architectural element, whose forms are associated with the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders?

In Rome, a famous freestanding column is wrapped in a spiral relief narrating the conquest of Dacia in two campaigns early in the second century CE. Which emperor’s victories does the monument commemorate?

In many musical ensembles, this low-pitched string instrument anchors the bottom of the harmony, in either an amplified solid-body form or a large upright acoustic form. Players associated with its electric and upright forms include Jaco Pastorius and Charles Mingus; what is this instrument category called?
Among electric-bass players, which American virtuoso joined Weather Report in 1976 and composed “Portrait of Tracy,” a fretless showcase on his self-titled debut album?

Thomas Eakins’s 1875 canvas shows a surgeon demonstrating an operation to medical students in an amphitheater, while a distressed woman recoils in the foreground. What is the painting’s commonly used title?

In The Gross Clinic, the central surgeon leads an operation before an audience of students at Jefferson Medical College. The painting is named for this influential Philadelphia physician, who also wrote A System of Surgery; who was he?

First publicly announced in 1839, this artistic and documentary practice creates images by recording light on film or an electronic sensor. Its practitioners make choices about framing and exposure while using cameras to document events or create artworks. What is this medium?
In early Photography, what process created a unique image on a polished, silver-coated copper plate? Publicly introduced in 1839, it often required long exposure times.

An American composer and bandleader, he served as director of the U.S. Marine Band from 1880 to 1892 before leading a civilian touring band. Known as “The March King,” who wrote many of the best-known U.S. military marches?
John Philip Sousa’s best-known patriotic march is designated the national march of the United States. Its final strain features a celebrated piccolo obbligato; what is the march’s title?
John Philip Sousa composed this march, which became the official march of the U.S. Marine Corps. Its Latin title means “always faithful,” matching the Marine Corps motto; what is the title?
John Philip Sousa helped develop this brass instrument for marching bands, adapting the helicon design so its bell projects sound upward and over the players. What is the instrument called?
After leaving his U.S. Marine Corps musical post in 1892, John Philip Sousa organized a civilian touring ensemble that performed widely under his leadership. What was this ensemble called?
Mozart’s final opera is a two-act German-language Singspiel whose plot follows Tamino and Pamina through a series of initiation trials. What is this work commonly called in English?
The Magic Flute has a German libretto by this actor-manager, who also portrayed Papageno in the opera’s first production. Who was he?
The Magic Flute is identified in the Köchel catalogue by this number. What is its catalogue number?
The Magic Flute premiered at the Theater auf der Wieden on September 30, 1791. In what Austrian city was the theater located?

This traditional maritime work song is famous for a brisk call-and-response refrain built around a recurring question, followed by a sequence of proposed remedies. One verse suggests keeping a crew member aboard a small vessel until he has recovered. Which shanty is it?
In “Drunken Sailor,” one verse recommends keeping the unsteady crewman in the ship’s smaller auxiliary craft until he is sober. What is that type of boat called?

At age 25, he made his New York Philharmonic conducting debut at Carnegie Hall after stepping in at short notice for the ailing Bruno Walter. He later served as the orchestra’s music director from 1958 to 1969 and presented televised Young People’s Concerts; name this American composer, conductor, pianist, and educator.

Leonard Bernstein composed the score for this 1957 Broadway musical, which reimagines Romeo and Juliet amid a Manhattan rivalry between the Puerto Rican Sharks and the white Jets. What is the musical’s title?
This British patriotic hymn sets words by a diplomat to a melody adapted from the central theme of the “Jupiter” movement in Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite The Planets. What hymn is it?
answer: I Vow to Thee, My Country

question: The words of I Vow to Thee, My Country derive from a poem drafted in 1908 under the title “Urbs Dei, or The Two Fatherlands.” Which British diplomat, who later served as ambassador to the United States during World War I, wrote the poem?
In this 1937 Surrealist canvas, three white water birds stand beside spindly trees, while their reflections form massive animals with broad ears and long trunks. What is the painting’s title?
Swans Reflecting Elephants is a double-image work by a Spanish Surrealist who also painted The Persistence of Memory and spent much of his later life at Portlligat. Which artist created it?

Commissioned for the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra’s 1942 season by conductor Eugene Goossens, this ceremonial work by Aaron Copland uses brass and percussion. Copland said it was inspired by a speech from the same year. What is the work?
Fanfare for the Common Man was inspired by a 1942 speech that called for a “Century of the Common Man.” Which U.S. vice president delivered that address?
In orchestral and popular music, this small metal percussion instrument is struck with a beater and commonly made by bending a metal rod into an open, three-sided shape. What is it called?

The Triangle was among the instruments Eduard Hanslick alluded to when he mocked a composer's first piano concerto as a “triangle concerto.” That composer also wrote the 1853 B-minor piano sonata associated with double-function form; who was he?

This Japanese art uses flowers, branches, and other plant materials in deliberately structured compositions, treating line and balance as essential parts of the arrangement. Its traditional principles connect the terrestrial, human, and celestial realms. What is this art?
In ikebana, a formal composition is traditionally interpreted as a model of a three-level cosmos, rather than merely a display of blossoms. Which three realms does the practice bring into harmony?

Andy Warhol’s 1961–62 group of 32 paintings repeats the image of a grocery product in a standardized 20-by-16-inch format, with each canvas showing a different variety. What is the commonly used title of this series?

Campbell’s Soup Cans first went on public view in July 1962 at a Los Angeles art venue on La Cienega Boulevard, where the paintings were displayed together in a row. Which venue hosted the exhibition?
After Campbell’s Soup Cans was exhibited, this Los Angeles art dealer preserved the original 32 canvases as a single group. The Museum of Modern Art later acquired them from him in 1996; who was he?
Campbell’s Soup Cans remained together in Irving Blum’s collection until 1996, when this New York institution acquired all 32 original canvases. Which institution acquired the series?

Unlike a functional support built into a wall, this freestanding monumental gateway commemorates a military victory or another major event and may be decorated with reliefs and inscriptions. What architectural monument is it?

Which Parisian triumphal arch stands at the center of Place Charles de Gaulle, where twelve avenues converge? Beneath it lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, beside an eternal flame rekindled each evening.

Which Japanese composer, born Mamoru Fujisawa, became internationally known through his long creative partnership with Hayao Miyazaki? He wrote scores for Studio Ghibli films including My Neighbor Totoro and Princess Mononoke.

Joe Hisaishi composed the score for this 2001 Studio Ghibli film, in which Chihiro’s parents are transformed into pigs and she works at a bathhouse for spirits. The film won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.
An Oslo example is known for a broad sloping roof that pedestrians are invited to walk across. These buildings are designed to stage sung dramas with orchestral accompaniment; what are they called?
Among opera houses, which Australian city is home to the landmark at Bennelong Point, notable for its white, sail-like concrete shells whose supporting ribs Ove Arup helped engineer?

Composed in 1893, this B-minor work was the last symphony Tchaikovsky completed and the last of his compositions to premiere during his lifetime. Its second movement sets a waltz in an unusual five beats per bar; what is this symphony commonly called?

At a memorial concert 21 days after the premiere of Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74, which conductor led the work’s second performance? Tchaikovsky had made minor corrections after the premiere, making this performance the first in the form now recognized.
Tchaikovsky conducted the premiere of his Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74, on 28 October 1893, nine days before his death. In what city did the first performance take place?
Which German composer, born in Munich in 1864, wrote the tone poems Don Juan and Also sprach Zarathustra and collaborated with Hugo von Hofmannsthal on the operas Elektra and Der Rosenkavalier?
Richard Strauss’s 1896 tone poem was inspired by a philosophical work by Friedrich Nietzsche and became famous for its opening fanfare in 2001: A Space Odyssey. What is the tone poem’s title?
In standard Western pitch naming, this note is a perfect fifth above C and is the tonic of a major key with one sharp. That major key’s relative minor is E minor. What is the note?
The key related to G major by sharing its one-sharp key signature has a tonic a major third above C. What is the name of that key?

Which London museum holds the clay tablet recording Nanni’s complaint to the merchant Ea-Nasir about poor-quality copper ingots? Its collections also include the Parthenon sculptures, whose ownership has prompted debates over cultural repatriation.

The British Museum holds a tablet on which Nanni complained to Ea-Nasir about copper ingots around 1750 BCE. What ancient writing system was made by pressing a cut reed into clay to create wedge-shaped marks?

On medieval churches and other buildings, these carved projections often take the form of grotesque creatures. Their hollow bodies carry rainwater away from the masonry, commonly discharging it from the figure’s mouth. What are these architectural carvings called?
A gargoyle is more than a decorative carving: its projecting form directs rainwater away from a building’s walls. What architectural feature does it function as?

What is the name for an approach to visual art that emphasizes color, line, shape, texture, and form rather than realistically depicting recognizable subjects? It can range from simplifying observed nature to creating imagery with no recognizable subject.

Within abstract art, which early American artist drew on landscapes and natural cycles, reducing observed nature to expressive color and line? The Met describes him as the first American artist to make purely nonrepresentational imagery.

This American photographer became renowned for sharply detailed black-and-white landscapes of the American West. With Fred Archer, he developed a system for planning photographic exposure and development using numbered tonal zones; who was he?

In the 1940s, Ansel Adams received a federal commission to photograph protected scenic lands for a mural project. He photographed Yosemite landmarks such as Half Dome and El Capitan in this type of federally protected area; what was it?

Written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, this musical tells how residents of a Newfoundland town took in thousands of airline passengers diverted when U.S. airspace closed after the September 11 attacks. What is the musical’s title?
In Come From Away, what town in eastern Canada became a diversion point for transatlantic flights after the September 11 attacks, prompting local residents to shelter stranded passengers?

Recorded in 1959 under Miles Davis’s leadership, this Columbia album features the modal-jazz tracks “So What” and “Flamenco Sketches.” Its personnel included pianist Bill Evans and tenor saxophonist John Coltrane. What landmark recording is it?

On Kind of Blue, this tenor saxophonist joined Miles Davis’s sextet and played a solo on “So What.” He later led the quartet behind A Love Supreme and wrote the rapid-changing-chord composition “Giant Steps.” Who is he?
Sergei Prokofiev composed this three-act ballet based on a Shakespeare tragedy. Its score includes a stately, forceful number associated with the rival families of Verona. What is the ballet’s title?

In Prokofiev’s three-act ballet Romeo and Juliet, a weighty, march-like orchestral number accompanies the formal gathering of Verona’s aristocracy and is also known by a title invoking the two rival houses. What is the movement’s primary title?

Born on Crete as Domenikos Theotokopoulos, this Greek-born painter developed a distinctive Mannerist style in Toledo, marked by elongated figures, forceful gestures, and vivid, unconventional colors. What name is he commonly known by?

El Greco painted this rare landscape around 1600, showing a walled city under a dramatic sky, with the Alcázar prominently visible. Rather than serving as a strictly literal record, the scene’s arrangement reflects the artist’s expressive interpretation. What is the painting’s title?
This Italian Baroque composer and violin virtuoso spent much of his career teaching in Padua. He wrote a celebrated sonata renowned for its exceptionally demanding trills; who was he?

Giuseppe Tartini composed his celebrated sonata for a bowed instrument with four strings tuned G, D, A, and E. It is the highest-pitched standard member of the orchestral string family; what instrument is it?
At the western end of the National Mall, a neoclassical temple with 36 Doric columns houses a monumental seated marble statue by Daniel Chester French. Which Washington, D.C., landmark is this?
The monumental seated marble figure at the Lincoln Memorial was designed by this American sculptor, who also created The Minute Man in Concord, Massachusetts. Who was he?
In this traditional Inuit vocal performance, two people face each other and create short, rhythmic sounds in an interlocking exchange. What is this performance form called?
Katajjaq is performed by two people facing each other and making short, rhythmic sounds without conventional instruments. What is the sound-producing medium they use?

Set in Rome in June 1800, this Giacomo Puccini opera follows a celebrated singer, her painter lover, and the corrupt police chief who orders the lover’s execution. The singer kills the chief in an attempt to save her lover; what is the opera’s title?
In Tosca, the painter condemned to execution by Scarpia is the title singer’s lover. He sings “E lucevan le stelle” while awaiting the firing squad at Castel Sant’Angelo; what is his full name?

In Japanese traditional theater, these large painted stage figures are manipulated by a coordinated team of three performers. Their performances are accompanied by a narrator and shamisen, and the tradition influenced kabuki. What are these figures called?
Bunraku puppets are operated by three specialists: one controls the head and right hand, while the others guide the left hand and legs. What is the Japanese title for the lead operator?

Which stage musical adapts Disney’s 1994 animated film about a young prince who must reclaim his place in the animal kingdom and features the songs “Circle of Life,” “Hakuna Matata,” and “Be Prepared”? Its Broadway production is noted for combining human performers with masks and puppetry.

In The Lion King, which director and designer led the Broadway production and shaped its celebrated use of masks, puppets, and visible performers? She became the first woman to win the Tony Award for Best Direction of a Musical for this production.
This polished, egg-like sculpture is associated with perfect beauty and the primordial origins of life. What is the title of the work?
The Beginning of the World is a work by the Romanian-born sculptor whose ensemble at Târgu Jiu includes the monumental Endless Column, created to honor World War I dead. Who was the artist?
What painting medium suspends pigments in water and is commonly applied to paper, producing transparent washes that often allow the surface beneath to remain visible?

In watercolor, pigments are carried in water; what method did Helen Frankenthaler adapt to large, unprimed canvases, where diluted paint spread through the fabric instead of forming a conventional surface layer? This approach helped shape Color Field painting.

In building design, this roofed platform or gallery is attached to a structure’s entrance or exterior wall, offering a sheltered transition between indoors and outdoors. Late-19th-century advocates of fresh-air treatments encouraged builders to add this feature to homes and other buildings.

During the 1896 presidential race, this Ohio Republican remained in Canton rather than making a nationwide speaking tour, receiving delegations at his home. The strategy became associated with speeches delivered from the home's porch.
What concept organizes beats into recurring groups or bars and is conventionally indicated by a time signature? It provides a rhythmic framework for performances across many traditions.

In musical meter, what classification describes bars with two main beats, each subdivided into three equal parts, as commonly found in music written in 6/8? Although six eighth notes appear in each bar, they are felt as two groups of three.
In Japanese origami, this bird model has a long neck and tail, a pointed beak, and broad wings. It is traditionally folded in sets of one thousand to make a wish.

Paper crane folding is closely associated with this Hiroshima girl, who developed leukemia after surviving the 1945 atomic bombing. Her story helped make the folded bird an international symbol of peace.

Born in New Orleans in 1901, this jazz trumpeter and singer became known for his gravelly voice, inventive solos, and nicknames including Satchmo and Pops. He recorded “What a Wonderful World.” Who was he?

Louis Armstrong performed “Melancholy Blues,” one of the musical selections included in a collection of sounds and music dispatched aboard a pair of NASA deep-space probes launched in 1977. What is the collection called?

Louis Armstrong made several collaborative albums with this vocalist, including a 1959 recording of selections from *Porgy and Bess*. Known as the “First Lady of Song,” she was also celebrated for her scat singing. Who was she?

In 1957, as nine Black students attempted to integrate Arkansas’s Central High School, Louis Armstrong publicly criticized the government’s handling of the confrontation. What is the name commonly given to this desegregation crisis?
Around 1922, Louis Armstrong moved to Chicago to join the Creole Jazz Band led by this cornetist, who was his mentor and was nicknamed “King.” Who was the bandleader?

Born Ieoh Ming Pei in Guangzhou in 1917, this Chinese-American modernist designed the East Building of the National Gallery of Art and a glass-and-steel landmark for the Louvre. Which architect received the Pritzker Prize in 1983?

In the courtyard of a famous Parisian former royal palace, I. M. Pei added a transparent geometric entrance that became one of the city’s best-known modern landmarks. What is this glass structure called?

I. M. Pei drew inspiration from Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings for this angular research complex built for the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado. What building brought him his first major recognition after its completion in 1967?

Born in Cheraw, South Carolina, this American trumpeter and bandleader helped shape 1940s bebop through virtuosic improvisation and unusually complex harmonies. He worked closely with Charlie Parker and wrote standards including “A Night in Tunisia” and “Salt Peanuts”; which musician is described?
Dizzy Gillespie’s signature instrument is a three-valved brass instrument whose sound is made by buzzing into a mouthpiece; his famous version had a bell bent upward. What instrument did he play?
Dizzy Gillespie composed this jazz standard, often associated with an Afro-Cuban rhythmic feel, whose original working title was “Interlude.” What is the composition’s familiar title?

Born in Luxembourg and raised in the United States, this artist worked as both a painter and photographer and became a leading figure in Photo-Secession. He later directed the photography department at the Museum of Modern Art and organized the 1955 exhibition The Family of Man. Who was he?

Edward Steichen made this 1904 image near Mamaroneck, New York, building its blue-green appearance with successive hand-applied layers of light-sensitive gum. Which early color photograph became one of his best-known works?

Opened in downtown Los Angeles in 2003, this performing-arts venue is home to the Los Angeles Philharmonic. Its sweeping, sculptural stainless-steel exterior was designed by Frank Gehry; what is this venue called?

The Walt Disney Concert Hall’s sweeping stainless-steel exterior was designed by an architect whose other major works include the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris. Who is this architect?

A 1932–1933 cycle of 27 fresco panels covers all four walls of the Garden Court at a major American art museum, portraying workers, machinery, and manufacturing. After visiting Ford’s River Rouge complex, which work did its Mexican artist create?

The Detroit Industry Murals include large panels that combine views of factory buildings to show stages in making an automobile engine and transmission. Which Mexican muralist created the cycle after sketching at Ford’s River Rouge factories?

Written in 1936 for the Moscow Central Children’s Theatre, this narrated symphonic fairy tale gives its characters and animals distinct orchestral themes, with strings representing its young protagonist and the bassoon his grandfather. What is the Sergei Prokofiev work?

In Peter and the Wolf, each animal is introduced by a characteristic orchestral timbre: the clarinet belongs to the cat, while a section of instruments plays the low, menacing theme of the pursuing predator. Which instruments carry that theme?

He opened his own Chicago practice in 1893 and later established a studio at his Oak Park, Illinois, home. He promoted an approach he called “organic architecture,” seeking harmony between buildings and their surroundings. Who was this American architect associated with the Prairie School and Usonian homes?

Edgar Kaufmann commissioned this Pennsylvania weekend house, where concrete terraces cantilever above Bear Run and the building is integrated with a waterfall. What landmark did Frank Lloyd Wright design for him?

In Chicago’s Hyde Park neighborhood, this residence for a local businessman is marked by strongly horizontal brick bands, expansive overhangs, and art-glass windows. Which Prairie-style building designed by Frank Lloyd Wright is this?
Born in Paris in 1840, this French sculptor first conceived The Thinker as a figure called The Poet for The Gates of Hell. His works also include The Burghers of Calais. Who was he?

Auguste Rodin created this public monument depicting six citizens who faced execution after offering themselves to England’s Edward III during the siege of their city. Each figure has a distinct pose and emotional expression. What is the sculpture called?

This Spanish Golden Age painter served as court artist to Philip IV and created a 1656 scene featuring Infanta Margarita, her attendants, and the artist at an easel. He also painted a canvas showing Ambrosio Spinola receiving the keys to Breda. Who was he?

In Diego Velázquez’s 1656 court scene, Infanta Margarita stands among her attendants while the painter depicts himself at work. A mirror in the background reflects the king and queen. What is this painting called?
In 1914, suffragette Mary Richardson attacked a Diego Velázquez painting showing a nude figure from behind gazing into a mirror held by Cupid. What is this work commonly called?
Completed in 1788, this is the second of the three final symphonies Mozart wrote and carries Köchel catalogue number 550. What is its title?
Symphony No. 40 in G minor was completed between Mozart’s Symphony No. 39 and the “Jupiter” Symphony. Which Köchel catalogue number identifies it?

Which electronic musical instrument generates tones from waveforms and shapes them with filters, envelopes, and other signal-processing components? Wendy Carlos helped popularize its use in recordings such as *Switched-On Bach*.

On a synthesizer, what sound property is associated with frequency and described by listeners as high or low? Raising an oscillator’s frequency raises this property, while lowering it makes the sound lower.

Anish Kapoor’s monumental polished stainless-steel sculpture stands in Chicago’s Millennium Park, where its elliptical surface reflects the surrounding skyline and visitors. Though it is popularly nicknamed “The Bean,” what is the work’s official title?

Cloud Gate’s mirrorlike elliptical surface is assembled from a precisely counted set of highly polished stainless-steel sections rather than formed as a single sheet. How many sections make up the sculpture?

This two-act ballet premiered in 1892 with music by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky and is set during a Christmas celebration. After a girl receives a wooden toy that leads her into a fantasy world, the story features a battle with mice and dances including the Trepak and the Sugar Plum Fairy’s solo. What ballet is it?

In The Nutcracker, Tchaikovsky gives the Sugar Plum Fairy’s music a delicate, bell-like sound using a keyboard instrument whose keys cause metal plates to ring. What instrument supplies that distinctive timbre?
The Nutcracker follows an 1844 French retelling of E. T. A. Hoffmann’s earlier story about a toy and a Mouse King. Which French writer created that intermediate adaptation?

Artists create this broad class of objects by shaping clay or other ceramic materials, then hardening them through firing. Its forms range from everyday vessels to sculptural works, and makers may shape them on a wheel or decorate them with slips and glazes. What is this craft and its resulting objects commonly called?
Within pottery, this high-fired ceramic body is made with a clay mixture that includes kaolin. It is prized for its smooth white surface, which can be semi-translucent. What is this material called?

This French composer (1862–1918) wrote the orchestral work *La mer*, the opera *Pelléas et Mélisande*, and the piano piece *Clair de lune*. Often associated with musical Impressionism, a label he rejected, who was he?
Claude Debussy completed only one opera, whose 1902 Paris premiere helped bring him international fame. Based on a symbolist play by Maurice Maeterlinck, what is its title?

Claude Debussy conceived this three-movement orchestral work as an alternative to the traditional symphony. Its middle movement depicts waves at play, and its opening movement follows the scene from dawn to midday; name the work.
In Claude Debussy’s *Suite bergamasque*, what piano movement takes its title from a French phrase meaning “moonlight” and became one of his best-known works?
Claude Debussy’s 1894 orchestral work was inspired by a poem by Stéphane Mallarmé about a mythological woodland creature. Its opening flute solo is especially famous; name this symphonic poem.
In music, what rhythmic action produces percussion when performers bring their hands together, and also serves as a common form of audience applause?
Which American minimalist composer wrote a 1972 work for two performers whose only sound comes from clapping, as one performer gradually shifts a repeating rhythm against the other's steady pattern?

This large concert instrument changes string pitches through a foot-operated mechanism, letting it play in any key. Its standard orchestral form has 47 strings and spans about six and a half octaves; what is it called?

The pedal harp is made by a major concert-harp company founded in 1950 by this harpist and instrument maker. Born in Chicago to Italian parents, he later established his manufacturing business in Italy; who was he?

The pedal harp also figures in jazz through this musician, who played harp and piano and was married to a renowned saxophonist and bandleader. Her recordings include *Journey in Satchidananda* and *Ptah, the El Daoud*; who is she?

Which monumental Mannerist canvas by Paolo Veronese, now displayed in the Louvre, depicts Jesus turning water into wine during a biblical banquet? Its vast composition fills a refectory-scale scene with biblical and contemporary guests.

The Wedding Feast at Cana was originally painted for the refectory of a Benedictine monastery on the island of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice. After French troops removed the enormous canvas from Venice in 1797, it was taken to what Paris museum?
In a symphony orchestra, what group comprises violins, violas, cellos, and double basses, distinct from the brass, woodwind, and percussion players?

In the orchestral string section, which instrument generally plays the lowest register and is physically larger than a cello? It is commonly played upright, with the musician standing or using a tall stool.

A member of a multigenerational Italian musical dynasty, this composer became known for operas that include a tragedy about young artists in Paris and an unfinished drama set in imperial China, completed by Franco Alfano after his death. His style began in late-Romantic Italian opera and later moved toward verismo; who was he?

Giacomo Puccini set this opera among struggling young artists in Paris, including the poet Rodolfo and the seamstress Mimì. It premiered in 1896, and its story later inspired the musical Rent; what is the opera?
In Giacomo Puccini’s Rome-set opera, a celebrated singer kills the police chief Baron Scarpia after he tries to use her lover, painter Mario Cavaradossi, as leverage. What is this opera?
Giacomo Puccini’s opera follows a young Japanese woman in Nagasaki who waits for U.S. Navy lieutenant Pinkerton to return. She sings “Un bel dì” as she imagines his homecoming; name the opera.

Giacomo Puccini’s final opera centers on a Chinese princess who sets suitors three riddles, while Prince Calaf risks execution to win her hand. Puccini left the score unfinished at his death, and Franco Alfano completed it; what is the opera?

Which notation symbol places F below middle C on the fourth line of a five-line staff, marked by two dots bracketing that line? It is commonly used for cello and trombone parts and for the left-hand staff in piano notation.
In the Bass clef, the two dots identify the staff line assigned to F. What alternate name for this clef refers to that pitch?

In Vivaldi’s *The Four Seasons*, the opening E-major violin concerto pairs an Allegro with a sonnet describing birds celebrating, while a viola figure represents a barking dog. Which season does the concerto depict?

Spring opens a cycle of violin concertos by Antonio Vivaldi, published in 1725 as Op. 8 and also known by the Italian title *Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione*. What is this cycle commonly called in English?
Built for Seattle’s 1962 world’s fair, this futuristic observation tower stands on three splayed legs and has a broad, saucer-shaped top. What is this landmark called?
The Space Needle was built as a signature landmark for Seattle’s 1962 world’s fair, which showcased visions of the future. What was the official name of that fair?

This setting of the Catholic Mass for the dead was begun in Vienna in late 1791, but its composer died before finishing it. Its standard posthumous completion is associated chiefly with a composer who supplied much of the missing music.
In the standard posthumous completion of Requiem in D minor, K. 626, this Austrian composer supplied much of the music left unfinished by Mozart, following contributions by Joseph Eybler. Who was he?

Requiem in D minor, K. 626, was commissioned for a February 1792 memorial service for Anna, the wife of a nobleman. Which nobleman placed the commission and probably intended to present the work as his own composition?

A sustained note can be shaped by a regular fluctuation above and below its central pitch, produced vocally or by a violinist rocking a finger on the string. This pitch modulation is distinct from a change in loudness; what is the technique called?
Vibrato periodically changes a sustained note’s pitch, while a related musical effect periodically changes the sound’s amplitude instead. What is that amplitude-based effect called?

This Chinese contemporary artist served as an artistic consultant on Beijing’s 2008 National Stadium, nicknamed the Bird’s Nest, and made a performance in which he photographed himself dropping a Han-dynasty ceramic urn. Known for politically engaged work across sculpture, photography, and installation, who is he?

To commemorate children killed in the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, Ai Weiwei covered the façade of Munich’s Haus der Kunst with thousands of brightly colored school backpacks arranged to form a sentence quoted from a bereaved mother. What is the title of this installation?

This chamber ensemble consists of two violins, a viola, and a cello; music written for the same lineup became a major genre during the Classical era. What is the natural name for this ensemble and genre?

This Austrian composer helped shape the string quartet in the mid-18th century, developing it around four relatively equal musical partners. His 68 quartets include works nicknamed “Sunrise” and “Emperor.” Who was he?

In Beethoven’s string quartet output, what eponymous name is given to the three works published as Op. 59, Nos. 1–3? Commissioned by a Russian diplomat, the set includes music that draws on Russian folk material.

This 1943 musical, Rodgers and Hammerstein’s first collaboration, adapts Lynn Riggs’s play *Green Grow the Lilacs*. It follows Laurey Williams as she weighs the courtship of cowboy Curly and farmhand Jud. What is the musical’s title?
In *Oklahoma!*, Laurey’s romantic uncertainty becomes an Act I dream ballet that imagines possible outcomes involving Curly and Jud. Which choreographer created this pivotal sequence?

Founded in 1897, this group of Austrian artists broke with the conservative Künstlerhaus establishment and organized exhibitions for modern art. Its exhibition pavilion, designed by Joseph Maria Olbrich, displays the motto “To every age its art, to art its freedom.” What was the movement called?

The Vienna Secession published this illustrated magazine as its official journal from 1898 to 1903, featuring work by artists such as Gustav Klimt and Koloman Moser. Its Latin title translates roughly as “Sacred Spring.” What was the magazine called?

Which Dutch modernist movement sought geometric abstraction through horizontal and vertical lines, often combining them with the primary colors, black, and white? Its principles are closely associated with grid-based paintings and compositions of simple rectangles.
The Dutch painter behind *Broadway Boogie Woogie* also created numerous grid-based *Compositions* using black lines and blocks of primary color. Which artist associated with De Stijl is described?

Submitted to the Society of Independent Artists’ 1917 exhibition under the name “R. Mutt,” this readymade turned a mass-produced urinal into a controversial work of art. What is the title of the work?
The artist behind Fountain also created L.H.O.O.Q., a Dada work that altered a reproduction of the Mona Lisa with a mustache and goatee. Which French artist made both works?
This kind of monument portrays a mounted rider and often commemorates a ruler, military leader, or civic founder. What is this form of sculpture called?
Designed by Étienne Maurice Falconet, this equestrian statue of Peter the Great stands in St. Petersburg atop the enormous granite Thunder Stone. What is the statue called?

Born in Hamlet, North Carolina, and later based in Philadelphia, this saxophonist played with Miles Davis before becoming a bandleader and composer. His work helped shape modal and free jazz, and his harmonic innovations inspired a namesake progression. Who was he?

John Coltrane played this woodwind instrument, which has a single reed and is commonly made in alto and tenor versions. Charlie Parker and Kenny G are also well-known players of it. What is the instrument?
John Coltrane’s 1959 album on Atlantic Records includes the tracks “Naima” and “Mr. P.C.” Its title piece is known for rapid harmonic movement through a series of tonal centers. What is the album?
John Coltrane recorded this 1965 suite for Impulse! Records. Its four parts include “Acknowledgement,” “Resolution,” “Pursuance,” and “Psalm.” What is the suite called?
John Coltrane’s second wife was a pianist and harpist who became a bandleader in her own right. Her recordings include the 1971 album Journey in Satchidananda. Who was she?
Which Banksy stencil artwork shows a small silhouetted figure in a dress, one arm extended toward a floating red heart shape? Its pared-down image is among the artist’s best-known works.
After a framed version of Girl with Balloon partially passed through a concealed shredder moments after a 2018 Sotheby’s auction, what new title was given to the altered work?
What drawing technique creates texture, shading, or depth by arranging small dots, often using a single color rather than overlapping lines?

Unlike stippling, which commonly uses dots in a single color for shading, what late-19th-century painting technique builds images from separate colored dots that blend optically at a distance? Georges Seurat used it in *A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte*.
A musical note can sound high or low even when its loudness stays the same. What perceptual property of sound, determined primarily by frequency, describes this difference?
On a synthesizer, a low-frequency oscillator can periodically modulate pitch, creating a wavering effect around a sustained note. What is this expressive effect called?

Designed by Eero Saarinen and completed in 1965, this 630-foot stainless-steel monument stands beside the Mississippi River in St. Louis. It has an inverted catenary profile and is the centerpiece of the national park that bears its name. What is this landmark?

The Gateway Arch’s profile follows a mathematically defined curve rather than a circular arc. It is the shape formed by a uniform chain hanging freely from two fixed endpoints; what is this curve called?
Gioachino Rossini’s 1817 comic opera reworks the Cinderella story around Angelina, Prince Ramiro, and Don Magnifico’s family. What is the opera’s title?
In La Cenerentola, Prince Ramiro exchanges clothes with his valet so he can observe Angelina and her family while disguised. What is the valet’s name?

This large-scale orchestral genre became a major form of independent concert music in eighteenth-century Europe. Its Classical-era works often use contrasting movements in a fast, slow, minuet or scherzo, and finale sequence, though earlier examples could have three movements. What is this kind of composition?

Which Bohemian composer and violinist helped shape the symphony through his work leading the Mannheim court orchestra in the mid-eighteenth century? His orchestra became known for its disciplined playing and striking dynamic effects.

This concert overture and early tone poem grew out of Felix Mendelssohn’s visit to Fingal’s Cave on the Scottish island of Staffa. Its undulating orchestral writing evokes the waves around the cave. What is the work’s natural title?
The Hebrides is an orchestral concert overture by this German Romantic composer, whose travels also inspired Symphony No. 4, commonly known as the Italian Symphony. Who is the composer?

Formed when limestone recrystallizes under heat and pressure, this metamorphic stone is composed chiefly of calcite and can obscure fossils from its original rock. Its translucence, polish, and capacity for fine carving made it a favored material for Greek statuary and architecture. What is this stone called?
A marble Hellenistic sculpture discovered in 1820 on the Greek island of Melos is famous for having lost both arms and is now displayed in the Louvre. By what name is this statue widely known?

Which American musical organization, one of the “Big Five,” became known for a distinctive sound under a conductor who led much of the music in Disney’s *Fantasia*? Its regular concert venue is Verizon Hall at the Kimmel Center.
Which conductor led the Philadelphia Orchestra from 1936 to 1980, succeeding Leopold Stokowski and becoming one of its most closely associated musical leaders?
Which lively French music-hall dance features a chorus line performing high kicks? It is prominently heard in the “Infernal Galop” from Orpheus in the Underworld.
The can-can is prominently associated with the “Infernal Galop,” a showpiece in Orpheus in the Underworld. Which French composer wrote that comic opera and also composed The Tales of Hoffmann?

Traditionally associated with Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, this wind instrument is often a long hollow tube. A player vibrates their lips to produce its resonant drone. What instrument is it?
A player of the didgeridoo can keep its drone sounding by storing air in the cheeks and inhaling through the nose. What technique makes this possible?

This British-Nigerian contemporary artist uses Dutch wax-print textiles, historical references, and often headless figures in sculptures and installations exploring colonialism, cultural identity, and hybridity. Who is this artist?

Yinka Shonibare created a headless, Dutch-wax-clad reinterpretation named as being “after” a French Rococo painter. Its source painting shows a young woman in a shepherdess hat kicking off a shoe while a putto signals silence and a concealed admirer watches from the bushes; what painting is reimagined?
What eighteenth-century European art style developed as a later phase of the Baroque and became known for playful aristocratic scenes, delicate colors, and elaborate, curving ornament?
In Rococo art, which French painter helped establish the fête galante genre, depicting elegantly dressed couples in garden settings? His best-known works include *The Embarkation for Cythera*.
This dramatic partner dance emerged in the dance halls of the Río de la Plata. Its sound is strongly associated with the bandoneón and the compositions of Astor Piazzolla. What dance is it?

In tango ensembles, this bellows-driven free-reed instrument gives the music its characteristic plaintive sound. It typically has buttons on both sides rather than a piano-style keyboard. What instrument is it?
In this classical genre, a solo keyboard player is featured in musical dialogue with an orchestra. What is the name of the genre?
Sergei Rachmaninoff wrote four works in the Piano Concerto genre, and the tonic of his second has E-flat major as its relative major. In what key is that concerto?

Developed by African American musicians in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, this American style became closely associated with piano. Its melody places accents on weaker or unexpected beats over a steadier, march-like accompaniment; what genre is it?

In Ragtime, what term describes the characteristic rhythmic effect in which a melody accents weaker or unexpected beats against a regular underlying pulse? It is heard in piano writing where the right hand’s tune contrasts with the left hand’s steady alternation of bass notes and chords.

This Japanese traditional theater form features elaborate puppets manipulated by teams of operators, a narrator who voices the drama, and musical accompaniment. What is this distinctive puppet-theater tradition?
In Bunraku, a player accompanies the narration and puppetry with a plucked, three-stringed Japanese lute whose music helps shape the mood and pacing of a performance. What is this instrument called?

This single-reed woodwind family has a usually brass, conical body, with a reed vibrating against a mouthpiece and keys that open and close tone holes. Its members include soprano, alto, tenor, and baritone registers; what is the family called?
The saxophone was invented in the early 1840s by a Belgian instrument maker, who secured a patent for it on June 28, 1846. What was this maker’s name?
In the modern saxophone family, soprano and tenor models share a transposing key, distinct from the one used by alto and baritone models. Which key is shared by soprano and tenor saxophones?

In Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s 1559 village scene, more than a hundred figures act out Dutch and Flemish sayings. Among them, one person bangs his head against a wall and another places a blue cloak on her husband; what is the painting’s commonly used English title?
The artist of Netherlandish Proverbs also painted The Hunters in the Snow and The Peasant Wedding. This sixteenth-century Flemish painter’s sons carried on his artistic dynasty; who was he?

What dance tradition, associated especially with Egypt and the Middle East, emphasizes rhythmic movements of the hips and torso and may be accompanied by finger cymbals? Its performers often use shimmies and shivers while moving to percussion rhythms.

In belly dance, what is the name of a common Egyptian four-beat rhythm whose Arabic-derived name means “divided”? Often played with low dum strokes and sharper tek accents, it provides a familiar foundation for hip movements.

This unfinished painting shows only the head and neck of the first U.S. president. Painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1796, it became one of the most widely reproduced likenesses of its sitter. What is the painting commonly called?
The Athenaeum Portrait is an unfinished 1796 likeness of the first U.S. president. Which American painter created it and also painted the Lansdowne portrait of the same sitter?

After beginning as a San Francisco portrait photographer, this American documentary photographer was hired by the Farm Security Administration to record Depression-era poverty and later documented the early conditions at Manzanar for the War Relocation Authority. She made a famous 1936 image of Florence Owens Thompson at a California pea-pickers’ camp and worked with economist Paul Taylor on reports about migrant labor. Who was she?

In a 1936 photograph by Dorothea Lange, Florence Owens Thompson looks into the distance while three children gather close around her at a California pea-pickers’ camp. The image became a widely circulated emblem of farmworkers’ hardship during the Great Depression; what is its title?

This Dutch painter worked as an art dealer and later as a Protestant missionary in Belgium before devoting himself to painting. In Arles, he created vivid sunflower still lifes, and his later work included a famous nocturnal scene with a cypress beneath swirling stars. Which artist is described?
Vincent van Gogh depended financially on his younger brother, who worked as an art dealer and exchanged a long series of letters with him. What was this brother’s name?

Vincent van Gogh moved to this southern French town in 1888, where he painted a series of sunflower still lifes and lived in a yellow house he depicted. His brief artistic partnership with Paul Gauguin took place there before ending in a crisis. Which town was it?
While residing at Saint-Rémy, Vincent van Gogh created this 1889 painting, combining a dominant foreground cypress with a village, crescent moon, and turbulent blue sky. What is the painting’s title?

Following his breakdown in Arles, Vincent van Gogh admitted himself to an asylum in this Provençal town, where he painted works including one with a swirling night sky and cypress. What is the town’s full established name?

This 1913 ballet and orchestral work, created for the Ballets Russes, depicts pagan ceremonies and the selection of a young woman for sacrifice. Its Paris premiere became notorious for the uproar in the audience. What is the work?
The Rite of Spring opens with an exposed, unusually high solo from this double-reed woodwind, the lowest-pitched instrument in the standard orchestral woodwind family. What instrument is it?
In the original production of The Rite of Spring, this celebrated Ballets Russes dancer created the angular, unconventional choreography. Who was he?
The Rite of Spring premiered on 29 May 1913 at this Paris theater, designed by architect Auguste Perret. What was the venue?
For The Rite of Spring, this Russian artist and archaeologist designed both the original stage settings and costumes, drawing on his knowledge of ancient cultures. Who was he?
Beethoven completed this C-sharp minor piano work in 1801; its catalog designation is Op. 27, No. 2, and its opening movement is marked Adagio sostenuto. What is the work best known by?
In the Moonlight Sonata, Beethoven made a dedication in 1802 to one of his piano pupils, a young countess. Which woman received the dedication?
The Moonlight Sonata was composed by a Bonn-born musician whose other piano works include the Pathétique and Waldstein sonatas. Who was the composer?
The Moonlight Sonata’s familiar nickname grew from an image comparing its opening movement to moonlight on Lake Lucerne. Which German poet and music critic proposed that image?
In the Moonlight Sonata, the first movement begins with a two-word Italian instruction that indicates a slow pace and a sustained manner of playing. What is the exact marking?
In classical ballet, which of the five basic foot placements has one foot in front of the other with the heels aligned?
In ballet, a dancer can begin this springing action from Fifth Position by bending into a demi-plié, then rising into relevé. What is the action called?

In this 1927 painting, a woman wearing a yellow hat sits alone at a small table and holds a mug. Reflections of two rows of ceiling lights appear in the dark window behind her. What is the painting called?

The artist who painted Automat also created a 1942 scene of four people in a brightly lit city diner, viewed through a broad window with no visible entrance. Which American artist made both paintings?
What concept is an ordered sequence of pitches that performers often practice in ascending and descending forms? Major, minor, and chromatic versions are common examples.
A musical scale that moves through every semitone within an octave uses all twelve pitch classes before reaching the octave’s repeated note. What is this scale called?

A German composer and critic created the fictional alter egos Florestan and Eusebius, who appear among the musical portraits in *Carnaval*. He also composed symphonies nicknamed “Spring” and “Rhenish.” Who was he?

Robert Schumann championed this younger German composer in an 1853 essay, predicting that he would bring new musical paths to light. The composer later wrote *A German Requiem* and the *Hungarian Dances*. Who was he?

This Norwegian Romantic composer drew on folk traditions in works such as his Piano Concerto in A minor. He also wrote the incidental music for a Henrik Ibsen play featuring the songs “Morning Mood” and “In the Hall of the Mountain King.” Who was he?

Edvard Grieg composed music for a Henrik Ibsen drama about a boastful wanderer whose adventures take him from Norway to North Africa. The music includes “Solveig’s Song” and “Anitra’s Dance.” What is the title of the drama?
Near Bergen, the former home of Edvard Grieg and his wife Nina became a museum; the property also includes a small composer’s hut by the water. What is the name of the estate?
Which 1959 Dave Brubeck Quartet album explored unusual meters, opening with “Blue Rondo à la Turk” in 9/8 and featuring a celebrated 5/4 track that became one of jazz’s best-known recordings?
On the Dave Brubeck Quartet’s album Time Out, which alto saxophonist composed “Take Five” and played the album’s alto saxophone parts?
This orchestral movement from Edvard Grieg’s Peer Gynt music begins with a quiet, repeating tune and grows steadily faster and louder as Peer is pursued by trolls. What is the movement called?
answer: In the Hall of the Mountain King

question: In the Hall of the Mountain King is part of the incidental music for Henrik Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt. Its composer also wrote the Holberg Suite and was a leading Norwegian Romantic composer; who was he?

Edward Burne-Jones helped revive this art, while Louis Comfort Tiffany used it to create elaborate lampshades. What architectural medium combines colored panes—often joined by lead cames—into images or patterns?
Marc Chagall created a predominantly blue work in stained glass that is displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago and commemorates the United States’ bicentennial. What is this work’s title?

In Sergei Prokofiev’s symphonic fairy tale, this boy ignores his grandfather’s warning to stay inside and ventures into the meadow. With the bird’s help, he loops a rope around the wolf’s tail so the hunters can capture it; what is the boy’s name?

In the 1936 symphonic fairy tale featuring Peter, the bird, duck, cat, hunters, and wolf each have a distinctive orchestral theme. Which Russian composer wrote the work to introduce children to the sounds of orchestral instruments?

This domesticated equid is commonly shown beneath a rider in equestrian sculpture. It appears in the monument atop the Thunder Stone in Saint Petersburg and in Donatello’s statue honoring Erasmo da Narni; what animal is depicted?

A monumental metal horse-and-rider statue in Saint Petersburg depicts Peter the Great and stands on the Thunder Stone, a massive boulder moved for the project. Designed by Étienne Falconet, by what familiar title is this equestrian monument known?

Construction of this unfinished basilica in Barcelona began in 1882 under Francisco de Paula del Villar, before another architect took over a year later and radically reshaped the design. Its plan calls for 18 towers, while branching columns inside create a forest-like effect. What is the basilica called?

The Sagrada Família’s nature-inspired geometry and ambitious structural design reflect the vision of the architect who took over the project in 1883. Which Catalan architect transformed the original design into the basilica recognized today?

What architectural structure consists of a succession of steps that provides a route between floors or other levels? M. C. Escher made this structure’s impossible, looping geometry famous in one of his prints.
Which 1960 M. C. Escher lithograph shows robed figures traversing an impossible, self-returning staircase on a rooftop structure, seemingly never reaching a different level?

Born in Halle in 1685, this German-born composer settled in London and became a naturalised British subject. He wrote a famous oratorio containing the “Hallelujah” chorus and the coronation anthem “Zadok the Priest.” Who was he?
Handel’s English-language oratorio includes “For Unto Us a Child Is Born,” and its second part culminates in a chorus whose text repeats “Hallelujah.” What is the title of this work?
Commissioned for a royal party aboard barges on the River Thames in 1717, this orchestral work by Handel includes dance movements such as “Alla Hornpipe.” What is its title?

Born Jacopo Robusti in Venice around 1518 or 1519, this painter received a nickname meaning “little dyer” because of his father’s occupation. He painted *The Miracle of the Slave* and spent decades decorating the Scuola Grande di San Rocco; who was he?
Tintoretto’s 1548 breakthrough painting shows Saint Mark intervening to save a bound man from torture, as the executioners’ tools break or fail. What is the title of this work?
Completed in 1942, this oil painting shows four people inside a brightly lit downtown diner while the surrounding street is dark and nearly deserted. What Edward Hopper work is it?
Nighthawks is one of the best-known paintings by this American artist, who also painted Automat and Chop Suey and often used his wife Jo as a model. Who was he?
Within months of its completion, Nighthawks was purchased for $3,000 by which museum, located at 111 South Michigan Avenue?
Nighthawks is classified within which art movement, associated with recognizable depictions of everyday life and urban settings?
Which French 20th-century composer belonged to Les Six and wrote both the opera *Dialogue of the Carmelites* and the concerto *Concert champêtre*?

Francis Poulenc composed *Concert champêtre* for Polish musician Wanda Landowska. The concerto’s solo part is written for an older keyboard instrument whose strings are plucked rather than struck by hammers; what is that instrument?
Which prolific German Baroque composer published Tafelmusik, whose subscribers included George Frideric Handel, and also wrote the Fantasias for Viola da Gamba Solo?
Georg Philipp Telemann wrote 12 solo Fantasias for this woodwind instrument, which was also played by Frederick the Great and has a smaller relative called the piccolo. What is the instrument?

This large keyboard wind instrument can have several hand keyboards, called manuals, and a pedalboard for the feet. Stops let the player combine ranks of differently voiced tones, which are sustained by pressurized air rather than struck strings; what is the instrument?

In a pipe organ, this chamber-like component receives pressurized air from the blower and distributes it beneath the pipes. Its valves admit air to selected pipes when the player presses keys; what is it called?

Born in Saint Petersburg in 1906, this Russian-born Soviet composer gained international attention when his First Symphony was performed in 1926. His output included fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets. Who was he?
In Shostakovich’s Eighth String Quartet, a four-note musical signature built from German note names for his initials appears prominently in every movement. What is this musical signature called?

Camille Saint-Saëns composed this humorous orchestral suite as a musical portrait gallery of creatures, with movements evoking lions, tortoises, and fossils. Its finale features a lyrical solo from a low-register string instrument to portray a graceful bird.
In The Carnival of the Animals, the finale gives its lyrical melody to a bowed string instrument with a rich, low register. Which instrument lies below the viola and above the double bass?

This over-two-meter Hellenistic marble figure of Aphrodite has stood among the Louvre’s most famous antiquities since 1821. Its original arms are missing, leaving their poses uncertain; what is this celebrated sculpture commonly called?

The Venus de Milo is commonly attributed to this sculptor because of a now-lost inscription, although the inscription’s connection to the statue is disputed. What is the name associated with that attribution?
The Venus de Milo has been displayed since 1821 in this Paris institution, where it became a major work in the antiquities collection after the Napoleonic Wars. What institution is it?

This Washington, D.C., installation consists of two polished black granite walls meeting in a V, inscribed with the names of U.S. service members who died or remain missing in the Southeast Asian conflict of 1955–1975. What is its established name?

The Vietnam Veterans Memorial’s winning design was chosen in a national competition from more than 1,400 entries. Its creator was then a 21-year-old architecture student at Yale; who was the American designer?

Maurice Ravel composed this 1928 orchestral work for a ballet commissioned by Ida Rubinstein, which premiered in Paris that November. Its melody is passed among instruments while the orchestration and volume gradually intensify; what is the work called?
In Boléro, one percussion instrument maintains the same repeating ostinato throughout as the melody moves among winds and strings. Which instrument supplies this persistent rhythmic foundation?
What Cuban music-and-dance genre developed from danzón, incorporated swing influences, and became internationally popular in the mid-20th century?
Which Cuban bandleader and pianist became a leading figure in the mid-century Mambo craze and recorded the 1955 hit version of “Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White”?

In Baroque counterpoint, one voice introduces a principal theme, which is then taken up successively by other voices at different pitches. The voices continue to imitate and transform that theme as the piece develops. What is this musical form?

In Baroque discussions of Fugue, this collection by J. S. Bach stands out for its two ricercars based on a royal theme supplied by Frederick II, one in three parts and one in six. It also contains a trio sonata for flute; what is the collection’s title?

What performance approach, descended from Stanislavski’s System and later influential in U.S. theater and film through the Group Theatre and Actors Studio, asks performers to investigate a character’s inner life, aims, and past rather than simply copy outward gestures? Practitioners may use imagination and sensory or personal memories to make behavior feel psychologically truthful.

Within Method acting, which American actor-teacher developed a particularly influential adaptation that placed special emphasis on affective, or emotional, memory, drawing on performers’ sensory and emotional recollections? His approach built on but was not identical to Stanislavski’s System.
In classical ballet, dancers use this technique to support their body weight on the ends of their toes, relying on specially constructed shoes with stiffened fronts. What is this technique called?
When a dancer works en pointe, a stiffened compartment at the front of the shoe surrounds and supports the toes. What is this part of the shoe called?

Traditional painting instruction treats a pigment-based trio as foundational for mixing, in contrast with the additive system used for screens and the more accurate subtractive model used in printing. What is the name of this traditional pigment-based model?

Which Bauhaus educator developed influential color-theory courses and later published *The Art of Color*, helping carry traditional ideas about the RYB primary colors into art instruction? His teaching used systematic exercises to explore color relationships.

Which Dutch art movement associated with Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg favored horizontal and vertical lines, geometric compositions, and a restricted palette that included the RYB primary colors? Its Dutch name translates as “The Style.”

This American jazz vocalist won an amateur contest at Harlem’s Apollo Theater, later led Chick Webb’s band after his death, and recorded Song Book albums devoted to composers such as Cole Porter and Duke Ellington. What singer, celebrated for precise technique and scat improvisation, was known as the “First Lady of Song”?

Ella Fitzgerald rose to prominence after winning an amateur talent contest at this Harlem venue, whose celebrated Amateur Night has helped launch many performers’ careers. What theater hosted the contest?
In folk and family music, what kind of song or musical piece is traditionally sung to a young child, often with a gentle, repetitive melody, to soothe them toward sleep?

A lullaby by this 19th-century German composer was published as “Wiegenlied,” Op. 49, No. 4, and dedicated to Bertha Faber in connection with her son. The composer also wrote *A German Requiem* and the *Hungarian Dances*. Who was he?

Written for Paul Whiteman’s “Experiment in Modern Music,” this 1924 concert work combines solo piano with jazz ensemble colors and begins with a rising clarinet glissando. What is the name of this George Gershwin composition?
In rehearsals for Rhapsody in Blue, Gershwin had written a scale-like run for the clarinet at the opening. Which clarinetist transformed it into the famous glissando?
Completed in 113 CE in Rome, this roughly 30-meter marble monument is wrapped in a continuous spiral relief depicting the emperor’s two campaigns against the Dacians. What monument is it?
The continuous relief on Trajan’s Column depicts two Roman campaigns against this kingdom north of the Danube, which Rome annexed after its defeat in 106 CE. What was the kingdom called?

Raphael’s *The School of Athens* and Diego Rivera’s *Detroit Industry* cycle are celebrated examples of this kind of architectural painting. It is made directly on walls, ceilings, or other permanent surfaces, and is called a fresco when painted on wet plaster; what is this art form?
The mural cycle *Detroit Industry* fills the Garden Court of the Detroit Institute of Arts with scenes of manufacturing and labor. Which Mexican artist created it?

This American jazz pianist, composer, and bandleader led an orchestra that helped define big-band jazz. His works include “Mood Indigo” and the extended suite Black, Brown, and Beige. What was his name?
Duke Ellington’s longtime composing and arranging partner joined his orchestra in 1939. He wrote the melody for “Take the A Train,” which became the band’s signature tune. Who was he?

John Trumbull painted this commander with his horse Blueskin, while Emanuel Leutze portrayed him crossing an icy river in a famous painting. The same man appears on the one-dollar bill and was the subject of Jean-Antoine Houdon’s marble statue in Virginia’s State Capitol; who is he?

In Richmond’s Virginia State Capitol, a marble life portrait of George Washington shows him standing with one hand on a cane and the other resting on a bundle of fasces. Which French sculptor traveled to America to model Washington from life and created this statue?

Created by Katsushika Hokusai around 1831, this Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock print opens a series devoted to views of Japan’s highest mountain. It shows three boats struggling beneath an enormous curling crest, with the mountain small on the horizon; what is the print’s title?

In The Great Wave off Kanagawa, a small peak can be seen beyond the turbulent water, contrasting with the enormous foreground wave. What Japanese mountain, also the focus of Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views, is depicted there?
In The Great Wave off Kanagawa, the sea’s saturated color comes from a recently imported European pigment that helped reshape Japanese woodblock printing. What synthetic iron-based pigment is it?
