The Great Wave off Kanagawa was published as the opening image in a Hokusai series that also includes Fine Wind, Clear Morning. The series presents views of Japan’s highest mountain; what is its title?

Born in Hamburg in 1809, this German early Romantic composer later led Leipzig’s Gewandhaus Orchestra and helped establish Germany’s first conservatory. He also conducted a landmark 1829 performance of a major work by J. S. Bach; name the composer.
Which large-scale sacred work by J. S. Bach did Felix Mendelssohn conduct in 1829, helping renew public interest in Bach’s music? It is one of Bach’s surviving settings of the final days of Jesus.

This Rodgers and Hammerstein stage production follows a novice nun who becomes governess to the children of a widowed Austrian naval officer and falls in love with him. When Nazi rule reaches Austria, the family escapes across the Alps.

The Sound of Music features the song “My Favorite Things,” which a jazz musician recast as an extended modal performance on a 1961 album. Which saxophonist, also known for the albums Giant Steps and A Love Supreme, recorded that interpretation?

Born in Oxford in 1945, this British cellist became closely identified with Edward Elgar’s Cello Concerto, especially through her 1965 recording with the London Symphony Orchestra and John Barbirolli. Multiple sclerosis ended her performing career in the early 1970s; who was she?

In Jacqueline du Pré’s celebrated 1965 recording of Elgar’s Cello Concerto with the London Symphony Orchestra, which conductor led the orchestra? The British musician was also music director of the Hallé Orchestra for 25 years.

Opened in 1927 in Chicago’s Grant Park, this monumental waterwork was modeled after a tiered feature in the gardens of Versailles and became an iconic part of the city’s lakefront parkland. What is its name?

Buckingham Fountain was modeled on a tiered water feature in Versailles’ gardens, where sculpted peasants are shown transforming into frogs after provoking a goddess and her children. What is that feature called?

Composed for the 1830 tricentennial of the presentation of the Augsburg Confession, this orchestral work’s finale incorporates Martin Luther’s hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God.” Mendelssohn composed it in 1830, but it was published only in 1868, two decades after his death, and was consequently assigned No. 5. What is its natural name?
The Reformation Symphony was written by a German composer whose other symphonies include the Italian and Scottish. Who was this early Romantic composer?
Which 1888 symphonic suite by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov depicts episodes from *One Thousand and One Nights* and includes movements titled “The Sea and Sinbad’s Ship” and “Festival at Baghdad”?
In Rimsky-Korsakov’s *Scheherazade*, which plucked instrument accompanies the solo violin’s recurring theme for the title character and uses pedals to change the pitches of its strings?
Opened to the public in 1793 during the French Revolution, this Parisian institution occupies a former royal palace and holds the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. Name this art institution.
At the Louvre Museum, a glass pyramid inaugurated in 1989 serves as the landmark entrance to an underground lobby connecting the museum’s wings. Which Chinese-American architect designed the pyramid?

What Renaissance system depicts three-dimensional space on a flat surface by making receding parallel lines converge toward a vanishing point? It also typically shows more distant objects as smaller, creating an illusion of depth.

Which Florentine artist-architect demonstrated linear perspective with a mirror and lost the competition for the Florence Baptistery doors to Lorenzo Ghiberti? He later designed the great octagonal brick dome of Florence Cathedral.

In this late-19th-century canvas, a red-haired woman folds herself around a seated man, her face pressed to his neck as he buries his face in his arms. Edvard Munch said the scene showed a kiss on the neck, though it is commonly given a supernatural interpretation. What is the painting commonly called?
The painting commonly called Vampire was made by the Norwegian artist whose many versions of The Scream helped make that work an emblem of modern anxiety. What was this artist’s name?
This French royal residence was substantially expanded under Louis XIV and became renowned for its extensive gardens and its Hall of Mirrors. What is its natural name?

At the Palace of Versailles, Jean-Antoine Watteau worked in an art style sometimes regarded as the later phase of the Baroque. What style is associated with his painting of a scene in which a portrait of Louis XIV is being packed away?

Which title belongs to the ten-book cycle of 66 short piano compositions whose opening work, “Arietta,” shares its melody with the closing “Remembrances”? The cycle also includes a composition depicting a wedding celebration at Troldhaugen.

Lyric Pieces is a ten-book collection of short piano works by a Norwegian composer who also wrote the incidental music for Henrik Ibsen’s Peer Gynt, including “Morning Mood” and “In the Hall of the Mountain King.” Who is the composer?

Pablo Picasso created this monumental 1937 oil painting in a stark palette of black, white, and gray after an air raid devastated a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. It fills the composition with a gored horse, grieving figures, and a bull; what is the painting called?
The Spanish painter behind Guernica also made The Old Guitarist during his Blue Period and co-founded an influential movement with Georges Braque. Who was this artist?

Guernica’s fractured figures and sharply angular forms are associated with this movement, which Picasso and Georges Braque helped pioneer. Louis Vauxcelles popularized its name after criticizing Braque’s landscapes at L’Estaque; what movement is it?
After international travels, Guernica entered the collection of this Madrid museum, where it is now displayed. The institution is Spain’s national museum of 20th-century art; which museum is it?

Guernica was first shown at the 1937 International Exposition in Paris, in a dedicated national building commissioned by the Republican government fighting Franco’s Nationalists. What was the name of that country’s exhibition venue?

Which Mozart comic opera, first performed in Vienna in 1786, uses an Italian libretto about a count’s servant and his fiancée outmaneuvering their employer? Its plot follows the characters introduced in Beaumarchais’s play The Barber of Seville.
In The Marriage of Figaro, which Italian poet and librettist wrote the text for Mozart? He also collaborated with Mozart on Don Giovanni and Così fan tutte.

Which Brazilian singer and guitarist developed an understated, softly syncopated guitar style that helped establish bossa nova? A landmark album he made with American tenor saxophonist Stan Getz also featured an English-language vocal by the guitarist’s wife.

On which 1964 album did João Gilberto pair his bossa nova guitar with an American tenor saxophonist, and on which did a female singer perform the hit English-language version of “The Girl from Ipanema”?

A young player in a feathered hat is being cheated by a disguised accomplice, who signals to another accomplice through a hole in his glove. A concealed six of clubs is tucked into the victim’s belt; what is the title of this painting?

The Cardsharps is an early genre scene by this Italian painter, known for using dramatic light and shadow. He also painted The Calling of St. Matthew, where a shaft of light falls across the tax collector; who was he?
In traditional choral music, this standard voice part occupies the lowest vocal range. It also begins the Kyrie fugue in Mozart’s Requiem. What is this voice part?

The Bass part begins the Kyrie fugue in this Austrian composer’s unfinished Requiem in D minor, which Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed after the composer’s death. The composer also wrote Eine kleine Nachtmusik; who was he?

Which 1977 Broadway musical, with a book by Thomas Meehan and songs by Charles Strouse and Martin Charnin, follows a spirited orphan in Depression-era New York who is taken in by billionaire Oliver Warbucks? Its opening number introduces the children at the orphanage run by Miss Hannigan.
In Annie, the title orphan visits the White House and meets the president who took office in 1933 and launched the New Deal. Which president appears in the musical?
Which musical key has C as its tonic and a signature that lowers B, E, and A? Its natural scale proceeds C, D, E-flat, F, G, A-flat, and B-flat.
In C minor, which relative key shares the same key signature but places its tonal center three semitones above C?

Congress created this U.S. cultural and research complex in 1846 using a bequest from a British scientist who had never visited the United States. It now operates dozens of museums and research centers, including Washington venues devoted to flight and space exploration and to visual cultures from Africa.

Operated by the Smithsonian Institution, this Washington venue’s home on the Mall opened in 1987 and is dedicated to the visual cultures of societies south of the Sahara. Its collection includes royal objects from Benin, including carved ivory works.

A Renaissance canvas presents a nude goddess upright on a scallop shell as wind carries her toward shore, while a waiting figure offers her a flowered cloak. What is the title of this Sandro Botticelli painting?

The Birth of Venus is one of this Florentine Renaissance painter’s best-known mythological canvases; he also created the large mythological scene of dancing Three Graces in an orange grove commonly called Primavera. Which artist painted The Birth of Venus?

The Birth of Venus has remained in a major art museum in Florence, alongside Botticelli’s Primavera. What is the name of that institution, whose collection also includes works by Michelangelo and Leonardo?

In The Birth of Venus, the goddess is shown arriving from the sea fully grown rather than being born as an infant. What classical art-historical term names this traditional image of Venus emerging from the water?

The Birth of Venus is often discussed alongside another large mythological panel by Botticelli, though the two were not necessarily conceived as a pair. What is the name of the other Uffizi work, recognized by its orange grove, dancing Three Graces, and figures including Flora and Zephyrus?

In mosque architecture, what is the name of the elevated structure traditionally used by a muezzin to give the call to prayer? Famous examples stand in Delhi’s Qutb complex, and similar structures were added to Hagia Sophia after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople.
Which landmark in Delhi’s historic mosque complex is a five-storey minaret begun around 1199 by the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate and later extended by Iltutmish?
Which Japanese contemporary artist is known for covering paintings and installations with polka-dot motifs and for creating immersive Infinity Mirror Rooms?
In a 1966 performance, Yayoi Kusama walked through New York City wearing a brightly colored kimono, an action recorded in photographs. What is the title of this work?
An Indian sitar virtuoso and composer, he helped bring Indian classical music to international audiences. He also taught George Harrison of the Beatles about the sitar. Who was this musician?
Ravi Shankar collaborated with this Beatles guitarist, who helped organize the 1971 Concert for Bangladesh. Which musician was it?

What name is given to prehistoric images made with mineral pigments or charcoal directly on the walls and ceilings of natural caverns? Famous examples include animal scenes at Lascaux in France and sites in Maros Regency, Indonesia.
Cave paintings at this Paleolithic site in southwestern France include a famous chamber filled with large bulls and other animals. The complex was discovered near Montignac in 1940.
Its prelude begins with a famously unresolved sonority built from F, B, D-sharp, and G-sharp, and its final scene culminates in the heroine’s “Liebestod” over her dead lover. Name this opera.
The composer of Tristan und Isolde was a 19th-century German composer whose four-opera Ring cycle includes The Valkyrie, with its famous “Ride of the Valkyries.” Name this composer.

Claude Monet painted several views of the Gare Saint-Lazare, while J. M. W. Turner depicted a Great Western Railway locomotive rushing over the Maidenhead Railway Bridge in a celebrated 1844 canvas. What broad subject of art brings such scenes together?

Within Trains in Nineteenth-Century Painting, identify J. M. W. Turner’s 1844 canvas showing a locomotive racing across the bridge at Maidenhead over the Thames. A small hare runs ahead of the engine in this scene.
answer: Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway

question: Gustav Mahler composed this six-song work in 1908–09 for tenor, alto (or baritone), and large orchestra, drawing its texts from German adaptations of ancient Chinese poems. Although its title page called it a symphony, he left it without a number; its long concluding song reflects on farewell and transience. What work is this?

The texts Mahler reshaped for Das Lied von der Erde came through a 1907 German-language collection of adaptations of Chinese poetry titled Die chinesische Flöte. Which German poet compiled that collection?

What is the name of the Western Christian liturgical repertory made chiefly of unaccompanied, single-line melodies and traditionally associated with Pope Gregory I? Its melodies were later adapted for use in polyphonic works.

Gregorian chant uses melodies associated with the medieval church-scale system, whose patterns later influenced jazz. Which scale has a minor third and a natural sixth and, in its standard form, uses the white keys from D to D?
This traditional Scottish song is based on a poem by Robert Burns and is widely sung at midnight on New Year’s Eve. What is its familiar title?
The poem behind Auld Lang Syne is credited to this Scottish poet, whose other well-known works include “To a Mouse” and “Tam o’ Shanter.” Who is he?
These fortified passages pierced a city’s defensive walls, allowing people to enter and leave while offering a way to control access. What are such entrances in a city wall called?

Among Rome’s city gates, one was associated with a two-faced deity who presided over entrances and transitions. Its doors were traditionally shut in peacetime and opened during war; which deity was it named for?
This broad musical family produces tones when stretched wires vibrate; its examples range from the erhu and pipa to the violin and cello. What is the family called?

Among string instruments, what traditional Chinese two-string fiddle is featured in the solo work Sai Ma, where sliding pitches and rapid bowing evoke a horse’s neighing and gallop? Its small resonator is traditionally covered with snakeskin.

What is the name of the ceramic art tradition of the Late Bronze Age Greek civilization associated with the palatial citadels of Tiryns and Pylos, whose vessels often feature floral motifs and scenes from myth?

Among examples of Mycenaean pottery, what is the conventional name of the famous krater whose frieze shows helmeted figures marching with spears and shields, while a woman gestures toward them from one side?

These percussion instruments often make sound when a stretched membrane vibrates after being struck, though some related forms produce sound through a resonant wooden body. Across traditions, they can accompany dance and ritual or communicate signals. What are these instruments?

Among drums, this Mexica slit instrument is distinguished by two differently hollowed wooden tongues that produce two tones when struck. The Met describes its use in religious, royal, and military contexts. What is this instrument called?

In this meter, each measure contains three beats, with the first beat typically receiving the main accent. It is commonly used for waltzes, minuets, and many scherzos; what is this meter naturally called?
Which partnered ballroom dance, whose name comes from a German word meaning “to turn,” became a defining feature of 19th-century Viennese balls and is conventionally danced to music in 3/4 time?

Born near Warsaw in 1810, this Polish-French Romantic composer settled in Paris as a young adult and wrote music chiefly for solo piano. His works include the “Revolutionary” Étude, numerous mazurkas and nocturnes, and two piano concertos; name the composer.

Chopin was born in this small Polish village west of Warsaw, before his family moved to the capital, where he grew up. The manor house associated with his birth now serves as a museum; name the village.

Chopin helped establish an instrumental form whose name had previously been associated with narrative song and poetry. His four solo-piano examples include a G-minor work with an intense, fiery closing coda; what is this genre called?
Chopin left Warsaw in 1830 just weeks before a Polish revolt against Russian rule broke out there. What is the conventional name of that revolt?

Chopin’s D-flat-major solo piano work, Op. 28, No. 15, has a nickname inspired by a sound associated with the weather; recurring A-flat and G-sharp notes underpin its contrasting middle section. What is the piece’s familiar nickname?

Construction of this medieval cathedral on the Île de la Cité began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully. Famous for its flying buttresses and rose windows, it suffered extensive damage in an April 2019 fire; what is its natural name?
During the 19th-century restoration of Notre-Dame de Paris, this French architect designed a new spire that was later destroyed in the 2019 fire. Who was he?

Notre-Dame de Paris is a celebrated example of a medieval building style characterized by pointed arches, rib vaults, and flying buttresses. Which style developed from Romanesque forms and flourished before the Renaissance?

Among the composer’s chamber pieces, this four-movement work was composed in 1893 during his stay in an Iowa settlement founded by Czech immigrants. Written for two violins, viola, and cello, it is associated with pentatonic melodies and folk-like rhythms; what is its title?
answer: String Quartet No. 12 in F major, Op. 96, “American”

question: Dvořák composed String Quartet No. 12 in F major, Op. 96, “American” during the summer of 1893 in a Czech-speaking community in northeast Iowa. What town was his summer retreat?

This 11th-century embroidered cloth consists of nine joined linen panels stitched with wool and measures nearly 68 metres. Its account of events leading to the Norman Conquest breaks off with the English retreat after a decisive battle in 1066; what is this famous medieval work?

The Bayeux Tapestry culminates in the English retreat after this October 1066 battle, fought between Harold Godwinson’s army and the invading forces of William, Duke of Normandy. Which battle marked the decisive Norman victory that began the conquest of England?

This Egyptian-style stone shaft stands on the National Mall and commemorates the first president of the United States. Construction halted for decades, leaving a visible change in the marble’s color where work resumed. What is this memorial called?

The Washington Monument’s design was selected in 1836 from a proposal by this American architect. His original plan paired the obelisk with a circular colonnade and a statue of George Washington. Who was the architect?

These Bronze Age ceramic vessels and decorative objects were produced by the civilization centered on Crete. Many are known for carefully shaped forms and vivid painted designs. What is this tradition called?

Within Minoan Pottery, one celebrated style takes its name from a cave on Mount Ida and is known for finely made vessels decorated with vivid, multicolored motifs against a dark ground. What is the name of this style?

Born in Venice in 1678, this composer was ordained a priest at age 25 and became known as the “Red Priest” because of his hair. He taught violin for many years at the city’s Ospedale della Pietà and wrote a cycle of concertos depicting the seasons. Who was he?

Antonio Vivaldi published this group of violin concertos in 1725 as part of *Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione*; each concerto is paired with a sonnet and uses musical effects such as birdsong, storms, and hunting to depict scenes from nature. What is the set called?

Antonio Vivaldi spent decades composing and teaching for this Venetian charitable institution, whose resident female musicians performed behind a screen and became renowned across Europe. Founded to care for orphaned and abandoned girls, it supplied the ensemble for many of his concertos and sacred works. What was the institution called?

Antonio Vivaldi’s Opus 3, published in Amsterdam in 1711, is a collection of twelve concertos whose bold contrasts helped establish his international reputation; J. S. Bach later adapted several of its concertos, including one for four harpsichords. What Italian-titled collection is this?

This nineteenth-century circle of Russian composers gathered around a leader and mentor in St. Petersburg, drawing on folk traditions to promote a distinctively Russian direction for art music. Its members included Modest Mussorgsky, Alexander Borodin, and Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. What was the circle called?
The Five helped establish a nationalist direction in Russian art music, and their ideas were promoted by a prominent music critic. Which critic popularized the group’s nickname “Mighty Handful”?
This American jazz bassist and composer led a group that recorded the politically charged “Fables of Faubus” and wrote “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat,” a tribute to saxophonist Lester Young. Who was he?
Charles Mingus released a 1959 Columbia album that opens with “Better Git It in Your Soul” and includes his tribute to Lester Young, “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat.” What is the album’s title?
In Indian classical music, this melodic framework organizes characteristic pitches, recurring motifs, and patterns of melodic movement. What is this framework called?
In Indian classical music, a performer developing a raga may follow a repeating rhythmic cycle that organizes beats and subdivisions. What is this cycle called?

Mahler wrote this expansive E-flat-major work for orchestra, vocal soloists, and chorus, setting a Latin Pentecost hymn in Part I and the closing scene of Goethe’s *Faust* in Part II. What is the title of this work?
In Mahler’s Symphony No. 8, the opening part sets a Latin hymn traditionally associated with Pentecost and addressed to the Holy Spirit. What is the hymn’s title?

Which 19th-century French architect and architectural theorist became known for restoring medieval buildings in a Gothic Revival style, including Notre-Dame de Paris? He also designed the cathedral’s spire that was destroyed in the 2019 fire.

During Eugène Viollet-le-Duc’s 19th-century restoration, this cathedral on the Île de la Cité received a spire that later collapsed in the 2019 fire. Its west façade once displayed statues of 28 kings of Judah; what landmark is it?
In South Dakota’s Black Hills, this monumental granite sculpture depicts four U.S. presidents carved into a mountainside. What is this landmark called?

A nearby unfinished sculpture in the Black Hills has been under construction since 1948 and honors a Lakota leader who fought at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. Which leader’s memorial stands near Mount Rushmore National Memorial?

An Italian violinist, guitarist, and composer born in 1782, he gained continental fame through extensive touring beginning in 1809. He was celebrated for dazzling violin technique and showmanship, and his career helped shape modern violin playing. Who was this virtuoso?

Niccolò Paganini’s best-known compositions include a set of 24 technically demanding pieces for the smallest standard member of the orchestral string family, usually held beneath the chin and played without accompaniment. The collection became a landmark in that instrument’s repertoire and inspired later composers, including Franz Liszt. What is the collection called?
By 1805, Niccolò Paganini was serving as first violin in the court of the ruler of Lucca. This political patron was a sister of the French emperor and governed Lucca at the time. Who was she?
After ending his concert career in 1834 amid declining health, Niccolò Paganini spent his final years in a city on the French Riviera. He died there in 1840, aged 57. What was the city?

In Sergei Prokofiev’s ballet Romeo and Juliet, this imposing orchestral movement accompanies the entrance of the male guests at the Capulets’ ball. It is recognizable for its ominous, pulsing low-brass opening followed by a broad string melody; what is the movement called?

Dance of the Knights is one of the best-known orchestral excerpts from a ballet based on Shakespeare’s tragedy Romeo and Juliet. Which Russian composer wrote that ballet, as well as the children’s orchestral tale Peter and the Wolf?
Born Emmanuel Radnitzky, this American modernist worked as a photographer, painter, and filmmaker and became associated with both Dadaism and Surrealism. What name did he use professionally?
In a 1926 photograph by Man Ray, Kiki de Montparnasse rests her head on a table beside an African mask, with the two heads positioned as contrasting forms. What is the title of the photograph?

In this full-length 1796 portrait, George Washington stands beside a table with an ornate gold-colored leg, extending one hand while holding a sword in the other. Gilbert Stuart painted the work, whose title honors a British marquess; what is the painting called?

In the Lansdowne Portrait, Washington gestures beside a table while a sword and classical architectural details reinforce the image of republican leadership. Which painter, who created several other portraits of Washington, painted this 1796 work?
In musical texture, a chord may be heard all at once or unfolded pitch by pitch, with its notes commonly moving upward or downward. What is the term for the successive sounding of a chord’s notes?

An arpeggio can trace the tones of a chord in either direction rather than sounding them together. What is the name for the version that starts on the chord’s lowest pitch and proceeds to its highest?

This three-act Italian opera, based on a play by Carlo Gozzi, is set in an imagined China where a princess tests her suitors with three riddles, with failure carrying a death sentence. Its exiled prince Calaf sings “Nessun dorma” in Act III. What is the opera?

Puccini died in 1924 before finishing the ending of Turandot, leaving sketches that another Italian composer used to complete it. Who completed the ending before the opera premiered at La Scala in 1926?

An American Pop artist enlarged comic-book panels into paintings with bold outlines, flat colors, and Ben-Day dots. He created the dramatic diptych *Whaam!* and the image of a woman overwhelmed by a wave in *Drowning Girl*; who was he?

Roy Lichtenstein based this 1963 painting on a panel from a DC romance comic. It shows a woman in the water beneath a large curling wave, with a thought balloon referring to a man named Brad; what is the work’s title?

What partnered ballroom and folk dance takes its name from the German word *Walzer*, meaning “to roll or revolve”? Traditionally set in triple meter, it features a turning motion and an accompanying “oom-pah-pah” rhythm.
Which composer is often called the “King of the Waltz”? He wrote “The Blue Danube” and “Tales from the Vienna Woods.”
Which composer wrote four works in the waltz tradition inspired by Mephistopheles? His Transcendental Études include “Mazeppa” and “Feux follets.”
Which Polish composer wrote the “Minute” waltz and the E-flat-major *Grande valse brillante*? His waltzes also include a brief D-flat-major piece dedicated to Delfina Potocka.

This English composer studied at the Royal College of Music under Charles Villiers Stanford. After an arm condition ended his hopes of becoming a pianist, he earned a living playing trombone professionally. Who was he?
Gustav Holst’s seven-movement orchestral suite opens with “Mars, the Bringer of War” and ends with “Neptune, the Mystic.” What is the title of this work?
From 1907 to 1924, Gustav Holst directed music at this London institution, where he taught music to adult students. What was the institution called?

Opened in 1997 beside the Nervión River in Spain’s Basque Country, this contemporary art institution is known for its sweeping, ship-like forms clad in titanium. Designed by Frank Gehry, it became a landmark of the city’s waterfront redevelopment; what is its name?

The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao’s titanium-clad, undulating design was created by a Canadian-born American architect who also designed Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles and the Dancing House in Prague. Who is this architect?

A late-fifteenth-century wall painting in a convent refectory portrays Jesus immediately after he announces that one of the Twelve will betray him. Its composition gathers the apostles into animated groups around a central figure, making it one of the most celebrated works of the High Renaissance. Name the painting.

The Last Supper was painted by a Renaissance polymath who also created the Mona Lisa and the Vitruvian Man. This artist used an experimental tempera mixture for the mural rather than traditional fresco technique. Name the artist.
The Last Supper occupies a refectory wall inside a church and convent complex in Milan. What is the name of this complex?
The Last Supper was commissioned during renovations to its Milanese church and convent complex. Which Duke of Milan, a patron of Leonardo, sponsored the work?

Which musical follows an Egyptian police orchestra whose tickets send them to the wrong destination, leaving the musicians to spend an unexpected night with residents of a small Israeli town? This 2018 Tony Award winner for Best Musical is adapted from a 2007 Israeli film.

In The Band's Visit, what fictional Israeli town do the Egyptian police musicians reach after a ticketing misunderstanding? The orchestra spends the night there with local residents while waiting to continue its journey.

This American sculptor is known for monumental steel works, including Equal-Parallel. His site-specific sculpture Tilted Arc was installed in a New York City plaza and later removed after a public controversy. Who is he?
Richard Serra designed this curving steel wall for New York City’s Federal Plaza. Its placement led to a public hearing, and the work was dismantled in 1989. What is the title of the sculpture?

Born in Russia in 1882, this composer studied under Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov while enrolled in law school and later became a French and American citizen. He wrote three landmark ballets for the Ballets Russes that transformed 20th-century music. Who was he?

Igor Stravinsky wrote a ballet whose 1913 Paris premiere provoked a notorious audience uproar. It depicts a pagan ritual in which a chosen young woman dances herself to death; what is the ballet’s title?
Igor Stravinsky’s early ballet trio was commissioned for the Ballets Russes by which Russian impresario, who founded the company and brought it to prominence in Paris?
While attending law school in St. Petersburg, Igor Stravinsky studied music with which older Russian composer, continuing until that teacher’s death in 1908?

Igor Stravinsky composed a neoclassical stage work based on Sophocles’ tragedy about the king of Thebes who discovers he killed his father and married his mother. What is the title of this work, written for a narrator, soloists, chorus, and orchestra?
Which French Impressionist painter, who was Édouard Manet’s sister-in-law, created *Harbor at Lorient* and *The Cradle*?
Berthe Morisot painted this intimate domestic scene showing a woman watching over her sleeping daughter. What is the title of the work?

This stage musical adapts Gaston Leroux’s 1910 novel about a masked musical genius who secretly trains soprano Christine Daaé beneath the Palais Garnier and competes with her childhood friend Raoul. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s adaptation premiered at London’s Her Majesty’s Theatre in 1986 and features “The Music of the Night.” What musical is it?

In The Phantom of the Opera, Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote the music while this British lyricist wrote lyrics for the original stage musical alongside Richard Stilgoe, who also contributed lyrics and co-wrote the book. Who was this lyricist, credited for songs including “All I Ask of You”?

This Italian opera by Giacomo Puccini is set in Nagasaki and follows a young geisha who believes her marriage to U.S. Navy officer Pinkerton is a lasting commitment. After he leaves, she waits for his return and imagines their reunion in a famous Act II aria. What is the opera?
In Madama Butterfly, Cio-Cio-San sings this Act II aria while imagining the day Pinkerton will return to Nagasaki. Its Italian title begins with the words “Un bel dì.” What is the aria’s full title?
These monumental funerary structures were built for pharaohs and elites, with major examples on the Giza plateau and an early stepped form at Saqqara. What are these monuments called?
Among ancient Egyptian pyramids, Djoser’s monument at Saqqara is distinguished by tiers of mastaba-like stages. Which architect and high official is traditionally credited with designing it?
Which Pierre-Auguste Renoir painting depicts friends dining on a balcony overlooking the Seine, beneath a pink-striped awning?
In Luncheon of the Boating Party, the woman seated in the foreground plays with a small dog. She was a seamstress who later became Renoir’s wife; what was her name?

This French-American Dada artist submitted an ordinary urinal to an art exhibition under the signature “R. Mutt.” He also added facial hair to a reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci’s portrait of Lisa Gherardini. Who was this artist?

Marcel Duchamp submitted this readymade to the 1917 Society of Independent Artists exhibition under the signature “R. Mutt.” It was a porcelain urinal displayed on its side, and the exhibition’s organizers rejected it. What work was it?

Marcel Duchamp used this feminine pseudonym for several works and appeared in photographs by Man Ray as this alter ego. The name is also associated with Duchamp’s perfume-bottle readymade Belle Haleine, Eau de Voilette. What was the pseudonym?

This landmark residence in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands was commissioned by the Kaufmann family as a weekend retreat. Its terraces project over a waterfall on Bear Run, closely connecting the house to its natural setting. What house museum is it?
Fallingwater was designed by an American architect who also created the Robie House in Chicago and developed the Prairie School style. Who was the architect?
At Fallingwater, the house spans the stream whose cascade gives the residence its name. What is the name of this stream in southwestern Pennsylvania?
Fallingwater has been operated as a public attraction since 1963, and tours began the following year. Which Pittsburgh-based conservation organization took on its operation?

An Austrian modernist composed a Passacaglia for Orchestra in 1908 and a Concerto for Nine Instruments in 1934. Known for concise works that influenced serialist music, who was this member of the Second Viennese School?

Anton Webern’s association with the Second Viennese School connects his modernist circle to the city where Arnold Schoenberg developed twelve-tone technique. Which Austrian capital gave the school its name?
Which Rodgers and Hammerstein musical follows a British schoolteacher brought to Siam to tutor King Mongkut’s children? It features the songs “Getting to Know You” and “Shall We Dance?”

In The King and I, what is the name of the Welsh-born British schoolteacher who travels to Siam to teach King Mongkut’s royal children? The musical portrays her lessons at the royal court and her relationship with the king.
What hard, dense material, obtained chiefly from elephant tusks, has been carved into artworks, ceremonial objects, and decorative crafts?
An ivory pendant mask from Benin court art depicts this woman, remembered as the kingdom’s first Iyoba, or Queen Mother. Her son Esigie became an Oba in the 16th century; who is she?
Which Norwegian painter and printmaker drew on illness, bereavement, and his own emotional life to develop a psychologically charged style that helped shape Expressionism?

Edvard Munch said the idea for this 1893 work came to him during a sunset walk in Kristiania, where he felt he heard a sound he described as “enormous” and “infinite.” What painting shows a distressed figure against a vivid, swirling sky?
Edvard Munch organized paintings exploring love, anxiety, jealousy, and betrayal into what interconnected series?
Which Italian Baroque painter, active in Rome, Florence, Naples, and London, became renowned for dramatic biblical scenes featuring women such as Judith and Jael?

Artemisia Gentileschi spent a formative period in this Tuscan city, where she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Her *Judith Slaying Holofernes* is now displayed in the city’s Uffizi Gallery. Which city is it?
At Art Basel Miami Beach in 2019, a conceptual artwork by Maurizio Cattelan drew attention for presenting a fresh banana fixed to a gallery wall with duct tape. What was this work titled?
Comedian is the 2019 wall-mounted banana artwork that became a much-discussed work of contemporary art. Which Italian artist conceived it?
Completed in 1946, this Surrealist painting places a small kneeling desert monk beneath a rearing horse and elephants balanced on extremely long, spindly legs. What painting by Salvador Dalí is it?

The Temptation of Saint Anthony was created for a competition organized by producers seeking a painting for a film based on Guy de Maupassant’s *Bel-Ami*. Dalí’s entry was not selected; which artist’s winning version appeared in the film?
In Greek myth, which string instrument did Hermes make from a tortoise shell and later give to Apollo in exchange for cattle? Apollo played it in a musical contest against the satyr Marsyas.

Which legendary musician played the lyre so beautifully that he persuaded Hades and Persephone to let him bring his dead wife back from the Underworld? He lost her again when he looked back before reaching the surface.

Hector Berlioz’s 1834 symphony makes a solo instrument the recurring musical observer, and its literary inspiration is Lord Byron’s poem about a traveler journeying through Europe. What is the title of this orchestral work?
In Harold in Italy, the featured soloist plays a four-string instrument tuned C–G–D–A, pitched between violin and cello, and commonly notated in alto clef. What instrument is it?

Woven in Persia in 1539–40 for the shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din in northwestern Iran, this celebrated textile has a large central medallion and an inscription naming its maker, Maqsud Kashani. What is this work commonly known as?
Since 1893, the larger surviving example of the Ardabil Carpet has belonged to a South Kensington institution founded to promote excellence in design and manufacturing. Which institution holds it?

An American painter associated with abstract expressionism, he placed large canvases on the floor and poured, dripped, or flicked paint across them. Which artist made the 1950 painting *Autumn Rhythm* and became renowned for this technique?

In 1950, Jackson Pollock made a monumental enamel-on-canvas work now held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art; it is also identified in catalogs as Number 30. What is the painting’s commonly used title?
In Indonesia, this traditional musical ensemble features interlocking tuned metallophones, gongs, and drums, with the kendang often guiding the rhythm. What is the name of this musical tradition?
Within a gamelan ensemble, this hand-played, double-headed drum helps direct tempo and signal transitions to the other musicians. What is this instrument called?

Commissioned by the French state in 1880 for a planned museum of decorative arts that was never built, this monumental portal draws on Dante’s Inferno. More than 200 modeled figures crowd its doors, and Auguste Rodin’s project remained unfinished at his death. What is this work?

For The Gates of Hell, Rodin designed a seated figure for the lintel above the doors, first imagining him as Dante contemplating the sinners in the Inferno. The figure later came to represent thought and creativity more broadly; what is this sculpture?
Claude Debussy’s three orchestral sketches evoke the sea through shifting harmonies and whole-tone passages; one of their sections is titled “Jeux de vagues.” What is the set called?
La mer was composed by the French musician who also wrote Clair de lune and the orchestral Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. Name that composer.

Three 1851 oil-on-canvas versions share the title of this history painting by Emanuel Leutze. It depicts the covert Christmas-night river passage that preceded the Continental Army’s surprise victory at Trenton; what is the painting called?

The 1851 history painting Washington Crossing the Delaware was created by this German-American artist, who was born in Württemberg and became known for large-scale historical canvases. Who painted it?

The original 1851 version of Washington Crossing the Delaware belonged to this German art institution, whose supporting art association was established in 1823; a British bombing raid destroyed the painting in 1942. Which institution owned it?
One surviving version of Washington Crossing the Delaware is held by this major New York City museum, whose collections span ancient art through modern works. Name the museum.

A version of Washington Crossing the Delaware that had previously hung in the White House was purchased in March 2015 for exhibition at this arts institution in Winona, on the Mississippi River. What institution received it?

In this late-18th-century canvas, sailors in a small boat reach into Havana harbor to pull a boy from the water as a large predator lunges beneath him. The work by an American painter dramatizes a real attack that left its subject with a lifelong injury; what is the painting called?
Watson and the Shark was painted by an artist born in Boston in 1738 who later became a leading portraitist in London. He also painted The Death of Major Peirson; who was he?
Which American composer became a major figure in musical minimalism, with music often built from repeating patterns and gradual changes? He wrote the operas *Einstein on the Beach* and *Satyagraha*.

When considering Muse’s classical influences alongside Philip Glass, which Polish composer’s music is quoted in the band’s song “United States of Eurasia”? He also composed the Minute Waltz and Fantaisie-Impromptu.

What is the commonly used name for Cassius Marcellus Coolidge’s humorous series of paintings depicting anthropomorphic animals gathered around card tables? The scenes place the animals in humanlike settings, often with drinks or cigars.
Within Dogs Playing Poker, which painting shows one dog secretly passing a card beneath the table to another, while the players above focus on their hand?

Mozart composed this serenade in G major in 1787 for two violins, viola, cello, and bass. Its surviving four movements are an Allegro, a Romance, a minuet and trio, and a rondo, although Mozart’s catalog lists an additional movement that has been lost. What is the work’s German title?

Mozart’s catalog dates Eine kleine Nachtmusik to August 10, 1787, and records this city as the place where he composed it. Then the capital of the Habsburg monarchy, it was also home to Mozart during much of his career. Which city is it?

A Catalan architect created Park Güell and Casa Milà in Barcelona and devoted the later decades of his life to the Sagrada Família. Known for sculptural forms inspired by nature and richly colored mosaics, who was this architect?

Antoni Gaudí transformed a Barcelona residence on Passeig de Gràcia with a rippling stone façade, mask-like balconies, and a roof of vivid ceramic tiles resembling a dragon’s back. What is the building commonly called?

This palace-fortress complex stands on a hill in Granada and was built primarily during the Nasrid dynasty. It is celebrated for its Islamic architecture and richly decorated courtyards. What is the complex called?
At the Alhambra, this courtyard in the Comares Palace is centered on a long reflecting pool bordered by clipped evergreen hedges. What is this courtyard called?

This wooden-bar keyboard percussion instrument is played by striking tuned bars with mallets and is especially associated with Guatemala and southern Mexico. Its distinctive sound also became familiar to many people as the name of a classic iPhone ringtone. What is the instrument?
Which virtuoso helped popularize the marimba in the United States by leading a traveling, all-female orchestra of more than 100 performers?

In this comic opera, a quick-witted local fixer helps Count Almaviva win Rosina, who is being kept under guard by Dr. Bartolo. The score includes Figaro’s showpiece aria “Largo al factotum,” and the lovers’ wedding is secured through disguises and deception. What is the opera?

The Barber of Seville was composed for its 1816 Rome premiere by an Italian composer whose later opera William Tell features the famous “March of the Swiss Soldiers.” Who composed The Barber of Seville?

A leading male star of Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, this dancer choreographed both *The Rite of Spring* and *L’Après-midi d’un faune*. His performance as the Faun in the latter ballet scandalized Paris audiences in 1912. Who was he?
Vaslav Nijinsky created the choreography for this Igor Stravinsky ballet, whose 1913 premiere at Paris’s Théâtre des Champs-Élysées became notorious for audience uproar. What is the ballet called?

Born in Nuremberg in 1471, this German Renaissance artist became renowned for precise woodcuts and engravings that helped establish printmaking as an art form. His celebrated works include *Melencolia I* and *Knight, Death, and the Devil*; who was he?

In 1515, Albrecht Dürer made a woodcut based on a written description and another artist’s sketch rather than firsthand observation. Its image of an animal with armor-like plates and an extra horn on its back influenced European depictions of the creature for centuries; what is the print called?

Recorded by John Coltrane’s quartet on December 9, 1964, this four-part spiritual suite was issued in 1965 and unfolds through “Acknowledgement,” “Resolution,” “Pursuance,” and “Psalm.” Near the end of its opening movement, Coltrane chants the phrase that supplies the suite’s title; what is this landmark work?

On A Love Supreme, the opening movement is built around a recurring bass figure that introduces the suite and returns throughout the piece. Which bassist in Coltrane’s quartet played that part alongside pianist McCoy Tyner and drummer Elvin Jones?

Written in 1935 for viola and orchestra, this concerto by Paul Hindemith draws on German folk-song material. Its three movements include “Between Mountain and Deep Valley” and “Now, Little Linden Tree, Grow Leaves!” What is the work called?
Der Schwanendreher is a 1935 viola concerto that incorporates German folk songs. Which German composer, also known for the opera Cardillac and the orchestral work Mathis der Maler, wrote it?

Air from the lungs passes through the larynx and makes a pair of tissue bands vibrate, while the throat, mouth, and nose help shape and resonate the resulting sound. This bodily instrument provides the sound used for speech, singing, and choral performance; what is it?

In the human voice, these paired tissue bands sit in the larynx, remain apart during quiet breathing, and vibrate when air from the lungs passes between them. What are these sound-producing structures called?
Which 1844 oil painting by J. M. W. Turner shows a locomotive hurtling across Brunel’s Maidenhead Bridge, its form half-lost in a blur of light and vapor?
answer: Rain, Steam, and Speed – The Great Western Railway

question: The artist behind Rain, Steam, and Speed – The Great Western Railway also painted The Fighting Temeraire and The Slave Ship, and became renowned for his atmospheric treatment of light. Which British Romantic artist is meant?

Carved from marble by Michelangelo between 1501 and 1504, this monumental sculpture depicts the biblical hero before his battle with Goliath. It was first planned as one of twelve prophets for Florence Cathedral’s roofline, but was instead installed in the city’s civic square; name the work.
The sculptor of David also painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, including the fresco in which God reaches toward Adam, and carved the Pietà. Name this Italian Renaissance artist.

After David was unveiled in 1504, it stood in this Florence square in front of the city’s seat of government. A replica was installed at that original site in 1910, after the sculpture itself had moved to the Galleria dell’Accademia.

Rebuilt after the Great Fire of London under the direction of Sir Christopher Wren, this Anglican church is one of the city’s best-known landmarks. Its vast dome has long dominated the London skyline. What is the name of this landmark?

The rebuilding of St. Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London was overseen by this English architect, who also designed the Royal Hospital Chelsea. He served as Surveyor of the King’s Works and became one of the leading architects of his age. Who was he?

What artistic technique makes a two-dimensional surface suggest depth and three-dimensional space? It includes systems based on converging lines as well as methods that use changes in color or clarity to imply distance.

In linear perspective, what is the name for the location on the horizon where parallel lines receding into the distance appear to converge? Artists use it to establish the direction of depth in a composition.

Which Mozart opera has a title commonly translated as “Thus do all women,” and follows Ferrando and Guglielmo as they disguise themselves to test the faithfulness of their fiancées, Dorabella and Fiordiligi?
Così fan tutte was written to a libretto by which Italian poet and librettist, who also collaborated with Mozart on The Marriage of Figaro and Don Giovanni?

This practical musical family includes objects sounded by striking, shaking, scraping, or rubbing, from timpani and snare drums to cymbals and triangles. Its members can belong to several different scientific classifications. What is this family called?
Within percussion instruments, what technique creates rhythms by clapping, stamping, or striking the performer’s own torso or limbs instead of using a separate instrument?
Among percussion instruments, what scientific class includes cymbals and the triangle, which produce sound through vibration of the instrument’s own body rather than a stretched membrane?

In ancient Rome, this monumental freestanding structure was erected to celebrate military victories. A surviving example stands on the Via Sacra and commemorates an emperor’s victory in Judea. What is this type of monument called?
On the Via Sacra in Rome, a Roman triumphal arch features a relief of soldiers carrying spoils from Jerusalem, including the Temple menorah. What is the name of this monument?
What dance-oriented popular style became a defining sound of 1970s clubs, pairing steady four-on-the-floor beats with grooves designed for extended dancing?
On Beyoncé’s 2022 album Renaissance, which lead single opens with a sample from Big Freedia’s “Explode,” including the repeated “yaka” vocal, in a track drawing on disco music?

An anonymous British street artist whose graffiti career began in Bristol in the 1990s became known for stencil images that blend visual wit with political and social criticism. Which artist also became famous for secret museum installations and provocative art-market pranks?
In 2018, a work based on Banksy’s Girl with Balloon began shredding shortly after it sold at auction. What title was given to the altered work?

Which Mississippi Delta blues singer and guitarist, born in 1911, made influential recordings including “Hellhound on My Trail” and “Love in Vain”? His later fame was amplified by a crossroads tale in which he supposedly traded his soul for musical skill.

Robert Johnson recorded a 1937 song whose narrator watches a departing train carry away a lover; the Rolling Stones later covered it on their 1969 album *Let It Bleed*. What is the title of that song?

Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov wrote this vivid orchestral interlude for his opera *The Tale of Tsar Saltan*, using rapid chromatic runs to evoke the erratic buzzing movement of a small insect. What is the interlude’s familiar title?

In *Flight of the Bumblebee*, rapid chromatic scales convey an insect’s flight in a passage originating in the opera *The Tale of Tsar Saltan*. Which Russian composer wrote the opera and its famous interlude?

This French Romantic composer left medical studies in Paris to pursue music. He wrote a five-movement symphony featuring a recurring idée fixe and a widely influential treatise on orchestration. Who was this composer?

In Hector Berlioz’s 1830 programmatic symphony, a recurring melody associated with the beloved returns in altered forms across five movements. Its final movement depicts a witches’ sabbath, following a march to the scaffold. What is this work called?
What is the name of the device that gives musicians a steady audible tick or visual pulse, often using an adjustable pendulum to set a tempo in beats per minute?
György Ligeti’s 1962 conceptual composition uses 100 metronomes, wound and started together, whose clicks gradually fall silent as they run down. What is the title of this work?

What term describes live musical performances presented to an audience, whether in a small hall or a large arena? Unlike a recording, each one takes place in real time before listeners gathered at a venue.

Concerts and other large music gatherings have sometimes become cultural landmarks. In August 1969, a farm near Bethel, New York, hosted a three-day event billed as “3 Days of Peace & Music”; what was it called?

Blinded by diphtheria at age three, this Spanish composer went on to write a guitar concerto whose slow movement became internationally famous and was later adapted by Miles Davis on *Sketches of Spain*. What is his name?
Joaquín Rodrigo composed a concerto for classical guitar and orchestra whose lyrical second movement was later adapted by Miles Davis for *Sketches of Spain*. What is the title of this concerto?

Which keyboard work did Johann Sebastian Bach organize into two books, with a prelude-and-fugue pair in every major and minor key? The first book was completed in 1722, and the collection became a landmark exploration of all 24 keys.

The Well-Tempered Clavier comprises two books of keyboard preludes and fugues spanning all 24 major and minor keys. Which German Baroque composer created it and also wrote the Brandenburg Concertos and the Goldberg Variations?
Which Austrian pianist and composer, born in Vienna in 1791, studied piano with Beethoven and later became known for collections such as *The School of Velocity*?
Carl Czerny taught this Hungarian-born child prodigy in Vienna in the 1820s. The pupil later composed the *Hungarian Rhapsodies* and the *Transcendental Études*.

This fresco panel on the ceiling of Vatican City’s Sistine Chapel shows the Creator leaning toward a reclining first human, with their nearly touching fingers forming the focal point. Painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512 as part of the ceiling’s Genesis sequence, what is this celebrated work called?

The Creation of Adam is among the Genesis scenes this Florentine Renaissance artist painted on the Sistine Chapel ceiling from 1508 to 1512. He also sculpted the marble David and Pietà; which artist created the fresco panel?

This Broadway musical reframes the Oz story around the unlikely friendship of Glinda and Elphaba, tracing how Elphaba comes to be known as the Witch of the West. Its score includes the song “Defying Gravity,” and its story begins before Dorothy arrives in Oz. What is the musical’s title?

The Broadway musical Wicked is adapted from a 1995 novel that retells Oz from the perspective of the future Wicked Witch of the West. Who wrote the novel, whose full title is *Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West*?

This American artist gained attention in 1980s New York with chalk drawings on unused subway-advertising panels. His thick outlines, simplified figures, and motion marks became a distinctive visual language. Who was he?
Keith Haring painted a vivid anti-drug mural in 1986 on a handball-court wall in East Harlem. What is this public artwork widely called?
A scale of this type contains five distinct notes within an octave. On the piano, the five black keys provide a familiar example of it; what is the scale called?
Many Japanese enka melodies use a named scale formed by omitting the fourth and seventh degrees of a major scale. As a specific example of the pentatonic scale, what is this Japanese scale called?

An English-language opera first performed in Boston in 1935 follows a disabled street beggar trying to rescue a woman from her violent lover and a drug dealer. With music by George Gershwin and a libretto by DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin, what opera is set in a fictional Charleston community?
The composer of Porgy and Bess wrote the lullaby “Summertime” and the orchestral work Rhapsody in Blue. Which American composer also wrote An American in Paris?
In Porgy and Bess, the action centers on a fictional Charleston neighborhood where Porgy, Bess, and their neighbors live. What is the name of this community?
Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, this wrought-iron lattice landmark stands on Paris’s Champ de Mars. What is its familiar name?

The Eiffel Tower was designed by the engineering company of a French civil engineer who also completed the Statue of Liberty’s metal framework after its original engineer died. Which engineer led the company?
A solitary, skull-like figure presses both hands to its cheeks while two people recede along a railing beneath an unnaturally fiery, swirling sky. What is the name of Edvard Munch’s 1893 artwork?

The Scream belongs to Munch’s Frieze of Life series. Its creator recalled seeing sunset clouds turn “blood red” and sensing a cry passing through nature; which Norwegian artist made the work and its multiple versions?
The Scream’s landscape is usually associated with a path beside a fjord overlooking this Norwegian capital. Which city is meant?
The Scream helped shape a movement that emphasized subjective emotion and distorted forms over naturalistic representation. Which art movement is this?
One version of The Scream, made in this dry medium, fetched a record-setting public-auction price in 2012. The material consists of pigment and binder formed into sticks; name the medium.

Developed in the 1940s, this jazz style favored rapid tempos, intricate chord progressions, and virtuosic improvisation over dance-band arrangements. Associated with musicians such as Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, what is this style called?
Which alto saxophonist, nicknamed “Bird,” helped define bebop with recordings such as “Ko-Ko” and “Ornithology”? He was also a major musical collaborator of Dizzy Gillespie.
In tonal harmony, a musical structure formed when multiple pitches sound simultaneously may be major, minor, diminished, or augmented. What is this structure called?
In tonal harmony, which musical chord is built on the lowered second scale degree and typically appears in first inversion as a predominant, often notated ♭II6?

Commissioned by King Ludwig II in the 19th century, this Romantic Revival palace stands above Hohenschwangau in the Bavarian Alps. Its dramatic towers and mountain setting later helped inspire the design of the palace in Disney’s Sleeping Beauty. What is this landmark?
The Bavarian monarch who commissioned Neuschwanstein Castle also built Linderhof Palace and Herrenchiemsee. Known as the “Fairytale King,” what was his regnal name?

Which Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice stage musical dramatizes Eva Perón’s rise from aspiring performer to Argentina’s first lady and political figure? Its story follows her life alongside Juan Perón’s rise to power.
In Evita, which song does Eva Perón sing from the balcony of the Casa Rosada to address the crowds below? The number became the musical’s best-known song.

This Mexican muralist created *The Epic of American Civilization*, a large cycle depicting Indigenous history and the development of the Americas. The work is installed at an Ivy League college in Hanover, New Hampshire. Which artist painted it?
José Clemente Orozco painted *The Epic of American Civilization* as a mural cycle for Baker Library. On the campus of which New Hampshire institution can visitors see the work?

Which ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician is traditionally associated with explaining musical consonance through simple numerical ratios? A later story links his investigation of pitch to hearing a blacksmith’s hammers.

Pythagoras of Samos is associated with the idea that ratios between string lengths shape consonant intervals. On a monochord, what interval is heard when a string is shortened to half its original sounding length?
In a musical score, what technique assigns individual parts to particular instruments? The term also describes adapting a solo or small-ensemble work for orchestra.

In Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestration of Scheherazade, which plucked instrument accompanies the solo violin in the title character’s recurring theme? A concert version of this instrument has 47 strings and pedals that change their pitches.

Which Paris museum occupies a monumental former railway station on the Left Bank of the Seine, across from the Louvre, and is renowned for its Impressionist and Post-Impressionist collection? Its central hall retains the station’s prominent Beaux-Arts clock.

The former Gare d’Orsay, now home to Musée d’Orsay, opened for the 1900 Exposition Universelle as a Beaux-Arts railway terminal. Which French architect designed it and also designed Tours’s Hôtel de Ville?

This German harpsichordist and composer studied with Bach and served Count Hermann Karl von Keyserlingk in Dresden. His surname became attached to Bach’s keyboard cycle of an aria and 30 variations, though his role in its first performance is debated. Who was he?

Johann Gottlieb Goldberg is associated with a keyboard cycle reportedly commissioned by Count Keyserlingk to help soothe his sleepless nights. Which composer wrote this work, whose 30 variations include a canon at every third variation?

This architectural offshoot sets abundant greenery against monumental concrete and blocky forms, often pairing planted terraces or facades with environmentally conscious design. What is this synthesis of a stark postwar aesthetic and ecological design called?

In eco-brutalism, architects may extend greenery onto a building’s uppermost horizontal surface with plantings that can help manage stormwater and reduce heat absorption. What is this feature commonly called?
Emerging in the 1950s, this functionalist architectural style favors monumental geometric forms and extensive use of exposed concrete and steel. What is this style called?
Which residential complex in Montreal exemplifies Brutalism with 354 identical prefabricated concrete modules arranged in varied configurations? Designed by Moshe Safdie, it was created for Expo 67.

This half-length oil portrait was painted on a white poplar panel and is famous for its sitter’s enigmatic smile and softly blended forms. Traditionally identified as the wife of Florentine merchant Francesco del Giocondo, it is a defining work of the Italian Renaissance. What painting is it?
The Mona Lisa is traditionally said to portray which Italian woman, the wife of Florentine merchant Francesco del Giocondo? Her married name is reflected in the painting’s Italian title, La Gioconda.
The Mona Lisa entered the French royal collection after which monarch acquired it following Leonardo da Vinci’s death? This king also initiated construction of the Château de Chambord.
In 1911, the Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre by which Italian former museum worker? His attempted sale of the painting in Florence led to its recovery in 1914.
Since 1797, the Mona Lisa has normally been displayed at which Paris landmark? Its collection also includes the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace.
Which French Impressionist painter became especially known for scenes of dancers, bathers, and urban life? He also painted the café scene *The Absinthe Drinker*.
Edgar Degas often depicted performers at the barre and backstage, in scenes featuring tutus and rehearsal spaces. What classical performance art were these performers practicing?

In this ukiyo-e landscape, Mount Fuji appears deep red beneath a band of clouds, with the foreground slopes largely in shadow. It is the second print in the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji; what is its title?
Fine Wind, Clear Morning belongs to a celebrated series of landscape prints that also includes The Great Wave of Kanagawa. Which Edo-period ukiyo-e artist created the series?

This Italian Baroque artist worked as a sculptor and architect, creating works for powerful patrons in Rome. He united sculpture, architecture, and theatrical effects in a chapel scene of a saint’s vision and in a fountain with an obelisk surrounded by river figures. Who was he?

Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed this Piazza Navona landmark, arranging personifications of the Nile, Ganges, Danube, and Río de la Plata around a basin beneath an obelisk. What is this monumental work called?
answer: The Fountain of the Four Rivers

question: What copper-based alloy, traditionally made chiefly from copper and tin, has been used for tools and weapons as well as cast sculptures? It is also the material named in the common nickname for the plaques and figures from the Kingdom of Benin.

In March 2022, which U.S. museum-and-research organization announced plans to return its collection of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria? It operates both the National Museum of African Art and the National Air and Space Museum.

This musical family produces sound when a player blows air through a tube, with pitch changed using keys or open holes. Its members include single-reed and double-reed types, as well as flutes that produce sound by splitting an airstream.

Within the woodwind instruments, which single-reed instrument opens Gershwin’s *Rhapsody in Blue* with a famous rising glissando? Its register spans several octaves, and it is a standard member of both orchestras and concert bands.

This three-part English-language oratorio sets a biblical compilation by Charles Jennens, moving from prophecy and the Nativity to suffering, resurrection, and thanksgiving. Its second part ends—not the whole work—with a famous chorus proclaiming that the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. What is the oratorio called?

The biblical text for Messiah was assembled from passages in both the Old and New Testaments by this English librettist. His compilation gives the oratorio a contemplative structure rather than a conventional drama with speaking characters. Who assembled the text?

An American Pop artist became known for bold, text-based works using simple letters and numbers. Which artist made a signature sculpture by arranging four block capitals in a square, with one letter tilted?

Robert Indiana’s best-known text design uses four block capitals arranged in a square, with the second letter rotated diagonally; the 1960s image was later made into monumental sculptures. What word does the design spell?
In George Frideric Handel’s oratorio *Messiah*, this celebrated passage concludes Part II and sets repeated praise of the “King of Kings” and “Lord of Lords.” What is its familiar title?
The Hallelujah Chorus belongs to a three-part English-language oratorio by George Frideric Handel. What is the oratorio’s title, whose first performance took place in Dublin in 1742?

This 1533 double portrait shows two French diplomats beside a table crowded with scientific instruments, books, and a globe. A distorted skull stretches across the foreground; what painting by Hans Holbein the Younger is it?
The Ambassadors was painted by a German-born artist who later became court painter to Henry VIII. He also painted portraits of Christina of Denmark and Jane Seymour; who was he?

Which Japanese origami artist pioneered wet-folding, a technique that uses damp paper to create sculptural shapes? With Samuel Randlett, he also helped develop a widely used system for diagramming origami instructions.
Akira Yoshizawa helped standardize a widely adopted notation system for origami folding diagrams, which uses arrows and symbols to show how paper moves. What is this system called?

This coiled brass orchestral instrument has a flared bell, and its players often place a hand inside the bell while performing. In Prokofiev’s narrated tale, its section supplies the musical theme for the animal that threatens Peter. What is the instrument?
In Prokofiev’s narrated orchestral tale, the French horn section provides the recurring theme for the dangerous animal that Peter eventually captures. Which animal is represented?
What painting technique uses varying shades of gray to model forms so they appear sculptural, and can also create an entirely monochromatic image?

Amy Sherald used grisaille for the skin tones in a portrait set against an aqua background. The subject was fatally shot in her Louisville apartment in 2020, an event that sparked nationwide protests; who was she?

Born in Dhaka in 1929, this Bangladeshi-American engineer developed structural innovations that helped make very tall buildings more efficient to design. He was a key structural engineer on Chicago’s John Hancock Center and Sears Tower; who was he?
Fazlur Rahman Khan devised a structural method for Chicago’s Sears Tower in which multiple linked vertical sections function together as a single load-bearing unit. What is this method called?
At ballroom events, performers may use elaborate costumes, makeup, lip-syncing, dance, and theatricality to present stylized versions of gender. What performance practice is described?

Voguing battles are often featured at drag competitions, and voguing developed in the ballroom scene of a New York neighborhood. The Apollo Theater, a landmark venue for Black performers, is also located there. Which neighborhood is it?

Which German Romantic painter, born in Greifswald in 1774, became known for atmospheric landscapes featuring solitary figures contemplating nature? His best-known works include *Wanderer above the Sea of Fog*.
Caspar David Friedrich painted this work, exhibited in Berlin in 1810, showing a tiny solitary figure on a shore beneath a vast, nearly empty sky. What is the painting’s title?

This famous mezzo-soprano aria from Georges Bizet’s opera opens over a repeating ostinato with a descending chromatic melody. Its singer compares love to a rebellious bird, while the chorus warns, “Prends garde à toi.” What is the aria called?
The Habanera is sung by the title character of this Georges Bizet opera before she throws a flower to Don José. The same work includes Escamillo’s “Toreador Song”; what is its title?
Opened in 2004, this downtown public institution designed by Rem Koolhaas is known for its irregular faceted glass exterior and bright yellow escalators. What is its full name?
Seattle Central Library’s faceted glass exterior and vivid yellow escalators are part of a design by which Dutch architect, founder of OMA and 2000 Pritzker Architecture Prize laureate?

This French photographer helped pioneer candid street photography and, in 1947, co-founded a photographer-owned cooperative agency with Robert Capa and David Seymour. He became closely associated with capturing a fleeting scene at its most meaningful instant. Who is he?

Henri Cartier-Bresson joined Robert Capa, David Seymour, George Rodger, and William Vandivert in founding this cooperative agency in 1947, created so photographers could retain control over their pictures and stories. What agency became a major international home for documentary photographers?

Aaron Copland’s one-act ballet, choreographed by Agnes de Mille, premiered in 1942 and follows a cowgirl seeking acceptance and romance in a Western community. Its score inspired the orchestral suite *Four Dance Episodes*, which includes “Hoe-Down.” What is the ballet called?
For the original production of *Rodeo*, which choreographer also danced the lead Cowgirl when the ballet premiered at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York on October 16, 1942?

Classical-music lore links this superstition to composers such as Beethoven, Schubert, and Bruckner. It claims that a composer who writes the symphony after their eighth may die before completing another major symphonic work; what is the superstition called?
In discussions of the Curse of the Ninth, which Austrian composer avoided numbering *Das Lied von der Erde* as a symphony, later completed his Ninth Symphony, and died before finishing his Tenth?

Painted in 1930, this work pairs a stern-looking man holding a pitchfork with a woman in front of a pointed-arch farmhouse in Eldon, Iowa. It became an iconic painting of the Regionalist movement; what is its title?
The artist who created American Gothic also painted Daughters of Revolution, a satirical work featuring figures posed in front of a famous Revolutionary War scene. What was this artist’s name?
The rural dwelling depicted behind the two figures in American Gothic was modeled on a real Gothic Revival property in Eldon, Iowa. What is that property’s name?
American Gothic is held in the collection of this museum on Michigan Avenue, which also displays Edward Hopper’s Nighthawks. What is the museum’s name?

In 1919, a French Dadaist turned a postcard reproduction of a celebrated Renaissance portrait into an irreverent work by adding a moustache and goatee and writing a title beneath it. The title’s letters form a bawdy pun when pronounced in French; what is the name of this artwork?

The artist behind L.H.O.O.Q. also submitted a urinal signed “R. Mutt” under the title Fountain, challenging conventional definitions of art. He became known for readymades and was a leading figure in Dada; who was this French artist?

This late-19th-century movement centered among Paris-based artists and became known for loose, visible brushwork, painting outdoors, and capturing changing light in scenes of modern life. It gained prominence through independent exhibitions in the 1870s and 1880s. What is the movement called?

Within Impressionism, a French critic gave the movement its name in a satirical 1874 review for the newspaper Le Charivari, written after he saw a sketch-like harbor sunrise painting. Who was the critic?

The title of this French painter’s 1872 harbor scene supplied the name for Impressionism. He later painted water lilies at Giverny and made several series depicting Rouen Cathedral in changing light. Who was he?
In Impressionism, this artist depicted Parisian leisure in scenes including a crowded outdoor dance at the Moulin de la Galette and a lunch gathering on the Seine. Which painter created both works?
This woman associated with Impressionism painted The Cradle, showing a mother watching her sleeping daughter. She was also the sister-in-law of Édouard Manet. Who was she?
Unlike soft ballet slippers, this specialized footwear has a reinforced toe box and a flat platform that lets trained dancers balance on the tips of their toes. What is it called?

Marie Taglioni became famous for dancing en pointe in this 1832 ballet, helping make pointe work a celebrated feature of Romantic-era dance. Which work is often cited as an early landmark in the history of pointe shoes?

In this performing art, a performer interprets a dramatic role through voice, movement, facial expression, gesture, and timing, making characters and their relationships legible to an audience. It can range from stylized performance to psychologically realistic behavior in theatre or film. What art and profession is this?
In acting, which American actor and teacher popularized the Method, an approach that builds on Konstantin Stanislavsky’s work and uses imagination and personal experience to develop a role?

In German-language Romantic music, what is the name for a poetic art song commonly written for solo voice and piano? Schubert composed many examples of this form, often setting poems by writers such as Goethe.

Which Schubert Lied sets Goethe’s ballad about a father riding through the night with his sick son? In the song, the child hears a supernatural figure calling to him, while his father offers natural explanations for what he perceives.

This early photographic process records a one-of-a-kind, highly detailed image on a polished silver-coated copper plate, sensitized with iodine vapor and developed using mercury vapor. What is this process called?
The Daguerreotype was publicly introduced in France in 1839. Which French artist and physicist gave the process its name?
Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1900 opera adapts Alexander Pushkin’s poem and includes a famous orchestral interlude depicting an insect’s frantic flight. What is the opera’s title?

In The Tale of Tsar Saltan, what is the name of the royal son who is sent away with his mother in a barrel, eventually rules the island of Buyan, and visits his father after the Swan-Bird transforms him?

This American composer studied in Paris with Nadia Boulanger and later developed an accessible style associated with spacious harmonies and American landscapes. His major works include a ballet built around the Shaker tune “Simple Gifts” and a brass-and-percussion fanfare inspired by Henry Wallace’s call to honor ordinary people. Who was this composer?

During World War II, Aaron Copland wrote this brass-and-percussion work at the request of Cincinnati Symphony conductor Eugene Goossens, who sought a piece honoring ordinary citizens. Its opening trumpet call helped make it one of Copland’s best-known short orchestral works. What is the work?

Aaron Copland composed a 1942 ballet for choreographer Agnes de Mille whose four dance episodes include “Buckaroo Holiday” and “Hoe-Down.” The latter draws on a fiddle tune associated with William Hamilton Stepp. What is the ballet’s title?

Painted in 1944 soon after spinal surgery, this oil-on-masonite self-portrait shows its artist alone, with tears, nails, and a body brace set against a fractured landscape. What is the work’s natural title?

In The Broken Column, a Mexican painter depicts herself with a fractured backbone represented by an architectural shaft, while tears and nails intensify the image of pain. Which artist made this work after ongoing problems connected to a traffic accident she suffered at age 18?
The Broken Column is held at a museum in Xochimilco, within Mexico City. Which museum houses the original painting?

The brace depicted in The Broken Column is one of several Kahlo used, and the actual brace is now preserved at the artist’s former residence, which became a museum in Coyoacán. What is that museum commonly called?
