Based on a hymn text by Charles Wesley first published in 1739, this Christmas carol is now commonly performed to a melody adapted from Felix Mendelssohn’s Festgesang. What is the carol’s title?

In Hark! The Herald Angels Sing, the familiar melody comes from the second section of this Mendelssohn festival cantata, written for the 1840 quadricentennial of Gutenberg’s printing press. What is the cantata called?
What type of glazed architectural opening became prominent in medieval church design, typically has a pointed arch, and often contains colored glass?
In a Gothic window, what is the name for a large circular opening with stone tracery radiating outward like spokes, often placed above a cathedral’s main entrance?

Over a career spanning roughly seven decades, this American modernist developed abstract charcoal drawings in 1915 before becoming known for enlarged flowers, animal bones, and landscapes of the American Southwest. She moved to New Mexico permanently in 1949; who was this artist?

In 1916, this art dealer and photographer exhibited Georgia O’Keeffe’s work, helping launch her public recognition; their professional and personal relationship later led to marriage in 1924. Who was he?

After Georgia O’Keeffe began spending time in New Mexico, the red-and-yellow cliffs around this property near Abiquiú became recurring subjects in her landscape paintings; she later kept a home there. What was the property called?
Georgia O’Keeffe’s 1936 painting pairs a deer skull with flowers set against a broad, sunlit Southwestern landscape. What is the title of this work?
This brass instrument is sounded by buzzing the lips against a mouthpiece, and most modern versions use three valves to alter pitch. Its most common form is pitched in B-flat; name the instrument.

The most commonly used version of the Trumpet is a transposing instrument: written notes sound a whole step lower than they appear on the page. What pitch designation is attached to this standard version?
A leading bebop player of the Trumpet wrote “A Night in Tunisia” and “Salt Peanuts”; he was famous for puffed cheeks and sometimes played a deliberately bent instrument. Which musician is described?

The Trumpet is often contrasted with this close relative: the latter's tube widens gradually along most of its length, giving it a conical bore, whereas the Trumpet's bore is chiefly cylindrical. What is this brass instrument?

The Trumpet family includes a small member that reaches the highest register in the brass family and is frequently used for demanding high Baroque parts, including the solo in Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 2. Name this instrument.
In 1986, a New York City mural warning about the dangers of a smokable cocaine derivative appeared on a handball court wall in East Harlem. What is the title of this work by Keith Haring?
The 1986 mural Crack Is Wack features bold outlines and vivid, cartoonlike figures, hallmarks of the artist’s public art. Which New York artist created it?
This 310-metre tower beside London Bridge was designed by Renzo Piano and became the tallest building in the United Kingdom upon completion in 2012. What London skyscraper is it?
Which Italian architect designed The Shard, the 310-metre London tower beside London Bridge? He also co-designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris with Richard Rogers.

This 1642 painting shows Captain Frans Banning Cocq’s Amsterdam civic militia company moving into action, with dramatic contrasts of light and shadow. Which work is Rembrandt’s monumental group portrait?
The Night Watch was painted by the Dutch artist who also created The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp and numerous self-portraits. Who was this painter, born in Leiden in 1606?
In a triad arrangement, its third is placed in the bass, with the root a sixth above it. What is this position called?
In common figured-bass shorthand, a first inversion chord is identified by the interval between its bass note and root. Which numeral indicates that the root is a sixth above the bass?

What German art song sets a poem by Christian Friedrich Daniel Schubart about a trout whose capture by a fisherman darkens the song’s mood? Its melody later became the basis for variations in a famous piano quintet.
Die Forelle is a German art song by which Austrian composer, who later incorporated its melody into variations in a piano quintet in A major? He also left his Eighth Symphony unfinished.
Featuring Miles Davis with orchestra on pieces such as “Concierto de Aranjuez” and “Will o’ the Wisp,” this 1960 album draws on Spanish classical and flamenco traditions. What is its title?
On Sketches of Spain, which longtime Miles Davis collaborator arranged the orchestral parts and conducted the album, helping shape its blend of jazz and Spanish musical influences?

Constantin Brâncuși's elongated, highly polished abstract sculptures reduce an airborne subject to a rising, tapered form. The series became central to a 1926 U.S. customs dispute over whether such modern sculpture qualified as art. By what title is this series best known?

In 1926, U.S. customs officials classified one of the abstract sculptures from Bird in Space as a manufactured object rather than a work of art, prompting a landmark 1928 ruling on modern sculpture. What was the name of the court case?
Which 1565 winter landscape shows a party of men carrying spears and their dogs returning toward a village, while people skate on frozen ponds and white-coated mountains rise in the distance?
The Hunters in the Snow is part of a celebrated series of seasonal landscapes by a Flemish Renaissance painter also known for The Tower of Babel and The Peasant Wedding. Who painted it?

Claude Debussy’s orchestral poem opens with a prominent solo flute line shaped by chromatic motion and takes its literary inspiration from a poem by Stéphane Mallarmé. What is this work commonly known by its English title?
answer: Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun

question: Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun draws on a poem titled L’Après-midi d’un faune by this French Symbolist poet. Who wrote the source poem?
This French painter left the naval career planned for him and instead became known for canvases such as Olympia and Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe. Who was he?
Édouard Manet’s Olympia reworked the composition of a famous reclining-nude painting by Titian. Which Titian work is identified by its subject’s recumbent pose and a small dog near the bed?
In Édouard Manet’s The Railway, a girl peers through an iron fence while a woman sits beside her, with rails and a cloud of steam behind them. Which Paris railway terminus provides the setting?

Édouard Manet’s history painting centers on the final moments of the Habsburg ruler installed as Mexico’s emperor by Napoleon III, who was defeated by republican forces in 1867. What is the commonly used title of the work depicting his death by firing squad?

This British-Indian sculptor created a monumental work in Chicago’s Millennium Park that is popularly nicknamed “the Bean.” He also drew controversy for securing exclusive commercial rights to the ultra-black pigment Vantablack. Who is this artist?

Anish Kapoor created this monumental, mirror-polished stainless-steel sculpture in Chicago’s Millennium Park, where its curved surface reflects the skyline and its visitors. What is the work’s official title?
This C-major chamber work is the third in Haydn’s Op. 76 set. Its slow second movement features the melody later adopted for Germany’s national anthem; by what name is the work commonly known?
The Emperor Quartet is part of a set of six quartets dedicated to Count Erdődy. Which Austrian composer, who served the Esterházy family for much of his career, wrote it?

In a musical score, this Italian direction may be shown as a hairpin that opens outward beneath a passage. It tells performers to increase the volume gradually over the indicated span; what is the direction?

Crescendo became so closely associated with the orchestral style of this Italian composer that he was nicknamed “Signor Crescendo.” He wrote the comic opera *The Barber of Seville* and the opera *William Tell*; who was he?

This American avant-garde composer, born in Los Angeles in 1912, transformed piano sounds by placing objects between the instrument’s strings. He also used I Ching chance procedures in works such as *Music of Changes*.
In this 1952 work by John Cage, a performer makes no intentional sounds during three timed movements, inviting the audience to notice sounds in the surrounding space. What is the work’s title?

In SATB choral music, this is the highest of the four standard voice parts, above alto. In opera, it commonly denotes a high female voice type often associated with trills, leaps, and other coloratura passages. What is this vocal range and voice type?
A Spanish soprano born in Barcelona became an international sensation after stepping in for Marilyn Horne in a 1965 Carnegie Hall performance of Donizetti’s *Lucrezia Borgia*. Which singer was it?

In Rome’s Cornaro Chapel, this theatrical marble group shows a Carmelite mystic reclining as an angel approaches with a spear. Golden rays and sculpted witnesses in chapel boxes frame the scene. What is the name of this work?

The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa was made by the Baroque sculptor who also created the Fountain of the Four Rivers in Rome’s Piazza Navona. He designed the bronze Baldacchino over the main altar of St. Peter’s Basilica. Who was this artist?
In this traditional Chinese and Japanese format, a long painting or illustrated manuscript is mounted horizontally and viewed by unrolling it section by section. What is this format called?
Handscrolls let viewers follow a long panorama a section at a time. Which Northern Song work by Zhang Zeduan depicts springtime life in Kaifeng and features a crowded bridge near its center?
answer: Along the River During the Qingming Festival

question: What are formally recognized patriotic songs adopted by countries as symbols of their collective identity?
Among National anthems, India’s “Jana Gana Mana” was written by this Bengali poet, who was born in Kolkata and is also known for the collection *Gitanjali*.

This jazz style became a major form of popular dance music during the big-band era. Its characteristic rhythmic feel often gives paired eighth notes unequal lengths rather than playing them straight. What is this style called?

Which clarinetist led the band whose 1938 Carnegie Hall concert helped bring swing into the concert hall? His small-group recordings with pianist Teddy Wilson and drummer Gene Krupa included the 1937 hit “Sing, Sing, Sing.”

Late-19th-century American percussionists brought together a foot-operated low-pitched part, a sharp backbeat, several differently pitched toms, and cymbals for one performer to play at once. This arrangement became central to jazz rhythm sections and later rock bands. What is it called?

On a standard drum kit, which component has two opposed cymbals mounted on a stand and a foot pedal that closes them? A drummer can use it for crisp timekeeping when closed or a sustained, washy sound when open.

This tenor aria appears in the final act of Turandot and is sung by Prince Calaf, who vows that the princess will learn his name by dawn. Its Italian title means “Let no one sleep.” What is the aria called?
Nessun dorma is part of Turandot, the opera in which Prince Calaf must answer three riddles to win the title princess. Who composed Turandot as well as La bohème and Madama Butterfly?

Nessun dorma reached a much wider audience after a televised performance during the 1990 FIFA World Cup by this Italian tenor. He later performed the aria with Plácido Domingo and José Carreras as one of the Three Tenors.

In a 1974 performance documented in photographs, an artist lay with his arms extended and was briefly nailed through the palms to the rear of a Volkswagen Beetle, evoking a crucifixion tableau. What is the title of this work?
The artist behind Trans-Fixed had previously staged Shoot, a 1971 performance in which an assistant fired a rifle and struck him in the arm. What was this American performance artist’s name?

In additive light, this is one of the three primary colors and combines with red and green to make white. In painting, its broad family includes hues made from woad, ultramarine, and Prussian pigments. What color is it?

This 17th-century Dutch painting by Johannes Vermeer shows a young woman turning toward the viewer against a dark background, wearing a blue-and-yellow turban. The bright Blue fabric was rendered with costly pigment ground from lapis lazuli. Which painting is it?

In a famous Jan van Eyck portrait, a small circular wall object shows a broad view of the room in a diminished reflection, and its frame is decorated with scenes from the Passion. What kind of curved reflective object is it?
Which Jan van Eyck painting features a convex mirror surrounded by scenes from the Passion, with a merchant and his wife standing beneath a chandelier bearing a single candle?

This Spanish painter and printmaker became a court painter and created a stark scene of captured Spaniards facing a French firing squad on 3 May 1808. What artist made that painting, now known as The Third of May 1808?

In 1799, Francisco Goya published a suite of 80 allegorical etchings that used satire and fantasy to criticize superstition and social folly. What is the title of this series, which includes The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters?

This instrumental genre became an important vehicle for music in Italy around 1600, and its name comes from an Italian verb meaning “to sound” or “to play an instrument.” Often written for a solo instrument or a small group, it commonly unfolds across several contrasting movements. What is this genre?

A sonata movement may use this structural plan, but the plan also appears in symphonies and string quartets. It typically presents themes in an exposition, reshapes them in a development, and brings them back in a recapitulation. What is this design called?

Commissioned by Pope Julius II for the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace, this fresco by Raphael gathers ancient thinkers beneath a monumental classical arch. At its center, one philosopher gestures upward while his companion gestures toward the ground; what is this work?
The School of Athens, painted for Pope Julius II’s Vatican apartments between 1509 and 1511, was made by which Urbino-born Renaissance master, also responsible for La Disputa and the Sistine Madonna?
The pope who commissioned The School of Athens for a suite of rooms in the Apostolic Palace also commissioned Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel ceiling. Which pope was this?

In The School of Athens, the floor and coffered architecture converge toward a shared location behind the two central philosophers, creating an illusion of depth on the flat wall. What system for depicting depth does this illustrate?

Johann Sebastian Bach assembled this collection of contrapuntal instrumental pieces after Frederick the Great supplied a royal theme; it includes two ricercars and a trio sonata. What is the collection’s title?
In The Musical Offering, the trio sonata features a woodwind instrument that Frederick the Great famously played. What is this instrument, held sideways and larger than a piccolo?

Which single-reed woodwind is pitched in B-flat and widely used in jazz combos and concert bands? Among its common sizes, it sits below the smaller, E-flat alto and above the larger, lower-pitched baritone.
On the final movement, “Psalm,” of his 1965 album *A Love Supreme*, the tenor saxophone carries a line he described as a musical recitation of a poem. Which jazz saxophonist led that recording?
Published in 1725 alongside eight other concertos, this collection of violin concertos uses sonnet-inspired scenes of birdsong, hunting, thunderstorms, and frozen landscapes. What is it called?
The Four Seasons was composed by a Venetian-born Baroque composer who connected the music with scenes described in sonnets. What was his name?

The Four Seasons appeared in 1725 as part of a larger print collection containing eight additional concertos. What is the original Italian title of that volume, translated as “The Contest Between Harmony and Invention”?
The Four Seasons was printed in 1725 by Michel-Charles Le Cène in this Dutch city, an important center for European music publishing. Which city was it?

In The Four Seasons, the second movement of one concerto assigns the viola a loud, sustained role depicting a barking dog while a goatherd sleeps. This concerto opens the collection and evokes the season of renewal; which one is it?

Which instrument uses magnetic pickups to convert vibrating strings into a signal sent to an amplifier, and is commonly built with six strings tuned E–A–D–G–B–E? In rock music, it can provide both chordal riffs and melodic solos.

Which American musician and inventor built a solid-body prototype called “The Log” and later had a Gibson model named after him? A pioneering electric guitar player, he also helped popularize multitrack recording.

Which Fender electric guitar model, introduced in 1954, is known for its contoured double-cutaway body, three single-coil pickups, and spring-loaded vibrato bridge? Jimi Hendrix famously played one, sometimes turning it upside down.

This four-movement piano composition by Claude Debussy was published in 1905 after earlier revisions. Its movements include “Prélude,” “Menuet,” the independently famous “Clair de lune,” and “Passepied”; what is the composition called?
Suite bergamasque was composed by the French musician who also wrote the piano suite Children’s Corner and the orchestral work Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune. Who was this composer?

This keyboard work by a Salzburg-born composer recasts a French song melody later associated with the English nursery rhyme “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” in a sequence of contrasting sections. What is the work, catalogued as K. 265?
answer: Twelve Variations in C Major on “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,” K. 265

question: Twelve Variations in C Major on “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,” K. 265 is a solo keyboard work by a Classical-era composer who was a celebrated child prodigy and was born in Salzburg. Who composed it?
What Manhattan theater district is internationally associated with professional stage productions and serves as a metonym for New York City’s commercial theater industry, especially its musicals?
A Neil Simon comedy that opened on Broadway in 1965 follows meticulous Felix Ungar after his wife leaves him and he moves in with his slovenly friend Oscar Madison. What is the play called?
Born in Belgium in 1898, this Surrealist painter created a 1929 work showing a pipe above the words “This is not a pipe.” He also painted The Son of Man and Time Transfixed. Who was he?

In René Magritte’s 1933 painting, an easel supports a canvas depicting the landscape visible beyond a window, making it difficult to tell where the painted view ends and the outside scene begins. What is the title of this work?

Painted in Paris in 1907, this monumental oil-on-canvas work presents five angular nude figures in a shallow, fractured space. Its mask-like faces and flattened forms made it a landmark of modern art, often described as proto-Cubist. What is the painting’s title?
The title of Les Demoiselles d’Avignon refers not to a French city but to a Barcelona street associated with sex work. What street supplied the title’s place-name?
This opening track of Miles Davis’s 1959 album *Kind of Blue* begins with a spare piano-and-bass introduction before the ensemble develops its modal jazz improvisation. What is the track’s title?
On the *Kind of Blue* recording of “So What,” which bandleader and trumpeter enters after the piano-and-bass introduction? The 1959 session also featured John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley.
This major art museum on Michigan Avenue houses Grant Wood’s painting of a pitchfork-holding farmer and a woman, as well as Edward Hopper’s scene of a late-night diner. Which institution is it?

At the Art Institute of Chicago, which Grant Wood painting shows a stern farmer holding a pitchfork beside a woman, with a house modeled on one in Eldon, Iowa, in the background? Its title alludes to the pointed-arch style of a window on that house.

This four-act opera premiered in Paris in 1875 and uses the opéra comique format, with spoken dialogue separating its musical numbers. Its story follows a free-spirited cigarette-factory worker and the soldier whose jealous passion ends in tragedy. What is the opera’s title?

The score of Carmen was written by a French composer who died suddenly after the opera’s 33rd performance, before it achieved international acclaim. He also composed The Pearl Fishers and the orchestral suite L’Arlésienne. Who was he?

In Carmen, the title character sings this aria while flirting with a crowd of men; its melody descends chromatically over a repeating cello figure. The chorus warns the men to beware of love’s capricious nature. What is the aria called?
Carmen adapts a novella first published in 1845 by this French writer, whose other works include Colomba and La Vénus d’Ille. Who wrote the source story?
This Italian Romantic-era composer wrote the operas Rigoletto, La traviata, and Aida, and his Nabucco includes the chorus “Va, pensiero,” later associated with Italian unification. Who was he?
One early Giuseppe Verdi opera centers on the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar and includes the chorus “Va, pensiero,” sung by Hebrew captives longing for their homeland. What is this opera’s title?

In this Giuseppe Verdi opera, an Ethiopian princess loves the Egyptian captain Radamès, and the two are ultimately entombed together; its score also contains the aria “Ritorna vincitor.” What is the opera’s title?
Giuseppe Verdi was born near this town in the modern province of Parma, where local patron Antonio Barezzi helped support his musical education. What is the town’s name?
Before Giuseppe Verdi became famous, this Busseto-based merchant and music patron helped finance his musical studies; he later became Verdi’s father-in-law. Who was this benefactor?
In Western music, this scale passes through all twelve pitches within an octave, moving by one equal-tempered half step at a time before reaching the octave repeat. What is its conventional name?
In a chromatic scale, each neighboring pair of notes is separated by this interval, which is half a whole tone in twelve-tone equal temperament. What is this interval called?
Which French painter, a leading Fauvist known for using bold, non-naturalistic color, created both *The Joy of Life* and *The Dance*?

Henri Matisse’s monumental 1910 painting shows five figures holding hands in a circle against a simplified landscape, with vivid red figures set against blue and green. What is the title of this work?
What Italian tempo marking calls for a slow, expressive pace, generally faster than largo or lento but slower than andante? It indicates a broad, unhurried character in a musical performance.

Samuel Barber’s widely performed orchestral Adagio began as the slow movement of which 1936 work? The original composition was scored for two violins, a viola, and a cello before Barber arranged the movement for orchestra.
An Italian Baroque composer produced a celebrated body of 555 keyboard sonatas, many associated with Infanta Maria Barbara. What was his name?
Domenico Scarlatti wrote many of his keyboard sonatas for an instrument whose jacks pluck strings rather than using hammers to strike them. What is this instrument called?

What international avant-garde movement took shape in 1920s Paris and drew on ideas about dreams and the unconscious to challenge the control of reason? Its artists and writers explored unexpected juxtapositions through forms ranging from poetry and painting to film.
Which French writer and organizer helped define Surrealism’s aims by publishing a manifesto in Paris in 1924?
This 1911 ragtime opera by the composer of “Maple Leaf Rag” centers on an educated young woman who challenges conjurers exploiting her community’s superstitions. What is the opera’s title?
In Treemonisha, the composer also wrote the libretto and was already famous for piano rags such as “The Entertainer.” Who was he?

Which theatrical dance tradition grew from European court entertainments into staged works and uses a codified vocabulary of steps linked through choreography? Its stories may be told through movement or omitted entirely, while pointe shoes and tutus became especially associated with its Romantic era.

In the early 20th century, this company made ballet a meeting point for choreographers, composers, and visual artists under impresario Sergei Diaghilev. Its Paris productions included Igor Stravinsky’s *The Firebird* and *The Rite of Spring*; what company was it?

In this large tempera-on-wood panel, nine mythological figures gather in a flower-filled orange grove, with Venus centered beneath Cupid and the Three Graces dancing at the left. What is the title of Sandro Botticelli’s allegorical painting celebrating the arrival of spring?
Primavera is generally dated to about 1480 and was created by a Florentine Renaissance painter whose other mythological works include The Birth of Venus. Which artist painted it?

Born in Bonn, this German composer and pianist moved to Vienna at 21, where he studied with Joseph Haydn and gained attention as a virtuoso performer. His music helped move Western art music from the Classical era toward Romanticism, even as progressive hearing loss later left him profoundly deaf. Who was he?

Beethoven’s Third premiered in 1805 and expanded the scale and dramatic scope of the orchestral form. He famously altered its original dedication after Napoleon crowned himself emperor; by what title is this work commonly known?

Beethoven dedicated this C-sharp minor piano work, Op. 27, No. 2, to his pupil Julie Guicciardi. Its first movement is marked Adagio sostenuto and unfolds over a flowing triplet accompaniment; what popular nickname is given to the work?
In Beethoven’s only opera, Leonore disguises herself as a young man to enter a prison and rescue her husband, Florestan, from a political enemy. What is the opera called?
Beethoven’s final completed work for full orchestra premiered in Vienna in 1824, and its finale sets Friedrich Schiller’s “Ode to Joy” with soloists and chorus. What number is this work?

Born in Vitebsk, this Belarusian-French painter drew on Jewish folklore and village life to create dreamlike modernist works. One of his signature paintings pairs a green-faced man with a farm animal, while one of his self-portraits refers in its title to an unusual number of fingers. Who was the artist?

Which 1911 painting by Marc Chagall brings together a large green-faced man, a white-faced animal, a small red figure, and angular houses in a dreamlike composition? Its distinctive imagery reflects his blend of folk traditions and modernist forms.

An artist cuts away parts of a wooden block, applies ink to the raised areas, then presses paper against it. The image transfers in reverse, and the same block can produce repeated impressions; what is this technique called?

In Japanese woodblock printing, this popular art form developed into a coordinated craft involving a publisher, designer, block cutter, and printer. Its prints often depicted kabuki actors, landscapes, and everyday urban life; what is this genre called?

Born Jacob Gershwine, this American composer and pianist wrote music that brought jazz and classical traditions together. His best-known works include an orchestral piece inspired by a train journey and an opera set in Charleston.

George Gershwin wrote this 1924 concert work for piano and orchestra at the request of bandleader Paul Whiteman. It opens with a famous clarinet glissando and helped bring jazz influences into the concert hall.
George Gershwin composed this opera with lyrics by his brother Ira Gershwin and DuBose Heyward. Set in Charleston’s Catfish Row, it includes the aria “Summertime.”

George Gershwin composed this political satire with lyrics by Ira Gershwin, and it became the first musical to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. Its fictional presidential candidate is John P. Wintergreen.

Victor Vasarely’s *Zebra* and Bridget Riley’s *Movement in Squares* use patterns that can seem to ripple or shift even though the images are physically still. What visual phenomena make these works appear different from their actual properties?

In artworks that explore optical illusions, artists use this technique to make a flat surface suggest depth. It arranges receding parallel lines so they appear to meet at a vanishing point; what is this technique called?

Premiering at London’s New London Theatre in 1981, this Andrew Lloyd Webber musical adapts poems from T. S. Eliot’s 1939 collection and centers on a tribe gathering for an annual ball. Grizabella’s solo “Memory” became one of its best-known songs; name the musical.
For the original London production of Cats, this British choreographer created the movement that made the Jellicle Ball and the performers’ catlike physicality central to the show. Who was she?
What dry artistic medium is made by combining pigment with a binder and forming the mixture into sticks for drawing or painting?
Pastel was used for two versions of a famous composition by Edvard Munch. In the image, a lone figure presses its hands to its head on a bridge beneath a turbulent red-orange sky; what is the work?
This French painter’s 1874 harbor scene gave a critic wording that became the name of an art movement. He also painted recurring series of haystacks, Rouen Cathedral, and water lilies. Who was he?
Before Claude Monet became known for painting outdoors, this older French landscape painter encouraged him to work directly from nature and introduced him to plein-air practice. Who was this mentor?

Claude Monet settled in this village in Normandy in 1883 and later developed a landscaped garden there, including the pond that became the setting for his long-running water-lily paintings. Name the village.

Claude Monet’s 1874 painting of an orange sun rising above the harbor at Le Havre was shown at an exhibition where critic Louis Leroy coined a label for the emerging style. What name did that artistic movement come to be known by?
Claude Monet made a group of paintings depicting this Paris rail terminal, exploring its iron-and-glass architecture, steam, and shifting light. What is the station called?

Commissioned by Amsterdam’s surgeons’ guild and dated 1632, this Rembrandt oil painting transforms a group portrait into a scene of anatomical instruction. A physician demonstrates the muscles of a dissected forearm as the assembled surgeons look on. What is the painting’s title?
answer: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp

question: In Rembrandt’s *The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp*, the dissected body represents a man who was hanged in Amsterdam on January 31, 1632. By what familiar name is he identified?

The Salon rejected an 1875 canvas by this French painter showing three laborers kneeling to scrape a parquet floor. He later exhibited the work at an Impressionist exhibition in Paris. Who painted it?

In Gustave Caillebotte’s 1877 canvas, sharply dressed pedestrians cross a broad intersection near Place de Dublin in the rain, with umbrellas and reflections above wet cobblestones. What is the title of this painting?

Which Stephen Sondheim musical uses a dark, episodic structure to portray people who assassinated or tried to assassinate U.S. presidents? Its characters include John Wilkes Booth, Charles Guiteau, and Lee Harvey Oswald.
In Assassins, which character sings “The Gun Song” and urges listeners that moving a little finger can change the world? He was the actor who assassinated President Abraham Lincoln.

Born in Paris to Chinese parents and raised in the United States, this musician became known for an extensive classical recording career. He founded an intercultural group inspired by historic exchange between Asia and Europe, and his playing is featured in Ang Lee’s Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. Which musician is described?

Yo-Yo Ma founded this international music project in 2000, bringing together artists from many traditions to explore cultural connections along the historic routes linking Asia with Europe. What is the project called?

Which 1910 ballet did Igor Stravinsky compose for Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, with original choreography by Michel Fokine? In its story, Prince Ivan receives help from a magical bird in his struggle against Koschei the Immortal.
For the original production of The Firebird, which choreographer created the dances, working from a scenario developed with Alexandre Benois and other collaborators?

The Firebird’s success helped bring Igor Stravinsky international fame. Which of his later ballets premiered in 1913 and became notorious for the uproar surrounding its radical music and choreography?

Monumental residences and civic buildings from the Renaissance period in this group pair classically ordered façades with prominent roles in city life. Examples include a Florentine house designed by Leon Battista Alberti for a wealthy merchant family and the city’s historic government seat; what architectural subject do they represent?

Within Italian Renaissance palaces, which Florentine residence is recognized for Leon Battista Alberti’s three-story façade, where pilasters organize each level and the masonry shifts from strong rustication below to a smoother, more refined treatment above?
In music theory, what interval spans eight scale degrees? Its upper note has twice the frequency of its lower note, as in the two C notes at the ends of a standard C-to-C span.

In an octave, the upper pitch has a particular whole-number relationship to the lower pitch in how rapidly they vibrate. Express the upper pitch’s vibration rate relative to the lower pitch as a pair of numbers.

Born in Ciboure in 1875, this French composer studied with Gabriel Fauré at the Paris Conservatoire and became renowned for his exacting orchestration. He wrote Le Tombeau de Couperin in memory of friends killed in World War I and a piano suite containing the nightmarish movement “Scarbo.” Who was he?

Commissioned for dancer Ida Rubinstein’s company, this orchestral work by Maurice Ravel passes a recurring melody and snare-drum rhythm among changing instrumental colors as the volume steadily rises. What is this ballet score?
Which American ballet dancer made history in 2015 when she became the first Black principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre?
Misty Copeland performs in specialized ballet shoes with reinforced toe boxes. What is the term for the technique in which dancers balance on the tips of their toes?

This 1863 painting scandalized viewers by showing a nude woman dining beside two fully clothed men in a wooded setting, with a bather visible in the background. What is its commonly known English title?
The Luncheon on the Grass was rejected by the official Salon and exhibited at the Salon des Refusés in 1863. Which French painter created this controversial scene?

In this oil painting, a canvas on an easel is positioned in front of a window, and its landscape aligns with the scenery visible beyond the glass. A second work by the same artist uses the same title but depicts a seascape; what is the name of the first painting?

The Human Condition makes an easel painting appear to continue the landscape seen through a window, blurring the boundary between artwork and reality. Which Belgian artist created this composition and its seascape counterpart?

Mozart finished this orchestral solo piece in 1791 for the Viennese virtuoso Anton Stadler, whose instrument had an expanded low register. The closing movement is a rondo with a buoyant recurring theme. Name this work.
answer: Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622

question: The Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622 was composed for a virtuoso who performed on a clarinet with an extended lower range. Which Austrian clarinetist was its intended soloist and dedicatee?

Which Brazilian composer drew on folk and urban traditions as well as European classical forms, creating both the Chôros cycle and Bachianas Brasileiras? His works made him a central figure in 20th-century Brazilian art music.

Heitor Villa-Lobos gave this name to a cycle of nine compositions written between 1930 and 1945, combining counterpoint associated with J. S. Bach and Brazilian musical idioms. What is this cycle called?

This Dutch graphic artist studied architecture before turning to printmaking, and his visit to the Alhambra helped inspire his repeating, interlocking patterns. He later created paradoxical prints such as *Waterfall* and *Ascending and Descending*. Who was this artist?
M. C. Escher studied the patterned tiles of this palace complex in Granada, Spain, whose geometric designs helped inspire his tessellations. What is the name of this historic site?

Edward Elgar composed a five-work orchestral series as Op. 39 between 1901 and 1930, with a later sixth assembled from his sketches. The first work’s trio became associated with “Land of Hope and Glory” and is often heard at graduations and the Last Night of the Proms; what is this series called?

Among the friends Elgar honored with dedications in the Pomp and Circumstance Marches, one was a conductor, while another was composer Granville Bantock and others were organists. Which conductor was a dedicatee?
A sixth entry to the Pomp and Circumstance Marches was not one of Elgar’s five completed originals. In 2006, a later composer assembled it from sketches Elgar had left behind; who was that composer?
Julia Ward Howe wrote this patriotic American song using the melody of “John Brown’s Body.” Its verses proclaim that God’s truth is marching on. What is the song’s natural title?
In Battle Hymn of the Republic, the chorus repeats a four-word refrain that combines a word of praise with a Hebrew expression of joy. What is the refrain?

After training as a goldsmith and sculptor in Florence, this Renaissance architect devised the cathedral’s vast octagonal dome, built with a double shell and herringbone brickwork without wooden supports. He also helped develop a method for representing depth on a flat surface. Who was he?

Filippo Brunelleschi is credited with developing a method that makes a flat image suggest three-dimensional space by showing parallel lines receding toward a single vanishing point. What is this technique called?

Born in Pesaro on February 29, 1792, this Italian opera composer studied music in Bologna and made his theatrical debut in Venice in 1810 with *La cambiale di matrimonio*. His final opera premiered in Paris in 1829; who was this composer of both comic and serious operas?

Gioachino Rossini’s final opera premiered in Paris in 1829 and is based on Friedrich Schiller’s play about a Swiss marksman compelled by Governor Gessler to shoot an apple balanced on his son Jemmy’s head. What is the name of this opera?

Its four strings are normally tuned in fifths from low C through G, D, and A, and players support it between their knees with its endpin resting on the floor. Which bowed violin-family instrument sounds lower than the viola but higher than the double bass?

Which musician, a Paris-born performer on the cello, founded the Silk Road Project in 1998 and later led its international ensemble? He also performed on the soundtrack to Ang Lee’s film *Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon*.
Among Johann Sebastian Bach’s six compositions for unaccompanied cello, the one catalogued as BWV 1007 opens with a Prelude of flowing broken chords. What is this work’s title?
answer: Suite No. 1 in G major, BWV 1007

question: The Czech composer behind the *New World Symphony* completed a large-scale work for cello and orchestra during his New York years in 1894–95. Leo Stern gave it its London premiere in 1896; what is the title of this composition?
answer: Dvořák’s Cello Concerto in B minor

question: Painted in June 1889 while Vincent van Gogh was staying at an asylum near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, this canvas places a dark cypress before an imagined village beneath a sky of curling blue strokes and radiant stars. What painting is it?
The Starry Night was made while this Dutch Post-Impressionist was staying at Saint-Paul-de-Mausole; he also painted Sunflowers and Bedroom in Arles. Which artist created it?
In 1941, the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest brought The Starry Night into the permanent collection of this New York institution, where it remains today. Which institution is it?

The Starry Night was inspired by the view from the room Vincent van Gogh occupied at this institution during his 1889 stay near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. What former monastery, then operating as an asylum, was it?

Taken in Havana on March 5, 1960, this portrait shows an Argentine revolutionary in a beret with a star, gazing beyond the camera during a memorial service for victims of the La Coubre explosion. It became one of the most widely reproduced images associated with revolutionary politics; what is its title?

Which Cuban photographer made Guerrillero Heroico while covering the Havana memorial service for victims of the La Coubre explosion? He later allowed Italian publisher Giangiacomo Feltrinelli to reproduce the image without charge.

Conceived by Auguste Rodin around 1880 for the top of a monumental portal inspired by the Inferno, this bronze depicts a muscular nude man leaning forward with his chin on his hand and elbow on his knee. What is this sculpture, later exhibited independently and enlarged by Rodin?
The Thinker was first titled The Poet and linked to this Italian writer, whose Divine Comedy includes the Inferno that inspired Rodin’s Gates of Hell. Who was the writer?

A 1939 protest song made famous by Billie Holiday, it turns Southern landscape imagery into a stark indictment of lynching. Abel Meeropol first wrote it as a poem after seeing a photograph of a lynching in Indiana; what is the song?

Strange Fruit began as a poem published under the pseudonym Lewis Allan before its author set it to music. Which New York City schoolteacher and songwriter wrote the work later famously recorded by Billie Holiday?
In Tchaikovsky’s ballet *The Sleeping Beauty*, the princess celebrates her sixteenth birthday before being cursed to sleep for a hundred years. What is her name?
At the end of Tchaikovsky’s *The Sleeping Beauty*, which visiting nobleman awakens Aurora with a kiss after her century-long sleep?
A nine-arched crossing in Hortobágy and a historic Danube crossing between Buda and Pest are two notable examples of this national collection of landmarks. What is the natural name for this topic?

Among Hungarian Bridges, which 19th-century suspension bridge became Budapest’s first permanent crossing of the Danube when it opened in 1849? It connects Buda and Pest and was rebuilt after its destruction in World War II.

Commissioned by Khedive Isma'il for Cairo’s Khedivial Opera House, this four-act opera premiered there on December 24, 1871. Its story follows an Ethiopian princess and an Egyptian commander whose love ends with the two sealed together in a tomb. What is the opera?
Aida’s score was composed by the Italian creator of Rigoletto and La traviata. Who was this composer, whose opera also premiered in Cairo in 1871?

This 17th-century Dutch painter depicted his hometown in a celebrated cityscape and also created scenes of a woman pouring milk and a young woman wearing a pearl earring. Which artist is known for these works?
In one of his domestic interiors, Johannes Vermeer centers a woman carefully pouring milk beside a table holding bread. What is the painting commonly known as?
In this painting, a woman and a young girl stand beside a railing and look out over Paris. Which work by French Impressionist Berthe Morisot depicts this scene?
answer: Woman and Child on the Balcony

question: Woman and Child on the Balcony shows a woman and girl looking over Paris from beside a balcony railing. Which French artist, one of the few prominent women of the Impressionist movement, painted it?
A quick-witted barber and servant helps Count Almaviva court Rosina in Rossini’s Seville-set comic opera, then returns as the groom at the center of a Mozart opera. What is this character called?

In Rossini’s The Barber of Seville, Figaro celebrates being everyone’s indispensable fixer in a fast-moving entrance aria whose refrain repeats his name several times. What is the conventional title of this showpiece?
Salvador Dalí’s 1931 Surrealist canvas places limp watches in a barren, dreamlike Catalonian landscape, with ants gathered on an orange watch near the edge. What is the title of this famous painting?
The Persistence of Memory was painted by an artist born in Figueres who also created Lobster Telephone and The Temptation of St. Anthony. Which Spanish Surrealist artist made it?
After The Persistence of Memory sold for $250, an anonymous donor gave it in 1934 to a major New York institution devoted to modern art. Which institution received the painting and holds it today?

The Persistence of Memory was first shown publicly in 1932 at a Manhattan art venue founded by a dealer who helped introduce Surrealism to American audiences and mounted shows for Dalí. What was the name of the venue?
The Persistence of Memory is also known by a Catalan title, reflecting the language of the northeastern Spanish region where Dalí was born. What is that title?

This celebrated late-15th-century French millefleur cycle consists of six hangings in which a richly dressed woman appears with the same fantastical, long-horned creature. Five are commonly interpreted as the senses, while the meaning of the sixth remains debated. What is the cycle called?
In The Lady and the Unicorn, the enigmatic sixth panel shows the woman beside a jewel casket beneath a tent. What French motto is woven across the tent?

Born in 1844 in Allegheny City, this American painter and printmaker was invited by Edgar Degas to exhibit with the Impressionists in 1877. Her work is especially known for intimate scenes of women and children. Who was this artist?

In Mary Cassatt’s 1893 painting, a seated woman supports a small figure while washing its feet in a basin, and the scene is viewed from above. What is the title of this work in the Art Institute of Chicago’s collection?

Commissioned by Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge and premiered in 1944, this ballet follows a Bride and a Husbandman celebrating their marriage in a nineteenth-century Pennsylvania settlement. Aaron Copland composed the score, and Martha Graham choreographed the original production; what is the ballet’s title?

In Appalachian Spring, this choreographer created the original dances and performed the role of the Bride in the 1944 premiere. She later became the namesake of a dance company whose repertory still includes the ballet; who was she?
Copland’s score for Appalachian Spring includes variations on an 1848 Shaker song attributed to Joseph Brackett of the Sabbathday Lake Shaker community. What is the title of that hymn?

A late-15th-century drawing by Leonardo da Vinci depicts a nude male figure with overlapping limbs positioned within a circle and a square, illustrating ideal human proportions. What is this work commonly called?

In Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man, a nude figure is arranged to fit both a circle and a square. Which ancient Roman architect and author of De architectura supplied the proportional principles the drawing illustrates?

Born in Rocky Mount, North Carolina, in 1917, this American jazz pianist developed an unmistakable style marked by angular melodies, unexpected silences, and dissonant harmonies. He composed jazz standards including “Round Midnight” and “Straight, No Chaser”; who was he?

Thelonious Monk composed this slow, chromatic jazz ballad in the 1940s, and it became a standard after early recordings by Cootie Williams and later performances by Miles Davis. What is the title of the piece?

J.M.W. Turner portrayed an aging naval vessel being towed to its final berth in a celebrated maritime painting. Along with sail-powered and steam-powered craft, what broad class of watercraft is a recurring subject of nautical paintings?

The subject of Ships also appears in Winslow Homer’s 1899 maritime canvas, which shows a Black fisherman bracing in a small boat amid rough, shark-infested water, with a vessel on the distant horizon. What is the title of this painting?

It serves the public on a continuing basis by collecting, preserving, researching, and interpreting visual art. Its exhibitions can combine works it owns with works borrowed from elsewhere; what kind of institution is described?

At its Fifth Avenue home in New York City, this art museum brings together curatorial, conservation, and scientific research teams to study, exhibit, and care for its encyclopedic collection. Which institution is described?

Completed in 1656, this court scene places a young princess and her attendants in a room at Madrid’s Royal Alcázar, while the painter stands beside a canvas at the left. A mirror at the back reflects the monarchs, making the viewer’s position part of the painting’s puzzle. What is this painting called?

In Las Meninas, this painter includes himself beside a large easel, wearing the red cross of the Order of Santiago. He served as court painter to Philip IV and also painted The Surrender of Breda. Who is he?

Las Meninas is displayed at this Madrid institution, Spain’s national art museum, which opened to the public in 1819. Its collection also includes Goya’s The Third of May 1808. What is the institution called?

In Las Meninas, the five-year-old child at the center of the group is the daughter of Philip IV and Mariana of Austria. Her entourage includes maids of honour, a chaperone, and court dwarfs. What is the princess’s name?
A trumpeter, composer, and educator from New Orleans, he serves as artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center and wrote the jazz oratorio *Blood on the Fields*. Who is this musician?
Wynton Marsalis’s *Blood on the Fields* became the first jazz composition to receive this Pulitzer honor in 1997. What is the award?
What Cuban dance and musical style is associated with a festive procession of dancers moving rhythmically in a linked line, one behind another? The same name is also used for the line itself.

Conga lines were popularized in American entertainment by Cuban musician and actor Desi Arnaz, who appeared in a 1950s sitcom alongside his real-life wife. What was the name of the comedian who sold Vitameatavegamin and starred in the famous chocolate-factory episode?

In this religious painting by William Holman Hunt, Christ holds a lantern while knocking at a closed door buried in weeds and ivy. The door has no handle on the outside, reflecting the idea that it must be opened from within. What is the painting called?

The Light of the World was painted by this English Pre-Raphaelite artist, who also created The Scapegoat and The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple. Which artist was responsible for all three works?

A French painter trained in Jacques-Louis David’s studio depicted Napoleon tending a plague-stricken soldier in an 1804 scene set in Jaffa, and later painted Napoleon among the casualties after the Battle of Eylau. Which artist created these Napoleonic history paintings?

Antoine-Jean Gros’s monumental 1808 history painting commemorates the French victory over Russian and Prussian forces at a 1807 battle, placing the French emperor on horseback amid a snow-covered field strewn with wounded soldiers. What is the title of this work?
answer: Napoleon on the Battlefield of Eylau

question: Taken by Voyager 1 in 1990 from the outer Solar System, this image shows Earth as a tiny speck suspended in a ray of sunlight. What is this photograph called?
The Pale Blue Dot photograph inspired a 1994 book reflecting on humanity’s place in the cosmos. Which astronomer and science communicator wrote that book and helped popularize the image?

Born in Nyack, New York, this American realist painter studied with William Merritt Chase and Robert Henri at the New York School of Art. His scenes of diners, apartments, and New England landscapes use stark light and shadow to suggest solitude. Who is he?
Edward Hopper’s 1942 canvas places three customers and a counterman inside a brightly lit urban diner, seen through a broad plate-glass window against a dark street. What is this painting called?
Edward Hopper married this fellow artist in 1924; she modeled for many of his paintings and helped manage his career. What was her full name?

Built in Central Java around the ninth century, this monumental Buddhist sanctuary rises in stacked terraces and features extensive narrative relief panels and Buddha images. What temple complex is it?
Borobudur stands on Java, one of the major islands in the Southeast Asian archipelago whose national capital is Jakarta. What modern country contains the temple?

In equal-tempered music, this interval spans six semitones, or three whole tones, and divides the octave exactly in half. It can be notated as either an augmented fourth or a diminished fifth. What is it called?
In tonal harmony, the four-note sonority C–E–G–B♭ contains the tritone E–B♭, whose guide tones typically resolve to F–A. What is this sonority called?

Developed in 12th-century France, this medieval building style succeeded Romanesque and preceded the Renaissance. Pointed arches, rib vaults, and flying buttresses are among its defining features. What is this style?

The rebuilding of the choir at the Basilica of Saint-Denis, begun around 1140, is often cited as a formative early example of Gothic architecture, with an ambulatory and radiating chapels designed to admit more light. Which senior cleric sponsored the project?
Joseph Haydn composed a final group of twelve orchestral works for his visits to England in the 1790s, numbered 93 through 104. What is this group commonly called?
Among the London symphonies, which one features a second movement whose sudden loud passages add triangle, cymbals, and bass drum for a Turkish-style effect?

Gustav Holst composed this seven-movement orchestral suite between 1914 and 1917, giving each movement an astrological title. It opens with “Mars, the Bringer of War” and ends with “Neptune, the Mystic.” What is the work?

The Planets, Op. 32, was written by an English composer who taught at St. Paul’s Girls’ School. He adapted a melody from the movement “Jupiter” into the hymn tune “Thaxted,” associated with “I Vow to Thee, My Country.” Who composed the suite?

At the invited-audience premiere of The Planets at Queen’s Hall on September 29, 1918, this English conductor led the performance. He was a friend of Holst; the suite’s first complete public performance followed in 1920 under Albert Coates. Who conducted the 1918 premiere?

In adults, this bony framework usually consists of 22 bones, with a cranium that protects the brain and facial bones that shape the face. In vanitas art, it is also a familiar memento mori, often shown beside fading flowers or extinguished candles. What is this structure?
In a 1628 Dutch vanitas still life, this painter placed a gap-toothed human skull beside a tipped glass and a lamp with a dying wick to suggest life’s brevity. Who made the painting?

This art material combines color-giving particles with a medium that binds them, and artists apply it to supports such as canvas, wood, plaster, or stone. Its varieties include oil, watercolor, egg tempera, and glue-based forms. What is this material?

In paint, pigment supplies the color, while this component holds pigment particles together and helps determine how the material handles and dries. Drying oil, egg, and glue can each serve this role in different types of paint. What is this component?

Created for the 1902 Vienna Secession exhibition, this monumental work depicts humanity’s quest for happiness and its struggle against allegorical forces. Its central section places three Gorgons beside the monstrous Typhoeus. What is the work’s name?
The Beethoven Frieze was created by this Vienna Secession co-founder, who also painted The Kiss and the portraits of Adele Bloch-Bauer. Name the artist.
In Christian art, this devotional scene shows the Virgin Mary holding the dead Christ across her lap after the Crucifixion. What is this scene commonly called?
A famous marble Pietà completed in 1499 is displayed in St. Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City. Which Renaissance sculptor also carved the colossal David now in Florence?
Born in Vienna in 1797 and dead at 31, this Austrian composer wrote more than 600 Lieder, including “Erlkönig,” and left an Eighth Symphony with only two completed movements. Who was he?
Franz Schubert set poems by Wilhelm Müller for this song cycle, which opens with “Gute Nacht” and ends with “Der Leiermann,” or “The Hurdy-Gurdy Man.” What is the cycle called?
Franz Schubert’s A-major chamber work for piano, violin, viola, cello, and double bass includes variations on one of his songs in its fourth movement. By what familiar nickname is this work known?

In Franz Schubert’s dramatic setting of a Goethe poem, one singer portrays a narrator, a father, a child, and a supernatural tempter, while rapid piano triplets evoke a galloping horse. What is the lied called?

Which 32-work body of solo-keyboard repertoire includes an early work whose slow movement is marked Adagio cantabile and a late work with a massive fugue finale? The composer behind the collection also wrote the Eroica Symphony.
answer: Piano sonatas by Ludwig van Beethoven

question: Within the piano sonatas by Ludwig van Beethoven, which work sets a tranquil theme and variations in D-flat major as its second movement, followed attacca by a stormy F-minor finale? It was dedicated to Count Franz von Brunswick.

Born in Leiden in 1606, this Dutch Golden Age painter and printmaker moved to Amsterdam around 1632, where he built a successful workshop. His portraits, history paintings, and technically inventive etchings helped define seventeenth-century Dutch art. Who was he?

In 1642, Rembrandt transformed the conventional Dutch civic-guard portrait into an animated scene, showing Captain Frans Banning Cocq and Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch amid guards preparing to march. What painting is this?

This Russian and Soviet composer, pianist, and conductor left Russia in 1918 and spent years working abroad before returning to the USSR in 1936. His works include the ballet *Romeo and Juliet* and an orchestral tale in which instruments represent characters. Who was he?

Sergei Prokofiev wrote this 1936 symphonic fairy tale for narrator and orchestra, assigning distinct instruments to its characters—for instance, a flute to a bird and an oboe to a duck. What is the work’s title?

This American artist and designer developed an iridescent glassmaking style known as Favrile and became famous for stained-glass windows and richly patterned lamps. He was the son of the founder of the jewelry company whose name became associated with those lamps. Who was he?
Louis Comfort Tiffany used a trademarked name for the iridescent, handmade material produced at his studio and shaped into decorative vessels and lamp shades. What was that name?

What period and style of Western art music, spanning approximately 1600 to 1750, came before the Classical period? Its composers worked across European church, court, and operatic settings rather than sharing one uniform sound.

In Baroque music, what practice pairs a written bass line with chordal accompaniment that players may realize from numerical shorthand? The accompanying group often combines a keyboard or lute with a bass instrument such as a cello.
What staged musical form tells a dramatic story by combining singing, instrumental music, and theatrical action? It commonly uses speech-like passages alongside more melodic arias.

In an opera, what speech-like style of singing typically carries dialogue and advances the plot between more melodic arias? It follows the rhythms of spoken language rather than the sustained lyrical shape of an aria.

Released by Atlantic in 1960 after being recorded the year before, this John Coltrane-led LP was his first Atlantic album as a bandleader and his first released LP made entirely of his own compositions. It includes “Naima,” “Mr. P.C.,” and “Countdown”; what is the album’s title?

In the title composition of Giant Steps, the harmony cycles rapidly through three major keys a major third apart, creating a demanding progression that became influential in modern jazz. What name is commonly given to this characteristic harmonic approach?

Roman artists used this technique to create durable scenes and patterns on the floors of homes and public buildings, while Byzantine artists used colored glass and gold-backed versions to decorate churches. It forms images by arranging small pieces of stone, ceramic, or glass; what is this art form called?

In a Mosaic, small pieces of stone, ceramic, or glass are fitted together to create a design. Roman works might combine several materials, while Byzantine church interiors often featured glass pieces against gold backgrounds; what is the established term for these individual pieces?

Which Dutch painter co-founded De Stijl with Theo van Doesburg and became known for abstract compositions built from black horizontal and vertical lines, white spaces, and primary colors? His late painting Broadway Boogie-Woogie evokes the grid of Manhattan streets and the rhythm of jazz.

Piet Mondrian helped shape this Dutch avant-garde movement alongside Theo van Doesburg. Its artists pursued geometric abstraction through simplified forms, straight lines, and a restricted palette of primary colors, black, and white.

This French painter trained in Paris under François Boucher and won the Prix de Rome in 1752 before studying in Italy. He became a leading Rococo artist, known for playful scenes of romance and leisure, including one in which a woman’s slipper flies as she swings toward a concealed admirer. Who was he?

In Jean-Honoré Fragonard’s famous garden scene, a young woman in a pink dress is suspended from ropes as she kicks her slipper toward a hidden admirer while an older man pushes her from behind. A nearby putto gestures for silence; what is this painting called?

Which French Impressionist painter portrayed dancers mingling at an outdoor Montmartre dance hall in a celebrated 1876 canvas? He also painted a riverside gathering of friends dining at the Maison Fournaise.
In which painting did Pierre-Auguste Renoir depict friends sharing a meal on a balcony at the Maison Fournaise, overlooking the Seine? A small dog appears near the diners in the foreground.
This Armenian-Soviet composer drew on Armenian folk music and wrote the ballets *Gayane* and *Spartacus*. A lively episode from the first ballet became the famous “Sabre Dance.” Who was the composer?
Aram Khachaturian’s ballet set in an Armenian collective farm follows a young woman whose wedding is disrupted by a rival’s attack. What is the ballet from which the “Sabre Dance” was extracted?

Built on a strong, regular, accented pulse, this musical form was historically used to keep soldiers moving in step. It is now closely associated with military and wind bands; what is this form called?
This American bandleader, often nicknamed the “March King,” wrote enduring works such as “The Stars and Stripes Forever” and “Semper Fidelis.” What is his full name?

The second movement of this Beethoven symphony is a somber funeral march, followed by a scherzo and finale. Beethoven originally dedicated the work to Napoleon Bonaparte, but later withdrew the dedication; which symphony is it?
The third movement of this composer’s Piano Sonata No. 2 in B-flat minor is a famous funeral march marked Lento. Which Polish composer wrote the sonata?

Richard Wagner placed a large-scale funeral march near the end of this music drama, following Siegfried’s death and recalling themes associated with the hero. What is the title of the final opera in Wagner’s Ring cycle?
This celebrated Song-dynasty handscroll presents a sweeping springtime panorama of city life, including crowded streets, boats, and a prominent arched bridge. What is the painting called?
answer: Along the River During the Qingming Festival

question: In Along the River During the Qingming Festival, the arched Rainbow Bridge appears amid a bustling urban panorama painted by Zhang Zeduan. Which Northern Song capital does the handscroll depict?
What annual American theater honors recognize achievement in Broadway productions and performances and are named for actress and producer Antoinette Perry?
The Tony Awards are named in honor of this actress, director, and producer, who helped found the American Theatre Wing and served as its president. What name is she commonly known by?

In a standard sonata-form movement, this opening principal section introduces the main themes and often moves from the tonic toward a contrasting key. It comes before the section that develops and transforms those themes.
After the exposition and development in a sonata-form movement, which section brings back the principal themes, generally placing them in the tonic key?
What keyboard instrument uses keys to raise jacks whose plectra pluck strings, producing a bright, crisp sound? Prominent in Renaissance and Baroque music, it preceded the modern piano.
In Baroque music, the harpsichord often supplied chords beneath a melody, usually reinforced by a bass instrument. What is this accompanying practice called?
This English composer wrote *Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis* and *A Sea Symphony*, his first symphony, which sets poems by Walt Whitman. Who was he?
Ralph Vaughan Williams adapted poems from Walt Whitman’s *Leaves of Grass* for his first large-scale choral-orchestral work, which premiered in 1910. What title did he give it?
In Act II of a famous ballet about a girl’s Christmas Eve journey, this sovereign welcomes visitors to the Land of Sweets. Which character performs the grand solo associated with that realm?
The Sugar Plum Fairy appears in the second act of The Nutcracker, whose ballet premiere took place in St. Petersburg in 1892. Which Russian composer wrote its score?

Developed in Black communities in the United States during slavery, these Christian folk songs often draw on biblical stories and feature call-and-response and syncopated rhythms. The Fisk Jubilee Singers later helped bring them to concert audiences. What is this musical genre?

Which vocal ensemble, formed by students at a historically Black university in Nashville in 1871 to raise money for their school, helped introduce African-American spirituals to concert audiences through its tours?

Written in 1792 in Strasbourg by Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle as a call to arms for the Army of the Rhine, this song later became France’s national anthem. Tchaikovsky also used its melody to represent Napoleon’s invading forces in his 1812 Overture. What is the song?

In an 1880 orchestral work commemorating Russia’s victory over Napoleon, the composer uses La Marseillaise to represent the advancing French army. The overture’s title names the year of that invasion, and its climactic performance often includes cannon fire. Who composed it?

A small, two-panel English devotional altarpiece from the late fourteenth century shows a kneeling monarch on one side being presented by saints to Mary and the Christ Child on the other. What is this work commonly called?
In the Wilton Diptych, the kneeling monarch on the left wears a white-hart badge and is presented by three saints to the Virgin and Child. Which English king is depicted?
This German electronic musician composed much of the music associated with a block-building video game, including the tracks “Subwoofer Lullaby” and “Stal.” What name does he release his music under?

C418’s ambient tracks are associated with a sandbox game where players gather resources and build with cubic blocks, while hostile creepers can explode and damage their creations. What is the name of this game?

Which Italian High Renaissance painter and architect, born in Urbino, moved from Umbria through Florence to Rome and worked for two popes in his final years? He is traditionally named alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo as one of the period’s three great masters.

Raphael painted this large fresco for the Stanza della Segnatura in the Vatican’s Raphael Rooms. At its center, Plato points upward while Aristotle gestures toward the ground, surrounded by philosophers and mathematicians of antiquity; what is the work?

Which pope invited Raphael to Rome in 1508 and commissioned him to decorate apartments in the Vatican, including the rooms later associated with the artist? Often called the “Warrior Pope,” he also commissioned Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Auguste Rodin’s sculptural group depicts six prominent citizens of a French port city who offered themselves as hostages to end its 1347 siege by English forces. What is the title of this work?
Which French sculptor created The Burghers of Calais, the group portraying six citizens who volunteered as hostages during the Hundred Years’ War?

Taken by the Apollo 17 crew on their journey to the Moon in December 1972, this color photograph shows the fully illuminated Earth, with Africa and Antarctica visible against the darkness of space. What is this famous image commonly called?

The Blue Marble was photographed during a December 1972 lunar mission whose crew included Eugene Cernan, Ronald Evans, and Harrison Schmitt. It was the final mission to land astronauts on the Moon; what was its designation?

In this celebrated 17th-century Dutch work, a young woman turns toward the viewer against a nearly black background, wearing a blue-and-yellow head covering. Often classified as a tronie rather than a formal portrait, it is held by the Mauritshuis in The Hague. What is the painting?
Girl with a Pearl Earring is among the best-known works by which Delft-born Dutch Golden Age painter, whose other celebrated paintings include The Milkmaid and View of Delft?

A 1513 engraving shows an armored rider proceeding through a rugged landscape, accompanied by a rotting corpse holding an hourglass and a goat-headed figure carrying a halberd. What is the title of this print by Albrecht Dürer?

The artist behind Knight, Death, and the Devil also created the 1514 engraving Melencolia I, which shows a winged figure seated among geometric and carpentry tools. Which German Renaissance artist made these works?

This American choreographer studied at the Cornish School in Seattle and danced with Martha Graham’s company before founding his own dance company in 1953. His long artistic partnership with a composer helped introduce chance procedures into modern dance. Who was he?

A longtime collaborator of Merce Cunningham, this American composer used chance procedures in music and dance, including methods drawn from the I Ching. He also composed a famous work in which performers make no intentional sounds for four minutes and thirty-three seconds. Who was this composer?
In Western music, this key is built on D, and its key signature contains a single flat, B-flat. What is the key?

Johannes Ringk’s manuscript is the earliest known source for this famous organ work, catalogued as BWV 565. The work is in D minor and opens with a dramatic flourish followed by a descending passage and a sustained chord; what is its title?
answer: Toccata and Fugue in D minor

question: This dramatic legend adapts Goethe’s tale of a scholar who bargains with the devil and begins with the Rákóczi March, a melody associated with a Hungarian national hero. What is the title of the work?
La Damnation de Faust is a dramatic legend based on Goethe’s Faust and opens with the Rákóczi March. Which French composer wrote it, also known for Symphonie fantastique?

A French civil engineer designed a 300-meter iron lattice tower for the 1889 Exposition Universelle in Paris. Built on the Champ de Mars, it became one of the world’s most recognizable landmarks. Who was the engineer?

After the original engineer died, Auguste Bartholdi asked Gustave Eiffel to design the iron framework inside a colossal copper sculpture that France gave to the United States. What monument did the framework support?

Developing in the rural American South around the turn of the twentieth century, this African American genre drew on field hollers, work songs, spirituals, and string ballads. Its expressive vocals, bent pitches, and recurring harmonic patterns later influenced jazz, rock, and country music. What is the genre?
In Blues, a singer may deliver a phrase that is answered by a chorus or an instrument, echoing a practice found in field hollers and work songs. What term names this musical technique?

This performing art consists of selected or improvised rhythmic body movements, performed alone or in groups, and may express aesthetic or symbolic meaning with or without musical accompaniment. What is this art form?

Within Dance, ceremonial forms can express cultural identity. The All Blacks, New Zealand's national rugby union team, perform this Māori ritual before matches, marked by forceful movements and vocal calls. What is the performance called?

Dance can intersect with combat training in this Afro-Brazilian practice, which developed among enslaved Africans in Brazil and pairs rhythmic movement with music played on instruments such as the berimbau. What is the practice called?

Which mid-20th-century art movement drew on advertising, comic strips, product packaging, and celebrity imagery, treating mass-produced consumer culture as a subject for fine art? Its artists often borrowed the bold graphics and repetition of commercial media rather than relying on traditional academic subjects.
Within Pop Art, what 1963 Roy Lichtenstein diptych adapts a scene from a war comic, depicting a fighter jet launching a rocket at another plane, with the explosion narrated in a bold speech balloon?

This one-act opera follows the daughter of Agamemnon as she becomes consumed by the need to avenge his murder. Richard Strauss composed its music to a libretto by Hugo von Hofmannsthal; what is the opera’s title?

In Elektra, the forceful, highly dissonant score was written by the German composer who also collaborated with Hugo von Hofmannsthal on Der Rosenkavalier and composed the tone poem Also sprach Zarathustra. Who was the composer?
This Finnish composer wrote a seven-symphony cycle and the tone poem *Finlandia*, and drew on the *Kalevala* for works including *Kullervo* and *Tapiola*. Who is he?

Jean Sibelius based *Kullervo* and the *Lemminkäinen Suite* on stories from this Finnish national epic, assembled by Elias Lönnrot from oral poetry and first published in 1835. What is the epic called?
This French modernist composer wrote the piano collections Gymnopédies and Gnossiennes, known for their spare textures and unusual harmonies. He also collaborated with Jean Cocteau on a 1917 ballet.

Erik Satie composed the score for this 1917 ballet, created for Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes with a scenario by Jean Cocteau and designs by Pablo Picasso. Its Paris premiere caused a notorious disturbance.
The Rapa Nui people carved these monumental human figures from volcanic stone on Easter Island; a 2022 wildfire damaged some near Rano Raraku. What are these statues called?
Many moai were carved from volcanic tuff at the crater that served as Easter Island’s principal quarry, where unfinished figures remain. What is the name of this crater?
An Italian contemporary artist became widely known for a 2019 Art Basel work featuring a banana duct-taped to a wall. He also created America, an 18-karat-gold functioning toilet. Who is this artist?

Maurizio Cattelan’s 2019 Art Basel Miami Beach work consisted of a banana duct-taped to a gallery wall. Artist David Datuna later ate the fruit during an intervention he called a performance. What was the title of the work?
This building feature is an opening in a wall or roof, often fitted with glass, that admits daylight and may provide ventilation or a view. What is this architectural element called?

In some houses, this feature projects outward from the exterior wall, often with a central pane and angled side panes that create an interior alcove and views in several directions. What is this projecting arrangement of windows called?
What 1872 Claude Monet painting shows boats in a Normandy harbor at dawn, with an orange sun reflected on the water? Its title later gave its name to the movement most closely associated with Monet.
The harbor depicted in Impression, Sunrise is in which French port city in Normandy? Monet spent much of his early life there after his family moved from Paris.

A leading figure in the Young British Artists movement, this British contemporary artist created a work featuring a tiger shark preserved in formaldehyde. His art often confronts death and medicine; who is he?
Damien Hirst designed the cover for a 2021 album featuring rows of pregnant-woman emojis. The album includes “Way 2 Sexy” and “Knife Talk”; which Canadian rapper released it?

In Tchaikovsky’s ballet, Rothbart’s spell turns a princess into a white swan, and the role is conventionally performed by the same ballerina who dances the black-swan character Odile. What is the princess’s name?
Odette is the enchanted princess in this Tchaikovsky ballet, which premiered at Moscow’s Bolshoi Theatre in 1877. What is the ballet called?
Born in Figueres, Catalonia, this Spanish painter became a leading Surrealist and is famous for a 1931 canvas of limp clocks in a stark landscape. Who was he?
Salvador Dalí's best-known 1931 painting places soft watches across an arid landscape, including one draped over a branch and another across a distorted face. What is the title of this painting?
Salvador Dalí's wife, born Elena Ivanovna Diakonova, became his muse and is commonly known by what one-word name?
In a 1954 painting by Salvador Dalí, Christ is viewed from above, suspended over a bay on the cross-shaped net of a four-dimensional hypercube. What is the painting's established title?

Salvador Dalí's 1946 canvas for the Bel Ami International Art Competition shows a saint in a barren landscape as a rearing horse and long-legged elephants approach. What is the title of this painting?

Born in rural Romania in 1876, this sculptor settled in Paris in 1904 and became a pioneer of modern abstract sculpture. He created the Bird in Space series and designed the Târgu Jiu memorial ensemble for those who died defending the city during World War I.

In the 1937–38 Târgu Jiu memorial ensemble created by Constantin Brâncuși, this outdoor work rises in a stack of repeated rhomboid modules. It forms part of a memorial to those who died defending the city during World War I.
What is the name for a pitch system with a characteristic scale pattern organized around a final or tonic? Examples of these systems appear in Gregorian chant and jazz improvisation.

Which musical mode uses the same pitches as a natural minor scale except that its sixth degree is raised? On a piano, its notes are the white keys from D up to the next D, and jazz musicians often use it for improvisation.
