The Shenandoah River joins this larger river near Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. This river also flows past Washington, D.C., and is the largest river in the Chesapeake Bay watershed. What is it?
Which city is Iceland’s capital and most populous municipality, located on the country’s southwest coast? Its name means “Smoky Bay,” referring to steam rising from nearby hot springs.
In the traditional, unconfirmed account of Reykjavík’s settlement, which Norse figure is said to have chosen the site after pillars he cast into the sea came ashore?

Which historic region stretched along the Caribbean shore of present-day Honduras and Nicaragua? Britain once exercised significant influence there, including through a protectorate that ended in the 19th century.

On the Nicaraguan stretch of the Mosquito Coast, which Caribbean port became an important center of British trade and is now the capital of the South Caribbean Coast Autonomous Region? Its name is often linked to the Dutch privateer Abraham Blauvelt.
Named for its many small islands, this western Pacific region includes the Caroline, Gilbert, Mariana, and Marshall island groups. What is the region called?
Within Micronesia, the Federated States of Micronesia has its national government on the island of Pohnpei. What is the name of the country’s capital there?

This Alabama port city lies at the head of a namesake bay, where Interstate 10 meets Interstate 65. It is associated with one of the oldest Mardi Gras traditions in the United States; what city is it?
Mobile is situated beside a broad Gulf Coast estuary that receives the Mobile and Tensaw rivers and opens southward into the Gulf of Mexico. What is the name of this bay?
Which historic county and Celtic nation occupies England’s southwestern peninsula? Its western tip reaches the mainland’s most westerly point, and it is associated with Tristan in Arthurian legend.
At the far western tip of Cornwall, what granite headland is commonly identified as the westernmost point of mainland England?

What name is commonly given to Australia’s vast, sparsely populated interior, where cattle stations and jackaroos became defining features of rural life? The 1932 Emu War is also associated with this remote region.

At an Outback station, Banjo Paterson wrote a song about a swagman camping beside a billabong; its imagery also features a tucker bag and a sheep. What is this song, often regarded as an unofficial Australian anthem?

This east-central Canadian province is the country’s most populous and second-largest by area. It contains Toronto, its provincial capital, as well as the national capital chosen in 1857, and it borders four of the Great Lakes. What is this province?
In Ontario, which city was selected by Queen Victoria in 1857 as Canada’s capital? It is home to Parliament Hill and lies across a major river from Gatineau, Quebec.

This Mid-Atlantic commonwealth contains Philadelphia, its largest city, and Pittsburgh, its second-largest metropolitan center. Its capital lies between them, and the state borders six other U.S. states. What state is it?
Pennsylvania has no ocean coastline, but its northwestern shore meets a Great Lake that also borders Ohio and lies across the water from Ontario. Which lake is it?
Pennsylvania’s eastern edge follows a tidal river that runs past Philadelphia and forms much of the state’s boundary with New Jersey. What river is it?
In northeastern Pennsylvania, this Appalachian resort area is known for forested ridges, lakes, and ski destinations. What region is it?
Pennsylvania’s capital sits on the Susquehanna River in the south-central part of the state, between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. What is the capital city?

This country occupies South America’s northern Atlantic coast, with Georgetown as its capital and borders with Venezuela, Brazil, and Suriname. Its population reflects substantial South Asian, African, Indigenous, and European influences. What country is it?
Guyana’s eastern neighbor is separated from it in large part by the Corentyne River. Which country lies between Guyana and French Guiana?
This port city in southern Yemen occupies a volcanic peninsula and became a key British coaling station on the route to India after Britain seized it in 1839. What is the city?

Aden lies east of this narrow maritime chokepoint, through which vessels pass between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The strait separates Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula from Djibouti and Eritrea in Africa. What is it called?

Which New England state lies between New York and Rhode Island, with Massachusetts on its northern border and Long Island Sound to its south? Its capital is Hartford, and it became the fifth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution in 1788.

Which city in Connecticut has been the state’s sole capital since 1875? It stands on the state’s major south-flowing river and is associated with the oak tree where the colony’s charter was hidden from Governor Edmund Andros.
Which major port city in southern China, on the Pearl River, was known to Western traders as Canton and served as the principal center of the Qing-era foreign trade system?

During the Qing era, Guangzhou was the sole authorized port for most Western maritime trade, which was regulated by an official known as the Hoppo and conducted through licensed merchants. What was this restrictive trade arrangement called?
Which Central American country has the region’s largest Garifuna population and a long coastline along the Caribbean Sea? It fought El Salvador in the 1969 conflict known as the Soccer War.
Honduras has the largest Garifuna population, but in which neighboring Central American country is a substantial Garifuna community concentrated around the coastal town of Dangriga?
Which Spanish-speaking Caribbean country occupies the eastern part of Hispaniola and shares the island with Haiti? Its capital is Santo Domingo.
The Dominican Republic occupies the eastern portion of this Caribbean island, while Haiti occupies the western portion. What is the island called?

This Nordic island country occupies the North Atlantic between Europe and North America, and it straddles a boundary between two tectonic plates. Volcanoes, glaciers, geysers, and geothermal springs mark its landscape; what country has Reykjavík as its capital?

Iceland sits astride a submarine mountain chain formed where the North American and Eurasian plates move apart. This chain rises above sea level in a rift zone at Þingvellir National Park; what is it called?
Iceland’s capital and largest city stands on the southwestern coast beside Faxaflói Bay. It is also the country’s center of government and culture; what city is it?
The inhabited island of Grímsey lies north of Iceland’s mainland and is crossed by a major named latitude line. What is the line called?
Iceland’s high latitude might suggest a much colder climate than it has. Which warm Atlantic current is commonly cited for carrying heat toward the island and moderating its climate?

One of the two great rivers associated with Mesopotamia, this river rises in eastern Turkey’s Taurus Mountains and flows south into Iraq. It passes through the country’s capital before joining the Euphrates to form the Shatt al-Arab. What is the river’s name?
The Tigris River passes through Iraq’s capital, which was founded as an Abbasid capital in 762 CE under Caliph al-Mansur. What city is it?
What Egyptian capital lies on the Nile near the southern edge of its delta? It is the country’s largest city and a major political and cultural center of the Arab world.
Cairo stands on this river, which flows north through Egypt before spreading into a broad delta that meets the Mediterranean Sea. What is the river’s name?

This region of the North Atlantic has no land boundaries; its limits are defined by the currents of the subtropical gyre. Its floating seaweed mats shelter marine life and provide the breeding grounds where European eels spawn. What is this sea?

This catadromous fish spends much of its adult life in freshwater rivers and coastal waters, then migrates thousands of kilometers to reproduce in the Sargasso Sea. Its transparent, leaf-shaped larvae cross the Atlantic to reach rivers from Iceland and Norway south to North Africa. What species is it?

Enclosed entirely within Rome, this sovereign city-state is the world’s smallest country by area and serves as the seat of the pope and the headquarters of the Catholic Church. What is this independent state?
In Vatican City, what monumental plaza at the entrance to its principal basilica is framed by sweeping colonnades designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini and has an ancient Egyptian obelisk at its center?

At the heart of Beijing, this vast civic plaza lies directly south of the Forbidden City and is flanked by major state buildings. It became globally associated with the 1989 protests and a photograph of a lone man facing a column of tanks. What is this public space called?
A granite obelisk completed in 1958 stands at the center of Tiananmen Square and bears an inscription by Mao Zedong. What memorial honors those who died in China’s revolutionary struggles?
This is Europe's longest river, rising in western Russia and flowing southeast to the Caspian Sea. A canal also links its basin to the Don River.
The Volga River rises in this upland region of Tver Oblast, near the village of Volgoverkhovye. What is this source region called?

What is the name of the historic and present-day region in northwestern France that faces the English Channel, includes five departments today, and derives its name from the Norse phrase meaning “men of the North”?
In Normandy’s early history, what 911 agreement between Frankish king Charles the Simple and Viking leader Rollo established a territory that developed into the Duchy of Normandy?

At the southern tip of the world’s second-largest continent, this sovereign country has coastlines on both the Atlantic and Indian oceans and completely encloses the landlocked kingdom of Lesotho. What is the country’s natural name?

South Africa’s executive branch and national administration are based in this city, where the Union Buildings overlook the city. Unlike Cape Town, it is not the country’s legislative capital. What is the city?
South Africa completely surrounds this independent, mountainous kingdom, whose capital is Maseru and whose territory lies entirely above 1,000 meters in elevation. What country is it?
Along South Africa’s eastern highlands, this prominent highland chain forms part of the Great Escarpment and reaches its highest point at Thabana Ntlenyana in Lesotho. What is the range called?

South Africa’s first president elected in a nationwide multiracial election in 1994 was an anti-apartheid leader who spent 27 years in prison. He later wrote the autobiography Long Walk to Freedom. Who was he?

This autonomous community occupies Spain’s northeastern corner, stretching from the Pyrenees along the Mediterranean coast and bordering France and Andorra. Its capital is Barcelona, and its parliament and government exercise powers set out in a Statute of Autonomy. What region is it?

In Catalonia, what is the name of the institutions that include the region’s parliament, president, and government? Their powers and relationship with the Spanish state are set out in the region’s Statute of Autonomy.

Which Greek island, the largest of the Dodecanese and located near the coast of southwestern Turkey, was governed by the Knights Hospitaller until Ottoman forces captured it in 1522? The island is also traditionally associated with a monumental statue of Helios, counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

Erected on Rhodes in the 3rd century BCE after the island resisted a siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes, this enormous bronze statue honored the sun god Helios. It toppled in an earthquake several decades later; what was the statue called?
This North African country lies between Algeria and Libya and includes the island of Djerba in the Gulf of Gabès. It is also home to the ruins of a Phoenician city that became a major rival of Rome.

Near Tunis in Tunisia, this ancient Phoenician city became Rome’s chief rival in the Punic Wars. Its archaeological remains include the Baths of Antoninus, among the largest Roman bath complexes in Africa.

This South African city is Gauteng’s largest urban center and a major financial and commercial hub. In Alan Paton’s *Cry, the Beloved Country*, Stephen Kumalo travels there while searching for his son. What city is it?
What large township in southwestern Johannesburg takes its name from the initials of “South Western Townships” and became a focal point of the 1976 student uprising?

This Midwestern state entered the Union as the 21st state on December 3, 1818, and its capital moved from Kaskaskia to Vandalia before settling in Springfield. It is nicknamed the Prairie State and includes Chicago. What state is it?

In Illinois, the state capital has been located in this city since 1837, after earlier capitals at Kaskaskia and Vandalia. Abraham Lincoln also lived and pursued public life here before becoming president. Name the city.
What is the name of the Baltic Sea’s northern arm between Finland and Sweden, whose two main subdivisions are the Bothnian Bay and the Bothnian Sea?
Within the Gulf of Bothnia, what is the northernmost of its two principal subdivisions, lying north of the Kvarken strait and bordered by northern Sweden and Finland?
Which major city on South Africa’s southwestern coast is one of the country’s three capitals, alongside Pretoria and Bloemfontein? It is also the seat of the national legislature.
Cape Town is the seat of the national legislature. What is the institution called, given that its two chambers are the National Assembly and the National Council of Provinces?

This Midwestern state takes its name from a river whose name derives from a Seneca word often translated as “good river” or “great river.” It borders Lake Erie and five states, and Columbus is its capital; name the state.

In Ohio, a federally protected natural area follows a winding river through the gorge between Cleveland and Akron, with the historic Ohio & Erie Canal towpath running through it. What is its full name?
At the large U.S. military aviation base near Dayton, Ohio, this institution displays historic aircraft including the Memphis Belle and planes used by U.S. presidents. What is its full official name?
answer: National Museum of the United States Air Force

question: In Ohio’s Adams County, this ancient earthwork stretches roughly 1,300 feet along a ridge above Brush Creek. Its winding animal form includes an oval feature at one end; name the earthwork.

Rather than a single structure built at once, this northern Chinese defense network grew over many centuries and includes fortified barriers, watchtowers, forts, and passes. UNESCO’s listed system extends for more than 20,000 kilometers; what is it called?

Around 220 BCE, this Qin ruler linked some earlier northern frontier barriers into a broader system now known as the Great Wall of China. He unified the Warring States and was buried with the famous terracotta army; who was he?

What Polynesian archipelago in the central Pacific stretches about 1,500 miles and consists of volcanic peaks built up from the ocean floor? Its islands’ age pattern records the Pacific Plate moving northwest over a comparatively fixed source of magma.

Across the Hawaiian Islands, volcanic activity is concentrated at the southeastern end, while progressively older islands and submerged seamounts extend northwest. What relatively stationary mantle feature does the Pacific Plate move over to produce this age pattern?

Which city is Russia’s capital and largest city, situated on the Moskva River and known in Russian as Moskva? Its earliest written mention dates to 1147, and its historic core grew around a fortified center of government and religious life.

In Moscow, what fortified complex developed as a center of state and religious power and is described by UNESCO as the city’s oldest part? Its walls, towers, churches, and palaces stand beside Red Square in a World Heritage site.

This western South American country has a Pacific coastline and borders Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Bolivia, and Chile. Its varied landscapes include arid coastal plains, the Andes, and tropical rainforest in the Amazon Basin. What country is it?

In Peru, this extensive chain of high peaks follows South America's western edge, forming the continent's longest continuous cordillera. It divides the Pacific-facing coastal strip from the lower, wetter region drained by the Amazon. What is it called?
Shared by Peru and Bolivia, this large high-altitude lake lies in the Andes along their international border. It is commonly described as the world’s highest navigable lake. What is its name?
Peru’s capital and largest city lies on the country’s arid Pacific coast, near the mouth of the Rímac River. What city is it?
Which sovereign country in Western Europe borders France, the Netherlands, Germany, and Luxembourg? It became independent following a revolution in 1830 and adopted a constitution the next year.
Belgium’s capital is also one of the three official seats of European Union institutions. What city is it?
What vast, remarkably level expanse in northwestern Utah is famous for attempts to set land-speed records? It formed from mineral sediments left behind as a prehistoric lake receded.
The Bonneville Salt Flats formed from sediments left behind when what vast Ice Age lake receded? Its former waters covered much of present-day Utah.

Which southeastern U.S. state borders Tennessee to the north and Florida and the Gulf of Mexico to the south? Its major Civil Rights Movement sites include Birmingham, Selma, and Montgomery, where Rosa Parks’s arrest helped spark a bus boycott.
In Alabama, which city is the state capital and was the destination of the 1965 voting-rights marches that began in Selma? Rosa Parks’s 1955 arrest there helped spark a bus boycott.
This Japanese city served as the imperial capital from 794 until Emperor Meiji moved the court to Tokyo in 1868. Its historic landmarks include Kiyomizu-dera and the Gion district. What is the city?
Kyoto was established as Japan’s capital in 794 under Emperor Kanmu, with a grid-planned layout inspired by the Chinese capital Chang’an. What was the city originally called?
A long-distance hiking route through the eastern United States links Springer Mountain in Georgia with Mount Katahdin in Maine. What is this route called?
The Appalachian Trail ends at this mountain in Maine, its northern terminus and the state’s highest peak. What is the mountain’s name?

This medieval Gothic Catholic cathedral on the Seine’s Île de la Cité is renowned for its flying buttresses and rose windows. Its roof and spire were severely damaged in a major fire in 2019. What is its name?
Notre-Dame de Paris stands on an island in the Seine that is also home to the Sainte-Chapelle and the Palais de Justice. What is the island called?

This Pacific Northwest city sits on an isthmus between Puget Sound and Lake Washington, and the Space Needle was built there for the 1962 World's Fair. It is the most populous city in Washington State; name it.
Seattle is the largest city in this U.S. state, but Olympia is its capital; British Columbia lies along the state's northern border. What state is it?
Seattle and Tacoma border this large inlet, which connects to the Pacific Ocean through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and helps define Washington's Olympic Peninsula. What body of water is it?

The settlers who first landed at Alki Point in 1851 moved to the eastern shore of Elliott Bay the following year, helping establish the settlement that became Seattle. By what collective name is this founding group known?
This U.S. state is bordered by seven other states, including Virginia and Missouri, and its northern boundary largely follows the Ohio River. Its capital is Frankfort.
In Kentucky, this city hosts the annual Kentucky Derby at Churchill Downs and was the site of Breonna Taylor’s 2020 killing. It sits on the Ohio River across from southern Indiana.

In Washington, D.C., this neoclassical residence has served as the official home and workplace of U.S. presidents since John Adams moved in during 1800. What building is located at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue?
The White House complex includes the Oval Office and offices for the president’s senior staff in a section created during Theodore Roosevelt’s 1902 renovation. What is this section called?
Which named route links Moscow with Russia’s Far East, crossing Siberia and northern Asia on a major east-west corridor?
On the Trans-Siberian Railway, which Russian port city on the Sea of Japan serves as the eastern terminus and a major Pacific gateway?

At Prinsengracht 263 in Amsterdam, this historic site sheltered a Jewish teenager, her family, and four other Jewish people during the German occupation. She wrote much of her diary while in hiding there. What is the name of this museum and historic site?
At the Anne Frank House, one of Otto Frank’s trusted employees helped prepare and sustain the hiding place. Anne referred to him by the pseudonym Mr. Kraler in her diary; what was his real name?
Which major Israeli city sits on the Mediterranean coast and anchors the country’s largest metropolitan area? It is also a leading center of Israel’s technology sector.
Alongside Tel Aviv, this older port settlement forms the second half of the municipality’s name, often written with a hyphen. What is the settlement’s Hebrew name?

This federation on a peninsula in the Middle East consists of seven constituent states and has coasts on both the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Six states formed it in December 1971, and a seventh joined the following year. What country is it?
In the United Arab Emirates, this city is the country’s largest and is home to the Burj Khalifa, the world’s tallest skyscraper. What city is it?

Established in 1796 by surveyors for the Connecticut Land Company, this northeastern Ohio settlement stands on the southern shore of Lake Erie. It was incorporated as a city in 1836 and grew into a major port and industrial center. What city is it?

In Cleveland, the former dock-and-factory district called the Flats occupies low-lying land along this river. The waterway runs through the city to Lake Erie, and its channel helped support shipping and industry. What river is it?

This Essex County city was once a major colonial seaport and later became nationally associated with the 1692–1693 witch trials. It is also home to the Peabody Essex Museum, whose collections grew in part from the East India Marine Society. What is this city’s name?

At the Peabody Essex Museum in Salem, Massachusetts, a Qing-era merchant residence originally built in Anhui Province was dismantled, shipped to the United States, and reconstructed for visitors. What is the name of this historic house?
Which county on England’s southern coast contains the New Forest, where commoners have grazing rights for ponies, and gave its name to a U.S. state east of Vermont and southwest of Maine?
In Hampshire, which port city was the Titanic’s point of departure on its maiden voyage in April 1912? The city’s SeaCity Museum also explores its connection to the ship.

This city on the southern edge of Alaska’s Seward Peninsula became a boomtown after gold was discovered near Anvil Creek in 1898 and in nearby beach sands the following year. It is also the western finish city of the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race. What city is it?
Nome is a regional hub on the Seward Peninsula, where archaeological evidence shows people used the area long before the gold rush. What is the city’s local Iñupiaq name?

This landlocked country lies at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, with the Hindu Kush separating its northern and southwestern plains. It borders Pakistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and China; what country is it?
Afghanistan’s capital and largest city occupies a valley in the country’s east-central region, along the river that shares its name. Which city is this?
In Afghanistan, this mountain range separates the northern plains from the southwestern plains, and its passes include the route through the Salang Tunnel. What is the range called?

Afghanistan’s narrow northeastern strip runs between Tajikistan to the north and Pakistan to the south, reaching a short border with China in the Pamir Mountains. What is this strip of Afghan territory called?

This isolated volcanic massif in northern Tanzania rises to 5,895 metres, making it the highest mountain in Africa. Its three principal volcanic peaks are Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira; what mountain is it?
On Mount Kilimanjaro, which of its three principal volcanic peaks contains the 5,895-metre summit? It is higher than rugged Mawenzi and the plateau formed by the older, collapsed Shira cone.

Which 1962 American drama follows George and Martha as a late-night visit from the younger couple Nick and Honey turns into a series of psychologically charged party games? The four characters’ tense exchanges expose the fractures in the hosts’ marriage.
In Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, the playwright also wrote Seascape, which brings the human characters Nancy and Charlie into conversation with the reptiles Leslie and Sarah. Who wrote both plays?

Born in Yate, Gloucestershire, this British novelist created a seven-book fantasy saga set partly at Hogwarts. She also wrote detective novels featuring Cormoran Strike under the pen name Robert Galbraith. Who is this author?
J. K. Rowling's seven-novel fantasy series follows an orphaned boy who discovers his magical heritage, studies at Hogwarts, and battles the dark wizard Voldemort. What is the name of this series?

John Milton’s blank-verse epic opens with the subject of humanity’s first disobedience and follows the temptation of the first humans, their expulsion from Eden, and the poem’s effort to address divine justice. What is the title of this work?

The author of Paradise Lost also wrote the political prose work Areopagitica and the sonnet that begins by considering how his light is spent. Blind in later life, he served as Latin secretary to Oliver Cromwell. Who was this poet?

In Paradise Lost, this fallen angel leads a revolt in Heaven, is cast into Hell, and later enters Eden in disguise to tempt its inhabitants. He also declares that the mind can make its own Heaven or Hell. Who is this character?

In Paradise Lost, the fallen angels build this immense palace as their capital and gather there for a council after their defeat. Its name later became an English word for a scene of noisy confusion. What is the palace called?

The 1667 first publication of Paradise Lost was divided into ten books, but Milton later reshaped the poem into twelve books, following the form of a classical epic such as Virgil’s Aeneid. In what year did that revised twelve-book version appear?

In this Sophoclean tragedy, a Theban princess defies Creon’s decree by performing burial rites for her brother Polynices, whom the king has left unburied. Her act sets off a deadly conflict with the ruler. Name the play.

In Sophocles’ Antigone, this blind Theban prophet warns Creon that the gods reject his sacrifices while Polynices remains unburied, and foretells disaster for the king’s household. The same seer tells Oedipus that he killed Laius. Who is he?
What is the name of Aeschylus’s only surviving complete tragic trilogy, whose three plays trace Agamemnon’s murder, Orestes’ vengeance, and his trial at Athens?
In the Oresteia’s final play, which goddess establishes the court on the Areopagus to judge Orestes and casts the deciding vote when the jurors are evenly divided?
Born in New Albany, Mississippi, and raised in Oxford, this American modernist won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature. His fiction often returns to an imagined Mississippi county. Who was he?
William Faulkner based this fictional Mississippi setting on the real Lafayette region, where he lived for years, and returned to it in many of his works. What is the setting’s name?
William Faulkner’s 1929 novel, shortened from a manuscript titled *Flags in the Dust*, was the first published work set in his fictional county. What title did the novel appear under?
After moving to New Orleans, William Faulkner wrote this first novel, published in 1925, about a wounded aviator returning from World War I. What is the novel’s title?
In this William Faulkner novel, the Bundren family carries Addie’s coffin to Jefferson to fulfill her burial wish, and the story is told through multiple narrators. What is the title?

In this 2007 young-adult novel, Spokane teenager Arnold Spirit Jr. leaves his reservation school in Wellpinit to attend Reardan High School. The story includes his cartoons and his efforts to find a place between the two communities; what is the novel?
answer: The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian

question: The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian follows Arnold Spirit Jr. as he transfers from Wellpinit to Reardan High School. Who wrote the novel and the short-story collection The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven?
Published in 1937, this novel follows Janie Crawford from her youth through three marriages as she pursues love, independence, and self-realization in Florida. What novel by Zora Neale Hurston is it?

In Their Eyes Were Watching God, Janie returns to Eatonville after Tea Cake’s death and recounts her life story to a trusted friend who has brought her dinner and defended her against the townspeople’s gossip. Who is this friend?
Zora Neale Hurston completed Their Eyes Were Watching God in seven weeks while staying in this Caribbean nation, where she also conducted anthropological research. What country was she in?

This 1899 novella was first published as a three-part serial in Blackwood’s Magazine. Its frame narrative places a group of listeners aboard the Nellie as a sailor recounts a journey into central Africa to find an ivory trader. What is this novella?

In Heart of Darkness, this sailor narrates his journey up the Congo for a Belgian company after being hired to captain a steamer in Africa. He tells the story to listeners aboard the Nellie; what is his name?

In Heart of Darkness, the Belgian company’s African outposts evoke this historical territory, which King Leopold II initially held as his personal possession before Belgium annexed it. What was the territory called?

What Persian national epic by Ferdowsi recounts the legendary and historical rulers of Iran? Its tragic episodes include Rostam killing Sohrab in battle before discovering that the young warrior was his son.
The Shahnameh was composed by a Persian poet born in Tus, in Khorasan, who spent decades working on the epic and completed it around 1010 CE. Who was this poet?

Born in Charleville in 1854, this French poet wrote “The Drunken Boat” and Illuminations. After an intense poetic career of only a few years, he stopped writing and spent much of his later life traveling and working abroad. Who was he?
Arthur Rimbaud arranged the publication of only one of his books himself. Written in 1873, this prose-poetry work reflects a period of personal and spiritual crisis. What is its title?

In this Langston Hughes poem, the speaker says he is sent to eat in the kitchen when company comes, then asserts his place in the nation. It responds to Walt Whitman’s “I Hear America Singing.” What is the poem’s title?

In I, Too, Langston Hughes responds to this poet’s “I Hear America Singing” with a speaker who insists on African American inclusion in the national identity. This 19th-century poet also wrote Leaves of Grass. Who is he?

Which English Catholic writer created the priest-detective Father Brown and wrote a novel about an anarchist council whose members are secretly police officers? His other works include *The Everlasting Man*.

G. K. Chesterton’s 1908 novel follows poet Gabriel Syme as he joins a secret police force to infiltrate an anarchist council whose members are identified by the days of the week. What is the novel’s title?

In the Old English epic, this monstrous outsider repeatedly raids King Hrothgar’s hall, killing and eating the Danes. The poem links him to Cain’s lineage, and Beowulf mortally wounds him by tearing off one of his arms. Who is this antagonist?

In Beowulf, King Hrothgar’s great mead-hall is where his people gather before Grendel’s repeated attacks. Beowulf confronts the monster in this hall, whose name is associated with a hart. What is the hall called?

In Stephen King's 1974 horror novel, a bullied high-school student discovers she can move objects with her mind. After classmates humiliate her at prom by dousing her with pig's blood, she unleashes her powers on the town; what is the student's name?
Carrie White is the telekinetic student at the center of a 1974 horror novel set in the fictional Maine town of Chamberlain. Which American author wrote it and also wrote The Shining?

Which Peruvian novelist and essayist won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Literature, wrote *Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter*, and fictionalized the final days of Rafael Trujillo in *The Feast of the Goat*? He was also a prominent literary rival of Gabriel García Márquez.

In Mario Vargas Llosa’s historical novel, an exiled woman returns to the Dominican Republic, while the story revisits the final days of the Trujillo regime. What is the title of the novel that fictionalizes the dictator’s assassination?

A late-seventeenth-century French author and collector transformed oral folktales into literary fairy tales, including versions of “Cinderella,” “Sleeping Beauty,” and “Little Red Riding Hood.” Who was this writer?
In Charles Perrault’s version of this tale, a girl carrying food to her grandmother meets a wolf, and both are eaten. What tale is it?
The British Victorian novelist who wrote Middlemarch and The Mill on the Floss published her fiction under a pseudonym rather than her birth name. What name did she use?
George Eliot's novel follows Maggie and Tom Tulliver, whose family struggles with debt near the River Floss; years later, a flood brings the siblings together again. What is the novel's title?
What is the name of the experimental literary practice that treats search-engine output as found language, often retaining accidental or awkward phrases and recombining them into poems?

Flarf poetry’s use of found language has a precedent in an early 20th-century avant-garde movement associated with collage and the cut-up technique. What movement included figures such as Hugo Ball and Tristan Tzara and is said to take its name from a French word for “hobbyhorse”?
Which 1726 satirical prose work follows an English ship’s surgeon and captain on voyages to tiny Lilliput, giant-inhabited Brobdingnag, and other imaginary societies?
In Gulliver’s Travels, who is the English surgeon and sea captain whose first-person account recounts visits to tiny islanders, giants, and an airborne scholarly society?
In Gulliver’s Travels, what country does the traveler reach after being abandoned by his companions, where the inhabitants are enormous relative to him and a farmer exhibits him for money?
In Gulliver’s Travels, what flying island is inhabited by intellectuals so absorbed in abstractions that servants called flappers tap them to get their attention?
In Gulliver’s Travels, what is the name of the rational, articulate horses whose orderly society contrasts with the brutish Yahoos?

Edgar Allan Poe’s Gothic short story follows an unnamed visitor to a decaying ancestral estate, where its owner and his twin sister are caught in a fearful sequence of illness, premature burial, and disaster. What is the story’s title?
answer: The Fall of the House of Usher

question: In The Fall of the House of Usher, the unnamed narrator visits a childhood companion whose letter describes his nervous illness and whose twin sister is Madeline. Which Usher sibling welcomes the narrator to the mansion and performs music as his condition worsens?

In Victor Hugo’s 1862 novel, this police officer rises from prison guard to relentless pursuer of Jean Valjean after Valjean breaks parole. His rigid belief that the law admits no exceptions leads to a crisis when Valjean spares his life. What character is described?
Inspector Javert pursues Jean Valjean throughout this 1862 novel by Victor Hugo, which also follows Valjean’s efforts to raise Cosette amid upheavals in France. What is the novel?
Inspector Javert is arrested as a suspected spy by student insurgents manning Paris barricades during this 1832 uprising, which forms the historical backdrop to the novel. What is this revolt called?

In Jane Austen’s novel, this witty, detached father of five daughters calls his wife’s repeatedly mentioned nerves his “old friends.” He also jokes that he would disown Elizabeth if she married the pompous clergyman who proposed to her. Who is he?

In the novel featuring Mr. Bennet, Elizabeth initially refuses a wealthy landowner whose first marriage proposal criticizes her family, but accepts his later proposal after learning of his help to her sister. What is the title of the novel?

Which Shakespeare play intertwines a bond demanding a pound of flesh from a Venetian debtor with his friend’s courtship of an heiress who must choose among three caskets? The drama is also widely discussed for its depiction of Jewish-Christian prejudice.
In The Merchant of Venice, which wealthy heiress disguises herself as a young male legal scholar called Balthazar and argues before the Duke that the bond permits no blood to be shed?
Which Wallace Stevens poem begins with houses haunted by white night-gowns and ends with an old sailor asleep in his boots who catches tigers in red weather?

In “Disillusionment of Ten O’Clock,” the contrast between ordinary domestic life and imaginative visions comes from the work of which American poet, who also wrote “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird”?
Peter Carey’s novel follows literary editor Christopher Chubb as he confronts the consequences of promoting a poet who was invented as part of a literary hoax. What is the novel’s title?

In *My Life as a Fake*, Carey draws on a famous Australian literary hoax in which two poets invented a modernist writer whose poems appeared in the journal *Angry Penguins*. What name did they give their fictional poet?

Born in 1856 in Chittenango, New York, this American author published a fantasy about a Kansas girl and a magical land in 1900, then wrote thirteen sequels. He also used the pseudonym Edith Van Dyne. Who was he?

In L. Frank Baum’s 1900 children’s fantasy, a cyclone carries Dorothy from Kansas to a land where she befriends a scarecrow, a tin woodman, and a lion. The companions follow a yellow-brick road to seek help from the land’s ruler. What is the novel’s title?
What 1928 Virginia Woolf novel follows an English noble who lives for centuries, changes from male to female, and moves through successive historical eras?
Virginia Woolf drew the central figure of Orlando: A Biography from this close friend and lover, a poet and novelist whose family owned the country estate Knole. Who was this writer?

In this Arthur Miller drama, an Ohio manufacturer faces the consequences of allowing defective aircraft engine parts to be shipped during World War II, causing the deaths of 21 pilots. A surviving member of his family presses him to confront his responsibility to the dead and their families. What is the play’s title?

In All My Sons, which factory owner authorized the shipment of defective aircraft parts during World War II and initially allowed his business partner to take the blame? His son Chris eventually forces him to face the deaths of the pilots.

Which American novelist and essayist, born in Ithaca in 1962 and raised in Illinois, studied philosophy and English at Amherst College, where his senior English thesis became his first novel? His best-known novel pairs a tennis academy with a halfway house for people recovering from addiction.

David Foster Wallace's final novel remained unfinished at his death and was published posthumously in 2011. Set largely at an Internal Revenue Service examination center and focused on the workers who audit tax returns, what is the novel's title?

This 1925 modernist novel follows Clarissa through postwar London as she prepares to host an evening party. Its shifting narration connects her memories with the experiences of a traumatized veteran over the course of a single day; name the novel.
The author of Mrs Dalloway also wrote To the Lighthouse and argued in A Room of One’s Own that women need money and a room of their own to write fiction. Who was this British modernist writer?

In Mrs Dalloway, a former soldier walks through Regent’s Park with his Italian wife, Rezia, while seeing his dead wartime officer Evans. Later, fearing that doctors will take him away, he jumps from a window; what is the veteran’s name?
Virginia Woolf developed Mrs Dalloway under a different working title before the novel appeared in 1925. What was the title used during its composition?

This epic novel interweaves the lives of Russian aristocratic families with philosophical reflections on history, set against Napoleon’s 1812 invasion of Russia. What is the work commonly titled in English?
War and Peace was written by a Russian novelist who also wrote Anna Karenina and often combined intimate family stories with questions about morality and history. Who was this author?
Before the complete 1869 publication of War and Peace, Tolstoy serialized an earlier version in The Russian Messenger from 1865 to 1867. What title did he give that version?
War and Peace first appeared in an earlier serialized version titled The Year 1805, published from 1865 to 1867 in a prominent literary periodical. What was that periodical called?

In War and Peace, Napoleon’s Grande Armée faced Kutuzov’s Russian forces in this major 1812 battle west of Moscow. Tolstoy depicts the clash as a chaotic encounter that challenges grand claims about military command. What battle was it?
In this story, a Bible seller trades a Wycliffe Bible for a volume with seemingly endless pages. Once a page is turned, it cannot be found again; what is the story’s title?
The Book of Sand is a short story by which Argentine writer, also known for “The Aleph” and “The Garden of Forking Paths”?

In this sonnet by Percy Bysshe Shelley, a traveler describes a shattered statue standing in a barren desert. Its pedestal bears a boastful command to the mighty, though only empty sands remain around it. What is the poem’s title?
Ozymandias is a sonnet by this English Romantic poet, who also wrote “Mont Blanc” and married the author of Frankenstein. Who is the poet?

In a Kate Chopin short story, a sudden downpour sends a former lover seeking shelter at a married woman’s Louisiana home while her husband and young son are away. The weather clears after the pair rekindle their intimacy, and the story ends by observing that everyone is happy. What is the story called?

In The Storm, Calixta is sewing at home when a former lover arrives to escape the approaching downpour. He stays with her while Bobinot and Bibi wait out the weather at Friedheimer’s store. What is the visitor’s name?

Written in prison by the late Roman statesman Boethius, this dialogue presents its author’s despair in a conversation with a woman who personifies wisdom. Through poetry and argument, she considers fortune, providence, and human freedom. What work is this?

The Consolation of Philosophy was written while its author was imprisoned after falling out of favor with the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. What sixth-century Roman statesman and philosopher appears as the dialogue’s imprisoned speaker?

Published in two volumes in 1852, this American antislavery novel follows an enslaved man whose experiences expose the violence of slavery and whose Christian faith remains central to the story. Its enormous readership helped strengthen abolitionist feeling before the Civil War; name the novel.
The author of Uncle Tom's Cabin was an active abolitionist, taught at Hartford Female Seminary, and came from a prominent religious family in nineteenth-century New England. What was her name?

In Uncle Tom's Cabin, this brutal plantation owner takes possession of Tom after the St. Clare household is broken up and orders him beaten. Name the enslaver whose cruelty drives the novel's final tragedy.
In Uncle Tom's Cabin, this enslaved mother flees the Shelby household with her young son rather than allow him to be sold, making a dramatic crossing over ice on the Ohio River. Identify her.

Uncle Tom's Cabin and Richard Wright's Native Son are discussed in the essay “Everybody's Protest Novel,” which criticizes the conventions and effects of protest fiction. Name the American writer who published that essay.

Published in 2012, this John Green novel is narrated by Hazel Grace Lancaster, a teenager with thyroid cancer that has spread to her lungs. At a support group, she meets Augustus Waters, a teenager who survived osteosarcoma, and the two fall in love. What is the novel?
The title of The Fault in Our Stars draws on a speech in this Shakespeare play, where Cassius tells Brutus that people—not fate or the stars—are responsible for their circumstances. What is the play?
The Fault in Our Stars is dedicated to this teenager, whose experience with thyroid cancer helped inspire John Green and who died in 2010 at age 16. Who is she?

This Roman poet wrote the didactic Ars Amatoria and a fifteen-book mythological narrative that begins with the creation of the world. Augustus later banished him to Tomis on the Black Sea; identify the poet.
Ovid composed this Latin narrative poem in fifteen books, tracing transformations in myth from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar. What is the title of the work?

In George Orwell’s farm allegory, which group takes charge of organizing the rebellion and then reserves the milk and windfall apples for itself? As the animals’ ruling class, it comes to embody revolutionary leaders whose pursuit of privilege hardens into dictatorship.

Among the pigs in Animal Farm, which silver-tongued spokesman repeatedly explains away changes to the commandments and assures the other animals that Napoleon’s rule benefits them? His polished rhetoric and selective claims make him the regime’s chief propagandist.

William Blake arranged this illuminated poetry collection in two contrasting sections: one presents childlike faith, while the other confronts suffering and corruption. Its poems include a gentle speaker asking about a lamb and a vision of a tiger’s “fearful symmetry.” What is the collection called?
answer: Songs of Innocence and of Experience

question: In Songs of Innocence and of Experience, the poet sets the trusting voice of “The Lamb” beside the awe-struck questions of “The Tyger,” using paired poems to explore contrasting human states. Who created this illuminated collection and wrote both poems?

John Gardner’s 1971 novel retells the Beowulf story from the perspective of the monster who terrorizes Hrothgar’s hall. Its narrator reflects on his encounters with the Danes, a dragon, and the power of storytelling. What is the title of the novel?

In Grendel, this blind court poet turns the Danes’ history into heroic songs, giving their violence a grand and meaningful shape. His music briefly draws the monster toward the human world. What is this character called?

In Eoin Colfer’s fantasy series, this young Irish heir uses his exceptional intellect to scheme against the hidden fairy world. In the first novel, he abducts an elf police officer and demands a ransom in gold; what is his full name?

In the first Artemis Fowl novel, Artemis Fowl II kidnaps a member of the Lower Elements Police to obtain a ransom of gold. What is the name of the LEPrecon captain whose capture sets the story’s central conflict in motion?
At a banquet hosted by Agathon, Socrates and other guests take turns praising Eros, and the late-arriving Alcibiades instead praises Socrates. What Platonic dialogue is framed by this gathering?
In the Symposium, which Athenian comic playwright explains desire through a myth in which Zeus split originally double-bodied humans, leaving them longing for their other halves?

In Louisa May Alcott’s Civil War-era story, this New England household is followed as four daughters with sharply contrasting temperaments grow from girlhood toward adulthood. One sister yearns for independence, while another is devoted to home and family; what is the family’s name?

In the March family’s story, the sisters use an earlier religious allegory about a traveler’s journey from the City of Destruction toward salvation. As children, they pretend their cellar is that city; what is the work’s title?

In Tennessee Williams’s tragedy, a former schoolteacher arrives in New Orleans from Laurel, Mississippi, to stay with her sister. She tries to preserve an image of gentility while hiding her age and avoiding bright light. Who is this tragic protagonist?
In *A Streetcar Named Desire*, Blanche DuBois comes to New Orleans to stay with her younger sister, who shares a cramped French Quarter apartment with her husband. What is her sister’s name?

Which Alexander Pope mock-epic poem portrays a goddess and her agents spreading stupidity, decay, and tastelessness across Britain? In its 1742 version, Colley Cibber replaced Lewis Theobald as the poem’s hero.
In Alexander Pope’s mock-epic The Dunciad, what personified goddess presides over the forces spreading stupidity and bad taste through Britain?
In this W. H. Auden poem, the speaker says the Old Masters understood suffering and describes ordinary life carrying on as a boy falls from the sky into the sea. What is the poem’s title?
In Musée des Beaux Arts, Auden describes a ship sailing calmly on while a boy falls into the sea. Which Flemish painter created the landscape painting that inspired this scene?

In this Shakespeare tragedy, a celebrated Scottish general receives a prophecy that he will become king and, urged on by his wife, murders his visiting monarch. At the end, soldiers conceal themselves with branches from Birnam Wood as Macduff confronts the usurper at Dunsinane. What is the play?

In Macbeth, three supernatural figures meet the returning general on a heath and hail him successively as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and future king. What name is commonly given to this prophetic trio?

In Macbeth, the title character’s wife initially mocks his fear and invokes spirits to harden herself before Duncan’s murder. Later, she walks in her sleep, rubbing at an imagined stain as she relives the crime; who is she?

In Macbeth, this Thane of Fife joins Malcolm’s forces against the tyrant after fleeing to England, and ultimately kills the ruler at Dunsinane. The witches’ assurance about no one born of a woman cannot protect the king from this nobleman, who was delivered by Caesarean section. Who is he?

In Macbeth, the monarch slain while a guest at Inverness is described as gracious and beloved; his sons Malcolm and Donalbain escape after discovering his body. Identify this Scottish king whose death sets the central usurpation in motion.
This American novelist created the A Song of Ice and Fire fantasy novels and also helped develop the mythology for FromSoftware’s 2022 game Elden Ring. What is his name?

George R. R. Martin helped create the history and setting for this 2022 FromSoftware role-playing game. Its Tarnished journey through the Lands Between and battle demigods in an attempt to repair a shattered source of power. What is the game’s title?

Edgar Allan Poe's tale is recounted long after a revenge committed during Carnival in an unnamed Italian city. Its narrator lures his rival into family catacombs with the promise of a rare sherry, then seals him behind a wall; what is the story's title?

In The Cask of Amontillado, a wine enthusiast attends Carnival dressed as a jester and follows Montresor into the family vaults after hearing there may be a prized cask below. What is the name of the man Montresor chains and walls in?
The Cask of Amontillado first appeared in the November 1846 issue of a U.S. periodical known for literature and fashion content. What was the magazine called?

This English novelist studied English literature at Balliol College, Oxford, and wrote a famous dystopia in which citizens take soma and worship Henry Ford. Which writer also authored Point Counter Point?

Aldous Huxley's 1932 dystopian novel depicts a future society divided into castes from Alpha to Epsilon, where people are conditioned from birth. What novel features John the Savage's confrontation with Mustapha Mond over the right to be unhappy?

Aldous Huxley's 1954 book recounts his experience with mescaline and considers whether the mind filters a wider reality. It takes its title from an idea in William Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell; what is the book?

Aldous Huxley's final novel contrasts a troubled outside world with Pala, a secluded society combining Buddhist practices, scientific medicine, and communal education. What is this 1962 utopian novel?

Which 2003 debut novel by Khaled Hosseini follows Amir from childhood in Kabul to adulthood in the United States, then back to Afghanistan as he tries to make amends for a betrayal of his closest childhood companion? Its childhood plot includes a Kabul contest in which participants sever opponents’ strings and children race to retrieve the fallen prizes.
In The Kite Runner, which boy is Ali’s son and Amir’s loyal childhood companion? After Amir wins a kite tournament in Kabul, he runs to retrieve the last cut kite for Amir.

First published in 1807 under its opening line, this poem was expanded from three six-line stanzas to four in an 1815 revision. Its speaker sees golden daffodils beside a lake and later finds pleasure in recalling them through the mind’s inward eye. What poem is it?
answer: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

question: In I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, Wordsworth’s remembered landscape drew on a 1802 walk with his sister Dorothy, whose journal recorded the daffodils beside the water. What lake in England’s Lake District was the setting of their sighting?
In Jane Austen’s novel, which witty second daughter of a gentleman is insulted by Mr. Darcy’s first impression of her, rejects his initial proposal, and eventually marries him?

In the novel centered on Elizabeth Bennet, wealthy bachelor Charles Bingley rents Netherfield, while his friend Darcy makes a disastrous first proposal and Lydia elopes with George Wickham. What is the title of this Jane Austen novel?

Which 1929 essay by Virginia Woolf grew out of lectures delivered at women’s colleges in Cambridge? Its first-person speaker moves between Oxbridge and the fictional women’s college Fernham while tracing how education, income, and privacy shape women’s opportunities to write fiction.
In A Room of One’s Own, Woolf’s first-person speaker treats her identity as unimportant and supplies several interchangeable names for herself. What two-word name appears first in that list?
What collective name identifies the married Victorian English poets in which the wife wrote a celebrated sequence of love sonnets and the husband became known for dramatic monologues?

Among works by The Brownings, Robert’s dramatic monologue features a duke showing an emissary a portrait of his deceased wife while revealing his possessiveness and the circumstances of her death. Name this poem.
A 1962 poem by Sylvia Plath dramatizes a speaker’s repeated survival after suicide attempts as a public spectacle. It was later included in her posthumous collection Ariel; what is the poem’s title?
Lady Lazarus first appeared in a collection published in 1965, two years after Plath’s death. What is the title of that collection?
The poet behind Lady Lazarus also wrote Daddy, whose speaker recalls a father figure through imagery associated with Nazi Germany. Who was this American poet associated with confessional writing?
In Jeff Kinney’s children’s series, this popular student is Greg Heffley’s main love interest. When Greg introduces himself, she asks whether his name is “Fregley.” Which character is she?
Holly Hills appears in a series by Jeff Kinney whose protagonist is Greg Heffley. Its installments include *Dog Days* and *Cabin Fever*. What is the title of the series?

In this 1865 fantasy novel, a girl follows a hurried White Rabbit underground and enters a world where she meets the Cheshire Cat and attends a tea party with the Mad Hatter. What is the title of Lewis Carroll’s book?
The original edition of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland featured 42 wood-engraved illustrations by this British artist. He was also a longtime cartoonist for the magazine Punch; who was he?
The author credited as Lewis Carroll on Alice's Adventures in Wonderland was an Oxford mathematician and logician who wrote under a pen name. What was his full birth name?

This folkloric storyteller is closely associated with traditional nursery rhymes and fairy tales. Illustrations often portray the figure as either a kindly grandmother or a maternal bird; what is the figure’s natural name?

The Mother Goose collection published in 1697 under the French title *Histoires ou contes du temps passé* includes literary versions of “Sleeping Beauty” and “Puss in Boots.” Which French writer assembled and published it?
In this Victorian science-fiction novel, a traveler journeys to the year 802,701 and encounters the gentle Eloi and the underground-dwelling Morlocks. What is the novel’s title?
The Time Machine was written by the English author who also created the invading Martians in The War of the Worlds and the island setting of The Island of Doctor Moreau. Who was this author?

Which English Renaissance playwright, poet, and actor was born around 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon and is traditionally credited with a dramatic canon that includes tragedies, comedies, and histories? He also wrote 154 sonnets and is often called the Bard of Avon.

In 1623, what posthumous collected edition of William Shakespeare’s plays was published by fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell? It contains 36 plays and helped preserve works that had not previously appeared in print.
William Shakespeare was born and raised in which Warwickshire town, a historic market town in the county? The town is also the place where he married Anne Hathaway at age 18.

In which Shakespeare play does the exiled Duke Prospero use magic to bring a ship carrying his brother Antonio and the King of Naples to an island? The island is also home to Prospero’s daughter Miranda, the spirit Ariel, and the enslaved Caliban.

Which Shakespeare play features two sets of separated identical twins: brothers both named Antipholus and their servants both named Dromio? Their mistaken identities cause a series of escalating mix-ups in Ephesus.

In Victor Hugo’s *Les Misérables*, this young nobleman and student becomes involved with a group of republican students during the lead-up to the June Rebellion. He falls in love with Cosette and eventually marries her. Who is he?
In *Les Misérables*, Marius Pontmercy joins this circle of Parisian republicans led by Enjolras, whose members make a stand at the barricade during the 1832 uprising. What is the group called?

First published in the United States in 1964, this children’s novel follows a poor boy who finds a Golden Ticket and tours the secretive confectionery works of the eccentric chocolatier Willy Wonka. What is the title of this Roald Dahl book?
The author of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory also wrote Matilda and The BFG, and recounted his wartime experiences in the memoir Going Solo. Who was this British writer?

Published in 1972 as the sequel to Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, this novel sends Charlie, Willy Wonka, and the Bucket grandparents soaring into orbit in a towering transparent capsule, where they encounter the Space Hotel USA. What is its title?
answer: Charlie and the Great Glass Elevator

question: Unlike a metaphor that treats one thing as another, this figure of speech explicitly compares two unlike things, typically using words such as “like” or “as.” What is it?

In ancient epic, a poet may pause the action to develop an elaborate comparison over several lines, often using familiar natural or domestic imagery to illuminate a heroic scene. What is the traditional name for this extended epic form of simile?

This impoverished Petersburg copying clerk spends his days transcribing documents and saves for a replacement garment after a tailor declares his old one beyond repair. Soon after obtaining it, he is robbed of it, and his attempt to seek help from a high-ranking official ends in humiliation.

Akaky Akakievich Bashmachkin is the protagonist of a celebrated Russian short story named for the garment he saves to buy, only to have it stolen soon afterward. Who wrote this story, as well as the novel *Dead Souls*?

Suzanne Collins’s three-book dystopian sequence follows a girl from District 12 who volunteers to take her younger sister’s place in a televised fight to the death, then becomes a symbol of resistance against Panem’s Capitol. What trilogy is this?
In The Hunger Games trilogy, which District 12 tribute volunteers to take her younger sister’s place in the arena, becomes a face of the rebellion, and is known for her skill with a bow?

In Harper Lee’s novel, Mayella Ewell accuses a Black farmhand of rape, and the defendant is represented by Scout and Jem Finch’s father. Testimony about the defendant’s badly injured left arm undermines the accusation, although the jury convicts him; what fictional courtroom proceeding is this?

During the Trial of Tom Robinson, which lawyer represents the accused and cross-examines Mayella Ewell about the injuries on the right side of her face? He is Scout and Jem’s father and argues that the defendant’s unusable left arm makes her account implausible.
Which American children's author wrote a debut novel about Opal Buloni and the stray dog she finds in Naomi, Florida, and later created a mouse hero named Despereaux?
Kate DiCamillo’s 2003 fantasy novel follows a large-eared mouse who is sent to the dungeon after speaking to Princess Pea. What is the book’s title?

Created and illustrated by Jeff Kinney, this children’s novel series presents Greg Heffley’s middle-school troubles as journal entries paired with cartoons. Its installments include Dog Days and Cabin Fever.
In Diary of a Wimpy Kid, which character is Greg’s older brother and the drummer and founder of the band Löded Diper? He drives a van bearing the band’s name and often torments Greg.

Published in 1820 as part of a collection attributed to Geoffrey Crayon, this American tale follows a village schoolmaster and ends with a nighttime pursuit by a rider without a head. What is the story’s title?
The Legend of Sleepy Hollow appeared in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., a collection its creator wrote while living in Birmingham, England. Which American author wrote the story?

In The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, this lanky, superstitious schoolmaster teaches in a rural Dutch settlement and courts the daughter of a prosperous farmer. He vanishes after a nighttime ride home from a harvest gathering. What is his name?

In The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, this wealthy farmer’s daughter draws the attention of both the local schoolmaster and a boisterous rival nicknamed Bones. She eventually marries the rival. What is her name?

In The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, local lore identifies this spectral rider as a Hessian soldier who lost his head to a cannonball during the Revolutionary War. What figure terrifies the schoolmaster on a nighttime ride?

Born in Lima in 1942 to Chilean parents and raised mostly in Chile, this novelist went into exile in Venezuela following Chile’s 1973 military coup. A letter she began to her dying grandfather in exile became the basis for her 1982 debut novel. Who is this author of *Eva Luna* and *Daughter of Fortune*?

Isabel Allende’s first novel grew from a letter she began to her dying grandfather while living in exile in Caracas. Published in 1982, it follows generations of the Trueba family amid Chilean political upheaval and supernatural events. What novel is it?

This American author created a wordplay-rich children’s fantasy in which Milo travels through a tollbooth into the Kingdom of Wisdom, meeting the watchdog Tock and the princesses Rhyme and Reason. Who is this author?
Norton Juster’s best-known children’s fantasy follows Milo into the Kingdom of Wisdom, where he helps rescue two imprisoned princesses from the Mountains of Ignorance. What is this novel called?

This 1914 short-story collection by James Joyce is arranged in four stages of life: childhood, adolescence, maturity, and public life. It concludes with a story whose closing image is snow falling across Ireland. What is the collection called?
In Dubliners, which final story follows Gabriel Conroy at the Morkan sisters’ annual dance, where a song leads his wife Gretta to recall Michael Furey?

This metaphysical poem describes two lovers parting without outward grief because their bond transcends physical distance. It compares their souls to the legs of a compass, with one leg leaning toward the other as they separate. Name the poem.
The author of A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning also wrote “The Flea” and the Holy Sonnet “Death, be not proud.” He later served as Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral in London. Name this poet.

An Alexandrian poet, he wrote “Ithaka,” whose speaker hopes for a long journey, and “Waiting for the Barbarians,” in which the barbarians’ arrival seems to offer a kind of solution. Who was this poet?
Constantine Cavafy wrote in the modern form of this language, whose ancient form Sophocles used for Oedipus Rex. What language was it?

This unfinished German-language modernist novel follows a bank officer who is arrested without being told the charge and finds the court system inaccessible. Written in 1914–15 and published posthumously in 1925, it ends with its protagonist’s execution; what is the novel’s natural title?

In The Trial, this bank officer is awakened by guards who announce his arrest but never explain the accusation. He encounters the court in hidden attic rooms and is eventually executed; what is his name?

A traveling salesman wakes after a night of uneasy dreams to find himself transformed into a monstrous vermin, and his family struggles to adapt to the change. What 1915 novella by Franz Kafka tells this story?
In The Metamorphosis, the traveling salesman whose transformation keeps him from going to work is later wounded when his father throws an apple at him. What is this protagonist’s name?

In The Metamorphosis, the protagonist’s sister initially brings him food and later plays violin for the family’s lodgers. She eventually insists that the family can no longer live with him. What is her name?
The Metamorphosis first appeared in October 1915 in a literary journal edited by René Schickele. What was the journal’s German title?
The Metamorphosis received its first book publication in December 1915 as part of a series edited by Kurt Wolff. What was the series called?

This American novelist wrote The Kitchen God's Wife and The Bonesetter's Daughter. Her debut novel explores the relationships and memories of Chinese immigrant mothers and their American-born daughters. Who is she?
Amy Tan's 1989 debut novel connects the stories of four Chinese immigrant mothers and their American daughters. Its four sections each open with a Chinese fable; what is the novel's title?

Born on Long Island in 1819, this American poet worked as a journalist and government clerk and spent part of the Civil War caring for wounded soldiers in Washington hospitals. He became especially known for a poetry collection that he kept revising and expanding throughout his life. Who was he?
In a Walt Whitman poem, the speaker celebrates his own identity and vows to sound a “barbaric yawp” over the roofs of the world. What long poem contains these lines?
Walt Whitman wrote two famous elegies after the 1865 assassination of a U.S. president: one mourns a fallen captain, while the other opens amid spring lilacs. Which president is memorialized in both?
Walt Whitman paid for the first edition of this poetry collection himself in 1855, then continued to expand and revise it for decades. What collection became his defining lifelong project?

Published in 1903, this adventure novel follows Buck, a domesticated dog kidnapped from California and forced into the Klondike-era sled-dog trade. The story tracks his adaptation to harsh life in the North under successive human owners; what novel is it?
The Call of the Wild appeared in 1903 under the name of this American author, who also wrote White Fang and drew on his experiences in the Klondike. Who was he?
Which thirteen-novel series by Lemony Snicket follows Violet, Klaus, and Sunny Baudelaire as they face repeated schemes by a theatrical villain after a fire destroys their home?
In A Series of Unfortunate Events, what villain repeatedly disguises himself to pursue the Baudelaire orphans and seize their fortune, including posing as the assistant Stephano in The Reptile Room?

Published by Chapman and Hall in 1843, this novella follows miserly Londoner Ebenezer Scrooge, whose night of December 24 is interrupted first by his dead former partner and then by three spirits who confront him with his past, present, and future. It launched Charles Dickens’s series of seasonal books. What is this work?
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge’s deceased business partner appears on Christmas Eve wrapped in chains made from objects such as cashboxes, keys, padlocks, and ledgers. What is the partner’s name?

Which Wilfred Owen poem, drafted in 1917 at a war hospital, follows exhausted soldiers caught in a gas attack and depicts one man dying after he fails to put on his mask? Its Latin title invokes a Roman patriotic maxim that Owen turns into bitter irony.
Wilfred Owen drafted *Dulce et Decorum Est* in 1917 while recovering from wartime service. What Edinburgh institution caring for recovering servicemen was he staying at?

Published in 1958, this novella by Truman Capote is narrated by a writer recalling his friendship with an enigmatic neighbor in a Manhattan apartment building. Its central character takes in a stray cat but insists that neither belongs to the other. What is the novella?

In Breakfast at Tiffany’s, this restless young woman in Manhattan creates a public identity while seeking acceptance. She takes in a stray cat, then sends it away while insisting that neither of them belongs to the other. What is her name?

This South African writer’s 1948 debut novel follows rural Anglican pastor Stephen Kumalo to Johannesburg and became internationally known for its portrayal of racial injustice. He later helped found South Africa’s Liberal Party and remained a prominent opponent of apartheid; who was the writer?

In Alan Paton’s novel, a Zulu Anglican pastor travels from Ixopo to Johannesburg after receiving news about his family, then learns that his son Absalom is accused of killing Arthur Jarvis. What is the title of the novel?

In this 1842 dramatic monologue by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, an aging king on Ithaca entrusts the rule of his kingdom to his son and urges his former sailors toward another voyage. The speaker’s closing resolve celebrates continued striving and exploration despite old age. What is the poem’s title?
Tennyson associated Ulysses with the need to press forward through life’s struggles after the death of this close friend in 1833. What was his friend’s name?
In oral traditions, this performer preserved and presented inherited poems, genealogies, or historical tales, sometimes with musical accompaniment. What is this traditional poetic storyteller called?

The ancient Greek bard traditionally credited with the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey* is also the subject of debate over whether those epics reflect one poet or generations of oral composition. Who is this poet?
In H.G. Wells’s *The Time Machine*, these pale subterranean people maintain machinery beneath future London and emerge at night to hunt the gentle inhabitants aboveground. What are they called?

In *The Time Machine*, the Morlocks prey on a childlike, physically weak people who live aboveground among the ruins of the distant future. Weena, whom the Time Traveller rescues from drowning, belongs to this people. What are they called?

In this short story, a first-person narrator in Buenos Aires receives a coin as change after attending a funeral. The coin gradually monopolizes his thoughts until ordinary experience seems to fade around it; what Borges story is this?
In “The Zahir,” a fictionalized narrator becomes obsessed with a coin until it dominates his thoughts. Which Argentine writer also created “The Aleph” and “Funes the Memorious”?

An impoverished former law student in Saint Petersburg murders a pawnbroker and her sister, then struggles with guilt and moral responsibility. Sonya reads him the biblical story of Lazarus as he moves toward confession and redemption; what novel is this?
Crime and Punishment appeared in twelve monthly installments in The Russian Messenger in 1866, and its author later created Ivan, Dmitri, and Alyosha Karamazov. Name this Russian novelist.

In Crime and Punishment, after confessing to the murders of Alyona Ivanovna and Lizaveta, Raskolnikov is sent to a penal settlement in this vast region of Russia. Sonya follows him there, and his sentence frames the novel’s closing movement toward spiritual renewal; what region is it?

This 14th-century Italian narrative poem opens with a pilgrim lost in a dark wood and follows his descent through a realm of punishments under the guidance of an ancient Roman poet. It is the first canticle of Dante’s larger three-part work. What is this canticle called?
In Inferno, a deceased Roman poet accompanies the pilgrim through the underworld and explains the fates of its inhabitants. The guide also wrote the Aeneid during his lifetime. Who is he?
The first-person pilgrim in Inferno shares the name of its author, a Florentine poet who wrote in Italian and used terza rima. What is the author’s full name?
Inferno arranges the damned in a descending sequence of concentric regions, with punishments reflecting different kinds of sin. What is this structure commonly called?
Inferno is the opening canticle of a three-part allegorical poem, followed by Purgatorio and Paradiso. What is the title of the complete work?

This English Romantic poet became famous after the first two cantos of *Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage* appeared in 1812. He later wrote the unfinished satirical narrative poem *Don Juan*; by what name is he commonly known?
Lord Byron’s unfinished comic narrative poem *Don Juan* uses a stanza of eight lines, with six alternating rhymes followed by a rhyming couplet. What is the name of this verse form?
Horace Smith’s poem about a vanished Egyptian civilization ends by asking what “powerful but unrecorded race” once dwelt in an “annihilated place.” What is the poem’s title?

The poem Ozymandias that appeared in The Examiner in 1818 was written as part of a friendly poetic competition with Shelley, who wrote another poem of the same title. This English poet’s version ends by imagining a hunter finding fragments where London once stood; who wrote it?

Published in 1929, this German-language antiwar novel follows young German soldier Paul Bäumer and his fellow recruits through the brutal trench warfare of World War I. Its portrayal of comradeship, fear, and loss became an international bestseller.
answer: All Quiet on the Western Front

question: The author of *All Quiet on the Western Front* drew on his own service in the German army during World War I, including being wounded in 1917 and losing comrades. Under what name was the novel’s 1929 German edition published?

In this lyric form, each couplet can stand as a self-contained unit while contributing to a shared mood, and the closing couplet may include the poet’s pen name. It often expresses longing for unattainable love and became prominent in Persian and Urdu poetry; what is the form?
A major poet of the Ghazal tradition, this 13th-century Persian mystic composed thousands of poems gathered in the Divan-e Shams, a collection named for Shams of Tabriz. Who was he?

In Harper Lee’s 1960 novel set in Maycomb County, Alabama, this widowed lawyer raises Jem and Scout and defends Tom Robinson at trial. What is the name of the principled father who teaches Scout to consider another person’s point of view?
Atticus Finch’s defense of Tom Robinson anchors this Harper Lee novel, narrated by his daughter Scout and set in the fictional Alabama town of Maycomb. What is the title of the book?
In The Catcher in the Rye, Holden’s younger sister is perceptive and affectionate, and she is one of the few people who truly understands him. What is her full name?
Phoebe Caulfield rides a carousel while Holden watches in this long, narrow stretch of Manhattan greenery, near its zoo. What is this famous site called?

A sailor recounts how he shot a bird that had appeared amid fog and ice, after which his crew suffered supernatural punishment, thirst, and a becalmed voyage. What Samuel Taylor Coleridge narrative poem frames this tale as an interruption of a wedding guest?
answer: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

question: In The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, this seabird appears as a welcome sign amid fog and ice, but the mariner shoots it with his crossbow, bringing the voyage under a supernatural curse. Which bird’s killing becomes the poem’s central transgression?

This medieval Italian narrative poem follows a pilgrim through three realms of the afterlife, moving from punishment toward purification and finally a vision of God. An ancient Roman poet guides him at first, before a woman associated with his earthly love takes over. Name this epic by Dante Alighieri.

In The Divine Comedy, which first section takes the pilgrim through nine descending circles where punishments reflect the sins of the dead? It includes encounters with Paolo and Francesca and with Count Ugolino.
In The Divine Comedy, which Roman poet, author of the Aeneid, guides the pilgrim through Hell and most of Purgatory as a symbol of human reason?
The Divine Comedy was written in a vernacular that helped establish the basis of standard Italian. What regional language variety, associated with Dante’s home city of Florence, did he use?
Which English novelist, born in 1775, published Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park, and Emma anonymously during her lifetime?

In Jane Austen’s 1813 novel, the opening sentence calls it a truth universally acknowledged that a wealthy single man must want a wife. Which novel follows Elizabeth Bennet’s changing opinion of the owner of Pemberley?

Jane Austen’s novel follows a wealthy young woman at Hartfield who meddles in Harriet Smith’s romantic prospects, despite claiming she has no wish to marry herself. Her longtime neighbor Mr. Knightley eventually becomes her husband; what is the novel’s title?
In this Jane Austen novel, Catherine Morland visits Bath, befriends Isabella Thorpe, and lets her love of Gothic fiction fuel suspicions about General Tilney’s home. What is the novel’s title?
