Jane Austen began but did not finish this novel about Mr. Parker’s plans to develop a seaside resort. Charlotte Heywood becomes involved with the Parker family after meeting them following Mr. Parker’s carriage accident; what is the novel’s title?

In this 1970 novel, Pecola Breedlove, a Black girl growing up in Ohio, longs for blue eyes as she confronts racism and destructive beauty standards. Its chapter headings draw on increasingly fragmented versions of the “Dick and Jane” reader. What is the novel’s title?
The Bluest Eye was the first novel published by this American writer, who later won the Pulitzer Prize for Beloved and the Nobel Prize in Literature. Who is she?

Which modernist short-story writer created Bertha Young, whose overwhelming happiness in “Bliss” is associated with a flowering pear tree? She also wrote “Prelude” and “How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped.”
Katherine Mansfield was born in Wellington in 1888, and Māori characters appear in her story “How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped.” In what country is Wellington located?

Aristotle describes this dramatic form as the enactment of a serious, complete action rather than a story told by a narrator. It often depicts a protagonist’s suffering or downfall, arouses pity and fear, and is traditionally contrasted with comedy. What genre is this?
In Aristotle’s account of tragedy, this term names an effect associated with the audience’s experience of pity and fear. Scholars continue to debate its precise meaning. What is the term?

Which sixteenth-century Ming-dynasty novel fictionalizes a Buddhist monk’s pilgrimage from China to India, blending the expedition’s historical outline with fantasy, satire, and religious traditions? The monk travels with a stone-born monkey disciple and two other supernatural companions.
In Journey to the West, which monkey disciple is born from a stone egg on Flower Fruit Mountain and learns Taoist arts, combat, and the ability to transform into 72 different forms?
Which British translator made Journey to the West widely known to English-speaking readers with a 1942 abridgment titled Monkey?

An American poet wrote the villanelle “One Art,” whose speaker insists that losing is an art one can master, and the dramatic monologue “Crusoe in England,” which reimagines Defoe’s castaway after his return home. Who was this poet?

In an Elizabeth Bishop poem, the speaker looks back on twenty-eight years marooned on an island with Friday, then reflects on being back in England. Which castaway from a Daniel Defoe novel is the poem’s speaker?

Which English Romantic poet wrote the ballad in which a mariner stops a wedding guest and recounts shooting an albatross, as well as a fragmentary dream-vision about a pleasure dome at Xanadu? He also collaborated with William Wordsworth on an influential 1798 poetry collection.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge joined this English poet in publishing the 1798 collection *Lyrical Ballads*, a landmark often associated with the beginning of British Romanticism. The same poet wrote “Tintern Abbey” and “I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud”; who was Coleridge’s collaborator?

Published in 1851, this novel follows a voyage aboard the Pequod, where Captain Ahab pursues the enormous white creature that took his leg in an earlier encounter. Its narrator opens with the famous words, “Call me Ishmael.” What is the novel’s full title?

In Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, this first-person narrator signs aboard the Pequod after deciding to go to sea. He shares a room at the Spouter-Inn with Queequeg and survives the shipwreck by clinging to a coffin. Who is he?
In Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, Ahab commands this Nantucket whaling ship, whose voyage becomes a hunt for a particular white whale. What is the ship’s name?

In Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, this tattooed harpooneer befriends Ishmael after they share a room at the Spouter-Inn. After an illness prompts him to have a coffin made, that coffin later serves as Ishmael’s life buoy. Who is he?
Moby-Dick; or, The Whale was published in 1851, first appearing in London under the shortened title The Whale. Which American author, drawing partly on his own seafaring experience, wrote it?

A grandmother tries to persuade her son not to take the family to Florida, partly because she has read that an escaped criminal is headed there. After the family’s cat causes a car crash, they encounter the criminal and his companions, and the grandmother is the last to be killed. What short story is this?
answer: A Good Man Is Hard to Find

question: The short story A Good Man Is Hard to Find appears in a 1955 collection by this writer, who also wrote “Good Country People” and “Everything That Rises Must Converge.” Who is the author?

In A Good Man Is Hard to Find, this escaped convict travels with Hiram and Bobby Lee and debates the grandmother about Jesus before shooting her. He says that Jesus has “thrown everything off balance.” What is the convict’s nickname?
In A Good Man Is Hard to Find, Bailey’s family leaves Atlanta on a road trip to Florida. The story’s author was also born in Savannah; in what state are both cities located?

Flannery O’Connor described the stories in the collection that includes A Good Man Is Hard to Find as being concerned with a Catholic doctrine about humanity’s fallen condition. What doctrine did she identify?

This Greek king is distinguished by his cunning as well as his skill as a warrior. After the fall of Troy, he spends ten years trying to return to Ithaca, including escaping the Cyclops Polyphemus by claiming his name is Nobody. Who is this hero?
In this epic attributed to Homer, Odysseus recounts encounters with Polyphemus and the enchantress Circe during his long journey home from Troy. What poem tells of this homecoming to Ithaca?

This stage drama by Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee reimagines the 1925 Scopes trial as a courtroom fight over whether a Tennessee teacher may teach evolution. Its fictional defense attorney is Henry Drummond, and its title echoes a biblical passage. What play is it?

In Inherit the Wind, the schoolteacher called Bertram Cates is a fictionalized counterpart of the real Tennessee high-school science teacher prosecuted in 1925 for teaching evolution. What was that teacher’s name?

Orson Scott Card expanded an earlier short story into this novel about a gifted child recruited to train against an alien enemy. Its young cadets practice mock battles in zero gravity at an orbiting school, and the novel won both the Nebula and Hugo Awards for Best Novel in consecutive years. What is the novel’s title?
In Ender's Game, young recruits settle tactical rivalries in a chamber where gravity is absent and their weapons freeze opponents in place. What is this mock-combat arena called?

Which medieval French epic poem recounts how Charlemagne’s rearguard is ambushed at Roncevaux after a betrayal by a Frankish baron? Its hero sounds an ivory horn to summon aid, but dies before Charlemagne can reach him.

In The Song of Roland, which Frankish baron conspires with the Saracen ruler Marsile to expose Roland’s rearguard to an ambush at Roncevaux? After the treachery is proved in a trial by combat, he is executed by being drawn and quartered.

E. E. Cummings’s short poem follows four girls who go down to the beach: one finds a singing shell, another befriends a stranded star, another is chased by a bubble-blowing creature, and the fourth brings home a smooth round stone. What is this poem called?
answer: maggie and milly and molly and may

question: The poem “maggie and milly and molly and may” was written by the poet who also authored “anyone lived in a pretty how town.” Who is this poet?

In a famous Emily Dickinson lyric, the speaker is unable to pause for a courteous visitor, who instead stops for her and shares a carriage ride past a school, fields of grain, and the setting sun. What personified figure accompanies her?
In the carriage lyric where Death courteously escorts the speaker, the first stanza names one additional passenger besides the two of them. What abstract figure is that third occupant?

Which American playwright wrote a two-part drama in which Prior Walter receives a diagnosis of AIDS and visions of an angel, while Roy Cohn faces his own illness? The playwright also wrote *A Bright Room Called Day*.
Which play by Tony Kushner follows Agnes Eggling, a Berlin actress living through the Nazi rise to power, and includes later scenes in which contemporary Americans debate political responsibility?

Set in a decaying Kyoto during the late twelfth century, this short story follows a dismissed servant who shelters in a ruined city gate and finds an old woman pulling hair from corpses to make wigs. After she argues that desperation excuses her actions, he uses her reasoning to justify taking her kimono. What is the story?
The Japanese author of Rashōmon, first published in 1915, also wrote “In a Grove” and “The Spider’s Thread.” Who was this writer?
Which Langston Hughes poem connects African-American history and identity to ancient waterways, with its speaker recalling the Euphrates and the Mississippi?
The Negro Speaks of Rivers was written by which poet, who also wrote “Harlem,” the poem that asks what happens to a dream deferred, and published the collection The Weary Blues?

This American playwright became the first U.S. playwright to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, winning it in 1936. His four Pulitzer Prizes for Drama include awards for *Beyond the Horizon* and *Long Day’s Journey Into Night*; who was he?

Eugene O’Neill drew on his family history in this play, which follows the Tyrone family through a single day as illness and morphine addiction deepen their conflicts. Published after his death, it received the 1957 Pulitzer Prize for Drama; what is its title?
In Voltaire’s satirical work, this philosopher tutors Candide and repeatedly argues that the world is “the best of all possible worlds.” What is his name?
Dr. Pangloss tutors the title character in this satirical work by Voltaire, which was published with the subtitle “Optimism.” What is the work’s title?

In a poem from William Blake’s 1794 collection, the speaker addresses a creature “burning bright / In the forests of the night” and asks what immortal hand or eye could frame its “fearful symmetry.” What is the poem titled?
The Tyger and “The Lamb” are poems by this English poet, who also wrote “London” and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. Who is the poet?
The Tyger appears in this 1794 collection, which Blake paired with an earlier collection centered on innocence and childhood. What is the collection called?
Who was the English poet, printmaker, and visionary (1757–1827) who created *Songs of Innocence and of Experience* and wrote “The Tyger” and “London”?

In a lyric by William Blake later set to music by Hubert Parry as a patriotic hymn, the speaker asks whether “those feet in ancient time” walked England’s mountains and speaks of “dark Satanic mills.” What sacred city does the poem imagine being built there?
William Blake’s wife helped print and color many of his illustrated books, contributing to the making of his artistic works. Whom did he marry in 1782?

William Blake’s illuminated work combines prose, poetry, and engraved illustrations, and includes a section of paradoxical aphorisms, among them “The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom.” It challenges conventional moral oppositions with the assertion “Without Contraries is no progression.” What is the work’s title?
answer: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

question: Published in 1987, this nonfiction work by journalist Randy Shilts traces the early history of the HIV/AIDS epidemic and examines the political response to it. What is the title of the book?

And the Band Played On criticizes the federal government’s slow response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic during the tenure of a two-term U.S. president who served from 1981 to 1989. Which president was in office during that period?

In this comic story, two hapless kidnappers take a boy from Summit, Alabama, intending to collect money from his father. The captive’s nonstop games and rough make-believe drive them to offer the father money to take him back; what is the story’s title?

The Ransom of Red Chief was written by the same American short-story writer who created Soapy, the vagrant who tries to get arrested in “The Cop and the Anthem,” and the newlywed couple in “The Gift of the Magi.” What pen name did this author use?

Written by W. B. Yeats in September 1916, this political lyric commemorates the armed revolt in Dublin and its executed leaders while questioning whether their sacrifice was necessary. Its recurring refrain holds admiration and horror together by describing a “terrible beauty” being born. What is the poem’s title?

In Easter, 1916, Yeats’s closing stanza names four men executed after the Rising. Which poet and revolutionary, who read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside Dublin’s General Post Office, is the final figure named?
Set in Denmark, this Shakespearean tragedy follows a prince who seeks to avenge his father’s murder by the uncle who takes the throne and marries his mother. What is the play’s title?
Hamlet survives in three early printed versions with differences in their wording and passages. Which one appeared in 1603, before the 1604 version and the 1623 First Folio?
In Hamlet, the prince asks visiting actors to stage a play reenacting a king’s death by poison, hoping the performance will expose Claudius’s guilt. What is the name of this play-within-the-play?

This 1891 novel by Thomas Hardy follows its title character, a young woman whose life is shaped by her family’s claim to aristocratic ancestry and her relationships with Alec and Angel Clare. After killing Alec at Sandbourne, she is captured at Stonehenge and executed; what is the novel’s title?
The author of Tess of the d’Urbervilles also wrote The Return of the Native and the poem “The Darkling Thrush.” Which English novelist created Tess Durbeyfield?

In this 1932 novel, itinerant worker Joe Christmas kills Joanna Burden, and her house is later burned. A parallel story follows pregnant Lena Grove as she travels through Mississippi searching for Lucas Burch. What is the novel’s title?

Light in August is set partly in Yoknapatawpha County, a fictional Mississippi setting that recurs in this writer’s novels. The same author wrote The Sound and the Fury and As I Lay Dying. Who is the author?

What lyric poetic form, originating in ancient Greece, addresses, praises, or meditates on a person, object, idea, or natural phenomenon? Its elevated expression and formal design distinguish it from many other kinds of lyric poem.

Which ancient Greek poet’s choral victory poems celebrating athletic festival winners became the model for one traditional kind of ode? His surviving poems include works honoring victors at the Olympic Games.
In ancient Greek performances of an ode, what stringed instrument was especially revered and used to accompany sung poetry? It was plucked, unlike the wind instrument known as the aulos.

In an Emily Dickinson poem, the speaker says she could not stop for this courteous visitor, who accompanies her past a school, fields, and the setting sun toward a grave. What concept does the visitor personify?
In A. E. Housman’s poem about Death, a champion runner is carried shoulder-high in a coffin, recalling how the townspeople once carried him after he won their race. What is the title of the poem?

An orphaned girl tells this coming-of-age story in an intensely personal first-person voice, moving from a harsh childhood school to work as a governess at an isolated country estate. Her romance with the estate’s master is disrupted by a secret in the house; name the novel.
Jane Eyre was issued in 1847 with the subtitle *An Autobiography*, but its title page credited a pseudonymous author rather than Charlotte Brontë’s full name. What pen name appeared there?
In Jane Eyre, the heroine takes a governess post at this estate, where Rochester’s planned wedding is interrupted by the discovery of a hidden resident. What is the name of the manor house?
In Jane Eyre, this woman is Rochester’s existing wife, kept in a locked room at Thornfield Hall. She tears Jane’s wedding veil and later sets the estate ablaze; name her.
Jane Eyre is often classified using a term for a novel that traces its protagonist’s development from childhood into adulthood, including psychological and moral growth. What is this literary term?

Born in Villers-Cotterêts in 1802, this French novelist and playwright became renowned for historical adventure fiction. He published a story of d’Artagnan and three companions in 1844 and a revenge novel about Edmond Dantès in 1845–46; who was this writer?

In Alexandre Dumas père’s 1844 adventure novel, the young Gascon d’Artagnan befriends Athos, Porthos, and Aramis after arriving in Paris. What is the title of this story, whose motto is “All for one and one for all”?
This late-Republic Roman lyric poet wrote about Lesbia’s sparrow and attacked critics named Aurelius and Furius in one of his poems. What was his full name?

Which Greek lyric poet from Lesbos wrote the original poem reworked in poem 51 by Gaius Valerius Catullus? Catullus’s version describes the speaker’s physical symptoms while watching a beloved converse with someone else.

A legendary German scholar is said to have bargained with a supernatural tempter for magical power and forbidden knowledge. Which figure became the subject of major dramas by Christopher Marlowe and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe?
In Goethe’s Faust, what is the name of the scholar’s demonic bargaining partner? This tempter offers Faust a pact in exchange for serving him.

A boy named Stanley Yelnats is sent to the desert juvenile facility Camp Green Lake, where a harsh daily digging regimen is presented as character-building. This 1998 Louis Sachar novel weaves that punishment together with an inherited family curse and the legend of an outlaw’s buried fortune; what is the work’s title?
In Holes, what is the nickname of the former Green Lake schoolteacher who becomes an outlaw after Sam is murdered and later hides her fortune in a lipstick tube?
In the second part of Jonathan Swift’s *Gulliver’s Travels*, what land does Lemuel Gulliver visit, where its inhabitants are giants and he is treated as a tiny curiosity?

In Brobdingnag, what is the name of the farmer’s young daughter who becomes Gulliver’s nurse and protects him after her father exhibits him for money? She later accompanies Gulliver to the royal court and cares for him there.

In Shakespeare’s tragedy set in Verona, this young woman meets Romeo at a family feast before learning he belongs to the rival Montague house. After questioning whether a name defines a person, she secretly marries him and later takes a potion that makes her appear dead; who is she?

When Juliet Capulet is pressured by her father to marry Count Paris, she seeks help from this cleric, who arranges her secret marriage to Romeo and gives her a potion intended to help her escape the wedding. Name this character.

Isabel Allende’s debut novel traces several generations of the Trueba family amid political upheaval, blending family history with clairvoyance and other supernatural events. What is the novel’s title?
In The House of the Spirits, which family member keeps notebooks chronicling her family’s history and is known for clairvoyance and telekinetic abilities?
Published in 1979, which V. S. Naipaul novel follows Salim, a trader whose life in an unnamed newly independent African country is reshaped by political upheaval and an authoritarian ruler?

In A Bend in the River, the merchant at the center of the story leaves his coastal home to run a shop in an inland town, where he witnesses the rise of the Big Man’s regime. What is this protagonist’s name?

What movement favors ordinary characters, recognizable social settings, and plausible events over idealized heroes or supernatural explanations? Its careful attention to concrete detail seeks to portray human behavior and everyday life as they are.

Which related mode keeps Literary realism’s attention to everyday settings and social detail while treating fantastic or supernatural happenings as part of ordinary life? It is often associated with the fiction of Gabriel García Márquez.

This Japanese writer published *Confessions of a Mask* and the tetralogy *The Sea of Fertility*. He also wrote the autobiographical essay *Sun and Steel* and died by seppuku after a failed coup attempt in 1970. By what pen name was Kimitake Hiraoka known?

In Yukio Mishima’s 1956 novel, the stuttering acolyte Mizoguchi becomes obsessed with the beauty of a famous Kyoto Buddhist landmark and ultimately sets it ablaze. What structure gives this novel its title?
answer: The Temple of the Golden Pavilion

question: Yukio Mishima established this private militia in 1968, and its members accompanied him during the 1970 hostage-taking at a Self-Defense Forces headquarters. What was the group called?

Wallace Stevens’s poem opens by saying that one must have a mind of winter to regard frost and the boughs, then ends with a listener who is “nothing himself” perceiving what is and is not there. What is the poem’s title?
In The Snow Man, the speaker says that perceiving frost and bare boughs without projecting human misery requires a particular mental stance. What brief phrase names that stance?
Which American poet and activist became the first U.S. National Youth Poet Laureate? At Joe Biden’s 2021 inauguration, she recited a poem about the country’s hopes and divisions.
At Joe Biden’s January 2021 inauguration, Amanda Gorman delivered an original poem reflecting on national unity and resilience. What was the poem’s title?

This 1837 Danish literary fairy tale follows the youngest daughter of a sea king, who trades her voice to a sea witch for human legs, hoping to win a prince and attain an immortal soul. What is the tale’s natural English title?

The Little Mermaid was written by the Danish author who also created “The Snow Queen” and “The Emperor’s New Clothes.” In another of his tales, the mermaid’s story ends with her becoming a daughter of the air. Who was this writer?
A bronze sculpture inspired by The Little Mermaid stands on a waterside promenade in the city where Andersen’s tale was written and first published. What Danish capital is its home?

In this Grimm tale, a princess traveling to marry a foreign king is tricked by her maid into surrendering her royal clothes and is later assigned to herd geese. Her identity is restored after the king investigates the strange daily encounter she has with her dead horse.
In The Goose Girl, what is the name of the princess’s talking horse, whose severed head is hung beneath a gateway and still responds when she passes?

This Old Comedy was first performed at the Lenaia in Athens in 405 BCE and follows Dionysus and his slave Xanthias into the underworld. There, Dionysus judges a poetic contest between Aeschylus and Euripides and ultimately chooses Aeschylus to return to the living; what is the play’s title?
The Frogs is an Old Comedy by the same Athenian playwright who wrote Peace and The Wasps. Who is this comic dramatist, whose plays often satirized civic life and politics?

In The Frogs, this tragedian defeats Euripides in a debate judged by Dionysus, with the poets’ verses weighed on a balance. The winner returns from the underworld to advise Athens and is also the author of the Oresteia; who is he?

This Irish writer studied classics at Trinity College Dublin and Oxford, became a leading figure in London’s Aesthetic movement, and was celebrated for his epigrams and social wit. Imprisoned following his 1895 conviction, he wrote a major reflective letter while behind bars; identify this author.

Oscar Wilde’s only novel first appeared in 1890 and centers on a young man whose portrait bears the signs of age and moral corruption while he retains his youthful appearance. What is this Gothic work?

In this Oscar Wilde comedy, Jack Worthing’s attempt to marry Gwendolen is obstructed by Lady Bracknell, while Algernon’s courtship of Cecily depends on a fabricated friendship with an invalid. What is this play?
During his imprisonment, Oscar Wilde addressed an extended, deeply personal letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, reflecting on their relationship and on spiritual suffering. What is the title of this work?
Which 17th-century French poet published the first collection of his verse Fables in 1668, adapting stories from Aesopic and other earlier traditions?
In a verse fable by Jean de La Fontaine, a fox flatters a black-feathered bird perched in a tree, prompting it to open its beak and drop a piece of food. What is the title of this fable?
This American postmodern novelist wrote *The Crying of Lot 49* and the sprawling 1973 novel *Gravity’s Rainbow*. He is also famous for keeping a remarkably low public profile. Who is he?
In Thomas Pynchon’s 1973 novel, former U.S. Army lieutenant Tyrone Slothrop’s sexual encounters seem to correspond to V-2 rocket impacts across wartime Europe. What is the novel’s title?

This English writer worked as a journalist and political writer, producing pamphlets and periodicals as well as fiction. Later generations chiefly associated him with a 1719 castaway narrative linked to Alexander Selkirk’s experience, and he also wrote *Moll Flanders* and *A Journal of the Plague Year*. Who was he?

In Daniel Defoe’s 1719 novel, a sailor survives a shipwreck and spends twenty-eight years on an island near the mouth of the Orinoco River. He rescues a man from cannibals and gives him the name Friday. What is this novel?

In this drama, the regulars at Harry Hope’s Greenwich Village saloon cling to comforting pipe dreams until a traveling salesman urges them to face reality and reveals that he murdered his wife. What is the title of this Eugene O’Neill play?
The Iceman Cometh was written by this American playwright, whose other works include Long Day’s Journey into Night and Mourning Becomes Electra. What is his name?

This 1902 supernatural horror story by W. W. Jacobs centers on a dried, cursed object said to grant three wishes to each of three men. The White family’s wishes bring devastating consequences in this story, which was collected in *The Lady of the Barge*. What is its title?
In *The Monkey’s Paw*, which veteran brings the White family the dried talisman, recounts how a fakir enchanted it to warn against interfering with fate, and later throws it into the fire?

Published in 1899, this novel follows Edna Pontellier as she questions the roles expected of her while living in New Orleans. Its story ends with her drowning in the Gulf of Mexico. What is the novel’s title?
The Awakening was written by a Louisiana-born author whose other works include the short stories “The Story of an Hour” and “Désirée’s Baby.” Who was this author?

This Victorian English poet wrote the 44-poem cycle *Sonnets from the Portuguese* and the verse novel *Aurora Leigh*. She married a fellow poet six years her junior and settled with him in Italy; who was she?
Elizabeth Barrett Browning published this 44-poem love sequence in 1850, drawing on poems she had privately given her future husband during their courtship. What is the collection's title?

Published in 1989, this novel follows four Chinese immigrant mothers and their American-born daughters in San Francisco through interconnected narratives. Its four sections each begin with a Chinese fable, and the mothers’ mah-jong gatherings provide a meeting point for their stories. What is this novel?
In The Joy Luck Club, which American-born daughter takes her late mother Suyuan’s place at the mah-jong gatherings and later travels to China to meet the twin daughters her mother left behind?

Born in Bombay in 1865, this British writer returned to India as a teenager and worked as a journalist before publishing the novel *Kim* and the poem “Gunga Din.” In 1907, he became the first English writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Who was he?
Rudyard Kipling published this 1894 collection featuring stories about Mowgli and the mongoose Rikki-Tikki-Tavi. Its other well-known characters include Baloo and Shere Khan. What is the title?
This Mexican poet and essayist examined national identity in *The Labyrinth of Solitude*. His long poem *Sunstone* has 584 lines, a count associated with the cycle of Venus. Who was he?

In 1990, Octavio Paz became the first Mexican writer to receive this international literary honor. The award recognized his passionate writing, marked by wide horizons and sensuous intelligence. What was it?

This nineteenth-century English novelist and poet published her only novel under the pseudonym Ellis Bell. The novel centers on the destructive relationship between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff. Who was the author?

In Emily Brontë’s only novel, this foundling is raised at Wuthering Heights and grows up deeply attached to Catherine Earnshaw. After disappearing for several years, he returns with wealth and seeks revenge on those he believes wronged him. Who is he?

In Suzanne Collins’s dystopian trilogy, this District 12 archer volunteers for the arena in place of her younger sister, then becomes a symbol of rebellion against the Capitol. What is the name of this protagonist, also associated with the mockingjay symbol?

Katniss Everdeen’s fellow District 12 tribute is the son of a baker who once secretly gave her bread during her family’s hardship. His camouflage talent later helps him evade opponents in the arena; what is his name?
Born in Atlanta in 1900, this American novelist worked as a reporter for the Atlanta Journal before publishing a single novel that became a major bestseller and the basis of a 1939 film. Who was she?

Margaret Mitchell’s only published novel follows Scarlett O’Hara through the Civil War and Reconstruction in Georgia, as she struggles to save her family’s plantation, Tara. What is the title of this work?

This long autobiographical poem traces the development of its author's mind and was subtitled “Growth of a Poet's Mind.” Conceived as an introductory work for a larger philosophical poem called The Recluse, what is its title?

The Prelude is the autobiographical poem of this English Romantic poet, who collaborated with Samuel Taylor Coleridge on Lyrical Ballads. His poem “Tintern Abbey” reflects on a return to the Wye Valley with his sister Dorothy; who was he?

This Nigerian writer became the first African recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986. His plays include a comedy about village beauty Sidi and schoolteacher Lakunle, as well as a tragedy centered on Elesin Oba.

Which Wole Soyinka comedy pits schoolteacher Lakunle against village elder Baroka, as both seek to marry Sidi, the village beauty? Set in Ilujinle, the play explores tensions between Western modernity and local traditions.

Published in 1944, this collection brings together stories from El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan and Artificios, including tales of an infinite structure of hexagonal galleries and a labyrinthine Chinese garden. What is the title of Jorge Luis Borges’s celebrated collection?
One story in Ficciones imagines a universe of endless hexagonal chambers whose books contain every possible combination of letters. What is the title of this story?

Lorraine Hansberry’s 1959 Broadway drama follows the Younger family as they weigh how to use an insurance payout after the death of their patriarch. What play takes its title from a Langston Hughes poem about a deferred dream?
In A Raisin in the Sun, the Younger family plans to move to this Chicago neighborhood, prompting Karl Lindner to offer them money to stay away. What neighborhood is it?
The title of A Raisin in the Sun alludes to this Langston Hughes poem, which asks what happens to a dream deferred. What is the poem’s title?

A Guy de Maupassant story follows a mixed group of French travelers fleeing Rouen by coach during the Prussian occupation. At an inn, the respectable passengers pressure a fellow traveler to comply with a Prussian officer, then shun her afterward; what is the story’s title?
In Boule de Suif, a radical democrat travels with the coach party and repeatedly whistles the French national anthem while they are delayed in occupied territory. What is this character’s name?
Set amid the Trojan War, this Shakespearean problem play follows a Trojan prince’s doomed courtship of the daughter of the priest Calchas. What is the play’s title?
In Troilus and Cressida, which character is Cressida’s uncle and arranges the lovers’ secret meeting? He also urges her toward Troilus during their encounter.

In this French lyric, the speaker vows to leave at first light and walk alone, ignoring the scenery as he travels to a grave. He ends by laying a bouquet of green holly and flowering heather there. What is this Victor Hugo poem called?
In “Tomorrow, at Dawn,” the daughter whose grave the speaker visits had drowned with her husband, Charles Vacquerie, at Villequier in 1843. What was her name?

Born in England and later part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, this 17th-century poet published *The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America*. She also wrote verse defending women’s intellectual abilities. Who was she?
In a poem by Anne Bradstreet, the speaker says, “If ever two were one, then surely we,” and values her beloved’s love above riches. What is the poem’s title?
answer: To My Dear and Loving Husband

question: Which poem by Wallace Stevens is structured as a sequence of brief, numbered vignettes about shifting perceptions, including one in which a bird whirls in autumn winds as a small part of a pantomime?
answer: Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird

question: In *Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird*, the final section places a blackbird in cedar limbs as snow falls. Which American modernist poet wrote this poem?
What 1843 short story by Edgar Allan Poe follows William Legrand as he deciphers a cryptogram leading to treasure associated with Captain Kidd?
In The Gold-Bug, what impoverished former Charleston resident living on Sullivan’s Island discovers a gold-colored beetle and deciphers the cipher that leads to Captain Kidd’s treasure?

Which 1883 memoir and travel narrative by Mark Twain recounts his years learning to pilot the great North American river that flows past St. Louis and New Orleans? It blends personal recollections with observations of river travel and communities along its banks.

In Life on the Mississippi, Twain describes training to pilot this kind of river vessel. Its commercial development is associated with Robert Fulton’s Clermont and adaptations of James Watt’s engine designs.

It includes picture books for beginning readers as well as longer novels aimed at younger audiences. Eric Carle’s picture book about an insect that eats through a week’s worth of food and Neil Gaiman’s tale of a girl who discovers a sinister parallel home are both examples of this broad literary field. What is the field called?

In children’s literature, which Eric Carle picture book follows a small larva as it eats its way through different foods before transforming into a butterfly? Its pages have holes showing where the insect has eaten.

A Yale-educated bond salesman from the Midwest rents a modest house in West Egg and is a cousin of Daisy Buchanan. As the reflective first-person narrator of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Jazz Age novel, he grows disillusioned with the East and eventually returns to the Midwest. Who is this character?

Nick Carraway narrates this F. Scott Fitzgerald novel, in which a self-made millionaire hosts extravagant parties on Long Island and a distant green light symbolizes his hope of reuniting with Daisy Buchanan. What novel is it?

In *The Great Gatsby*, an abandoned billboard above a desolate stretch of road displays two immense eyes behind spectacles. The eyes belong to a fictional eye doctor whose name is printed on the advertisement; what is his name?

In *The Great Gatsby*, the billboard bearing Dr. T. J. Eckleburg’s enormous eyes overlooks a gray industrial wasteland between West Egg and New York City, where George Wilson runs a garage. What is this region called?

Esther Greenwood narrates this semi-autobiographical novel, which follows her from a summer internship at a New York women's magazine into a deepening mental-health crisis. Her efforts to reconcile her ambitions with restrictive expectations for women shape the story; name the novel.

The Bell Jar is the semi-autobiographical story of Esther Greenwood's struggle with mental illness and the social expectations placed on women. Which American poet wrote it and also wrote the poems “Daddy” and “Lady Lazarus”?

Born in Boston in 1932, this American writer studied at Smith College and later at Cambridge as a Fulbright student at Newnham College. She wrote a semi-autobiographical novel about Esther Greenwood and the poems “Daddy” and “Lady Lazarus”; who is she?

In Sylvia Plath’s semi-autobiographical novel, protagonist Esther Greenwood interns at a New York fashion magazine and imagines her future as a fig tree with branches representing different possible lives. What is the title of this 1963 novel?

At a 1959 Boston University creative-writing seminar attended by Sylvia Plath and Anne Sexton, the instructor was a prominent American poet whose collection *Life Studies* helped shape the confessional movement. Which poet led the seminar?

Sylvia Plath’s posthumous 1965 poetry collection includes “Daddy,” “Lady Lazarus,” and “Tulips.” Its title comes from the name of a horse in a poem about a brisk ride at dawn; what is the collection called?

This 14th-century Italian prose collection frames one hundred tales as the entertainment of seven women and three men who leave plague-stricken Florence and tell stories over ten days. What is the work’s natural title?

The frame narrative of The Decameron takes place during the 1348 plague, and its stories helped establish vernacular Italian prose as a literary art form. Which Italian writer composed the collection?

In one story, a Bengali American couple share revelations during scheduled power outages; in another, a driver for a doctor's family guides tourists around India while interpreting for them. What is Jhumpa Lahiri's 1999 collection of stories, which won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?

The author of Interpreter of Maladies was born in London to Bengali parents and grew up in Rhode Island. She later wrote the novels The Namesake and The Lowland; which writer won the 2000 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for that debut collection?

Born in Jamaica, this poet and novelist moved to New York in 1914 and became a major figure in the Harlem Renaissance. His 1919 sonnet “If We Must Die” responds to racial violence and urges resistance. Who was this writer?

Claude McKay’s 1928 novel follows Jake, a Black veteran who leaves military service in France and returns to New York, where he encounters the city’s nightlife and working-class communities. What is the title of this influential novel about Black urban life?
In Claude McKay’s 1933 novel, Bita Plant returns to her Jamaican community after years of missionary schooling and must reconcile that upbringing with local life. What is the title of the novel?

In this four-act drama, the revolutionary John Tanner writes a handbook outlining his political ideas, and a dream sequence stages a philosophical conversation with Don Juan in Hell. What is the title of the play?
The playwright of Man and Superman also wrote Pygmalion, in which Professor Henry Higgins attempts to pass off Eliza Doolittle as a duchess. Who was this playwright?

In Orson Scott Card’s novel, this gifted child commander trains at Battle School and leads a unit called Dragon Army before discovering that the supposedly simulated campaigns against the Formics were real. What is the name of this protagonist?

Ender Wiggin is assigned a newly formed Battle School formation whose members are younger than usual, and Bean becomes one of its standout soldiers. What is the name of this unit that remains undefeated under his command?

Published in 1928, this collection by a Granada-born poet reworks the Spanish romance tradition through Andalusian landscapes, folklore, and mythic imagery. It includes the famous poem whose refrain repeatedly longs for green. What is the collection called?

Gypsy Ballads combines traditional Spanish ballad forms with Andalusian folklore and mythic imagery. Its author also wrote Blood Wedding and the elegy “Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías.” Who was the poet?

Published in 1813, this novel follows Elizabeth Bennet as she reconsiders her judgments of a wealthy gentleman amid the Bennet family’s concerns about marriage, class, and inheritance. Its opening reflects on the supposed desire of a wealthy unmarried man for a wife. What is the novel’s title?

The author of Pride and Prejudice also wrote Emma, about a young woman who tries to arrange matches for others, and Persuasion, featuring Anne Elliot and Captain Wentworth. Who was this English novelist?

In Pride and Prejudice, this second-eldest of five sisters refuses Mr. Collins’s proposal and initially rejects Darcy’s proposal at Hunsford. After learning more about Darcy and reconsidering her own assumptions, she eventually marries him. Who is she?

In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet family lives at an estate subject to an entail that will pass the property to Mr. Collins rather than to Mr. Bennet’s daughters. What is the name of the family home?

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth visits this Derbyshire estate with the Gardiners and encounters Darcy’s housekeeper, who speaks highly of her employer. The estate’s grounds and house help change Elizabeth’s impression of Darcy. What is it called?

Born in Alabama and raised in Eatonville, Florida, this writer later used the town as a setting for much of her work. She was a Harlem Renaissance novelist and anthropologist whose best-known novel centers on Janie Crawford’s life story. Who was she?
Published in 1937, this Zora Neale Hurston novel follows Janie Crawford as she recounts her life to her friend Phoeby Watson. What is the novel’s title?
Zora Neale Hurston drew on her fieldwork in North Florida for this 1935 book, a collection documenting African American folklore. What is the book’s title?

This 1974 novel follows a young Harlem woman who becomes pregnant while her fiancé is imprisoned after being falsely accused of rape. Narrated by the woman, it centers on her family's efforts to clear him and bring him home. What is the novel's title?

In If Beale Street Could Talk, what nickname is used for Tish's fiancé, a young sculptor imprisoned after Victoria Rogers identifies him as her rapist? Tish and her family try to prove his innocence while she carries his child.

What Jules Verne adventure novel follows a precise Englishman who wagers at his London club that he can circle the globe before a stated deadline? It was serialized in Le Temps from November 6 to December 22, 1872, before appearing as a book from Hetzel in 1873.
answer: Around the World in Eighty Days

question: Who wrote Around the World in Eighty Days, as well as Journey to the Center of the Earth and Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea? This French novelist’s works were collectively known as the Extraordinary Adventures.

A surgeon named Tomas, his wife Tereza, the artist Sabina, and the professor Franz form the central cast of this philosophical novel. Their private lives are disrupted by the 1968 Prague Spring and the Soviet-led invasion that followed; name the novel.
The Unbearable Lightness of Being was written by a Czech-born novelist from Brno who left Czechoslovakia for France in 1975 after the Soviet-led crackdown on reform. What is his name?
In Chinua Achebe’s 1958 novel *Things Fall Apart*, what fictional Igbo clan is the home community of Okonkwo and the principal setting for the story?

In Umuofia, which famous wrestler and warrior is chosen by the elders to serve as guardian of Ikemefuna, a boy taken as a peace settlement after a conflict with another clan? He is later exiled after accidentally killing Ezeudu’s son.

In George Orwell’s dystopia, which Outer Party employee at the Ministry of Truth keeps a forbidden diary and alters old records to fit the Party’s current claims? He lives in Airstrip One and is eventually tortured in Room 101.

In Winston Smith’s story, which fellow Outer Party member from the Fiction Department secretly begins an affair with him after passing him a note that says “I love you”? They later meet in a room above Mr. Charrington’s shop.

This anonymous Middle English alliterative romance is set in King Arthur’s court and follows one of its courtiers, who accepts a beheading challenge from a strangely verdant visitor. After striking the visitor, he must seek him out a year later at a remote chapel to receive a return blow.
answer: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

question: In Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Gawain spends Christmas at this lord’s castle, Hautdesert, where a three-day exchange-of-winnings bargain unfolds alongside the beheading challenge. The host is ultimately revealed as the same figure who wielded the enormous axe at Arthur’s court.

In Aldous Huxley’s dystopian novel, this Western European World Controller meets John the Savage and defends the World State’s censorship and engineered stability. He acknowledges that preserving social order means sacrificing art, freedom, and genuine happiness. Which character is he?

Mustapha Mond is a high-ranking official in this 1932 Aldous Huxley novel, where citizens are divided into biologically engineered castes and conditioned to value consumption and the drug soma. What is the title of the novel?

In Joseph Heller’s World War II satire, this 28-year-old captain serves as a bombardier in the 256th Squadron and keeps trying to be excused from dangerous missions. What is the name of the protagonist stationed on Pianosa?

John Yossarian is the combat-weary bombardier at the center of Joseph Heller’s 1961 satirical novel, in which a paradoxical military rule makes a sane airman’s request to be grounded evidence that he is fit to fly. What is the novel’s title?

John Yossarian flies bombing missions aboard a twin-engine medium bomber used by the Army Air Forces during World War II. The same aircraft type flew the 1942 raid on Tokyo launched from the carrier Hornet; what model was it?
As a child, this fictional woman is taken into Hikaru Genji’s household and raised by him. She later becomes his principal companion, and her death leaves him grieving; what is she known as?
In what classic Japanese court novel is Murasaki adopted by Hikaru Genji and later mourned after her death? The work centers on the “Shining Prince” and depicts aristocratic life in the Heian period.

Published in 1958, this debut novel is set in the fictional Igbo community of Umuofia. It follows an influential leader whose pursuit of strength and status is shaped by his rejection of his father’s life and challenged by Christian missionaries and British rule. Name Chinua Achebe’s novel.

In Things Fall Apart, which celebrated wrestler earns fame after defeating Amalinze the Cat, yet is driven by fear of seeming weak and of resembling his father? His accidental killing of a boy at an elder’s funeral leads to a seven-year exile.

In Things Fall Apart, which boy from Mbaino is sent to Umuofia as a settlement for the killing of a village woman and then lives in Okonkwo’s household? After the oracle orders his execution, Okonkwo strikes the fatal blow despite an elder’s warning not to take part.

In Things Fall Apart, name the village where Okonkwo’s maternal kin shelter him during the seven years of exile imposed after his gun accidentally kills Ezeudu’s son at a funeral. Its location in his mother’s homeland distinguishes it from his home village of Umuofia.
Things Fall Apart takes its title from a line in “The Second Coming,” a 1919 poem whose image of a falcon unable to hear its falconer precedes that line. Name the Irish poet who wrote the poem.

In a cycle of tales associated with One Thousand and One Nights, this Baghdad adventurer returns after seven extraordinary voyages marked by shipwrecks, strange islands, and perilous encounters. He recounts his adventures to a poor porter who shares his name. Who is this legendary voyager?

The tales of Sinbad the Sailor are commonly associated with this framed collection, in which Scheherazade tells stories to postpone her execution, ending each session at a suspenseful moment. What is the collection’s familiar English name?

This Shakespeare tragedy follows a Moorish general in Venetian service whose ensign manipulates him into suspecting his wife of infidelity. A handkerchief becomes false evidence, and the general kills his wife before taking his own life. What is the play’s title?

In Othello, which ensign engineers the general’s jealousy by insinuating that Cassio and Desdemona are lovers and by using Desdemona’s lost handkerchief as supposed proof? Emilia exposes his scheme after discovering the handkerchief. Who is this ensign?

In this poem, the speaker first sees “three long mountains and a wood,” then imagines taking in the whole world and is overwhelmed by its weight. Rain and the scent of an orchard eventually restore her. What is the title of Edna St. Vincent Millay’s breakthrough poem?
Renascence follows a speaker who imagines the world’s suffering, lies in a grave, and experiences renewal after hearing rain and encountering nature’s beauty. Which poet wrote this breakthrough poem?

This 1854 work recounts a deliberate experiment in self-sufficient living at a cabin near a Massachusetts pond, combining practical accounts of daily necessities with reflections on nature and society. Its opening chapter is titled “Economy,” and it includes the observation that many people “lead lives of quiet desperation.” What book is it?
answer: Walden; or, Life in the Woods

question: In Walden; or, Life in the Woods, the narrator builds his cabin on land owned by a Concord essayist who had served as Thoreau’s mentor. That landowner also published Nature, an influential work associated with American Transcendentalism; who was he?
Published in June 1924, this Spanish-language collection helped establish its Chilean author’s fame when he was 19. Its lyrics explore erotic longing, memory, and heartbreak. What is the work?
answer: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair

question: The author of Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair was born Neftalí Ricardo Reyes Basoalto in Chile and later adopted a pen name. He won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature. What name is he best known by?

In 1969, this American poet published an English translation of Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair. He later served as U.S. Poet Laureate and won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry for The Shadow of Sirius. Who was the translator?

In Mary Shelley’s novel, she is raised in the Frankenstein household as Victor’s beloved companion and eventually becomes his wife. The creature murders her on their wedding night to punish Victor. Who is she?
Elizabeth Lavenza is killed by the being created by this Genevan scientist, who studies at Ingolstadt and tells his life story to the Arctic explorer Robert Walton. Who is the scientist?

Published in 1954 as William Golding’s debut novel, this story follows British schoolboys stranded on an uninhabited island as their attempt at self-government collapses into violence. What is the novel’s title?
The 1954 novel Lord of the Flies was this British writer’s first novel. He later received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Literature; who was he?
In Lord of the Flies, which bespectacled, asthmatic boy uses his glasses to help make fire and is killed when a boulder falls on him at Castle Rock?
In J. R. R. Tolkien’s epic fantasy, Frodo carries a powerful artifact from the Shire toward Mount Doom, where it can be destroyed to break Sauron’s power. What novel follows this quest?
In The Lord of the Rings, this Elven refuge is ruled by Elrond and hosts the council where representatives decide the fate of the One Ring. What is the refuge called?

Which Yasunari Kawabata novel follows the detached Tokyo visitor Shimamura on trips to a remote hot-spring town, where he becomes involved with the geisha Komako? First published in installments, it is known for its spare modernist style and wintry landscapes.
Snow Country was written by which Japanese novelist, who received the 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature and also authored The Sound of the Mountain and Thousand Cranes?
In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel, which socially detached flapper is a competitive golfer and a friend of Daisy Buchanan? Nick recalls a report that she moved her ball during a tournament.
Jordan Baker appears in which 1925 F. Scott Fitzgerald novel, whose title character is a wealthy Long Island host famous for lavish parties and his pursuit of Daisy Buchanan?

Which Latin epic by Virgil follows a Trojan survivor who escapes the fall of Troy and journeys to Italy, where his descendants are destined to found Rome? Along the way, he visits Carthage and meets his father in the underworld.
In The Aeneid, which Carthaginian queen welcomes the Trojan refugees and falls in love with their leader? After he leaves to fulfill his destiny in Italy, she dies upon a funeral pyre.
Born in Boston in 1809, this writer became known for Gothic stories, poems, and influential literary criticism. He died in Baltimore in 1849; who was he?

In an Edgar Allan Poe short story, a narrator insists his heightened senses prove he is sane while describing how he murdered an old man because of his pale, film-covered eye. He hides the victim beneath floorboards, but the sound he imagines hearing ultimately makes him confess; what story is it?

Edgar Allan Poe’s poem begins on a dreary midnight in December, as a grieving speaker encounters a bird that repeatedly answers his questions with the same bleak word. The speaker mourns Lenore, and the visitor settles above his chamber door; name this poem.

In Edgar Allan Poe’s The Murders in the Rue Morgue, what is the name of the Parisian amateur detective who solves the apparently impossible murders of Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye by interpreting physical evidence? He also appears in The Mystery of Marie Rogêt and The Purloined Letter.

In an Edgar Allan Poe tale, Montresor claims he will sample a rare vintage with his acquaintance Fortunato, then exploits Fortunato’s vanity and cough to lead him deep into underground catacombs. Which story concludes with Montresor sealing him behind masonry?
In medieval British romances, Gawain serves at the court of this legendary ruler, whose fellowship gathers at the Round Table. He is associated with Camelot and the sword Excalibur. Who is he?

In legends about King Arthur, this prophetic enchanter acts as the king’s adviser and is often credited with arranging for the infant heir to be raised in Sir Ector’s household. What is the name of this figure?

In this 1965 comedy, recently divorced Felix Ungar moves into the apartment of his untidy friend Oscar Madison, a sportswriter whose regular poker games bring a group of friends into the household. What is the name of this play?
Who wrote The Odd Couple, the stage comedy about the contrasting roommates Felix Ungar and Oscar Madison? This American playwright also wrote Barefoot in the Park and Plaza Suite.

In Geoffrey Chaucer’s pilgrimage narrative, this veteran warrior is praised for his honor, generosity, and courtesy, and he has traveled widely on military campaigns. After the pilgrims draw lots, he is chosen to tell the first tale. Who is this pilgrim?
The Knight tells a romance about Palamon and Arcite, rivals who love Emily. Which later play by William Shakespeare and John Fletcher adapts this story?

In Charles Dickens's novel *Great Expectations*, what is the familiar name of the orphaned narrator who is raised by Mrs. Joe and receives a gentleman's education through the secret patronage of Abel Magwitch?

Pip's story of sudden expectations, visits to the reclusive Miss Havisham at Satis House, and complicated attachment to Estella are central to which Charles Dickens novel? The story follows him from childhood in Kent into London society.

Born in Oklahoma City in 1914, this American writer studied music at Tuskegee Institute before moving to New York and becoming associated with the Harlem literary scene. His novel about an unnamed Black narrator won the 1953 National Book Award; who was the novelist and essayist?

In Ralph Ellison’s novel, an unnamed Black narrator recounts his life from a hidden underground room in New York, where he taps electricity from Monopolated Light & Power. The book won the 1953 National Book Award for Fiction; what is its title?
Born in York in 1907 and later a U.S. citizen, this English-American poet wrote “Musée des Beaux Arts” and “September 1, 1939.” Who was he?
In which W. H. Auden poem does the speaker ask for clocks to be stopped and telephones cut off, then describe the deceased as “my North, my South, my East and West”?

Which English novelist and journalist began his major popular success with serial installments in 1836, later used serialized publication for many novels, and wrote about London’s debtors’ prisons and child poverty? His works include a Christmas novella featuring Ebenezer Scrooge and a historical novel set during the French Revolution.

Charles Dickens’s first major publishing success began in monthly installments in 1836 and became a sensation after the introduction of a servant whose catchphrases helped inspire merchandise and spin-offs. What is this comic novel, named for its central gentleman traveler?

Before establishing his fame under his own name, Charles Dickens published sketches and early pieces under a short pen name borrowed from a character in Oliver Goldsmith’s The Vicar of Wakefield. What was that name?
In Charles Dickens’s 1853 novel, the generations-long inheritance lawsuit called Jarndyce and Jarndyce consumes litigants and satirizes the delays of England’s Court of Chancery. What is this novel?

Charles Dickens’s 1843 novella follows a miser visited on a winter holiday’s eve by three spirits representing the past, present, and future. Afterward, he changes how he treats his clerk Bob Cratchit and Cratchit’s son Tiny Tim. What is the title?

What literary genre is primarily set on the nineteenth-century American frontier and often features cowboys, sheriffs or marshals, outlaws, ranch disputes, and conflicts between law and lawlessness? Owen Wister’s 1902 novel helped establish its familiar cowboy hero and climactic shootout.

Which 1902 novel by Owen Wister helped establish Western fiction’s familiar pattern of a cowboy hero, a code of the West, and a climactic shootout? Its title identifies the central cowboy by his home state.

Born and raised in Newark, New Jersey, this American novelist explored Jewish-American identity through comic, self-conscious fiction, including a psychoanalytic confession that brought him wide attention. He also created the recurring writer-character Nathan Zuckerman and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for *American Pastoral*. Who was he?

In Philip Roth’s fiction, this recurring writer-character first appeared in *The Ghost Writer* and later narrates *American Pastoral*, Roth’s Pulitzer-winning novel centered on Seymour “Swede” Levov. What is the character’s name?
In Margaret Atwood’s dystopian novel, this is the name of Gilead’s secret police force, which spies on citizens and enforces the regime’s rules. What is the force called?
In The Handmaid’s Tale, the Eyes are Gilead’s secret police, operating in the theocratic state that controls Offred’s life. Which Canadian author wrote this novel and its sequel, The Testaments?

This Tang dynasty poet wrote “Quiet Night Thoughts,” in which moonlight appears like frost and prompts the speaker to look toward the moon before remembering home. Who was this widely traveled poet, born around 701 and regarded as one of the era’s leading literary figures?

Li Bai met this fellow Tang poet in 744, and the two became friends whose poems referred to one another. Which contemporary poet is also recognized as one of the leading voices of Tang dynasty literature?

In Jeff Kinney’s illustrated middle-grade series, this character is Greg’s older brother and the drummer in the garage band Löded Diper. His habit of teasing Greg makes him a major source of sibling conflict; who is he?

The author of the illustrated series Diary of a Wimpy Kid has said that Rodrick was partly inspired by his own older brother, who played drums in a basement band, while noting that the fictional character differs from his sibling. Who is the author who shared this story?

Published in 1956 under the name of a Massachusetts senator who later became president, this book examines U.S. senators who risked political standing to act on principle. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography; what is its title?

In accounts of the creation of Profiles in Courage, which longtime Kennedy aide—a lawyer and speechwriter who later served as special counsel to the president—is often credited with substantial research and drafting?
In Salman Rushdie’s 1990 children’s novel, a boy journeys to the dark land of Chup to stop Khattam-Shud from poisoning a magical sea. What is the novel’s title?
answer: Haroun and the Sea of Stories

question: Haroun and the Sea of Stories was written by this British-Indian author, whose novel The Satanic Verses prompted Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to issue a fatwa against him in 1989. Who is the author?

First published serially in the Russian magazine *Epoch* in 1864, this novella follows an unnamed former civil servant whose reflections challenge rationalist ideas about human behavior and freedom. What is the work?
Notes from the Underground was written by which Russian novelist, who also created Raskolnikov, the protagonist of *Crime and Punishment*, and the brothers in *The Brothers Karamazov*?

In *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*, which younger brother of Lucy, Susan, and Peter is bribed with enchanted Turkish delight by the White Witch and betrays his siblings by revealing their plans? He later receives Aslan’s forgiveness and fights in the battle to end her rule.

In *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*, Edmund Pevensie passes through a wardrobe into a land held in perpetual winter by the White Witch. What is the name of that country, where Aslan eventually returns?

Geoffrey Chaucer’s unfinished Middle English frame narrative follows pilgrims who set out from a London inn to visit the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket, telling stories along the way. What is the name of this collection?
The Canterbury Tales is considered the major achievement of the poet who also wrote Troilus and Criseyde and The Parlement of Foules. Who was this English writer?
In The Canterbury Tales, what Southwark inn is the gathering place where Harry Bailly proposes a storytelling contest to the pilgrims bound for Canterbury?
The Canterbury Tales begins with this section, which describes April’s spring rains and introduces roughly thirty pilgrims before they tell their stories. What is the section called?

What is the title of Pablo Neruda’s fifteen-part poetry collection that traces the history and landscapes of the Western Hemisphere from a Hispanic American perspective? Its opening section is “A Lamp on Earth.”
Which Chilean poet wrote Canto General and “The Heights of Macchu Picchu,” whose speaker urges, “Arise to birth with me, my brother”?

Published in 1969, this nonlinear antiwar novel draws on its author's experience as a prisoner of war in World War II. Its protagonist moves unpredictably through time and survives the bombing of Dresden. What is the novel's title?

In Slaughterhouse-Five, the protagonist is an American optometrist who serves as a chaplain's assistant during World War II. After being captured by German forces, he recounts being taken to an alien zoo. Who is he?
In Slaughterhouse-Five, Billy Pilgrim is held as a prisoner of war in this German city, which was devastated by Allied bombing in February 1945. What city is central to the novel's wartime events?
In Slaughterhouse-Five, aliens abduct Billy Pilgrim and take him to this planet, where he is placed in a zoo alongside actress Montana Wildhack. What is the planet's name?
In Slaughterhouse-Five, this brief refrain repeatedly follows mentions of death, linking the novel's wartime losses with the many other deaths Billy encounters. What is the refrain?

Created by Dav Pilkey, this children’s-book superhero is the alter ego of an elementary-school principal whom two prank-loving students hypnotize with a ring. What is the name of the character who stars in the series?

In Captain Underpants, what is the name of the stern principal at Jerome Horwitz Elementary School whom George and Harold hypnotize with a 3-D Hypno Ring? He transforms into a costumed superhero whenever he snaps his fingers.
Which American playwright wrote the confrontational 1962 drama in which George and Martha host Nick and Honey, as well as the later play Seascape featuring two human characters and two lizards?

In Edward Albee’s one-act play The Zoo Story, Jerry meets Peter on a bench in Manhattan’s best-known expanse of landscaped greenery, and their encounter ends with Jerry impaling himself on Peter’s knife. What Manhattan landmark is the setting?

A traveler halts beside trees owned by someone who lives in a village, while his horse shakes its harness bells at the unexpected pause. Which Robert Frost poem ends with the speaker repeating that he has promises to keep and miles to go before sleep?
answer: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening

question: The poet of Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening called it his “best bid for remembrance” in a letter to Louis Untermeyer. This same poet wrote “The Road Not Taken” and “Fire and Ice”; what is his name?
Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening was written in 1922 and first published the following year in a volume named for a state in New England. What is the title of that 1923 collection?

This genre of dramatic and performance works aims to amuse audiences and provoke laughter, in contrast to tragedy. It can appear in theatre, books, film, television, radio, and stand-up performance. What is this genre?

In contrast to comedy, this Shakespearean tragedy follows a prince seeking to expose his uncle’s treachery. In the graveyard scene, the prince holds Yorick’s skull and reflects on the dead jester’s wit. Who is the title character?

Comedy in ancient Athens included this play by Aristophanes, whose chorus imitates croaking amphibians. The god Dionysus journeys to the underworld in it to bring a tragic playwright back to life. What is the play’s title?

In Charles Dickens’s *Great Expectations*, the wealthy owner of Satis House has every clock stopped at twenty minutes to nine and continues to wear her decaying bridal gown. What past event is she preserving in this frozen tableau?
In *Great Expectations*, after Miss Havisham’s abandoned wedding, she raises a girl and teaches her to reject love and break men’s hearts. What is the girl’s name?

This ancient Greek epic follows a king’s prolonged voyage back to his island kingdom after the Trojan War. Traditionally divided into 24 books and attributed to the same poet as the Iliad, what is this poem called?

The Odyssey is traditionally credited to the same ancient Greek poet who composed the Iliad, although scholars debate whether the poems were written by one historical individual. What is the name conventionally given to this epic poet?
In The Odyssey, this king of Ithaca spends ten years trying to return from Troy and escapes Polyphemus by claiming that his name is “Nobody.” What is the name of this hero?

In The Odyssey, this queen of Ithaca delays remarriage by weaving a burial cloth by day and secretly undoing it at night, until her husband returns. What is the name of his wife, who tests him after his arrival?
The Odyssey is often discussed as an epic shaped by this Greek idea: a hero’s return to his homeland after absence and wandering. What is the term for this homecoming motif?

In Jane Austen’s 1813 novel, this wealthy gentleman arrives at the Meryton assembly with Charles Bingley and is initially judged proud and disagreeable. He later overcomes his first disastrous proposal and marries Elizabeth Bennet. Who is he?
Fitzwilliam Darcy is one of the central characters in which 1813 novel by Jane Austen, whose opening sentence reflects on a wealthy single man’s supposed need for a wife?
Fitzwilliam Darcy owns an imposing Derbyshire estate that Elizabeth visits with her aunt and uncle, the Gardiners; its grounds and house change her impression of him. What is the estate called?
This American fantasy author created Alagaësia, the setting for a four-volume sequence that begins with Eragon and continues through Eldest, Brisingr, and Inheritance. Who is the author?

In Christopher Paolini’s four-volume young-adult fantasy series, a farm boy discovers a dragon egg, and the hatchling Saphira draws him into the ancient order of dragon Riders. What is the name of the series?

This fourteenth-century English poet helped establish Middle English as a literary language and wrote both *The Canterbury Tales* and *Troilus and Criseyde*. He also served the English crown as a diplomat and civil servant; name him.
In this frame-story collection by Geoffrey Chaucer, a group of pilgrims set out from the Tabard Inn toward the shrine of Thomas Becket and pass the journey telling stories. What is the work’s title?

Geoffrey Chaucer wrote this instructional work in English for his ten-year-old son Lewis. It explains how to use a medieval astronomical instrument to determine time and track celestial positions; what is the work?
In this dream-vision poem by Geoffrey Chaucer, an assembly of birds debates and chooses mates on St. Valentine’s Day. What is the poem’s title?
Geoffrey Chaucer was the first writer buried in this area of Westminster Abbey, which later became a place of commemoration for British writers. What is this section called?

A speaker in this narrative poem finds two paths splitting through a yellow wood and reflects on how choosing one may shape the story he tells about his life. He imagines recounting the choice “ages and ages hence.” What is the poem’s title?
The Road Not Taken was written by the poet whose other works include “Mending Wall” and “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening.” Who was this poet?
The Road Not Taken first appeared in the August 1915 issue of which magazine, before being published the following year in Frost’s collection Mountain Interval?

In Herman Melville’s novel, which first-person sailor is the only member of the Pequod’s crew to survive the final wreck? After Queequeg’s coffin becomes a life buoy, he clings to it until the Rachel rescues him.

Ishmael signs on to this whaling vessel, whose captain nails a gold doubloon to its mast and directs the voyage toward the white whale. The ship is destroyed during the final pursuit. What is its name?

This American novelist, screenwriter, and journalist began his career with short stories before publishing the 1948 novel *Other Voices, Other Rooms*. He later became closely associated with New Journalism and wrote a celebrated account of a Kansas farm-family murder.

Truman Capote spent six years developing this account of the 1959 murders of the Clutter family in Holcomb, Kansas, interviewing convicted killers Perry Smith and Richard Hickock. Often described as a nonfiction novel, it became a landmark of modern true-crime writing.
Truman Capote wrote this novella about Holly Golightly, a young woman who socializes with wealthy New Yorkers. Its 1961 film adaptation starred Audrey Hepburn in the lead role.

Fyodor Dostoevsky’s final novel follows Alyosha, Dmitri, and Ivan through a family crisis centered on their father’s murder, while exploring faith, morality, and free will. What novel was published serially from 1879 to 1880?
In The Brothers Karamazov, what Russian town inspired the novel’s main setting and was where Dostoevsky composed much of the work?
In what periodical did The Brothers Karamazov appear in installments from January 1879 through November 1880?
Bram Stoker introduced this Transylvanian aristocratic vampire as the title antagonist of his 1897 Gothic novel. What is the character’s name?
In Bram Stoker’s novel featuring Count Dracula, which English solicitor keeps a journal of his business journey to the Transylvanian castle, where he becomes the vampire’s prisoner?

Although Bram Stoker may not have known of the connection, later accounts often associate Count Dracula with which 15th-century prince who ruled Wallachia and became notorious for impaling his enemies?

This American playwright and novelist wrote a three-act play in which the Stage Manager narrates the lives of residents of Grover’s Corners, with actors miming many objects on a mostly bare stage. He also wrote a novel about a friar investigating the deaths of five people in the collapse of a Peruvian bridge; who was this author?

In Thornton Wilder’s Pulitzer-winning drama, a Stage Manager introduces a small New Hampshire town and follows Emily Webb and George Gibbs from youth to marriage. Later, Emily returns from the dead to revisit an ordinary day among the living; what is the play?

This Bengali poet and creative polymath became the first non-European recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913. He wrote the lyrics later used for India’s national anthem and translated poems that brought Gitanjali to wide international attention. Who was he?
Rabindranath Tagore founded an experimental school at Santiniketan in 1901, seeking to bring Indian and Western traditions together. What institution did the school become in 1921?

An unnamed speaker insists that heightened perception proves sanity, then recounts stalking an old man for seven nights before killing him over a disturbing eye. After hiding the dismembered body beneath the floorboards, the speaker hears a rhythmic sound and confesses to the police; name the story.
The Tell-Tale Heart was written by the American author who also created Roderick Usher and Montresor. What is that author’s name?
The Tell-Tale Heart first appeared in January 1843 in a literary magazine associated with editor James Russell Lowell. What was the magazine’s title?

In The Tell-Tale Heart, the narrator says the old man had never harmed them and claims the murder was driven by a physical feature, not greed or revenge. What bird-of-prey comparison names the old man’s pale, film-covered eye?

L. M. Montgomery’s novel follows a red-haired orphan whose lively imagination and mishaps transform life after she is mistakenly sent to live with siblings Matthew and Marilla on Prince Edward Island. What is the novel’s title?
In Anne of Green Gables, the older of the two siblings who adopt Anne becomes a devoted father figure and gives her the puffed-sleeve dress she had long wanted. What is his name?

Which Russian drama by Anton Chekhov follows an estate manager whose stagnant life is upended when Professor Serebryakov returns with his much younger wife? The manager’s resentment culminates in a failed attempt to shoot the professor.
In Uncle Vanya, which character is Professor Serebryakov’s daughter and Vanya’s niece, and quietly loves Dr. Astrov? In the final scene, she reassures Vanya that they will work and eventually rest.

A Victorian dramatic monologue opens with wind and rain driving a woman into a cottage, where the speaker watches her tend the fire and arrange her hair. He later describes using her long hair to kill her and sitting beside her body through the night. Name the poem.
In “Porphyria's Lover,” an unnamed speaker delivers a dramatic monologue, a form its poet also used in “My Last Duchess” and “Andrea del Sarto.” Which Victorian poet wrote these works?

Published in 2001, this fantasy novel begins with Shadow leaving prison after his wife’s death and accepting work from a mysterious traveler. What Neil Gaiman novel follows their journey amid a supernatural struggle between deities brought to the United States by immigrants and newer powers shaped by modern culture?

In American Gods, a mysterious con man recruits Shadow shortly after his release from prison, then travels across the country seeking old deities for a brewing supernatural conflict. Which character becomes Shadow’s employer and traveling companion?

This 1940 novel by Ernest Hemingway follows American volunteer Robert Jordan, who works with Republican guerrillas during the Spanish Civil War. Ordered to help destroy a bridge, he falls in love with Maria during the mission. What is the novel?
The title of For Whom the Bell Tolls comes from a passage in Meditation XVII, which includes the phrase “No man is an island.” Who wrote that meditation?

Born in Odense in 1805, this Danish writer published literary fairy tales in nine volumes and also wrote novels, plays, poems, and travelogues. His best-known stories include one about a mermaid who longs to become human and another about a child freezing on New Year’s Eve. Who was he?

In Hans Christian Andersen’s tale, a splinter from a devilish mirror distorts Kai’s sight and lodges in his heart, leading an icy ruler to carry him to her palace. Gerda journeys through a series of dangers to rescue him; what is the title of the story?

Hans Christian Andersen’s homeland has a capital where Edvard Eriksen’s statue of the Little Mermaid stands by the harbor, while Tivoli Gardens is a prominent attraction in the city center. The city is connected to Malmö by the Øresund Bridge; what is it?

In this satirical tale by Hans Christian Andersen, swindlers claim their fabric is invisible to anyone unfit for office or foolish. A child finally punctures the court’s pretense as the ruler processes through the city wearing nothing; what is the story’s title?

Attributed to Homer, this ancient Greek epic is arranged in 24 books and uses dactylic hexameter. Its central action concerns a champion’s wrath during the final weeks of the war at Troy and concludes with Hector’s burial; what poem is it?
In The Iliad, this close companion of Achilles enters battle wearing Achilles’ armor to help repel the Trojans. Hector kills him, and his death prompts Achilles to return to combat; who is he?
In The Iliad, Agamemnon’s seizure of this captive woman from Achilles precipitates the quarrel that drives the poem’s opening action. Who is she?

What Latin term names the narrative technique in which a story opens during ongoing events rather than at its chronological beginning? Horace discusses the technique in his Ars Poetica, and Homeric epics are often cited as examples.
Which Homeric epic, whose action begins with Odysseus detained on Calypso’s island while the gods debate his return to Ithaca, is a classic example of in medias res?

First published in 1759, this French satirical novella sends a sheltered young man through war, disaster, and repeated misfortune while mocking the doctrine that events are arranged for the best. Its ending favors practical work over abstract assurances. What is the work’s title?
