In Candide, a tutor’s confident defense of optimism is repeatedly challenged by suffering and catastrophe. Which French Enlightenment writer created the novella and was imprisoned in the Bastille after criticizing authority?

In Candide, this tutor applies Leibnizian optimism to the hero’s misfortunes, insisting that events fit into the best possible world. He is with the young man at Baron Thunder-ten-Tronckh’s castle before both are cast out; name the tutor.

In Candide, Candide and Cacambo reach a secluded country where gold and jewels are so common that people treat them as ordinary stones. They eventually leave with red sheep laden with treasure; what is this fabled country called?
Which 18th-century Chinese novel follows Jia Baoyu and portrays the decline of the aristocratic Jia family? It is traditionally counted among China's Four Great Classical Novels.

In Dream of the Red Chamber, which precious material appears in Jia Baoyu’s name and is associated with the stone he carries from birth? In Chinese traditions, this stone is often carved into pendants and associated with virtue and protection.
Published in 1929, this novel follows an American ambulance volunteer on the Italian front during World War I. Its wartime narrative is intertwined with his relationship with an English nurse.
In A Farewell to Arms, which English nurse meets American ambulance driver Frederic Henry during World War I and becomes his romantic partner?

Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 story follows an unnamed woman whose physician husband confines her to an upstairs room after childbirth and discourages her from writing. As she studies the room's patterned wall covering, she becomes convinced a woman is moving behind it; what is the story's title?

In The Yellow Wallpaper, the narrator’s husband John forbids her from writing and prescribes isolation and near-total inactivity to address her postpartum condition. What nineteenth-century treatment, famously associated with physician Silas Weir Mitchell, does this regimen represent?
In this short story, the universe is imagined as a vast arrangement of hexagonal rooms containing every possible 410-page book made from a fixed set of characters. What is the story’s title?
The Library of Babel is one of the works of this Argentine author, who was also a librarian and wrote “The Aleph” and “The Garden of Forking Paths.” Who is he?

The Library of Babel first appeared in Spanish in this 1941 Borges collection, whose title translates as The Garden of Forking Paths; the collection was later included in Ficciones. What is the earlier collection’s Spanish title?
answer: El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan

question: In Mark Twain’s satirical novel, a nineteenth-century American firearms-factory superintendent is knocked unconscious and wakes in the Britain of a legendary medieval king. He tries to use modern technology and ideas to transform the society he finds there. What is the novel’s title?
answer: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court

question: In A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, the central character is a nineteenth-century superintendent at a Connecticut firearms factory who is knocked unconscious in a fight and awakens in King Arthur’s Britain. What is his name?

The author of an 1851 novel follows Ishmael aboard the whaling ship Pequod, commanded by Captain Ahab. The same writer created a Wall Street copyist who persistently declines his employer’s requests. Who was this American author?
Herman Melville’s first book was a travel-adventure narrative inspired by his stay among island communities in the Marquesas; its sequel was Omoo. What is the title of that first book?
In 1841, Herman Melville joined a whaling voyage aboard this vessel, which he later left in the Marquesas Islands. What was the name of the ship?

Set in a Wall Street law office, this Herman Melville story centers on a copyist whose repeated, polite refusals disrupt his employer’s routine. The clerk ultimately dies in prison. What is the story’s title?

Herman Melville left this work unfinished at his death, and it was published posthumously in 1924. It follows a young crewman who kills the master-at-arms after being falsely accused of mutiny, then is sentenced to death by Captain Vere. What is the work’s title?

What modernist novel follows its narrator from childhood in Combray through his relationships and artistic development? Its opening section recalls a madeleine dipped in tea, while an earlier childhood episode features a magic lantern projecting the story of Golo and Geneviève de Brabant onto a bedroom wall.
In In Search of Lost Time, Bloch admires a line from this French tragedian’s play Phèdre for its “supreme merit of meaning absolutely nothing.” The line refers to the daughter of Minos and Pasiphaë.

First published in 1894, this is a collection rather than a continuous novel, pairing stories about Mowgli with independent animal tales, including one about a mongoose defending a family from cobras. Its prose is accompanied by poems and songs.
The Jungle Book was written by this British author, who also wrote Kim and the poem “Gunga Din.” He became the first English-language writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Margaret Atwood’s sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale alternates among the accounts of Aunt Lydia, Agnes, and Daisy, using their testimonies to illuminate Gilead’s downfall. What is the title of this novel?

In The Testaments, one of the three narrators records a secret history in the Ardua Hall Holograph and uses her authority within Gilead’s inner leadership to help expose the regime. Which character is this?

This Japanese travel diary recounts Matsuo Bashō’s journey through the northern region of Oku, weaving prose passages with haiku. Its first edition appeared posthumously in 1702; what work is it known as in English?
answer: The Narrow Road to the Deep North

question: The Narrow Road to the Deep North combines travel prose with haiku, a pairing associated with a particular Japanese literary form. What is this prose-and-haiku form called?
The Narrow Road to the Deep North was composed by the Japanese poet who wrote the famous old-pond verse in which a frog jumps into water. Identify that poet.
William Carlos Williams shaped a five-book modernist poem around a New Jersey city’s streets, history, and changing relationship between language and place. Which city gives the poem its title?

The five-volume modernist poem Paterson links the city’s physical landscape to questions of history and language. Its author also wrote “The Red Wheelbarrow” and “This Is Just to Say”; who was this poet?
This four-act psychological drama, first performed in 1891, follows a newly married woman who burns Eilert Løvborg’s manuscript and later dies by suicide. What is the play’s title?
The four-act psychological drama Hedda Gabler was written by this Norwegian playwright, whose other works include A Doll’s House and The Wild Duck. Who is he?

In Murasaki Shikibu’s Heian-period court novel, the son of Emperor Kiritsubo gives up imperial status and receives the Minamoto surname. Celebrated for beauty so exceptional that it inspires an epithet meaning “Shining,” what is the name of this central fictional protagonist?
In Murasaki Shikibu’s story of Hikaru Genji, which emperor is his father and favors Genji’s mother, a woman of lower court rank?

Which Euripidean tragedy depicts the god of wine arriving in Thebes, where King Pentheus rejects his worship and is ultimately killed by ecstatic female followers? Its title refers to those devotees collectively.

In The Bacchae, which young king of Thebes tries to suppress the visiting god’s rites and disguises himself to spy on the women on Mount Cithaeron? His mother Agave mistakenly brings his severed head back to the city.

James Baldwin’s essay argues that fiction written to advance social reform can reduce complex people to symbols, and criticizes both the violence of Richard Wright’s *Native Son* and the sentimentality of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s antislavery writing. What is the title of this essay?

In “Everybody’s Protest Novel,” Baldwin calls the protagonist of Richard Wright’s *Native Son* a descendant of a character in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s antislavery novel titled for that character’s cabin. Which character does Baldwin identify as the predecessor?
In this World War II novel narrated by Death, a foster girl in Nazi Germany steals books and shares them with a Jewish man hidden in her family’s basement. What is the novel called?
The Book Thief was written by an Australian novelist whose other works include I Am the Messenger and Bridge of Clay. What is his name?
Which novel is narrated by an orphan whose fortunes change after he encounters an escaped convict in a Kent churchyard? Charles Dickens’s story first appeared in serial form in 1860–61.
Who wrote Great Expectations, first publishing it in his weekly periodical All the Year Round? This Victorian novelist also created Ebenezer Scrooge and Oliver Twist.
In Great Expectations, who narrates the story as an orphan raised by his sister and her kind blacksmith husband? After a secret benefactor pays for his move to London, he tries to become a gentleman.

In Great Expectations, which escaped convict confronts the young narrator in a churchyard and demands food and a file? Years later, this man’s fortune becomes the secret source of the narrator’s new expectations.

In Great Expectations, who raises Estella at Satis House and tries to shape her into a heartbreaker? She remains in her old wedding dress and keeps her clocks stopped after being abandoned on her wedding day.
Born in 1832 and raised in New England in a family associated with transcendentalism, this American writer drew on her childhood with three sisters for her best-known novel. Who was she?
Louisa May Alcott served as a nurse during the American Civil War and later drew on that experience in this work, which brought her critical success in the 1860s. What is the title of the work?
Louisa May Alcott sometimes published adult sensation novels and lurid short stories under this pen name, rather than her own name. What was the pseudonym?

In this short lyric, the speaker invites another outsider into a private alliance and mocks public fame by comparing a celebrated person to a frog croaking to an admiring bog. What poem presents this playful contrast between being unknown and being “Somebody”?

The poem “I’m Nobody! Who are you?” was written by a reclusive 19th-century poet from Amherst, Massachusetts. The same poet wrote “Because I could not stop for Death” and “I heard a Fly buzz—when I died.” Who was she?

Published in 1981, this South African political novel follows Bam and Maureen Smales and their children as they flee a violent revolution and take refuge in the village of their Black servant, who had worked for them in the city. What is the novel’s title?
Nadine Gordimer, author of July’s People, was named the 1991 laureate of this prize, awarded by the Swedish Academy. What is the prize’s full name?

This English novelist and poet also worked as an architect, and many of his tragic novels are set in a semi-fictional region of southern England. His works include *Far from the Madding Crowd* and *Tess of the d’Urbervilles*; who was he?

Thomas Hardy set many novels in this semi-fictional region, rooted in a medieval Anglo-Saxon kingdom and later encompassing parts of Dorset, Wiltshire, Somerset, Devon, Hampshire, and Berkshire. What is the name of this literary setting?

In this Thomas Hardy novel, a stonemason from rural Wessex dreams of a scholarly life in Christminster, the author’s fictional version of Oxford, but encounters barriers of class and circumstance. What is the novel’s title?

In Ernest Cline’s *Ready Player One*, players scour the OASIS for the Easter Egg hidden by its creator, James Halliday. What informal name is given to these dedicated egg hunters, in contrast to the Sixers working for IOI?

In *Ready Player One*, the Gunters’ hunt for Halliday’s Easter Egg is opposed by the Sixers, who are recruited and equipped by a corporation seeking control of the OASIS. What three-letter abbreviation names that corporation?

Beginning in 1732, this annual publication combined calendar information with weather forecasts and practical advice, and became especially famous for witty aphorisms that entered common use. Which work did Benjamin Franklin publish annually under a literary persona?
Poor Richard's Almanack was presented as the work of a fictional almanac-maker and astrologer, rather than being signed openly by its actual publisher. What name did Franklin give this persona?

In Charlotte Brontë’s novel, she is Edward Rochester’s first wife, kept in an upper room at Thornfield Hall under Grace Poole’s watch. Her escape and the fire she sets reveal the secret that prevents Rochester from marrying Jane. Who is this character?
In *Jane Eyre*, Bertha Mason escapes confinement and sets fire to the estate where Rochester lives and plans to marry Jane. What is the name of this estate?

In Mark Twain’s novel *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer*, this girl is the daughter of a local judge and rejects Tom’s proposal after learning he had been engaged to Amy Lawrence. Later, she and Tom become lost together in McDougal’s Cave. Who is she?

Becky Thatcher appears in this 1876 novel set in the fictional town of St. Petersburg, Missouri, where she and Tom Sawyer become lost in McDougal’s Cave. The novel’s author also wrote *The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn*. What is the author’s name?
In Margaret Atwood’s novel set in the Republic of Gilead, women who indoctrinate, discipline, and supervise the Handmaids hold a title drawn from a family relationship. What is that title?
Among the Aunts in Margaret Atwood’s *The Handmaid’s Tale*, which stern instructor oversees the Red Center where Offred and other Handmaids are trained, and later narrates part of *The Testaments*?

Robert Louis Stevenson’s *Treasure Island* is chiefly narrated by the young son of the Admiral Benbow innkeeper, who discovers the map among Billy Bones’s belongings and later hides in an apple barrel aboard the treasure ship to overhear Long John Silver’s mutiny plans. What is this cabin boy’s name?

On Jim Hawkins’s voyage to the island, this ship carries Squire Trelawney’s expedition and is captained by Alexander Smollett. Jim hides in an apple barrel aboard it and overhears Long John Silver’s mutiny plans. What is the ship called?

Published in 1962, this Madeleine L’Engle novel follows Meg Murry, Calvin O’Keefe, and Charles Wallace as they cross vast interstellar distances to rescue Meg’s missing father from a planet ruled by a sinister intelligence. What is the novel’s title?

In A Wrinkle in Time, what is the name of the planet where Meg, Calvin, and Charles Wallace encounter Charles Wallace under the control of the novel’s tyrannical intelligence? Its identical houses and children bouncing balls in perfect unison reflect the world’s enforced conformity.
Carl Sandburg’s brief imagist poem places a silent, catlike presence over a harbor, arriving on little feet. What atmospheric phenomenon is the poem named for?

The poem “Fog” turns its subject into a cat moving quietly over a harbor. Its author also wrote “Chicago,” whose famous portrait calls the city “Hog Butcher for the World” and “City of the Big Shoulders.” Who was this American poet?
This 1959 novel by Günter Grass follows Oskar Matzerath, who decides at age three to stop growing and narrates his life amid the upheavals of twentieth-century Europe. What is the novel’s title?
In The Tin Drum, the central character receives a drum at age three and thereafter refuses to grow, later using his shrill screams to shatter glass. What is this character’s name?
In Harper Lee’s novel set in Maycomb, Alabama, this household centers on a lawyer who defends Tom Robinson and his two children, one of whom narrates the story. What is the family called?
In the Finch family’s Maycomb neighborhood, which reclusive man leaves small gifts for the children in a tree’s knothole? He later carries them to safety when Bob Ewell attacks them.

An American writer whose fiction includes many stories about the Glass family also created a celebrated novel about a disaffected teenager expelled from prep school. What writer, born Jerome David and known by his initials and surname, wrote these works?

In J. D. Salinger’s best-known novel, a Pencey Prep student expelled shortly before Christmas wanders Manhattan, criticizes “phonies,” and seeks out his younger sister Phoebe. What novel follows this teenager’s narration?

In a novel by J. D. Salinger, this teenager is expelled from Pencey Prep, remembers his late brother Allie, and asks cabdrivers where Central Park’s ducks go in winter. What is the name of the narrator who goes to visit Phoebe in Manhattan?

J. D. Salinger’s 1948 New Yorker story centers on Seymour Glass, who befriends a young girl named Sybil at a Florida resort before the story ends with his death. What story takes its title from an unusual image Seymour describes to Sybil?
J. D. Salinger’s 1953 collection opens with his story about Seymour Glass and also includes “For Esmé—with Love and Squalor.” What short-story collection brings these pieces together?

This Russian physician and writer said that a writer’s duty was to state problems correctly rather than solve them. He wrote The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard; who was he?

In this play by Anton Chekhov, aspiring actress Nina gives the writer Trigorin a medallion bearing a message that he may take her life if he needs it. Rejected by Nina, Konstantin Treplev later dies by suicide. Name the play.

In this play by Anton Chekhov, Lopakhin buys the estate belonging to Madame Ranevskaya and announces that the estate’s grove of trees will be cut down. The sound of trees being felled closes the drama. Name the play.
In 1898, this theater company staged a celebrated revival of Anton Chekhov’s play after its poor reception in 1896. Konstantin Stanislavski was associated with the production. Name the company.

In this Anton Chekhov story, a Moscow banker named Gurov meets Anna Sergeyevna while she is staying in Yalta with a small dog. Their relationship continues after they return to their separate lives. Name the story.

This Belgian refugee and former police officer becomes a private detective whose investigations rely on method, psychology, and his celebrated “little grey cells.” His immaculate appearance and carefully groomed moustache are among his signature traits. Who is this Agatha Christie character?
Hercule Poirot made his published debut in this 1920 mystery, Agatha Christie’s first novel. Set at an English country estate, it centers on the poisoning of wealthy Emily Inglethorp. Name the novel.
Eugene O’Neill reshaped the Oresteia as a three-play family tragedy set in post-Civil War New England, replacing the House of Atreus with the Mannon family. What is the title of this cycle of plays?

Beyond writing Mourning Becomes Electra, this American dramatist created The Iceman Cometh, in which traveling salesman Hickey upends the regulars at Harry Hope’s saloon by confessing he killed his wife. Who was this playwright?

What 1854 narrative poem commemorates the doomed British cavalry’s advance at Balaklava during the Crimean War? Its six stanzas repeatedly invoke the “six hundred” and include the line “Someone had blunder’d.”
answer: The Charge of the Light Brigade

question: The Charge of the Light Brigade was written soon after news of the Battle of Balaklava reached London. Which British poet also wrote “Crossing the Bar” and “Ulysses”?

This sixteen-year-old narrator is expelled from a Pennsylvania prep school and spends several days wandering New York City. He dislikes people he considers “phonies” and asks a cab driver where the Central Park ducks go in winter. Who is this protagonist?

Holden Caulfield narrates this 1951 novel, recounting his departure from Pencey Prep and his unsettled days in New York City. Its title comes from his imagined role of catching children before they fall from a rye field’s edge. What is the novel?
Holden Caulfield was created by this American author, who also wrote “A Perfect Day for Bananafish” and the Glass family stories. The author published The Catcher in the Rye in 1951. Who was he?
Holden Caulfield’s younger sister is an intelligent, red-haired child who is upset when she learns he has been expelled. He watches her ride a carousel near the end of the novel. What is her name?

Holden Caulfield is expelled from this fictional boys’ school in Agerstown, Pennsylvania, after failing most of his subjects. Before leaving, he loses the fencing team’s equipment on a New York subway. What is the school called?

A short story follows George and Lydia Hadley, whose automated home includes a nursery that projects whatever their children imagine. When the parents try to shut down an African grassland scene populated by lions, the nursery turns the children’s play into a deadly trap; what is the story’s title?

In The Veldt, Peter and Wendy Hadley become fixated on a nursery that renders an African savanna so convincingly that their parents seek help from psychologist David McClean. What American writer created this story and also wrote Fahrenheit 451?
Judy Blume's children's novels follow Peter Hatcher as he copes with his mischievous younger brother, Farley Drexel, and a family turtle named Dribble. What is the name of this series?
In the Fudge series, what is the name of the older brother who narrates Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing and often finds himself exasperated by his younger sibling's antics?

This 1929 novel traces the decline of a Mississippi family through sections told from differing perspectives, including those of Benjy, Quentin, and Jason Compson. Its final section centers on Dilsey, a longtime member of the household. What is the novel’s title?
The Sound and the Fury is among the novels set in Yoknapatawpha County by which American writer? He also wrote As I Lay Dying, about the Bundren family’s journey to bury Addie.

A leading 19th-century American regionalist, this writer drew on California Gold Rush camps and frontier life in stories such as “The Outcasts of Poker Flat” and “The Luck of Roaring Camp.” Who was this author?
In a story by Bret Harte, a baby is born to Cherokee Sal in an isolated California mining settlement, and the miners take responsibility for raising him. What is the title of this story?

In Gwendolyn Brooks’s “We Real Cool,” seven pool players speak in clipped, defiant lines from a named Chicago pool hall. Terrance Hayes later borrowed that venue’s name for a poetic form built around the final words of its lines; what is the hall called?
The Golden Shovel is a poetic form in which the end words of a newly written poem follow the words of an existing poem. Which American poet introduced the form in his 2010 collection *Lighthead*?

In Alan Paton's novel set in South Africa, this young man is the son of a rural priest who travels to Johannesburg to find him. After taking part in a burglary at Arthur Jarvis's home, he shoots Jarvis and is sentenced to death. Who is he?
Absalom Kumalo is the son of this Zulu Anglican priest from Ndotsheni, who journeys to Johannesburg after learning that his son is missing. What is the priest's name?

Published in 1952, this novella follows an aging Cuban fisherman through a days-long struggle to catch a giant marlin. It first appeared in full in *Life* magazine before Scribner’s released it as a book. What is its title?
answer: The Old Man and the Sea

question: In *The Old Man and the Sea*, an elderly Cuban fisherman sets out alone after going many days without catching a fish. What is the name of the fisherman who hooks the great marlin?

In *The Old Man and the Sea*, this boy had fished with Santiago before his parents made him join another boat, which they considered luckier. He later brings food to the old fisherman and finds him asleep after his return. What is the boy’s name?

In 1953, *The Old Man and the Sea* received an annual American literary honor administered by Columbia University and established through the will of a Hungarian-American newspaper publisher. What award did the novella win?
This sonnet begins with its speaker reflecting that his “light is spent” and considers how he can serve God after losing his sight. By what title is the poem commonly known?
On His Blindness is a sonnet by an English poet who also wrote Paradise Lost, an epic about Satan’s rebellion and the Fall of humanity. Which poet wrote both works?

In John Steinbeck’s novella, this powerful ranch laborer travels with George and dreams of tending rabbits on a farm. After accidentally killing Curley’s wife, he waits at a riverside clearing, where George finds him before the other ranch hands arrive. Who is this character?

Lennie Small’s closest companion is a quick-witted ranch hand who repeatedly protects him from trouble and shares his dream of owning a farm. In the novella’s final scene, this man speaks to Lennie about their plans before shooting him. Who is he?

Which 1927 British modernist novel follows the Ramsay family at their Scottish summer house before and after World War I? Its three sections move from a family's anticipated outing, through years of absence and loss, to the surviving characters' completion of a long-delayed trip to a coastal beacon.
The author of To the Lighthouse also wrote Mrs Dalloway and the essay A Room of One’s Own. Which English writer created the Ramsay family and published the novel in 1927?

In To the Lighthouse, what Scottish island is the setting for the Ramsay family’s summer visits? Its rocky coastline is where their summer house stands, near the destination of Mr. Ramsay’s repeatedly postponed excursion.

In To the Lighthouse, the narration shifts among the perceptions of several members of the Ramsay family, giving their private thoughts more prominence than spoken exchanges. What narrative technique describes this movement among different points of view?

This early 11th-century Japanese court novel follows a brilliant imperial son who is removed from the line of succession and given the surname Minamoto. Its later sections move beyond his life to the stories of Kaoru and Niou. What is the title of this work?

The Tale of Genji is traditionally attributed to this Heian-period noblewoman, poet, and lady-in-waiting. She is also known for keeping a court diary that records daily activities and observations of life at court. Who was she?

The Tale of Genji was written mostly in this Japanese phonetic script, which was associated with women’s writing during the Heian period. It was used instead of relying mainly on the more prestigious kanji script. What is this script called?
This British scholar produced an almost complete English translation of The Tale of Genji between 1925 and 1933, though he omitted chapter 38. Who was this translator?

The original physical format of The Tale of Genji consisted of sheets pasted together and folded alternately in opposite directions, creating a concertina-like book. What is the Japanese name for this format?

Published in 1962, this book by Rachel Carson exposed the ecological and wildlife hazards of synthetic pesticides, especially DDT. Its warnings helped spur the modern environmental movement. What is the book’s title?
Silent Spring described how birds exposed to DDT laid these reproductive structures with abnormally thin shells, making them more likely to break before hatching. What structures were affected?
Which Samuel Beckett play is the bleak absurdist drama in which Hamm and his servant Clov inhabit a sealed room, while Nagg and Nell emerge from ashbins?
In Endgame, which blind, wheelchair-bound character directs Clov’s actions from the center of the room and is cared for by Nagg and Nell?

In Lincoln Peirce’s comic series, this stern social studies teacher at Public School 38 is a frequent nemesis of Nate Wright. Nate’s hostility toward her leads him to use nicknames such as “Godzilla.” Who is she?

Clara Godfrey is a stern social studies teacher at Public School 38 in a Lincoln Peirce comic series, where the class-clown protagonist often gets detentions and spends time with friends Teddy and Francis. What is the series called?
In a Dickinson lyric, this autonomous inner self “selects her own Society” and then “shuts the Door” against an unwelcome visitor. What recurring concept is portrayed this way?

Alongside her poems about the Soul, Emily Dickinson wrote a lyric narrated by a speaker accompanied by a courteous driver in a carriage. Their route passes a school, fields, and the setting sun; what is the poem’s title?
answer: “Because I could not stop for Death”

question: This English mystery writer created Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple. Her works include *The Mysterious Affair at Styles* and *The Murder at the Vicarage*. Who was she?
Agatha Christie’s Belgian detective is famous for referring to his “little grey cells.” He investigates the stabbing of Samuel Ratchett aboard a train stranded by snow. What is his name?
Agatha Christie’s murder-mystery play began as a radio play called *Three Blind Mice* and opened on the London stage in 1952. What is the play’s title?

In this Agatha Christie novel, ten strangers are summoned to an isolated island off the Devon coast. Their deaths echo a nursery rhyme, and figurines on the dining-room table disappear one by one. What is the novel?
Agatha Christie introduced this elderly amateur sleuth from the village of St Mary Mead in *The Murder at the Vicarage*. What is the character’s name?

Published as a children’s fantasy series under the collective pseudonym Erin Hunter, this saga follows groups of wild cats organized into rival Clans. Its books include subseries such as The Prophecies Begin. What is the series called?

In Warriors, the four living Clans seek guidance from a spiritual Clan believed to consist of their deceased ancestors. Medicine cats act as intermediaries with this group and look to it for signs. What is this ancestral Clan called?

Ernest Hemingway described prose that presents only a small part of a story’s meaning explicitly, leaving readers to infer much of what remains unstated. What is this minimalist literary technique called?
The Iceberg Theory is closely associated with the American novelist who wrote *The Old Man and the Sea* and *A Farewell to Arms*. Who is this author?

In Philip Roth’s 2000 novel, a longtime classics professor at Athena College loses his position after students interpret his literal description of two absent students as a racial insult. As Nathan Zuckerman recounts the professor’s concealed past and its consequences, what is the novel’s title?

In The Human Stain, which former dean and classics professor at Athena College is at the center of a scandal over the word “spooks,” and whose concealed Black ancestry makes passing central to his story?
Published in 1953, this was Ian Fleming’s first novel featuring an MI6 agent known as 007. Its central mission has the agent try to ruin a financially powerful opponent in a baccarat game.

In Casino Royale, what French-named agent of SMERSH is the target of Bond’s effort to bankrupt him at baccarat? He manages a large financial network and seeks to recover his losses at the gaming table.

He is the Italian writer behind *Cosmicomics*, whose recurring character Qfwfq appears in stories that blend scientific ideas and fable. His experimental novel begins by directly addressing a reader about to read a book titled *If on a Winter’s Night a Traveler*. Who is this author?

In Italo Calvino’s 1972 novel, Marco Polo reports fantastical destinations to the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan; the chapters are arranged in recurring thematic groupings. What is the title of this work?

Set in the dystopian nation of Panem, this novel follows District 12 tributes Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark as they compete in a nationally televised fight to the death. What is the title of Suzanne Collins’s book?

In The Hunger Games, which former victor from District 12 is assigned to mentor Katniss and Peeta before the 74th Games? Known for his heavy drinking and cynicism, he urges them to avoid the initial bloodbath at the Cornucopia.
Which American novelist drew extensively on upper-class New York society in works including *The Age of Innocence* and *Ethan Frome*? She won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for the former novel.
In Edith Wharton's *The Age of Innocence*, which New York lawyer is engaged to May Welland but becomes increasingly drawn to her cousin Ellen Olenska after seeing her at a performance of *Faust*?

In a landmark early-20th-century dramatic monologue, the speaker imagines awkward social encounters, frets about growing older, and wonders whether he dares to eat a peach. What is the full name of this hesitant speaker?
J. Alfred Prufrock is the speaker in a poem whose social scene includes women discussing Michelangelo and whose title calls itself a love song. Which modernist poet also wrote *The Waste Land*?

Which Henry James novella, first published in 1898, follows an unnamed governess hired to care for Miles and Flora at an isolated English estate? There, she believes the children are being visited by the dead former valet Peter Quint and former governess Miss Jessel.

The Turn of the Screw first appeared as a serial in Collier’s Weekly in 1898 and was later published alongside “The Jolly Corner” in a volume titled The Two Magics. Which American-born author wrote it?

Tradition credits this ancient Greek poet with composing two foundational epic poems, one centered on the Trojan War and the other on a hero’s long journey home. His historical identity remains uncertain.

Homer is traditionally credited with an epic that opens by asking the Muse to sing of a warrior’s anger. Its plot centers on a quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles during the Trojan War. What is this poem?
In Homer’s other major attributed epic, a Greek hero encounters the Cyclops Polyphemus and the enchantress Circe while trying to return to his wife and son in Ithaca. What is this poem?
The uncertain identity of Homer, and the debate over whether one poet composed both of his traditionally attributed epics, are central to what scholarly debate?
The poems attributed to Homer use a literary language blending Ionic and Aeolic features, with predominantly Eastern Ionic influence. What is this language commonly called?

This Indian-born novelist earned a history degree from the University of Cambridge in 1968 and was knighted in 2007 for services to literature. His 2012 memoir recounts the years he spent living under threat following a controversy over one of his novels. Who is this author?

In Salman Rushdie’s 1981 novel, Saleem Sinai is born at the precise moment India gains independence and later discovers a telepathic connection to other people born in that hour. The book won the Booker Prize in its publication year. What is the novel?

Salman Rushdie’s 1988 novel begins with Gibreel Farishta and Saladin Chamcha surviving the explosion of an airliner. Its controversial reception led Iran’s Ruhollah Khomeini to issue a fatwa calling for the author’s death in 1989. Name this novel.

This 2012 memoir by Salman Rushdie recounts the effects of a fatwa and his years living under police protection, including his adoption of a cover identity during that period. What is the memoir called?
In an 1844 adventure novel, this young Gascon travels to Paris hoping to join the king’s musketeers and soon befriends Athos, Porthos, and Aramis. What is the name of the protagonist?

Which 1844 Alexandre Dumas novel follows d’Artagnan as he joins forces with Athos, Porthos, and Aramis, while they contend with the schemes of Cardinal Richelieu’s agents? Its title refers to the three companions rather than the newcomer.

In Flannery O’Connor’s 1953 short story, this escaped convict explains his nickname by saying the punishment he received did not fit his crime. He debates the consequences of Jesus’ resurrection with the grandmother before his associates kill her family. What is this character called?

In the short story featuring The Misfit, the grandmother and her family set out from Atlanta for Florida, then crash on a Georgia back road where the escaped convict catches up with them. What is this Flannery O’Connor short story called?
answer: “A Good Man Is Hard to Find”

question: What fantasy-novel series follows a young wizard through his education at a school of magic, where he and his friends confront the dark wizard responsible for his parents’ deaths?
In the Harry Potter series, what is the boarding school of witchcraft and wizardry where the title character studies and students are sorted into Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, or Slytherin?

Born in Skien in 1828, this Norwegian playwright became a leading figure of nineteenth-century drama and helped make social realism central to modern theater. His major works include Brand, Peer Gynt, and Ghosts. Who was he?

Henrik Ibsen's drama centers on Nora Helmer, who secretly borrows money and forges her father's signature to finance a journey intended to save her husband. After Torvald reacts with self-interest rather than the moral courage she expected, she leaves their home in the play's final scene; what is the play?

In a Henrik Ibsen drama, the title character is married to scholar George Tesman and is later trapped by Judge Brack after burning Eilert Lovborg's manuscript. Her circumstances end in suicide; name the play.

Henrik Ibsen first won broad recognition with this verse drama, whose restless title figure encounters trolls, travels widely, and is eventually confronted with the consequences of a life spent avoiding a true self. Solveig remains devoted to him through the play; what is this work?
Henrik Ibsen was born in Skien, in a Scandinavian country whose capital was called Christiania during much of his lifetime and is now known as Oslo. What was his native country?

Created by H. P. Lovecraft and introduced in a 1928 short story, this Great Old One is linked to an ancient cult and strange dreams. A sculpted image depicts it with a tentacled head, a scaly body, and rudimentary wings; name this figure associated with the sunken city of R’lyeh.
In “The Call of Cthulhu,” investigators connect disturbing dreams and an ancient cult to a vast creature beneath a sunken stone city. What is the name of the city where Cthulhu waits dreaming?

This fifth-century BCE Athenian tragedian wrote a surviving trilogy that begins with the murder of Agamemnon and ends with the establishment of a court to judge Orestes. In Aristophanes’ The Frogs, he defeats Euripides in a contest and is chosen to return from the underworld. Who is he?

Aeschylus wrote this trilogy of tragedies, whose three plays follow the aftermath of Agamemnon’s homecoming, Orestes’ revenge for his father, and the resolution of the resulting cycle of violence in Athens. What is the trilogy called?

Which British playwright, awarded the 2005 Nobel Prize in Literature, wrote The Birthday Party and The Homecoming? His spare dialogue, charged pauses, and atmosphere of menace became hallmarks of his drama.

In which Harold Pinter one-act play do the hitmen Ben and Gus wait in a basement while receiving increasingly strange food orders through a speaking tube? The play ends with one of them hearing a whistle from the tube.

What Latin title is given to Horace’s didactic poem addressed to the Pisos, which sets out principles of poetic composition? It mocks an artistically incoherent figure made by joining a horse’s neck to a human head.
In Ars Poetica, the author discusses how poets should shape their work and avoid jarring combinations. Which Roman poet also wrote the Odes and the line “dulce et decorum est pro patria mori”?
Maya Angelou’s poem contrasts a creature free to claim the sky with another confined behind bars, whose song expresses longing for freedom. What is the poem’s title?
In “Caged Bird,” which American poet and memoirist contrasts a bird able to fly freely with one confined behind bars and singing for freedom?

In Book 18 of the Iliad, after Patroclus’s death leaves the Greek hero without his armor, this object is made at Thetis’s request. Homer describes it as bearing scenes of the heavens, two cities, agriculture, and dancing.
In the Iliad’s episode about the Shield of Achilles, which Olympian craftsman makes replacement armor for Achilles after Thetis appeals to him?

Stories featuring magic, supernatural forces, invented worlds, and mythic or heroic elements belong to what broad literary genre? J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings and Terry Pratchett’s Discworld books are well-known examples.

Within fantasy literature, which British author created Discworld, where four elephants carry a world atop a giant turtle? The inept wizard Rincewind first appeared in this author’s novel The Colour of Magic.
This English novelist and essayist wrote a 1945 allegory about farm animals who overthrow their human owner and a dystopian novel set under the rule of Big Brother. What pen name did he use?

George Orwell’s 1945 allegorical novella begins with a rebellion against Mr. Jones by the creatures he owns. The pigs later take power and alter the commandments that were meant to guide their community. What is the novella’s title?

In George Orwell’s dystopian novel, Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth, where he revises historical records to match the Party’s claims. The regime’s slogans include “War is Peace” and “Freedom is Slavery.” What is the novel’s title?

George Orwell’s account of serving with a militia on the Republican side of the Spanish Civil War recounts both his experiences at the front and political conflict in Barcelona. What is the title of this nonfiction book?
In George Orwell’s 1937 nonfiction book, he investigates poverty and working-class life in industrial northern England, including the conditions faced by coal miners. What is the title of this work?

In Lewis Carroll’s *Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland*, this feline talks with Alice while perched in a tree and offers her directions through Wonderland. It can disappear gradually, leaving its smile visible after the rest of it is gone. What character is it?
The Cheshire Cat is among the strange inhabitants Alice meets in a fantasy novel first published in 1865. What pen name did the English author of *Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland* use?

In this lyric, an abstract virtue is imagined as a small bird that perches in the soul and sings through storms. The speaker notes that it has never asked for even a crumb in return for its comfort. What is the poem’s title?

The author of “Hope is the thing with feathers” was a reclusive poet from Amherst whose poem “Because I could not stop for Death” describes a carriage ride with Death and Immortality. Who was this poet?

An American realist writer, she created Edna Pontellier, a married woman whose search for independence drives a landmark Louisiana-set novel. She also wrote “The Story of an Hour.” Which author was she?

In Kate Chopin’s novel, a married woman spends the summer on Grand Isle and grows increasingly alienated from the domestic expectations surrounding her. The story ends with her entering the Gulf of Mexico alone. What novel is it?

In Margaret Mitchell’s novel set during the Civil War and Reconstruction, this headstrong daughter of an Irish-born Georgia planter schemes to save her family’s plantation and pursues Ashley Wilkes despite his marriage to Melanie. Which protagonist is known for declaring that she will think about her troubles tomorrow?
In *Gone with the Wind*, Scarlett O’Hara returns to this Georgia family plantation after the Civil War and vows to keep it from being lost. What is the name of the estate?
Which Sanskrit drama by Kalidasa follows a woman raised in a hermitage who is cursed to be forgotten by King Dushyanta, until a fisherman finds a ring that restores the king’s memory?
Shakuntala is one of three surviving dramas attributed to this classical Sanskrit poet, alongside Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvashiyam. He also composed the poem Meghaduta. Who was he?

This American playwright first drew major acclaim when a memory play about the Wingfield family reached Broadway in 1944. He later wrote dramas featuring Blanche DuBois and Maggie the Cat; by what name is he best known?

In this 1944 memory play by Tennessee Williams, Amanda Wingfield tries to arrange a suitable caller for Laura, whose collection of delicate figurines includes a unicorn. When visitor Jim O’Connor accidentally breaks the ornament, which play is underway?

Tennessee Williams’s 1947 drama sends Blanche DuBois to live with Stella and Stanley Kowalski in a cramped New Orleans apartment, where her genteel self-presentation clashes with Stanley’s suspicion. What play ends with Blanche being led away after saying she has depended on the kindness of strangers?

In this Tennessee Williams drama first staged in 1955, a wealthy Mississippi family gathers for Big Daddy’s birthday while Brick’s drinking and strained marriage to Maggie complicate the struggle over the family estate. What play is it?
answer: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof

question: Tennessee Williams set this 1961 play at a run-down Mexican hotel, where defrocked minister and tour guide T. Lawrence Shannon takes refuge with a group of Baptist schoolteachers and the hotel proprietor, Maxine Faulk. Name the play.

In Gustave Flaubert’s novel, this provincial doctor’s wife moves to Yonville, has affairs with Rodolphe Boulanger and Léon Dupuis, and accumulates debts through extravagant spending. When she cannot repay the moneylender, she takes arsenic; who is this title character?

Emma Bovary’s husband is a country doctor who attempts to treat the ostler Hippolyte’s clubfoot after encouragement from the pharmacist Homais. The operation fails, and Hippolyte ultimately requires an amputation; what is the doctor’s name?

Born in Rutherford, New Jersey, this American modernist poet earned an MD at the University of Pennsylvania in 1906, then practiced medicine while writing. He made ordinary scenes central to poems such as “The Red Wheelbarrow” and “This Is Just to Say”; who was he?

William Carlos Williams shaped this five-volume modernist epic around a New Jersey city, publishing its books separately between 1946 and 1958. The work develops the principle “no ideas but in things”; what is its title?

Writing under a pen name, the English author and mathematician Charles Lutwidge Dodgson published *Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland* and its sequel, *Through the Looking-Glass*. What name did he use for these literary works?

Lewis Carroll’s fictional heroine is widely associated with a real girl whose father served as dean of Christ Church, Oxford, though Carroll denied that she was his model. What was the girl’s full name?

In *Through the Looking-Glass*, Lewis Carroll included a nonsense poem whose opening coins words such as “brillig” and “slithy,” and whose monster is attacked with a “vorpal” blade. What is the poem’s title?

At the center of Anton Chekhov’s final play, a debt-ridden aristocratic family returns to its Russian estate after years abroad, only to lose it at auction. The new owner, a merchant whose father had been a serf on the property, plans to clear its famous flowering trees; name the play.
In The Cherry Orchard, which merchant—whose father had been a serf on Ranevskaya’s estate—buys the property at auction and proposes replacing the orchard with summer cottages?
Which Australian novelist won the 1973 Nobel Prize in Literature? His fiction includes a novel centered on a German-led expedition across the continent’s remote interior.
Patrick White’s novel about a disastrous expedition across the Australian interior pairs a German explorer with Laura Trevelyan, who remains in colonial society. What is the title of the novel?
What Agatha Christie stage mystery opened in London’s West End in 1952 and centers on a murder among guests snowbound at a country guesthouse? It became the world’s longest-running play.
In The Mousetrap, what is the name of the country guesthouse where the visitors become stranded by snow and Sergeant Trotter investigates the murder?

Published in Buenos Aires in 1967, this Colombian novel follows generations of the Buendía family in a town whose history repeatedly echoes itself. Gabriel García Márquez’s landmark work ends as Melquíades’s parchments are deciphered and the town is swept away; name the novel.

In One Hundred Years of Solitude, José Arcadio Buendía establishes this isolated settlement, whose founding, rise, and destruction frame the family’s generations. What is the fictional town where Melquíades first amazes the patriarch by bringing ice?

In One Hundred Years of Solitude, which patriarch leads his companions away from the coast and founds Macondo? Fascinated by Melquíades’s discoveries, including magnets and ice, he is eventually tied to a chestnut tree.

One Hundred Years of Solitude is often treated as a defining example of this narrative mode, in which fantastical events—such as a woman ascending into the sky—are recounted alongside ordinary family and social life in a matter-of-fact tone. Name the mode.

In Jonathan Swift’s 1726 satire, this first-person narrator begins as a ship’s surgeon and later becomes a captain, recounting voyages to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa, and the country of the Houyhnhnms. What is the traveler’s name?

Lemuel Gulliver is the narrator of this author’s satirical account of fantastic voyages, which uses unfamiliar societies to criticize human nature. The same Irish writer also published the satirical essay A Modest Proposal; who was he?
Born in Edinburgh in 1859 and trained as a physician, this Scottish writer created a consulting detective who shared rooms at 221B Baker Street with Dr. Watson. What was the writer’s name?
Arthur Conan Doyle introduced his consulting detective and Dr. Watson in an 1887 novel whose title combines a scientific discipline with a color. What is the novel?

After public outcry over his detective’s apparent death at Reichenbach Falls, Arthur Conan Doyle brought him back for this novel. Holmes and Watson investigate a threatened family estate on Dartmoor, where a spectral beast from a family legend is blamed for a series of deaths. What is the novel?
Arthur Conan Doyle introduced an irascible scientist in The Lost World, a novel about an expedition to a South American plateau where prehistoric creatures survive. What is the scientist’s name?

Arthur Conan Doyle’s Holmes stories began appearing monthly in The Strand Magazine with a case in which Irene Adler outmaneuvers the detective and keeps a compromising photograph from a European king. What is the title of that story?
This picture book by Kamala Harris encourages young readers to see people in their communities and well-known public figures as examples of courage and kindness. What is its title?
The author of Superheroes Are Everywhere served as a U.S. senator from California before becoming vice president, and was the first woman to hold that office. Who is she?

In Robert Louis Stevenson's novella, Richard Enfield recalls that this man trampled a child and paid the family after a confrontation. Later, he is implicated in the killing of Sir Danvers Carew, and a note supposedly written by him matches Dr. Jekyll's handwriting. Name this character.

The novella featuring Mr. Hyde was written by a Scottish author whose other works include *Kidnapped* and *Treasure Island*. The story follows London lawyer Gabriel Utterson as he investigates the disturbing connection between a respected doctor and a violent man. Name the author.

Set during the Mexican Revolution, this novel follows Tita, the youngest daughter in a family where tradition requires her to remain unmarried and care for her mother. Recipes frame its chapters, and Tita’s emotions affect the food she prepares. What is the novel called?
In Like Water for Chocolate, Tita’s mother enforces the family tradition that the youngest daughter must remain unmarried and care for her until her death. What is the name of this strict matriarch?
Born in 1850 and dying in 1893, this French realist writer was a protégé of Gustave Flaubert and became renowned for economical short stories with sharply turned endings. Who was he?

In Guy de Maupassant’s 1880 story, a group of travelers fleeing the Prussian occupation of Normandy includes a patriotic prostitute named Elizabeth Rousset. What is the title of this story, often translated as “Ball of Fat”?
Guy de Maupassant was mentored by this French novelist, whose works include *Madame Bovary* and the short story “A Simple Heart.” Who was this author?

In this Guy de Maupassant story, Mathilde Loisel borrows jewelry from Madame Forestier for a Ministry of Education ball, then spends years repaying the cost of a replacement after losing it. What is the story’s title?

In Madeleine L’Engle’s *A Wrinkle in Time*, this disembodied antagonist exerts a sinister control over the inhabitants of Camazotz. It captures Charles Wallace and tries to bend Meg to its will; what is this entity called?
In *A Wrinkle in Time*, what planet is ruled by IT, where the children encounter a neighborhood whose residents bounce their balls in eerie unison?

Created by Ann M. Martin, this long-running children’s novel series follows adolescent friends in fictional Stoneybrook, Connecticut, whose babysitting jobs lead them to organize a neighborhood service. Its original core members include Kristy Thomas, Mary Anne Spier, Claudia Kishi, and Stacey McGill. What is the series called?

In The Baby-Sitters Club, which founding member proposes organizing a babysitting service after realizing families in her neighborhood need a reliable way to find sitters? She becomes the club’s president and is often shown wearing a baseball cap.

Published in 1532, this Renaissance treatise examines how rulers acquire and preserve power. It famously says an effective ruler should combine the force of a lion with the cunning of a fox. What work is it?
The Prince was written by which Florentine diplomat and political thinker, who served the Republic of Florence before the Medici returned to power and later wrote the Discourses on Livy?
In Sophocles’ Theban tragedy, which daughter of Oedipus defies the king’s order by burying her brother Polynices? She is sentenced to be sealed alive in a cave for performing the forbidden rites.

In Sophocles’ Antigone, which ruler forbids the burial of Polynices and sentences his niece for disobeying the decree? After the blind prophet Tiresias warns him, he reverses his decision too late to prevent tragedy.

In Mary Shelley’s 1818 Gothic novel, this intelligent being is secretly created by a university student and rejected by his maker and by human society. After learning language by observing a family in hiding, he asks his creator for a companion and later seeks revenge when refused. What character is this?

The story featuring Frankenstein’s monster is framed by letters from Arctic explorer Robert Walton and follows a student at the University of Ingolstadt who pursues the creation of life. What is the title of Mary Shelley’s novel, whose subtitle alludes to a mythological figure who stole fire from the gods for humanity?

The novel featuring Frankenstein’s monster was first published anonymously in 1818 and later revised by this English author. She was the daughter of political philosopher William Godwin and published the novel at age twenty. Who was the author?

This Chinese-American novelist's debut centers on the Lee family after middle daughter Lydia is found dead in a lake in 1970s Ohio. Her later novel follows the intertwined lives of the Richardson family and artist Mia Warren in Shaker Heights.
In Celeste Ng's novel *Little Fires Everywhere*, what Cleveland-area suburb is home to the Richardson family and the setting for their conflict with artist Mia Warren?

In Dr. Seuss’s 1957 Christmas book, this green recluse lives above Whoville on Mount Crumpit and disguises himself as Santa to take the Whos’ holiday goods. When he hears them singing anyway, his heart grows three sizes. Who is this character?
In the Grinch’s story, what is the name of his loyal dog, whom he outfits with an antler to serve as a reindeer during the Christmas-night theft?

In Chaucer’s Canterbury collection, a knight condemned after assaulting a maiden avoids execution only by undertaking a year-and-a-day quest to discover what women desire most. What is the name of this narrative?
In The Wife of Bath’s Tale, the knight’s assault on a maiden brings him before King Arthur’s court. Which queen grants him a year and a day to discover what women desire most?

In Arthur Conan Doyle’s original stories, this mathematical scholar directs an international criminal network, and Sherlock Holmes compares him to a spider at the center of a web. He confronts Holmes at Reichenbach Falls in a story first published in 1893; who is this principal nemesis?
Professor Moriarty’s confrontation with Sherlock Holmes at Reichenbach Falls is the central event of which 1893 short story? It appeared in The Strand Magazine and was written by Arthur Conan Doyle.
answer: The Adventure of the Final Problem

question: Professor Moriarty’s epithet “Napoleon of crime” echoes a description of a real 19th-century criminal who helped inspire Doyle’s fictional mastermind. That criminal was also notorious for stealing Thomas Gainsborough’s portrait of the Duchess of Devonshire; who was he?

Born in Romania and later a French citizen, this dramatist became a central figure in the Theatre of the Absurd. He wrote *The Bald Soprano* and *Rhinoceros*, a play in which townspeople transform into beasts.
In Eugene Ionesco’s landmark one-act play, two English couples meet in a bourgeois living room, but banal exchanges unravel into disconnected speech and escalating absurdity. What is the play?

This Irish modernist writer spent much of his adult life in Trieste, Zurich, and Paris while making Dublin central to his fiction. His experiments with interior monologue and a novel structured around a single day in 1904 became landmarks of modern literature. Who was he?

James Joyce’s novel follows advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom and aspiring writer Stephen Dedalus through Dublin on June 16, 1904. Its episodes echo Homer’s Odyssey while shifting among markedly different literary styles; what is the novel’s title?

James Joyce’s 1914 short-story collection includes “Ivy Day in the Committee Room” and closes with a story in which Gabriel Conroy reflects on mortality as snow falls across Ireland. What is the collection’s title?

James Joyce first published this novel in book form in 1916, after it appeared serially in The Egoist. It follows Stephen Dedalus from childhood through his growing rejection of family, church, and nation and his decision to leave Ireland; what is the novel’s title?
answer: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

question: Which Japanese Taishō-era modernist writer wrote “Rashōmon,” “In a Grove,” and “Hell Screen”? His name was also given to a major Japanese literary prize.

In a Ryūnosuke Akutagawa Buddhist parable, the condemned thief Kandata is granted a chance to leave hell after the Buddha recalls a small act of kindness from his life. What story ends when Kandata tries to prevent other sinners from following him toward salvation, causing his escape route to fail?

Which Ryūnosuke Akutagawa story presents conflicting accounts of a samurai’s death through testimonies from a woodcutter, a priest, a bandit, the samurai’s wife, and a medium speaking for the dead man?

A hardworking insect stores food through the warm months while another spends the summer singing. When winter arrives, the hungry singer asks for help and is told to dance instead. What is this fable called?
The Ant and the Grasshopper belongs to a tradition of moral animal fables conventionally attributed to an enslaved storyteller of ancient Greece. What is the name of this fabulist?

After reading her husband's letter about the Weird Sisters' prophecy, she calls on spirits to strip away her compassion and later challenges his courage as they plot a killing. Which Shakespearean character eventually sleepwalks while trying to wash imagined blood from her hands?
Lady Macbeth helps arrange the murder of this ruler during his visit to Inverness; after his death, the crime is blamed on the drugged attendants. Which Scottish king is killed in the play?

In Margaret Atwood’s dystopia, these women are assigned to elite households in the Republic of Gilead and compelled to bear children for the ruling class amid widespread infertility. They wear red uniforms and include a woman known as Offred. What are they called?
The Handmaids are central figures in a novel by this Canadian author, who later returned to Gilead in The Testaments and also wrote Oryx and Crake. Who is the author?
A Muggle-born witch sorted into Gryffindor, she becomes one of Harry Potter and Ron Weasley’s closest friends and is renowned for her exceptional knowledge of magic. What is her name?
Hermione Granger later marries this red-haired wizard, the youngest child of Arthur and Molly, who raise their large family at the Burrow. He becomes one of Harry Potter’s closest friends. Who is he?

Written in 1919 by an Irish poet, this modernist poem frames postwar social disintegration through Christian apocalyptic imagery. It features a falcon that can no longer hear its falconer and ends with a rough beast moving toward Bethlehem; what is its title?

The Second Coming first appeared in the November 1920 issue of this American literary magazine. During its modernist era, the journal was edited by Scofield Thayer and James Sibley Watson and published writers such as T. S. Eliot; name it.
The Second Coming was included in a 1921 Yeats collection whose title pairs an esoteric figure from his writings with a performer in motion. What is the name of that volume?

Published in 1964, this picture book follows a boy whose relationship with a generous woodland companion changes as he grows older. The companion gives him its apples, branches, and trunk, leaving only a stump on which the elderly boy can rest; what is the book’s title?
The Giving Tree was written and illustrated by an American poet and cartoonist who also authored the poetry collections Where the Sidewalk Ends and A Light in the Attic. What is his name?

The story opens with fellow judges discussing a newspaper notice about a colleague, then follows the judge’s conventional life as it unravels after a seemingly minor injury while hanging curtains. Which Tolstoy novella centers on his confrontation with mortality?

In The Death of Ivan Ilyich, which young household servant treats the dying judge with compassion while his family avoids facing his condition? He brings relief by supporting the judge’s legs on his shoulders.

Which American modernist poet is known for unconventional typography, punctuation, syntax, and frequent lowercase usage, and wrote “maggie and milly and molly and may” as well as “anyone lived in a pretty how town”?
E. E. Cummings wrote a poem in which an unnamed man and woman pass through courtship, marriage, aging, and death as the town’s seasons recur. What is the title of that poem?
answer: “anyone lived in a pretty how town”

question: This novella follows aging writer Gustav von Aschenbach as he becomes captivated by the boy Tadzio during a stay in an Italian port city. Despite warnings of a cholera outbreak, Aschenbach remains there. What is the title of this work by Thomas Mann?
In Death in Venice, who created Gustav von Aschenbach, the writer whose fixation on Tadzio unfolds amid a cholera outbreak? This German novelist also wrote The Magic Mountain.
This ancient Sanskrit Hindu epic, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, recounts Rama’s exile, Sita’s abduction, and the war in Lanka that ends with Ravana’s defeat. What is the epic called?
In the Ramayana, this devoted ally of Rama crosses the ocean to Lanka to search for Sita and later carries a mountain of medicinal herbs to save Lakshmana. What is the name of this vanara hero?
Anne Carson’s 1998 novel-in-verse reimagines the Greek myth of a red-winged monster slain by Herakles as a modern coming-of-age story. What is the title of this work?
In *Autobiography of Red*, the ancient monster at the center of the myth becomes a red, winged adolescent who writes poetry and travels with Herakles. What is the protagonist’s name?

A 1939 story in The New Yorker follows an ordinary husband through town errands, interrupted by fantasies of piloting a Navy hydroplane and performing a daring operation. What is this comic story called?
answer: The Secret Life of Walter Mitty

question: The Secret Life of Walter Mitty appeared in The New Yorker in 1939, using everyday errands and marital frustrations as a frame for extravagant adventure fantasies. Which American humorist wrote it?
Which fictional Colombian town, created by Gabriel García Márquez, is founded by the Buendía family and becomes the setting for a story involving an insomnia plague and years of rain?

Macondo is the principal setting of this 1967 novel, which follows the Buendía family across generations from the town’s founding to its destruction. Its story includes Melquíades’s parchments and a baby born with a pig’s tail; what novel is it?
Which American children's author wrote novels such as *No Talking*, *The Landry News*, and *Lunch Money*, as well as a story about a student whose invented word catches on nationwide?

In an Andrew Clements novel, fifth-grader Nick Allen gives a new name to a common writing tool after a classroom discussion about how words are created. The term spreads well beyond his classroom and eventually appears in a dictionary; what is the novel’s title?

Which American author and essayist contributed to The New Yorker for decades and helped revise a concise guide to English usage first written by his former Cornell professor? He also created the characters Stuart Little and Wilbur the pig.

In E. B. White’s children’s novel, a farm pig named Wilbur faces slaughter until a spider draws attention to him by weaving admiring words into her web. A rat named Templeton helps with the scheme in exchange for food.

An Australian novelist made a wager over transporting a glass church central to *Oscar and Lucinda*, then wrote *True History of the Kelly Gang*, a fictionalized account of a nineteenth-century bushranger. Who is this two-time Booker Prize winner?
In Peter Carey’s Booker Prize-winning novel, a notorious nineteenth-century bushranger tells his story in letters intended for his daughter. Which outlaw is the central figure?
Which 1903 essay collection by W. E. B. Du Bois opens with “Of Our Spiritual Strivings” and explores the color line, African American life, and the image of a veil?
In The Souls of Black Folk, what concept names the “two-ness” Du Bois describes: seeing oneself both through one’s own perspective and through the eyes of a society that devalues Black people?
This 1951 Langston Hughes poem asks what happens to a dream deferred and develops the question through images including a drying raisin, a festering sore, and a heavy load. What is the poem’s title?
Langston Hughes’s Harlem asks what becomes of a deferred dream, and one image in the poem inspired the title of Lorraine Hansberry’s 1959 play about the Younger family. What is the play?

Its opening contrasts happy families, said to be alike, with unhappy families, each unhappy in its own way. This novel follows a married aristocrat’s affair with a cavalry officer and ends with her death beneath a train. What is the novel’s title?

Anna Karenina first appeared serially before being published in book form in 1878, and its author called it his first true novel. The same Russian writer also composed War and Peace, his epic of Napoleon’s invasion of Russia. Who was he?

In Anna Karenina, this cavalry officer meets the title heroine at a railway station after a railway worker is killed. He becomes her lover, and the two travel together to Italy. What is the officer’s name?

In Anna Karenina, this rural landowner proposes to Kitty and devotes himself to managing his estate and working alongside peasants. Near the novel’s end, his reflections on faith and moral purpose lead to a spiritual resolution. Who is he?

In Anna Karenina, this young member of the Shcherbatsky family is courted by both Levin and Vronsky, but Vronsky turns his attention to Anna at a ball. She later marries Levin and has a son with him. Who is she?
An English folk hero in medieval ballads, he leads the Merry Men from Sherwood Forest and is famed for archery and robbing the rich to give to the poor. What is his name?
In Sir Walter Scott’s historical novel, Robin Hood appears under the name Locksley and aids a disinherited Saxon knight returning from the Crusades. What is the novel called?
Which Shakespeare tragedy opens with Roman tribunes confronting citizens celebrating a ruler’s triumph, then follows a conspiracy that ends in his murder on the Ides of March?

In Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, which conspirator defends joining the assassination by telling the Roman crowd that he loved Caesar but loved Rome more? He speaks before Antony delivers the opposing funeral oration.

Born in Savannah in 1925, this American Catholic writer created Southern Gothic stories filled with grotesque characters and moral struggles over grace. Who wrote two novels and 31 short stories, including “A Good Man Is Hard to Find”?

In a Flannery O’Connor story, a grandmother secretly brings her cat Pitty Sing along in a basket as her family drives toward Florida. After a car crash, the family encounters an escaped convict known as the Misfit; what is the story’s title?
answer: “A Good Man Is Hard to Find”

question: Flannery O’Connor’s short fiction was gathered in this posthumous volume, which won the 1972 National Book Award for Fiction. What is the collection’s title?
Flannery O’Connor was born in Savannah and spent much of her adult life at Andalusia, near Milledgeville. In which U.S. state are both places located?

First appearing as an untitled work in the 1855 edition of *Leaves of Grass*, this 52-section free-verse poem moves among nature, bodily experience, everyday work, death, and encounters with other people. Its speaker’s celebration of himself repeatedly expands to include the reader and a broad human community. Name the poem.

The poet behind *Song of Myself* repeatedly revised *Leaves of Grass* over the course of his life. In the poem’s final section, he declares that he sounds a “barbaric yawp” over the roofs of the world. Name this American poet.

Two young lovers in Babylon communicate through a crack in a wall after their families forbid them to meet. A lioness bloodies one lover’s veil, leading the other to believe that the beloved has been killed; Shakespeare’s craftsmen perform this tragedy as a play within a play. What classical love story is it?
Pyramus and Thisbe is retold in Book IV of the Metamorphoses, a Latin narrative poem that connects myths through tales of transformation. Which Roman poet composed the work?
In this 1819 ode, the speaker imagines leaving ordinary human consciousness for a wooded scene, then pictures himself dead beneath a sod while a bird’s song continues. Name the poem.
Ode to a Nightingale sets a mortal speaker’s uncertainty about waking or dreaming against a song that seems to outlast human life. Which English Romantic poet wrote it?
Ode to a Nightingale first appeared in the July issue of a periodical. Name the publication that printed it.

A Roman statesman allied with Caesar, he survives the assassination and is granted permission by Brutus to address the funeral crowd, provided he does not openly condemn the conspirators. He uses a repeated, ostensibly respectful description of them to turn the citizens against them; who is this character?
Mark Antony appears in this English tragedy, whose plot follows Brutus and Cassius’s conspiracy against Caesar and later concludes with their defeat at Philippi. Who wrote the play?

This four-part poem by Edgar Allan Poe moves from winter sleigh rides and a wedding to a fire and a funeral, shifting from delight to dread. Its insistent repetitions and changing rhythms imitate the sounds at the heart of each scene. What is the poem?
The complete text of The Bells appeared shortly after Poe’s death, in November 1849. What periodical first published it?
After the Dashwood family is forced to leave Norland Park, the sisters Elinor and Marianne settle at Barton Cottage and face contrasting romantic experiences. What novel follows their story?
Sense and Sensibility was published in 1811, initially credited only to “A Lady.” Its author also wrote Mansfield Park and Northanger Abbey; who was she?

In Mark Twain’s 1876 novel set in the fictional Missouri town of St. Petersburg, this mischievous schoolboy lives with Aunt Polly and persuades other boys to pay for turns whitewashing a fence. What is the title character’s name?
In Tom Sawyer, this daughter of a local judge becomes the schoolboy’s love interest. After she and Tom lose their way in McDougal’s Cave, he finds an exit that leads them to safety. What is her name?

In Gwendolyn Brooks’s 1960 poetry collection, an elderly couple share a modest meal in a rented back room crowded with beads, receipts, dolls, and cloth. The volume also includes “We Real Cool”; what is the collection called?
The Bean Eaters is one collection by this poet, whose book Annie Allen won the 1950 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, making her the first African American to receive that award. Who was the poet?

In Joseph Heller’s satirical World War II novel, this mess officer treats a bomber squadron’s operations as opportunities for profit and builds a vast syndicate around his deals. His egg trade famously turns a lower resale price than purchase price into a supposed profit. Who is this character?

Milo Minderbinder’s schemes unfold alongside the story of bombardier John Yossarian, who tries to escape combat missions on the island of Pianosa. What is the title of Joseph Heller’s novel, named for a paradoxical rule that traps the airmen in its bureaucracy?

This Anglo-Irish writer, essayist, and Anglican cleric became dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin in 1713. His 1729 economic satire proposed a grotesque solution to Irish poverty involving the sale of infants as food. Who was this author?

Jonathan Swift wrote a four-part prose work whose shipwrecked narrator encounters the tiny inhabitants of Lilliput, the flying island of Laputa, and the rational horse-like Houyhnhnms. What is the title of this satirical work?

In a 1729 pamphlet, Jonathan Swift adopts the voice of a calculating economic reformer who argues that impoverished Irish families might ease poverty by selling infants to wealthy consumers. What work uses this deliberately monstrous scheme to expose indifference toward the poor?

Jonathan Swift’s 1726 poem addressed to Esther Vanhomrigh gave literary currency to a woman’s name reportedly formed from part of her surname and a form of her first name. What name did the poem help popularize?

Jonathan Swift adopted this name for the mock-almanac writer behind his 1708 predictions, then helped stage a literary hoax by announcing that astrologer John Partridge had died. What pseudonym did Swift use?

In Haruki Murakami’s fiction, a domestic animal repeatedly appears as an elusive or missing presence, most notably when Toru Okada is asked to search for one in a novel about his increasingly strange life. What animal is this recurring motif?
In which Haruki Murakami novel does Toru Okada search for a missing household pet named after his wife’s brother? Cats are among the story’s recurring mysterious presences.
In George Orwell’s dystopian novel set under Big Brother’s surveillance, a young woman defies Party rules and begins a secret affair with the protagonist after passing him a note. What is her name?

In Nineteen Eighty-Four, Julia begins a clandestine relationship with a man who keeps a diary criticizing the Party and works at the Ministry of Truth rewriting historical records. What is his full name?
In Nathaniel Hawthorne's novel, Hester Prynne is compelled to wear an embroidered red initial as public punishment for adultery. What is this emblem called?

In Nathaniel Hawthorne's novel, Hester Prynne's scarlet letter A marks her public punishment, while her daughter is a spirited presence who often accompanies her in the forest. What is the daughter's name, which is also shared by a precious gemstone?

What literary mode, often discussed as a style rather than a settled genre, places supernatural events alongside recognizable social history and everyday detail, presenting the marvelous without surprise or explanatory pause? Though strongly associated with Latin American writing, it is also used to describe works from other regions.
In discussions of magical realism, which Cuban novelist introduced the idea of “lo real maravilloso” (“the marvelous real”) to the Americas in 1949, in the prologue to *The Kingdom of This World*?

In William Faulkner’s novel about a family’s journey to bury its matriarch, which youngest child bores holes in his mother’s coffin lid and accidentally pierces her face? His response to seeing a cleaned fish becomes one of the novel’s best-known lines.

Vardaman Bundren appears in which William Faulkner novel, where the Bundren family carries Addie’s coffin on a difficult journey to Jefferson to fulfill her burial wish? The novel uses shifting interior monologues and is set in Yoknapatawpha County.

In this nonfiction form of life-writing, the author is also the person whose life is recounted, selecting and interpreting memories in a retrospective narrative. Unlike a biography, it tells the author’s own story; what is this genre?
What work is Maya Angelou’s autobiography about her childhood in Stamps, Arkansas, from roughly age three to sixteen? Published in 1969, it became the first volume in a series about her life.
answer: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

question: Born John Griffith Chaney, this American novelist and journalist drew on his experiences as a sailor and adventurer in works about the Klondike and the South Pacific. He wrote about Buck in The Call of the Wild and the wolfdog in White Fang. Who was this author?

In this Jack London novel, Buck is taken from a California home and shipped north during the Klondike Gold Rush. After working as a sled dog, he bonds with John Thornton before responding to the wilderness. What is the novel’s title?
This Jack London dystopian novel depicts an oligarchy crushing a socialist movement and is framed by editorial notes on the memoir of Avis Everhard. What is the novel’s title?

Maya Angelou’s second autobiographical memoir, published in 1974, follows her as a young mother navigating work and survival in postwar California. What is the title of this book, which continues the life story begun in *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings*?

In *Gather Together in My Name*, the narrator recounts her own early adulthood in postwar California. Which poet and memoirist began a seven-volume autobiographical series with *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings*?
