Born in Beaconsfield in 1948, this English novelist created a comic-fantasy series whose flat world travels through space on four elephants standing on Great A’Tuin. He also co-wrote a comic end-of-the-world story with Neil Gaiman; who was this author?

Terry Pratchett’s first Discworld novel, published in 1983, introduces the hapless wizard Rincewind and the tourist Twoflower, whose sentient wooden chest follows him on dozens of little legs. What is the title of this novel?

Born in St. Petersburg in 1899, this multilingual writer left Russia after the Revolution, wrote novels in Berlin, and later taught at Cornell while studying butterflies at Harvard. Who was the novelist whose intricate, allusive fiction made him a major twentieth-century stylist?

In Vladimir Nabokov's novel, a 999-line poem by the fictional John Shade is followed by a foreword, commentary, and index written by Charles Kinbote. What is the title of this work, whose scholarly apparatus develops a narrative of its own?

What 1860 narrative poem by a leading American poet dramatizes a colonial messenger’s warning journey from Boston through Middlesex County before the Battles of Lexington and Concord, with church lanterns signaling the movement of British troops?
The 1860 poem *Paul Revere’s Ride* was written by which American poet, also known for *The Song of Hiawatha* and *Evangeline*?

In this 1922 fantastical satire from *Tales of the Jazz Age*, sixteen-year-old John Unger visits his schoolmate Percy Washington’s secluded Montana estate and discovers that the family’s fortune comes from a gigantic gemstone beneath the property. What F. Scott Fitzgerald work uses this incredible discovery to satirize the wealthy?
answer: The Diamond as Big as the Ritz

question: *The Diamond as Big as the Ritz* appeared in this American writer’s 1922 collection *Tales of the Jazz Age*. The same writer created Nick Carraway, the narrator who observes Jay Gatsby’s lavish world in a novel set around West Egg. Who is the writer?

Published in 1955, this Vladimir Nabokov novel is narrated by Humbert Humbert, whose ornate, self-justifying account invites readers to question what he conceals. A purported scholarly foreword by John Ray, Jr., frames the manuscript; what is the novel?

In Lolita, the first-person narrative is preceded by a fictional scholarly foreword that presents Humbert Humbert’s manuscript and comments on the people involved. Which fictional scholar is credited with writing that foreword?

Published in 1939 after appearing in installments as “fragments from Work in Progress,” this experimental novel begins with “riverrun, past Eve and Adam’s” and ends with a line whose unfinished syntax carries into that opening. What is the novel’s title?

The Irish writer who created Finnegans Wake had earlier written Ulysses, which follows Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through Dublin on June 16, 1904. He also wrote A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man; what was his name?

In Finnegans Wake, the father of Shem, Shaun, and Issy is identified by a recurring three-letter set of initials and is the subject of an obscure rumor that his wife ALP tries to rebut. What initials designate this central figure?

In Fyodor Dostoevsky’s 1866 novel *Crime and Punishment*, which poverty-stricken former student lives in a cramped Petersburg garret and murders a pawnbroker after forming a theory about exceptional people who may transgress moral laws?

In *Crime and Punishment*, which examining magistrate conducts probing interviews with Rodion Raskolnikov after the pawnbroker’s murder? He challenges the argument that extraordinary people may break the law and gradually pressures the suspect toward confession.

Which Flannery O’Connor short story follows Julian and his prejudiced mother on a newly integrated Southern city bus? The matching hats worn by his mother and a Black passenger, followed by the mother’s condescending offer of a penny to a child, lead to a devastating confrontation.

In Flannery O’Connor’s “Everything That Rises Must Converge,” this young college graduate accompanies his mother on a desegregated city bus and tries to provoke her, even as he sees himself as opposed to her racism. What is his name?
In Shakespeare’s tragedy about a Scottish king undone by the witches’ prophecies, which Thane of Fife avenges his family and ultimately kills Macbeth?
Macduff escapes to England to oppose Macbeth and joins forces with which son of Duncan? This prince later returns with an English-backed army to reclaim the Scottish throne.

In Rick Riordan’s novels, this demigod is the daughter of Athena and joins Percy Jackson on the quest in *The Lightning Thief*. A companion-book profile describes her as athletic, blonde-haired, gray-eyed, and guided by the advice, “Always, always have a plan.” Who is she?
Annabeth Chase joins this son of Poseidon on the quest in *The Lightning Thief*. His dyslexia and ADHD are explained as signs of his demigod heritage. Who is he?

First serialized from 1869 to 1870, this Jules Verne adventure follows Professor Pierre Aronnax, Conseil, and harpooner Ned Land after they are taken aboard a submarine commanded by Captain Nemo. Its title measures the distance traveled, not the ocean’s depth. What is the novel?
answer: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

question: In Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, which Canadian harpooner is captured alongside Professor Aronnax and Conseil after joining an expedition to hunt a supposed sea monster? Aboard the Nautilus, he repeatedly looks for a chance to escape.

In Orwell’s dystopia, Party linguists continually revise the official language by deleting words and narrowing meanings, with the aim of making politically rebellious ideas impossible to express. What is this deliberately restricted language called?

In Nineteen Eighty-Four, which philologist working on the Newspeak dictionary tells Winston that a future edition will drastically reduce the vocabulary? He later disappears from official records as an “unperson.”
Set in a Port Elizabeth tea room during apartheid, this Athol Fugard drama follows a white teenager whose treatment of two Black employees becomes increasingly cruel. What is the play?

In Master Harold...and the Boys, which of the two Black employees recalls building a kite with Hally and is an enthusiastic ballroom dancer? His reflections on dancing also give the play its image of a world where people move without colliding.
In this play by John Patrick Shanley, Sister Aloysius becomes suspicious of Father Flynn’s relationship with a student at a Catholic school. What is the play’s title?

In Doubt: A Parable, characters debate whether a school pageant should feature secular or religious songs for this holiday. James Joyce’s “The Dead” also centers on a family gathering held during its season. What holiday is it?

In Ray Bradbury’s story, a wealthy client joins a commercial safari into the distant past to hunt a Tyrannosaurus, with strict instructions to stay on a path so the present will not be disturbed. After he panics, leaves the path, and returns with a crushed butterfly on his boot, the election results and language of the future have changed. What is the story called?

In A Sound of Thunder, the travelers return to find that the butterfly crushed by Eckels has changed the outcome of a U.S. presidential election. Which candidate, described as a fascist, is now reported to have defeated Keith?

In a tale absent from established Arabic editions of *One Thousand and One Nights*, a poor tailor’s son is tricked by a sorcerer into entering a cave to retrieve an oil lamp. What young hero escapes with help from a jinni summoned by a ring, then uses the lamp’s jinni to gain wealth and marry a princess?
In 1709, this Syrian storyteller told Antoine Galland the tale of Aladdin, which Galland later included in his French version of *One Thousand and One Nights*. Who was the storyteller?

During the American Civil War, Union soldiers prepare to hang Peyton Farquhar from this wooden railroad structure in Alabama. Ambrose Bierce’s story uses it as the setting for both the execution and the imagined escape that follows.

At Owl Creek Bridge, this Alabama planter and Confederate sympathizer is bound and prepared for execution by Union soldiers. Bierce’s story follows his apparent escape before revealing that it occurred only in his imagination.

After a storm, a poor couple finds a frail, elderly stranger in their courtyard, and the villagers argue about whether his remarkable feathered limbs mean he is an angel. Which Gabriel García Márquez short story tells this tale?
answer: A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings

question: In A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings, what is the name of Pelayo’s wife, who turns the crowds’ curiosity about the visitor into paid admission and later uses the proceeds to build a mansion?

In Herman Melville’s novel, a former whaleman preaches at the Whaleman’s Chapel in New Bedford. He climbs a rope ladder to a pulpit shaped like a ship’s bow before delivering a sermon about a prophet who fled from God’s command. Who is this preacher?

Before Ishmael and Queequeg sail, Father Mapple delivers a sermon at the Whaleman’s Chapel about a biblical prophet who tries to escape by sea, is swallowed by a great fish, and is sent to preach at Nineveh. Which prophet is the sermon about?

In a Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale, two swindlers claim to weave a splendid garment that cannot be seen by people who are foolish or unfit for their positions. During a public procession, a child breaks the spell of the deception by saying aloud what everyone can see. What is the title of the tale?
The Emperor’s New Clothes is one of the best-known fairy tales by this Danish writer. His other stories include “The Snow Queen” and “The Little Mermaid.” What is his name?

In Roald Dahl’s children’s novel, a book-loving girl with extraordinary intelligence discovers she can move objects with her mind after confronting the cruel headmistress of Crunchem Hall. What is the title of the novel?

In Matilda, the formidable headmistress of Crunchem Hall is a former Olympic hammer thrower who terrorizes pupils and flees after believing that chalk is writing a message on the classroom board. What is her name?

Which Platonic dialogue opens with Socrates recalling a discussion of the ideal city before a Pythagorean philosopher from southern Italy gives an account of the cosmos’s creation and structure? Its planned continuation recounts a war between ancient Athens and a powerful island civilization.

In Plato’s Timaeus, Egyptian priests tell Solon of an island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, larger than Libya and Asia together, that was destroyed by earthquakes and floods. What lost island do they describe?

A first-person narrator named Jim Burden recalls his childhood on the Nebraska prairie, where he befriends a Czech immigrant girl from the Shimerda family who later builds a life with Anton Cuzak. What 1918 novel by Willa Cather centers on her story?
In My Ántonia, Jim Burden recounts his life among immigrant homesteaders in Nebraska. Which author, who also wrote O Pioneers! and The Song of the Lark, wrote this novel?

Which Chinese historical novel, traditionally attributed to Luo Guanzhong, portrays the fall of the Han dynasty and the conflicts among Wei, Shu, and Wu? Drawing on historical records and popular storytelling, it is counted among the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature.

Romance of the Three Kingdoms is traditionally attributed to which 14th-century Chinese writer? The same writer is sometimes credited with an early version of the vernacular novel Water Margin, though that attribution has been debated.

In Romance of the Three Kingdoms, which battle on the Yangtze in 208 CE becomes a major victory for the alliance of Liu Bei and Sun Quan over Cao Cao? The novel depicts fire destroying Cao Cao’s fleet and halting his southward advance.

Washington Irving used this fictional Dutch antiquarian as the supposed author of *A History of New York* and as the source of tales later collected in *The Sketch Book*. What name did Irving give this recurring narrator?

Which collection by Washington Irving, published in installments in 1819–20, includes “Rip Van Winkle” and “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” tales presented as coming from Diedrich Knickerbocker’s papers?
answer: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.

question: This sonnet describes divine presence as gathering like oil and argues that human trampling and industry have not exhausted the natural world. It closes with a sacred spirit brooding over that world. What is the poem?
The sonnet God's Grandeur was written by a Victorian poet whose distinctive sprung rhythm also appears in “The Windhover.” This Jesuit priest and poet also wrote “Pied Beauty.” Who was he?

In this lyric, a speaker recounts the stillness of a deathbed as mourners wait for the expected final moment. A fly briefly crosses the speaker’s field of vision just as the speaker’s sight begins to fail; what is the poem’s title?
answer: “I heard a Fly buzz—when I died—”

question: “I heard a Fly buzz—when I died—” is one of this poet’s lyrics, alongside “Because I could not stop for Death” and “Hope is the thing with feathers.” Identify the 19th-century American poet who wrote these works.

Miguel de Cervantes published this Spanish novel in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. Its hidalgo protagonist, after obsessively reading chivalric romances, sets out as a knight-errant with a practical squire.

In Don Quixote, this practical farm laborer becomes the protagonist’s squire and is promised the governorship of an island. His earthy proverbs and appetite often contrast with his master’s lofty chivalric rhetoric.
In Don Quixote, the title character gives this name to his old, thin horse. The grand-sounding name contrasts with the animal’s former status as an ordinary working nag.
In Don Quixote, the protagonist dedicates his exploits to a woman whom he imagines as a noble lady, though she is actually the peasant Aldonza Lorenzo. What name does he give his idealized beloved?

In Don Quixote, the knight charges at these devices after imagining they are giants. Their turning sails knock him from his horse and expose the gap between his imagined adventures and ordinary reality.

Which English novelist, born in 1904 and deceased in 1991, became a Roman Catholic in 1926? His fiction includes a fugitive priest pursued during religious persecution in Mexico and a satirical story of espionage in Cuba.

In which Graham Greene novel does vacuum-cleaner salesman James Wormold, living in Cuba, become a reluctant intelligence agent and invent reports about nonexistent installations? Greene classified this satirical spy story as an “entertainment.”

Scott O'Dell's 1960 children's novel follows Karana after she is left behind when her people sail away from their island off the California coast. Which book tells of her struggle to survive alone, including her efforts to tame a wild dog?
In Island of the Blue Dolphins, Karana captures and eventually tames the leader of the wild dog pack that killed her brother, Ramo. What name does she give this dog?
Jean Rhys’s 1966 novel centers on Antoinette Cosway’s life in the Caribbean and reimagines the history behind the imprisoned first wife in *Jane Eyre*. What is the title of this novel?
In *Wide Sargasso Sea*, Antoinette’s English husband rejects her Caribbean identity and uses the name associated with Rochester’s attic-bound wife in *Jane Eyre*. What name does he impose on her?

A speaker addresses a small field animal whose nest has been overturned by a plough just before winter, then reflects that even carefully made plans can fail. Name this 1786 poem, whose Scots phrase “gang aft agley” captures that idea.

In “To a Mouse,” the speaker calls the animal an “earth-born companion” and a “fellow-mortal.” Which Scottish poet wrote these lines and used Scots expressions such as “wee” and “gang aft agley” in the poem?
In this satirical novel, car dealer Dwayne Hoover encounters science-fiction writer Kilgore Trout, as the story pokes fun at American culture. What is the novel’s title?
Breakfast of Champions features Dwayne Hoover and Kilgore Trout. Which American novelist wrote it and also created Billy Pilgrim, the protagonist of Slaughterhouse-Five?

In epic poetry, what is the literary term for a descriptive name or phrase repeatedly attached to a person or thing? Homeric examples include stock descriptions of a hero’s speed or a goddess’s appearance.

Alongside the use of an epithet, ancient Greek epics often develop a comparison over several lines, connecting a battle scene with an image from nature or everyday life. What is this extended epic comparison called?

Born in Manhattan in 1783 to a merchant family, this American writer made his literary debut with observational letters in the Morning Chronicle under a pseudonym. He later became one of the first U.S. authors to win acclaim in Europe and wrote famous tales about a long-sleeping villager and a schoolteacher pursued by a specter. Who was this author?

Washington Irving serialized this collection from 1819 to 1820 while temporarily in England on family business. It includes his Catskills tale of a man who sleeps for 20 years and his story about a schoolteacher pursued by a headless specter. What collection is it?
answer: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.

question: In 1802, Washington Irving published observational letters in the Morning Chronicle using this assumed name, beginning his literary career. What pseudonym did he use?
During the 1840s, Washington Irving served as the United States’ ambassador to this European country. Which country was the location of his diplomatic post?
Washington Irving encouraged this younger American author, whose best-known works include the poem “The Raven” and the short story “The Tell-Tale Heart.” Which writer is described?

T. S. Eliot gathered this sequence of interrelated poems, first published separately, into a single work. Beginning with a meditation on an unrealized garden in “Burnt Norton,” it reflects on time, spiritual life, and renewal; what is the sequence called?
In Four Quartets, which poem takes its title from a village in Somerset associated with Eliot’s family history and includes the refrain “In my beginning is my end”?

Published by Random House in 1952, this first-person novel follows an unnamed Black narrator from the South to Harlem, where others fail to recognize or truly see him. He eventually makes an underground room his refuge, illuminating it with 1,369 stolen lightbulbs. What is the novel?

In *Invisible Man*, the unnamed narrator’s journey takes him to Liberty Paints and into the Brotherhood, an organization that claims to fight for oppressed people. Who wrote the novel and became the first Black author to win the National Book Award, receiving it in 1953?

Which 1934 novel by Evelyn Waugh follows Tony Last, an English country gentleman whose marriage falls apart and who becomes stranded in the Brazilian jungle? Its title echoes a phrase from T. S. Eliot’s *The Waste Land*.
In *A Handful of Dust*, Evelyn Waugh alludes in the title to a phrase from this 1922 poem by T. S. Eliot, whose sections include “The Burial of the Dead” and “A Game of Chess.” What is the poem?

In Thomas Mann’s 1924 novel, young engineer Hans Castorp visits his cousin at a Swiss sanatorium intending to stay only a few weeks, but remains there for seven years. What is the title of this novel?
In The Magic Mountain, which Italian humanist at the Berghof champions reason, progress, and democratic ideals, and frequently argues with the Jesuit-trained Leo Naphta?

Born in Kyoto in 1949 and raised in Kobe, this Japanese novelist studied at Waseda University and later ran the jazz café Peter Cat. His 1979 debut novel, *Hear the Wind Sing*, won the Gunzo Prize for New Writers. Who is this author?

In a Haruki Murakami novel, unemployed Toru Okada searches for his missing wife, Kumiko, and a lost cat. His journey takes him to a dry well, where strange encounters blur the line between dreams and waking life. What is the novel?
In the Mahabharata, she is the daughter of Vishvamitra and Menaka, raised in the forest hermitage of Kanva. She marries King Dushyanta and gives birth to Bharata; what is the heroine’s name?
In Kālidāsa’s Sanskrit drama about Shakuntala, Dushyanta’s memory of their marriage is restored after a fisherman finds an object swallowed by a fish and returns it to court. What is the object?

In Stephen Crane’s Civil War novel, this young Union private enlists imagining that battle will prove his courage, but runs from his first major engagement. He later returns with a head wound inflicted by another soldier and carries his regiment’s flag during a renewed advance; what is his name?

Henry Fleming’s experiences as a young Union private are at the center of this 1895 Stephen Crane novel. After fleeing a battle, he returns to his regiment and later helps lead an advance while carrying its colors; what is the title of the work?

After immersing himself in chivalric romances, this rural hidalgo reinvents himself as a knight-errant and travels through Spain with Sancho Panza, famously mistaking windmills for giants. What name does Cervantes give this deluded but idealistic protagonist?
In Don Quixote, the self-styled knight gives his thin, worn-out horse a grand name to match his new identity as a chivalric hero. What is the horse called?

This Spanish tragedy premiered in Madrid on March 8, 1933, after its author wrote it the previous year. Set in rural Andalusia, it follows a bride who flees with Leonardo, setting off a fatal knife fight.
Blood Wedding was written by this Spanish playwright, whose other rural tragedies include Yerma and The House of Bernarda Alba. He also wrote the poetry collection Gypsy Ballads.
In Shakespeare’s tragedy about a Scottish thane’s rise to the throne, three supernatural figures meet him on a heath and foretell his future. What is the familiar name of this prophetic group?
In Shakespeare’s Macbeth, which Thane of Fife is described as having been “from his mother’s womb untimely ripped,” fulfilling the Three Witches’ cryptic prediction and killing Macbeth?

This Augustan-era Roman poet wrote the Odes, Epodes, Satires, and Epistles, as well as a verse treatise on poetic craft. He is also associated with the Latin line “dulce et decorum est pro patria mori.”

Horace addressed this verse epistle to the Pisos, opening with a comic image of a painter joining a horse’s neck to a human head. It discusses principles of poetic composition and is commonly rendered in English as “The Art of Poetry.”
In William Golding’s postwar novel about schoolboys stranded on an island, which asthmatic, intelligent boy champions rules and has his spectacles used to ignite the group’s signal fire?

Piggy’s spectacles become vital for making fire on the island where a group of British schoolboys are stranded after a crash. What 1954 novel by William Golding follows their struggle to maintain order?
Joseph Heller’s debut novel, first published in 1961, follows U.S. Army Air Forces bombardier Captain John Yossarian and satirizes military bureaucracy during World War II. What is this novel called?
In Catch-22, the author drew on his own experience as a U.S. Army Air Forces bombardier in World War II. Who published this novel as his debut in 1961?
In Catch-22, the fictional 256th U.S. Army Air Squadron is stationed on this Mediterranean island west of Italy, the novel’s main setting. What is the island called?
In Catch-22, this mess officer creates M&M Enterprises, turning military supplies into a sprawling syndicate. Which character famously argues that everyone has a share in the business?

At Covent Garden, a young flower seller’s Cockney speech catches the attention of a phonetics professor, who takes on the challenge of changing her speech and manners. What is the flower seller’s name?

Eliza Doolittle becomes the subject of a wager in which Professor Henry Higgins tries to pass her off as a duchess after training her speech, with Colonel Pickering as his fellow participant. What George Bernard Shaw play tells this story, with a title drawn from the Greek myth of a sculptor who creates an ideal woman?

In Harper Lee’s novel, this longtime cook in Atticus Finch’s household helps raise Scout and Jem and becomes a trusted maternal figure to them. She also takes the children to worship with her at Maycomb’s Black church. Name this character.
In *To Kill a Mockingbird*, Calpurnia takes Scout and Jem to this church in Maycomb, where Reverend Sykes leads the service and the congregation worships with them. What is the church called?
Which Swedish playwright and novelist, associated with modernist drama, wrote the chamber play *The Ghost Sonata* and the tragedy *Miss Julie*?
Which 1888 naturalistic play by August Strindberg unfolds during a Midsummer’s Eve celebration, as a count’s daughter and her father’s valet Jean become entangled in a destructive relationship?

This 1988 novel begins with Gibreel Farishta and Saladin Chamcha surviving an explosion aboard an aircraft over the English Channel. It blends magical realism with themes of migration, identity, and religious revelation. What is the novel?
The Satanic Verses was written by the British-Indian novelist who also wrote Midnight’s Children, a novel narrated by Saleem Sinai and set against India’s independence. Identify this author.
The Satanic Verses won this British literary prize for Novel of the Year in 1988, although it was only a finalist for that year’s Booker Prize. What prize did it win?
The Japanese translator of The Satanic Verses was stabbed to death in 1991 amid the international controversy surrounding the book. Name the translator.
In a German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm, an enchantress imprisons a girl in a tower. A prince reaches her by climbing her exceptionally long hair; what is the tale’s title?

Rapunzel appears in a German collection first published in 1812 under a title commonly translated as *Children’s and Household Tales*. Which two German folklorists gathered the stories for this collection?

Which French poet, born in 1821 and dead in 1867, wrote controlled, rhyming lyric verse and also worked as an essayist, translator, and art critic? His influence on later poets including Verlaine, Rimbaud, and Mallarmé helped make him a foundational figure in modern poetry.

Charles Baudelaire’s best-known lyric collection includes “The Albatross,” “The Swan,” and “To the Reader,” and responds to the rebuilding of nineteenth-century Paris. What is the title of this collection?
What French concept did Charles Baudelaire use for the fleeting experience of urban life and the artist’s responsibility to capture its present moment?

Allen Ginsberg’s landmark poem, composed in 1955 and published the following year, portrays a generation ravaged by madness and social pressures. Its three parts are driven by the recurring words “who” and “Moloch,” followed by an address to Carl Solomon.
Howl was first read publicly at this San Francisco venue on October 7, 1955, in an event that became an important moment in Beat poetry. What was the venue’s name?

This 19th-century American writer was born and died in Concord, Massachusetts, and spent 1845–47 living in a cabin he built beside a nearby pond. He later turned the experiment into a book and wrote an essay first published as “Resistance to Civil Government”; who was he?
Henry David Thoreau’s 1854 book reshapes his two years living near a Massachusetts pond into a single year for artistic unity, and its opening chapter is titled “Economy.” What is this work?

What is the name of the 1798 poetry collection jointly published by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge that helped launch English Romanticism? It includes Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.”
In the 1800 edition of Lyrical Ballads, which poet wrote the influential preface advocating ordinary subjects and everyday language in poetry? He also wrote the autobiographical poem The Prelude.

Which English modernist writer helped pioneer stream-of-consciousness narration and, with her husband Leonard, founded the Hogarth Press in 1917? Her novels include works about Clarissa Dalloway and the Ramsay family.
In this Virginia Woolf novel, Clarissa prepares for an evening party in postwar London while veteran Septimus Warren Smith struggles with the effects of the war. What is the novel called?

Which Virginia Woolf novel follows the Ramsay family at their summer home in the Hebrides? In its final section, Lily Briscoe completes her painting as James and Cam finally reach the island's beacon after a long-delayed journey.

In this Virginia Woolf essay, a fictional sister of Shakespeare named Judith illustrates the barriers women faced as writers. The essay argues that women need financial independence and privacy to write fiction; what is its title?

After moving to London, Virginia Woolf became a founding member of this informal circle of writers, artists, and critics. Its members included her sister Vanessa Bell and writer Lytton Strachey; what was the circle called?

Its first-person narrator describes a childhood shaped by a cruel stepfather, factory work, and a journey to live with his aunt, Betsey Trotwood. The novel follows his education, relationships, and moral development.
David Copperfield was written by the Victorian novelist who created Ebenezer Scrooge and Pip. He also wrote A Tale of Two Cities, set during the French Revolution.
This Italian lyric collection by Petrarch brings together sonnets, canzoni, and other poems, many reflecting on an idealized beloved named Laura. What is the collection known by its Italian title?
In Il Canzoniere, which woman is the idealized beloved whose presence and absence inspire many of Petrarch’s poems?

In this carpe diem poem, a speaker imagines spending centuries admiring his beloved, with his “vegetable love” growing slowly and vast. He then invokes the approaching “Time’s winged chariot” to argue that they should seize pleasure while they can. What is the poem?

To His Coy Mistress was written by an English poet whose other works include “The Garden” and the country-house poem “Upon Appleton House.” He also served as a Member of Parliament and held a government post under Oliver Cromwell. Who was he?

This American author studied psychology at Brooklyn College and is best known for a story about an experimental attempt to increase a man’s intelligence, later expanded into a novel. He also wrote the novel The Fifth Sally. Who was he?

In Daniel Keyes’s novel, bakery worker Charlie Gordon undergoes an experimental operation intended to increase his intelligence, and his progress reports chart his rise and decline. The laboratory mouse used in the same experiment provides another important measure of its effects. What is the novel’s title?

Which Irish avant-garde playwright and novelist wrote a drama in which Vladimir and Estragon wait beside a tree for someone who never arrives, as well as another centered on Hamm and Clov in a nearly bare room?
In Samuel Beckett’s play, Hamm and his servant Clov share a sparse shelter while Hamm’s parents, Nagg and Nell, live in ashbins and cannot kiss. What is the title of this work?
Created by Edgar Rice Burroughs, this jungle-raised hero was brought up by apes and first appeared in a 1912 novel. What is his name?
In a Sandra Cisneros novel, Esperanza works with film negatives at Peter Pan Photo Finishers and breaks her arm while trying to imitate Tarzan. What is the novel’s title?

A newly married town marshal returns by train to his Texas town with his new wife, while a local gunfighter expects their customary confrontation. When the gunfighter finds the marshal accompanied by his wife, the anticipated showdown loses its force. What short story is this?
answer: The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky

question: The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky is one of this American writer’s short stories. The same author created Henry Fleming, the young Union soldier at the center of The Red Badge of Courage, and wrote the shipwreck story The Open Boat. Who is the author?

Rick Riordan’s first Percy Jackson & the Olympians novel follows a New York schoolboy who learns that Greek gods are real and is sent on a cross-country quest after Zeus’s master bolt goes missing. What is the novel’s title?
In The Lightning Thief, this twelve-year-old son of Poseidon is accused of taking Zeus’s master bolt and sets out with Annabeth Chase and Grover Underwood to retrieve it. What is his name?
Born François-Marie Arouet, this French Enlightenment writer and philosopher became renowned for sharp satire and advocacy of religious freedom. What pen name did he use?

In Voltaire’s satirical novel, the title character is expelled from Baron Thunder-ten-Tronckh’s castle and travels with his tutor Pangloss and the servant Cacambo. What work ends with the advice to cultivate one’s garden?

George Bernard Shaw dated this five-act play to 1912 and subtitled it “A Romance in Five Acts.” Its plot centers on a phonetics professor’s wager that he can train a London flower seller to pass as a duchess. What is the title of the play?
In Pygmalion, which professor of phonetics bets Colonel Pickering that he can train Eliza Doolittle to pass as a duchess by changing her speech?

This American young adult novelist worked as an editor at Scholastic and became known for LGBTQ+-themed fiction. He also coauthored a novel with John Green whose two teenage narrators share the same name. Which author is this?
In David Levithan’s 2003 debut novel, a gay teen named Paul navigates first love at a high school where a student who plays quarterback is also elected homecoming queen. What is the novel’s title?
Which Chicago-born American poet wrote “We Real Cool” and “The Bean Eaters,” and became the first African American to win the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry?
Which poetry collection by Gwendolyn Brooks received the 1950 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry? Its recognition made her the first African American to win a Pulitzer Prize.
Gwendolyn Brooks lived in this Illinois city throughout her life, and its South Side community inspired her collection A Street in Bronzeville. What is the city?
During 1985–86, Gwendolyn Brooks held the federal counterpart of her earlier Illinois state literary appointment. What was the title of that office?
In 1976, Gwendolyn Brooks became the first African-American woman inducted into which prestigious literary institution?
answer: American Academy of Arts and Letters

question: In this short story, two landowners whose families have feuded for generations become trapped beneath a fallen tree while hunting on disputed forest land. They reconcile as they wait for help, but the story ends when wolves approach instead of rescuers. What is the story’s title?

The Interlopers was written by a British author who published under a one-word pen name. This author also wrote “The Open Window,” in which Framton Nuttel is led to believe that three hunters have died in a bog. Who was the author?
Anthony Burgess published this 1962 dystopian novel, whose teenage narrator Alex leads a gang of droogs and frequents the Korova Milk Bar. What is the novel's title?
In A Clockwork Orange, Alex narrates in a youth argot that mixes English with Russian vocabulary; words like “droog” and “tolchock” belong to it. What is this fictional language called?

This J. D. Salinger story first appeared in the January 31, 1948, issue of The New Yorker and later opened the collection Nine Stories. It moves from Muriel Glass’s phone call with her mother to Seymour’s beach conversation with a child, then ends with a sudden death in a hotel room. What is the story’s title?

In “A Perfect Day for Bananafish,” Seymour Glass speaks with a young girl on a Florida beach while his wife is at the hotel. The girl joins him in the water and listens to his strange fable about fish that gorge themselves on bananas; what is her name?

In Robert Louis Stevenson's *Treasure Island*, this ship's cook wins Jim Hawkins's trust while secretly organizing a mutiny aboard the Hispaniola. A former seaman with one leg, he later escapes with some of the buried treasure; who is he?
In *Treasure Island*, Long John Silver is the cook aboard this vessel, which carries Jim Hawkins and Squire Trelawney's expedition to the island under Captain Smollett. What is the name of the ship?
Anne, Charlotte, and Emily were nineteenth-century English novelists who published under the pen names Acton, Currer, and Ellis Bell. What are these writers collectively known as?

Among the novels by the Brontë sisters, which Charlotte Brontë work follows an orphaned governess who takes a post at Thornfield Hall, where she discovers that Bertha Mason is confined? The estate’s master, Edward Rochester, becomes central to her story.

A shipwreck separates two pairs of identical twins: the Antipholus brothers and their Dromio servants. Years later, their accidental reunion in one city drives a chain of mistaken identities and comic confusion; what Shakespeare play is this?

In The Comedy of Errors, which ancient city does Antipholus of Syracuse enter, where his twin has long lived and the mistaken-identity plot unfolds? Its duke presides over the opening judgment of Egeon.
Born in Kabul and trained as a physician in California, this Afghan-American novelist wrote The Kite Runner and A Thousand Splendid Suns. Who is this author?
In Khaled Hosseini’s 2003 novel, Amir returns to Afghanistan to try to rescue Sohrab, the son of his childhood friend Hassan. What is this novel’s title?

In Shakespeare’s island drama, this enslaved inhabitant is the son of the dead witch Sycorax and resents being taught the language of his master. After drinking Stephano’s wine, he pledges himself to Stephano as his true subject. Who is this character?

In The Tempest, this former Duke of Milan rules the island where Caliban lives and uses magic to bring his brother Antonio’s ship ashore. He relies on the spirit Ariel to carry out his plans before agreeing to leave the island. Who is this ruler?
An Old English attention-getting interjection opens the poem about the Spear-Danes and Beowulf’s battles with Grendel and the dragon. What is this word, often translated as “Listen” or “Lo”?
In her 2020 translation of Beowulf, this American novelist rendered Hwæt! as “Bro!” She compared its force to a man in a bar pounding his glass to demand another. Who is the translator?

Born in Monroeville, Alabama, this American novelist published a 1960 novel that won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction the following year. She later received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Who was she?

Harper Lee’s best-known novel is narrated by Scout Finch and set in the fictional Alabama town of Maycomb during the Great Depression. It follows Atticus Finch’s defense of Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of raping Mayella Ewell. What is the novel’s title?

Harper Lee assisted this close friend with research for his 1966 book about the murders of the Clutter family in Kansas. The book helped establish a landmark form of nonfiction storytelling. Who was the author?
Which English Jesuit priest and poet developed sprung rhythm, a metrical style that shaped his distinctive verse? He wrote both “The Windhover” and “The Wreck of the Deutschland.”

Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote this long poem in response to an 1875 shipwreck that killed five Franciscan nuns traveling to America, and he dedicated it to them. Which poem opens by addressing God as “giver of breath and bread”?

This confessional poem was composed by Sylvia Plath on October 12, 1962, shortly after her separation from Ted Hughes. Its speaker confronts an oppressive father figure through charged personal and historical imagery, then declares, “you bastard, I’m through.” What is the poem’s title?

In Sylvia Plath’s “Daddy,” the speaker’s father figure draws on the poet’s own father, a German-born entomologist and biology professor who died from undiagnosed diabetes shortly after her eighth birthday. What was his name?
In “Daddy,” the poem appeared posthumously in a 1965 collection alongside “Tulips” and “Lady Lazarus.” What is the collection’s title?

Which nineteenth-century English literary family was raised at Haworth Parsonage in West Yorkshire and included Charlotte, Emily, Anne, and Branwell, with the sisters writing *Jane Eyre*, *Wuthering Heights*, and *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall*?
In the Brontë family, which sister published *Wuthering Heights* under the pen name Ellis Bell and helped Anne create the imaginary world of Gondal?

Which 1952 John Steinbeck novel follows the intertwined Trask and Hamilton families across generations in California’s Salinas Valley? Its family conflicts echo the story of Cain and Abel and explore whether people can choose their own path.
In East of Eden, Lee consults his Chinese relatives about a Hebrew passage connected to Cain’s story. What word do they interpret as expressing that a person may choose how to act?

Truman Capote’s nonfiction novel recounts his reporting on the 1959 murders of four members of the Clutter family in Holcomb, Kansas. What is the title of the work that first appeared in four installments in The New Yorker in 1965?

During his 1959 research trip to Holcomb for In Cold Blood, Capote was accompanied by New Yorker fact-checker Sandy M. Campbell and a fellow American novelist. Which writer later became famous for To Kill a Mockingbird?

This American writer and filmmaker of Spokane and Coeur d’Alene heritage published the story collection *The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven*. He also wrote the screenplay for its film adaptation, *Smoke Signals*, and the novel *The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian*. Who is he?

Sherman Alexie’s novel follows Spokane teenager Arnold Spirit Jr., known as Junior, as he leaves his reservation school to attend Reardan. He joins the school’s basketball team and draws cartoons about his experiences. What is the novel’s title?
answer: The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian

question: As a Hogwarts student, he opened the Chamber of Secrets using a memory preserved in a diary, then later divided his soul among objects to evade death. What name did the leader of the Death Eaters use as Harry Potter’s chief enemy?

Lord Voldemort concealed fragments of his soul in objects and a living creature to anchor himself to life, and murder was required to create each one. What is the term for a receptacle made to contain such a soul fragment?

Published in 1857, this realist novel follows a country doctor’s wife whose romantic longings, affairs, and extravagant spending lead to crushing debt and a fatal dose of arsenic. Set in provincial France, it is known for Gustave Flaubert’s restrained narration. What is the novel?
Which 19th-century French novelist wrote Madame Bovary, the controversial 1857 work about Emma’s dissatisfaction with provincial life? His other novels include Sentimental Education and Salammbô.

First serialized in Le Siècle in 1844, this French adventure novel opens with a young Gascon arriving in Paris and becoming entangled with three royal guardsmen named Athos, Porthos, and Aramis. The four companions swear a motto expressing their mutual loyalty. What is this novel by Alexandre Dumas?
The Three Musketeers began appearing in installments on March 14, 1844, in a Paris newspaper, before its publication as a book later that year. What newspaper first serialized the novel?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy set at Elsinore, this newly crowned Danish ruler presents his marriage to his brother’s widow as a political union, yet privately admits that the crime which won him the crown still weighs on him. Who is this king?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy featuring Claudius, this dead Danish ruler appears to his son on the battlements at Elsinore and recounts that poison was poured into his ear while he slept. What is the identity of this apparition?

Which English metaphysical poet represented Kingston upon Hull in the House of Commons and served as Latin secretary to John Milton? He also wrote the carpe diem lyric in which the speaker hears “Time’s winged chariot” approaching.
Andrew Marvell’s lyric first imagines a courtship unconstrained by time, then turns to mortality and urges the lovers to seize the present. Which poem opens with “Had we but world enough and time”?

Born to Linda after she was left behind during a visit, this character grows up in Malpais, a New Mexico community outside the World State. He later travels to London and invokes Shakespeare while condemning the society’s use of soma and its controls on individual life. Who is this outsider in Aldous Huxley’s novel?

In Brave New World, John the Savage spends his childhood in a New Mexico community beyond the World State’s control, where he learns English and encounters Shakespeare. What is the name of that community, which Bernard and Lenina visit before bringing him to London?

A British vacuum-cleaner salesman living in Cuba is recruited by intelligence officers and starts sending them fabricated reports to satisfy his new employer. What is the title of Graham Greene’s comic espionage novel about him?

Our Man in Havana was written by the British novelist who also wrote The Power and the Glory, about a fugitive whiskey priest in Mexico, and Brighton Rock, centered on Pinkie Brown. Who is that writer?
An imaginative boy travels from Meridian to Maycomb each summer and becomes close friends with Scout and Jem Finch. What is the name by which this childhood friend is commonly known?
Dill Harris appears in what novel, set in Maycomb, Alabama, where Atticus Finch defends Tom Robinson against a false accusation by Mayella Ewell?

This Italian novelist and scholar of semiotics became internationally known for a medieval murder mystery set in a monastery, investigated by a Franciscan friar and his novice. He later wrote a novel in which three Milanese editors invent a far-reaching Templar conspiracy that begins to take on a life of its own. Which writer is described?

In this Umberto Eco novel, three Milanese editors devise a sprawling secret history linking the Knights Templar to modern events as a private game, but their invention draws the attention of people who believe it is real. What is the novel’s title?

This prose technique presents a character’s private mental activity as it unfolds, often moving through memories and associations rather than orderly exposition. What literary technique is being described?

Julio Cortázar’s experimental novel invites readers either to follow its chapters in printed order or to use a “Table of Instructions” beginning at Chapter 73; its fractured narrative also draws on stream of consciousness. What is the novel’s title?

This Welsh-born British author wrote about a poor boy whose golden ticket earns him a tour of a chocolate factory and a gifted schoolgirl who uses telekinesis against a cruel headmistress. Who is the writer of *Charlie and the Chocolate Factory* and *Matilda*?

In a novel by Roald Dahl, a neglected young reader discovers she can move objects with her mind, and her sympathetic teacher Miss Honey helps her confront the tyrannical headmistress Miss Trunchbull. What is the novel’s title?

In a novel by Roald Dahl, an orphaned girl is carried off to Giant Country by a kindly dream-catching giant whose speech includes comic verbal mistakes. They later enlist the Queen of England to stop the man-eating giants; what is the novel’s title?

This American Beat poet read a landmark poem at a San Francisco art venue in October 1955, before its publication in 1956 and the obscenity trial that followed. He also wrote “Kaddish” and “A Supermarket in California.” Who was this poet?
At which San Francisco venue did Allen Ginsberg give the first public reading of “Howl” in October 1955? The poem was published the following year.

Born in London in 1797 to political philosopher William Godwin and the author of *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, this English Romantic novelist began her best-known Gothic novel during a ghost-story challenge near Geneva in 1816. Who was she?

In the summer of 1816, Mary Shelley stayed near Lake Geneva with Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron, and John Polidori, and a rainy-weather contest inspired the group to devise ghost stories. What was the name of the Cologny estate where they gathered?

This 1897 Irish Gothic novel is told through diaries, letters, and newspaper reports. It follows an English solicitor’s visit to a Transylvanian nobleman and the vampire’s attempt to establish himself in England.

Dracula was published in 1897 by an Irish writer who served for nearly three decades as business manager of London’s Lyceum Theatre, working closely with actor Henry Irving. What was the writer’s name?

Arthur Miller’s 1953 four-act play dramatizes the Salem witch trials of 1692–1693 and uses the accusations as an allegory for the anti-communist persecution of his own era. What is the title of this play?

The playwright of The Crucible used the Salem witch trials to explore mass hysteria, accusation, and moral integrity. He also wrote Death of a Salesman, which won the 1949 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. Who wrote The Crucible?

In The Crucible, this Salem farmer is pressed to death after refusing to enter a plea, hoping to protect his property from forfeiture. During the torture, he reportedly urged his tormentors to add more weight. Who is he?

This 1947 drama follows Blanche DuBois as she arrives in New Orleans to stay with her sister Stella and brother-in-law Stanley Kowalski. It made its Broadway debut on December 3 of that year; name the play.
The writer of The Glass Menagerie and The Rose Tattoo also created A Streetcar Named Desire, the drama about Blanche DuBois’s troubled stay with the Kowalskis. Who was this American playwright?
In A Streetcar Named Desire, this former Southern belle comes to New Orleans after the loss of her family estate and stays with her younger sister and her sister’s husband. Which character is she?
The 1951 film adaptation of A Streetcar Named Desire was directed by this filmmaker, who also directed On the Waterfront and East of Eden. Who was he?

In Rudyard Kipling’s jungle stories, this boy is raised by the Seeonee wolf pack and learns the Law of the Jungle from Baloo and Bagheera. He becomes the target of Shere Khan, the tiger who resents his presence among the animals. Who is he?
Mowgli’s adventures appear in this 1894 story collection by Rudyard Kipling, which also includes “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi” and “Toomai of the Elephants.” What is the collection’s title?

In this allegorical novella, a revolt drives Mr. Jones from his estate, but the pigs who led it later establish a new dictatorship. George Orwell connected the political upheaval to the Russian Revolution and the Stalinist era; what is the title of this work?

The English writer born Eric Arthur Blair described Animal Farm as a satire against Stalin and sought to unite political purpose with artistic purpose. What pen name did he use as the author of Animal Farm?
In Animal Farm, the animals’ rebellion begins on Mr. Jones’s farm, which is later given a new name. What was the farm called before the uprising?
Animal Farm was first published in England after Orwell completed writing it in February 1944. On what date in 1945 did the novella first appear?
When Animal Farm was first published, its title was followed by a short subtitle that American publishers dropped for the 1946 edition. What was that subtitle?

In Shakespeare’s play, an exiled former Duke of Milan uses magic to strand his enemies on an island where he lives with his daughter, Miranda. What play ends with the duke regaining his position and renouncing his magic?
In The Tempest, this spirit helps Prospero stage the shipwreck and guide the castaways through the island’s spectacles. At the end, Prospero grants this servant the freedom he has promised.

What pen name did William Sydney Porter use for his short stories about characters such as Della and Jim, and the homeless man Soapy? This American writer became known for concise narratives and surprise endings.

A newly married couple each parts with a cherished possession to buy the other a Christmas present: Della sells her hair, while Jim sells his watch. What O. Henry short story centers on this exchange?
In an O. Henry story, two kidnappers seize a mischievous boy and demand money from his father, who ultimately pays them to take the boy back. What story is it?

O. Henry began writing this linked-story book while in Honduras, and its fictional Central American setting is called Anchuria. The work also helped introduce the phrase “banana republic”; what is its title?
O. Henry’s collection of New York stories takes its title from the city’s estimated population and includes both “The Gift of the Magi” and “The Cop and the Anthem.” What is the collection?
This American author wrote a novel about Margaret Simon’s questions about faith and puberty, as well as a story about Peter Hatcher’s exasperation with his younger brother Fudge. Who is this writer?
Judy Blume’s novel follows fifth-grader Jill Brenner as she joins in bullying classmate Linda Fischer, then finds herself on the receiving end of the cruelty. What is the novel’s title?

In this Thomas Hardy poem, a speaker surveys a frost-stricken landscape at the close of the nineteenth century, where winter has left the countryside bleak and lifeless. An old, frail bird suddenly sings from tangled branches, and the speaker wonders whether it knows of a hope he cannot see. What poem is this?

The Darkling Thrush was written by the English poet and novelist who set The Return of the Native around Egdon Heath and created Tess Durbeyfield in Tess of the d’Urbervilles. What is this writer’s name?

In this short story, neighbors gather for an annual drawing in an ordinary village, where a shabby black box holds folded slips of paper. The black-spotted slip identifies Tessie Hutchinson, and the villagers stone her.
Who wrote The Lottery, the 1948 New Yorker story whose matter-of-fact village setting gives way to communal violence? This author also wrote The Haunting of Hill House.
O. Henry’s linked stories about political maneuvering, commercial schemes, and expatriate life are set in a fictional Central American republic. What is the title of this collection?

Cabbages and Kings is a linked collection set in Anchuria, written by an American short-story writer also known for “The Gift of the Magi” and “The Cop and the Anthem.” What pen name did that writer use?

Born in Salem in 1804 and a Bowdoin College graduate, this 19th-century American writer became known for fiction steeped in New England history, moral ambiguity, and Puritan legacies. He wrote both The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables; who was he?

Nathaniel Hawthorne’s 1850 novel follows Hester Prynne, who is compelled by a Puritan community to wear an embroidered letter “A,” and features the minister Arthur Dimmesdale and Hester’s daughter Pearl. What is the novel’s title?
In 1837, Nathaniel Hawthorne gathered short fiction that had previously appeared in periodicals into this collection. It includes stories such as “The Minister’s Black Veil”; name the collection.

Nathaniel Hawthorne graduated in 1825 from this institution of higher education in Brunswick, Maine, where his classmates included future president Franklin Pierce and poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. What is the institution’s name?
Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in this New England port city, whose Puritan past and 1692 witch trials figure prominently in the region’s history and literary imagination. Which city was it?

Published in 1912, this Arthur Conan Doyle adventure follows Daily Gazette reporter Edward Malone as he joins an expedition to a remote South American plateau where supposedly extinct animals still live. What is the novel’s title?

In The Lost World, which combative scientist insists that prehistoric life survives on a South American plateau and leads an expedition to prove his claim? His companions include journalist Edward Malone, hunter Lord John Roxton, and Summerlee.

In Rick Riordan’s Norse-mythology series, this homeless Boston teenager discovers he is the son of the god Freyr. After dying while confronting the fire giant Surt, he is taken to Valhalla and becomes the hero of *The Sword of Summer*. Who is he?
Which 2015 novel introduces Magnus Chase, a homeless Boston teenager who learns he is a son of Freyr and is brought to Valhalla after dying in a confrontation with Surt?
This Czech writer’s 1920 play about manufactured workers helped introduce the word “robot.” He also wrote a novel about intelligent newts that wage war on humanity; who was he?
In Karel Čapek’s 1920 play, a factory creates artificial workers who eventually revolt against humanity. What is the play, known by the initials of its Czech title?

Born in Paris in 1905, this French intellectual developed an existentialist philosophy emphasizing human freedom and responsibility, and wrote philosophy, fiction, and drama. He declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature after publishing works including *Being and Nothingness* and *Nausea*. Who was he?

In this Jean-Paul Sartre play, three characters are confined in a Second Empire-style room, and a valet with no eyelids ushers them in. One character’s declaration that “Hell is other people” captures the play’s central conflict. What is the play?

Born in 1749, this German writer and polymath became a central figure in German-language literature and helped shape the cultural life of Weimar. His major works include *Faust* and *The Sorrows of Young Werther*; who was he?
In Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s celebrated drama, a scholar makes a pact in blood with Mephistopheles and later encounters Helen of Troy. What is the scholar’s name?

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s 1774 epistolary novel follows a man whose unrequited love for Lotte leads him into despair; he reads Ossian to her before eventually dying by suicide. What is the novel’s title?

Jane Austen’s *Lady Susan* is told through correspondence, while Bram Stoker’s *Dracula* combines letters, diary entries, and telegrams. What literary form is built from written communications exchanged between characters or addressed to a recipient?
In epistolary literature, which C. S. Lewis work presents advice sent by a senior demon to his nephew Wormwood, a junior tempter assigned to influence a human?

Set in 1327 at a wealthy Italian abbey, this historical mystery follows a Franciscan friar investigating seven deaths amid a labyrinthine library and debates over theology, logic, and laughter. Which novel by Umberto Eco is it?

In The Name of the Rose, which Franciscan friar arrives at the abbey with novice Adso of Melk to investigate the monks’ deaths? A former inquisitor, he uses observation and logical deduction to unravel the library-centered mystery.

In Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s 1855 narrative poem, this fictional Ojibwe warrior courts Minnehaha and experiences adventures shaped by Indigenous traditions. What is the name of the poem’s central character?

Hiawatha’s courtship of Minnehaha and encounters with figures such as Pau-Puk-Keewis appear in which 1855 narrative poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow? The work is written predominantly in trochaic tetrameter.
This 1957 poem by a Mexican writer consists of 584 lines, echoing the length of a cycle in the Aztec calendar and its associated symbolism. What is the poem’s title?
Sunstone is a major poem by which Mexican poet and diplomat, also known for The Labyrinth of Solitude and awarded the 1990 Nobel Prize in Literature?
What fourteen-line poetic form typically divides into three quatrains followed by a closing couplet, using an ABAB CDCD EFEF GG rhyme scheme?
In a Shakespearean sonnet, what meter is commonly used, typically giving each line five repetitions of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one?
Which Canadian short-story writer won the 2013 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote fiction often set in small-town Ontario? Her works include a linked-story book following Del Jordan’s coming of age.
Alice Munro published this 1971 work, a sequence of linked stories about Del Jordan growing up in the fictional Ontario town of Jubilee. What is its title?

In John Steinbeck’s novel about the Joad family’s journey from Oklahoma to California, this former preacher becomes a labor organizer among migrant workers. He is killed while trying to organize a strike.
In *The Grapes of Wrath*, after Jim Casy is killed while organizing migrant workers, which recently paroled son of the drought-stricken Oklahoma family kills the attacker?

This ancient Greek storyteller is traditionally credited with a body of moral tales, many featuring animals with human traits. No writings by him survive, and even his historical existence is uncertain; Aristotle and Herodotus are among the ancient authors who mention him. Who is this fabulist?

An episodic life story traditionally associated with Aesop portrays him as an enslaved person who wins his freedom through cleverness and later advises rulers and city-states. Scholars generally regard this account as highly fictional; what is the work called?

In a fable attributed to Aesop, a hungry animal repeatedly leaps for fruit hanging out of reach from a vine. After failing to get it, the animal dismisses the fruit as sour; what is the title of this tale?

A scholar's despair over the limits of knowledge leads him to bargain with a demonic tempter, while the tragedy's central human story follows a young woman whose seduction ends in imprisonment and a verdict of salvation. What is the natural title of Goethe's dramatic tragedy featuring these events?
In Faust, Part One, which young woman is given a sleeping potion that leads to her mother's death, later imprisoned after killing her infant, and refuses the tempter's offer of escape?

This 1944 memory play is narrated by Tom Wingfield and centers on his mother, Amanda, and his sister, Laura, whose life changes when a co-worker visits as a suitor. During the evening, the visitor accidentally damages Laura’s miniature unicorn. What play is it?

The playwright behind The Glass Menagerie later wrote A Streetcar Named Desire, whose New Orleans story pits Blanche DuBois against Stanley Kowalski. What professional name did this American dramatist use?

The Glass Menagerie premiered on December 26, 1944, in the city where critics Ashton Stevens and Claudia Cassidy helped turn an initially shaky production into a success. Which city hosted its first production?

After The Glass Menagerie opened in Chicago, a favorable review from a leading Chicago Tribune drama critic helped draw audiences to the struggling production and support its move to Broadway. What was this critic’s name, alongside Ashton Stevens in championing the play?

This dramatic principle says that a conspicuous detail introduced into a story should later prove consequential rather than remain idle. It is famously summarized through a stage weapon that, if displayed, should eventually be fired; what is this principle called?

Chekhov's gun is often explained through a rule about a displayed weapon eventually being used. In which play by the principle's namesake does Konstantin Treplev shoot a bird and give it to Nina, before later dying by suicide?

After an uneasy night, a traveling salesman awakens to find that he has become a monstrous insect-like creature. He tries to conceal a picture of a woman in furs when his furniture is being removed. Who is this protagonist of Franz Kafka’s novella?

The novella about Gregor Samsa was published by Kafka in 1915, first appearing in the October issue of *Die weißen Blätter* before a book edition followed that December. What is its commonly used English title?
In Gregor Samsa’s family, which sister initially brings food to his room, later insists that the household must get rid of the creature, and had hoped to study violin at a conservatory?

A Colombian novelist and journalist, he became a leading exponent of magical realism, bringing extraordinary events into otherwise everyday settings. He received the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote a celebrated multigenerational story about the Buendía family.

Gabriel García Márquez's novel follows generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo. It opens with Colonel Aureliano Buendía recalling the day his father took him to discover ice.
In Gabriel García Márquez's fiction, this fictional village is the setting for the Buendía family's saga and was chiefly inspired by his birthplace, Aracataca. What is the village called?
Gabriel García Márquez received this major literary honor in 1982, becoming the first Colombian laureate in its category. What was the award?
Gabriel García Márquez was born in this Colombian town, which is commonly cited as the principal inspiration for Macondo. What is the town's name?

This short story follows a young married couple who each sell a prized possession to afford a Christmas surprise for the other. Its ending pairs combs that cannot be used with a chain that has no watch to adorn. What O. Henry story is it?
The Gift of the Magi was written by the American short-story writer also known for “The Ransom of Red Chief” and “A Retrieved Reformation.” What byline did this writer use?
In The Gift of the Magi, which spouse has only $1.87 and sells her long hair to buy a watch chain for Jim? What is her name?
In The Gift of the Magi, which husband sells a gold watch inherited from his grandfather to buy combs for his wife’s hair? Give his familiar name.
The Gift of the Magi was included in book form in April 1906 in this O. Henry collection, whose title refers to New York City’s population. What is the collection called?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy, this Capulet kinsman challenges Romeo after Romeo refuses to fight, then kills Mercutio when he intervenes. Romeo later kills him, further inflaming the feud between the two households. Which character is this?
Tybalt fatally wounds this witty friend of Romeo after the two duel in a Verona street. Earlier, this character delivers the speech about Queen Mab. Who is he?

In Juan Rulfo’s 1955 novel, a young man named Juan Preciado travels to the Mexican town of Comala to fulfill a promise to his dying mother by seeking the father he never knew. The town’s inhabitants gradually reveal themselves as voices of the dead. What is the novel’s title?

In Pedro Páramo, which son of Dolores travels to Comala after promising his dying mother he would seek the father he never knew? His arrival provides the novel’s opening frame before the town’s many voices take over.

H. P. Lovecraft's short story pieces together a sculptor's clay relief, Professor Angell's records of disturbing dreams, and a Norwegian sailor's account of a monstrous city rising from the sea. Which story uses these separate reports to introduce an ancient being worshiped by a secretive cult?

In The Call of Cthulhu, Norwegian sailor Gustaf Johansen describes a city of immense, non-Euclidean architecture that surfaces in the Pacific. What is the name of this city, where the Great Old One's tomb is opened?

Born Albert Chinualumogu in colonial Nigeria, this novelist used English shaped by Igbo proverbs and storytelling to challenge colonial depictions of African life. His 1958 first novel became a landmark of modern African literature; who was this writer?

In Chinua Achebe’s novel, a celebrated wrestler and clan leader accidentally kills Ikemefuna, is sent into seven years of exile, and later confronts the arrival of British rule. Which novel follows Okonkwo’s fate in Umuofia?

In his 1975 lecture, Chinua Achebe criticized Joseph Conrad’s portrayal of Africans in a famous novella, arguing that it relies on racist assumptions and denies Africans full humanity. What title did Achebe give this influential essay?

In Chinua Achebe’s novel set in the Igbo community of Umuaro, Ezeulu is the chief priest of Ulu and refuses the British administration’s pressure to serve as a warrant chief. Which work follows the resulting clash between religious authority, colonial rule, and his own people?

Born in Besançon in 1802, this French Romantic writer became a leading literary figure through dramas such as *Hernani* and novels including *Les Misérables*. He spent years in political exile after opposing Napoleon III. Who was he?
In Victor Hugo’s novel, former convict Jean Valjean tries to rebuild his life after stealing silver from Bishop Myriel, while Inspector Javert relentlessly pursues him. What is this novel called?
Set in 15th-century France, this Victor Hugo novel follows the bell-ringer Quasimodo and the Romani dancer Esmeralda, whose fate is entangled with Archdeacon Claude Frollo. What is the novel’s title?

This American novelist, poet, journalist, and short-story writer was born in 1871 and died of tuberculosis in Germany at age 28. His works include a Civil War novel that brought him international acclaim and a Bowery story often regarded as an early American Naturalist novel. Who was he?

Stephen Crane’s 1895 Civil War novel follows Henry Fleming, a young Union soldier who fears battle, flees during his first engagement, and later returns to fight. What novel takes its title from the visible injury Henry hopes to acquire as evidence that he has faced combat?

Stephen Crane’s 1893 novel set in Manhattan’s Bowery follows a young woman whose poverty and abusive home life lead her into prostitution. Often considered the first work of American literary Naturalism, what is this novel called?
answer: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets

question: After the SS Commodore sank on Stephen Crane’s voyage toward Cuba, he and three other men spent about 30 hours adrift in a dinghy. Which short story draws on this ordeal to portray shipwreck survivors struggling at sea?
In Katherine Mansfield’s short story, the wealthy Sheridan family prepares a celebration while Laura learns that a working-class neighbor, Mr. Scott, has died. What is the name of this story?
The Garden Party was written by Katherine Mansfield, who was born in Wellington and grew up in the country where Māori are Indigenous. What country was it?

Published in 1925, this novel follows a mysterious Long Island millionaire who hopes to reunite with Daisy Buchanan. Its first-person narrator, Nick Carraway, observes the pursuit amid Jazz Age wealth and disillusionment. What is the novel?

In The Great Gatsby, whose lavish West Egg parties attract crowds who often have never met their host? He hopes to rekindle a romance with Daisy Buchanan and gazes across the water toward a green light on her dock.
In The Great Gatsby, which East Egg resident is Nick Carraway’s cousin and the woman Gatsby hopes to win back? She is married to Tom and is driving the car that kills Myrtle Wilson.
The Great Gatsby is narrated by this Midwesterner, who rents a modest home beside Gatsby’s mansion in West Egg. He is Daisy’s cousin and arranges for her to meet Gatsby again.
In The Great Gatsby, what desolate industrial area lies between West Egg and Manhattan? A billboard showing the eyes of an optometrist looms over George and Myrtle Wilson’s garage there.

This American author and Vietnam War veteran wrote the novel *Going After Cacciato*, about a soldier who imagines deserting his unit and walking to Paris, and the linked-story collection *The Things They Carried*. Who is he?
In Tim O’Brien’s collection *The Things They Carried*, which story follows the narrator’s return to Vietnam with his daughter Kathleen, where he takes her to the spot where Kiowa died?

In this 1985 novel, the narrator’s red uniform marks her as one of the fertile women forced to bear children for elite households in a theocratic state that has replaced the United States. Known as Offred, she recounts her life under this system; what is the novel’s title?
The Handmaid’s Tale and its sequel, The Testaments, were written by the Canadian novelist who also created Oryx and Crake and The Blind Assassin. Who is this author?

In The Handmaid’s Tale, Offred learns the name of this clandestine resistance movement from Ofglen, another Handmaid. Its name is also used as an international radio distress call; what is the movement called?

Margaret Mitchell’s 1936 novel follows Scarlett O’Hara from the Civil War through Reconstruction, with much of the story centered on her family’s Georgia plantation. Its final line promises that “tomorrow is another day”; what novel is this?
In Gone with the Wind, Scarlett O’Hara returns to this family plantation after Atlanta falls and vows that she will never go hungry again. What is the name of her home?

This 1895 American war novel follows a young Union private whose fear and shame after fleeing battle matter as much as the fighting itself. Its title evokes the wound he hopes will mark him as a hero. What Stephen Crane novel is it?

The Red Badge of Courage was written by a novelist born after the Civil War who had never experienced battle firsthand. He also wrote Maggie: A Girl of the Streets and “The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky”; who was he?

In The Red Badge of Courage, this young Union private flees from battle and later longs for a wound that might serve as proof of his bravery. When his regiment fights again, he carries its flag. What is his name?
In The Red Badge of Courage, this tall soldier is a friend of the protagonist and has said he would run if everyone else ran. After being shot in the side, he dies during the retreat. Who is he?
The Red Badge of Courage places a Union regiment in combat against Confederate troops, though the novel does not identify its fictional battle by name. What conflict provides the setting?

In Harper Lee’s story set in Maycomb, Alabama, Scout and Jem Finch spend years trying to glimpse this reclusive neighbor, whose gifts appear in a tree’s knot-hole. On Halloween night, he intervenes to save the children from Bob Ewell. Who is he?
Boo Radley is one of the mysterious Maycomb residents in this Harper Lee novel, which follows Scout Finch’s childhood and her father Atticus’s defense of Tom Robinson. What is the novel’s title?

In Lewis Carroll’s 1865 novel, this curious girl follows a waistcoat-wearing White Rabbit down a hole and finds that eating or drinking can radically alter her size. She returns in the sequel, where she crosses a mirror into a chessboard world.

Alice’s two fantasy novels were published under the pen name Lewis Carroll, but their author used a different name in his private life. What was the full name of the Oxford mathematician who wrote them?

This Shakespearean tragedy opens with an aging monarch asking his three daughters to declare their love before he divides his kingdom. After disowning the daughter whose answer is restrained rather than flattering, he faces betrayal, a storm, and madness; what is the play?

In King Lear, which daughter is disowned after declining to compete with her sisters’ extravagant declarations of affection? She later returns to Britain with a French force, but the tragedy ends with her death alongside her father.
This Chilean poet and educator was born Lucila Godoy Alcayaga and became the first Latin American to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1945. What name did she publish under?
Gabriela Mistral’s first major poetry collection was published in New York in 1922 and includes her celebrated sequence “Los sonetos de la muerte.” What is the collection’s title?
Which 1879 realist drama follows a wife who secretly borrows money to save her husband, then leaves him after the truth about the loan transforms their understanding of their marriage? Name the play.
In A Doll's House, Nora and Torvald's marriage is shaped by the social constraints of their time. Which Norwegian playwright also wrote Peer Gynt and Hedda Gabler?
At which Copenhagen theater did A Doll's House premiere on December 21, 1879? The venue is Denmark's national theater.
In A Doll's House, Nora performs a dance to distract Torvald from reading Krogstad's letter, growing increasingly wild as he watches. What is the name of this dance?

In Thornton Wilder’s drama set in the fictional town of Grover’s Corners, this unnamed figure speaks directly to the audience and guides the story. He presides over Emily Webb and George Gibbs’s wedding and later allows Emily to revisit her twelfth birthday.
The Stage Manager narrates this Thornton Wilder play, set in Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire. Its sparse staging uses few pieces of furniture and ladders as props; what is the play’s title?

What 1960 novel follows Scout and Jem Finch growing up in Maycomb, Alabama, while their father defends Tom Robinson against a false accusation? Its treatment of racial injustice and childhood loss of innocence made it a classic of modern American literature.
To Kill a Mockingbird was the debut novel of this Alabama-born author, who received the Pulitzer Prize for the book in 1961. She published no other book until Go Set a Watchman appeared in 2015.
In To Kill a Mockingbird, Scout and Jem initially fear this reclusive neighbor, whose small gifts they find hidden in a tree. He later saves them from Bob Ewell after a Halloween pageant.
In To Kill a Mockingbird, this Finch family cook takes Scout and Jem to her church, First Purchase African M.E. Church. She is also a mother figure to the children.
In To Kill a Mockingbird, this Black man is falsely accused by Mayella Ewell, and Atticus Finch serves as his defense lawyer. His left arm was badly injured in a cotton gin accident.

Maya Angelou’s 1969 autobiographical memoir follows her from childhood in Stamps, Arkansas, through adolescence in St. Louis and San Francisco, ending when she is seventeen. What is the title of this first volume in her life-writing series?
answer: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

question: In *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings*, this teacher and family friend encourages young Maya to read poetry aloud and memorize literary works, helping her regain confidence in her voice. Who is she?

In the dragon episode of an Old English epic, this young Geatish retainer is the only one of the king’s companions who returns to help after the others flee. He fights beside the king and later rebukes the deserters. Who is he?

Wiglaf appears near the end of this Old English epic, whose Geatish hero previously defeated Grendel and Grendel’s mother. The poem concludes with the hero’s fatal battle against a dragon and the mourning of his people. What is the poem’s title?

Born in St. Louis, this poet moved to England and later became a British subject. He became a leading modernist whose best-known works include “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” and “The Waste Land.” Who is he?
T. S. Eliot’s 1922 poem opens with the declaration that “April is the cruellest month.” Its final section, “What the Thunder Said,” ends with the repeated word “Shantih.” What is this poem?

In a dramatic monologue by T. S. Eliot, the speaker worries about disturbing the universe and asks, “Do I dare to eat a peach?” He also hears women “talking of Michelangelo.” What is the name of this speaker?
T. S. Eliot wrote this 1935 verse play about the martyrdom of Archbishop Thomas Becket. What is the title of the play?
