T. S. Eliot received this major international literary honor in 1948, recognized for his pioneering contribution to poetry. What was the honor?

This 1950 science-fiction story cycle links accounts of Earth expeditions to Mars, encounters with its ancient civilization, and the later settlement of the planet. In the complete form its author came to prefer, 28 story-chapters trace exploration, exploitation, and eventual abandonment of Mars; what is the work’s title?
The Martian Chronicles was first published in the United States in 1950, but its British first edition appeared in 1951 under a different title. What title did that British edition use?

Published in 1990, this Michael Crichton science-fiction thriller follows a genetic engineering company that recreates dinosaurs using DNA recovered from insects preserved in amber. Visitors tour its island theme park until the animals escape their enclosures; what novel is it?

In Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park, InGen builds its dinosaur attraction on a fictional island off Costa Rica, distinct from the larger island used as the setting for the sequel. What is the original novel’s park island called?

In Jules Verne’s adventure novel, this wealthy London gentleman wagers 20,000 pounds at the Reform Club that he can circle the globe and return within 80 days. He travels with his French valet, Passepartout, and rescues Aouda in India. Who is this protagonist?
Phileas Fogg is the protagonist of an 1872 French adventure novel whose French title is *Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours*. Which author wrote this novel?
In a Grimm fairy tale, a young woman is kept in a tower with no door, and a prince reaches her by climbing the long hair she lowers from its window. What is the name of this character?
In the Grimm tale of Rapunzel, what is the name of the enchantress who takes the child after her parents give her up in exchange for greens stolen from the enchantress’s garden?

In Henrik Ibsen’s drama, this woman secretly borrows money for a trip to Italy that helps save her husband’s life, signing her late father’s name on the loan papers. When her husband reacts to the blackmail scandal by worrying about his reputation, she leaves their home to seek independence. Who is she?
Nora Helmer performs this increasingly frantic dance to distract Torvald from checking the letterbox, where a letter from Krogstad is waiting. What dance is she performing?

In Goethe’s tragedy, this supernatural tempter first appears to the scholar Faust as a black poodle and later offers him companionship in an agreement signed in blood. He describes himself as part of a power that wills evil yet brings about good; name this witty, shape-changing figure.

In Part One of Goethe’s *Faust*, Mephistopheles helps Faust approach a young woman by supplying a jewel casket, setting in motion a romance that ends in her imprisonment after she kills her newborn child. What familiar name is given to this woman, whose brother Valentine also dies in the tragedy?

In this dystopian novel, twelve-year-old Jonas is selected at the Ceremony of Twelve to inherit memories from an older man and becomes troubled by what his community has sacrificed for order. Near the end, he flees with the infant Gabriel. What is the novel’s title?

Which author wrote The Giver, the dystopian novel in which Jonas is chosen to train as Receiver of Memory? The same author also wrote Number the Stars, a historical novel set in Nazi-occupied Denmark.

An English soldier-poet, he wrote about the horrors of trench combat and gas warfare rather than celebrating war. His best-known poems include “Dulce et Decorum Est” and “Anthem for Doomed Youth.” Who was he?

Wilfred Owen’s sonnet begins by asking, “What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?” It replaces church funeral rites with battlefield imagery, including “the stuttering rifles’ rapid rattle.” What is the poem’s title?

Wilfred Owen’s poetry was strongly influenced by this fellow English soldier-poet, whose works include “Counter-Attack.” The two met while recovering at Craiglockhart War Hospital. Who was Owen’s mentor?

Wilfred Owen served as an infantry officer in the conflict that began in 1914 and brought trench warfare and poison-gas attacks to Europe. He was killed in action one week before the November 1918 armistice that ended it. What conflict was this?

Isaac Asimov’s short story follows successive generations of people asking increasingly advanced descendants of Multivac whether entropy can be reversed. After the universe has gone dark, the final computer finds a way to begin creation anew; what is the story’s title?
In The Last Question, technicians Alexander Adell and Bertram Lupov first ask a planet-spanning computer whether entropy can be reversed. What is the computer called?

This demigod is the son of mortal Sally and Poseidon, and his sword Anaklusmos disguises itself as a pen. In Rick Riordan’s first novel about him, he joins Grover Underwood on a quest involving Zeus’s stolen master bolt. Who is this hero?

In the Percy Jackson stories, this daughter of Athena joins Percy and Grover on the quest to recover Zeus’s stolen master bolt in The Lightning Thief. She is known for calling Percy “seaweed brain.” Who is she?

Born in Panama in 1928 and later recognized as a Mexican writer, this novelist became a leading figure of the Latin American Boom. His 1962 novel follows a dying former power broker through three narrative viewpoints and time periods; who wrote it?

Carlos Fuentes’s 1985 novel imagines the fate of American writer Ambrose Bierce in revolutionary Mexico, exploring the border as a source of cultural and political tension. What is the title of this work?
Suzanne Collins’s 2008 dystopian novel follows Katniss Everdeen after she volunteers to take her younger sister’s place in an annual televised fight to the death. What is the novel called?
In The Hunger Games, Katniss lives in a post-apocalyptic nation ruled by the Capitol and divided into districts. What is the name of that nation?

This Shakespearean tragedy follows a Venetian military commander whose marriage to Desdemona is undermined by a subordinate’s deception and a handkerchief used to fuel suspicion. After believing his wife has been unfaithful, the commander kills her and then himself. What play is it?

In Othello, this ensign manipulates the general’s trust, persuades him that Desdemona has been unfaithful, and uses her handkerchief as false evidence. He also urges Roderigo to “put money in thy purse” while advancing his schemes. Who is this villain?

Which 1987 novel by Chinua Achebe is set in the fictional West African nation of Kangan and follows the intertwined lives of Chris Oriko, Ikem Osodi, and Beatrice Okoh amid military rule and political repression?
In Anthills of Savannah, journalist Ikem Osodi and commissioner Chris Oriko live under the rule of Sam, the military Head of State. What is the name of their fictional West African country?

An orphaned storyteller recounts her life amid political upheaval and personal turmoil, using her gift for invention to shape the people and events around her. What 1987 novel by Isabel Allende bears this storyteller’s name?
Eva Luna is one of several novels by the Chilean writer who made her fiction debut with the family saga The House of the Spirits and later wrote Daughter of Fortune. What is this author’s full name?

In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Jazz Age novel, she is the cousin of the narrator and an East Egg socialite whose voice Gatsby associates with wealth. She is married to a wealthy former Yale football player. Who is she?
Daisy Buchanan’s cousin rents a modest house in West Egg next door to Gatsby, works in the bond business, and narrates the novel’s events. Who is he?

In J. K. Rowling’s seven-book fantasy series, this orphaned wizard is sorted into a house with a lion emblem and becomes close friends with Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. He survives the Killing Curse as a baby and is later called “the Boy Who Lived.” Who is the central character?

In the Harry Potter novels, which Hogwarts house places the young wizard in the same student group as Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger? Its emblem is a lion, and its traditional virtues include courage and daring.
Born in Litchfield, Connecticut, in 1811, this American author became a prominent abolitionist after publishing a hugely influential antislavery novel in 1852. What was her name?

Harriet Beecher Stowe published this 1852 antislavery novel, whose subtitle was *Life Among the Lowly* and whose plot includes Eliza fleeing with her son, Harry. Simon Legree orders the title character beaten after he refuses to reveal where two other enslaved people have gone; what is the novel?
Harriet Beecher Stowe set this 1859 novel in colonial-era Newport, Rhode Island; its characters include Mary Scudder, Samuel Hopkins, and sailor James Marvyn. What is the title of this work?

In this 1856 novel, an enslaved man who escaped bondage leads a community of fugitives in a vast marshland on the Virginia–North Carolina border, while plantation heiress Nina Gordon’s story runs alongside his. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote this antislavery work; what is its title?
answer: Dred: A Tale of the Great Dismal Swamp

question: In this E. B. White children's novel, Fern Arable raises a runt pig named Wilbur, who later becomes the focus of a barnyard scheme involving a spider and a food-loving rat named Templeton. What is the novel's title?
In Charlotte's Web, which girl insists that the newborn runt pig should be allowed to live, raises him until he is moved to her uncle's farm, and later visits him at the county fair?

A Heian-period Japanese court writer served Empress Shōshi and recorded court life in a diary, including celebrations surrounding the birth of Shōshi’s son. Tradition also credits her with composing a landmark narrative about Prince Genji; who was this writer?

Murasaki Shikibu is traditionally credited with writing a long Heian court narrative about a fictional imperial prince who is made a commoner and pursues an eventful romantic and political life. Its later Uji chapters follow a younger generation after the protagonist’s death; what is the work?

In William Golding’s island novel, this bespectacled, asthmatic schoolboy argues for reason and rules, and his glasses are vital for making fire. Roger kills him by sending a boulder crashing down at Castle Rock. Which character is it?
Piggy appears in which William Golding novel, where a group of British schoolboys stranded on an uninhabited island use a conch to call assemblies before their fragile order breaks down?

Born in Harlem in 1924, this American writer became a teenage preacher before publishing his autobiographically informed first novel, *Go Tell It on the Mountain*. He later wrote influential fiction and essays addressing race, sexuality, and American society; who was he?

In a 1949 essay, James Baldwin criticizes the violence of Richard Wright’s *Native Son* and the sentimentality of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s *Uncle Tom’s Cabin*. What is the title of this essay about the way fiction addresses racial injustice?
Which nineteenth-century French novelist created the vast linked cycle La Comédie humaine and wrote The Wild Ass’s Skin and Eugénie Grandet?

In Honoré de Balzac’s novel about an aging former vermicelli maker, law student Eugène de Rastignac lives at the Maison Vauquer alongside the title character. The man’s daughters, Anastasie and Delphine, neglect him as his fortune dwindles.

Published in 1848 under the pseudonym Acton Bell, this novel by Anne Brontë is framed as Gilbert Markham’s account and includes Helen Graham’s diary recounting a troubled marriage. What is the novel’s title?
In The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, what is the name of Helen Graham’s husband, a charming but selfish gentleman whose alcoholism and infidelity lead her to flee with their young son?

Sophocles’ tragedy begins with an aged, blind exile entering a grove sacred to the Eumenides in a village outside Athens. Theseus eventually offers him refuge, and the exile’s mysterious death brings the plot to its close; what is the play’s title?
In *Oedipus at Colonus*, which Athenian king grants the blind, aged exile protection after he arrives at the sacred grove, despite pressure from Creon to surrender him?

Born in San Francisco in 1916, this American writer became known for fiction that turns ordinary homes and communities unsettling. Her 1948 story about a village’s deadly annual ritual and her novels about a haunted mansion and the Blackwood family are among her best-known works. Who was she?

Shirley Jackson’s 1959 novel follows Eleanor Vance, who joins a small group investigating a mansion reputed to be haunted. As Eleanor becomes increasingly drawn to the residence, the story ends with her driving into a tree. What is the novel’s title?

In this traditional fairy tale, a girl carrying food to her grandmother is diverted by a wolf in the forest, and the animal reaches the house first and disguises itself as the grandmother. What story is it?

In the 1697 collection *Histoires ou contes du temps passé*, which French writer published a version of Little Red Riding Hood in which the girl and her grandmother are eaten, with no huntsman arriving to rescue them?
First published in 1678, this English Christian allegory follows a traveler who leaves the City of Destruction and journeys toward the Celestial City. What work is it?
In The Pilgrim's Progress, Christian and Faithful pass through a bustling place where the devilish trio Beelzebub, Apollyon, and Legion sell worldly pleasures. What is this place called?

The Pilgrim's Progress was written by this English nonconformist preacher, who began composing it during one of his imprisonments for holding religious services outside the established church. Who was he?

This English Augustan poet wrote a 1711 work on literary judgment that includes the warning “a little learning is a dangerous thing.” He was also celebrated for his mastery of rhymed heroic couplets and translated Homer’s Iliad. Who was he?
Alexander Pope transforms a quarrel over the cutting of Belinda’s hair into a mock epic, using the grand style of heroic poetry to magnify a fashionable social slight. What is the title of this poem?

J. M. Coetzee’s 1999 novel follows a Cape Town professor whose sexual assault of student Melanie Isaacs leads to a university inquiry and upheaval in post-apartheid South Africa. What is the novel’s title?
In Disgrace, which Cape Town professor faces a university inquiry after sexually assaulting student Melanie Isaacs? He resigns and later goes to his daughter Lucy’s farm in the Eastern Cape.
Born Samuel Langhorne Clemens, this American humorist grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, and wrote novels about Tom Sawyer and Huck Finn. What pen name did he use?

Mark Twain’s novel follows a boy who fakes his death and later travels down the Mississippi River on a raft with an escaped enslaved man named Jim. It also features two con men who claim to be a duke and a king. What is the novel’s title?
Mark Twain spent much of his childhood in this river town, which later inspired the fictional setting of his novels about Tom Sawyer and Huck Finn. What town was it?

Mark Twain gained international attention with an 1865 comic tale narrated by Simon Wheeler at a California mining camp. Wheeler recounts a gambler whose prized amphibian loses a contest after a stranger secretly loads it with lead shot. What is the tale’s title?
answer: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County

question: Mark Twain worked as a steamboat pilot on the river that flows past Hannibal and New Orleans, and later drew on that experience in a book blending memoir, history, and travel. What is the book’s title?
In Victor Hugo’s novel, this deaf bell-ringer lives in Notre-Dame Cathedral and was raised by Archdeacon Claude Frollo. What is the name of the novel’s title character?
Quasimodo rings the bells of this Gothic Paris landmark on the Île de la Cité, whose construction began in 1163. What building is the central setting of Hugo’s novel?

In Victor Hugo’s novel, this former convict receives a lengthy prison sentence after stealing a loaf of bread, with repeated escape attempts extending his term. After a bishop shows him mercy, he builds a new life as a factory owner and mayor under the name Monsieur Madeleine. Who is this character?

After Jean Valjean is caught with stolen silver, which elderly cleric tells the police that the silver was a gift and gives him two candlesticks as well? He holds the highest local church office in Digne and is among the novel’s first major examples of compassion.

During the Dust Bowl, this Oklahoma tenant-farming family loses its home and travels west along Route 66 in search of work. They are the central family in John Steinbeck’s novel about Depression-era migrant labor, whose closing scene features one member nursing a starving man.

The Joad family are at the center of a 1939 novel by this American author, who also wrote *Of Mice and Men* and *East of Eden*. Born in Salinas, California, he received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature.

Which Mark Twain novel, begun in 1876 and completed for typesetting in 1884, is narrated by a boy who fakes his death to escape his abusive father and then travels by raft on the Mississippi with an enslaved man seeking freedom?

In The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, what is the name of the enslaved man who escapes and travels down the Mississippi with Huck? Their growing friendship challenges beliefs Huck has absorbed about slavery and morality.

A 1928 novel by Aldous Huxley portrays intertwined relationships and intellectual debates in English society. One of its plotlines follows journalist Walter Bidlake’s love for Lucy Tantamount; what is the novel’s title?
In Aldous Huxley’s Point Counter Point, which journalist becomes romantically involved with Lucy Tantamount, forming one strand in the novel’s network of social entanglements?

In Chaucer's collection of stories narrated by pilgrims, this work follows two Theban cousins imprisoned in Athens who become rivals after falling in love with the same Athenian woman; their contest is settled through a tournament arranged by the city's ruler. What is the work's title?
In The Knight's Tale, which duke of Athens discovers Palamon and Arcite fighting in the woods, imprisons them, and later arranges a tournament to decide which may marry Emily?

In Douglas Adams’s Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy series, this robot is extraordinarily intelligent but trapped in a body with personality circuits that leave him perpetually miserable. He travels with Arthur Dent and Ford Prefect aboard a ship powered by an experimental drive. Which character is this?
Marvin the Paranoid Android serves aboard this starship, whose experimental drive enables travel by passing through every point in the universe at once. What is the name of the ship?

The British author of *American Gods* also created a comic saga in which Dream, one of the Endless, is captured and later seeks to reclaim his realm. Who is this writer, who co-wrote *Good Omens* with Terry Pratchett?

In which Neil Gaiman novel does ex-convict Shadow Moon become the bodyguard of Mr. Wednesday, traveling across the United States as ancient mythological figures clash with personifications of modern life?

A 1959 poem by a Chicago poet is headed with the descriptions “The Pool Players” and “Seven at the Golden Shovel.” Its brief, syncopated declarations repeatedly end with “We,” before the final words abruptly turn the speakers’ bravado toward mortality. Name this poem.

In “We Real Cool,” seven pool players speak in a terse, syncopated collective voice. The poem appeared in this 1960 collection, whose title poem portrays “Two who are Mostly Good” and says their dinner is “a casual affair.” Name the collection.

This 1948 novel follows Zulu priest Stephen Kumalo from his rural home to Johannesburg as he searches for his son, who is on trial for murdering a white farmer’s son. What novel by South African writer Alan Paton is it?
Cry, the Beloved Country includes a brief appearance by its author as the head of a reformatory, reflecting his experience directing a reformatory school. Who was this South African novelist?
A 1949 musical adaptation of Cry, the Beloved Country had a book by Maxwell Anderson and music by Kurt Weill. What was the musical’s title?

Which Shakespeare comedy intertwines the tangled courtship of four Athenian lovers with a quarrel between fairy monarchs and a troupe of craftsmen preparing a wedding performance? First printed in 1600, it culminates in reconciled couples and a comic staging of a tragic legend.

In *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, which mischievous attendant to Oberon uses an enchanted flower’s juice to confuse the lovers and mistakenly redirects Lysander’s affections? He also gives the craftsman Bottom an ass’s head.

A sonnet by an English Romantic poet tells of a traveler who finds a shattered ruler’s statue in the desert. Its boastful inscription survives, but the empire it celebrates has vanished; what is the poem called?
In Ozymandias, the ruined statue is described through the account of a traveler from an ancient land. The poet also wrote “Mont Blanc” and “To a Skylark”; who was he?
What 1936 satirical science-fiction novel by a Czech writer follows intelligent amphibians first exploited for pearl fishing, then demanding lebensraum and threatening human civilization?
The War with the Newts is a satirical science-fiction novel by which Czech writer? His play R.U.R. introduced the word “robot.”

Published in 1831, this French Romantic novel follows a bell-ringer who lives in a famous Paris cathedral and becomes entangled with Esmeralda and the archdeacon Claude Frollo. What novel by Victor Hugo is it?
In The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, which archdeacon becomes obsessed with Esmeralda and stabs Captain Phoebus after finding him with her?

In *The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle*, Kumiko’s concern over a vanished family pet sends Toru Okada on an errand that brings him to Malta Kano. In *Kafka on the Shore*, Nakata earns money by helping owners whose same kind of household companion has disappeared; what recurring activity links the novels?

In *Kafka on the Shore*, which elderly man lost his ability to read and write after a childhood wartime incident, can speak with cats, and takes paid jobs locating them? His role is a prominent example of finding lost cats in Haruki Murakami’s fiction.
Published in 1949, this novel follows Ti Noël amid the Haitian Revolution and is known for its use of marvelous realism. What is the title of this work by Cuban writer Alejo Carpentier?
In The Kingdom of This World, Ti Noël’s story unfolds amid the Haitian Revolution, and the novel is regarded as a landmark of marvelous realism. Which Cuban author wrote this 1949 work?

This American author and muckraker wrote a 1906 novel whose revelations about Chicago meatpacking helped spur federal food-safety laws. He later campaigned for governor of California as a Democrat. Who was he?

In Upton Sinclair’s 1906 novel, Lithuanian immigrant Jurgis Rudkus and his family struggle in Chicago’s Packingtown, where filthy slaughterhouse practices and brutal labor conditions are depicted. What is this novel?
Upton Sinclair shifted his muckraking from industrial labor to the press in this 1919 book, an exposé of American journalism that criticized paid-for coverage and other malpractice. What work is it?
Upton Sinclair won this 1943 literary award for Dragon’s Teeth, his novel about a German family amid the rise of Nazism. What award did he receive?

Robert Burns recorded and reshaped older Scots material in a poem whose title is commonly translated as “for old time’s sake.” Associated with Hogmanay and New Year’s farewells, it recalls shared walks and journeys before offering a “cup o’ kindness”; what is this work?

The melody most often heard with Auld Lang Syne was printed in 1799 in a collection of Scottish airs, although Burns’s words had appeared earlier. Which Scottish music publisher and editor issued that collection?

In this narrative poem, two rural neighbors meet each spring to reset fallen stones along a property line. The speaker questions why apple trees and pines need a barrier, while the neighbor repeats inherited advice about fences and neighborliness; what is the poem called?
Robert Frost’s 1914 collection, his second book of poems, first included Mending Wall. What is the title of that collection?

This American playwright and essayist wrote a 1949 tragedy about Willy Loman, a traveling salesman whose pursuit of success strains his family. He also dramatized the Salem witch trials in a play that became a response to political persecution in his own era. Who was he?

Arthur Miller’s 1949 tragedy follows Willy Loman and his sons, Biff and Happy, as they struggle with his ambitions and disappointments. The play received the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and became a landmark of American theater. What is its title?

In Arthur Miller’s 1947 family tragedy, a manufacturer conceals that he knowingly shipped defective aircraft-engine parts, leading to the deaths of 21 pilots. Chris Keller confronts him after learning the truth. What is the play’s title?
Ernest Cline’s science-fiction novel follows Wade Watts as he searches a virtual-reality world for a hidden Easter egg left by its creator, James Halliday. What is the novel’s title?
In Ready Player One, Wade Watts uses the avatar Parzival to search this vast virtual-reality world for James Halliday’s hidden Easter egg. What is the world called?

Which short story follows Confederate civilian Peyton Farquhar as Union soldiers execute him for attempting to disrupt a railroad line? Its apparent escape sequence is revealed to be an imagined experience in the moments before his death.
answer: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge

question: The author of An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge served as a Union officer in the Civil War and later wrote the satirical work The Devil’s Dictionary. Which American writer created this story?
A Langston Hughes poem opens by asking what happens to a dream deferred. It follows with images of a dried raisin, a festering sore, and a heavy load; what is the poem’s title?
In “Harlem,” the speaker considers whether a postponed dream might dry up like a raisin or explode. Which poet, also known for “The Weary Blues,” wrote the poem?

A bored boy named Milo travels through a mysterious checkpoint in a toy car and arrives in the Lands Beyond. His adventures include rescuing Princesses Rhyme and Reason, who were banished by Azaz and the Mathemagician. What children’s novel by Norton Juster is this?
In The Phantom Tollbooth, Milo meets a companion in the Doldrums who is both a dog and a timepiece. This watchdog has a clock built into his body and joins Milo on his journey. What is his name?

In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Jazz Age novel, this wealthy former Yale football star lives in East Egg with Daisy and takes Nick Carraway to meet his mistress in the Valley of Ashes. After Jay Gatsby is killed, he tells George Wilson that Gatsby owned the car involved in Myrtle’s death. Who is this character?

Tom Buchanan appears in this novel narrated by Nick Carraway, whose mysterious title character throws lavish parties while longing for Daisy across the bay. The novel’s final image recalls boats borne back ceaselessly into the past. What is its title?

Published in 1901, this Frank Norris naturalist novel follows San Joaquin Valley wheat growers whose conflict with a powerful transportation monopoly exposes the reach of corporate power. Norris planned it as the first volume in his unfinished Epic of the Wheat trilogy; what is the novel?

In The Octopus: A California Story, the wheat farmers confront a fictional rail corporation whose president is named Shelgrim and whose freight rates and land policies drive the conflict. What is the name of that company?
A tragedy follows two young lovers from feuding households in Verona, whose deaths finally bring their families’ long conflict to an end. What is the natural title of this Shakespeare play?
The tragedy Romeo and Juliet is attributed to the English playwright who also wrote Hamlet and A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Who was this author?
In Romeo and Juliet, the Prince of this northern Italian city intervenes in the feud between the Montagues and Capulets. The play’s opening street fight takes place there. What is the city?
In Romeo and Juliet, this witty friend of Romeo delivers the Queen Mab speech and is fatally wounded by Tybalt after Romeo refuses to fight. Who is he?
The doomed romance in Romeo and Juliet inspired this Leonard Bernstein musical, which relocates the conflict to 1950s New York and pits the Jets against the Sharks. What is the musical’s title?

A Danish prince opens his most famous soliloquy with a stark formulation of the choice between continued existence and nonexistence. The speech then weighs enduring suffering against escaping it. What is the line?
answer: To be, or not to be, that is the question

question: The line “To be, or not to be, that is the question” appears in a Shakespearean tragedy about a Danish prince who investigates his father’s murder and seeks revenge against his uncle, the new king. What is the title of the play?

This four-act play by Anton Chekhov follows aspiring actress Nina, playwright Konstantin Treplev, and successful writer Trigorin. After its disastrous 1896 reception, Konstantin Stanislavski’s Moscow Art Theatre revived it to acclaim in 1898. What is the play?
The Seagull is one of four major plays by this Russian physician and writer, alongside Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard. Who wrote these works?
After The Seagull’s poor 1896 reception, this theatre company, led by Konstantin Stanislavski and Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko, revived the play to acclaim in 1898. What was the company called?

In Washington Irving’s 1819 tale, a Dutch-American villager enters the Catskills, drinks with mysterious men playing ninepins, and wakes twenty years later, after the American Revolution. What is the title of the story?

Rip Van Winkle and The Legend of Sleepy Hollow are both stories by the same nineteenth-century American author. In the latter, schoolteacher Ichabod Crane competes with Brom Bones for Katrina Van Tassel and encounters a spectral rider; who wrote both stories?
Rip Van Winkle appeared in a volume that also included The Legend of Sleepy Hollow. What is the title of this collection of tales?
answer: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.

question: In Rip Van Winkle, what upland region of New York is the setting for the title character’s encounter with mysterious men playing ninepins and his twenty-year sleep? Irving said he had not visited the area when he wrote the story.

This American graphic novelist wrote comic-book continuations of *Avatar: The Last Airbender* and created the National Book Award finalist *American Born Chinese*. He also wrote *Boxers* and co-created DC's Chinese counterpart to Superman; who is he?
In DC's *New Super-Man*, written by Gene Luen Yang, a teenager from Beijing is chosen for a government program that gives him powers inspired by Superman. What is the name of this young hero?

Its protagonist works in a government department that alters old newspaper reports, while the ruling Party promotes slogans such as “War is Peace” and “Ignorance is Strength.” What 1949 dystopian novel follows Winston Smith under Big Brother’s rule?
The English novelist who wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four also wrote Animal Farm, a fable about farm animals who overthrow their human owner. What was this writer’s pen name?
In Nineteen Eighty-Four, the Party uses this name for Great Britain, which has become a province of the superstate Oceania. What is the name of the territory where Winston Smith lives?

In Nineteen Eighty-Four, a Party philologist named Syme helps compile the eleventh edition of this deliberately restricted language. The Party intends its shrinking vocabulary to make unorthodox thoughts harder to express. What is the language called?
In Nineteen Eighty-Four, Winston is taken to this chamber in the Ministry of Love, where the Party exploits his fear of rats to force him to betray Julia. What is the chamber’s designation?

This great talking lion is the son of the Emperor-Beyond-the-Sea and the ruler of Narnia. In *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*, he willingly gives his life in Edmund’s place and later returns to life.

In this C. S. Lewis prequel, Aslan sings Narnia into existence after Digory Kirke and Polly Plummer arrive through the Wood between the Worlds. The story also reveals how the wardrobe’s wood came from a tree grown from a magical apple.

Which Jane Austen novel follows Catherine Morland, an inexperienced reader of Gothic romances, as she travels to Bath and later visits the Tilney family’s country home, where she mistakes ordinary clues for evidence of a dark secret?

In Northanger Abbey, which clergyman’s daughter befriends Isabella Thorpe in Bath and becomes romantically attached to Henry Tilney? Her suspicions about General Tilney’s household reveal how Gothic fiction shapes her imagination.

In this 1844 fairy tale, a shard from a magic mirror lodges in Kay’s eye and heart, and Gerda travels through strange lands to bring him home. What Hans Christian Andersen story centers on her rescue?
The Snow Queen is one of the best-known works of this Danish writer, whose other fairy tales include “The Ugly Duckling,” “The Little Mermaid,” and “The Little Match Girl.” Who was this author?
In Alexander Pope’s poem, a suitor secretly cuts a strand from Belinda’s hair, sparking an elaborate conflict among fashionable society. What is the name of this work?

In The Rape of the Lock, Pope treats a fashionable dispute over a stolen curl with supernatural interventions, battles, and the grand conventions associated with legendary heroes. What literary mode names this comic elevation of a trivial subject?

Published in 1939, this novel follows the Joad family, tenant farmers driven from Oklahoma by drought, foreclosures, and economic hardship. Their westward journey takes them toward California in search of work during the Dust Bowl.
The Grapes of Wrath and Of Mice and Men are both novels by this American writer, who also wrote East of Eden. Who was he?
In The Grapes of Wrath, the Joads leave Oklahoma and head toward this Pacific Coast state, hoping to find work as migrant farm laborers. Name their destination.
A 1940 film adaptation of The Grapes of Wrath starred Henry Fonda as Tom Joad. Which director helmed the adaptation?

In Goethe’s epistolary novel, this young man falls in love with Charlotte, who is engaged to Albert, and later dies by suicide with pistols borrowed from Albert. What is the protagonist’s commonly used name?

Werther is the protagonist of a novel by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who wrote primarily in this language. Friedrich Schiller also wrote his play *William Tell* and the poem “Ode to Joy” in it. What language is it?

Born in London in 1608 and educated at Christ’s College, Cambridge, this poet later became blind while serving the English Commonwealth, yet continued writing by dictation. He authored a prose defense of unlicensed printing and composed an epic about humanity’s first disobedience; who was he?

John Milton dictated this blank-verse Christian epic to assistants after he became blind. First published in 1667 in ten books, it depicts Satan’s rebellion and the fall of Adam and Eve; a revised edition expanded it to twelve books. What work is it?
What early twentieth-century poetry movement, associated with a London-based circle, called for precise images, direct expression, and concise language?
Which American-born poet helped launch Imagism, published “A Few Don’ts by an Imagiste” in 1913, and later wrote The Cantos?

In poetry, a reader may reach the end of a verse line while its syntax is still grammatically incomplete, with the phrase continuing into the next line rather than pausing for a full stop. What is this poetic technique called?

Unlike Enjambment, this technique places a syntactic or rhetorical pause at the end of a poetic line, often reinforced by punctuation, so the sentence does not run onward into the next line. What is this line-ending practice called?

Which Persian allegorical poem by Farid ud-Din Attar follows thirty feathered creatures on a quest for a sovereign bird, only for the seekers to discover that the Simurgh reflects their own collective identity?
The Conference of the Birds is a Persian Sufi poem about thirty birds seeking the Simurgh. Which Persian poet and mystic composed this work?

Which Irish author created a teenage criminal mastermind who encounters technologically advanced fairies in a bestselling fantasy series, and later wrote *And Another Thing...*, a continuation of Douglas Adams’s *The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy*?

In Eoin Colfer’s fantasy series about an underground fairy civilization, which young mastermind uses his bodyguard Butler’s help to abduct LEPrecon officer Holly Short and demand a ransom in gold in the opening novel?

Which work by Friedrich Nietzsche is subtitled *A Book for All and None* and presents the Übermensch and eternal recurrence through the speeches of a prophet who descends from the mountains to address humanity?

In *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, Nietzsche presents a doctrine that asks whether a person could embrace life so fully as to will every event’s return in precisely the same sequence, endlessly. What is this doctrine called?

In Edith Wharton's novel The Age of Innocence, this privileged New York lawyer is engaged to May Welland when he becomes increasingly drawn to her cousin, Ellen Olenska. He must choose between pursuing a life with Ellen and preserving his place in Manhattan society. Who is this protagonist?

Newland Archer is the protagonist of this 1920 Edith Wharton novel, whose title refers to the strict social codes of upper-class New York in the 1870s. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1921. What is the novel?

Which American novelist wrote about the Glanton gang and Judge Holden in a story set along the U.S.-Mexico border, then depicted a father and son traveling through an apocalyptic landscape toward the coast? His novel about a West Texas drug deal inspired a film featuring the killer Anton Chigurh, played by Javier Bardem.

Cormac McCarthy’s 1985 novel follows a Tennessee-born adolescent known only as “the kid” as he joins a scalp-hunting expedition across the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Judge Holden is one of the gang’s most memorable figures; what is the novel’s title?

What name is given to the literary genre that depicts societies made oppressive or severely damaged, often in an unsettling future or alternate social order? Its stories may warn about the consequences of political, social, or technological choices.

Aldous Huxley’s widely studied work of dystopian fiction depicts babies produced in an artificial hatchery, assigned to one of five castes, and conditioned to accept their place in society. What is the novel?

In the verse of *Pearl* and *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight*, this poetic technique creates a sound pattern by repeating the same initial sound in prominent stressed words. What is the technique called?
Alliteration is prominent in this anonymous Middle English dream vision, in which a grieving father dreams of meeting his young daughter in Heaven after her death. What is the poem’s title?

This literary nonfiction account grew out of a 1996 Mount Everest expedition during which a storm and delays near the summit contributed to eight climbers’ deaths. Its author, a journalist who was on the mountain, later reconstructed the disaster and the decisions that shaped it. What is the book’s title?

In Into Thin Air, the first-person narrator is an American journalist and mountaineer who joined the 1996 Everest expedition while reporting for Outside magazine. He also wrote Into the Wild and Under the Banner of Heaven; who is he?

A New York City boy and his toddler sister fall through a grate in their apartment building into a subterranean realm inhabited by pale humans and enormous creatures. After arriving, the boy becomes caught up in a prophecy involving the realm’s rats and bats; what Suzanne Collins middle-grade fantasy novel tells this story?
In Gregor the Overlander, what is the name of the hidden civilization beneath New York City, where humans live alongside giant rats, bats, cockroaches, and spiders?
In William Golding’s postwar novel *Lord of the Flies*, this increasingly cruel boy joins Jack Merridew’s hunters, tortures Wilfred, and ultimately kills Piggy by dislodging a boulder. Who is he?

In *Lord of the Flies*, Roger kills this bespectacled, asthmatic boy by sending a boulder crashing down from Castle Rock. Earlier, Jack’s group had taken the boy’s glasses to make fire. Who is the victim?

This English Lake Poet collaborated with Samuel Taylor Coleridge on a 1798 poetry collection that helped usher in a new literary age. He served as Britain’s Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death in 1850. Who was he?

William Wordsworth repeatedly revised a semi-autobiographical long poem about his early life, once generally known as “The Poem to Coleridge.” His wife supplied its familiar title and arranged its publication after his death. Name the poem.

William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge jointly published this 1798 collection, which includes Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.” Its later preface articulated principles associated with ordinary language and poetic feeling. What is the collection?
What 1919 Sherwood Anderson short-story cycle portrays the inhabitants of a fictional Midwestern town, with many stories connected through the young reporter George Willard?
In Winesburg, Ohio, which minister watches Kate Swift from his church’s bell tower and, after the experience, resolves to work harder on his sermons?

This American author of children’s and young-adult fiction wrote a World War II story about two friends in Nazi-occupied Denmark and a dystopian novel about a boy chosen to receive memories. She won Newbery Medals for those two novels in 1990 and 1994; who is she?
In Lois Lowry’s historical novel set in Nazi-occupied Denmark, ten-year-old Annemarie Johansen helps her Jewish friend Ellen Rosen escape persecution. What is the title of this novel?
In traditional Japanese poetry, certain words create a pause, emphasis, or rhetorical break rather than merely adding to a poem’s imagery. What is the Japanese term for these words?
A haiku may use Kireji to create a break, while a separate conventional marker signals the season—for example, “first snow” suggests winter. What is the Japanese term for that seasonal reference?

This poet, born in West Africa and enslaved as a child in Boston, published *Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral* in 1773, becoming one of the first African American authors to publish a book. Who was she?

In Phillis Wheatley’s 1775 poem addressed to the commander of the Continental Army, she urges him to “Proceed, great chief, with virtue on thy side” and links his leadership to Columbia’s cause of freedom. Which Revolutionary War general is addressed?
This English Romantic poet wrote “Ozymandias,” “Mont Blanc,” and “Ode to the West Wind.” He died at age 29 after drowning in the Gulf of Spezia in 1822. Who was he?
In Percy Bysshe Shelley’s sonnet, a traveler describes a shattered statue in the desert, and its pedestal bears the boast, “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” What is the title of the poem?
Percy Bysshe Shelley’s second wife published an 1818 novel subtitled “The Modern Prometheus,” featuring Victor Frankenstein and the being he creates. Who was this novelist?

Percy Bysshe Shelley published this four-act lyrical drama in 1820. It reimagines a myth in which a captive Titan is freed by Hercules and the rule of Jupiter is ultimately challenged. What is the work’s title?

In this Elizabethan comedy, Don Pedro arranges overheard conversations that lead Benedick and Beatrice to believe the other loves them, while Don John’s deception causes Claudio to reject Hero at their wedding. What is this play?
In the 1993 film adaptation of Much Ado About Nothing, which Northern Irish actor played Benedick and directed the film? He also directed film adaptations of Hamlet and Henry V.

This British novelist made the accidental umbrella mix-up after Helen Schlegel hears Beethoven’s Fifth a memorable incident in a novel about the Schlegels, Wilcoxes, and Leonard Bast. He also wrote A Room with a View and A Passage to India. Identify him.

In E. M. Forster’s novel set in British-ruled India, Dr. Aziz arranges an excursion for Adela Quested and Mrs. Moore to a series of limestone hollows whose echo becomes central to a disputed accusation. What are these formations called?

This lyric follows an aging speaker visiting a convent school, where the young pupils prompt reflections on his youthful beloved, the passage of time, and philosophical ideas about education. Its final stanza asks how one can know the dancer from the dance. Name the poem.

Among School Children moves from a classroom visit to meditations on Plato, Aristotle, and Pythagoras, before ending with an image of a chestnut tree and the unity of dancer and dance. Which Irish poet wrote it?

Alice Walker’s epistolary novel follows Celie, an African American woman in the early-20th-century South, through letters addressed first to God and later exchanged with her sister Nettie. What is the title of this novel?
In The Color Purple, Celie’s life is rooted largely in a rural state of the Deep South. Margaret Mitchell’s Gone with the Wind is also set in this state; which one is it?

In this 1947 novel by John Steinbeck, an ensemble of travelers on a California bus route becomes stranded, and one chapter shifts to the perspective of crooked car salesmen peddling defective “jalopies.” What is the title of the novel?

The Wayward Bus is among the novels by this California-born writer, whose other works include Of Mice and Men and The Grapes of Wrath. He received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature. Who is this author?

This seven-volume autobiographical sequence begins with a 1969 memoir of a Black girl's childhood in Stamps, Arkansas, and concludes with a 2013 account of the writer's relationship with her mother. What body of work is described?

The opening volume of Maya Angelou's autobiographies was published in 1969 and recounts her childhood in Stamps, Arkansas, including years spent largely silent after a traumatic experience. What is the title of this book?
answer: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

question: In Aristotle’s Poetics, this dramatic form is associated with a serious action that arouses pity and fear and brings about catharsis. Unlike comedy, it often centers on human error, reversals of fortune, and misfortune.
This fifth-century BCE Athenian playwright wrote Oedipus Rex and Antigone, two enduring works of Greek tragedy. Ancient tradition also credits him with introducing a third actor to the stage.

In this dialogue, Socrates and his companions investigate what justice is by imagining a city built from the ground up. Its discussion of education and political rule includes the claim that the best rulers must become philosophers. What is this work called?

In The Republic, Socrates describes people confined since childhood who mistake images before them for reality; one person’s release and turn toward the light illustrates the path from ignorance to knowledge. What is this philosophical image called?

A German-Jewish teenager kept a diary while her family hid from Nazi persecution in a concealed annex in Amsterdam. Her account became one of the most widely read firsthand narratives of the Holocaust; who was she?
Anne Frank’s firsthand account, written while her family hid in Amsterdam, was first published in Dutch in 1947 as *Het Achterhuis*. Under what familiar English title was this work published?
answer: The Diary of a Young Girl

question: In Harriet Beecher Stowe’s 1852 anti-slavery novel, this enslaved Christian man is sold to Simon Legree and remains faithful to his beliefs despite brutal pressure to help Legree control other enslaved people. He is killed after refusing to reveal where Cassy and Emmeline have fled. Who is this central character?

In a 1949 essay, James Baldwin criticizes the “self-righteous, virtuous sentimentality” of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s novel and calls Bigger Thomas from Richard Wright’s *Native Son* a descendant of its enslaved protagonist, Uncle Tom. What is the title of Baldwin’s essay?
Created by Arthur Conan Doyle, this fictional British consulting detective lives at 221B Baker Street and solves cases through close observation and deduction. What is his name?
In the Sherlock Holmes stories, this former army surgeon meets the detective after returning from service in Afghanistan and becomes his friend, flatmate, and frequent narrator. What is his name?
In Sherlock Holmes’s first appearance, the detective meets Dr. Watson after Watson returns to London and is introduced to a peculiar, laboratory-minded lodger. What 1887 novel introduced them?
Sherlock Holmes’s first series of short stories began in 1891 in this London publication, where “A Scandal in Bohemia” first appeared. What was the publication’s title?

In the Sherlock Holmes story “The Final Problem,” this criminal mastermind confronts the detective at the Reichenbach Falls, where both are presumed to die. What is the name commonly given to Holmes’s nemesis?
This ancient Indian poet and playwright wrote the drama *The Recognition of Shakuntala* and the lyric poem *The Cloud Messenger*. Who was this influential Sanskrit author?
Kalidasa composed his poetry and dramas in this classical language of ancient India. It was also the language in which the Vedas were composed.

In Shakespeare’s tragedy about a Roman dictator’s assassination, this senator tells Brutus that “the fault… is not in our stars, / But in ourselves” and recounts rescuing Caesar from the Tiber. Which character is speaking?

After Cassius and Brutus participate in Caesar’s assassination in Shakespeare’s Roman tragedy, this political ally of Caesar delivers a funeral oration beginning, “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.” Who is the speaker?

This Russian-language writer of Ukrainian origin drew on Ukrainian folklore in his early stories and later satirized corruption in works such as *Dead Souls* and a comedy about officials deceived by a low-ranking visitor. Who was he?

In a short story by Nikolai Gogol, a barber discovers a severed facial feature inside a loaf of bread, while its owner later encounters it dressed as a high-ranking official. What is the story called?

In this stage comedy by Nikolai Gogol, officials in a provincial town mistake an impecunious traveler for an important visitor from the capital and try to win his favor. Their efforts unravel when they read a letter revealing what the traveler thinks of them, just before news arrives that a genuine dignitary has reached town. What is the play?

Which Russian novelist, short-story writer, and playwright (1818–1883) began publishing a series of hunter-narrated sketches about rural life in 1847? His compact novels and translations of his work helped bring Russian literature to readers in Western Europe and the United States.

In which 1862 novel by Ivan Turgenev does the young doctor Bazarov challenge the older generation with his nihilist views? The novel’s debates helped popularize “nihilist” as a label for Russian radicals of the period.

This Italian poet and early humanist composed a celebrated vernacular sequence addressed to Laura. A letter recounting his 1336 climb of Mont Ventoux became a famous emblem of humanist curiosity and inward reflection. Which writer was he?

Petrarch’s 14th-century collection of 366 Italian lyric poems, mostly sonnets, follows the speaker’s love for Laura and is traditionally divided into poems from before and after her death. By what familiar title is this work known?

This American poet, playwright, novelist, and essayist became a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance and an early innovator of jazz poetry. His first poetry collection was published in 1926; who was he?

Langston Hughes titled one of his best-known short poems for this Manhattan neighborhood; the poem asks what happens to a dream deferred. Which neighborhood also became the namesake of the cultural movement in which Hughes was a central figure?
Langston Hughes’s 1926 debut poetry collection includes a title poem in which a musician plays piano late into the night, singing in syncopated rhythm. What is the collection’s title?

After leaving Columbia before completing his studies, Langston Hughes later graduated from a historically Black institution in Chester County, Pennsylvania, founded in 1854 as Ashmun Institute. What is its current name?
From 1942 to 1962, Langston Hughes wrote a weekly opinion column for a major Black-owned newspaper founded by Robert S. Abbott in 1905. What was the paper’s name?

This fifth-century BCE Athenian tragedian was born at Colonus and, according to ancient estimates, wrote more than 100 dramas, of which only seven survive complete. He composed *Antigone* and *Oedipus the King*, though those plays were not planned as a single trilogy. Who was this playwright?

In Sophocles’ tragedy first staged in 409 BCE, Odysseus and Neoptolemus travel to Lemnos to persuade an archer abandoned there years earlier to join the expedition against Troy. The wounded exile possesses a bow once given to him by Heracles. What is the title of this play?

Langston Hughes’s poem depicts a musician playing beneath an old gaslight in Harlem, where a droning, syncopated performance leaves him asleep “like a rock or a man that’s dead.” What is the poem’s title?
The Weary Blues portrays a Harlem musician performing a syncopated song. Its author also wrote “Harlem,” which asks what happens to a dream deferred, and “Theme for English B.” Which poet wrote it?

In Richard Adams’s 1972 novel, Fiver’s warning prompts Hazel and a band of rabbits to flee their threatened warren and search for a safe place to settle. What is the title of this story about their journey across the English countryside?

In Watership Down, this rabbit becomes the expedition’s leader through his good judgment and ability to bring others together, rather than through strength or seniority. He later serves as chief rabbit of the refugees’ new warren.
Published posthumously in 1965, this poetry collection includes Sylvia Plath’s “Lady Lazarus” and “Daddy.” What is the collection’s title?
Ariel is the collection by the poet who wrote “Daddy,” whose speaker describes a “man in black with a Meinkampf look.” This poet also wrote “The Colossus”; who was she?
In Charles Dickens’s Oliver Twist, this confident young pickpocket leads Oliver into Fagin’s circle of thieves. What nickname is given to the boy known for his skill at picking pockets?
In the novel featuring the Artful Dodger, what orphaned boy is sent from a workhouse to apprentice with an undertaker? He later asks for more gruel in one of the story’s best-known scenes.

This two-volume graphic memoir intertwines a Polish Jewish man’s account of persecution and imprisonment at Auschwitz with scenes of his adult son recording those memories. Its animal imagery depicts Jews as mice and Germans as cats; what work is being described?

In Maus: A Survivor’s Tale, the adult son interviews his father, Vladek, while the narrative explores their strained relationship and the lasting effects of the Holocaust. Which cartoonist and writer created this graphic memoir?

In this José Saramago novel, the Iberian Peninsula breaks away from Europe and drifts into the Atlantic. Its travelers include a woman whose scratch in the earth sets events in motion and a man followed by starlings. What is the novel’s title?
The Stone Raft depicts the Iberian Peninsula drifting away from Europe. Who wrote this novel, as well as Blindness and The Gospel According to Jesus Christ?

This English writer and critic spent years compiling the 1755 A Dictionary of the English Language and later wrote Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets, including biographies of Milton, Dryden, and Pope. What was his name?
Samuel Johnson’s close companion was a Scottish lawyer who traveled with him through the Hebrides and later published a celebrated biography of him. What was this biographer’s name?

Set in Pittsburgh’s Hill District in 1957, this August Wilson drama follows former aspiring baseball player Troy Maxson and the tensions between him and his son Cory over football opportunities. It premiered at Yale Repertory Theatre in 1985 and later won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama; name the play.
August Wilson’s Fences is one installment in this ten-play sequence, whose plays trace Black life in the United States across the 1900s. What is the name of this sequence?
Ray Bradbury completed this dystopian novel in 1953. Its fireman protagonist eventually rebels against a society that outlaws books and sends crews to burn them; what is the novel’s title?

In Fahrenheit 451, which fireman begins to question his work after a teenage neighbor asks whether he is happy? After seeing an elderly woman choose to die with her books, he secretly starts keeping volumes at home.
In Fahrenheit 451, what is the name of the curious teenage neighbor who walks with Guy Montag, notices details of nature, and asks him, “Are you happy?”
Which French director adapted Fahrenheit 451 into a 1966 film starring Oskar Werner as the fireman and Julie Christie in two roles? It was his first film shot in color.

Lord Byron’s lyric opens by likening a woman’s graceful movement to a cloudless night filled with stars, then says that “all that’s best of dark and bright” meet in her face and eyes. What is the poem’s title?

In “She Walks in Beauty,” Byron presents a woman’s beauty through the balance of darkness and light, alongside an emphasis on feeling and idealized imagery. What major nineteenth-century literary movement, also associated with poets such as Wordsworth and Shelley, does the poem exemplify?

Kurt Vonnegut’s satirical novel follows a writer named John as he researches the scientists behind the atomic bomb and travels to San Lorenzo, where he encounters the religion of Bokononism. What is the title of this novel?
In Cat’s Cradle, what fictional substance, invented by scientist Felix Hoenikker, can act as a seed crystal that freezes water at room temperature and sets the novel’s catastrophe in motion?
In this poetic meter, each line is conventionally organized into five metrical feet, and each foot typically moves from an unstressed syllable to a stressed one. What is the meter’s natural name?
Iambic pentameter is the usual meter of this unrhymed poetic form, used extensively for Shakespearean dramatic dialogue and in Milton’s *Paradise Lost*. What is this form called?
This ancient Indo-Aryan language is the language of the Vedas, and its later classical form became a major vehicle for South Asian literature, religion, and scholarship. What is this language?
Classical Sanskrit grammar was codified in the compact eight-chapter treatise called the Aṣṭādhyāyī, whose rules shaped the language for centuries. Which ancient Indian grammarian composed it?

Daniel Keyes's novel follows an adult bakery employee who submits progress reports while researchers test on him a brain operation that previously boosted a mouse's intelligence. The procedure temporarily makes him a genius before its effects reverse. What is the novel called?

In Flowers for Algernon, which bakery worker is chosen for an experimental operation after his teacher recommends him to researchers? His progress reports chart the rise and later decline of his intelligence.

This poem opens with “The curfew tolls the knell of parting day” and reflects on the lives and unrealized potential of villagers buried in a rural burial ground. It imagines, among them, “some mute inglorious Milton” and “some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood.” What is the poem?
answer: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

question: The author of Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard also wrote “The Bard” and “Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College.” Who was this English poet?

This American novelist and travel writer frequently set his fiction in California’s Salinas Valley and wrote sympathetically about ordinary and dispossessed people. He received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature and authored both a novel about the Joad family’s migration and a novella about ranch workers George and Lennie. Who was this writer?

In this 1939 John Steinbeck novel, the Joad family leaves Oklahoma for California during the Dust Bowl, while brief interchapters widen the story into a portrait of migrants and hardship. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1940; what is the novel?
John Steinbeck’s 1937 novella follows ranch hands George Milton and Lennie Small, whose dream of owning a small farm is undone by a fatal encounter at a California ranch. What is this work’s title?
John Steinbeck recounts a cross-country journey in this nonfiction book, driving a camper he named Rocinante with his French poodle as a companion. What is the title of this account?

In 1962, John Steinbeck was awarded this major literary distinction, with the Swedish Academy praising the realism, imagination, sympathetic humor, and social perception in his work. What honor did he receive?
Published in 1984 by Mexican-American author Sandra Cisneros, this coming-of-age novel follows a young Chicana growing up in a Chicago neighborhood. What is the title of the novel?
In The House on Mango Street, a 12-year-old girl experiences a year in a Hispanic neighborhood of Chicago as she enters adolescence. What is the name of this central character?
The House on Mango Street is told through brief, self-contained scenes rather than continuous chapters with one uninterrupted plot. What is the literary term for these short narrative pieces?

Emerging in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, this literary and artistic movement prized imagination, individual emotion, and the power of nature in reaction to Enlightenment rationalism and industrialization. What movement is it?
Within the Romantic Movement, which English Lake Poet collaborated with Samuel Taylor Coleridge on *Lyrical Ballads* and wrote the poem *Tintern Abbey*?

Born into a Russian noble family in 1828, this novelist drew on his military service in the Crimean War for *Sevastopol Sketches*. His works include the semi-autobiographical trilogy *Childhood, Boyhood and Youth* and influential novels of realist fiction. Who was this writer?

In this immense novel by Leo Tolstoy, Pierre Bezukhov, Andrei Bolkonsky, and Natasha Rostova live through the upheavals surrounding Napoleon’s 1812 invasion of Russia. Its title joins two ideas that shape the story: armed conflict and its opposite. What is the novel?

Leo Tolstoy opens this novel with a famous observation that happy families resemble one another, while unhappy families are unhappy in their own ways. Its title character’s affair with Count Vronsky ends in tragedy at a railway station. What is the novel?

This 1886 novella by Leo Tolstoy follows a respected official whose fatal illness forces him to reconsider the life he has led. His decline begins after he injures himself while putting up curtains. What is the novella?

Leo Tolstoy’s writings on nonviolent resistance influenced this Indian independence leader, who corresponded with the Russian author and named a South African communal settlement in his honor. Who was this leader?

Originating in Japan as the opening stanza of a linked-verse form, this short poetic form traditionally uses three phrases totaling 17 morae, often arranged in a 5–7–5 pattern. Its classical conventions include a seasonal reference and a word that creates a pause or emphasis; English versions are often printed in three lines.
In traditional haiku, what Japanese term names the seasonal word or image—such as cherry blossoms or snow—that places a poem in the annual cycle?
Traditional haiku may use a word that marks a pause, break, or emphasis in the poem; in English translations, punctuation sometimes conveys its effect. What is this Japanese poetic term?
Which Edo-period poet wrote the famous haiku about a frog jumping into an old pond, as well as the travelogue Oku no Hosomichi?

This anonymous Old English heroic epic is set in pagan Scandinavia and follows a Geatish warrior who aids a Danish king by confronting a monster attacking his mead hall. After becoming king of his own people, the hero dies battling a dragon. What poem is it?
The sole surviving manuscript of Beowulf is bound with other texts, including Judith, and is named after a sixteenth-century antiquarian who wrote his name in it. What manuscript preserves the poem?
In Beowulf, this Danish king’s hall, Heorot, is repeatedly attacked by Grendel until a Geatish hero arrives to help him. Which king is this?
The 1999 translation of Beowulf that begins “So. The Spear-Danes in days gone by...” was made by which Irish poet, whose version won the Whitbread Book of the Year award?

In Shakespeare’s comedy, this mischievous spirit serves the fairy ruler Oberon and mistakenly uses a love potion on Lysander. The same character gives Nick Bottom an ass’s head and, in the closing speech, asks the audience to think of the events as a dream. Which character is it?

In Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Puck carries out this fairy ruler’s orders, including the search for a flower whose juice makes a person fall in love with the first creature they see. This ruler also quarrels with Titania over an Indian boy. Who is he?

This South African novelist and short-story writer examined apartheid and political change in works including *Burger’s Daughter* and *July’s People*. She received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991. Who was she?

In which Nadine Gordimer novel does a white South African family flee an uprising in Johannesburg and take refuge in a rural village with the help of their Black servant? Published in 1981, the book imagines a political upheaval that overturns the family’s former life.

An American poet and playwright, she won early acclaim for a poem whose speaker sees “three long mountains and a wood.” She was also known for lyric poetry and an openly bisexual public identity. Who was she?

In Edna St. Vincent Millay’s poem “Renascence,” the speaker feels buried and remains in the grave until she hears this substance falling overhead. Its arrival precedes a breeze carrying the scent of an orchard. What is it?

Which nineteenth-century American poet, associated with the New England fireside poets, taught at Bowdoin and Harvard before leaving teaching in 1854? He wrote *Evangeline* and became the first American to complete a translation of Dante’s *Divine Comedy*.
In Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s narrative poem, an Indigenous culture hero’s adventures include his courtship of Minnehaha. Which poem opens with the words “By the shores of Gitche Gumee”?

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem depicts a midnight rider sent to warn that British troops are advancing toward Lexington and Concord. The rider’s church-tower lantern signals indicate whether the troops are traveling by land or by sea; what poem is it?

This 1850 historical romance is set in Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony and follows a woman punished for adultery by being made to wear an embroidered red emblem. Its author also wrote The House of the Seven Gables. Name this novel.
The Scarlet Letter was written by the same New England author who created the characters in “Young Goodman Brown” and The House of the Seven Gables. Who was this author?

In The Scarlet Letter, this woman is publicly shamed for adultery and required to wear an elaborately embroidered red badge. She raises the child whose paternity becomes central to the novel’s conflict. Who is she?

In The Scarlet Letter, Hester raises this lively daughter, whose name also means a precious gem. Governor Bellingham considers taking the child from her, but a minister intervenes. What is the daughter’s name?

In The Scarlet Letter, this revered minister hides his role in Hester’s adultery while Roger Chillingworth secretly probes his guilt. During the Election Day procession, he acknowledges his connection to Pearl and dies shortly afterward. Who is he?

This ancient Sanskrit epic recounts a dynastic struggle between two branches of a royal family that leads to a devastating war. Traditionally attributed to a sage, it also contains a celebrated dialogue on duty between a prince and his charioteer. Name this work.
The Mahabharata is traditionally attributed to this sage, who also appears in the epic as a seer connected to the Kuru dynasty. Indian tradition also credits him with compiling the Vedas.
The Mahabharata contains this philosophical dialogue, set on the battlefield just before fighting begins. In it, Krishna counsels the troubled warrior Arjuna about duty and right action.
In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas and Kauravas fight an eighteen-day battle on a plain in northern India. Name this conflict, whose battlefield setting frames Krishna’s counsel to Arjuna.

In the Mahabharata, this princess of Panchala becomes the wife of all five Pandava brothers after Arjuna wins her in an archery contest. Her public humiliation at the Kuru court after a dice game becomes a pivotal episode in the epic.

Which English novelist, editor, and critic wrote a novel centered on the unraveling marriage of Edward and Leonora Ashburnham, as well as a four-volume sequence following Christopher Tietjens through World War I?
Ford Madox Ford edited this influential literary periodical, which published early work by Ezra Pound and provided a platform for modernist writers. What was the periodical called?

In this lyric, the speaker imagines a modest cabin of clay and wattles, nine rows of beans, and a beehive, longing to leave the city for a quiet island retreat. What poem by W. B. Yeats describes this self-sufficient life?
The Lake Isle of Innisfree is inspired by a small island near Sligo town, with wooded shores and other islands nearby. In which lake is the island located?

This American novelist drew on his own life in Paris for *Tropic of Cancer* and later wrote *The Rosy Crucifixion*, a trilogy of autobiographical novels. Both works faced bans and obscenity prosecutions; who was the author?

Henry Miller’s semi-autobiographical novel follows an American writer living among artists and expatriates in Paris between the world wars. First published in Paris in 1934, it became the subject of a major U.S. obscenity ruling after its American publication in 1961; what is the novel?

Which absurdist one-act play follows two hired killers, Ben and Gus, waiting in a basement room as a service lift delivers increasingly puzzling food orders? Their routine is disrupted by messages from an unseen employer.
The Dumb Waiter is a postwar British play whose clipped dialogue and pauses help turn a basement waiting room into a setting of menace. Which playwright wrote this drama about the hitmen Ben and Gus?
This Archaic Greek lyric poet is known for choral works, especially maiden-songs performed by girls’ choruses. Who was the poet?
Alcman’s maiden-songs are associated with choruses in this Peloponnesian city-state, whose king Leonidas led the famous defense at Thermopylae. What was the city-state’s name?

The American writer behind the essay “The Case for Reparations” also published a memoir addressed to his son about living in a Black body in the United States. He later wrote a historical novel about Hiram Walker and the enslaved community known as the Tasked. Who is this author?

In Ta-Nehisi Coates’s novel *The Water Dancer*, Harriet Tubman tells Hiram Walker that “memory is the chariot.” Which biblical leader, associated with leading the Israelites out of Egypt, does she parallel?

Published in 1926, this modernist novel follows wounded American veteran Jake Barnes, Lady Brett Ashley, and their expatriate circle from Paris to Spain. Its climactic scenes take place during the San Fermín fiesta, amid bullfighting in Pamplona. What Ernest Hemingway novel is it?
In The Sun Also Rises, Jake Barnes and his companions travel to this Spanish city for the San Fermín fiesta, where they watch bullfights and the running of the bulls. What is the city?
Which Victor Hugo novel, first published on 31 March 1862, follows an ex-convict’s search for redemption amid social injustice and culminates against the backdrop of a Paris uprising in 1832?
In Les Misérables, which former convict is imprisoned for stealing a loaf of bread, later adopts Cosette, and takes the identity Monsieur Madeleine?
In Les Misérables, which law officer relentlessly pursues Jean Valjean, but ultimately drowns himself in the Seine after Valjean spares his life?
In Les Misérables, what 1832 Paris uprising forms the novel’s climactic historical backdrop, with Enjolras and the Friends of the ABC fighting at the barricades?

First published in 1857, this landmark French poetry collection opens with “To the Reader,” which condemns folly, sin, and ennui, and includes poems such as “The Albatross” and “Correspondences.” What is the collection’s title?
The author of Les Fleurs du mal was a French poet born in Paris in 1821, known for poems including “The Albatross” and “Correspondences.” Which poet wrote the collection?

Published as a novel in 1951, this first-person coming-of-age story follows a teenager expelled from Pencey Prep as he wanders New York City and reflects on the people he considers “phonies.” What novel is it?
The author of The Catcher in the Rye also wrote the short story “A Perfect Day for Bananafish,” which introduces Seymour Glass, and many of his stories feature the Glass family. Who was this author?
In The Catcher in the Rye, this first-person narrator leaves Pencey Prep after being expelled and asks a cab driver where Central Park’s ducks go in winter. What is his name?
In The Catcher in the Rye, Holden buys a “Little Shirley Beans” record for this younger sister, whom he secretly visits in New York. Who is she?
In The Catcher in the Rye, Holden is expelled from this fictional boarding school before he leaves for New York City. What is the school’s name?

Born in Azinhaga in 1922, this Portuguese novelist trained as a mechanical locksmith before working as a journalist and writing The Stone Raft and The Gospel According to Jesus Christ. In 1998, he became the first writer working in Portuguese to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Who was he?

In José Saramago’s 1995 novel, an unexplained epidemic causes nearly everyone to lose their sight, while the doctor’s wife remains able to see and guides a group of survivors. What is the novel called?

Born in Rouen in 1821, this French novelist made his debut with a 1857 novel about Emma Bovary and became famous for painstakingly testing prose for the exact right word. He also mentored Guy de Maupassant; who was he?

In Gustave Flaubert’s 1857 novel, a dissatisfied doctor’s wife in Yonville pursues affairs with Rodolphe Boulanger and Léon Dupuis, while her husband Charles’s failed operation on Hippolyte’s clubfoot deepens the household’s troubles. What is the novel’s title?
Gustave Flaubert encouraged this younger French writer, who became known for compact stories including “The Necklace,” “Ball of Fat,” and “The Piece of String.” Which writer was Flaubert’s protégé?

Gustave Flaubert set this historical novel amid the mercenary revolt against Carthage after the First Punic War. Its central figure is a priestess and daughter of Hamilcar Barca, and the conflict turns around a sacred veil called the zaimph. What is the novel called?

Daniel Defoe’s 1719 adventure novel is presented as a sailor’s first-person account. Its castaway survives for twenty-eight years by salvaging supplies, building shelter, and cultivating food before eventually returning to England. What is the novel’s title?

Robinson Crusoe is often linked to this Scottish sailor, who lived as a castaway on an island from 1704 to 1709, before Defoe’s novel appeared. His experience is considered a possible inspiration for the book, alongside other voyage accounts. Who was he?

Thomas Keneally's Booker Prize-winning historical novel follows a German industrialist who used his factories and fortune to protect Jewish prisoners from Nazi persecution during the Holocaust. What is the novel's original title, published in the United States under a different title?
Schindler's Ark is the Booker Prize-winning Holocaust novel by which Australian author, born in Sydney in 1935, whose other novels include The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith?

In Rick Riordan’s Percy Jackson universe, which daughter of Atlas is imprisoned on an island where heroes arrive but she cannot leave? Percy considers her his “biggest what if,” and she later falls in love with Leo Valdez.
In Rick Riordan’s Percy Jackson universe, Calypso is confined to this remote island, where she encounters heroes including Odysseus and Leo Valdez. What is the island’s name?
V. S. Naipaul’s 1961 novel follows a man who marries into the powerful Tulsi family and spends decades trying to secure a home independent of his in-laws. What is the novel called?
In A House for Mr Biswas, the newly married Mohun is drawn into the Tulsi family’s crowded residence in Arwacas, presided over by Mrs. Tulsi. What is the name of this house?

This American writer spent nearly all his life in Providence, Rhode Island, and developed tales in which ancient, alien forces dwarf human concerns. He encouraged other authors to write within the shared fictional background later associated with his creations. Who was he?
H. P. Lovecraft’s later stories helped popularize a mode of fiction in which the universe is vast and hostile, and humanity’s place in it is insignificant. What is this mode commonly called?

What title is given to Edward FitzGerald’s 1859 English rendering of selected quatrains attributed to an 11th-century Persian astronomer-poet? Though it initially sold poorly, the work became widely popular in the English-speaking world later in the 19th century.
The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyam became famous in English through a rendering published in 1859, rather than as an English original. Which British poet and translator produced that version?
The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyam draws on quatrains attributed to a poet whose literary language was also used by Ferdowsi for the Shahnameh, Iran’s national epic. What is that language?

This 1898 British science-fiction novel follows a narrator in southern England as Martians emerge from cylinders, attack with tripod fighting machines and heat-rays, and spread a red weed across the landscape. Their invasion collapses when they succumb to Earth’s microorganisms; what is the novel’s title?
Who wrote The War of the Worlds, the 1898 British novel in which Martians invade England using tripod fighting machines and heat-rays, only to die from terrestrial microorganisms?
