Two German scholarly siblings born in Hanau in 1785 and 1786 published the first two volumes of *Children’s and Household Tales* in 1812 and 1815. What collective name is used for this pair, known for collecting and revising traditional stories?

Among the narrators who supplied tales to the Brothers Grimm, this storyteller from Hesse was an important source for their collection. She was born in 1755 and later became known as the “fairy-tale woman” of Niederzwehren. Who was she?
An Irish-born playwright and Whig politician, he became one of the leading comic dramatists of the late 18th century. His best-known play is the comedy of manners *The School for Scandal*.

Richard Brinsley Sheridan praised Samuel Johnson’s reference work in a prologue to Richard Savage’s *The Tragedy of Sir Thomas Overbury*. What was the title of the work whose entry for “oats” quotes Jonathan Swift?
answer: A Dictionary of the English Language

question: Published in 1755 after a major project led by Samuel Johnson, this landmark reference work uses literary quotations to illustrate word meanings. Its famous entry for “oats” contrasts their use as horse feed in England with their role as food for people in Scotland. What is the work’s title?
answer: A Dictionary of the English Language

question: In A Dictionary of the English Language, the entry for “oats” draws on a satirical writer’s contrast between English and Scottish diets. This Anglo-Irish author also created the traveler Lemuel Gulliver. Who is the author?

This American novelist served in World War II, was captured during the Battle of the Bulge, and survived the Allied firebombing of Dresden while held as a prisoner. He later drew on those experiences in the antiwar novel Slaughterhouse-Five. Who was this author?

In this Kurt Vonnegut novel, Billy Pilgrim becomes “unstuck in time” and is abducted to the planet Tralfamadore. Its title refers to the Dresden building where American prisoners were confined during the firebombing. What is the novel?

Kurt Vonnegut’s 1963 novel follows a writer named John to the fictional Caribbean island of San Lorenzo, where he encounters the religion of Bokononism. The story also features ice-nine, a substance that can freeze water on contact. What is this novel?

Kurt Vonnegut’s first novel imagines a future in which machines have taken over much of the work once done by people. Its protagonist, engineer Paul Proteus, becomes involved with the displaced workers. What is this 1952 novel?

In this Kurt Vonnegut novel, car dealer Dwayne Hoover’s life takes a turn after he meets science-fiction writer Kilgore Trout at an arts festival in Midland City. The title echoes a cereal slogan. What is the novel?

Published serially in 1859, this historical novel moves between London and Paris during the French Revolution and opens by contrasting an age of wisdom with an age of foolishness. It follows Dr. Manette’s reunion with Lucie and ends with a lawyer taking Charles Darnay’s place at the guillotine; name the novel.

In A Tale of Two Cities, what English lawyer, whose earlier life is marked by cynicism and wasted promise, takes Charles Darnay’s place in prison and is executed in his stead? He makes this sacrifice to save Darnay and Lucie Manette’s family.

After a rhinoceros kills the young protagonist’s parents, he is sent to live with his cruel aunts, then finds a way to travel inside an enormous fruit alongside talking insects. Which Roald Dahl novel follows this unlikely voyage across the Atlantic to New York?
In James and the Giant Peach, which insect companion provides violin music during the group’s airborne journey from England to New York? He is the novel’s elderly musician among the travelers.

This episodic literary form follows a poor, socially marginal rogue through changing households and encounters, with survival depending on wit and improvisation rather than heroic status. What is this genre called?

A landmark Spanish work in the picaresque tradition, this anonymously published 1554 narrative is told by a poor boy who serves a blind man, a miserly cleric, and an impoverished squire. What work is it?

In John Milton’s epic poem, this defeated rebel angel rallies his followers in Hell after their nine-day fall through Chaos, then journeys to Eden in serpent form to persuade Eve to eat the forbidden fruit. Who is this central antagonist?
In Book IX of Paradise Lost, Satan approaches this first woman in serpent form and persuades her to eat the forbidden fruit. Her choice helps bring about humanity’s Fall. Which character is this?
This fifth-century BCE Athenian playwright wrote surviving comedies including *Peace* and *The Wasps*, and his sharp political satire helped define Old Comedy. Who was he?

In Aristophanes’ comedy, Dionysus travels to Hades with his slave Xanthias and holds a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides to decide which tragic poet to bring back to Athens. What is the title of this play?

In Daniel Keyes’s novel *Flowers for Algernon*, this New York bakery worker keeps progress reports while doctors Strauss and Nemur test an operation that first dramatically increases and later diminishes his intelligence. What is the name of the character whose changing reports narrate the story?

In Charlie Gordon’s story, what is the name of the white laboratory mouse who undergoes the intelligence-enhancing operation before him, competes against him in maze tests, and later declines in a way that foreshadows Charlie’s own?
In Shakespeare’s tragedy, this nobleman of Verona is approved by Lord Capulet as a suitor for the family’s daughter. He confronts Romeo at the Capulet tomb and is killed there.

Count Paris seeks to marry a member of the Capulet family in this tragedy, whose prologue describes its central pair as “star-cross’d lovers.” Its final scene ends the feud between the Montagues and Capulets after the young lovers die.

A Danish prince in Shakespeare’s revenge tragedy learns from a ghost that his uncle murdered his father, then stages a play echoing the alleged crime to test the new king’s reaction. He also delivers the soliloquy beginning “To be, or not to be.” Who is this prince?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy about Prince Hamlet, this daughter of Polonius is rejected by the prince and later descends into madness after her father’s death. She is found drowned, though the circumstances of her death remain uncertain. Which character is she?

Created by Lincoln Peirce, this mischievous sixth-grader attends Public School 38 and often gets into trouble alongside his friends Teddy and Francis. His adventures appear in a newspaper comic strip and a children’s book series. Who is he?
In stories about Nate Wright, which Public School 38 social-studies teacher is his frequent detention-giver and the target of his nicknames “Godzilla” and “She Who Must Not Be Named”?

This ancient Mesopotamian literary work took shape from Sumerian and Akkadian stories preserved on clay tablets. Its best-known Babylonian narrative follows the king of Uruk and his friend Enkidu, and the king’s search for eternal life after Enkidu’s death.

In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the hero meets this survivor of the great flood, who recounts how he built a boat after receiving a divine warning. The gods granted him and his wife immortality after the catastrophe; who is this figure?

Which narrative mode addresses the reader or another character directly as “you,” making that addressee the grammatical focus rather than referring to them as “he,” “she,” or “they”? It is one of the three standard grammatical persons used in narrative voice.

In Italo Calvino’s metafictional novel, Second-Person Narration places a reader at the center of the action as they try to finish a succession of books whose beginnings are repeatedly interrupted. What is the title of this novel?
answer: If on a Winter’s Night a Traveler

question: Its action unfolds over one day in the Tyrone family’s summer home, where Mary’s morphine dependence and Edmund’s tuberculosis sharpen old resentments among parents and sons. What autobiographical drama by Eugene O’Neill centers on this family?
Long Day’s Journey Into Night portrays a troubled day in the Tyrone family and draws on its playwright’s own family history. Which American dramatist wrote it?

Sophocles’ tragedy begins with Thebes suffering a plague, and its king vows to discover what has brought the city low. An oracle links the city’s salvation to the unresolved murder of Laius; what is the play’s title?
In Oedipus Rex, this blind prophet initially resists naming Laius’s murderer, then accuses the king himself when pressed. Who is the Theban seer?
In this Victorian dramatic monologue, a duke shows a visiting envoy a portrait of his late wife and reveals his resentment of her warmth toward others. What poem is this?
Which British poet, who also wrote “Porphyria’s Lover” and “The Bishop Orders His Tomb at Saint Praxed’s Church,” composed My Last Duchess?

Born at the stroke of midnight on 15 August 1947 in Bombay, this narrator’s life becomes entwined with the history of independent India. His unusually large, perpetually runny nose helps him discover telepathic powers and connect with other children born around the time of independence. Who is he?

Saleem Sinai narrates this Salman Rushdie novel, recounting his family’s story alongside the upheavals surrounding the end of British rule and the first decades of independent India. Its title refers to those born in the hour after independence, many of whom have extraordinary abilities. What is the novel?
An English author and Christian apologist, he created the fantasy world of Narnia and wrote the memoir *Surprised by Joy*. Which writer is this?

In C. S. Lewis’s memoir *Surprised by Joy*, he describes how reading *The Everlasting Man* helped draw him toward Christianity. Which English author of that book also created the priest-detective Father Brown?

In this one-act drama, Estelle, Garcin, and Inez are confined for eternity in a room in hell, where bricked-up windows and the absence of mirrors leave them exposed to one another. Rather than physical torture, their punishment comes from judging and revealing one another; what is the play’s title?
No Exit is a one-act French existentialist play that opened in Paris in 1944 and was originally titled Huis Clos. Which philosopher and playwright wrote it?

This four-stanza lyric by the author of “Ulysses” begins with sunset and the evening star, then imagines a final departure over a sandbar into an immeasurable sea. The speaker hopes to meet his “Pilot” face to face; name the poem.
Crossing the Bar is a late poem by this British Poet Laureate, who also wrote “In Memoriam A.H.H.” and “The Lady of Shalott.” Who is the poet?

This wizard was headmaster of Hogwarts for much of Harry Potter’s schooling and defeated Gellert Grindelwald in a famous 1945 duel. His youthful alliance with Grindelwald later became a painful part of his history. Who is he?
In the Harry Potter novels, Albus Dumbledore serves as headmaster of this wizarding school, where students are sorted into Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, or Slytherin. What is the school’s name?

Which young Danish noblewoman in Shakespeare’s *Hamlet* is Polonius’s daughter and Laertes’s sister? After her father is killed, she appears at court singing and distributing flowers, and the queen later recounts her drowning.
In *Hamlet*, which queen gives the account of Ophelia’s drowning, describing her fall from a willow beside a brook and her garments spreading on the water before she sinks?

In the final tale of Day Ten of Boccaccio’s *Decameron*, a poor young woman marries a marquis who subjects her to years of cruel tests, including falsely claiming that he has killed their children. What is the title of this novella?
In *The Patient Griselda*, the Marquis of Saluzzo takes Griselda as his wife and devises the ordeals meant to test her obedience. What is his name?

What unfinished allegorical epic by Edmund Spenser was planned as a twelve-book work celebrating virtues through the adventures of knights? Its first book follows the Redcrosse Knight, while its idealized queen is named Gloriana.
In The Faerie Queene, this virtuous princess accompanies Redcrosse on a quest to free her parents from a dragon. After she and the knight become separated, a lion comes to her aid.

This nonsense poem appeared in 1871 as part of a sequel to *Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland*. Its speaker tells of a son who sets out to slay a fearsome creature, and its opening begins, “’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves.” What is the poem called?
Jabberwocky appeared in which 1871 book by Lewis Carroll, a sequel in which Alice enters a world on the other side of a mirror, where things are reversed?

In medieval romances, these armed nobles travel beyond their own lands in search of quests, often defending the vulnerable and pursuing honor; later parodies exaggerate their adventures. What is the natural name for this literary type?
In this famous parody of knights-errant, an aging hidalgo renames himself and rides out with Sancho Panza, mistaking windmills for giants. What work is it?
This 1922 modernist poem is arranged in five titled sections, moves among shifting voices and cultural allusions, and opens with the line “April is the cruellest month.” What is the poem?
In The Waste Land, which section opens the poem by presenting spring as a painful renewal and includes the line “I will show you fear in a handful of dust”?
The Waste Land draws on an Arthurian fertility myth centered on a wounded ruler whose land is barren. What is this legendary king commonly called?

Born in Sighet in what is now Romania, this Jewish writer survived Auschwitz and Buchenwald and later became an internationally recognized witness to the Holocaust. He received the 1986 Nobel Peace Prize for his work promoting human dignity and peace; who was he?

In Elie Wiesel’s autobiographical account, Moishe the Beadle returns to Sighet after escaping a cattle train and tries to warn the townspeople about mass killings, but they dismiss him. The narrator is later deported with his father to Auschwitz; what is the title of this memoir?

James Baldwin’s 1953 semi-autobiographical novel follows a Harlem teenager through conflicts involving faith and family, culminating in an intense religious experience. What is the title of this novel?
answer: Go Tell It on the Mountain

question: In Go Tell It on the Mountain, which fourteen-year-old Harlem boy confronts his stepfather’s religious authority and undergoes a spiritual crisis during a church service?

In this Robert Frost poem, the speaker first imagines a boy swinging bent branches, then explains that winter ice storms bowed them. The boy’s game becomes an image of brief escape, though the speaker hopes to return to earthly life and love. What is the poem’s title?
Robert Frost’s “Birches” appears in a collection that also includes “The Road Not Taken” and “Out, Out—.” The volume bears a 1916 copyright date. What is the collection’s title?

This Roman poet wrote the pastoral Eclogues, the farming-themed Georgics, and an epic about Aeneas and Rome’s origins. The epic was unfinished when he died in 19 BCE, and tradition says Augustus ordered that it be preserved rather than burned. Who was this poet?

Virgil spent eleven years composing this Latin epic, which follows Trojan prince Aeneas from the fall of Troy to Italy and connects his descendants with Rome’s origins. What is the title of this unfinished work?

In the folktale about the forty thieves, which poor woodcutter discovers their hidden cave after hearing the secret command that opens it? His brother’s greed brings further danger, and a clever servant ultimately saves him.

In the tale of Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, which resourceful servant discovers robbers hiding in oil jars and pours boiling oil into them to save her master? She later recognizes the thieves’ leader when he returns disguised as a merchant.
In this Eddic flyting, the gods gather in the hall of a sea-associated host, and Loki trades accusations with the assembled deities while defending his practice of sorcery. What poem is it?
In Lokasenna, the insults begin at a feast held in the hall of a sea-associated figure who brews ale for the gods. Who hosts the gathering?

In John Bunyan’s allegory, this deceptive market was established by Beelzebub and his companions to tempt travelers with worldly goods and pleasures. When Christian and Faithful refuse to buy its wares, they are put on trial, and Faithful is executed.

John Bunyan’s allegory follows Christian on his journey from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City. It includes the episode at Vanity Fair, where Christian and Faithful face persecution for refusing to conform to the town’s customs. What is the title of the work?

A Wall Street lawyer employs a quiet copyist whose repeated response, “I would prefer not to,” gradually disrupts the office. This short story ends with the lawyer learning that the copyist had once worked in a dead-letter office; what is the story’s title?
The author of “Bartleby, the Scrivener” also wrote a novel narrated by Ishmael about the Pequod’s pursuit of a white whale under the command of Captain Ahab. What was this author’s name?

Born to Laius and Jocasta but raised by Polybus and Merope after an attempt to abandon him, this Theban prince later solved a monster’s riddle and unknowingly fulfilled a prophecy by killing his father and marrying his mother. What legendary figure is the tragic hero of Sophocles’ Theban plays?

In the story of Oedipus, the king summons this blind prophet to investigate the plague and the murder of Laius. The prophet eventually reveals that the king himself is the killer. What Theban seer delivers this revelation?

Sophocles’ tragedy about Oedipus opens with citizens carrying olive branches and pleading for relief from a plague in Thebes. The king’s investigation of Laius’s murder drives the plot toward a revelation about his own identity. What is this first play in Sophocles’ Theban trilogy called?

In the legend of Oedipus, this mythic creature terrorizes Thebes by challenging travelers with a riddle. After he answers that the creature is a human being, it plunges to its death. What creature did he defeat?
What poetic form laments a death or other profound loss, often reflecting on mortality and remembrance? Unlike a brief factual account, it typically gives grief a sustained, meditative treatment.

One famous English elegy opens with the curfew tolling “the knell of parting day” and reflects on the uncelebrated lives of villagers buried in a rural parish burial ground. Its epitaph describes “a youth to Fortune and Fame unknown.” What is the poem’s title?
answer: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

question: Born in St. Paul, Minnesota, in 1896, this novelist attended Princeton before leaving college to enlist in the U.S. Army during World War I. He became a defining chronicler of the Jazz Age and wrote about the wealth and disillusionment of 1920s America; who was he?

In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1925 novel, a narrator named Nick Carraway rents a home in West Egg and becomes drawn into the orbit of an immensely wealthy neighbor whose mansion hosts lavish parties. The neighbor’s longing is symbolized by a green light across the bay; what is the novel’s title?

F. Scott Fitzgerald’s first novel follows Amory Blaine, who attends Princeton and pursues a romantic relationship with Rosalind Connage, only to be rejected when she chooses a wealthier match. What is the novel’s title?

In a later F. Scott Fitzgerald novel, American psychiatrist Dick Diver marries Nicole Warren, a wealthy patient he has treated. Their glamorous life among expatriates on the French Riviera gradually unravels; what is the novel’s title?
F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1922 story collection includes “May Day,” “The Diamond as Big as the Ritz,” and “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button.” What title did he give this collection?

Oscar Wilde’s only novel follows a young aristocrat whose portrait bears the marks of his sins while his own face remains youthful. First published in an 1890 issue of *Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine*, what is the novel’s title?
In *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, which artist paints the portrait that becomes a supernatural record of Dorian’s aging and corruption? He also introduces Dorian to Lord Henry Wotton.
Born in 1932 and raised in Port Elizabeth, this South African playwright, actor, and director wrote anti-apartheid dramas including The Blood Knot and Master Harold...and the Boys. What is his name?

Athol Fugard co-wrote this play with John Kani and Winston Ntshona. Set around prison life on Robben Island, it reveals apartheid’s cruelty through the experiences of imprisoned men. What is the play?

This postwar American literary movement included writers such as Allen Ginsberg, Jack Kerouac, and William S. Burroughs. Its authors challenged conventional storytelling and materialism while exploring spiritual searching and candid depictions of experience. What movement was it?
The Beat Generation found a major gathering place in this Northern California city, where Lawrence Ferlinghetti’s City Lights bookstore became an important literary hub. What city was it?
Jack Kerouac drew on his cross-country travels to write this 1957 novel associated with the Beat Generation. Its narrator, Sal Paradise, travels across America with Dean Moriarty. What novel is it?

This modernist novel follows Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through Dublin over the course of a single day, using parallels to episodes and figures from Homer’s Odyssey. First published in full in Paris in 1922, what is the novel’s title?
In Ulysses, the events take place on June 16, 1904, a date readers later adopted for an annual celebration honoring the novel. What is that commemorative day called?

Ulysses was serialized in The Little Review before its first complete book edition appeared in Paris on February 2, 1922. What was the name of the bookseller who published that edition through her Shakespeare and Company bookshop?
Ulysses ends with Molly Bloom’s long, largely unpunctuated interior monologue. What title is given to this final episode?

Established under the 1895 will of a Swedish chemist and inventor, this international honor was first awarded in 1901 and recognizes outstanding literary work across forms such as poetry, fiction, drama, and historical writing. Its laureate is selected by a Swedish cultural institution.
For the Nobel Prize in Literature, a committee reviews nominations, but which institution makes the final choice of laureate? Founded by King Gustav III in 1786, this cultural body has 18 members.

This Scottish writer published a novella about a respectable doctor whose secret persona commits violent crimes, as well as an adventure novel following David Balfour after he is abducted and taken aboard a ship. Who was this author?

In Robert Louis Stevenson’s adventure novel, a boy named Jim Hawkins finds a map associated with the dead pirate Captain Flint and joins a voyage in search of buried riches. What is the name of the destination island?

A former journalist and wartime intelligence officer, this British novelist published *Casino Royale* in 1953, introducing an MI6 agent who became famous by the codename 007. Who wrote the original series of spy novels featuring that agent?
In Ian Fleming’s first novel about his MI6 agent, the protagonist travels to a French gaming resort to defeat Le Chiffre at baccarat, and meets Vesper Lynd. What is the novel’s title?

In the final voyage of an eighteenth-century satirical travel narrative, the protagonist encounters rational horses who are repulsed by the brutish, humanlike Yahoos. What is the name of this horse people?
In Jonathan Swift’s satirical novel, its narrator visits the land of the Houyhnhnms after earlier journeys to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, and Laputa. What is the novel’s commonly used title?

Published in 1920, this novel follows a young man through his intellectual and romantic development, including his years at Princeton and his painful loss of Rosalind Connage. What is the novel’s title?
In This Side of Paradise, which socialite ends her engagement to Amory Blaine because she fears a life of poverty, then marries Dawson Ryder?
Created by Johnston McCulley, this masked swordsman and folk hero hides his identity as the nobleman Don Diego de la Vega. What is the character’s name?
Zorro first appeared in a 1919 novel by Johnston McCulley, set in Spanish colonial California. What was the novel’s title?

A fifth grader’s classroom rebellion begins when he invents a new name for an everyday writing tool, challenging his English teacher’s insistence on proper vocabulary. The word spreads far beyond his school and eventually earns a dictionary entry; what novel tells this story?
The author of Frindle also wrote No Talking, about a fifth-grade boys-versus-girls silence challenge, as well as The Landry News and Lunch Money. Which American children’s novelist wrote these books?
Walt Whitman wrote this long elegy in response to the assassination of a U.S. president. Its recurring images include a western star, a hermit thrush, and a sprig of spring flowers; name the poem.
answer: When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd

question: In When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd, Whitman mourns the U.S. president whose assassination in April 1865 prompted the poem. Which president’s death is at the center of the elegy?
What brief narrative form is cataloged in the Perry Index and appears in collections by Jean de La Fontaine? Its stories often use animal characters to convey a moral or practical lesson.
Among Aesop’s Fables, which story pits a confident, swift runner against a slow but steady competitor, who ultimately wins their race?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy set partly in Venice and Cyprus, this ensign turns Othello against Cassio by exploiting the general’s suspicions about Desdemona. He reveals his deceptive nature with the line “I am not what I am.” Which character is the play’s chief plotter?
Iago engineers this Venetian military commander’s jealousy by making a handkerchief seem like evidence of his wife’s infidelity. Desdemona is his wife, and he gives the tragedy its title. Who is he?

In Edgar Allan Poe’s narrative poem about a student visited by a raven, the speaker mourns an absent woman he describes as a “rare and radiant maiden.” What is the name of this idealized deceased beloved?

Lenore is the deceased beloved mourned in a poem whose midnight visitor perches on a bust of Pallas and answers the speaker’s questions with a repeated one-word refrain. Which American author wrote that poem?
This lyric poem by Matthew Arnold begins with a view of the moonlit sea and the coast of France, then turns to the image of the “Sea of Faith” withdrawing from the world. What is the poem called?
In Dover Beach, which ancient Greek tragedian is named as having heard the “eternal note of sadness” beside the Aegean?
A compact nine-line poem by Robert Frost imagines two opposing elements as possible forces that could end the world, linking one with desire and the other with hatred. What is the poem?
In December 1920, what periodical title first carried Robert Frost’s “Fire and Ice,” before the poem appeared in his 1923 collection New Hampshire?

Born in 1547 and dead in 1616, this Spanish Golden Age writer fought at the Battle of Lepanto and spent five years in captivity after being captured by Barbary pirates. He wrote a two-part novel published in 1605 and 1615 that is often called the first modern novel. Who was he?

In this novel by Miguel de Cervantes, an aging man adopts the identity of a knight-errant, rides Rocinante, and takes Sancho Panza as his squire. What novel features a hero who mistakes windmills for giants?
Miguel de Cervantes was wounded while fighting in this 1571 naval clash between the Holy League and the Ottoman Empire, near the western coast of Greece. What battle was it?

Published in 1585, this pastoral romance was Miguel de Cervantes’s first significant novel; it follows shepherds and their romantic entanglements. What work did Cervantes later hope to continue with a sequel?

In this Nathaniel Hawthorne tale, a newly married Puritan leaves his wife Faith at sunset for a journey into the woods, where he encounters a gathering attended by people he had regarded as upright members of his community. After finding a pink ribbon and witnessing the assembly, he returns to Salem distrustful of those around him; name the short story.

In Young Goodman Brown, which elderly woman who taught the protagonist his catechism recognizes him on a forest path and takes the stranger’s serpent-like staff? She later appears among the people gathered for the nocturnal ceremony.

In this mystery novel, ten people with seemingly unrelated pasts arrive on a remote island after receiving invitations signed by the mysterious U. N. Owen. A nursery rhyme and a row of small figures track the guests’ deaths one by one; what is the novel’s title?
And Then There Were None was written by which British mystery novelist, creator of Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, whose other books include The Murder of Roger Ackroyd and Death on the Nile?

This medieval collection draws on Middle Eastern and South Asian traditions and has no single canonical sequence of tales. Its frame story follows a woman whose nightly storytelling delays her execution. What is the collection’s natural English name?
In One Thousand and One Nights, which woman tells stories to King Shahryar night after night, stopping each tale at a suspenseful point to postpone her execution?
In One Thousand and One Nights, which French translator introduced tales such as Aladdin and Ali Baba to European readers after hearing them from a Syrian storyteller?
Which Syrian storyteller told Antoine Galland tales including Aladdin and Ali Baba, which later circulated in editions of One Thousand and One Nights?
One Thousand and One Nights includes a cycle about this seafarer, whose seven voyages feature a giant roc and a valley of diamonds. What is the name by which this mariner is best known?

Louisa May Alcott’s coming-of-age novel follows Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy March during the American Civil War era. First published in two volumes in 1868 and 1869, it was combined into one novel in 1880; what is its title?
In Little Women, which of the four sisters writes newspaper stories under a pseudonym, rejects Laurie’s proposal, and later marries Professor Bhaer?

In Little Women, the March sisters’ childhood play is shaped by an allegory whose protagonist Christian travels from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City. What John Bunyan work provides the sisters with a model of spiritual burdens?
In the United Kingdom, the separately issued second volume of Little Women was given a title by its publisher. What title did that volume bear?
The sequel Little Men continues the story introduced in Little Women, with Jo and Professor Bhaer running a school for boys at their estate. What is the name of the estate and school?

In this short story from Nathaniel Hawthorne’s 1837 collection *Twice-Told Tales*, Reverend Mr. Hooper appears in Milford with a piece of crape covering most of his face. It symbolizes the hidden sins people conceal from one another, while the story leaves Hooper’s own reason unresolved. Name the story.

*The Minister’s Black Veil* is one work by this American writer, who also created Hester Prynne and Arthur Dimmesdale in his novel *The Scarlet Letter*. His other well-known short stories include “Young Goodman Brown” and “The Birth-Mark.” Name the writer.
In Markus Zusak’s World War II novel, this personified narrator tells Liesel Meminger’s story and gathers the souls of people who die amid the conflict. What is the narrator called?
In Markus Zusak’s novel, Death narrates the story of Liesel Meminger, a girl who steals books and is fostered by Hans and Rosa Hubermann in Nazi Germany. What is the novel’s title?

In this Sherlock Holmes novel, Dr. Watson investigates on Dartmoor while Holmes is apparently in London, after the death of a wealthy baronet and amid an old family legend about a supernatural beast. Holmes eventually exposes a scheme connected to the inheritance. What is the novel’s title?

The Hound of the Baskervilles was serialized in The Strand Magazine from August 1901 through April 1902. Its author had previously sent Holmes over Reichenbach Falls in “The Final Problem”; who wrote the novel?

This 1937 fantasy novel follows a comfort-loving resident of the Shire who joins a company of thirteen dwarves on a journey to reclaim their ancestral treasure. Their destination is the Lonely Mountain, where a dragon guards the hoard.

In The Hobbit, this reluctant member of the dwarves’ expedition finds a ring in tunnels beneath the Misty Mountains. He escapes those underground passages after taking part in a riddle contest with Gollum.

Which 1989 historical novel follows Danish schoolgirl Annemarie Johansen as she helps her Jewish friend Ellen Rosen escape Nazi persecution in occupied Denmark? Its title alludes to a biblical image that offers comfort in a time of danger.
Who wrote Number the Stars, the historical novel about Annemarie Johansen and Ellen Rosen set during the Nazi occupation of Denmark? The same author created Jonas’s dystopian community in The Giver.

This fictional family is represented by three orphaned siblings: an inventive eldest sister, a book-loving middle brother, and a youngest child known for her sharp teeth. Count Olaf repeatedly pursues them in an effort to seize the fortune their parents left behind.

In which Lemony Snicket novel series does the Baudelaire family appear, beginning with a story about the children being sent to live with Count Olaf? Its installments follow Violet, Klaus, and Sunny through a succession of disastrous guardians and schemes.

Which English novelist and social critic, born in Bromley in 1866 and trained in biology under T. H. Huxley, helped shape speculative fiction with stories of journeys through time, invisibility, and invasion from Mars?
In which 1898 H. G. Wells novel do Martians invade Earth using three-legged fighting machines and heat-rays?

In J. R. R. Tolkien’s *The Hobbit*, this intelligent dragon drives the Dwarves from their home beneath the Lonely Mountain and claims their treasure. During Thorin Oakenshield’s expedition, Bilbo enters the mountain to confront it. Who is this dragon?
When Smaug attacks Lake-town, which archer learns from a thrush that the dragon has an unarmored patch on its left breast and brings it down with the Black Arrow?

Born in Florence and later exiled amid the city’s political conflicts, this medieval poet wrote in the Tuscan vernacular and helped shape literary Italian. His best-known narrative poem follows a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven. Who was he?

Dante Alighieri’s 100-canto narrative poem is divided into three sections tracing a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven. In its opening section, the pilgrim is guided by the Roman poet Virgil. What is the name of the complete poem?
Dante Alighieri is closely associated with this verse form, in which three-line stanzas link their rhymes across a sequence, as in ABA BCB CDC. What is this interlocking rhyme scheme called?

Dante Alighieri wrote this unfinished Latin treatise defending the expressive power of vernacular speech and considering the qualities of an illustrious Italian literary language. What is the work called?
Set during an anti-Catholic campaign in revolutionary Tabasco, this novel follows a fugitive cleric nicknamed the “whisky priest” as he tries to evade capture. What is the novel’s title?
The Power and the Glory was written by which British novelist, whose other works include The End of the Affair and Brighton Rock? His fiction often explores Catholic belief and moral conflict.

In this Emily Dickinson poem, the speaker accepts a courteous carriage ride with a personified escort while Immortality accompanies them. They pass schoolchildren, fields of grain, and the setting sun before stopping at a house resembling a mound; the final stanza looks back across centuries toward Eternity. What poem is it?
answer: Because I could not stop for Death

question: In “Because I could not stop for Death,” the speaker rides in a carriage with Death and one other passenger. Named in the poem’s opening stanza, this companion represents the possibility of life beyond the grave. Who is it?

Which 1774 German epistolary novel is told largely through letters its sensitive protagonist sends to his friend Wilhelm? Its central plot follows his unreturned love for a woman named Charlotte and ends with his suicide.
The Sorrows of Young Werther brought this German writer widespread fame after its 1774 publication. He later spent much of his career in Weimar and authored the dramatic work Faust.
This American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist became associated with the Lost Generation in 1920s Paris and later won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. What was his name?

Ernest Hemingway’s 1926 debut novel follows Jake Barnes, an American expatriate journalist, and Brett Ashley as their circle travels from Paris to Pamplona for the running of the bulls. What is this novel?

Ernest Hemingway drew on his World War I experience as an ambulance driver for this novel, whose protagonists are American lieutenant Frederic Henry and British nurse Catherine Barkley. What is the title?

In Ernest Hemingway’s 1952 novella, elderly Cuban fisherman Santiago spends days battling a giant marlin, while the boy Manolin and baseball star Joe DiMaggio figure in his thoughts. Which work is this?
answer: The Old Man and the Sea

question: Ernest Hemingway used an analogy in which a small visible portion rests above a much larger hidden mass to describe a prose method that leaves much of a story’s underlying meaning unstated. What is this technique commonly called?

In Chinua Achebe’s *Things Fall Apart*, this celebrated wrestler and warrior builds his standing in Umuofia, but his fear of seeming weak leads him to take part in Ikemefuna’s death. After an accidental killing brings exile, his resistance to colonial rule ends in tragedy. Who is this protagonist?

In *Things Fall Apart*, Okonkwo violates this sacred period by beating his wife Ojiugo, drawing a rebuke from Ezeani, the priest of Ani. Observed before the planting season, it is meant to preserve harmony and secure a good harvest. What is this period called?

Tony Kushner’s two-part drama follows Prior Walter’s AIDS diagnosis amid Reagan-era politics, sexuality, and religious visions. Subtitled “A Gay Fantasia on National Themes,” what is the play’s title?
In Angels in America, what is the name of the closeted Mormon law clerk whose wife is Harper and whose career is drawn toward Washington by Roy Cohn?
Which Japanese novelist and filmmaker wrote about Hashi and Kiku, boys abandoned as infants in coin lockers who later encounter the polluted city of Toxitown?
In which Ryu Murakami novel do Hashi and Kiku, abandoned as infants in separate storage compartments at a railway station, grow up and become entangled with the polluted city of Toxitown?

William Shakespeare's historical tragedy, believed to have been first performed in 1599, dramatizes a conspiracy against a Roman dictator and the civil war that follows. Shakespeare drew much of its historical material from Sir Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's *Parallel Lives*. What is the play's title?

In *Julius Caesar*, this senator joins Cassius's conspiracy but presents his decision as serving Rome's public good rather than personal hatred. After his forces are defeated at Philippi, he asks a companion to hold his sword as he runs upon it. Who is he?

In *Julius Caesar*, this ally of the murdered ruler asks permission to speak at the funeral, then turns the crowd against the conspirators by repeatedly calling them “honourable men.” His oration opens, “Friends, Romans, countrymen.” Who delivers the speech?

In *Julius Caesar*, this battle in Macedonia is where the forces of Mark Antony and Octavius defeat the armies of Brutus and Cassius. It brings the conspirators' military cause to an end. What is the battle called?

In *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*, Lucy comes upon Mr. Tumnus beside this iron fixture in a snowy wood; *The Magician’s Nephew* later explains that it grew from an iron bar in the newly made world. What landmark is it?
In *The Magician’s Nephew*, an iron bar planted in the ground of newly created Narnia grows into the lamppost in Narnia. Which former queen of Charn planted the bar?
A dark wizard can conceal a fragment of his soul inside an object, creating a magical safeguard against death even if his body is destroyed. What is this object called in the Harry Potter series?

One Horcrux in the Harry Potter series preserved a teenage memory of the dark wizard, who used it to manipulate Ginny Weasley into reopening the Chamber of Secrets. Harry later destroyed the object with a basilisk fang beneath Hogwarts; what was it called?

What collective name identifies the set of major lyric poems that includes works about a nightingale, a Grecian urn, and melancholy? One poem in this group cautions the reader against seeking oblivion in Lethe.

Within Odes by John Keats, which poem addresses a “light-winged Dryad of the trees” and imagines Ruth “in tears amid the alien corn”? Its speaker later wonders whether the experience was a vision or a waking dream.
What literary form tells a novel’s story primarily through letters, diaries, or other written documents?

Which 2019 epistolary novel by Ocean Vuong is framed as a letter from its narrator, Little Dog, to his mother Rose, who cannot read it? The novel follows their family history and Little Dog’s coming of age in Connecticut.

Which Daniel Defoe novel is narrated by an English castaway who spends twenty-eight years on a remote island? After meeting a companion there, the narrator recounts their life together in this landmark of British adventure fiction.

In Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe, what name does the castaway give the man he rescues from a group of cannibals? The name commemorates the day they meet, and the man later becomes his close companion on the island.

Born in Dublin in 1856, this Irish playwright combined social satire with political argument across more than sixty plays. He received the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote Pygmalion and Saint Joan; identify him.
In George Bernard Shaw’s comedy, Professor Henry Higgins wagers Colonel Pickering that he can train Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower seller, to pass as a duchess. What is this play’s title?

George Bernard Shaw’s first public success centers on Raina Petkoff, who finds a Swiss mercenary named Captain Bluntschli sheltering in her bedroom during the Serbo-Bulgarian War. What is the title of this comedy, in which Bluntschli’s fondness for chocolate creams contrasts with his soldierly role?

This English novelist was the elder sister of Emily and Anne, and her 1847 novel *Jane Eyre* first appeared under a pen name. Her earlier novel, *The Professor*, was rejected by publishers before her best-known work was published. Who was she?

In Charlotte Brontë’s 1847 novel, the title character is educated at Lowood School and later becomes a governess at Thornfield Hall. The story ends with her declaration, “Reader, I married him.” What is the novel?

Charlotte Brontë wrote this novel before *Jane Eyre*, but publishers rejected it, and it appeared only after her death. Its protagonist, William Crimsworth, leaves England to teach in Brussels. What is the novel?

Jane Austen’s comic novel, published in late 1815, is set in Highbury and follows a wealthy young woman whose attempt to match Harriet Smith with Mr. Elton goes awry when he reveals that he is interested in her instead. What is the novel’s title?

In Emma, Austen’s narration sometimes adopts a character’s thoughts and phrasing without setting them off as direct speech, creating irony between the character’s perspective and the larger narrative. What is this narrative technique called?

Born in Coney Island, this American novelist served as a B-25 bombardier in the U.S. Army Air Forces during World War II and flew 60 missions over Italy. He later drew on that service in a landmark novel about wartime bureaucracy; who was he?

Joseph Heller’s first novel follows bombardier Yossarian as he tries to survive repeated missions over Italy while military officers keep increasing the required number of sorties. The story also features mess officer Milo Minderbinder and his sprawling syndicate; what is the novel’s title?

First serialized in Bentley’s Miscellany from 1837 to 1839, this Victorian novel follows an orphan born in a workhouse. After he is punished for asking for more food, he flees to London and is drawn into Fagin’s circle of young thieves; name the novel.
answer: Oliver Twist; or, The Parish Boy’s Progress

question: The author of Oliver Twist also wrote about Pip in Great Expectations and Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol. What was this Victorian novelist’s name?
Which American fantasy novelist created the Cosmere, wrote Warbreaker and The Stormlight Archive, and revealed that he had secretly written five novels during the COVID-19 pandemic?
In Brandon Sanderson’s novel Warbreaker, a sentient sword is awakened through BioChromatic magic and speaks in a blunt, distinctive voice. What is the sword called?

Goethe began shaping this German poetic drama in the 1770s, published its first part in 1808, and its second part posthumously in 1832. Centered on a scholar’s pact with the devil, what two-part tragedy became one of the major works of German literature?

In Goethe’s Faust, this tempter wagers with God in the Prologue in Heaven that he can lead the restless scholar astray. He later appears in Faust’s study after first taking the form of a poodle; what is the name of this devilish companion?

Born in Chicago in 1930, this playwright drew on her family’s fight against racially restrictive housing covenants in a drama about a Black family confronting a move into a white neighborhood. The work won the New York Drama Critics’ Circle Award for Best American Play, and its Broadway opening made its author the first Black woman to have a play staged there. Who was she?

Which play by Lorraine Hansberry follows a Greenwich Village intellectual who runs a small newspaper and becomes involved in a local election, while his marriage faces strain? It opened on Broadway in 1964 and was her final play to premiere during her lifetime.
answer: The Sign in Sidney Brustein’s Window

question: Which Edgar Allan Poe lyric tells of a speaker whose beloved dies in a kingdom beside the sea, yet whose nightly vigil at her tomb affirms that their souls remain joined?
Annabel Lee is a lyric by the 19th-century American writer who also composed The Raven and The Bells. Who is the poet?

A girl from Moonstone, Nebraska, leaves her childhood home to pursue musical training after her remarkable voice is noticed by people in town. Willa Cather’s novel follows her development into a successful opera singer, including a formative period among artists in Arizona; what is the novel’s title?

In The Song of the Lark, which Moonstone physician recognizes Thea Kronborg’s musical gift and encourages her ambitions before she leaves town for further training? He remains one of the supporters of her developing opera career.

This didactic poem attributed to Hesiod invokes the Muses and traces the origins and genealogies of the gods, from the earliest cosmic beings through the rise of Zeus. What work recounts these divine origins?
In Hesiod’s Theogony, an anvil is said to take nine days to fall to earth from this mountain. Ruled by Zeus, it is also the home of the gods in Greek mythology. Name this mountain.
In Carlo Collodi’s children’s novel, this wooden puppet sets out to become a real boy and repeatedly gets into trouble. His nose grows when he lies. What is his name?
In Pinocchio, what is the name of the elderly woodcarver who makes the puppet from a piece of wood and becomes his father figure?
In Roald Dahl’s novel, this kind-hearted boy lives in poverty with his parents and four grandparents, then finds one of five Golden Tickets hidden in a chocolate bar. What is his name?

In Charlie Bucket’s story, the reclusive owner of the chocolate factory hides five Golden Tickets inside candy wrappers and invites their finders to tour his workshops. What is the name of this eccentric confectioner?
This American essayist examined the Haight-Ashbury counterculture in a title essay published in 1968. She later collected essays including the 1979 work The White Album. Who is she?
Joan Didion’s essay “Slouching Towards Bethlehem” draws its title from a poem whose opening describes a falcon turning in a widening gyre. Which poet wrote that poem?
An early-20th-century Imagist poet and a later poet known for “Skunk Hour” both came from this prominent Boston literary clan. What is the name of the family?
A member of the Lowell family, this poet’s collection *Life Studies* includes “Skunk Hour,” a landmark poem of American confessional poetry. Which poet wrote it?

Born in Zlín in 1937 and raised in Britain after his family fled Europe during World War II, this playwright became known for intellectually playful dramas, including one centered on two courtiers from Hamlet and another set at an English country estate across two eras. Who is the playwright?

In Tom Stoppard’s play, the action moves between 1809 and the present at Sidley Park, where a teenage mathematical prodigy and her tutor explore questions involving heat, determinism, and the changing English landscape. What is the play?

In L. Frank Baum’s novel, this ruler of the Emerald City is revealed to be an ordinary former performer from Omaha who arrived in Oz by balloon. He uses elaborate stage effects to appear powerful to visitors; what is this character called?
In The Wizard of Oz, the ruler explains that he came to Oz by balloon after leaving his home in Nebraska. Which city does he identify as his hometown?
Which fictional Fleet Street barber from a Victorian penny dreadful murders his customers and sends their bodies to a pie-maker to be used as filling?
Which Victorian penny dreadful first introduced Sweeney Todd? Published in serial form in 1846–47, it later inspired numerous stage and screen adaptations.
An overconfident fast animal challenges a slow, diligent one to a race, then loses after pausing while its rival keeps going. Numbered 226 in a standard index of Aesopic fables, which story is this?

The Tortoise and the Hare is traditionally counted among the fables associated with this ancient Greek storyteller, whose other familiar tales include “The Fox and the Grapes” and “The Ant and the Grasshopper.” Who is the fabulist?
The Tortoise and the Hare appears as entry 226 in a reference catalog that assigns numbers to Aesopic fables. What is this catalog called?

Its author famously included just one equation, believing that each additional equation would reduce the readership. Its chapters include “The Origin and Fate of the Universe” and a discussion of how space and duration fit together. What is its title?
answer: A Brief History of Time: From the Big Bang to Black Holes

question: The author of A Brief History of Time: From the Big Bang to Black Holes was a British theoretical physicist who predicted that black holes emit radiation and gradually lose mass. What was his name?
Which German novelist won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote both *Buddenbrooks* and *Death in Venice*?
In Thomas Mann’s novel, young Hans Castorp travels to a Swiss mountain sanatorium to visit his cousin and remains there for seven years. What is the title of this novel?

Born in Moscow in 1821, this Russian novelist was arrested in 1849 for association with the Petrashevsky Circle and spent four years in Siberian hard labor after a last-minute reprieve from execution. His psychologically intense fiction includes *Crime and Punishment* and *The Brothers Karamazov*; identify him.

In this 1864 novella by Fyodor Dostoevsky, an isolated former civil servant rejects the idea that people always act according to rational self-interest. In its second part, he recounts a humiliating dinner with former schoolmates and an encounter with a young woman named Liza; name the work.

After Fyodor Dostoevsky spent four years in Siberian hard labor, he drew on his prison experience for this work, published in installments from 1860 to 1862. It portrays convict life through the notes of a fictional former nobleman named Aleksandr Goryanchikov; what is the book?

Fyodor Dostoevsky’s first novel is written as correspondence between impoverished clerk Makar Devushkin and Varvara Dobroselova. Published in 1846, it brought the young writer into Saint Petersburg literary circles; name the novel.

In Ambrose Bierce’s story, as a condemned man awaits hanging, an ordinary object’s amplified ticking becomes a sharp, metallic sound like a blacksmith striking an anvil. What object seems to mark his final moments before execution?

In Ambrose Bierce’s story, Peyton Farquhar’s watch seems to tick as loudly as a hammer while he awaits execution. The plot follows his apparent escape downriver and through the countryside, then reveals that the escape occurred in the moments before his death; what is the story’s title?
answer: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge

question: Born in Andalusia in 1898, this Spanish poet, playwright, and theatre director became associated with the Generation of ’27. He was assassinated at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War in 1936, and his remains have never been found. Who was he?

Federico García Lorca first gained widespread fame with this 1928 poetry collection, which combines Andalusian themes with avant-garde styles. It includes the poem “Romance sonámbulo,” with its recurring green refrain. What is the collection’s title?

In this rural tragedy by Federico García Lorca, a bride runs away with Leonardo, leading to a fatal confrontation between Leonardo and the groom. In the final act, woodcutters discuss the events and Death appears as a character. What is the play’s title?
Federico García Lorca’s writings from his 1929–1930 stay in Manhattan were collected in this volume, published posthumously in 1942. What is the title of the collection?

Born in Cambridge in 1952 and educated in English literature at Cambridge, this English humorist created a comic science-fiction saga that began as a late-night BBC radio comedy before expanding into novels and other adaptations. Who was this author?

Douglas Adams first developed this comic science-fiction story as a late-night BBC radio comedy before expanding it into a five-novel sequence and other adaptations. It follows Arthur Dent’s escape from Earth with Ford Prefect after the planet is demolished to make way for a hyperspatial express route; name the work.
answer: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy

question: Born in partitioned Poland and later a British subject, this novelist drew on service in the French and British merchant navies to write fiction about maritime life, imperialism, and moral uncertainty. He became a master of English prose even though he learned the language only as an adult. Who is this author?

In this Joseph Conrad novella, Charles Marlow recounts a journey upriver through the Congo Free State to find an ivory trader whose final words are “The horror!” The story is framed by a gathering aboard the yacht Nellie.

This Joseph Conrad novel follows a young seaman who abandons passengers aboard the Patna, then seeks to redeem himself in a remote community. His efforts end tragically after the arrival of the pirate Gentleman Brown.
In his lecture “An Image of Africa,” this Nigerian novelist and critic condemned the portrayal of Africa in a famous Joseph Conrad novella as racist. He is also known for writing Things Fall Apart.
Which British novelist debuted with *White Teeth*, a multigenerational novel about Jamaican, Bangladeshi, and English families in North London, and later wrote *On Beauty* and *NW*?

Zadie Smith’s *On Beauty* follows rival academic families in a fictional New England college town and reworks a novel by E. M. Forster. What Forster novel, named for an English country house, provides its main model?

Published at Christmas 1871, this sequel to Lewis Carroll’s 1865 fantasy about a girl who follows a White Rabbit sends its heroine into a mirrored world laid out as a chess game. Its opening diagram casts her as a White Pawn whose route ends with her becoming a Queen in eleven moves. What is this novel?
answer: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There

question: In *Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There*, Alice encounters a nonsense poem printed in mirror writing. Humpty Dumpty later explains several of its invented words, including “slithy” and “mimsy.” What is the poem called?

In this children's novel, ten-year-old India Opal Buloni moves with her preacher father to Naomi, Florida, where she befriends a stray dog she finds in a grocery store. What novel is named for that dog?
Because of Winn-Dixie follows Opal Buloni and the stray dog she befriends in Naomi, Florida. Which American author also wrote The Tale of Despereaux?
In Jane Austen’s novel, this wealthy, good-natured bachelor leases Netherfield Park near the Bennets’ home and becomes attached to the eldest Bennet daughter. What is his name?
Charles Bingley appears in the 1813 novel *Pride and Prejudice*, whose author also wrote *Emma* and *Sense and Sensibility*. Who was this author?
A Florentine diplomat and political writer, he composed *The Prince* after being removed from public office. He also wrote *Discourses on Livy* and *The Art of War*. Who was this Renaissance author?
In which work does Niccolò Machiavelli explore republican government by examining Rome’s early republican history, including the conflict between patricians and plebeians?

In Cervantes’s novel, this practical, proverb-speaking peasant neighbor agrees to serve as a squire after being promised an island to govern. During the famous windmill encounter, he correctly tells his master that the apparent giants are windmills. Who is this companion of Don Quixote?

In Part II of *Don Quixote*, Sancho Panza is briefly appointed governor of this place. Although it is presented as an island, it is actually a village used as part of a practical joke. What is it called?

Published in 1906, this Jack London novel follows a part-wolf, part-dog born in the Yukon during the Klondike Gold Rush. Its protagonist is bullied by a larger camp puppy, and his journey from wilderness toward human companionship reverses the broad arc of *The Call of the Wild*. What is the novel?
In *White Fang*, the young protagonist is repeatedly attacked by a larger puppy at the camp. The novel links this persecution to his growing isolation and fierceness; what is the bully’s name?
What is the title of Rick Riordan’s young-adult fantasy series that follows a modern-day demigod son of Poseidon through adventures involving Camp Half-Blood and the Greek gods?

In Percy Jackson & the Olympians, which daughter of Athena was found at age seven by Thalia Grace and Luke Castellan and brought to Camp Half-Blood? As a child, she was also plagued by spiders that hid whenever her stepmother entered the room.

First staged on Broadway in 1949, this Arthur Miller tragedy follows a traveling commercial representative whose confidence in charm and popularity masks his failing career and strained family relationships. It ends with him deliberately crashing his car in the hope that the insurance money will benefit his family. What is the play?

In Death of a Salesman, this aging salesman believes that being well liked is the key to success and struggles to accept his son Biff’s rejection of his ambitions. After losing his job, he dies in a car crash intended to leave his family insurance money. Who is he?

Born in Amherst, Massachusetts, in 1830, this reclusive poet wrote nearly 1,800 poems, only ten of which appeared in print during her lifetime. What American poet’s posthumous work became a cornerstone of U.S. literature?

In an Emily Dickinson poem, a speaker takes a carriage ride with Immortality and a courteous male escort, passing children at recess, fields of grain, and the setting sun before reaching a grave. What is the poem’s title, conventionally given by its opening line?
answer: Because I Could Not Stop for Death

question: After Emily Dickinson died, this sister discovered a cache of her poems in the poet’s desk, helping preserve the manuscripts for later publication. What was her name?

Emily Dickinson’s first posthumous collection, published in 1890, was edited to fit the poetic conventions of the day. Which scholar’s 1955 complete collection restored her poems closer to their original form?
Before Emily Dickinson briefly attended Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, she studied at this institution in her hometown. What was the name of the school?

Toni Morrison’s 1987 novel follows Sethe, an escaped enslaved woman living with her daughter Denver at 124 Bluestone Road, where a haunting draws her back to her past and the choice she made to keep her child from reenslavement. What is the title of this novel, which won the 1988 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?

While compiling The Black Book, Toni Morrison encountered the historical case of an enslaved woman who escaped Kentucky to Ohio and killed her young daughter rather than allow her return to slavery; her story inspired Beloved. What was this woman’s name?

Published in 1847 under the pseudonym Ellis Bell, this Gothic novel frames the story of the Earnshaw and Linton families through a visitor’s notes about a housekeeper’s recollections. What is the title of the novel set around a manor on the Yorkshire moors?
In Wuthering Heights, which housekeeper recounts to the visiting Lockwood the history of the Earnshaw and Linton families, forming the central layer of the novel’s frame narrative?

A 1995 novel by a Portuguese writer follows an epidemic that leaves people suddenly unable to see and brings society to the brink of collapse. An ophthalmologist and his wife are among those caught up in the crisis, but she alone retains her sight; what is the novel’s title?
Who wrote Blindness, the 1995 novel about an epidemic of sudden blindness, and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998?

In Charles Dickens’s Christmas novella, this London miser refuses his nephew’s holiday invitation and treats his clerk Bob Cratchit harshly. After visits from spirits show him his past, present, and possible future, he resolves to change. Who is this character?

In *A Christmas Carol*, what deceased former business partner of Ebenezer Scrooge appears burdened with chains made from ledgers and cashboxes? He warns Scrooge to change before three other visitors arrive.
This Argentine writer and poet became director of the National Public Library in 1955. He wrote “The Garden of Forking Paths” and “The Library of Babel”; who was he?
In a story by Borges, the narrator visits Carlos Argentino Daneri’s cellar and sees a point that contains every other point in the universe. What is the title of this story?
Borges’s 1944 collection includes “The Garden of Forking Paths” and “The Library of Babel.” What is the collection’s title?
Jorge Luis Borges was born in Buenos Aires in 1899, and his family returned to this South American country in 1921 after living in Switzerland. Which country was it?
Borges shared a literary honor with Samuel Beckett in 1961, helping bring his work wider attention. What was this distinction called?

In this 1930 modernist novel, members of the Bundren family take their mother Addie’s coffin on a difficult journey to Jefferson to fulfill her burial wish. Set in Yoknapatawpha County, what is the novel’s title?
As I Lay Dying was written by the Mississippi-born modernist novelist who created Yoknapatawpha County and also wrote The Sound and the Fury and “A Rose for Emily.” Who was this author?

Isaac Asimov’s science-fiction cycle follows a psychohistorian’s plan to preserve civilization and shorten a period of chaos after predicting the Galactic Empire’s collapse. What is this series commonly called?

In the Foundation series, Hari Seldon uses a mathematical discipline to forecast the behavior of vast populations and the future course of civilization, rather than predicting the choices of individuals. What is this discipline called?

Which American poet, born in Head Tide, Maine, won three Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry and became known for early sonnets as well as dramatic character poems including “Miniver Cheevy” and “Richard Cory”?

In Edwin Arlington Robinson’s dramatic poem, townspeople admire a wealthy, courteous man and envy his seemingly perfect life. What is the title of the poem whose final line reveals that he dies by suicide?
This fixed poetic form traditionally has fourteen lines arranged according to a set rhyme scheme and meter. What is this form, whose name derives from the Italian word for “little song”?

The sonnet took shape in 13th-century Sicily, where this poet and notary served at the court of Emperor Frederick II. Literary tradition credits him with helping establish the form in its early Italian use; who was he?
The sonnet tradition is strongly associated with this 14th-century Italian poet, whose Canzoniere includes poems addressed to Laura. Who was he?

In this novel, a young seaman abandons the pilgrim ship Patna after believing it is about to sink, then spends years seeking a chance to live up to his ideal of courage. His later life in Patusan ends in disaster when Gentleman Brown’s attack leads to the death of Dain Waris. What is the title of Joseph Conrad’s novel?

The novel Lord Jim follows a seaman whose decision to leave the Patna becomes a lasting source of shame, and its story is largely framed by the recurring narrator Charles Marlow. Which Polish-born British writer also wrote Heart of Darkness and Nostromo?

In the Harry Potter novels, this red-haired Gryffindor comes from a large wizarding family and becomes one of Harry Potter’s closest friends after meeting him on the Hogwarts Express. During their first year, he uses his skill at wizard chess to help Harry and Hermione get past a life-sized chessboard. Who is this character?

Ronald Weasley kept a pet rat for years, taking it with him to Hogwarts before its identity was revealed as Peter Pettigrew, a wizard long believed to be dead. By what name did Ronald Weasley know the rat?

The speaker addresses a silent ancient artwork and considers a carved lover pursuing his beloved alongside a procession to a sacrifice. What 1819 ode by John Keats uses these frozen scenes to reflect on art’s permanence and human experience?
In Ode on a Grecian Urn, the speaker calls the vessel an “unravish’d bride of quietness” and a “foster-child of silence and slow time.” Which English Romantic poet wrote this work?
Ode on a Grecian Urn appeared anonymously in 1819, before the poem was gathered in book form. Which periodical published it first?
In Ode on a Grecian Urn, one carved scene shows a priest leading a lowing heifer toward an altar, while the homes of the inhabitants are left empty. What communal rite is depicted?

In Ryu Murakami’s *Coin Locker Babies*, Hashi’s story ends inside one of these institutions. In Haruki Murakami’s *Norwegian Wood*, Naoko receives residential care at the Ami Hostel, where she meets Reiko. What type of institution is represented in both works?

Haruki Murakami’s novel follows Toru Watanabe as he recalls his university years and the impact of Kizuki’s suicide. Naoko, one of its central characters, stays at the Ami Hostel, a psychiatric hospital in the story. What is the novel’s title?

In the frame narrative of *One Thousand and One Nights*, this woman marries King Shahryar and tells him stories night after night, stopping at a suspenseful point so he will postpone her execution. What is her name?
In the frame story involving Scheherazade, this king orders his new brides executed at dawn until her nightly tales persuade him to delay the sentence. What is his name?

An aging speaker opens by rejecting a land of youthful sensuality with the line “That is no country for old men,” then seeks escape from bodily decay by imagining himself as a golden bird perched on a bough, singing to an imperial court. What poem is this?
The Irish poet who wrote Sailing to Byzantium also composed “Easter, 1916” and “The Second Coming.” He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923. Who was this poet?

In this 1988 novel, a manuscript from a supposed Templar named Ardenti prompts three Milanese publishing editors to invent an occult conspiracy called the Plan, weaving together hidden history and telluric currents. As real conspirators take their game seriously, the editors’ fabrication becomes dangerous; what is the novel?
The Italian novelist and semiotician who wrote Foucault’s Pendulum also created William of Baskerville, the Franciscan investigator in The Name of the Rose. Who is this author?

First written for live television in 1954 and later adapted for the stage, this drama follows twelve jurors deliberating a murder case. After one juror’s doubts shift the vote from 11–1, the jury ultimately reaches a not-guilty verdict. What work is it?
The original live television version of 12 Angry Men aired on CBS’s Studio One in 1954, and its creator later adapted it for the stage. Who was the writer?

In a famous lyric by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, the speaker measures love by the depth, breadth, and height her soul can attain, then describes loving through ordinary needs and the convictions she held as a child. Which numbered poem is it?

Sonnet 43 appears in *Sonnets from the Portuguese*, and its author also wrote a poem beginning “I thought once how Theocritus had sung.” Which Victorian poet, who was married to fellow poet Robert Browning, wrote it?

In the Harry Potter novels, what goblin-run institution manages the magical community’s gold and valuables, with underground vaults beneath Diagon Alley? One vault eventually contains an object that Voldemort turned into a Horcrux.
At Gringotts Wizarding Bank, which golden heirloom belonging to one of Hogwarts’ four founders is hidden in the Lestrange family vault and later revealed to be one of Voldemort’s Horcruxes?

This 1883 adventure novel follows young Jim Hawkins on a voyage aboard the Hispaniola after he discovers a map tied to a pirate’s buried riches. Its story includes a mutiny led by the ship’s one-legged cook.

The novel Treasure Island first appeared in the magazine Young Folks from 1881 to 1882 under the pseudonym “Captain George North.” Which Scottish author later published it as a book and also wrote Kidnapped?
In Treasure Island, which ship’s cook secretly organizes a mutiny while seeking the buried treasure? He is a one-legged sailor who travels with a parrot named Captain Flint.

This 1934 Hercule Poirot mystery begins when a snowdrift stops a luxury international train and an American passenger is found stabbed in his locked compartment. The isolated passengers form a closed circle of suspects; name the novel.
Murder on the Orient Express is a 1934 mystery by this English writer, who also created Miss Marple and drew on her own railway travels when shaping the novel’s setting. Who is the author?

Shakespeare’s English history play dramatizes a Yorkist duke’s ruthless seizure of the crown and his role in the deaths of his young nephews. Its opening soliloquy declares that he is “determined to prove a villain”; what is the play’s title?

In Shakespeare’s Richard III, the two sons of Edward IV—including the briefly crowned Edward V—are taken into royal custody and disappear from public view in 1483. What familiar collective name is given to the brothers?

At a New Year’s feast at Camelot, this supernatural challenger offers a beheading game: a volunteer may strike him once if he can return the blow a year later. He arrives on horseback carrying a great axe; what is this figure called in the Middle English poem?

In the Middle English romance, which member of Arthur’s court steps forward to accept the beheading challenge posed by The Green Knight so the king need not take it himself? A year later, he sets out from Camelot to meet the promised return blow at the Green Chapel.

A grieving speaker hears a mysterious bird repeat a single bleak word after he has mourned his beloved. Which narrative poem opens with a midnight visit during “bleak December” and follows the speaker’s torment over Lenore?

The Raven was first published in 1845, and its author later explained his deliberate approach to composing it in an 1846 essay titled “The Philosophy of Composition.” The same American writer also created the detective C. Auguste Dupin; who was he?
In The Raven, the speaker mourns a “rare and radiant maiden” and fears he will never again embrace her in the afterlife. What is the name of his lost beloved?
In The Raven, the bird perches on a pale bust above the chamber door, and the speaker names the classical goddess represented by the sculpture. What is her name?
One inspiration for The Raven was the talking raven Grip in this 1841 novel by Charles Dickens. What is the novel’s title?

This novel follows the al-Jawad family in Cairo under the authority of its patriarch, Ahmad Abd al-Jawad, against the backdrop of the 1919 Egyptian uprising. One of his sons, Fahmy, is killed during a demonstration against British rule; name the novel.
Palace Walk begins a Cairo-set trilogy by an Egyptian novelist who also wrote Midaq Alley. This author received the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature; who was he?

Written by Aristotle in antiquity, this influential treatise examines poetry as imitation and gives particular attention to the structure and effects of tragic drama. Its analysis of plot, reversal, recognition, and audience response became foundational in literary criticism. What is the title of this work?
In Poetics, Aristotle names the effect tragedy produces by arousing pity and fear and then purging or clarifying those emotions. What is this concept?
In Goethe’s two-part drama, what is the name of the scholar who considers drinking poison before Easter bells turn him from suicide, and who later makes a wager with a supernatural tempter?
In Goethe’s Faust, what is the familiar name of the young woman Faust seduces with Mephistopheles’s help, who is later imprisoned after drowning her newborn child?
Jean Craighead George’s novel follows Sam Gribley after he leaves New York City to survive on his own in a treehouse in the Catskill Mountains. What is the title of this book?
In My Side of the Mountain, Sam trains a bird named Frightful to help him hunt for food. What species of raptor is Frightful?

In Zora Neale Hurston’s novel *Their Eyes Were Watching God*, this woman returns to Eatonville after the death of her third husband, Tea Cake, and recounts her life to Pheoby Watson. Earlier, her experience beneath a pear tree shapes her understanding of love and desire. Who is this protagonist?
After returning to Eatonville following Tea Cake’s death, Janie Crawford tells the story of her life to a trusted friend who listens without condemning her. What is this confidante’s name?
Born in Waukegan, Illinois, this American author published Fahrenheit 451 and The Martian Chronicles and wrote a time-travel story in which a crushed butterfly changes history. What is his name?
Ray Bradbury’s 1950 sequence of linked stories begins with “Rocket Summer” and imagines humanity’s arrival on and settlement of Mars. What is the title of this work?
Ray Bradbury’s 1957 coming-of-age novel follows twelve-year-old Douglas Spaulding through a transformative summer in fictional Green Town, Illinois. What is the title of this novel?

In this Ray Bradbury time-travel story, a customer on a prehistoric safari leaves a designated path and steps on a butterfly; when the group returns, the small disruption has altered the outcome of a U.S. election. What is the story’s title?

In Milan Kundera’s novel, what recurring episodes torment the wife of surgeon Tomas with cats scratching her, degrading public spectacles, and images of dead women? These sequences repeatedly unsettle her and expose her fears of bodily vulnerability and loss of dignity.
answer: Tereza’s dreams in The Unbearable Lightness of Being

question: In Tereza’s dreams in The Unbearable Lightness of Being, she is forced into a humiliating procession alongside other women, moving around a place while watched. What kind of place is at the center of this scene?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy set in Verona, this household is one of two long-feuding families whose conflict drives the plot. Romeo belongs to it, as does his cousin Benvolio; what is the household’s name?
A member of the Montague family, this cousin of Romeo tries to restore peace during the opening street fight and later urges Romeo to attend the Capulets’ feast. Who is he?

In this O. Henry story, the homeless Soapy repeatedly tries to get arrested so he can spend the winter on Blackwell’s Island, but his schemes fail. After hearing music from a church and deciding to reform, he is arrested for loitering. What is the story’s title?
The Cop and the Anthem appears in The Four Million, a collection that also includes “The Gift of the Magi.” The author of both stories was born William Sydney Porter; what pen name did he use?

Shirley Jackson’s 1959 novel brings Eleanor Vance, Theodora, Luke Sanderson, and Dr. Montague together at an isolated mansion to investigate reports of supernatural activity. Its opening reflects that no living organism can long exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality. What is the novel’s title?

In The Haunting of Hill House, which invited investigator joins Dr. Montague’s study after years of caring for her invalid mother? She drives to the mansion in a car she has borrowed from her sister without permission.
In Nathaniel Hawthorne’s novel, what is the name of Hester and Arthur Dimmesdale’s daughter, whose spirited behavior repeatedly draws attention to the secret behind her birth?
Pearl Prynne appears in what 1850 novel by Nathaniel Hawthorne, whose title refers to the embroidered scarlet A Hester is condemned to wear?

Which 1990 comic fantasy novel, co-written by Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett, turns an impending Armageddon into a story about an angel and a demon trying to prevent the end of the world after the Antichrist is misplaced?

Good Omens was co-written by this author, whose Discworld novels take place on a flat world carried through space by four elephants standing on a giant turtle. What is this British fantasy writer’s name?

In this 2006 novel, an unnamed father and his young son travel through a devastated United States, pushing a shopping cart and hoping the coast offers safety. What Cormac McCarthy novel follows their post-apocalyptic journey?

In The Road, a father and son cross a burned, ash-covered America, and the novel won the 2007 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Which American author, also known for Blood Meridian and No Country for Old Men, wrote it?
