This French novelist, poet, and playwright wrote pioneering adventure stories set amid the scientific and technological advances of the nineteenth century. His best-known novels include Journey to the Center of the Earth, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, and Around the World in Eighty Days. Who was he?
In a Jules Verne novel, Professor Pierre Aronnax, his servant Conseil, and harpooner Ned Land are taken aboard the submarine Nautilus. What is the title of this novel about their undersea voyage?
answer: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

question: This French editor and publisher collaborated with Jules Verne to develop the Voyages extraordinaires series, issuing its installments in Magasin d’Éducation et de Récréation before many appeared as books. He also published works by Victor Hugo and George Sand. Who was he?

In Vladimir Nabokov’s novel, this middle-aged European protagonist narrates his own case in polished, self-justifying prose, repeatedly courting the reader’s sympathy as if before a jury. His obsession with a twelve-year-old American girl drives the plot, while his control over her story makes him an unreliable narrator. Which character is described?

In *Lolita*, Humbert Humbert imposes a pet name on a twelve-year-old American girl whose mother becomes his wife, filtering the girl’s story through his own perspective. What is the girl’s actual name?
What book-length narrative form uses sequences of visual panels and text to tell an extended story, rather than relying on prose alone?
Which graphic novel by Art Spiegelman recounts his father Vladek’s experiences during the Holocaust, portraying Jewish people as mice and Germans as cats?

After her younger brother dies during their journey to foster care, a German girl is placed with Hans and Rosa Hubermann on Himmel Street. She steals books and survives the destruction of her neighborhood in an Allied air raid. Who is she?

Liesel Meminger's story is narrated by Death and follows her life with a foster family on Himmel Street in Nazi Germany. Which Markus Zusak novel ends with the narrator reflecting, “I am haunted by humans”?

What early Jane Austen novella, written entirely as correspondence, centers on a widowed mother who tries to steer her reluctant daughter into a marriage with the wealthy Sir James Martin while attracting the attention of Reginald De Courcy?

In Lady Susan, letters exchanged among the title character, relatives, and acquaintances tell the story instead of a conventional third-person narrator. What term describes fiction composed through letters and similar documents?

Which poem by Robert Frost reflects on the American people’s relationship with their land and includes the line “the land was ours before we were the land’s”? Frost recited it at John F. Kennedy’s inauguration.
The Gift Outright was written by an American poet whose other works include “The Road Not Taken” and “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening.” Who was this poet?

Which 2016 political-thriller novel was written by the conservative commentator who became the youngest nationally syndicated columnist in the United States at age 17? It is classified as a work of mystery, crime, and adventure fiction.
True Allegiance was written by a commentator who co-founded The Daily Wire and became the youngest nationally syndicated columnist in the United States at age 17. Who is the author?

In this adventure novel, Professor Otto Lidenbrock deciphers a mirrored message left by Arne Saknussemm and sets out with his nephew Axel and guide Hans through the Icelandic volcano Snæfellsjökull. What is the novel’s title?
answer: Journey to the Center of the Earth

question: Journey to the Center of the Earth was written by the French novelist who also created Captain Nemo and the submarine Nautilus in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. Who was this author?
In Charles Dickens’s Victorian novel, an orphan raised in a parish workhouse is apprenticed to an undertaker and later becomes entangled with Fagin’s London gang. What is the name of this novel?
Which English novelist wrote Oliver Twist, first published in serial installments from 1837 to 1839, and also wrote David Copperfield and Bleak House?

Born in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, in 1885 to a coal-miner father, this English writer first published poetry before becoming known for novels about working-class life, sexuality, and industrial society. Who was he?

D. H. Lawrence privately printed this novel in 1928; its frank treatment of sexuality led to censorship disputes. The plot centers on an aristocratic woman’s affair with her husband’s gamekeeper. What is the novel’s title?

A World War II veteran and optometrist from Ilium, New York, this protagonist is captured by Germans during the Battle of the Bulge and survives the bombing of Dresden in a slaughterhouse cellar. Later, he claims that extraterrestrials from Tralfamadore abduct him and that he has become unstuck in time; who is he?

Billy Pilgrim is at the center of Kurt Vonnegut’s novel that recounts the Dresden firebombing through a fragmented narrative and repeatedly punctuates accounts of death with a recurring refrain. What is the novel’s title?
Haruki Murakami’s novel follows Toru Okada, whose search for a lost cat becomes entangled with the disappearance of his wife. What is the novel’s title?
In The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, Toru Okada’s wife disappears while he is searching for their lost cat. What is her name?
In this fairy tale, a young bird is mocked and rejected by the other animals, then endures a harsh winter before discovering that he has grown into a swan. What is the title of the story?
The Ugly Duckling is one of the best-known fairy tales by which Danish author? His other stories include “The Snow Queen” and “The Little Mermaid.”

Born in Ueno in 1644 and active during Japan’s Edo period, this poet helped establish the opening verse of linked poetry as an independent form. He is also known for a famous poem about a frog and an old pond. Name this writer.
Matsuo Bashō shaped this haibun travel work from his 1689 journey through northern Japan, blending prose with poetry as he described places along the route. What is the work’s Japanese title?

In L. Frank Baum’s 1900 fantasy, a cyclone carries Dorothy from Kansas into a magical land where she travels toward a green city with the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Cowardly Lion. What is the land called?
L. Frank Baum’s 1900 children’s fantasy introduced Oz and was illustrated by W. W. Denslow; its popularity prompted thirteen sequels. What is the title of this book?
What poem by Maya Angelou did she read at Bill Clinton’s 1993 presidential inauguration? It opens by invoking three enduring features of the natural world: a rock, a river, and a tree.
In On the Pulse of Morning, which American poet begins the poem by addressing a rock, a river, and a tree? She also wrote the autobiographical work I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

In this short story, a student named Giovanni Guasconti rents a room in Padua and watches a secluded garden where Dr. Rappaccini cultivates deadly plants. The physician’s experiments have made his child poisonous; what is the title of Nathaniel Hawthorne’s story?
Rappaccini’s Daughter is a work by this 19th-century American author, who also wrote The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables. Who is the author?

Its speaker invites a companion through “half-deserted streets,” hears women discussing Michelangelo, and wonders whether to “disturb the universe.” What poem concludes with the speaker asking whether he dares to eat a peach?
answer: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock

question: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock appeared in 1915 in Poetry and was later included in Prufrock and Other Observations. Its writer also composed The Waste Land and Four Quartets; who was this poet?

The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock became its author’s first professionally published poem when it appeared in a Chicago-based literary periodical in 1915. Founded by Harriet Monroe in 1912, which magazine printed it?
Henrik Ibsen’s final play centers on a sculptor and a woman from his past who climb a mountain together. Their ascent ends in an avalanche that kills them both; what is the play’s title?
In When We Dead Awaken, a renowned sculptor encounters Irene, a former model whose past is bound up with his artistic success. What is the sculptor’s name?

He commands the Pequod and replaces the leg bitten off by the white whale with an ivory prosthesis. His whaling voyage becomes a single-minded revenge hunt; identify this character in Herman Melville’s novel.
Captain Ahab turns this whaling vessel’s voyage into a pursuit of the white whale after it bites off his leg. Ishmael sails aboard it as a member of the crew; what is the ship’s name?
Captain Ahab’s revenge hunt supplies the central conflict of this 1851 Herman Melville novel, which opens with the narrator’s words, “Call me Ishmael.” Name the work.
Wilfred Owen’s sonnet about the death of Europe’s great civilizations as World War I began is known by a year as its title. What is the poem called?
The sonnet 1914 portrays the outbreak of World War I as the death of Europe’s civilizations. Which English soldier-poet, also known for “Dulce et Decorum Est,” wrote it?

In this comic science-fiction novel, mild-mannered Arthur Dent escapes Earth’s demolition with Ford Prefect, an alien researcher sent to update an entry about the planet. Their journey brings them aboard a starship powered by an improbable new drive and accompanied by a famously gloomy robot. What is the novel?
answer: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy

question: In The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, a colossal computer spends millions of years calculating the answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything. What number does it eventually announce?

Born in Galesburg, Illinois, in 1878, this American writer used free verse to portray working people and city life. His poems include “Chicago” and “Fog,” whose opening image compares fog to a cat moving on quiet feet. Who was he?

Alongside his poetry and biography of Abraham Lincoln, Carl Sandburg collected and performed traditional folk songs from across the United States. What title did he give the 1927 volume in which he published many of these songs?

In Anthony Burgess’s dystopian novel *A Clockwork Orange*, what is the name of the youth argot used by Alex and his gang, mixing mostly English with many Russian-derived words? Its name echoes the Russian suffix associated with adolescence.
In Nadsat, Alex uses a slang term for a close friend adapted from the Russian word *drug* (друг). What is that term?

In African American animal folklore, this trickster is captured with the help of a tar-covered figure and pleads not to be thrown into a briar patch. His captors grant that wish, allowing him to escape through the very place he pretended to fear. Who is this character?

The tales of Br'er Rabbit reached a broad audience through the Uncle Remus stories, which drew on African American oral traditions. Which Georgia-born journalist and folklorist wrote and popularized those stories?
An Irish poet and playwright associated with the Irish Literary Revival received the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature. He wrote “Easter, 1916” and “Sailing to Byzantium”; who was he?
William Butler Yeats helped found this Dublin playhouse with Lady Gregory and John Millington Synge. It became a central venue for the Irish Literary Revival; what institution was it?
In a poem by William Butler Yeats, a falcon can no longer hear its falconer, the center cannot hold, and a rough beast approaches Bethlehem. What poem is this?
William Butler Yeats received this international literary award in 1923, recognized for poetry that gave expression to the spirit of a whole nation. What award did he receive?
In a poem by William Butler Yeats, the speaker plans to build a small cabin of clay and wattles and grow nine bean-rows on an island where peace comes dropping slowly. What poem is this?

In this 1942 novel by C. S. Lewis, an experienced demon sends advice to his nephew about tempting a human and undermining his faith. What is the title of the work presented through their correspondence?
The Screwtape Letters was written by the Oxford scholar and Christian apologist who also created The Chronicles of Narnia and wrote Mere Christianity. What was his name?

This American poet and memoirist recited a poem at Bill Clinton’s first inauguration in 1993 and wrote a seven-volume autobiographical series whose opening book drew on her childhood in Arkansas. What is her name?

Maya Angelou’s 1969 book follows her childhood and adolescence in Stamps, Arkansas, through age seventeen, and began the autobiographical series that brought her international recognition. What is the title of that first volume?
answer: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

question: Maya Angelou recited this poem at Bill Clinton’s first presidential inauguration in January 1993. Its opening images are a rock, a river, and a tree. Name the poem.
Maya Angelou’s 1971 debut poetry collection was nominated for a Pulitzer Prize. Its title ends with an unconventional spelling of a verb meaning “die.” What is the collection?
answer: Just Give Me a Cool Drink of Water ’fore I Diiie

question: In 1982, Maya Angelou became the first holder of an endowed Wake Forest University faculty post focused on the study of the United States. What was the professorship’s title?

An 11th-century Persian polymath, he wrote on mathematics and astronomy, but English readers know him chiefly through quatrains collected in a work featuring a book of verses, wine, bread, and a companion beneath a bough. Who was this poet?
In the Rubaiyat associated with Omar Khayyam, one quatrain describes a potter thumping this material, while another evokes human forms shaped from it on a wheel. What material is it?
Which English playwright and poet wrote *Every Man in His Humour* and *The Alchemist*, and created the comic hypocrite Zeal-of-the-Land Busy for *Bartholomew Fair*?
Ben Jonson named *Bartholomew Fair* for an annual fair held in this English capital. The same city was home to the Globe Theatre, where groundlings watched plays from the yard. Which city is it?

This 1937 novella follows two migrant ranch workers in California during the Great Depression: George, who looks after his physically powerful friend, and that friend, who dreams of tending rabbits on their own farm. What is the title of the work?
Which American novelist wrote Of Mice and Men, the story of George and Lennie, as well as The Grapes of Wrath, about the Joad family’s journey to California?
The title Of Mice and Men alludes to a poem whose speaker regrets having destroyed a mouse’s nest while plowing a field. Who wrote that poem, “To a Mouse”?

Born in Virginia and raised in Red Cloud, Nebraska, this American novelist drew on immigrant and pioneer life on the Great Plains in works such as *My Ántonia* and *The Song of the Lark*. Who was she?
In a Willa Cather novel, Thea Kronborg leaves her home in Moonstone, Colorado, to pursue a career as an opera singer, with support from Dr. Howard Archie. What is the novel’s title?
This short poem describes moonlight at the foot of the speaker’s bed, which he mistakes for frost before looking up at the moon and down toward home. What is its commonly known English title?
Quiet Night Thoughts is attributed to a celebrated Tang dynasty poet who was a contemporary of Du Fu, and whose works were translated by Ezra Pound. Which poet wrote it?
In this fable, a fox repeatedly leaps for clusters of fruit hanging high on a vine but cannot reach them. As it walks away, it dismisses the fruit as sour. What is the fable’s natural title?
The Fox and the Grapes is attributed to which ancient Greek fabulist, traditionally described as an enslaved storyteller? Other fables associated with him include “The Tortoise and the Hare.”
Xenophon’s prose work follows Cyrus the Great from his education through his rise to power, presenting an idealized portrait of his character and rule. What is this work’s title?
The Cyropaedia is attributed to an Athenian writer who also composed the Anabasis, an account of Greek mercenaries’ retreat after Cyrus the Younger’s expedition. Who wrote the Cyropaedia?

First published in book form by Doubleday in 1906 after appearing in a socialist newspaper, this naturalist novel follows a Lithuanian immigrant whose family enters Chicago's meatpacking district. Although its author hoped to spur support for socialism, readers were especially galvanized by its revelations about food processing. What is the novel?

The Jungle was written by this American journalist, who spent seven weeks investigating Chicago's Union Stock Yards in 1904. He later wrote the exposé The Brass Check and the novel Oil!, which inspired There Will Be Blood. Who was he?

In The Jungle, this Lithuanian immigrant comes to Packingtown with Ona and faces low-paid, hazardous work. After a series of personal losses and exploitation, he is introduced to socialist organizing by characters including Ostrinski and Nicholas Schliemann. Who is he?

The Jungle's Packingtown is a fictionalized version of the stockyard neighborhood in this Illinois city beside Lake Michigan. Its real Union Stock Yards were where Sinclair conducted his 1904 research, and Carl Sandburg later called the city the “Hog Butcher for the World.” What city is it?

The Jungle's revelations about adulterated food and filthy processing helped push Congress to enact this 1906 federal statute. It authorized federal officials to examine livestock and carcasses at slaughterhouses and required sanitary conditions in packing plants. What was the statute called?

An Argentine author wrote “Axolotl,” in which a man who repeatedly watches the amphibians at an aquarium comes to experience life from the other side of the glass. The same writer composed an experimental novel whose reading plan begins at Chapter 73 and lets readers follow a “Table of Instructions”; who is he?
Julio Cortázar set both “Axolotl” and much of Hopscotch in which European capital, where he was later buried in Montparnasse Cemetery?
This form of autobiographical literary nonfiction records an author’s personal experiences and observations close to when they occur, often in a sequence of dated entries. What is this form called?
While hiding with her family in occupied Amsterdam during World War II, Anne Frank addressed many entries in her diary to an imagined confidante. What name did she use for that addressee?

Thornton Wilder's three-act drama follows the Gibbs and Webb families in a fictional New Hampshire community from 1901 to 1913. In its final act, Emily returns briefly to her twelfth birthday after dying in childbirth. What play is this?

In Our Town, this figure introduces the audience to Grover's Corners, comments on the play's sparse staging, and presides over George and Emily's wedding. After Emily's death, he allows her to revisit a day from her childhood. Who is this character?

In Our Town, the fictional New Hampshire community lies near the real towns of Jaffrey and Peterborough. The daily lives of its residents between 1901 and 1913 provide the setting for the play. What is this town called?
Our Town premiered at the McCarter Theatre in Princeton in 1938 and later moved to Broadway. Which major American literary award did Thornton Wilder's play win that year?

Which 1950 C. S. Lewis fantasy novel follows the Pevensie siblings after they pass through a piece of bedroom furniture into Narnia, where they join Aslan’s struggle against a ruler who has trapped the land in winter?
answer: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

question: In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, which faun living near the lamppost is the first Narnian Lucy meets, shares tea with her, and later aids the children after initially promising the White Witch to turn her in?
What 1892 drama by Henrik Ibsen centers on an ambitious architect who fears being displaced by younger rivals? After Hilda Wangel urges him to climb to the top of a house, he falls to his death.
The Master Builder was written by this Norwegian playwright, whose other dramas include A Doll’s House and Ghosts. In A Doll’s House, an offstage door slam marks Nora’s departure from her husband.

This archaic Greek lyric poet from Lesbos was active around 630–570 BCE and composed verses intended for musical accompaniment. Ancient admirers called her the “Tenth Muse,” and most of her surviving work consists of fragments; who was she?

In Sappho’s only poem generally accepted as surviving complete, the speaker calls on a deathless goddess with an iridescent throne for help with painful, unreturned love. What is the poem’s conventional title?
Sappho’s home island in the eastern Aegean gave its name to the English word “lesbian,” while the poet’s name gave rise to “sapphic.” What was the island called?
Published in 1968, this collection of short fiction by Kurt Vonnegut includes “Harrison Bergeron,” a story in which government-imposed handicaps enforce equality. What is the collection’s title?

In Welcome to the Monkey House, the title story features Billy the Poet, a rebel who fights the government’s ethical birth-control program, while “Harrison Bergeron” imagines a society enforcing equality through handicaps. Which American author wrote this 1968 collection?
Allen Ginsberg’s poem follows a speaker wandering through a grocery store at night, where he imagines a conversation with an earlier American poet among the aisles. What is the title of this poem?
In A Supermarket in California, the speaker imagines encountering a nineteenth-century American poet whose landmark collection is Leaves of Grass. Who is this poet?

This English metaphysical poet combined intellectual argument with striking comparisons in works such as “The Flea” and the Holy Sonnets. He was ordained as an Anglican priest and became Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral in 1621. Who was he?

John Donne’s 1624 prose work *Devotions upon Emergent Occasions* includes a reflection on human connection and mortality that contains the famous image that no person is an island. What is the title of that reflection?

In James Thurber’s short story, this mild-mannered man escapes routine errands through fantasies in which he pilots a Navy hydroplane and performs surgery with a fountain pen. His wife sends him to buy overshoes while she gets her hair done. Who is this daydreaming protagonist?
Walter Mitty’s imagined adventures appear in a short story first published in The New Yorker in 1939. Which American writer and cartoonist wrote it?

This American novelist wrote The Underland Chronicles, beginning with a boy's discovery of a hidden world beneath New York City, and later created a dystopian trilogy centered on Katniss Everdeen. What is her name?

Suzanne Collins's first Underland Chronicles novel follows a boy who falls through an air duct in a New York apartment building and discovers a subterranean realm inhabited by humans and giant creatures. What is the book's title?

Which American poet, born in San Francisco in 1874, became closely associated with rural New England and won four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry? He wrote “Mending Wall” and “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening.”
In a poem by Robert Frost, a traveler pauses in a yellow wood where two paths diverge, then reflects that choosing one altered the course of his life. What is the poem’s title?
Robert Frost’s compact poem imagines the world’s destruction through two opposed elemental forces, associating one with desire and the other with hate. What is the title of this poem?

Robert Frost recited this poem at John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inauguration. It reflects on American national identity and includes the line about the land having belonged to the people before the people belonged to the land. What is the poem’s title?
In a 1939 prose essay, Robert Frost characterizes poetry as a revelation, or a sequence of revelations, shared by writer and reader. What is the essay’s title?

In H. G. Wells's *The Time Machine*, what is the name of the frail, surface-dwelling human race encountered far in the future? These people live above ground and are hunted by the subterranean Morlocks.
In *The Time Machine*, which Eloi woman does the Time Traveller rescue from drowning and who later gives him two white flowers?

A polite traveler from darkest Peru arrives in London carrying a small suitcase, and the Brown family takes him in after finding him alone. He is especially fond of marmalade sandwiches; what is his name?

Which British author created Paddington Bear, the polite bear from darkest Peru who comes to live with the Brown family in London? The character first appeared in the 1958 book *A Bear Called Paddington*.

Ambrose Bierce began publishing entries for this satirical reference work in a weekly paper in 1881. A partial 1906 edition appeared under another title, followed by an expanded A–Z edition in 1911. What is the work called?
In the publication history of The Devil’s Dictionary, what title did Bierce give the 1906 volume? It contained entries only through the letter L, before the expanded edition appeared in 1911.

Born Hector Hugh Munro in Akyab in 1870, this English writer became known for short stories that satirized upper-class manners with polished wit and sometimes macabre twists. By what one-word pen name was he known?

In a Saki short story, nervous visitor Framton Nuttel hears from young Vera that her aunt’s husband and brothers disappeared while hunting in a bog. When the men later approach the house, Nuttel flees, and Vera invents another explanation for his reaction; what is the story?

After winning the 50th Hunger Games as a District 12 tribute, this character becomes the mentor for Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark in the 74th Games. Known for heavy drinking and sharp cynicism, he urges them to flee the Cornucopia at the start of the competition.
Haymitch Abernathy lives in Panem’s poorest coal-mining region in Appalachia. Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark are also selected from this same part of Panem to compete in the 74th Hunger Games.

This literary tradition passes compositions between generations through speaking, singing, memorization, and performance rather than primarily through writing. The Epic of Sundiata, performed by West African griots, is one example. What is this tradition called?

In discussions of Oral Literature, scholars point to the repeated formulas in this scripture as evidence of transmission through spoken performance. Its recognized qira'at are distinct traditions for reciting it; name the text.

In this Ernest Hemingway story, an American on safari panics during a lion hunt, while his wife grows close to their professional guide. During a later buffalo hunt, she fires a shot that kills her husband; what is the story’s title?
answer: The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber

question: In The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber, who is the experienced professional hunter guiding the safari? He shoots the wounded lion after Macomber flees and later leads the buffalo hunt.

First published in 1897, this H. G. Wells novel follows a scientist whose optical experiments make him impossible to see. After arriving in the village of Iping, he uses his condition to terrorize those around him; what is the novel’s title?

In The Invisible Man, a bandaged stranger rents a room at the Coach and Horses in Iping, then later explains his optical experiments to Dr. Kemp. What surname identifies the scientist who tries to recruit Kemp into a violent campaign?
This Chilean poet adopted a pen name as a teenager, later served as ambassador to France under Salvador Allende, and received a major literary honor in 1971. What name is he best known by?
In 1971, Pablo Neruda received an award whose citation praised poetry that brought alive a continent’s destiny and dreams. What award was it?
Pablo Neruda’s 1924 poetry collection includes “Body of a Woman” and “Tonight I Can Write the Saddest Lines.” What is the title of this collection?
answer: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair

question: Pablo Neruda’s fifteen-part poetic epic traces the history and landscapes of Latin America. It includes “The Heights of Macchu Picchu” and begins with a section titled “A Lamp on Earth.” What is the work called?
Pablo Neruda was born in this Pacific-facing South American country, whose capital is Santiago and whose territory includes the Atacama Desert. What country was it?

A fifth-grade boy who hopes to become the fastest runner in his class befriends a new girl who beats him in a race. Together, they swing over a creek to reach an imaginary kingdom they have created. What 1977 novel by Katherine Paterson tells their story?
Bridge to Terabithia was written by an American author who also won the Newbery Medal for Jacob Have I Loved. What is the author's name?

In this satirical story by Nikolai Gogol, an impoverished Petersburg copyist spends months saving for a new winter garment, which is stolen soon after he gets it. After an official dismisses his pleas for help, the dead clerk returns as a ghost who targets passersby’s outerwear; what is the story called?

In The Overcoat, what is the name of the timid Petersburg government copyist who devotes himself to recopying official documents and painstakingly saves for a tailor-made winter garment? After the garment is stolen, he seeks help from a senior official, who brusquely sends him away.
This Prague-born German-language poet changed his first name from René to Rainer in 1897. After meeting Auguste Rodin in Paris, he wrote “The Panther” and “The Archaic Torso of Apollo.” Who was he?

Rainer Maria Rilke began writing this poetry cycle at a castle on the Adriatic coast in 1912 and completed it in Switzerland in February 1922. Published in 1923, it opens by asking who would hear the speaker cry among the angelic orders. What is the work?

In this Russian novel in verse, a detached young aristocrat rejects a country woman’s love and later regrets it after she has married. Earlier, he kills his friend in a duel after a quarrel over her younger sister. What is the work?
Eugene Onegin was written by the Russian poet who also authored The Bronze Horseman and the play Boris Godunov. Who was this writer, often regarded as a founder of modern Russian literature?

In Shakespeare’s tragedy *Romeo and Juliet*, this quick-witted friend of Romeo is a relative of the Prince of Verona and gives a speech about a tiny fairy who shapes people’s dreams. After Romeo refuses to fight Tybalt, this character takes up the challenge and is fatally wounded. Who is he?

In *Romeo and Juliet*, Mercutio responds to Romeo’s worry about dreams with a fantastical account of a tiny fairy who rides in a walnut shell and visits sleepers. What is the name of this fairy, whose visits are said to shape people’s dreams?

First published in 1938, this Gothic novel by Daphne du Maurier is narrated by a young woman whose name is never disclosed. After marrying the widower Maxim de Winter, she moves to his Cornish estate, where the housekeeper’s loyalty to his first wife casts a shadow over their marriage. What is the novel?

In Rebecca, what is the name of the imposing Cornish estate that the unnamed narrator enters as Maxim de Winter’s new wife? Its rooms and grounds remain closely associated with the memory of Maxim’s first wife.

Created by C. S. Lewis, this magical realm is the principal setting of a seven-book portal-fantasy series. Its history runs from its creation in *The Magician’s Nephew* to its destruction in *The Last Battle*; what is the realm called?
In Narnia, this great lion is the son of the Emperor-Beyond-the-Sea and sings the world into existence in *The Magician’s Nephew*. What is his name?
The original editions of the Narnia books, published between 1950 and 1956, were illustrated by this English artist, who also illustrated Tolkien’s *Farmer Giles of Ham*. What was her name?

Born in Prague in 1883, this German-language Jewish writer trained as a lawyer and later worked in insurance. His fiction includes the novels *The Trial* and *The Castle* and the story of Gregor Samsa’s transformation.

In Franz Kafka’s 1915 novella, traveling salesman Gregor Samsa wakes to find himself transformed into a monstrous vermin. His sister Grete initially cares for him, but a wound from an apple thrown by his father contributes to his decline. What is the novella’s title?

In Franz Kafka’s unfinished novel, Josef K. is arrested without being told his alleged crime and becomes trapped in an inaccessible legal system. The story ends with two men executing him “like a dog.” What is the novel?

Franz Kafka entrusted this friend with his literary papers and asked him to destroy the unpublished manuscripts after his death. Instead, the friend served as Kafka’s literary executor and arranged for works such as *The Trial* and *The Castle* to be published. Who was he?

In Franz Kafka’s story, an officer explains a specialized execution device to a visiting explorer on a remote island. The machine inscribes the condemned person’s sentence onto their body before killing them. What is the story’s title?

Emerging in the 1760s, this literary tradition often uses isolated castles or decaying houses, threatening atmospheres, mystery, and uncertainty about whether uncanny events are supernatural. What genre is it?
Often treated as the founding novel of Gothic fiction, this work was published by Horace Walpole in 1764 and was first presented as a translation of an old Italian manuscript. What is its title?

This 1977 novel follows Macon “Milkman” Dead III as he leaves his Rust Belt home to uncover his family’s origins. Its blend of African American folklore, family history, and questions of identity made it the author’s third novel.
Song of Solomon was the 1977 third novel of an American writer whose other works include Beloved and The Bluest Eye. Who was the writer?

A deadly plague drives Prince Prospero to seal himself and a group of nobles inside an abbey, where they hold a masquerade in seven rooms of different colors. The celebration ends when a mysterious intruder arrives in a costume that contains nothing tangible inside it. What is this Gothic short story?
answer: The Masque of the Red Death

question: In The Masque of the Red Death, which ruler tries to escape the plague by retreating to a secluded abbey with a thousand healthy nobles? He hosts the masked revel that unfolds through seven color-coded rooms.
Under the earlier title “The Mask of the Red Death: A Fantasy,” The Masque of the Red Death first appeared in May 1842 in which periodical?
Which actor portrayed Prince Prospero in Roger Corman’s 1964 film adaptation of The Masque of the Red Death? He was also known for starring in horror films such as House of Wax.

Which 19th-century American essayist and lecturer described himself in an essay as a “transparent eye-ball” while contemplating nature? A leading Transcendentalist, he also wrote “Self-Reliance” and delivered an influential address to Harvard’s Phi Beta Kappa Society.

In 1837, Ralph Waldo Emerson gave a Harvard Phi Beta Kappa address urging thinkers in the United States to develop their own intellectual voice rather than depend on European models. What is the title of this address?

Olga, Masha, and Irina’s bond is at the heart of a Chekhov drama, while the three prophetic witches in Macbeth form a supernatural counterpart. What literary concept names the relationship represented by these female trios?

In literary discussions of Sisterhood, what city do Olga, Masha, and Irina repeatedly hope to return to from the provincial Russian town where their family lives? Chekhov’s play makes that destination the focus of their shared longing.

Published anonymously in London on January 1, 1818, this Gothic novel follows a young scientist whose attempt to animate an assembled humanoid leads to murder and an Arctic pursuit. What is its full title?

The 1818 edition of Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously, while its revised 1831 edition named its author. Which English writer developed the story after the 1816 ghost-story challenge at Villa Diodati, where participants were invited to compose supernatural tales?

In Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, which Arctic expedition leader sends letters to his sister Margaret Saville, takes in Victor when the scientist is near death, and ultimately agrees to turn his ship back?

In Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, Victor leaves Geneva to study at which German institution of higher learning, where he becomes absorbed in natural philosophy and begins his life-making experiments?

In Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, which young woman in the Frankenstein household is falsely accused of murdering William after a miniature portrait is found among her possessions, then executed despite her innocence?

Two men remain beside a lone tree on a country road, expecting a figure neither has met. A boy tells them that the figure will not come that evening but may arrive the next day, and the same routine begins again. What play by Samuel Beckett follows this uncertain vigil?

The playwright who first wrote Waiting for Godot in French also created Endgame, whose elderly characters Nagg and Nell live in dustbins. Who was this Irish writer, whose play was first performed in Paris in 1953?

Published in 1722 as a purportedly true account, this Daniel Defoe novel follows its title heroine from birth in Newgate through a succession of marriages, criminal exploits, transportation to the American colonies, and eventual repentance. What is the novel’s title?

The author of Moll Flanders also created Robinson Crusoe, whose castaway spends 28 years on an island, and wrote A Journal of the Plague Year about London’s 1665 epidemic. Which English novelist and pamphleteer was this?

This farcical comedy premiered at London’s St James’s Theatre on 14 February 1895. It follows Jack Worthing and Algernon Moncrieff as they adopt the same first name while courting Gwendolen Fairfax and Cecily Cardew. What play by Oscar Wilde is it?

The Importance of Being Earnest was this Irish writer’s last drawing-room play. He also wrote a novel in which a portrait reflects its subject’s moral corruption while the subject himself remains youthful. Who was the writer?
In The Importance of Being Earnest, this formidable society matron rejects Jack’s marriage proposal after learning he was found as a baby in a handbag at Victoria Station. What is her name?

In The Importance of Being Earnest, Algernon invents this chronically ill friend as an excuse to escape his social obligations. Jack uses a similar pretense by claiming to have a troublesome brother named Ernest. What is Algernon’s invented friend called?

This Egyptian novelist began publishing in the 1930s and became the first Arabic-language writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, winning it in 1988. His major works include a three-generation family saga set in Cairo and the novel Midaq Alley. Who was he?

In Naguib Mahfouz’s first novel of the Cairo Trilogy, Amina visits the Al-Husayn Mosque without her husband’s permission and is sent back home. The story also follows her son Fahmy, who is killed by British soldiers during a demonstration. What is the novel’s title?

Naguib Mahfouz wrote his novels in this language, which has Classical, Modern Standard, and colloquial varieties. It is also the language of the Qur’an and of One Thousand and One Nights. What language is it?

Peter Carey's 1988 novel follows an English clergyman and a glass factory heiress whose shared love of gambling leads to a wager involving the transport of a glass church to a town in New South Wales. What is the novel's title?
Oscar and Lucinda is a 1988 novel by the Australian writer whose later Booker-winning book, True History of the Kelly Gang, tells the story of outlaw Ned Kelly. Who wrote Oscar and Lucinda?

Published in 1932, this novel depicts a technologically managed society that uses reproductive technology, conditioning, and sleep-learning to maintain a hierarchy from Alpha to Epsilon. What Aldous Huxley work also portrays citizens using soma to stay pacified?

Which English author wrote Brave New World and later revisited its ideas in a 1958 essay bearing the novel’s title? He also wrote the 1962 novel Island, often described as a utopian counterpart to it.

In Brave New World, citizens revere the American industrialist whose mass-production methods helped shape their society. The novel’s calendar counts from the first Model T produced by his company; who is this figure?

In Brave New World, which World Controller meets John the Savage and defends sacrificing art, religion, and individual freedom for social stability? He also authorizes the exile of Bernard Marx and Helmholtz Watson.

In Brave New World, Linda’s son grows up on a New Mexico reservation, learns about Shakespeare, and is later brought to London. What is the name commonly given to this outsider who rejects the World State’s values and demands the right to be unhappy?

This Canadian novelist, poet, and literary critic is best known for *The Handmaid’s Tale* and also wrote *The Testaments* and *Oryx and Crake*. A two-time Booker Prize winner, she has written dystopian fiction, poetry, and nonfiction. Who is she?

In Margaret Atwood’s 1985 dystopian novel, a woman called Offred is assigned to Commander Fred in the theocratic Republic of Gilead, where fertile women are compelled to bear children for ruling households. What is this novel called?
Margaret Atwood’s sequel to her Gilead novel has three female narrators, including Aunt Lydia, and presents part of its story as testimony preserved in Ardua Hall. Name this novel.

A survivor known as Snowman narrates this Margaret Atwood dystopia, set after a catastrophe involving genetic engineering and corporate-controlled biotechnology. It is the first novel in the MaddAddam trilogy. What is the novel’s title?

Margaret Atwood developed a remote-writing technology that lets someone sign a physical page from afar by using a digital tablet to control a robotic pen at another location. What is this device called?
This Lebanese-American poet and writer is best known for a book presenting Almustafa’s farewell teachings to the people of Orphalese. What is his name?

Kahlil Gibran’s *The Earth Gods* has been suggested to draw inspiration from *The Four Zoas*, an unfinished mythological poem by this English poet. He was also a painter who illustrated *Songs of Innocence and of Experience*.

A dissatisfied Parisian clerk’s wife borrows a sparkling piece of jewelry from a wealthy friend for a Ministry of Education ball, then she and her husband spend ten years replacing it after it disappears. At the story’s final reversal, the friend explains that the original was imitation jewelry; what Guy de Maupassant short story is this?
The Necklace is a French short story whose author also wrote “Boule de Suif” and “The Piece of String.” His compact stories are often recognized for their ironic reversals; name this author.
In The Necklace, the friend who lends Mathilde Loisel jewelry for a Ministry of Education ball later reveals that the missing original was imitation. What is this friend’s name?

This American horror novelist published Carrie in 1974 and became widely known for works such as The Shining, It, and Cujo. He also created the fictional Maine town of Castle Rock, which recurs across several of his stories and novels. Who is he?

In a Stephen King novella, four boys in 1959 follow railroad tracks to find a deceased boy whose disappearance has drawn their attention; Rob Reiner later adapted the story into the film Stand By Me. What is the novella's title?

Published in 1835 as part of La Comédie humaine, this novel centers on an impoverished former vermicelli-maker whose daughters neglect him. A young provincial law student attends his funeral. What Balzac novel is this?

In Father Goriot, what ambitious provincial law student boards at Madame Vauquer’s lodging house and, after the old man’s burial, turns toward Paris with a defiant challenge to the city? He later becomes one of Balzac’s recurring characters in La Comédie humaine.

Which 1970 Judy Blume novel follows a sixth-grader after her family moves from New York City to suburban New Jersey? As she forms a girls’ club with Nancy, Janie, and Gretchen, she wrestles with puberty and her search for a religious identity.
answer: Are You There, God? It's Me, Margaret.

question: Who wrote Are You There, God? It's Me, Margaret.? This American author also created Peter Hatcher, whose exasperation with younger brother Fudge anchors Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing and related books.
Which American novelist, born Chloe Ardelia Wofford, became the first Black female fiction editor at Random House in the late 1960s and received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature?

In Toni Morrison’s 1987 novel, the formerly enslaved Sethe lives at 124 Bluestone Road, where a mysterious young woman with a name connected to Sethe’s past appears. What novel won the Pulitzer Prize in 1988?

In Toni Morrison’s 1977 novel, Macon “Milkman” Dead III follows clues about his family’s past from Michigan to Virginia, while Guitar Bains belongs to a group called the Seven Days. What novel won the National Book Critics Circle Award?

In *Our Town*, Emily asks whether anyone ever truly realizes life while living it. The Stage Manager replies that, besides saints, a group exemplified by Robert Frost and Emily Dickinson might; what are these writers called?

Among the Poets named as examples in *Our Town*, which 19th-century American writer from Amherst became known for poems with unconventional capitalization and punctuation, many of which were published after her death?

In Joel Chandler Harris’s collections of African American animal tales, this fictional storyteller supplies the framing voice for accounts of Br’er Rabbit and other animals. What is the narrator’s name?

The fictional narrator Uncle Remus was created by this Georgia-born journalist, who collected and adapted African American animal tales in *Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings* (1880). Name the author.

This American author created a fantasy series that begins with a boy discovering he is the son of Poseidon, and later wrote the Kane Chronicles and Magnus Chase and the Gods of Asgard series. Who is the author?

In Rick Riordan’s fantasy series, this demigod carries a sword that disguises itself as a pen and is brought to Camp Half-Blood after discovering his father is a Greek god of the sea. What is the demigod’s usual name?

In Daniel Defoe’s adventure novel, a shipwrecked Englishman rescues this man from cannibals and teaches him English. The castaway names him after the day of the week on which he was saved; what name does he give him?
In the novel featuring Friday, an English sailor is stranded for twenty-eight years on an island near the mouth of the Orinoco River before he is rescued. What is the title of Daniel Defoe’s novel?

Born at the exact moment on August 15, 1947, when India became independent, Saleem Sinai discovers telepathic powers that connect him to nearly a thousand other people born during the country’s first hour of freedom. What Salman Rushdie novel links this fantastical premise to a family’s history and modern India?

Midnight’s Children, published in 1981, won the Booker Prize and is narrated by Saleem Sinai, whose birth coincides with Indian independence. Which British-Indian novelist also wrote The Satanic Verses?

Which Heian-period Japanese literary work, composed by a court lady serving Empress Teishi, ranges from observations of palace life to memorable lists such as “Hateful Things” and “Things That Make One’s Heart Beat Faster”?
The Pillow Book preserves the personal observations and courtly anecdotes of a woman who served Empress Teishi in late tenth-century Japan. What was this author’s name?

What nonfiction literary genre recounts a writer’s journeys while presenting firsthand observations of places, cultures, and encounters? It includes essays, memoirs, and other works shaped by the traveler’s experience.

In Travel Literature, which 1869 book draws on Mark Twain’s account of the Quaker City excursion, a steamship tour that included Europe and the Holy Land? Twain turned the travelers’ observations and comic reactions into a satirical narrative.

What historical language stage, used in England from roughly the late eleventh through the late fifteenth century, is the language of *Pearl* and *The Canterbury Tales*? It developed after the Anglo-Saxon period and before the early modern period.

Which Middle English Arthurian romance, generally attributed to the anonymous poet of *Pearl*, features a beheading challenge at King Arthur’s court and a later test of a visiting knight at Sir Bertilak’s castle? Its long alliterative stanzas conclude with a short “bob” followed by a rhyming “wheel.”
answer: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

question: Born in 712 and active in Tang China, this poet twice failed the imperial civil-service examinations before war and political upheaval shaped verse attentive to public events and ordinary suffering. Later readers called him both a “poet-historian” and a “poet-sage”; who was he?

Du Fu wrote about social crisis, family, friendship, and landscape, but is especially associated with a Chinese form of regulated verse marked by fixed patterns and tonal organization. What is this poetic form called?

This French adventure novel was serialized from 1844 to 1846 and follows Edmond Dantès, a sailor falsely accused of treason who escapes the Château d’If, discovers hidden treasure, and seeks revenge on those who betrayed him. What is the novel’s title?
The Count of Monte Cristo was first published in serial form before appearing as a book in 1846. Which French novelist created Edmond Dantès and this story of imprisonment, treasure, and revenge?

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Edmond Dantès is held in this fortress-prison on an island off Marseille after being falsely accused of treason. Its isolated setting becomes central to his imprisonment and escape. What is the prison called?

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès meets this learned fellow prisoner, who teaches him languages and history and reveals the location of hidden treasure on Monte Cristo. By what name is this priest known?

First privately printed in 1855, this poetry collection began with 12 untitled poems, one of which later became known as “Song of Myself.” Its author repeatedly revised and enlarged it, and the 1891–92 “deathbed” edition contained nearly 400 poems. What is the collection’s title?

In Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman mourned this assassinated U.S. president in an elegy framed by spring lilacs and in a poem that addresses him as a fallen captain. He was shot in 1865, shortly before the Civil War ended. Who was he?

Born in London to Bengali parents, this British-American author explored the Indian-immigrant experience in works including *The Namesake* and *Interpreter of Maladies*. Her debut story collection won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.
Jhumpa Lahiri’s 1999 debut short-story collection won both the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the PEN/Hemingway Award. What is the title of this collection?
After moving to this Italian capital in 2012, Jhumpa Lahiri began writing in Italian. She later published the Italian-language novel *Dove mi trovo* and the collection *Roman Stories*.
Born in Lincolnshire in 1809, this English poet was appointed Poet Laureate by Queen Victoria in 1850 and held the post until his death in 1892. He also wrote an elegy for his friend Arthur Hallam.
Which 1850 work by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, is a long elegy for his friend Arthur Hallam and includes the phrase “Nature, red in tooth and claw”?

Carl Sandburg’s free-verse poem addresses a Midwestern metropolis as “Hog Butcher for the World” and later calls it the “City of the Big Shoulders.” Which city does the poem celebrate while also acknowledging its roughness?

In his free-verse poem “Chicago,” the speaker calls the city “Hog Butcher for the World” and “City of the Big Shoulders,” combining civic pride with hard-edged criticism. Which American poet also wrote “Grass”?
In this Yoruba tragedy, Elesin Oba is expected to perform ritual suicide following the ruler’s passing, but British officer Simon Pilkings intervenes and prevents the rite. What is the play’s title?
Death and the King's Horseman was written by a Nigerian playwright who became the first African recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986. What is his name?
In this novel, a young shepherd named Santiago follows his Personal Legend after recurring dreams lead him to seek treasure near the Egyptian pyramids. What is the title of Paulo Coelho’s work?
In The Alchemist, Santiago learns that alchemy’s Master Work includes the Elixir of Life and a substance said to turn lead into gold. What is that substance called?
Born in Bloemfontein in 1892, this English philologist later taught at Oxford and created Middle-earth. He wrote *The Hobbit* and *The Lord of the Rings*. Who was he?
J. R. R. Tolkien’s son Christopher edited this posthumously published 1977 work, which gathers foundational myths and histories of Middle-earth. What is the work called?
Born in Alloway in 1759, this Scottish poet published *Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect* in 1786 and wrote “To a Mouse” and “A Red, Red Rose.” What is his name?
What was the title of Robert Burns’s first poetry collection, published in Kilmarnock in July 1786? It gathered poems written in the language of his native region and brought him rapid fame.

Born in Chaguanas, Trinidad, in 1932, this novelist and essayist later became a British citizen and received the 2001 Nobel Prize in Literature. He also wrote a landmark novel about Mohun Biswas’s struggle to claim a home of his own. Who is this writer?
In V. S. Naipaul’s 1961 novel, an Indo-Trinidadian journalist named Mohun marries into the Tulsi family and struggles to gain independence from his in-laws. What is the title of this novel?
Which German mathematician, born in 1845, founded modern set theory and used a proof involving an altered diagonal to show that the real numbers are uncountable?

In Georg Cantor’s proof that the real numbers cannot be arranged in a complete list, he constructs a number that differs from the nth listed number in its nth decimal digit. What is this proof technique called?

A data set in which every value is identical has this measure equal to zero. Unlike variance, it is expressed in the same units as the original observations, and the population version is commonly denoted by σ. What is this measure of spread?
When calculating standard deviation, deviations from the mean are squared and averaged before taking a square root. This intermediate measure is expressed in squared units; what is it called?

The Intermediate Value Theorem assumes this object is continuous on a closed interval, and standard notation such as f(x) names one of these rules. What mathematical object assigns a unique output to every allowed input?
For a function, the set containing every allowed input at which its rule is defined is distinct from the set of resulting outputs. What is this input set called?

In a right triangle, this trigonometric function is the ratio of the side opposite an acute angle to the hypotenuse. On the unit circle, its value is the vertical coordinate of the point corresponding to the angle. What is this function?
The sine function accepts every real angle, but its outputs stay within the unit circle’s highest and lowest vertical coordinates. What closed interval is its range?

For positive inputs, this function returns the exponent to which the constant approximately 2.71828 must be raised to obtain the input. It can also be defined as the signed area under y = 1/t from 1 to x; what is this function called?
The natural logarithm is undone by this function: for a real input u, it returns e^u, and its derivative is itself. What is this function called?

Which theorem established that the prime numbers contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length? Announced in 2004, its proof extended work on arithmetic patterns associated with Szemerédi’s theorem.

The Green–Tao theorem is named for this mathematician and Ben Green. An Australian-American number theorist, he received the Fields Medal in 2006 and coauthored the result on arithmetic progressions among primes. Who is he?
Which positive integer follows 1 and precedes 3, and is the first and only even prime?
In algebra, x+y is a polynomial with two separate terms, and polynomials with exactly that structure have a standard name. In the context of Two, what is this type of polynomial called?

At a point on a smooth surface, multiply the surface’s two principal bending rates—those along the directions of greatest and least normal bending—to obtain this scalar. It is unchanged by bending the surface without stretching it. What is this quantity called?

The intrinsic character of Gaussian curvature is central to the Theorema Egregium, which shows that it is preserved by local isometries of a surface. Which German mathematician published this theorem in 1827?
What is the set-theoretic measure of how many elements a set contains, conventionally written with vertical bars around the set and unchanged when a bijection pairs its elements with another set?

Which mathematician, the original formulator of set theory, used the diagonal argument to show that the real numbers have a larger cardinality than the natural numbers, proving that the reals are uncountable?
For a function f mapping a set into itself, an element x with f(x)=x is unchanged by the mapping. What is the standard name for x?
A permutation can send some elements to themselves; those elements are fixed points. What is the name for a permutation that has none, so every element moves to a different position?

Archimedes showed that a sphere inscribed in a certain solid has two-thirds the solid’s volume. The solid has two parallel, congruent circular bases joined by a curved surface; what is its standard geometric name?
For a right circular cylinder, the volume equals the area of its circular base multiplied by the perpendicular distance between its bases. What is this distance called?
In standard form, this degree-two equation is written as ax² + bx + c = 0, with a nonzero. When its left-hand side is graphed as a function, the result is a parabola. What is this equation called?

For a Quadratic Equation written as ax² + bx + c = 0, the quantity b² − 4ac determines whether its roots are two distinct real numbers, one repeated real number, or a complex-conjugate pair. What is this quantity called?

In right-triangle trigonometry, this function gives the ratio of the side opposite an acute angle to the adjacent leg. It can also be calculated by dividing sine by cosine. What is this trigonometric function?
The Tangent function has vertical asymptotes where cosine vanishes, but its values repeat after adding a fixed angle. What is its least positive period?

This operation reverses squaring: for a nonnegative number, it gives the nonnegative value that multiplied by itself returns the original number. For example, applying it to 25 gives 5. What is this operation?
In the notation for a square root, the symbol √ appears before the value being operated on. What is the term for the number written beneath that symbol?
In number theory, this theorem guarantees that for any integers a and b with b ≠ 0, there are unique integers q and r such that a = bq + r. It requires 0 ≤ r < |b|; what is the theorem called?
The Division Algorithm represents an integer a as bq + r, where b is nonzero and q and r are integers. What is the name for r, which is restricted to 0 ≤ r < |b|?

What is the name for the higher-dimensional analogue of a circle or ordinary sphere, defined as the set of points a fixed distance from a center in Euclidean space? The familiar spherical surface in three-dimensional space is one example.

A Ukrainian mathematician proved that the E8 lattice gives the densest packing of equal balls in eight-dimensional space, a result in the study of Hypersphere packing. Which 2022 Fields Medalist made this breakthrough?

The relation sets an exponential with the imaginary unit multiplied by the radian measure of a half-turn equal to negative one, then balances it by adding one; it is renowned for uniting five fundamental constants. What celebrated equation is this?
In Euler's Identity, which irrational constant forms the base of the exponential term, is approximately 2.71828, and has a natural logarithm equal to one?

In the hyperoperation sequence, what operation follows exponentiation and is defined by repeatedly applying exponentiation, just as exponentiation repeatedly applies multiplication? It can be represented as a power tower, with the height specifying the number of repeated exponentiations.

Tetration is commonly expressed as a↑↑b, placing a doubled operator between the base and height. This symbolic system is named for the American computer scientist who introduced it; what is the system called?
What is the name of the closed figure drawn on a sphere whose three boundary edges are arcs of great circles? Its boundary follows the curved surface rather than lying in a plane.
For a Spherical Triangle, what is the name of the amount by which the sum of its interior angles exceeds 180°? On a sphere of radius R, its area equals this amount multiplied by R².

Mathematicians use this concept for what has no finite bound or endpoint, and for sets that contain infinitely many elements. Its symbol resembles a sideways figure eight, but it is not an ordinary counting number. What is this concept?

In discussions of Infinity, a classic set-theoretic proof shows that no list can contain every real number between 0 and 1: by changing the kth decimal digit of the kth entry, it constructs a number missing from the list. What is this proof method called?
For any nonzero number, dividing 1 by it gives a value whose product with the original number is 1. What is this number called?
Which positive constant equals 1 plus its own reciprocal and is also the limiting value of quotients of consecutive Fibonacci numbers?
What branch of mathematics studies how the angles and side lengths of triangles are related? It also uses ratios of those sides to calculate unknown measurements.
In trigonometry, which function gives the ratio of a right triangle’s adjacent side to its hypotenuse for an acute angle? It is the function represented by “CAH” in the mnemonic SOHCAHTOA.

For a sample of n observations, calculating deviations from the sample mean imposes one constraint, leaving n−1 independent deviations. What is this count of independent quantities in a statistical calculation called?

In a one-sample inference procedure with an unknown population variance estimated from data, the reference curve is symmetric and heavier-tailed than the standard normal, with its shape indexed by degrees of freedom, typically n−1. What is this family called?
What name is given to transformations that turn an object around an axis, with the direction commonly described as clockwise or counterclockwise?

In three-dimensional geometry, rotations can be represented using a four-dimensional extension of complex numbers with three non-real basis units, commonly written i, j, and k. What is this number system called?

In algebra, what is a collection of two or more first-degree conditions on the same unknowns, where one assignment must make every condition true at once? The collection can have a unique solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solution.

When solving a system of linear equations, which procedure applies elementary row operations to an augmented matrix to put it in row-echelon form, after which back-substitution can find the variables? It is named for the mathematician associated with the story of summing the integers from 1 to 100 as a schoolboy.

The cross product is defined in this many dimensions and in three dimensions, but not in other dimensions. A regular polygon with this many sides has interior angles of about 128.6°, and the sum of two standard dice is most likely to equal it. What number is it?
The number Seven is central to Euler’s famous bridge-crossing puzzle, which asked whether a route could cross every bridge exactly once. In which Prussian city was the puzzle set?

For any triangle, dividing each side length by the value of the trigonometric function that gives the vertical coordinate on the unit circle at its opposite angle produces the same quotient. What theorem states this relationship?

The Law of Sines says that a triangle’s side-to-opposite-angle-sine ratios share one common value. That value is twice the radius of the circle passing through all three vertices; what circle measurement does it represent?
In graph theory, vertices receive labels from a shared palette, with the endpoints of every edge required to have different labels. What is this type of vertex assignment called?

Given a proper vertex coloring of a graph, what is the smallest number of colors that can be used while ensuring that adjacent vertices have different colors? This graph invariant is commonly written as χ(G).
A paper band becomes this surface when one end is given a half-twist before the ends are joined. It has only one side and is non-orientable; what is it called?

A Möbius strip is a classic example of a surface whose orientation cannot be defined consistently across the whole shape. What branch of mathematics studies spaces like this and properties preserved under continuous deformation?
This regular quadrilateral has four equal sides and four right angles. It is classified as both a rectangle and a rhombus; what plane figure is it?
In a square, drawing a diagonal creates a right triangle whose two legs are equal sides of the figure. Which theorem can be used to derive the diagonal’s length from those sides?

In plane geometry, this six-sided polygon has equal sides and angles, an interior-angle sum of 720°, and can tile the plane with repeated copies. Its three longest diagonals divide its interior into six equilateral triangles. What is the polygon?
A Regular Hexagon can be repeated edge to edge across the Euclidean plane with no gaps or overlaps. What is the name of this repeating arrangement of congruent polygons?

In topology and geometry, what quantity describes how many independent directions or degrees of extent a space has? It distinguishes a line, a plane, and ordinary space by assigning them one, two, and three, respectively.
In geometric measure theory, this refinement can assign a non-integer value to a fractal by analyzing coverings with sets of arbitrarily small diameter. What refinement of dimension is it?

In Euclid’s account of plane geometry, one axiom says that when a transversal cuts two straight lines and the interior angles on one side total less than two right angles, the two lines will meet on that side if extended. What is the name of this foundational axiom?

The Parallel Postulate is denied in one system where, through a point outside a given line, infinitely many distinct lines can avoid intersecting that line; the Poincaré disk is a standard model of this system. What is this system called?
In number theory, what are pairs of numbers greater than 1 called when each is divisible only by 1 and itself, and their difference is exactly 2? The pairs 3 and 5, and 11 and 13, are examples.
Which English number theorist received the 2022 Fields Medal for work including major contributions to prime gaps? He built on Yitang Zhang’s research related to twin primes.
In number theory, an integer belongs to this class if dividing it by two leaves a remainder of zero. Its parity is therefore described as zero.

This unproved assertion in additive number theory says that every even number greater than 2 can be expressed as the sum of two primes. It is named after a German mathematician who proposed it in a letter to Leonhard Euler.

In the focus-based definition of a conic, points are selected so their distance from a fixed point bears a constant ratio to their perpendicular distance from a fixed line. For a parabola, that ratio is one; what is the fixed line called?
For a parabola, the directrix is parallel to a special chord through the focus that is perpendicular to the axis of symmetry. The chord’s endpoints lie on the curve; what is it called?

Rational numbers can be expressed as quotients of integers, and this arithmetic operation determines how many times one quantity is contained in another. It is the inverse of multiplication; what operation is described?
In ordinary arithmetic, division by this denominator is undefined for a nonzero numerator, since no quotient multiplied by the denominator can recover that numerator. Which number is the denominator?

Starting from an initial estimate for a zero of a function, this iterative algorithm uses the tangent line at that estimate to predict a better one, then repeats the process. What is this algorithm called?
For a single-variable equation, each correction in Newton's method uses the function's value divided by the slope of its graph at the current estimate. What calculus quantity gives that local slope?

In abstract algebra, this structure consists of a set and an operation satisfying closure, an identity rule, an inverse rule, and a rule that makes the placement of parentheses irrelevant. What is this structure called?
For a group operation, combining three elements gives the same result whether the first two are combined first or the last two are combined first. What property of the operation does this describe?

In this stochastic process, once the current state is known, earlier history does not affect the probability distribution of the next state. Its possible states can be shown as vertices in a directed graph with weighted transitions. What is this process called?

For a Markov chain with a finite set of states, what square array lists the probability of moving from each current state to each possible next state? Each row gives a probability distribution over the possible next states.

In plane geometry, the area of a parallelogram can be found by multiplying the lengths of its diagonals by the sine of the angle between them, then applying this coefficient. The same coefficient appears in the area formula for a triangle given two side lengths and their included angle. What fraction is it?

One-half appears as the coefficient in an area formula using the lengths of a four-sided figure’s diagonals and the sine of the angle between them. This figure has two pairs of opposite sides that are parallel. What is the figure?
Which positive integer is the smallest odd prime? It also divides every base-ten integer whose digits add up to a multiple of that integer.

Four-digit numbers made from two 7s and two 8s have a digit sum of 30, so the topic 3 divides each of them. Two examples, 7887 and 8778, read the same in either direction; what is the term for a number with this property?
What mathematical structure has intricate detail at arbitrarily small scales and often exhibits similar patterns under magnification? Its scaling behavior can be described by a non-integer dimension.

This fractal is defined by the complex parameters for which repeatedly applying z → z² + c, starting from z = 0, produces a bounded sequence. Its boundary includes a large cardioid and smaller circular bulbs, with intricate detail revealed by magnification.
This fractal is built by repeatedly adding an outward triangular bump to every side of an equilateral triangle. The resulting boundary has infinite length even though the enclosed area is finite.

Unlike the familiar x-, y-, and z-values of rectangular space, this three-dimensional framework locates a point using its distance from the origin and two angles, commonly measured relative to the positive z-axis and around that axis. What is this framework called?

In the physics convention for the spherical coordinate system, one angle is measured from the positive z-axis and the other sweeps around that axis in the xy-plane. Which Greek letter commonly denotes the angle that sweeps around the axis?

For a differentiable map from n input variables to m outputs, this m-by-n array has the partial derivative of output i with respect to input j in row i, column j. At a point, multiplying it by a small input change gives a first-order estimate of the output change. What is this array called?
In a two-variable coordinate transformation, this scalar is computed from the Jacobian matrix, and its absolute value tells how much a tiny patch’s area is locally scaled. What is this scalar called?

In plane geometry, what is the name for a closed two-dimensional figure whose boundary is made from a finite number of straight line segments joined end to end? Triangles and quadrilaterals are familiar examples.
Unlike a Polygon, which lies in a plane, what is the simplest three-dimensional polytope, bounded by four triangular faces and shaped like a triangular pyramid?

For a differentiable function of two variables, suppose both first partial derivatives vanish at the same location, while nearby values rise in one direction and fall in another, so that location is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. What is this type of stationary feature called?

In multivariable calculus, determining whether a saddle point occurs at a critical point often involves evaluating the square array whose entries are all the function’s second partial derivatives. What is this array called?
In Hamilton’s number system, these are the three distinct non-real basis elements, each of which squares to −1; their cyclic product also equals −1. What are they collectively called?
answer: Quaternion units i, j, and k

question: The quaternion system built from the Quaternion units i, j, and k was devised by this Irish mathematician, who famously carved its defining relation into a bridge in Dublin in 1843. Who was he?

In geometric packing, this quantity is the greatest number of congruent, non-overlapping circles that can touch one congruent central circle; in the plane, its value is six. What is this quantity called?

In the planar Kissing Number problem, congruent circles are arranged around a fixed congruent central circle so that each outer circle touches it and no two circles overlap. What is the greatest number of outer circles that can touch the central one?
In three-dimensional topology, this composite object is formed by taking the connected sum of a trefoil with its reflected image, combining factors of opposite handedness. What is its standard name?
The square knot is equivalent, under ambient deformation in three-dimensional space, to its reflected version. What is this mirror-related property called?
It is the first and smallest positive integer, and multiplying any number by it leaves that number unchanged. By convention, it is neither prime nor composite. What number is this?
In arithmetic, multiplying any number by one leaves that number unchanged. What is the name for the element that has this role in multiplication?
In the base-two number system used in digital computing, the symbols are 0 and one; these commonly represent the off and on states. What is this number system called?
Which quadrilateral has two pairs of congruent adjacent sides, with the sides in each pair meeting at a shared vertex? What is its natural geometric name?

In a kite, the diagonal joining the vertices where the congruent side pairs meet crosses the other diagonal at a right angle and divides it into two equal segments. What is that diagonal, in relation to the other one, called?

A result published in 1837 says that infinitely many terms of a sequence are prime if it begins with a positive integer, repeatedly adds a fixed positive integer, and the starting value and increment have no common divisor greater than 1. What is this theorem naturally called?

In the standard analytic proof of Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions, these periodic, completely multiplicative functions modulo an integer are used to distinguish residue classes and define associated L-functions. What are they called?
In plane geometry, this quadrilateral has two pairs of opposite sides that are parallel. Its opposite sides are also equal in length, and its diagonals bisect each other. What is its standard name?
For a parallelogram, an area formula uses the lengths of both diagonals and the sine of the angle between them. What numerical factor multiplies that product?
In a fraction, the term below the fraction bar indicates how many equal parts make up the whole. What is this term called?
When a complex number appears as a denominator, multiplying the numerator and denominator by its complex conjugate can make the denominator real. What is the complex conjugate of 5 + i?

In combinatorics, what is the name for a set of vertices and edges whose vertices can be divided into two disjoint independent sets, with every edge joining vertices from opposite sets? Equivalently, its vertices can be assigned two colors so that adjacent vertices receive different colors.

Which named graph is the complete bipartite graph with three vertices in each part and all nine possible edges between the parts? It is one of the two graphs whose subdivisions characterize nonplanar graphs in Kuratowski’s theorem, alongside K₅.

At an input a, a function has this property when its value is defined, the limit as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals the function’s value at a. This property is also necessary for the function to be differentiable at that point. What is it?

When a function has continuity throughout a closed interval, this theorem guarantees that it attains every output between its outputs at the two endpoints somewhere in the interval. What theorem is this?
A proof method for claims over integers begins by verifying a chosen starting case, then shows that truth at an arbitrary value k forces truth at k+1. What is this technique called?

Within mathematical induction, the proof temporarily assumes a claim holds for an arbitrary value k in range, then uses that assumption to prove it holds for k+1. What is this temporary assumption called?

This topological invariant of a polyhedron is calculated by subtracting the number of edges from the number of vertices, then adding the number of faces. For every convex polyhedron, its value is 2. What is this invariant called?

For a connected planar graph, count the unbounded region as a face and compute the Euler characteristic by subtracting edges from vertices, then adding faces. What value does the Euler characteristic always have?

In an expression formed by adding terms that are coefficients times nonnegative integer powers of a variable, this quantity is the greatest exponent attached to a term with a nonzero coefficient, even if some intermediate powers are missing. It also limits how many distinct complex roots the expression can have. What is this quantity called?

The degree of a polynomial is central to this theorem, which says that every nonconstant polynomial has exactly as many complex roots as its degree when roots are counted with multiplicity. What is the theorem called?
