Which real-valued function sends every input to its nonnegative distance from zero, using the rule −x for negative inputs and x for nonnegative inputs? Its graph is continuous at the origin but has a corner there, where the left- and right-hand slopes differ.
For the absolute value function, changing an input x to −x leaves the output unchanged, and its graph is mirrored across the y-axis. What classification describes functions with this property?
Which conic section is formed by the graph of a quadratic equation and is characterized by an eccentricity exactly equal to one?
In a Parabola, the latus rectum is parallel to this line, which lies on the opposite side of the vertex from the focus. The vertex is midway between this line and the focus; what is the line called?
In quaternion multiplication, the units i, j, and k multiply together to produce this number. In the complex number system, i is defined as a square root of it; what number is it?
Negative one is the product of three units in this extension of the complex numbers, which includes j and k and has noncommutative multiplication. What is this number system called?
In mechanics, what operation accumulates a quantity with respect to elapsed duration rather than position? Applied to power, it gives the change in energy.
In Lagrangian mechanics, a time integral of the Lagrangian along a system’s history gives this scalar quantity. Its stationary value under small variations leads to the equations of motion.

Francis Guthrie raised a famous planar-map problem in 1852: could each region be assigned one of a uniformly bounded set of labels, with regions sharing a boundary segment assigned different labels? Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken resolved it in 1976; what theorem is named for this problem?
The 1976 demonstration of the Four-Color Theorem became a landmark because extensive case-checking relied on a machine rather than solely on hand calculations. What kind of demonstration was this?

For a circle, multiplying the two directed lengths measured from one fixed location to its two intersections with any line through that location gives an invariant, independent of the chosen line. What theorem states that this invariant is the same for every such line?

When a line from an external location touches a circle at T, while a second line from the same location crosses the circle at A and B, the Power of a Point Theorem says the square of the first distance equals the product of the distances to the two crossings. What is this particular relationship commonly called?

This positive integer comes immediately after seven and before nine. It is also the atomic number of oxygen and the number of valence electrons in a noble-gas atom with a full outer shell. What is the number?
Eight is the number of carbon atoms in the alkane whose name supplies the label for a gasoline measure of resistance to engine knocking. What is this measure called?

This triangle theorem extends the right-triangle relationship to oblique triangles: given two side lengths and the angle between them, it determines the third side. Its equation reduces to a² + b² = c² when that angle is 90 degrees. What is the theorem called?
In the Law of Cosines, the input is measured at the vertex where the two known sides meet, not at a vertex opposite either side. What is this input called relative to those sides?
When two quantities vary so that doubling one halves the other, their product remains fixed. What is this type of relationship called?

In inverse proportionality, a blackbody’s absolute temperature and the wavelength at which its emission curve peaks change oppositely, with their product fixed. What named law describes this relationship?
In plane geometry, this is the longest chord of a circle because it passes through the center. Its length is exactly twice the circle’s radius; what is this segment called?

In the classic result involving a circle’s Diameter, a triangle inscribed in the circle with that segment as one side has a right angle at the opposite vertex. What theorem, named for an ancient Greek mathematician, states this?
In plane geometry, this quadrilateral has four sides of equal length, though its angles do not all have to be right angles. What is its standard name?
A rhombus has two diagonals, and each diagonal splits the corner opening at each of its endpoints into two equal parts. What is each diagonal called in relation to those corner openings?

Which enormously large but finite integer served as an upper bound in a Ramsey-theoretic problem about forcing a monochromatic square in a two-coloring of edges between vertices of a high-dimensional hypercube? It was regarded at the time as the largest number used in a serious mathematical proof.

A 1977 Scientific American column helped popularize Graham's number and described it as the largest number then used in a serious mathematical proof. Which mathematics writer and puzzle columnist wrote the column?

Born in Warsaw and later working in France and the United States, this mathematician used computer experiments to study rough forms in nature and developed a new geometry for describing them. He coined a name for structures with intricate detail at arbitrarily fine scales; who was he?

Benoît Mandelbrot argued that coastlines, mountains, and clouds are better described by geometry that captures roughness across many scales than by smooth Euclidean forms. What term did he coin for structures of this kind, exemplified by the recursively constructed Cantor set?
For a function defined at both x and −x, those two inputs always produce the same output. Its graph is unchanged when reflected across a coordinate axis; what type of function is this?
An even function assigns equal outputs to each pair of opposite inputs, such as x and −x. Which vertical line through the origin is the mirror line that leaves its graph unchanged?
In integer arithmetic, it identifies numbers that cannot be paired completely into groups of two; for functions, it is the property expressed by f(-x) = -f(x). What is this property called?
For a graph, Oddness means that a half-turn about the point (0, 0) leaves the graph unchanged. What is this geometric relationship called?

Which irrational constant is the positive solution to x² − x − 1 = 0, approximately 1.618? It is also defined by dividing a segment so that the whole length divided by the longer part equals the longer part divided by the shorter part.
The golden ratio’s segment construction is described in this classical Greek geometry treatise as a division in “extreme and mean ratio,” rather than by its modern name. Which work is it?

In Book IX, Proposition 20 of the *Elements*, an argument considers a finite list of numbers divisible only by themselves and one, then forms one more than their product. What theorem establishes that this family has no largest member?
answer: Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes

question: In Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes, multiplying a proposed finite list of primes and adding one creates an integer that need not itself be prime. What kind of factor of that integer must be absent from the original list?
Which set consists of values expressible as the quotient of two integers, provided the denominator is nonzero? It includes integers, fractions, and terminating or repeating decimals.

In the definition of Rational Numbers, what arithmetic operation forms the quotient of one integer by another when the second integer is nonzero? It is the inverse of multiplication, and attempting it with zero as the divisor is undefined.
In geometry, the four-dimensional analogue of a square and a cube is a regular polytope whose boundary is made of eight cubic cells. What is this shape called?

A regular 4-polytope dual to a Hypercube has 16 tetrahedral facets, one corresponding to each vertex of the original, and eight vertices corresponding to its cubic facets. What is this dual polytope commonly called?
A positive integer greater than 1 that can be written as a product of smaller positive integers has a nontrivial factorization. What is this kind of number called?

A key result about the factor structure of every composite number states that each integer greater than 1 can be expressed as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors. What is this result commonly called?
In classical logic, this principle says that for any proposition P, either P is true or its negation is true. It is commonly written as P ∨ ¬P. What is the principle called?

Unlike classical systems that accept the Law of the Excluded Middle for every proposition, this constructive framework does not accept the unrestricted schema without proof of one side or the other. What is this framework called?

In calculus, this function or value describes the instantaneous rate at which another function changes. Geometrically, it gives the slope of the original function’s graph at a particular input. What is it called?

At a point where a curve is differentiable, the derivative gives the slope of the straight geometric object that passes through that point and locally matches the curve’s direction. What is that object called?
In number theory, this property applies to two integers whose greatest common divisor is 1, meaning they share no prime factor. What is the name of this property?
Which iterative procedure can test coprimality by repeatedly dividing and replacing a pair of integers with the smaller integer and the remainder, until the remainder is zero?

In Euclidean plane geometry, this relationship describes distinct coplanar lines that never meet and maintain the same direction. In slope-intercept form, it is indicated for two nonvertical lines when their m-values are equal. What is this geometric relationship called?

In coordinate geometry, parallelism between two nonvertical lines can be tested by comparing the coefficient that describes each line’s rate of rise over run. In the form y = mx + b, what is this coefficient called?
Consider an ordered sequence in which every adjacent pair differs by the same fixed amount, whether that amount is positive, negative, or zero. What is the standard name for this kind of sequence?
In an arithmetic progression such as 2, 5, 8, 11, subtracting each term from the next always gives the same value. What is the standard name for that fixed additive change?

In mathematics, these collections have no finite cardinality. They may be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers, or they may be too large to be listed in such a sequence. What is the standard name for them?

In discussions of Infinite Sets, which German mathematician used a diagonal argument to prove that the real numbers cannot be listed in a sequence and are therefore more numerous than the natural numbers? He is also credited as the founder of set theory.

This branch of mathematics assigns numerical values from 0 to 1 to the likelihood of events, with 0 representing impossibility and 1 certainty. It provides a formal way to analyze random outcomes and quantify uncertainty. What is this field?
Which French mathematician, whose research applies Probability to phase transitions and other problems in mathematical physics, received the 2022 Fields Medal for work on critical phenomena?

This average is found by summing the inverses of a set of nonzero values, dividing by the number of values, and then inverting that result. For a journey made up of equal-distance legs, it gives the average speed across the whole journey; what is this average called?

In the formula for the harmonic mean, each nonzero observation is first changed to a value that, when multiplied by the original observation, gives 1; those transformed values are then summed. What is the standard name for the transformed value of an observation?
Which natural number is both the atomic number of beryllium and the number of sides in a square? The same count appears in the Standard Model’s number of fundamental interactions.
A circuit associated with Four arranges four resistors in a diamond, using a detector across one diagonal to determine an unknown resistance. What is this circuit called?
In a conic section, what is the name of the chord that passes through a focus and meets the major axis—or, for a hyperbola, the transverse axis—at a right angle?
The latus rectum of this conic is a focal chord perpendicular to its major axis. Every point on the curve has the same sum of distances to its two distinct foci; what conic is it?

In this mathematical procedure, vertices or edges receive labels under constraints; for instance, endpoints joined by an edge cannot share a label. It also underlies the result that planar maps need no more than four labels; what is the procedure called?

A landmark result in graph coloring says that any planar map can be labeled so neighboring regions differ, regardless of how many regions the map contains. First proved with computer assistance by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken, what is the theorem called?

In plane geometry, this equilateral and equiangular polygon has five sides, and each of its interior angles measures 108°. Its diagonals are longer than its sides and all have the same length. What is this shape?
For a regular pentagon, the ratio of a diagonal’s length to a side’s length is the positive solution of x² − x − 1 = 0. What is this number, commonly represented by φ?

Bézout’s identity says that this value for a set of integers can be written as an integer linear combination of those integers. It is also the number used to simplify a fraction by dividing both its numerator and denominator.

This procedure repeatedly divides a pair of integers and replaces them with the divisor and the remainder until the remainder is zero. The last nonzero remainder gives the greatest common divisor of the original pair; what is the procedure called?

A positive integer belongs to this class when its proper positive divisors sum exactly to itself; 6 is its smallest member, since 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. What is the natural name of this number-theoretic concept?

For a perfect number, mathematicians give a particular name to the sum of all its positive divisors except the number itself. That sum equals the number in the defining condition; what is this divisor-sum called?
When 2ᵖ − 1 is prime, 2ᵖ⁻¹(2ᵖ − 1) is a perfect number; conversely, every even perfect number has this form. What is the name of the theorem establishing this relationship?

This ancient prime-finding procedure begins with a list of integers and repeatedly crosses out multiples of each smallest unmarked candidate, leaving primes behind. Named for a Greek mathematician from Cyrene who worked in Alexandria, what is the procedure?

In the Sieve of Eratosthenes, multiples of each newly identified prime are crossed off because they belong to a particular class of integers. What are integers greater than 1 that have a divisor other than 1 and themselves called?

Which statistical procedure compares observed counts in categorical groups with expected counts by adding, across categories, each observed-minus-expected difference multiplied by itself and divided by its expected count? The total is then evaluated against a distribution associated with a Greek letter.

In an ordinary goodness-of-fit chi-squared test with no parameters estimated, what quantity is one less than the number of categories? It also specifies the number of independent values that can vary under the test’s constraints.
What four-dimensional number system extends the complex numbers with units conventionally called i, j, and k, and has noncommutative multiplication?
The discovery of quaternions is traditionally linked to an 1843 walk along Dublin’s Royal Canal, when this Irish mathematician inscribed their defining relation on Brougham Bridge. Who was he?
Which special function is defined for real x as (2/√π) times the integral of e^(−t²) from 0 to x, and is used to express the standard normal cumulative distribution function?

The error function appears in a closed-form expression for the cumulative distribution function of this continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped distribution. The central limit theorem identifies it as the limiting law for suitably standardized sums of many independent observations; what is this distribution?
What branch of mathematics studies points, lines, shapes, areas, distances, and objects in two or three dimensions? Its subjects include figures such as circles and triangles.

Within Geometry, what statement says that through a point outside a given line, exactly one line can be drawn that does not intersect the given line? Its status as one of Euclid’s foundational assumptions distinguishes the system where triangle angles sum to two right angles from hyperbolic alternatives.

In any triangle, this associated circle passes through the three side midpoints, the three feet of the altitudes, and the midpoints of the segments joining the vertices to the orthocenter. What is this circle called?

For a triangle whose orthocenter and circumcenter are distinct, the center of the Nine-Point Circle is the midpoint of the segment joining those two points. What is the conventional name for the straight path through them?

Which ancient Greek mathematical treatise by Euclid is arranged in thirteen books and builds from definitions, postulates, and common notions? It systematizes geometry while also treating topics such as proportion and number theory.
In Euclid’s Elements, which famous result is proved in Book I, Proposition 47, relating the areas of the squares on the legs of a right triangle to the square on its hypotenuse?

For a discrete random variable, this quantity is calculated by multiplying each possible outcome by its probability and summing the results. For a continuous variable with density f(x), it is the integral of x f(x), and it is also known as the first moment. What is this probability-weighted average?
For a fair six-sided die numbered 1 through 6, Expected value weights each face equally and averages the possible outcomes. What number does it give, even though no single roll can produce it?

The sequence begins 0, 1, 4, 9, and 16, and each term is obtained by multiplying an integer by itself. The differences between consecutive terms are successive odd numbers. What are these numbers called?

In the study of Square Numbers, this theorem states that every positive integer can be represented as a sum of integer squares using a fixed upper bound on the number of terms, independent of the integer represented. Its namesake was born in Turin and later worked in Berlin and Paris. What is the theorem called?
In discussions of Square Numbers, what term describes a positive integer whose prime factorization contains no repeated prime factor, or equivalently, that has no square divisor greater than 1?
What is the geometric process of covering an entire flat surface with repeated shapes so that there are no gaps or overlaps? Regular octagons combined with squares are one familiar example.
In Tiling the Plane, which five-sided polygon has equal sides and angles of 108 degrees, and a diagonal-to-side ratio equal to the golden ratio?

In probability, what theorem says that as more independent observations are collected, their average approaches the distribution’s expected value? Its weak and strong forms differ in the mode of convergence, but both describe the stabilization of averages over repeated sampling.

The Law of Large Numbers describes what happens to this statistic as more independent observations are collected. It is computed by summing the observed values and dividing by the number of observations, and it approaches the population expectation.

For a number written as a + bi, this related number keeps a unchanged and reverses the sign of the coefficient of i. Multiplying the two numbers gives the real quantity a² + b². What is the related number called?

To remove the imaginary part from a denominator of 5 + i, a standard fraction-simplification step multiplies the numerator and denominator by its complex conjugate. Which binomial is used as the multiplier?

In topology, this object is formed by embedding a circle in three-dimensional Euclidean space, and it is studied up to continuous deformation without cutting or allowing strands to pass through one another. Invariants such as the Alexander polynomial help distinguish its different forms. What is this object called?

For a mathematical knot, this invariant is a Laurent expression derived from a presentation of the knot group's relations. It remains unchanged under ambient isotopy and can distinguish the trefoil from the unknot. What is it called?

For a binary operation on three inputs, this property says that changing [?m(a ★ b) ★ c[?m to [?m a ★ (b ★ c)[?m leaves the result unchanged, with the inputs kept in the same order. What is this property called?

In abstract algebra, the associative property is one of three standard requirements for this structure, alongside an identity element and inverses for every element. What structure consists of a set equipped with an operation satisfying those requirements?

In algebra and linear algebra, this is the mathematical partner that undoes an operation: composing it with a function returns the identity, while multiplying a square matrix by it also gives the identity matrix. What is this general term?

A function’s inverse can be defined over its full domain only when different inputs never produce the same output. On a graph, this condition is tested by checking that every horizontal line intersects it at most once; what property is this?

In this indirect method, a mathematician temporarily assumes the claim being proved is false, then uses accepted reasoning to reach an impossibility, such as a statement and its negation both holding. What is this approach called?
In classical logic, proof by contradiction is commonly justified by a principle that says for any proposition P, either P is true or its negation is true. What is the name of this principle?

In Euclidean plane geometry, what is the name of a polygon with three straight sides and three vertices whose interior angles total 180 degrees? Its area can be found by taking half the product of a chosen base and its perpendicular height.
Within a triangle, what is the common intersection point of its three medians, each connecting a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side? It also serves as the triangle’s balance point.
In a triangle, each altitude passes through a vertex and is perpendicular to the line containing the opposite side. What is the name of the point at which the three altitudes concur?

Which classical named result gives a triangle’s area using only its side lengths a, b, and c, by first setting s = (a + b + c)/2 and then taking the square root of s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)? It does not require a separately supplied altitude.

For a non-equilateral triangle, what is the name of the straight path containing its centroid, circumcenter, and orthocenter? In a typical case, the centroid lies between the other two centers, one-third of the way from the circumcenter to the orthocenter.
A polygon’s adjacent sides meet at one of these points, and the same term names a dot representing an object in a graph, where edges encode connections. What is this shared mathematical term?

In graph theory, a vertex can represent an airport, and its position in a drawing is irrelevant as long as its connections are preserved. What term describes a vertex with no incident edges, meaning its degree is zero?

Which sixth-century BCE Greek thinker grew up on an Aegean island and founded a disciplined religious community whose members connected number with the order of the world? His name later became attached to a rule about the sides of right triangles, though reliable evidence that he proved it is lacking.

Pythagoras of Samos is associated by later tradition with a rule for right triangles, although Babylonians knew the underlying relation earlier. What theorem states that the square on a right triangle’s hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on its other two sides?
Each altitude of a triangle passes through a vertex and is perpendicular to the opposite side or its extension. What is the name of the point where the triangle’s three altitudes intersect?
When a triangle has one corner measuring 90 degrees, its orthocenter coincides with that corner. What is this kind of corner called?

Every point on this closed conic section has distances to two fixed points whose sum is constant. Its major and minor axes meet at its center, and the circle is a special case. What is this shape called?
For an ellipse, this numerical measure of shape is zero in the circular special case and increases toward—but remains below—one as the curve becomes more elongated. What is this measure called?
This set combines rational and irrational values and corresponds to every point on a continuous line. It is uncountable and is conventionally denoted by a double-struck R; what is it called?

The real numbers cannot be listed in a sequence that pairs each one with a natural number. This proof technique supposes such a list of decimal expansions exists, then constructs a new decimal whose nth digit differs from the nth digit of the corresponding listed expansion; what is it called?

The real numbers have this order property: every nonempty subset that has an upper bound has a least upper bound. This property distinguishes them from the rational numbers and is central to their rigorous construction; what is it called?
Which meromorphic function extends the factorial to non-integer and complex inputs, takes the value (n−1)! at each positive integer n, and satisfies F(z+1)=zF(z)?

The Gamma Function appears in the identity B(x,y)=Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x+y). For positive x and y, the same two-variable function is given by the integral from 0 to 1 of t^(x−1)(1−t)^(y−1); what is its standard name?

Which function maps a nonnegative integer n to the product of all positive integers from 1 through n, with its value at zero defined as 1? In combinatorics, its value at n also counts the arrangements of n distinct objects.
For the factorial function, the product defining 0! has no factors and is conventionally assigned the value 1. What is the standard algebraic name for a product over a collection with zero members?

For large inputs to the factorial function, what asymptotic estimate uses an expression beginning with √(2πn)(n/e)^n? It is commonly used to estimate factorial growth without multiplying every integer in the product.

In linear algebra, two rectangular arrays can be combined by pairing each row of the first with each column of the second and summing the products of corresponding entries. The resulting array takes its row count from the first factor and its column count from the second; what is this operation called?
A left factor has dimensions m × n, and a right factor has dimensions n × p. In matrix multiplication, what are the dimensions of the resulting matrix?

Active in Egypt around 300 BCE, this ancient Greek mathematician organized geometry into a deductive system built from definitions, postulates, and propositions. His Elements also contains a proof that infinitely many primes exist. Who was he?

In Euclid of Alexandria’s axiomatic geometry, one famous fifth assertion concerns a line and a point outside it: exactly one line through that point never intersects the given line. What is this fifth assertion commonly called?

Euclid of Alexandria described a number-theoretic procedure that repeatedly divides two positive integers, then continues with the divisor and remainder until the remainder is zero. What is this method for finding the greatest common divisor called?

The expression n²+n+41 gives a number divisible only by 1 and itself for each of its first forty positive integer inputs, a pattern noted by an 18th-century Swiss mathematician. What is this famous formula known as?
Euler's Prime-Generating Polynomial is represented by n²+n+41, whose highest exponent is 2 and whose graph is a parabola. What is the standard degree-based name for this type of polynomial?

What mathematical function reverses exponentiation by finding the exponent to which a specified base must be raised to produce a given value? For instance, it solves for x in the relationship b^x = y.

In a sorted array, what procedure compares the target with the middle entry and repeatedly discards the half that cannot contain it? The number of comparisons grows in proportion to the logarithm of the array’s length.

He estimated Earth’s circumference by comparing the Sun’s angle at noon in Syene and Alexandria with the distance between the cities. He also devised a procedure for identifying prime numbers by eliminating their multiples; who was this ancient Greek mathematician?

For his measurement of Earth’s circumference, Eratosthenes of Cyrene compared Syene’s nearly overhead midsummer Sun with the shadow angle at the Egyptian city where he served as chief librarian. Which city supplied the second observation?

Area is characterized by length squared, while volume is characterized by length cubed; these descriptions help determine whether the units in a proposed equation are consistent. What attribute of a measurable quantity do these powers describe?

To test a proposed equation, physicists compare the physical dimensions of the quantities on each side and check whether their fundamental-unit powers agree. What is this consistency-checking method called?

This German mathematician and astronomer used least-squares methods to predict the orbit of Ceres after its discovery in 1801. He also proved that a regular 17-sided polygon can be constructed with ruler and compass. Who was he?

Carl Friedrich Gauss published this landmark Latin treatise in 1801, devoting much of it to number theory and giving a systematic treatment of congruences and quadratic reciprocity. What is the title of the work?
This term names a rearrangement in which every element of a set appears exactly once, or, formally, a bijection from the set to itself. What is it?
For a set of n distinct objects, the number of possible permutations is written n!; this notation represents the product of all positive integers from 1 through n. What is this function called?
The complete collection of permutations of an n-element set, with composition as its operation, is commonly denoted S_n. What is this structure called?
A permutation of a set can leave some elements mapped to themselves, but a particular kind leaves none in their original positions. What is this kind of permutation called?

What class of numbers consists of values one less than a power of two, where the exponent has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself? The family is named for a 17th-century French cleric and mathematician who studied these numbers.
Mersenne primes take their name from which 17th-century French cleric, mathematician, and music theorist, known for corresponding with many leading scholars of his era?

For an equation built from nonnegative integer powers of a variable, these are the values that make its left-hand side equal zero. They can be found even when no single formula works for every general equation of degree five or higher; what are these values called?
In the study of Polynomial roots, this result rules out a universal formula using radicals for solving every general polynomial equation of degree five or higher. What theorem is it?
Which measure of central tendency is calculated by adding every value in a data set and dividing by the number of values? It is commonly denoted x̄ for a sample and μ for an entire population.

When a data set contains unusually high or low observations, the arithmetic mean can be pulled toward them. Which measure of center, found by ordering the observations and taking the middle value (or the midpoint of the two middle values), is typically less affected by those extremes?

Which branch of mathematics studies equations and operations involving numbers and variables, and also includes the study of vector spaces and abstract structures? Its elementary problems often ask a student to isolate an unknown in an equation such as 3x + 4 = 0.

In the history of Algebra, which ninth-century Persian mathematician wrote a foundational treatise whose title includes the phrase al-jabr wa’l-muqabala (“completion and balancing”)? His Latinized name also gave English the word “algorithm.”

For a square matrix, this scalar is nonzero exactly when the matrix has an inverse. Its absolute value gives the factor by which the associated linear transformation scales area in two dimensions and volume in higher dimensions. What is this quantity?

For a square linear system with a nonzero determinant, this named method finds each variable using a ratio of determinants, replacing one column of the coefficient matrix with the constants column in the numerator. What is this method?

A 19th-century German number theorist proved that every arithmetic progression with coprime first term and common difference contains infinitely many primes. He is also credited with formulating a counting principle that forces at least two objects into one container when there are more objects than containers. Identify the mathematician.

Johann Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet described a counting argument in which distributing more objects than containers guarantees that at least one container receives two or more objects. What is this principle called?
This French mathematician’s 1637 work helped connect algebraic equations with geometric curves, and his name later became attached to a familiar coordinate system. Who was he?
In 1637, René Descartes published this mathematical treatise as part of the Discourse on the Method. It presented influential ways to use algebra to investigate geometric curves; what is its title?
Two figures are related when a slide, turn, or flip can place one exactly over the other, preserving every corresponding side length and angle measure. What is this relationship called?

In geometric congruence, slides, turns, and flips preserve all lengths and angle measures. Which rigid motion maps points to the opposite side of a fixed line, with that line halfway between each point and its image?

For a normal distribution, this statistical guideline estimates the proportions of observations falling within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean, following the sequence 68%, 95%, and 99.7%. What is this guideline called?
Under the Empirical Rule, approximately what percentage of values in a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean?

In calculus and mathematical analysis, this quantity describes the value approached by a function as its input nears a chosen point, or by a sequence as its index grows. It concerns nearby behavior, so the function need not be defined at that point or take that value there. What is this quantity?

For a quotient whose limit yields an indeterminate form such as 0/0 or ∞/∞, this calculus rule can—when its hypotheses are met—help evaluate it by differentiating the numerator and denominator and taking a new limit. What is this rule?

For a self-similar pattern, this quantity measures how completely it fills space and can be non-integer, unlike the whole-number values associated with a line, a plane, and a solid. What is this measure called?

One precise way to define fractal dimension considers coverings of a set by pieces whose sizes shrink toward zero, then finds the critical exponent at which a related measure changes from infinite to zero. Named for the German mathematician who introduced it, what is this dimension?

This continuous probability model is symmetric about a central value that is simultaneously its mean, median, and mode. Its spread is specified by its variance, and its density has the familiar bell-shaped form. What is this distribution?

The normal distribution’s density is associated with this German mathematician, who devised a straightedge-and-compass construction for a regular 17-sided polygon. His name is also attached to an elimination method used in solving systems of linear equations. Who was he?

In its classical form, this theorem says that standardized sums of independent, identically distributed observations with finite mean and variance approach the normal distribution as the sample size grows. What is this foundational result in probability?
These numbers cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers, and the square root of two is a familiar example. What are they called?

Irrational numbers such as the square root of two cannot be written as ratios of integers, while ancient Babylonian arithmetic used a different numeral system. A clay tablet records fifteen Pythagorean triples in that system, whose legacy is often linked to the 360-degree circle; what is the system called?
Unlike an ellipse, this conic section has eccentricity greater than 1 and consists of two separate branches. In a standard centered coordinate equation, its squared terms have opposite signs.

For a hyperbola centered at the origin with its transverse axis along the x-axis, the branches approach two diagonal lines as they extend outward. If the equation is x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, what are those lines called?
This plane curve consists of all points at a fixed distance from a central point. Among the conic sections, it has eccentricity zero and circumference 2πr. What is this shape?
In a circle, every point on the boundary is the same distance from the center. In the equation x² + y² = r² for a circle centered at the origin, what measurement does r represent?
In a circle, a straight segment joining two points on the boundary is a chord. What is the special chord that passes through the center and is twice the radius?

Starting with an equilateral triangle, this fractal is formed by repeatedly replacing the middle third of each side with an outward-pointing equilateral triangular bump. What is the resulting figure called?

In the Koch snowflake, each iteration replaces every boundary segment with four segments that are each one-third as long. The enclosed area remains finite as the construction continues, but what happens to the total boundary length?

What three-dimensional solid consists of all points at a fixed distance from one central point? Its volume is four-thirds pi times the radius cubed, and every plane through its center cuts it in a circle.
For a sphere, what is the name of the central point from which every point on its surface lies at the same distance? That distance is called the radius.

Which ancient Greek mathematician studied the sphere and famously requested that a sphere and a cylinder be depicted on his tomb? He also showed that the sphere’s volume is two-thirds the volume of its circumscribed cylinder.

In calculus, this task seeks inputs where a function attains its smallest or largest values; in one variable, setting the derivative to zero can locate candidates, while in several variables the gradient plays that role. The Hessian can then help classify the resulting critical points. What is this mathematical task?

During optimization of a multivariable function, a critical location can have a zero gradient without being a local minimum or maximum. If its Hessian has both positive and negative curvature directions, the graph rises in some directions and falls in others; what is this kind of critical location called?

For a quotient whose numerator and denominator both approach zero or both become unbounded, this method compares their derivatives to evaluate the original limit, when its hypotheses are satisfied. What is the name of this calculus method?

L'Hôpital's rule can be applied when a quotient has this pattern: as the variable approaches a point, both its numerator and denominator tend to zero. What compact quotient notation describes these paired limits?
Ancient Mesopotamian scribes used a positional numeral system whose place values are based on sixty. What is this system called?
The Sexagesimal Number System is reflected in the conventional division of a full turn into equal angular units. What numerical measure does this convention assign to one complete revolution?
In probability, this mathematical object assigns a numerical value to each possible outcome of a chance process, such as assigning a number to each result of a die roll. What is this object called?

For a random variable representing the result of a fair six-sided die roll, this quantity is 3.5. More generally, it is calculated by weighting each possible outcome by its probability; what is it called?

This mathematical problem asks for the exact sum of 1/1² + 1/2² + 1/3² + …, rather than merely a decimal approximation. Its surprising value is π²/6, linking reciprocal squares to the circle constant. What is this problem called?
The Basel Problem was solved in 1735 by the mathematician who established that the infinite sum of reciprocal squares equals π²/6. Which mathematician made this celebrated early contribution?

In a two-input truth table, this connective is false only in the false/false row, making three of the four possible input pairs true. It combines propositions inclusively, unlike the exclusive variant, which rejects the true/true case. What is this operation?

In propositional logic, Logical OR between propositions p and q is conventionally written with this wedge-shaped symbol, which is distinct from ⊕, often used for the exclusive variant. What is the standard symbol?
In probability, what property describes two events when learning that one occurred does not change the probability of the other? For events A and B, it is characterized by P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).

For a collection of random variables, what stronger form of statistical independence requires the joint probabilities of every finite subcollection to factor into the product of the individual probabilities, rather than requiring this only for pairs?
In linear algebra, this mathematical quantity has both magnitude and direction. Dot products and cross products are defined for this kind of object. What is it called?
A nonzero vector can be divided by its magnitude to produce this normalized vector, which has a magnitude of exactly one. What is this special kind of vector called?
In trigonometry, this function gives the reciprocal of cosine wherever cosine is nonzero. What is its standard name?
The Secant function is the reciprocal of this trigonometric function, whose value at 0° is 1. It is also the “CAH” part of the mnemonic SOHCAHTOA. Which function is it?

Which framework represents each point by an ordered pair of numbers measured from a common origin along two mutually perpendicular axes, conventionally labeled x and y? It lets geometric relationships be described using algebra.

The Cartesian Coordinate System is named for this French philosopher and mathematician, who developed analytic geometry and wrote La Géométrie as an appendix to Discourse on the Method. He is also associated with the dictum “I think, therefore I am.” Who is he?

In plane geometry, one complete rotation carries a ray around a circle and back to its starting direction; it also equals the combined interior-angle measure of any quadrilateral. What number names that turn in the standard angular system?
Within the measure of 360 degrees for a full turn, perpendicular rays divide the turn into four equal parts. What is the standard name for each part?

A function has this property at a point when its difference quotient approaches a finite limit there, giving it a well-defined derivative. For example, the absolute value function has this property everywhere except at zero. What is this property?

Differentiability implies this property, which means the function’s value at a point matches the limit of its values as the input approaches that point. The absolute value function has this property at zero even though it has no derivative there. What is this property?

In mathematics, a rule can define each term of a sequence using earlier terms, or solve a problem by applying the same procedure to smaller cases. Such a definition or procedure typically stops at a specified base case; what is this method called?
In Recursion, this familiar number pattern starts with 0 and 1; each later term is the sum of the two terms immediately before it. What is it called?

One part of this result says that differentiating an accumulated-area function recovers its integrand; another says a definite integral can be evaluated by subtracting endpoint values of an antiderivative. What theorem connects these two operations?

When applying the fundamental theorem of calculus to evaluate an integral, one seeks a function whose derivative is the integrand, then subtracts its value at the lower endpoint from its value at the upper endpoint. What is this function called?
In base ten, what kind of number has a digit sequence that is unchanged when read from left to right or right to left? The four-digit examples 7887 and 8778 both have this property.
Which four-digit palindromic number uses exactly two 7s and two 8s, begins and ends with 8, and places the two 7s in the middle? Reading its digits in reverse leaves it unchanged.
What set, denoted by the double-struck symbol ℤ, consists of zero together with all positive and negative whole numbers?
For integers, what theorem guarantees that a number is uniquely determined modulo the product of pairwise coprime moduli by its congruence class modulo each one?

A function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior, with equal values at the two endpoints, must have a point in the interior where its derivative is zero. What theorem guarantees this?

Rolle's theorem is the special case of a broader result in which the function has the same output at both endpoints, making the secant slope zero. Which theorem guarantees a point in the interval's interior where the derivative equals the secant slope between the endpoints?
What branch of mathematics studies limits, derivatives, integrals, and rates of change, and was developed independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz?
Which German polymath, who wrote *Monadology* and independently developed Calculus in the seventeenth century, introduced the differential notation dy/dx and the elongated S symbol for integrals?
The expression 2x + 2 is a polynomial, contrasted with the single-term expression 2x and the three-term expression x² + 3x + 1. What is the standard name for this kind of polynomial?
In the binomial 5x⁷ − 3x², which polynomial property is represented by 7? It is the greatest exponent among the variable terms, regardless of how many terms the polynomial has.

A famous claim first recorded in a 17th-century margin beside Diophantus’s *Arithmetica* says that no positive integers satisfy xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ for any integer n greater than 2. Andrew Wiles proved it in the 1990s; what is this theorem called?
Fermat’s Last Theorem was proved by this British mathematician, who announced a proof in 1993 and later repaired a gap in collaboration with Richard Taylor. Who is he?
This convex solid has four congruent equilateral-triangle faces, six edges, and four vertices. It is the simplest of the five Platonic solids; what is its natural name?
In tabletop role-playing games, what is the four-sided die commonly shaped as a regular tetrahedron, whose notation uses the letter “d” followed by its number of faces?
In set theory, this is the unique set that has no members. It can be written as a pair of braces with nothing between them. What is its natural name?
The Empty Set is commonly written either as braces with no entries or as a single typographic mark. What is the mark formed by a circle crossed by a diagonal stroke?

In calculus and coordinate geometry, this term names a line that gives a smooth curve’s instantaneous direction at a point. In trigonometry, it also names the function equal to sine divided by cosine. What is this mathematical term?
At a chosen point on a differentiable curve, the tangent line has a definite rise-over-run value that describes the curve’s instantaneous steepness there. What is this quantity called?
In mechanics, a small mark placed above a variable indicates its first derivative with respect to time; two such marks indicate the second derivative. What is this convention called?

In dot notation, one dot and two dots above a variable conventionally indicate its first and second time derivatives, respectively. This convention is associated with the mathematician who developed the method of fluxions, distinct from Leibniz’s differential notation. Who was he?

A mathematical thought experiment assigns a room to every positive integer, with all rooms initially occupied. It accommodates one more arrival by moving each current occupant from room n to room n+1; what is this scenario’s established name?

In Hilbert’s Grand Hotel, moving the guest in room n to room n+1 matches every originally occupied room with a different room numbered 2, 3, and onward. What mathematical relationship between the original rooms and those destination rooms does this illustrate?

For a square matrix A, this scalar λ satisfies Av = λv for at least one nonzero vector v, so A sends that vector to a multiple lying in the same one-dimensional span. Equivalently, it makes det(A − λI) equal to zero. What is this scalar called?
An Eigenvalue λ of a matrix is paired with a nonzero vector v satisfying Av = λv. What is the name of that vector, which the matrix sends to a scalar multiple of itself?

Unlike a mean, this summary statistic is one of the values observed in the data, chosen because it has the greatest count. If two values tie for the greatest count, both can qualify; what is this statistic called?
Mode identifies a data set’s most frequently occurring value. What term describes a frequency graph with two distinct peaks?

In propositional logic, an implication has a related statement formed by reversing its two parts and negating each one. This related statement always has the same truth value as the original implication; what is it called?

A mathematician wants to establish an implication but instead establishes the contrapositive, then uses their logical equivalence to conclude the original claim. What is this mathematical strategy called?

In mathematics, what is the name of the property associated with real numbers strictly above zero? It is required for the inner product of every nonzero vector with itself and describes a function whose second derivative makes its graph bend upward.

In the study of Positivity in linear algebra, what condition on a real symmetric matrix requires its quadratic form xᵀAx to be greater than zero for every nonzero real vector? Equivalently, all of the matrix’s eigenvalues lie above zero.

In positional notation, this integer lets 205 show that the tens place contributes no quantity. It is also the additive identity, since adding it to any number leaves that number unchanged. What is this value?
Zero’s role in the Hindu-Arabic positional numeral system spread through Europe in the Middle Ages. Which Italian mathematician helped popularize the system in Europe through his book *Liber Abaci*?
In linear algebra, a square matrix whose determinant is zero has no inverse, and its columns are linearly dependent. What is this kind of matrix called?

What integer pattern begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, … and is defined by taking each term after the first two to be the sum of the two preceding terms? The ratios of its consecutive terms approach the golden ratio.

Which 1202 treatise by Leonardo of Pisa includes a rabbit-breeding problem whose idealized population counts follow the Fibonacci sequence? The work also helped popularize Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe.

In plane geometry, what measure describes how much two-dimensional space a flat region covers, rather than the length of its boundary? It is expressed in square units, such as square centimeters, while perimeter is expressed in linear units.

In multivariable calculus, what operation gives the area of a plane region when applied to the constant function 1 over that region? It accumulates contributions across both coordinate directions rather than along a single interval.

For every integer greater than 1, this theorem guarantees a representation as a product of primes and says that, aside from rearranging the factors, no different prime product gives the same integer. What theorem is this?

Books VII and IX of this ancient Greek mathematical work develop number theory and include a proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. The work is best known for its systematic treatment of geometry. What is it?
What solid-geometry figure has a square base and four triangular lateral faces that meet at one point? Together, these faces form a polyhedron.

Which architect initially considered a square pyramid for the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and later used the form in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum in Cleveland? He also designed the glass pyramid at the Louvre.
For n positive values, multiply them all and take the nth root to obtain this alternative statistical measure. What is it called?

For two positive values, the geometric mean is the square root of a result formed from both values; for larger sets, the same operation is performed before taking the appropriate root. What operation combines the values?

What branch of mathematics studies basic operations such as addition and multiplication, especially when applied to whole numbers? It provides foundational calculation skills used before topics such as algebra.

In formal logic, what axiomatic system for arithmetic describes the natural numbers using a successor operation and rules for addition and multiplication? Gödel’s incompleteness theorems apply to sufficiently expressive systems of this kind.

What mathematical description assigns probabilities to the possible values of a random variable, with those probabilities accounting for all possible outcomes? Bernoulli and binomial are discrete examples, while the Gaussian is a continuous example.

Within a probability distribution, which named model gives a random variable two possible values, conventionally 1 and 0, with probabilities p and 1−p? It represents one trial and serves as the building block for the binomial model.

In mathematics, what is the basic object consisting of distinct members, commonly written inside braces? Its size is called its cardinality, and modern axiomatic foundations treat it as a primitive notion.

In Set theory, what representation uses overlapping closed curves to show relationships among collections, with shared regions representing elements common to them? Its familiar two-circle form can show both union and intersection.
For two sets A and B, what construction contains every ordered pair (a, b) with a drawn from A and b drawn from B? In general, reversing the order of the inputs can produce a different result.

This theorem guarantees that every nonconstant polynomial in one variable with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. Equivalently, such a polynomial factors completely into linear factors over the complex numbers. What is the theorem’s natural name?

The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra can be restated by saying that every nonconstant polynomial over the complex numbers splits into linear factors over that same field. What is the name for this property of a field?
In the expression 3⁴, this operation is represented by multiplying 3 by itself four times, giving 81. What is the operation called?
In exponentiation notation such as 5³, the raised 3 tells how many times the other number is used as a factor. What is the name for that other number?

In a major key, the dominant is the scale degree that supplies the root of the dominant triad, counted from the tonic with the tonic as one. A standard pentatonic scale contains the same number of distinct notes; what number is it?

In the tonal vocabulary that also gives Five its role as the dominant scale degree, a standard major scale follows the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half and reaches the tonic again at the octave. How many distinct notes does it contain before that octave repeat?
In a triangle, this point is where all three segments from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side meet. It is also the triangle’s geometric center of gravity. What is this point called?

In a triangle, the Centroid lies on each of these segments and divides it in a 2:1 ratio, with the longer portion closer to the vertex. Each segment connects a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. What is this segment called?
What mathematical representation places sets inside closed curves and uses shared regions to show common elements? Its regions can also illustrate which elements belong to either set or to neither.
In a Venn diagram of two sets, what is the name of the collection of elements that belong to both sets, shown in the curves’ shared region? In set notation, this operation is commonly written A ∩ B.

In probability and statistics, this measure describes how widely values are dispersed around a distribution’s mean. It is calculated as the average of the squared deviations from that mean and is the distribution’s second central moment. What is it?
For a data set, this measure describes its typical spread in the original units rather than in squared units. It is calculated as the nonnegative square root of the variance. What is it?

A consistent, effectively axiomatized formal theory capable of expressing sufficient elementary arithmetic cannot decide every sentence in its language: some sentences are neither provable nor refutable within the theory. A companion result also limits a sufficiently strong theory’s ability to prove its own consistency. What is the name of this result?

Gödel's incompleteness theorem is often discussed alongside a later undecidability result: no algorithm can determine for every program and input whether the computation will eventually stop. Which British mathematician and logician established this result in 1936 while introducing an idealized model of computation?
This three-dimensional polyhedron has four triangular faces, six edges, and four vertices; its faces need not be equilateral. What is its natural name?

For a tetrahedron, draw from each vertex a segment to the point where the three medians of the opposite triangular face meet. The four resulting segments intersect at one point; what is that point called?

For positive inputs, applying this function to each value and summing the results gives the denominator used to calculate a set’s harmonic mean. It is also the derivative of ln x, and its graph is the hyperbola xy = 1. What is the natural name of the function f(x) = 1/x?

On the graph of the Reciprocal Function f(x) = 1/x, the two branches approach but never cross a pair of perpendicular coordinate lines. One is horizontal and the other is vertical; what are these asymptotes?

In geometry, this property holds when a transformation—such as a rotation, reflection, or translation—leaves an object unchanged. Continuous families of such transformations can be modeled by Lie groups; what is this property called?

In the study of Symmetry, what kind of function satisfies f(-x) = -f(x), so its graph is invariant under a half-turn about the origin rather than a reflection across the y-axis? The cubic function f(x) = x³ is a standard example.

What term names a line or curve that a graph gets arbitrarily close to in a specified limit, whether near a particular input or toward an end of its domain? Such guides can be vertical, horizontal, or slanted, and describe limiting behavior rather than forming barriers the graph cannot cross.
For an asymptote represented by y = b, what is the name of the type that describes a graph’s output as x tends toward positive or negative infinity?

This closed, non-orientable surface has only one side and can be described by joining the ends of a cylinder after reversing one end. It cannot be embedded in ordinary three-dimensional space without passing through itself; what is it called?

A Klein bottle cannot be embedded in three-dimensional Euclidean space, but it can be represented there by a smooth map whose local patches remain regular even when distant parts of the surface intersect. What is this kind of map called?

This quantity describes both the steepness and direction of a straight line on a coordinate plane. It is calculated as the vertical change divided by the horizontal change, often called rise over run. What is it?

On a differentiable curve, the slope at a particular point is represented by a geometric object that shares the curve’s instantaneous direction there. It can be found as the limiting position of secants through that point and nearby points; what is it called?
In calculus, the slope of a function’s graph at x = a is computed as the limit of [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h as h approaches zero. What is the name of this quantity?

For a triangle with side lengths a, b, and c, this quantity is s = (a + b + c)/2. It represents half the triangle’s perimeter and is denoted by s in Heron’s area formula. What is this quantity called?

Which named rule for finding a triangle’s area uses the semiperimeter s together with the factors s − a, s − b, and s − c under a square root, so that the area can be calculated from the side lengths alone?

In set theory, these transfinite cardinal numbers are used to compare the sizes of infinite sets, and their first value gives the size of the natural numbers. What is this system of cardinal numbers called?

A famous proposition about Aleph numbers states that the cardinality of the real numbers is the immediate successor of the cardinality of the natural numbers, with no size of infinity strictly between them. What is this proposition called?

This 17th-century French lawyer and government official pursued mathematics alongside his work in Toulouse. He became renowned for number theory and is associated with both a theorem about powers modulo primes and a famous claim about sums of like powers. Who was he?

Pierre de Fermat left a famous claim in the margin of a book: no positive integers satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ when n is greater than 2. Andrew Wiles proved this claim centuries later; what is the theorem called?

For independent observations from a population with finite variance, this result says appropriately standardized sample means increasingly follow the same probability curve as sample size grows, even if the original population is not bell-shaped. What theorem is this?
In the central limit theorem, standardized sample means approach a symmetric bell-shaped curve centered at 0, with variance 1 and about 68% of its area between -1 and 1. What is this curve called?

This mathematical framework locates a point by its distance from a fixed origin and its angle measured from a reference direction. Points at a fixed distance from the origin form a circle centered there. What is this system called?
In Polar Coordinates, a point is specified using an angle and a distance from the origin, commonly denoted by r. What is this distance called?

In linear algebra and geometry, this object extends the familiar scalar, vector, and matrix cases, while its components transform in a prescribed way when the coordinate system changes. What is the name of this mathematical object?

In index notation for a Tensor, a repeated index appearing once as a superscript and once as a subscript signals that contributions for all its allowed values are combined, even when no explicit sigma symbol is written. What is this rule called?
In three-dimensional geometry, a cube has this many vertices, while a standard stop sign has this many sides. Which natural number is shared by those counts?
The number eight is the face count of this Platonic solid, whose six vertices and twelve edges distinguish it from the other regular polyhedra. Its faces are equilateral triangles; what is the solid?

For a three-sided plane figure, this measurement can be found by taking half the product of a base and its corresponding altitude. Heron’s formula provides another way to calculate it using the lengths of the three sides. What is being measured?
In Heron’s formula for the area of a triangle, the variable s represents a length equal to half the sum of the triangle’s three side lengths. What is this quantity called?
This positive integer has proper divisors 1, 2, and 3, which sum to the integer itself. It is also the number of sides in a hexagon. What number is it?
In number theory, Six is the smallest positive integer whose proper divisors sum to itself. What is the term for an integer with this divisor-sum property?

In Euclidean geometry, this ideal one-dimensional object has no thickness or endpoints and extends without limit in both directions. Unlike a segment or a ray, it continues indefinitely in both directions. What is it?

A nonvertical line’s equation can be arranged with y isolated, x multiplied by a coefficient, and a constant added; that constant is the y-coordinate where the graph crosses the vertical axis. What is this standard equation pattern called?

For a regular polygon, half the product of this measure and the apothem gives its area; for a rectangle, it is twice the length plus twice the width. The corresponding boundary measure for a circle is called circumference. What is the total distance around a closed plane figure called?

In plane geometry, perimeter is found by adding the side lengths of a polygon. For a circle, the analogous distance around its boundary can be calculated by multiplying its radius by 2π; what is this circular measure called?

An Irish mathematician introduced a four-dimensional extension of complex numbers whose imaginary units are conventionally written i, j, and k. His surname also names the function used with the wavefunction in the Schrödinger equation. Who was he?

What algebraic system did William Rowan Hamilton devise as an extension of complex numbers beyond the plane? It has one real component and three imaginary units, conventionally denoted i, j, and k, whose multiplication rules include ijk = −1.

What standard linear-algebra object is arranged in rows and columns, with dimensions such as m × n indicating its number of rows and columns? It can represent a linear transformation or organize coefficients in a system of equations.

Suppose matrix A has n columns and matrix B has n rows. What operation produces a matrix whose entries are dot products of rows of A with columns of B, and whose result may change if the order of the factors is reversed?
For a 2 × 2 matrix with entries a, b, c, and d arranged by rows, what scalar is calculated as ad − bc? For a square matrix of any size, this value is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible.
In matrix algebra, what square matrix has ones along its main diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so that multiplying a compatible matrix by it leaves the original matrix unchanged?
For a square matrix, what are the scalars λ that satisfy Av = λv for some nonzero vector v? They are also the roots of the matrix’s characteristic polynomial.

This Euclidean-geometry rule applies to right triangles, equating the area of the square built on the side across from the right angle with the combined areas of squares built on the other two sides. What is this theorem?
In the Pythagorean theorem, one side of a right triangle is singled out because it lies opposite the 90-degree angle and is longer than either of the other two sides. What is this side called?

The Pythagorean theorem is satisfied by a right triangle whose integer side lengths are 3, 4, and 5, the smallest integer-sided right triangle. What is the conventional name for this familiar example?
Which branch of mathematics studies features of spaces that persist under continuous deformations such as stretching and twisting, while setting aside exact lengths and angles?
In topology, what one-sided surface can be formed by giving a narrow paper band a half-twist and joining its ends? Cutting it down the middle produces one longer loop with two half-twists.

This triangular array begins with 1, places 1s along both edges, and forms each interior entry by adding the two entries directly above it. Numbering its top row as 0, its nth row gives the coefficients in the expansion of (a+b)^n. What is this array called?

In Pascal’s triangle, row n supplies the coefficients for expanding (x+y)^n, with each term having total degree n. What theorem gives this general expansion of the sum of two variables raised to a nonnegative integer power?

In arithmetic, which matched curved marks enclose part of an expression so it is handled as a unit and can override the usual precedence of operations? They appear as an opening and closing symbol around an expression such as a sum or difference.
Parentheses can regroup the terms of 3 + 4 + 5 without changing the total, and multiplication shares this feature while subtraction does not. What property is illustrated?
For pairwise coprime moduli, simultaneous congruences with specified remainders determine a unique residue class modulo the product of those moduli. What theorem in number theory states this result?

The Chinese remainder theorem is associated with an ancient Chinese text that preserves the classic problem of finding a number with remainders 2, 3, and 2 when divided by 3, 5, and 7, respectively. What is the title of this mathematical work?

What branch of mathematics represents networks using vertices joined by edges and studies properties such as paths and connectivity? Euler’s investigation of whether each of the seven bridges in Königsberg could be crossed exactly once became an early landmark in this field.

In an 18th-century puzzle that helped establish Graph Theory, Euler asked whether one walk could pass exactly once over every crossing spanning the Pregel River and its islands in a Prussian city. What historically famous collection was the subject of the puzzle?
In standard rally-scoring games of this sport, players usually compete to a set total, and a player must win by two if the score reaches 10-all. What is the usual game-point target?
Eleven is the usual point target in this indoor racket sport, where players hit a small ball against a front wall and try to control the T-shaped center of the court. What is the sport?
What geometric quantity measures the two-dimensional extent of a three-dimensional object's exterior? For a sphere, it is proportional to the square of the sphere’s radius.
For a sphere, surface area is calculated as four times pi multiplied by the square of this length. Measured from the sphere’s center to any point on its boundary, what is this length?

In plane geometry, this three-sided figure has two sides that meet at a 90-degree angle; the side opposite that angle is called the hypotenuse. It is the standard shape used to state the relation a² + b² = c².

For a right triangle, this result equates the area of the square on the hypotenuse with the combined areas of the squares on the two legs. It is commonly used to find the height a ladder reaches on a wall when its length and distance from the wall are known.

In set theory, a set has this property if its elements can be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers. The integers and rational numbers have it, even though both sets are infinite. What is this property called?
In the study of Countability, this proof technique considers a proposed list of decimal expansions and constructs a new number by changing the nth digit of the nth entry. What is this method called?

In the mechanics example, the angle of repose is found by applying an inverse trigonometric function to the coefficient of static friction. More generally, this function returns the principal angle whose tangent equals a given real number; what is it?
The standard real arctangent assigns each real input a single principal angle rather than the full family of coterminal solutions. What open interval is its range?

On a graph, this calculus operation finds the slope of the tangent at a point by taking a limit of slopes between nearby points. It can also turn a position function into instantaneous velocity. What is this operation called?
In differentiation, the expression [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h compares function values at two nearby inputs before a limit is taken as h approaches zero. What is this two-point slope expression called?

This dimensionless quantity describes the shape of a conic section, distinguishing circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas; for an ellipse, its value lies strictly between 0 and 1. What is this quantity called?
In the standard classification by conic-section eccentricity, which curve has a value of exactly 1, between the elliptical range below 1 and the hyperbolic range above 1?
This irrational constant is approximately 2.71828 and is the base of the natural logarithm. It is also the limit of \((1+1/n)^n\) as \(n\) grows without bound; what is it?

In a permutation of distinct objects, what is a rearrangement called if none of the objects remains in its original position? Euler's number is related to the limiting fraction of these rearrangements among all permutations, which approaches \(1/e\) as the number of objects increases.
In linear algebra, this square array has 1s along its main diagonal and 0s everywhere else. Multiplying a compatible matrix by it leaves that matrix unchanged. What is this matrix called?

The Identity Matrix plays a neutral role in matrix multiplication, much as 1 does in ordinary multiplication of numbers. What is the algebraic term for an element that leaves other elements unchanged under an operation?

When selecting members for a committee, rearranging the same chosen people does not create a different outcome. The number of ways to select k objects from n distinct objects is written C(n, k), or “n choose k.” What is this kind of selection called?
Unlike a combination, a podium assignment distinguishes first, second, and third place, even when the same three competitors are involved. What is the name for this kind of ordered selection?

In plane geometry, this is a corner-like opening measuring exactly 90°, or one quarter of a full turn. A small square at its vertex marks it in diagrams, even when the drawing does not look perfectly square. What is it called?
In geometry, two straight geometric objects meet to form a right angle, and the symbol ⟂ marks their relationship. What are these objects called?

In complex arithmetic, this number is conventionally represented by a lowercase letter and has a square equal to −1. It makes it possible to express square roots of negative numbers within an expanded number system.
In electrical engineering, the imaginary unit is often written with an alternate lowercase letter because the usual symbol can represent electric current. What letter is commonly used instead?
A number written in the form a + bi, with a and b real and the imaginary unit appearing in its second term, belongs to what number system?

In a two-dimensional Cartesian plane, the horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis cross at a shared reference point. What is this point, from which other locations’ horizontal and vertical displacements are measured, called?
For the origin in a Cartesian coordinate plane, what ordered pair gives its horizontal and vertical coordinates, in that order?
This kind of natural number is greater than 1 and has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. What is it called?

A proof about prime numbers by this ancient Greek mathematician assumes a finite list, multiplies its members, and considers a number one larger than their product. The argument shows that no finite list contains them all. Who was the mathematician?
This ancient procedure for finding prime numbers starts with integers from 2 up to a chosen limit and repeatedly crosses out multiples of each surviving candidate. What is the method called?
An unresolved claim about prime numbers asserts that every even integer greater than 2 can be written as the sum of two primes. What is this claim called?

This public-key encryption method publishes a modulus formed from two large prime numbers and uses exponentiation modulo that modulus. Its security is associated with the difficulty of factoring the modulus. What is the method called?

In real analysis, this theorem applies to a continuous function on an interval and guarantees that the function’s output includes every real number between its outputs at the interval’s endpoints. What theorem is it?
The Intermediate Value Theorem applies to a mathematical object that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input, often written using notation such as f(x). What is this kind of object called?

In an 18th-century Prussian city now called Kaliningrad, the Pregel River flowed around two islands, dividing the land into four regions connected by a set of crossings. What famous problem asked whether a walker could use every crossing exactly once, a feat later proved impossible?

In the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, which mathematician represented each land region as a vertex and each bridge as an edge? He used the resulting graph, with four vertices of odd degree, to show that no route could cross every bridge exactly once.

This 19th-century German mathematician made major contributions to complex analysis and geometry. His work on a zeta function led to a famous conjecture about the locations of its nontrivial zeros. Who was he?

Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann’s zeta function has nontrivial zeros that his famous conjecture predicts all have real part one-half. What is the name of the vertical locus defined by Re(s) = 1/2, where those zeros are predicted to lie?
Which three-dimensional polyhedron has six faces, each a parallelogram, with cubes and rectangular prisms as special cases?
In a parallelepiped, all four body diagonals intersect at their common midpoint. What is the standard geometric name for this point?

For a monic polynomial factored into linear factors, these identities connect its coefficients to sums of roots, sums of pairwise root products, and higher-order products. For a cubic, they make the sum of the roots the negative of the coefficient of the squared term and the product of the roots the negative of the constant term. What are these named relations?

In Viète's formulas, each coefficient is related, up to alternating signs, to a sum of products formed by choosing the same number of distinct roots at a time. What are these algebraic expressions called?

This mathematical system extends the real line by pairing a real component with a multiple of a unit whose square is −1. Its elements are written in the form a + bi, and the system is conventionally denoted by a double-struck C. What is it called?

William Rowan Hamilton devised this number system as an extension of the complex numbers, using three imaginary units commonly written i, j, and k. Its multiplication is noncommutative, and Hamilton famously carved its defining relation onto Broom Bridge in Dublin. What is this system called?

In Western music theory, what integer gives the number of distinct notes in a major scale before the octave repeats? It is also the scale-degree number of the note added to a dominant triad to create its familiar four-note chord.
