In a population with inherited variation, individuals whose traits lead them to leave more offspring tend to pass those traits on more often. What evolutionary process can make such traits more common over generations?

In accounts of natural selection, what term describes an individual's relative contribution of offspring to later generations, rather than simply strength or survival? This measure depends on the environment and reflects how successfully individuals pass their genes on.

Snakes periodically shed their skin, while insects and crustaceans cast an old exoskeleton as a larger replacement forms. What is the biological process of shedding and replacing an animal’s outer covering called?
Molting in arthropods leaves behind a cast-off cuticle, often visible as an empty shell after a cicada emerges. What is this shed outer covering called?

A British naturalist independently developed the theory of evolution by natural selection while studying species in the Malay Archipelago. In 1858, he sent Charles Darwin an essay outlining the idea, helping prompt their joint presentation of the theory. Who was he?

Alfred Russel Wallace observed a sharp change in animal life between Bali and Lombok, even though the islands are close together. What named biogeographic boundary marks this division between Asian and Australasian fauna?

This plant-derived elastomer is chiefly obtained from latex of Hevea brasiliensis and consists mainly of repeating isoprene units. Its stretch and resilience make it useful in products such as tires and erasers. What material is it?
In processing natural rubber, workers make shallow cuts in the bark of Hevea brasiliensis and collect the milky latex in vessels. What is this harvesting practice called?
Natural rubber consists mainly of a polymer formed from repeating isoprene units. What is the name of this polymer?
In managed honey-bee colonies, this phenomenon is marked by adult bees abruptly disappearing while the queen, immature bees, and food stores remain. What is this phenomenon called?

In colony collapse disorder, which caste is conspicuously absent even when the queen, developing young, and food stores remain? Members of this caste normally forage for nectar and pollen and perform much of the colony’s daily labor.
What class consists mostly of ectothermic vertebrates with scales and amniotic development? Its members typically lay shelled eggs, though some species give live birth.
Within reptiles, which limbless group includes the king cobra and Burmese python? Its members use a forked tongue to collect chemical cues, and many swallow prey whole.

Long recognized as the world’s deepest known underground natural system, this vertical karst feature lies in the Arabika Massif and extends more than two kilometers below its entrance. What is its established name?
Krubera Cave lies in the Arabika Massif near the Black Sea, within the Caucasus territory whose principal city is Sukhumi. What territory is it in?
An American computer scientist and U.S. Navy rear admiral, she helped shape early programming practices and became a leading advocate for making computers easier to program. Who was she?
Grace Brewster Murray Hopper helped develop a programming language intended to make business data processing more accessible. What language became widely used for commercial applications?

In kinetic theory, this physical quantity reflects the average kinetic energy of particles and describes the thermal state of matter. A thermometer measures it, commonly using scales such as Celsius, Fahrenheit, or kelvin.
Temperature is expressed in this SI base unit, whose symbol is K. Since 2019, its magnitude has been defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant.
Temperature on the Kelvin scale is referenced to this limiting point, assigned 0 K and equivalent to −273.15 °C. Experiments can approach it but cannot attain it.

Temperature measured on this scale assigns water’s freezing and boiling points 0 and 100 degrees, respectively, at standard atmospheric pressure. The scale is named after an eighteenth-century Swedish astronomer.
For certain systems with an upper bound on their energy, temperature can enter a regime that thermodynamics ranks as hotter than every positive-temperature state. What is this regime called?

Which American computer engineer co-founded Apple with another future Apple co-founder and designed the Apple I and Apple II? His work on these early machines helped establish the company’s reputation in personal computing.

Steve Wozniak designed this personal computer, introduced in 1977, with a built-in keyboard and color graphics. Its plastic case and expandability helped make it a successful home-computing system. What was this model called?

In the SI, this base unit is defined by fixing the frequency of a particular transition in cesium-133 at exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles per unit. It is represented by the symbol s and is commonly used to measure duration. What is the unit?
The SI second is defined using a microwave transition in the ground-state hyperfine structure of this isotope. Its frequency is fixed at 9,192,631,770 hertz for the definition. Which isotope is it?

In modern birds, what lightweight structures made chiefly of keratin provide insulation and form aerodynamic surfaces for flight? Fossil evidence suggests that some non-avian dinosaurs also bore them.
In birds, what is the collective term for feathers attached to the wings, including the primaries on the hand and the secondaries along the forearm, but not the tail feathers?

Vorticella and Stentor belong to this mostly unicellular protist phylum, whose members use hairlike structures for movement or feeding. Its cells typically have a large macronucleus and a smaller micronucleus; what is the phylum?

Within Ciliophora, which genus includes large freshwater ciliates with a trumpet-shaped body that can attach to surfaces by a holdfast and contract rapidly into a compact shape? Some species are strikingly blue-green and are known as trumpet animalcules.

This large, fast-moving snake is native to sub-Saharan Africa and has a dark lining inside its mouth, despite usually having olive, gray, or brown scales. Its scientific name is *Dendroaspis polylepis*; what is its common name?
The black mamba belongs to this family of front-fanged venomous snakes, which also includes cobras and kraits. What is the family’s name?
In modern chemistry, every atom of this pure substance has the same number of protons, which determines its atomic number. Hydrogen and bismuth are examples; what is this kind of substance?

In ancient Greek philosophy, this pre-Socratic thinker described four roots—air, water, earth, and fire—a scheme that predates the modern idea of a chemical element. He said Love and Strife governed how these roots combined; who was he?

What kind of vehicle is studied in ethical dilemmas where onboard automated systems must decide how to respond to an unavoidable crash? These vehicles can navigate roads and make travel decisions with limited or no human control.

Which crowdsourced research project presents people with unavoidable crash scenarios to investigate the ethical choices that self-driving cars might make, such as saving one group of road users over another?

At factories, this method combines nitrogen and hydrogen at high pressure and temperature, typically over a finely divided iron catalyst, to produce ammonia. What industrial synthesis process, first used at a full-scale plant in Oppau in 1913, is named for the chemist who demonstrated the reaction and the engineer who helped industrialize it?

The Haber–Bosch process produces this nitrogen hydride from nitrogen and hydrogen, and it is chiefly used as a starting material for nitrogen fertilizers. The compound can also be converted into nitric acid by the Ostwald process. What is it?

Among the six quark flavors, which is the lightest and carries an electric charge of +2/3 of the elementary charge? It appears twice among the three valence quarks in a proton, alongside one down quark.
An Up quark contributes +2/3e, while a down quark contributes −1/3e. What signed total results from adding two contributions of the first kind and one of the second?

This umbrella class includes thousands of fluorinated chemicals with strong carbon–fluorine bonds, many of which resist breaking down in the environment. Members have been used in nonstick coatings, water- and stain-resistant products, and some firefighting foams. What is the natural name of this chemical class?

Among per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, this eight-carbon perfluoroalkane sulfonate was a key ingredient in older Scotchgard water- and stain-repellent formulations. 3M began phasing out its production in 2000; what is this chemical?
This group-15 metalloid has atomic number 33 and the chemical symbol As. Its compounds were once used in pigments and cosmetics, despite the element’s toxicity. What element is it?
Arsenic was a key ingredient in a vivid 19th-century pigment made with copper compounds, used in wallpapers and sometimes cosmetics before its toxicity became notorious. What was this pigment called?
What process describes the gradual change in an ecosystem’s species composition and structure over time, whether on newly exposed ground or after a disturbance?

During primary ecological succession, newly exposed land may become habitable after the retreat of these immense, slow-moving bodies of ice. They can carve valleys and lose mass through melting and calving; what are they?

When water-saturated sediment experiences a rise in pore-water pressure, its strength and stiffness can collapse, causing it to temporarily behave like a fluid. What is this ground-failure process, often triggered by earthquakes, called?
During an earthquake, Soil Liquefaction can destabilize slopes and contribute to downslope movement. What compound term names this broad hazard category, which includes rockfalls and debris flows?

What gemstone name is used chiefly for either of two minerals, nephrite or jadeite? In Chinese history, this material was carved into ritual objects, burial goods, and ornaments, and held major cultural and religious importance.

Jade can refer to nephrite or to a sodium-aluminum pyroxene mineral. What is the name of that mineral, whose chromium-bearing green varieties are prized as imperial jade and whose major deposits occur in Myanmar?

This American pediatrician urged parents to rely on their own judgment rather than follow rigid formulas, a reassuring message that made his child-rearing guidance hugely influential among postwar families. He later became the People’s Party’s 1972 presidential nominee and a prominent opponent of the Vietnam War; who was he?
Benjamin Spock’s 1946 parenting manual became a highly influential guide for postwar families, encouraging a warmer, less authoritarian approach to raising children. What is the title of that work?
This marine bivalve attaches to hard surfaces and is widely cultivated for food; some varieties are also raised for pearls. What is its common name?

In oyster aquaculture, some stock is produced with three sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two. What is this ploidy condition, associated with oysters that do not have a normal spawning period?

Unlike a hard disk, this computer component stores data in nonvolatile semiconductor memory and has no spinning platters or read/write head. Many models connect over SATA or PCIe/NVMe and serve as secondary storage. What is it?
A solid-state drive commonly relies on this nonvolatile storage technology, whose name matches the logic gate that outputs false only when both inputs are true. What is this technology?

This elastic device stores energy when compressed, stretched, or twisted, then exerts a restoring force as it tends back toward its resting shape. In a common coil form, it appears in trampolines, pogo sticks, and vehicle suspensions; what is it?

For a mechanical spring at modest deflections, the restoring force is approximately proportional to its displacement from rest and points back toward equilibrium. What law is this linear model named for?
A mechanical spring of this design stores energy by being twisted rather than compressed or extended, and its output is torque related to angular deflection. What is this type of spring called?

For a mechanical spring, this quantity is the change in force divided by the corresponding change in deflection; for a linear extension or compression spring, its units are force per distance. What is this measure of stiffness called?

This catecholamine neurotransmitter is made in several brain regions and participates in motor control as well as reward-related signaling. Degeneration of neurons in a midbrain pathway that uses it is associated with Parkinson’s disease; name the chemical.

In Parkinson’s disease, the dopamine-producing neurons that degenerate are primarily located in this darkly pigmented midbrain nucleus. Its Latin name refers to its black appearance, which is caused by neuromelanin.

Fine solid grains in interstellar space scatter sunlight to create a faint glow along the ecliptic and absorb blue light, reddening distant stars. NASA’s Stardust mission returned samples of this material from comet Wild 2; what is it called?
Cosmic dust concentrated in the plane of the Solar System scatters sunlight into a diffuse, triangular glow that can be seen after twilight or before dawn. What is this phenomenon called?

This quantity measures how much thermal energy must be supplied to raise an object’s temperature by one degree. In its molar form, it is approximately 3R for many solids under the classical Dulong–Petit result. What is the quantity?
For many solids, the molar heat capacity approaches three times the gas constant in the classical high-temperature limit. What law, named for two French physicists, describes this result?
This group 17 element has atomic number 9 and the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale. At room temperature, its pure elemental form is a highly reactive, pale yellow-green gas. What is it?

In 1886, which French chemist isolated fluorine by electrolyzing potassium bifluoride dissolved in liquid hydrogen fluoride? His achievement solved a long-standing challenge involving this exceptionally reactive element.
What inflammatory disorder occurs when urate crystals accumulate in joints, causing sudden attacks of pain, redness, and swelling? It often first affects the joint at the base of the big toe.
In gout, the crystals that deposit in joints form from a waste product created when the body breaks down purines. What is this compound, which is normally removed from the body in urine?

Usually made primarily from silica, this amorphous solid forms when molten material cools rapidly without crystallizing. It can be blown into vessels and shaped into windowpanes and lenses; what is this material?
Glass has a naturally occurring volcanic form that can fracture into sharp edges. People in the Stone Age used this dark, naturally formed material to make arrowheads and knives; what is it?
About 90% of modern manufactured glass belongs to this type, which contains roughly 70% silica. What is this widely used composition, named for its two main non-silica ingredients?
Glass can be drawn into very thin strands that guide light over long distances and carry information through communications networks. What is this light-guiding strand called?

It is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest world in the Solar System, with an atmosphere composed mostly of hydrogen and helium. Its rapid rotation, completed in about ten hours, gives it a noticeably flattened shape. What planet is this?

On Jupiter, this long-lived anticyclonic storm appears as a reddish oval in the planet’s southern hemisphere and has been observed for centuries. Though it has been shrinking, it remains a defining feature of the planet’s atmosphere. What is this storm called?
Among Jupiter’s four Galilean moons, this one is the largest moon in the Solar System and is wider than Mercury. It is also the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field. What is its name?

Jupiter’s innermost Galilean moon is continually flexed by tidal forces, heating its interior and driving frequent volcanic eruptions. This makes it the most volcanically active world known. What is the moon’s name?

Which American programmer and entrepreneur left Harvard before completing his degree and co-founded the company that developed MS-DOS and Windows? He later became a major philanthropist through a foundation established with his then-wife Melinda.

Bill Gates and Melinda Gates teamed with the Berkshire Hathaway chairman nicknamed the Oracle of Omaha to launch what philanthropic campaign? It encourages the world’s wealthiest people to donate most of their fortunes to charity.

Chemists assign this formal electron-accounting value to an atom in a compound based on electrons it is considered to have gained or lost. It can help track which atoms are oxidized or reduced in a reaction. What is this quantity?

In potassium permanganate (KMnO₄), potassium has an oxidation state of +1 and each oxygen has an oxidation state of −2. Which element must have an oxidation state of +7 for the compound to be neutral?

This English naturalist joined a five-year scientific voyage aboard a British naval survey ship and later argued that species change over generations through a process that explains both life’s diversity and its shared ancestry. Who was he?

Charles Darwin served as the naturalist on a British naval surveying voyage from 1831 to 1836, commanded by Robert FitzRoy. What was the name of the ship that carried him to South America and the Galápagos Islands?
Charles Darwin published this 1859 book to present evidence for common descent and explain how favorable inherited traits can become more widespread. What is the title of the work?

In 1858, this naturalist sent Charles Darwin an essay outlining an independently developed theory of how species change; their ideas were then presented jointly to the Linnean Society. Who was this naturalist, whose fieldwork included the Malay Archipelago?

Charles Darwin compared this process to selective breeding, arguing that inherited variations associated with greater survival and reproduction tend to accumulate over generations. What is this mechanism of evolutionary change?

What semiconductor component can control current in a circuit, allowing it to act as either an electronic switch or a signal amplifier? Replacing bulky vacuum tubes with this solid-state device helped make radios and computers smaller.

After the first point-contact transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947, which physicist developed the junction design and shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Bardeen and Walter Brattain?

When seawater absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide, it forms carbonic acid, lowering the water’s pH and reducing carbonate ions available to many shell-forming organisms. What is this change in ocean chemistry called?
Ocean acidification is driven chiefly by seawater taking up this atmospheric greenhouse gas, whose concentration has been measured at Mauna Loa and plotted on the Keeling Curve. What gas is it?

For a rigid body, this relation gives the rotational inertia about a shifted line from its value about a line through the center of mass by adding the body's mass times the squared separation. What theorem is this?

In the Parallel-Axis Theorem, the value about a displaced axis is found from the value about a parallel axis through the center of mass, plus the body's mass times the squared separation. What rotational quantity is being related?

At the center of a mature tropical cyclone, this roughly circular region has the storm’s lowest surface pressure. Sinking air often leaves it relatively clear and less windy than the surrounding storm. What is this central feature?
The eye of a tropical cyclone is encircled by this ring of deep thunderstorms, where the storm’s strongest surface winds and heaviest rainfall occur. What is this ring called?
This enzyme class breaks down proteins by catalyzing the hydrolysis of peptide bonds. Digestive enzymes such as trypsin are members of this class. What is it called?

A protease produced by the pancreas is released as an inactive precursor and activated in the small intestine. It preferentially cleaves peptide bonds after lysine and arginine residues; which serine protease is described?

This data value is supplied to an algorithm to control operations such as encrypting, decrypting, signing, or authenticating information. In systems with asymmetric encryption, its access role may be designated public or private. What is it called?
A cryptographic key of this type can be shared openly; depending on the system, others use it to encrypt messages for its owner or to verify the owner’s digital signatures. What type of key is it?

Eight-legged arachnids build this silk structure to intercept prey, and its architecture may be orb-shaped, sheet-like, funnel-shaped, or an irregular tangle. In many orb designs, a sticky spiral crosses supporting threads.
As a spider constructs a spider web, silk passes through small movable structures on the underside of its abdomen. What are these silk-spinning organs called?

A eutectic mixture reaches this temperature below the corresponding temperatures of either pure component, and salt lowers water’s value enough to reduce winter road icing. What is the temperature at which a pure substance changes from solid to liquid at a specified pressure?

Incandescent bulbs used this refractory metal for their filaments because its melting point is exceptionally high. Its chemical symbol is W, reflecting its alternate name, wolfram. Which element is it?

A wave packet’s envelope travels at this speed, which is found by differentiating angular frequency with respect to wavenumber. What is this wave quantity, distinguished from the speed of individual constant-phase crests?
For a monochromatic wave, the ratio of angular frequency to wavenumber describes the speed at which its crests move. In a nondispersive medium, this speed matches group velocity; what is it called?

In a 1952 bacteriophage study, researchers labeled viral protein with radioactive sulfur and viral DNA with radioactive phosphorus, then used a blender and centrifuge to track which material entered bacterial cells. Which experiment provided evidence that DNA, rather than protein, carries hereditary information?

The Hershey–Chase experiment compared a phosphorus-tagged component of bacteriophages with sulfur-tagged viral protein during infection of bacteria. The phosphorus-tagged material entered bacterial cells and directed production of new phages; which molecule was thereby supported as the hereditary material?

This American political scientist’s 1979 book *Theory of International Politics* presented an influential account of how the international system shapes state behavior. Who developed this approach, explaining international outcomes in part through the distribution of power among states?

Kenneth Waltz argued that international politics is shaped not only by what individual states want, but also by the system’s anarchic structure and the distribution of capabilities among states. What school of thought, also called structural realism, is associated with this explanation?
What term names the intentional act of causing one’s own death? It is studied as self-destructive behavior and raises questions about ethics, culture, and public health.

What is the name of the scientific field that studies suicide and self-destructive behavior? Its scope includes examining patterns and risk factors rather than referring to one particular prevention program.
What Japanese term names a ritual form of suicide associated with the samurai era and historically linked to failure or protest? It is also known as harakiri.

What term describes coordinated efforts to reduce suicide risk through measures such as limiting access to lethal means, treating mental-health and substance-use disorders, and encouraging careful media reporting?

Which 1859 essay by John Stuart Mill discusses the boundaries between personal choice and state coercion, including the argument that freedom does not require permitting a person to sell themselves into slavery? Its discussion of suicide is part of that broader argument about self-regarding choices.

This British philosopher and logician used the sentence about the present king of France being bald to show how a statement involving a definite description can be meaningful even when no such king exists. He also coauthored *Principia Mathematica* with Alfred North Whitehead. Who was he?

Bertrand Russell analyzed phrases such as “the present king of France” as expressions that assert existence and uniqueness rather than as names for particular objects. What is his account of the logical form of such phrases called?
Which framework describes how mortality typically declines before fertility as societies develop, producing a period of rapid population growth followed by slower growth as birth rates also fall?
In the Demographic Transition Model, what measure of population change is calculated by subtracting deaths from births, without accounting for migration?
What term names the rivalry among firms or sellers that can limit market power? Its idealized form assumes many firms and no individual seller has the power to set the market price.

In discussions of competition, what market structure has a single firm supplying the market and substantial power over price? A firm in this structure could theoretically use first-degree price discrimination to capture all consumer surplus.

Economists use this term for the relationship between prices and how much of a good consumers are both willing and able to buy over a specified period. Unlike mere desire, it accounts for ability to pay and describes purchases across a range of prices rather than a single transaction. What is this market concept?

Whereas Demand describes a relationship across prices, what term refers to the specific amount consumers are willing and able to purchase at one stated price during a given period? This point-specific measure differs from the broader relationship being analyzed.

In discussions of Demand and aggregate production, which classical economic principle associated with Jean-Baptiste Say is often summarized by the claim that production creates the means to purchase output? John Maynard Keynes challenged this principle in arguments about deficient aggregate spending and prolonged economic downturns.

In Marxist theory, this class owns little or no productive property and must sell its labor power for wages. It is portrayed as standing in opposition to the owners of capital and as having revolutionary potential.

In Marxist theory, which class is the principal counterpart to the proletariat, owning and controlling the means of production? Marxist critiques associate its power with capital and the exploitation of wage workers.

Which organized-crime network emerged on the Italian island of Sicily and traditionally operated through local clan-like groups known as cosche? Its members have also been associated with a strict code of silence.

In accounts of the Sicilian Mafia, what term describes the code of silence that pressures insiders and witnesses not to report criminal activity or assist law enforcement? This norm has historically made investigations and prosecutions more difficult.

This West Germanic language is spoken primarily in the Netherlands and Belgium, and its historical varieties provided the basis for a language that developed in southern Africa. What is this language?

The Dutch language is the historical source of this language, which developed in southern Africa and is now one of South Africa’s official languages. It is also spoken in Namibia. What is this language?

During India’s 1975–77 Emergency, a mass campaign associated with Sanjay Gandhi used coercion to permanently eliminate targeted people’s ability to reproduce. What is the name of this practice, which was also upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in Buck v. Bell?

In the U.S. history of forced sterilization, which Supreme Court justice wrote the majority opinion in Buck v. Bell (1927), upholding Virginia’s eugenics law as applied to Carrie Buck? His opinion included the notorious line, “Three generations of imbeciles are enough.”

A dialogue framed as a report to Echecrates recounts Socrates’ final day, when he debates Simmias and Cebes before drinking hemlock. What is the title of this Platonic dialogue, which tests arguments for the soul’s survival after death?
In the Phaedo, which Theban interlocutor compares the soul to the harmony of a lyre, raising the possibility that it perishes when the body dies?

What major family includes Sanskrit, Persian, Greek, Russian, English, and the Romance branch? Its branches are also compared through the centum–satem distinction, based on how they reflect an ancient consonant in the word for “hundred.”

Within the Indo-European languages, what sound change in the Germanic branch transformed many inherited voiceless stops into fricatives? One example is the correspondence between the initial /p/ in Latin *pater* and the /f/ in English *father*.
Created in 1934 after the stock-market crash, this federal agency regulates U.S. financial markets and enforces laws against investment fraud and market manipulation. What agency is it?

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission accused this health technology startup and its founder Elizabeth Holmes of misleading investors about its blood-testing technology. The company claimed it could perform many tests using only a small blood sample. What company was it?

Born Kong Qiu during China’s Spring and Autumn period, this philosopher taught that personal virtue and proper conduct help create social harmony. His teachings later became the foundation of a major Chinese philosophical tradition. Who was he?
This text, assembled after Confucius’s death, preserves sayings and conversations associated with him, including teachings on proper conduct and relationships. What is the name of this collection?
In teachings associated with Confucius, this virtue involves loyalty to one’s family, respect for parents and elders, and care for them in later life. What is this virtue called?

In macroeconomics, what phenomenon is measured by an economy’s rising real output of goods and services over time, rather than by an increase in prices alone? The Solow–Swan framework and models that explain technological progress through decisions made within the economy both seek to explain its sources.

In analyses of Economic Growth, which neoclassical framework models capital accumulation and labor, assumes diminishing returns to capital, and treats technological progress as an external driver rather than something generated within the economy? Its long-run per-capita growth depends on that external technological progress.

Across southern Africa, hunter-gatherer communities including the !Kung and Ju/'hoansi are often grouped under a broad Indigenous name, despite substantial cultural and linguistic diversity. What is that collective name?
The San peoples have longstanding ties to this arid region, where Richard B. Lee conducted fieldwork among !Kung communities and which covers much of Botswana. What named region is being described?

Which French philosopher founded positivism and described intellectual development as progressing through theological, metaphysical, and positive stages? He also coined the terms “sociology” and “altruism.”

In which 1859 essay does John Stuart Mill criticize Auguste Comte’s proposed moral authority, warning that it could lead to a “despotism of society over the individual”? The work defends personal independence against social coercion.

Written by John Stuart Mill and first published in 1859, this short political-philosophy work argues against both governmental repression and the “tyranny of the majority” over individual conduct. What is its title?
In On Liberty, Mill argues that coercive power may be used against a competent adult only to prevent injury to others, not simply for that person’s own good. What principle is this?

Born in France in 1596, this philosopher and mathematician sought an indubitable starting point by methodically questioning beliefs that could be mistaken. He also helped unite algebra and geometry and argued that the existence of a thinking self survives radical doubt; who was he?
René Descartes organized this six-part philosophical work around radical skepticism, the example of a piece of wax, and arguments about the distinction between mind and body. Which work is it?
René Descartes’s approach to linking algebra and geometry represents points by numerical pairs on a plane, with each value measured along one of two perpendicular axes. What namesake system is this?

In the first of René Descartes’s Meditations, he temporarily sets aside any belief that might be mistaken, including sensory judgments, in order to find something absolutely certain. What is this systematic procedure called?

These rulers concentrate political power in one person and suppress meaningful opposition. They include the fictional leader in Miguel Ángel Asturias’s *El Señor Presidente* and the historical Rafael Trujillo. What are such rulers called?

In novels about Dictators, Miguel Ángel Asturias’s *El Señor Presidente* was among the early works to combine fantastical events with a naturalistic setting. Juan Rulfo and Isabel Allende are also associated with this literary mode; what is it called?

Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s 1762 treatise on raising children follows a pupil’s development from infancy toward adulthood, arguing that instruction should suit each stage of growth. Its final book considers the pupil’s marriage and entry into civic life; what is the work?

In Émile, or On Education, Rousseau advises the tutor to delay formal moral lessons and book learning, protecting the child from corrupting influences while the child learns through experience. What is this approach to education called?

Its members include people with diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, and many advocacy groups use a rainbow banner to represent their pride and solidarity. What broad identity-based group is commonly represented by that banner?

In the history of the LGBTQ+ community, a police raid at a Greenwich Village bar in June 1969 sparked several days of protests and resistance, and is often cited as a turning point in modern gay rights activism. What event was this?

Which political doctrine was written into the Chinese Communist Party’s constitution at its 19th National Congress in 2017 and later promoted through Chinese education and governance? Its official formulation presents it as a guide to socialism with Chinese characteristics for a new era.
In October 2017, a major party meeting in Beijing formally added Xi Jinping Thought to the ruling party’s constitution. What was the meeting called?
answer: 19th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party

question: What term describes a pragmatic approach to politics and diplomacy that prioritizes practical power and achievable outcomes over ideological principles? The approach is famously associated with Bismarck’s statecraft.

A 19th-century Prussian statesman used diplomacy and limited wars to unify many German states under Prussian leadership, then became the first chancellor of the German Empire. Which figure is commonly associated with Realpolitik?

Psychologists describe this cognitive faculty through encoding, storage, and retrieval, and distinguish brief sensory traces, processes for holding information briefly, and long-term forms. It supports retaining facts, personal experiences, and learned skills. What is this faculty?

In research on Memory, this American psychologist demonstrated the misinformation effect by changing the wording of questions about a filmed car crash and then testing participants’ recollections. Her findings showed that post-event language can influence what people report remembering. Who is she?

What land-use approach permits residential and commercial functions within the same building or district, often with homes above street-level shops instead of separating the uses into single-purpose zones?

In discussions of mixed-use zoning, planners often value the possibility of reaching shops and services on foot without driving. What quality of a neighborhood describes how easily pedestrians can access everyday destinations?
In the expenditure approach to calculating GDP, which fiscal-policy component is added to consumption, investment, and net exports? When it exceeds tax revenue, it can contribute to a budget deficit.

Government spending is one component of which measure of economic output, calculated as the market value of final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a given period? In the expenditure approach, it is combined with consumption, investment, and net exports.

This 15th-century Italian humanist proposed 900 theses spanning philosophical and religious traditions, including an effort to reconcile Kabbalistic teachings with Christianity. He introduced the project with an address arguing that human beings have exceptional freedom to shape their lives. Who was he?

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola prepared an address to introduce a proposed public disputation based on his 900 theses. The address became a celebrated Renaissance statement on human freedom and potential; what is its commonly used title?
answer: Oration on the Dignity of Man

question: Which branch of philosophy evaluates moral principles and judgments about right and wrong, including questions of duty, virtue, and how people ought to act?
In ethics, which ancient Greek philosopher's *Nicomachean Ethics* examines virtue and human flourishing, with the work's title traditionally associated with his son Nicomachus?

This political system takes its name from Greek words meaning “people” and “rule,” and gives political authority to the people through direct decisions or elected representatives. In ancient Athens, eligible citizens could speak and vote in an assembly, while women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners were excluded. What is this system?
In the development of Athenian democracy, which reformer reorganized citizens into ten tribes around 508 BCE, weakening inherited aristocratic ties?
These criminal organizations coordinate the manufacture, transport, and distribution of illicit substances such as heroin and cocaine. What is the common name for them?
Among drug cartels, which Colombian organization was led by Pablo Escobar and targeted by the vigilante group Los Pepes and Colombia’s First Search Bloc?

What is the name of the controversial conditioning study in which John B. Watson and a research assistant paired a sudden loud noise with an infant’s exposure to a white rat, producing a fear response that later generalized to some furry objects?
In the Little Albert experiment, which researcher coauthored the 1920 report “Conditioned Emotional Reactions” with John B. Watson and helped conduct the study at Johns Hopkins?

This American author and political activist, who had previously worked as a biology researcher, took low-wage jobs to investigate whether full-time work could cover basic living costs. She described the experiment in a 2001 book. Who was she?
Barbara Ehrenreich worked as a waitress, hotel housekeeper, and retail clerk while investigating the realities of low-wage work. What 2001 book recounts that experience?

This American writer, feminist theorist, and cultural critic wrote *Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism* and *Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center*. She adopted an all-lowercase pen name honoring her maternal great-grandmother. Who was she?

In a 2000 book, bell hooks describes a relationship ethic through six elements: care, commitment, knowledge, responsibility, respect, and trust. She argues that it should be understood as an action rather than merely a feeling. What is the title of this work?

What term describes the stable arrangement of governing authority and institutions through which a society makes and enforces public decisions? It refers to the durable framework of rule, rather than a particular leader or policy.

Which political scientist examined the formation of political order in his book *The Origins of Political Order: From Prehuman Times to the French Revolution*? He also wrote *The End of History and the Last Man*.

What discipline systematically investigates and interprets past human events using evidence such as written records and artifacts? Its early foundational practitioner is traditionally identified as Herodotus.

In History, which fifth-century BCE Greek author wrote the *Histories*, recounting the Greco-Persian Wars and describing the customs of various peoples? Later tradition calls him the “Father of History.”

Founded in 1885 by a couple in memory of their son, this private research institution opened in Palo Alto in 1891. Its founding vision combined coeducation and a nonsectarian setting with liberal arts, science, and engineering. What institution is it?

At Stanford University in 1971, this psychology professor ran a simulated prison study in which student volunteers were assigned roles as guards or prisoners. Planned to last up to two weeks, the study was halted after six days amid concerns about participants’ behavior. Who was the professor?
This German-born Jewish political thinker fled Nazi Germany in 1933 and later became a U.S. citizen. Her influential works examine totalitarian rule and political responsibility. Who was she?

Hannah Arendt covered the 1961 trial in Israel of a former Nazi official responsible for organizing the deportation of Jews, first reporting on it for The New Yorker. She expanded that coverage into a book subtitled “A Report on the Banality of Evil.” What is the title of that book?

This East Slavic language is spoken primarily in Russia and was the original language of *Crime and Punishment*, translated into English by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky. What is its natural name?

Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky’s first major English translation from the Russian language was a novel centered on a family whose sons include Alyosha, Dmitri, and Ivan. What is the novel’s title?

In transportation planning, what is the condition in which vehicle demand exceeds road capacity, causing vehicles to slow down or queue? Governments address it through policies such as road expansions and investments in alternative transportation.

Which Virginia state delegate campaigned on reducing traffic congestion along Route 28 in Prince William County, proposing fewer traffic lights and more overpasses? She represented the 13th House District and defeated longtime incumbent Bob Marshall in 2017.

In ethics, this term names the act of causing another person's death. It is the action at issue in trolley-problem scenarios that weigh one person's death against the deaths of several others. What is the term?

Killing figures in a famous challenge to this philosopher's categorical imperative: should someone lie to a would-be murderer asking where hidden children are? This Enlightenment thinker also wrote the *Critique of Pure Reason* and the *Critique of Practical Reason*. Who is he?

Emerging in the third century CE, this late-antique tradition reworked Plato’s metaphysics around the One, Intellect, and Soul, and became especially associated with Plotinus and his successors. What is this philosophical tradition called?
Within Neoplatonism, which third-century philosopher from Lycopolis studied in Alexandria under Ammonius Saccas, later taught in Rome, and whose writings Porphyry arranged into the *Enneads*?
What is the name of the socially constructed system used to categorize human populations that has often been falsely presented as a biological hierarchy and used to justify discrimination?

In discussions of race as a social rather than biological category, which American anthropologist wrote *The Chrysanthemum and the Sword* based on wartime research into Japanese society? She also described anthropology’s purpose as making the world safe for human differences.

Which 2007 nonfiction book by social psychologist Philip Zimbardo examines how situational and institutional pressures can lead ordinary people to commit harmful acts? It connects a prison simulation at a California university with prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib and also considers resistance and heroism.

In The Lucifer Effect, what 1971 study did Philip Zimbardo use as a central case for examining how assigned roles and institutional settings can shape behavior? Student volunteers were divided into guards and inmates, and the simulation ended after six days.

This contemporary approach to designing towns counters car-dependent sprawl with compact neighborhoods where homes, shops, and civic spaces are close together. Its designs emphasize walkability, mixed uses, and environmental sustainability. What is the movement called?

A planned community often cited as an early example of New Urbanism, Seaside was designed by Andrés Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk. On which U.S. state’s Gulf Coast is Seaside located—a state also home to Miami?

This emotion arises when someone perceives danger, and horror films commonly provoke it. In the suspension-bridge attraction study, participants sometimes mistook bodily arousal from crossing a high, shaky bridge for romantic interest in an interviewer; what emotion’s arousal was involved?

In the suspension-bridge attraction study, participants who crossed a high, shaky bridge were more likely than those who crossed a low, sturdy bridge to interpret their pounding heart and sweaty palms as attraction to an interviewer. What cognitive process, often discussed in explanations of Fear, describes assigning those bodily reactions to the wrong source?

What family of visual-gestural systems conveys meaning through coordinated handshapes and movements, facial expressions, and body position rather than audible speech? These complete, grammatically structured systems are used by Deaf communities around the world and vary from country to country.

One language in sign languages is used widely by Deaf communities in the United States and parts of Canada. Despite the shared spoken language, it is distinct from British Sign Language and has historical ties to French Sign Language; what is it?

In this form of associative learning, a neutral cue is repeatedly paired with a stimulus that naturally produces a response, until the cue alone can elicit a learned response. Unlike operant learning, it focuses on associations between stimuli; what is this process called?

The dog experiments that became a famous demonstration of classical conditioning grew out of this Russian physiologist’s research on digestion. He received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; who was he?

Which neurodevelopmental condition involves differences in social communication and interaction together with restricted or repetitive behaviors and interests? Its characteristics and support needs vary among individuals.

In research involving children with autism spectrum disorder, what classic false-belief task asks a child to predict where the character who first placed a marble in a basket will search after another character moves it while they are away?
What U.S. community is descended from immigrants and refugees from Vietnam, including many who arrived after the fall of Saigon, and includes writers such as Ocean Vuong and Viet Thanh Nguyen?

Among Vietnamese Americans, which writer won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for The Sympathizer, a novel about a communist double agent who leaves Vietnam for the United States after the fall of Saigon?

In cognition and microeconomics, researchers study the process by which people select one option from competing alternatives. Barry Schwartz’s work on how an abundance of options can affect this process helped make it a central topic in behavioral economics. What is this process called?
Barry Schwartz’s book on decision-making argues that having more options can sometimes make people less satisfied with their selections. What is the title of this book?

Which major Central Semitic language belongs to the Afroasiatic family, is written from right to left in an abjad, and serves as the liturgical language of Islam? It is also one of the United Nations’ six official languages and the language of the Qur’an and *One Thousand and One Nights*.

Arabic influenced this language, which developed from a Siculo-Arabic variety but is written in the Latin alphabet. It is the national language of Malta and the only Semitic language that is an official language of the European Union. What is it?

Arabic speakers commonly use this term for the eloquent formal register that encompasses both the classical literary form and its modern standard descendant. Western linguists often distinguish those forms, but what is this Arabic term?

A French existentialist philosopher examined how women are made into the social “Other” in a major 1949 work, and also wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity about freedom and moral responsibility. Which thinker authored both books?
Simone de Beauvoir's 1949 study argues that woman is positioned as man's “Other” and examines how femininity is socially formed rather than simply innate. What is the title of this work?

In the 1970s, Canadian psychologist Bruce Alexander compared rats living in standard isolated cages with rats in a spacious, stimulating colony that offered opportunities for social contact and play. What name did he give this study environment, where the group-housed animals showed less voluntary drug consumption?

The Rat Park experiment found lower morphine self-administration among socially housed rats than among isolated rats, challenging explanations that focused only on a drug’s chemical properties. Which psychologist led this research?

In producer theory, this result links derivatives of a firm’s optimized profit function to its choices: differentiating with respect to output price gives output supplied, while derivatives with respect to input prices gives the negatives of input demands. What is this named result?

Hotelling’s Lemma can recover a producer’s output decision without solving its profit-maximization problem again. Holding input prices fixed, what market quantity is obtained by differentiating the optimized profit function with respect to the producer’s output price?

What academic field examines interactions among sovereign states and other cross-border actors, including diplomacy, conflict, and global institutions? Its major theoretical approaches include Realism, Liberalism, and Constructivism.

In international relations, which American theorist’s book *Theory of International Politics* helped establish neorealism? His structural account emphasizes how the anarchic international system shapes states’ behavior.

This Scottish Enlightenment thinker was born in Kirkcaldy and published a landmark work on political economy in 1776. His writing discussed specialization in production and the way individual decisions can benefit society through market exchange. Who was he?

In Adam Smith’s 1776 book *The Wealth of Nations*, a pin factory illustrates how dividing production into specialized tasks can increase output. What is this organizing principle of production called?
What family of philosophical approaches seeks to establish God's existence a priori by analyzing the concept or necessary nature of a maximally perfect being, rather than by observing the world?

In the Ontological Argument's best-known medieval formulation, which eleventh-century Benedictine monk and theologian argues in the *Proslogion* that a being than which none greater can be conceived cannot exist only in the mind, since existing in reality would make it greater?

In a representative democracy, citizens use this formal practice to choose public officials or express a collective preference on a policy question. Their choices may be marked on a ballot or, in some settings, indicated by voice or a show of hands. What is this practice called?

In voting, what preferential electoral method lets people rank candidates and, if no candidate has a majority of first preferences, repeatedly eliminates the lowest finisher and transfers those ballots to the next-ranked eligible candidate?

In labor economics, this broad category includes hourly pay and piece-rate compensation, and can be measured in nominal or inflation-adjusted terms. It is labor income, as distinct from an employer’s profit or a property owner’s rent. What is this form of compensation called?

In studies of wages, George Akerlof and Janet Yellen used a framework in which an employer’s generous offer can be reciprocated with greater worker effort, even without an enforceable contract requiring it. What is this framework commonly called?

Published in New York in 1928, this anthropological monograph draws on fieldwork conducted in 1925–26 on Taʻū and focuses especially on adolescent girls in three villages. It argues that adolescent turmoil is not universal, attributing the differences Mead reported to cultural patterns. What is the title of this work?

The American anthropologist who conducted 1925–26 fieldwork on Taʻū wrote Coming of Age in Samoa, a 1928 study arguing that adolescent development is shaped by cultural context rather than following a universal pattern. What is her name?

This Romance language is official in Italy, San Marino, Vatican City, and Switzerland’s Ticino and part of the Grisons. It is associated with writers such as Dante and Petrarch and is widely used in opera libretti. What language is it?

In the Italian language, what is the phonological term for doubling a consonant, a feature that distinguishes short consonants from long ones? The process can change how a word is pronounced and understood.

The standardized form of the Italian language is based on the central Italian variety associated with Florence, where Dante and Boccaccio wrote in the vernacular. What variety provided this foundation?

This Cold War nuclear deterrence doctrine holds that two nuclear-armed adversaries would each retain enough retaliatory force to inflict catastrophic damage on the other, even after being attacked first. What is this doctrine called?
Within mutual assured destruction, what is the term for a state’s ability to survive an enemy’s initial nuclear attack and still launch a devastating retaliation?
In investment analysis, what quantity reflects both the possibility of an adverse outcome and the potential magnitude of its loss, and is commonly weighed against expected reward?

A 2016 study found that this measure was below three for 65 percent of 133 popular GitHub projects. In discussions of risk, it means the minimum number of contributors whose sudden departure would stall a project, and its name refers to being struck by a vehicle. What is the measure?

An everyday reflective object forms an image by reflecting light. In a classic animal-cognition task, researchers place a visible mark on an animal to see whether it uses its reflection to inspect itself. What object is central to that task and also used for ordinary household viewing?

In a mark test involving a mirror, an animal recognizes that the image is its own and investigates a mark on its body rather than treating the reflection as another animal. What cognitive ability is this behavior taken to indicate?

Under the U.S. Constitution, the House of Representatives can formally charge a federal official with serious misconduct, and the Senate may then hold a trial that can lead to removal from office. What is this constitutional process called?

During the impeachment of President Andrew Johnson in 1868, a central charge followed his dismissal of Secretary of War Edwin Stanton. The House alleged that the firing violated a federal law restricting the president’s removal of certain Senate-confirmed officials; what law was at issue?

A former investment banker who served as U.S. Treasury undersecretary for domestic finance during George H. W. Bush’s administration, he joined the Federal Reserve Board in 2012 and became its chair in 2018, succeeding Janet Yellen. Who is this American central-bank leader?
Jerome H. Powell chairs the U.S. central bank, whose monetary-policy committee adjusts the benchmark overnight lending rate and pursues maximum employment and stable prices. What institution is it?

This American cultural anthropologist served as curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History from 1946 to 1969 and became president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1975. Her 1928 ethnography about adolescence in Samoa brought her national attention. Who was she?
Margaret Mead’s first ethnographic book, published in 1928, drew on research on Taʻu in the South Pacific to examine adolescence and sexuality. What was its title?
In this 1935 book, Margaret Mead compared gender roles and personality through fieldwork among the Arapesh, Mundugumor, and Tchambuli peoples of Papua New Guinea. What is the book’s title?
answer: Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies

question: In economics, what factor of production consists of human effort used to make goods or provide services? It is often analyzed alongside land and capital, and specialization can make it more productive.

In The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith described a workshop where workers divided production into specialized tasks to show how labor specialization could raise output. What small metal fasteners were they making?
In labor economics, many workers may offer their labor while only one employer buys it. What market structure describes this arrangement, in which that buyer can influence wages or hiring?

A landmark study often cited in debates about monopsony examined fast-food employment before and after a 1992 minimum-wage increase. David Card and Alan Krueger compared restaurants in this state with those in neighboring Pennsylvania, where the minimum wage did not rise at that time; which state was it?
This Goidelic Celtic language is traditionally spoken in Ireland and is closely related to Scottish Gaelic and Manx. Welsh and Breton are Celtic relatives from a different branch; name this language.
The Irish language is designated Ireland’s national and first official language in the country’s constitution. What is its name in Irish, rather than the English name used in this question?
What is the process through which children develop the ability to understand and use language? It is often studied in connection with how early-life experience shapes language development.

In research on language acquisition, what proposal holds that early childhood offers a particularly favorable window for learning a language, with native-like mastery becoming more difficult after that window?

In macroeconomics, this proposition says that expected inflation can raise nominal interest rates by less than one-for-one, because it may encourage real investment and reduce the demand for money. What is this effect called?

In the Mundell–Tobin Effect, nominal interest rates rise by less than expected inflation. What benchmark proposition predicts a one-for-one rise in nominal interest rates when the real interest rate is held fixed?

Which constitutional-law doctrine allows courts to protect certain fundamental rights through the Due Process Clauses even though those rights are not explicitly listed in the Constitution? It remains a contested feature of American law, especially in cases involving privacy and personal autonomy.

In a landmark 1965 Supreme Court decision, the Court struck down a state ban on contraceptive use by married couples. The ruling is frequently discussed as an important application of substantive due process. What case was it?
What concise 1714 philosophical work presents reality as composed of simple, nonmaterial substances, each with its own perceptions and activity? Its account is organized into numbered sections.
The author of Monadology was a German polymath who independently developed calculus and argued in his theodicy that this is the best of all possible worlds. Who was he?

This ancient Greek philosopher from Abdera studied under Leucippus and became known for explaining the world through indivisible atoms. His deterministic views were later challenged by Lucretius’s account of a small deviation in atomic motion. Who was this philosopher?
Lucretius proposed a small, unpredictable deviation in the motion of atoms to counter the strict determinism associated with Democritus. What is this deviation called?

They are judgments about whether an action is right or wrong that seem to arise without extended step-by-step reasoning. Experimental philosophers study how people report these judgments when considering ethical thought experiments. What are they called?

This field investigates the psychological processes behind moral intuitions, including how emotions shape judgments of right and wrong. Jean Piaget’s studies of children’s moral development helped establish it as an area of research. What is this field called?

Karl Marx's multivolume analysis of wage labor and commodity production develops accounts of surplus value and the commodity form; its first volume appeared in 1867, and Friedrich Engels edited and published the later volumes. What work is it?
answer: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy

question: In Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, Marx explains how social relations among producers can appear as relations among commodities, making commodities seem to possess powers of their own. What concept names this appearance?

What seventeenth-century Japanese treatise on strategy and swordsmanship is divided into books named for Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Void? Its author also discusses fighting with two swords and applying martial discipline beyond combat.
The Book of Five Rings presents the teachings of a Japanese swordsman famed for his duels and for founding the two-sword style Niten Ichi-ryū. Who wrote the treatise?
First published in 1785, this foundational treatise develops an ethical theory centered on the categorical imperative and seeks principles of right conduct grounded in reason. What work is it?
answer: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

question: In Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, which German Enlightenment philosopher presents the test of whether a maxim could be willed as a universal law? He also wrote the Critique of Pure Reason.

In the United States, these deposit-taking institutions make loans and process payments; some also provide commercial and investment-banking services. Their historic separation from securities underwriting was loosened when the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act repealed part of Glass-Steagall—what are they?

Which 1999 U.S. law allowed banks to affiliate with securities firms and insurers by repealing key provisions of Glass-Steagall? Its passage loosened restrictions separating commercial and investment banking.

In classical Chinese thought, this concept can mean moral character in Confucian writings and inner efficacy or power in Daoist writings. It is the second element in the title commonly translated as the “Classic of the Way and ___.” What is the concept?

In Daoist thought, De is associated with the inner efficacy discussed in a classic traditionally attributed to a sage linked to the state of Chu. Tradition gives this sage the surname Li and an honorific meaning “Old Master”; who is he?

In U.S. graduate programs, students in this field often earn J.D. degrees and analyze appellate opinions through a Socratic casebook method. Its formalist tradition is commonly contrasted with an approach that emphasizes how judges actually decide cases. What field is this?

In debates about law, this early 20th-century American movement emphasized how courts actually decide cases and how social conditions can shape judicial outcomes. Karl Llewellyn and Jerome Frank were among its prominent figures. What movement is this?

What name is given to a family of proactive policies intended to reduce barriers and widen educational or employment opportunities for groups historically excluded from them? Depending on the setting, these policies may consider protected characteristics as one way to address discrimination or promote diversity.

Affirmative action entered modern federal policy language in a 1961 directive signed by President John F. Kennedy. It required federal contractors to take steps to ensure equal employment opportunity; what was the directive’s number?

An American psychologist and longtime Stanford professor, he became widely known for leading a 1971 simulated-prison study in which volunteers were assigned guard and prisoner roles. His work also explored time perspective, shyness, and the influence of situations on behavior.

In a study led by Philip Zimbardo, college volunteers were assigned roles as custodial officers or detainees in a simulated correctional facility at a California university. After six days, Christina Maslach objected to the conditions and the project was halted.

During Philip Zimbardo’s simulated-prison study, this psychologist’s reaction to seeing how participants were treated helped bring the project to an end. She later became known for research on workplace burnout and the inventory named after her.
Philip Zimbardo examined how ordinary people can be influenced by situational forces in this 2007 book, drawing parallels between the Stanford prison study and abuses at Abu Ghraib.

This regular sound change transformed Proto-Indo-European voiceless stops into voiceless fricatives in Proto-Germanic, among other consonant shifts. It helps explain correspondences such as Latin *pater* and English *father*. What is the name of this sound change?

Grimm's law accounts for the consonant correspondence between Latin *pater* and English *father*, with Greek *patēr* also preserving the older stop. Which voiceless stop at the start of the reconstructed ancestral form is reflected as /f/ in the Germanic languages?

Historically centered in northern China, this language variety is represented by the standardized speech based on Beijing pronunciation and serves as the official spoken standard in mainland China. What language is it?
In Mandarin Chinese, some Beijing pronunciations add a rhotic coloring to the end of a syllable, often without creating a separate syllable. What is this phonological process called?

Born in Geneva in 1712, this Enlightenment philosopher argued in *The Social Contract* that legitimate laws should express the people’s collective will. He also explored child-centered education in *Émile* and the development of inequality in a 1755 discourse. Who was this writer?

Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued in *The Social Contract* that legitimate laws should reflect the common interest of citizens rather than simply add up their private preferences. What term did he use for this shared political principle?

What is the semantic relation that holds when two words or expressions have the same or substantially equivalent meaning? In philosophy of language, explaining this relation became central to W. V. O. Quine’s challenge to defining analyticity.

In “Two Dogmas of Empiricism,” which American philosopher argued that explaining synonymy through analyticity, and analyticity through synonymy, is circular? His essay also challenged the distinction between analytic and synthetic truths.

In Maslow’s hierarchy, this broad class of motives concerns personal development and fulfillment rather than restoring something missing. It remains relevant beyond the reduction of deprivation and includes the drive to realize one’s capacities. What is this category called?
Growth needs in Maslow’s theory include an aim in which a person fulfills their potential and becomes what they are capable of becoming. What did Maslow call this highest-level process?
What universal human condition is understood as the cessation of biological life and explored as an existential, religious, and philosophical question about what may lie beyond it?

In poetry about death, which British poet wrote “Crossing the Bar,” whose speaker hopes to meet his “Pilot” after the final voyage, and also composed “The Charge of the Light Brigade” about the Battle of Balaclava?

An analysis of U.S. Stanford–Binet and Wechsler data estimated a 13.8-point rise in IQ scores from 1932 to 1978, reflecting a broader increase in average intelligence-test performance across generations. What is this pattern called?

The Flynn effect means that average scores can change across generations, making results from editions of an assessment standardized in different eras less directly comparable. What feature—the reference values used to interpret individual scores—can become outdated?

Born in Limerick in 1919, this British analytic philosopher wrote a landmark book on intentional action and an essay that helped renew interest in virtue ethics. She was also one of Ludwig Wittgenstein’s literary executors and translated his Philosophical Investigations into English. Which philosopher is described?

G.E.M. Anscombe’s 1957 book examines how an agent’s reasons and purposes shape what it means to act intentionally, and became an influential work in the philosophy of action. What is the title of the book?
What is the deliberate communication of something the speaker believes to be false, rather than an honest mistake? Kant argued that if everyone did this, trust in communication would be undermined.

In Kant’s ethics, what principle tests whether the maxim behind an action such as lying could be willed as a universal law? It is also known through formulations focused on universal law and respect for humanity.

A Roman emperor composed this collection of twelve books of personal reflections, often while on military campaigns, without preparing it as a polished work for publication. Its recurring exercises concern Stoic self-discipline, mortality, duty, and governing one’s judgments. What is this work?

In Meditations, the writer repeatedly urges himself to accept hardship calmly, focus on what lies within his control, and fulfill his duties to the human community. He ruled alongside Lucius Verus and campaigned against peoples along the Danube; who wrote these reflections?

An eleventh-century Benedictine theologian born in Aosta became abbot of Bec and later held England’s highest ecclesiastical office. He wrote the Proslogion, which presents a famous case concerning God’s existence. Who was he?

In the Proslogion, Anselm of Canterbury reasons from the idea of a being than which none greater can be conceived, claiming that such a being must exist in reality as well as in the understanding. What name is given to this proof for God’s existence?

In classical psychoanalytic theory, what is the name for a child’s unconscious attachment to the opposite-sex parent coupled with rivalry toward the same-sex parent? The concept is associated with early psychosexual development.
The Oedipus complex was central to the account of childhood psychosexual development advanced by which Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis and proposed the id, ego, and superego?

A municipality uses this regulatory system to divide land into districts with different rules for permitted uses, building forms, and development limits. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld this kind of regulation in its 1926 Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. decision. What is this system called?

Within zoning laws, what approach allows different uses—often street-level shops beneath residential floors—in the same building or development, instead of separating them into single-use areas? It is often promoted for supporting walkability and sustainability.

Added to federal law in 1996 as part of the Communications Decency Act, this provision generally prevents an online service from being treated as the publisher or speaker of content supplied by another person. It is also associated with protection for good-faith moderation of objectionable material. What provision is it?

Section 230’s separate moderation clause protects an interactive computer service from certain claims when it voluntarily restricts access to material it considers objectionable, even if that material may otherwise be constitutionally protected. What commonly used nickname identifies this clause?
Created by the Constitution, this officeholder presides over the Senate and may cast a vote to break a tie. The holder also stands first in the presidential line of succession. What is this office?
answer: Vice President of the United States

question: The first person to hold the Vice President of the United States office served under George Washington from 1789 to 1797, then became the nation’s second president. Who was this early Federalist leader?

Zeno of Elea’s arguments about motion include an arrow that seems stationary at every instant and a race in which Achilles cannot catch a tortoise. What general term names a statement, argument, or situation that appears to lead to a contradiction or self-defeating conclusion?

When a paradox admits several possible resolutions, what principle associated with the 14th-century Franciscan William of Ockham advises favoring the simplest adequate explanation and avoiding unnecessary assumptions?

What scientific field studies humanity across both the present and the past, examining cultures, societies, language, human biology, and variation among populations? Its broad scope includes contemporary communities as well as archaic humans.

In anthropology, which Polish-born researcher conducted long-term fieldwork among the Trobriand Islanders and described their regional exchange system in Argonauts of the Western Pacific? His approach became influential in the development of immersive field research.

Which branch of anthropology investigates how language shapes social life, including communication, identity, and relationships within communities? It connects the study of speech with the cultures and societies in which people use it.

In anthropology, what approach asks researchers to understand a society’s practices within that society’s own framework rather than judge them by another society’s standards? Franz Boas was an influential advocate of this approach.
In Leibniz’s metaphysics, what are the simple, indivisible, nonspatial substances that have no “windows” through which anything can enter, yet each represents the universe from its own perspective?
Which German polymath developed the doctrine of Monads, proposed a pre-established harmony between mind and body, and argued in his Theodicy that this is the best of all possible worlds?
What name is given to the 17th- and 18th-century European intellectual movement that emphasized reason and empirical inquiry while advocating social and political reform?

A leading figure in the Scottish branch of the Enlightenment, this moral philosopher and political economist published The Theory of Moral Sentiments in 1759 and The Wealth of Nations in 1776. Who was he?

Introduced nationally under Lester Pearson’s government, this publicly funded system provides universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services. It drew in part on an earlier health-care program in Saskatchewan. What is its commonly used name?

Canadian Medicare drew inspiration in part from Saskatchewan’s pioneering public hospital-insurance plan, introduced in 1947. Which Cooperative Commonwealth Federation premier led Saskatchewan when that plan was established?

Which standardized system uses letters and diacritics to represent speech sounds across languages, making it possible to record pronunciation independently of conventional spelling? Its symbols support both broad and detailed transcription.
In the International Phonetic Alphabet, what is the term for a single vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within the same syllable, as in the vowel sound in “boy”?

What financial practice systematically records and tracks transactions between individuals and organizations? Its double-entry form became associated with Renaissance commerce and appears in Benedetto Cotrugli’s treatise on merchants and trade.

In histories of bookkeeping, which Ragusan merchant and diplomat wrote *Della mercatura e del mercante perfetto*, a fifteenth-century treatise that likely includes an early description of the double-entry method?

Born in Leipzig in 1646, this German rationalist developed the notation for derivatives and integrals independently of Newton. He also summarized his metaphysics in the 1714 work *Monadology*. Who was he?

In Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's metaphysics, what term names the simple, immaterial substances he regarded as the basic constituents of reality, each lacking “windows” and not directly interacting with other substances?

This macroeconomic phenomenon is a sustained rise in the general prices of goods and services, reducing how much each unit of currency can buy. It may be driven by stronger demand or higher production costs. What is this phenomenon?

To measure inflation, statisticians compare the cost of a representative basket of household goods and services with its cost in a base period. In the United States, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes this widely cited measure, commonly known by a three-letter abbreviation. What is the measure?

When inflation expectations rise, this relationship predicts that nominal interest rates will tend to rise by a similar amount if the real interest rate remains unchanged. It is often expressed as nominal interest equaling real interest plus expected inflation. What is this relationship called?

This American investor was born in Omaha, Nebraska, and became known for value investing and his long leadership of Berkshire Hathaway. Along with Bill and Melinda Gates, he co-founded a philanthropic commitment encouraging billionaires to give most of their wealth to charity. Who is he?

Warren Buffett co-founded this initiative with Bill and Melinda Gates to encourage billionaires and other wealthy people to commit to donating most of their fortunes to charitable causes. What is it called?

What methodological principle advises against positing more entities or assumptions than necessary, favoring the simplest explanation that still adequately accounts for the evidence? It is named for a medieval Franciscan philosopher.
Occam’s razor is conventionally linked to this 14th-century English Franciscan scholastic, a major nominalist born in a village in Surrey. Who was he?
What position encompasses both the explicit denial that any gods exist and the view that belief in gods is unwarranted? It is a form of nonbelief discussed in philosophy of religion.

In discussions of atheism in classical Indian philosophy, which school is known for rejecting the authority of the Vedas and treating perception as the most reliable source of knowledge? Its materialist outlook is also associated with denying an afterlife.
As infants become more sensitive to unfamiliarity and unpredictability, they may grow wary or fearful of people they do not know. What is this common developmental response called?
