During the 1587 expedition to Roanoke Colony, this infant granddaughter of Governor John White was traditionally regarded as the first English child born in the Americas. What was her name?

After students in the GED classes he taught urged him to seek office, this Pennsylvania Democrat served 13 years as mayor of Braddock. He later became Pennsylvania’s 34th lieutenant governor and won a U.S. Senate seat in 2022 by defeating Mehmet Oz. Who is he?
John Fetterman won Pennsylvania’s 2022 U.S. Senate race against a Republican opponent who was a physician and television host, best known for presenting The Dr. Oz Show. Who was that opponent?

This Great Plains state entered the Union as the 34th state on January 29, 1861, under a free-state constitution. Before statehood, it saw violent clashes between pro-slavery supporters and Free-Staters, and in 1877 it became home to a settlement founded by formerly enslaved African Americans.
During Bleeding Kansas, this abolitionist led the 1856 Pottawatomie killings. He later led an unsuccessful raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry and was hanged for his role in it. Who was he?

Founded by former Confederate soldiers during Reconstruction, this secret organization used threats, assaults, and killings to suppress Black political participation and intimidate supporters of Reconstruction governments. What organization is it?
The Ku Klux Klan’s first incarnation chose this former Confederate cavalry general as its first Grand Wizard. He also commanded the Confederate forces involved in the 1864 Fort Pillow massacre.
This 1915 silent film by D. W. Griffith helped revive the Ku Klux Klan, and it was the first movie screened inside the White House. What is the film’s title?

In 1871, Congress passed this set of federal laws to combat Ku Klux Klan violence during Reconstruction. The laws enabled federal action against conspiracies that deprived people of civil rights and helped weaken the original organization.
The Ku Klux Klan first organized in this Tennessee town in 1865, when former Confederate soldiers formed a social club that later became a vehicle for racial terror. What town was it?
He became the 41st U.S. president in January 1989 and served one term, during which the Berlin Wall fell and a U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait. Who was he?
During George H. W. Bush’s administration, which secretary of state, formerly Ronald Reagan’s chief of staff, was a key U.S. negotiator during German reunification and the 1991 Gulf War?

The fifth president of the United States, he presided over the Era of Good Feelings and signed the Missouri Compromise into law. His administration also issued a 1823 warning against European intervention in the Western Hemisphere; who was he?

In an 1823 message to Congress, James Monroe declared that the Americas were no longer open to European colonization and warned that European efforts to extend political control in the hemisphere would be viewed as hostile. What foreign-policy principle came to be known by the name of that president?

After losing the 1800 election, John Adams rushed to fill newly created federal judicial posts with Federalists during his final days in office. Some commissions were not delivered before Thomas Jefferson took office. What are these late-term appointees commonly called?

Which 1803 Supreme Court case arose when a District of Columbia justice of the peace appointed among the midnight judges asked the Court to compel delivery of his undelivered commission, and established the Court’s power to declare federal laws unconstitutional?

On January 8, 1815, American defenders under Andrew Jackson repelled a larger British force at Chalmette, downriver from a port controlling access to the Mississippi River Valley. Fought after a peace treaty had been signed but before news of its ratification reached the armies, what engagement became a lasting source of U.S. national pride?

The Battle of New Orleans was fought while the armies still lacked news of a peace settlement signed on December 24, 1814. Hostilities were not to cease until both governments ratified it; what was the settlement called?

These steam-powered naval vessels carried protective plating made of iron or steel, and both Union and Confederate forces deployed them during the American Civil War. What is the name of this class of vessel?
In March 1862, the Union’s USS Monitor and the Confederacy’s CSS Virginia fought the first famous duel between ironclad warships near Norfolk, Virginia. What was this engagement called?

What is the name of the 1898 U.S. expansion that incorporated the Pacific island kingdom ruled by Queen Liliʻuokalani after her monarchy was overthrown? Congress approved it through a joint measure, and the islands later became a U.S. state.
During Hawaiian annexation, which congressional measure passed in July 1898 authorized the islands’ incorporation into the United States? It was named for its Nevada sponsor.

This Michigan territorial governor later served as Andrew Jackson’s secretary of war and as James Buchanan’s secretary of state. A Democratic presidential nominee in 1848, he resigned from the latter post in December 1860 after objecting to the administration’s response to secession; who was he?

Lewis Cass resigned as secretary of state in December 1860 after disagreeing with the president over the federal government’s response to secession. Which president, a Democrat who had won the 1856 election and served immediately before Abraham Lincoln, led that administration?
Which public institution of higher education in northeastern Ohio was the site of the May 4, 1970, anti-Vietnam War protest where National Guardsmen killed four students?
At Kent State University, which student photojournalist took the Pulitzer Prize-winning image of 14-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio kneeling over Jeffrey Miller after the May 4, 1970, shootings?
Edmonia Lewis claimed that one-quarter of her heritage came from this Anishinaabe people of the Great Lakes region. What people are they?

Edmonia Lewis’s Mississauga Ojibwe heritage informed works drawing on Indigenous themes. Which of her sculptures shows an older man teaching a young child to fashion a traditional hunting implement from wood and feathers?

The Constitution requires this federal enumeration at ten-year intervals, and its population totals support demographic statistics and representation in Congress. It is distinct from the estimates the federal statistical agency produces between full counts.
The first United States census, conducted in 1790, took place while this Virginian was serving as Secretary of State under George Washington. He later became the third U.S. president.

Population figures from each United States census are used to reapportion seats in this chamber of Congress, whose membership is allocated among states according to population. Unlike the Senate, it has 435 voting seats.

Born in Brooklyn in 1899, this gangster became the leader of Johnny Torrio’s Chicago organization in 1925 and built a fortune from illegal liquor during Prohibition. After a 1931 federal conviction for tax evasion, he served time at Alcatraz. Who was he?
Which 1929 Chicago gangland killing left seven members or associates of Bugs Moran’s mob dead? Al Capone’s organization was widely blamed, but his involvement was never proven.

Released publicly in April 2019, this Justice Department document presented findings from a special-counsel investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and possible coordination with the Trump campaign. What is this document commonly called?

The Mueller Report grew out of an investigation overseen by a special counsel appointed in May 2017. Which deputy attorney general signed the appointment order after Attorney General Jeff Sessions recused himself from the Russia investigation?

Passed in 1854, this law organized two territories west of the Missouri River and let settlers decide by popular sovereignty whether slavery would be allowed there. It also overturned the restriction on slavery established by the 1820 Missouri Compromise. What was this law called?
The Kansas–Nebraska Act was introduced in the Senate by an Illinois Democrat who chaired the Committee on Territories and championed popular sovereignty. What was the name of this senator?
Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay used a shared pen name for essays urging ratification of the Constitution. What name appeared beneath the Federalist Papers?
Among the three authors who wrote as Publius, which one contributed five Federalist essays and later became the first Chief Justice of the United States?
In late 1864, a Union army cut across Georgia from Atlanta to the Atlantic, destroying railroads and other military resources before reaching a major coastal port. What campaign was this?
At the conclusion of Sherman's March to the Sea in December 1864, which Georgia port city did Union forces occupy and Sherman famously offer as a Christmas present to President Abraham Lincoln?

This 1803 Supreme Court case arose after outgoing president John Adams’s judicial commissions were not delivered by Thomas Jefferson’s administration. Chief Justice John Marshall’s opinion invalidated a provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789 and established the courts’ authority to reject unconstitutional laws. What was the case?

In Marbury v. Madison, this chief justice authored the 1803 opinion declaring that Congress could not expand the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction by statute. He served as chief justice from 1801 to 1835, longer than anyone else in that office. Who was he?

In Marbury v. Madison, the Court ruled that it could not issue William Marbury a writ of mandamus because Congress had expanded the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction beyond constitutional limits. Which numbered provision in the 1789 statute governing the federal courts did the Court strike down?
answer: Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789

question: A congressional settlement in 1820 paired the admission of a slave state with a free state to ease sectional conflict. It also prohibited slavery in the remainder of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30′, except in the state being admitted as a slave state. What was this agreement called?

The Missouri Compromise set a geographic boundary for prohibiting slavery in most of the Louisiana Purchase, while exempting Missouri from that restriction. Which latitude did it designate as the boundary?

This former NASA astronaut flew four Space Shuttle missions and later represented Arizona in the U.S. Senate as a Democrat. Married to former congresswoman Gabby Giffords, he won a 2020 special election against appointed senator Martha McSally. Who is he?
Mark Kelly commanded the final mission flown by this NASA orbiter in May 2011. That flight also delivered the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer to the ISS. Which orbiter was it?

What name was given to the interracial civil rights activists who rode integrated buses through the segregated South in 1961? Their journeys challenged the failure to enforce federal rulings against segregation in interstate travel.

Which 1960 Supreme Court decision ruled that segregation in interstate bus terminal facilities violated federal law? The Freedom Riders sought to enforce this ruling during their 1961 journeys through the South.

What is the U.S. Navy’s primary special operations force, trained to conduct missions across maritime, land, and airborne environments? Candidates qualify through the demanding BUD/S course in Coronado, California.
In 2011, a raid in Abbottabad, Pakistan, killed the al-Qaeda leader responsible for orchestrating the September 11 attacks. What was the target of Operation Neptune Spear, carried out by Navy SEALs?

In 1957, a group of Black teenagers sought to attend a formerly all-white public school in Arkansas, facing resistance from the governor and receiving federal protection after President Eisenhower intervened. By what collective name are the students known?

The Little Rock Nine enrolled at this formerly all-white Arkansas public institution in 1957. Federal troops protected the students as they attended classes during the desegregation crisis. What was the institution’s name?

This Alabama governor became nationally notorious in 1963 when he stood in the doorway at the University of Alabama to resist the enrollment of two Black students, stepping aside after federal intervention. He also delivered an inaugural address defending segregation and later ran for president as a third-party candidate.

George Wallace ran as the American Independent Party candidate in a national race, earning 46 electoral votes and finishing third behind Richard Nixon and Hubert Humphrey. The Democratic National Convention that year nominated Humphrey amid protests in Chicago.

This Arkansas-born Democrat took office in January 1993 after defeating incumbent George H. W. Bush, then won reelection in 1996. He was the 42nd U.S. president and was in office when Maya Angelou read “On the Pulse of Morning” at an inauguration. Who was he?

A major pact signed during Bill Clinton’s first year in office and implemented in 1994 linked the United States, Canada, and Mexico, lowering barriers to commerce among the three countries. What was this pact called?

Bill Clinton nominated this jurist to the Supreme Court in 1993, after she had served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. She became the second woman to serve on the Court and was widely known by the initials RBG. Who was she?
In February 1999, the Senate voted on the articles brought against Bill Clinton but failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed to convict him. What outcome did the Senate reach?
In 2020, a St. Louis husband-and-wife legal team drew national attention after displaying firearms at Black Lives Matter demonstrators outside their home. What is this episode commonly known as?

The McCloskey gun incident brought national attention to Mark and Patricia McCloskey, who later spoke at the 2020 Republican National Convention. The convention faced criticism for using “Hallelujah” without permission from the estate of the Canadian singer-songwriter who wrote it; who was the artist?

In 1676, armed colonists in Virginia rose against Governor William Berkeley’s administration amid disputes over frontier security and the colony’s policy toward Native peoples. The revolt culminated in the burning of Jamestown; what is this uprising known as?

During Bacon’s Rebellion, which royal governor of Virginia was the rebels’ principal opponent and was later recalled to England after the uprising? He had governed the colony for much of the mid-17th century.

Formed by the House in 2021 and chaired by Mississippi Democrat Bennie Thompson, this bipartisan panel held televised hearings in 2022 about the Capitol attack and efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election. What was this panel called?

One of the two Republicans appointed to the United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack, this Wyoming representative was removed as House Republican Conference chair after supporting Donald Trump’s impeachment. Who was she?

What was the name of the April 1980 U.S. military mission authorized by President Jimmy Carter to rescue Americans held at the U.S. embassy in Tehran? Mechanical failures and an aircraft collision at a remote Iranian staging site forced the mission to be abandoned.

During Operation Eagle Claw, what was the codename for the remote Iranian staging site where the rescue force planned to refuel and transfer personnel before continuing toward Tehran? An RH-53D helicopter collided there with an EC-130, leading commanders to abort the mission.
Which UC campus is regarded as the flagship of its statewide public research system? Following student strikes in 1969, it became the first U.S. institution to establish an ethnic studies program.

While attending the University of California, Berkeley, LaNada War Jack became the school’s first Native American student before joining Indians of All Tribes. Beginning in 1969, the group occupied which island for 19 months, invoking the Treaty of Fort Laramie and proposing a Native American cultural center?

In late 1919 and early 1920, federal agents carried out coordinated arrests of suspected anarchists, communists, and other radicals amid postwar fears of political upheaval. What name is given to these U.S. government sweeps?
The Palmer Raids were conducted under this U.S. attorney general, who later sought the 1920 Democratic presidential nomination. Who was he?

What was the name of the federal detention and processing facility that operated on an island in San Francisco Bay from 1910 to 1940? It held many arrivals from China and Japan, and a fire in 1940 led to its closure.

At Angel Island Immigration Station, many arrivals from East Asia were detained and questioned under a federal law first passed in 1882 that barred most laborers from the country then ruled by the Qing dynasty from entering the United States. What was this law called?
After the Supreme Court’s 1954 Brown ruling, white Southern officials coordinated political and institutional efforts to block school desegregation. What was this campaign called?

This Virginia senator led a statewide political machine that advocated closing public schools rather than complying with court-ordered integration. His strategy became closely associated with Massive Resistance; who was he?

This English-born political writer emigrated to the American colonies and became a forceful advocate for independence. His pamphlets included one that urged separation from Britain and a wartime series that began with the words “These are the times that try men’s souls.”
Thomas Paine published this influential pamphlet in 1776, arguing that it was absurd for a continent to be ruled by an island. It called for the American colonies to separate from Britain.
Sacco and Vanzetti were anarchists convicted in Massachusetts for the 1920 Braintree murders and executed in 1927. What U.S. ethnic community did these two men belong to?

On September 16, 1920, a horse-drawn wagon exploded outside J.P. Morgan & Co.’s Manhattan headquarters, killing 38 people and injuring hundreds. Italian Americans in Luigi Galleani’s anarchist circle were investigated in connection with the attack, though its perpetrators were never conclusively identified. What event was this?

What 1972 crime involved operatives tied to President Nixon’s reelection campaign entering the Democratic National Committee headquarters in Washington, D.C., to install surveillance equipment? Its discovery by a security guard became the starting point of a major political scandal.

During the Watergate break-in, what security guard found tape placed over door latches at the office complex and alerted police? His discovery led officers to the DNC offices, where the burglars were caught.

Developed in the United States around World War I, this .45-caliber automatic firearm could use a distinctive drum magazine. It later became strongly associated with both bootleggers and law enforcement during Prohibition. What weapon is it?

The Thompson submachine gun became closely associated with this 1929 Chicago gangland killing. Seven members of George “Bugs” Moran’s gang were shot in a garage by attackers, some of whom were disguised as police officers. What event was it?

In 1973, a 7–2 Supreme Court ruling held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protected abortion choice before fetal viability and described a trimester framework for regulation. It struck down a Texas law that generally allowed abortion only to save the pregnant woman’s life; name this landmark case.

In Roe v. Wade, the plaintiff behind the pseudonym Jane Roe was a Texas woman whose challenge was litigated by Sarah Weddington and Linda Coffee. After the case, she publicly identified herself; what was her legal name?
In Roe v. Wade, this Chief Justice joined the 7–2 majority and led the Supreme Court during the 1973 decision. Appointed by Richard Nixon, he served as Chief Justice from 1969 to 1986; who was he?

From 1920 to 1933, the United States banned the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcoholic beverages under a constitutional amendment and a federal enforcement law. What is the natural name for this national policy and period?

During Prohibition, which 1919 federal law gave the Eighteenth Amendment practical force by defining prohibited intoxicating beverages and establishing enforcement rules? It also allowed limited exceptions, including sacramental wine and medicinal alcohol.
As Prohibition ended in 1933, which constitutional amendment repealed the amendment that had begun the nationwide ban? It is the only amendment adopted to repeal another constitutional amendment.

Nominated by George W. Bush to replace Sandra Day O’Connor, this conservative jurist joined the Supreme Court in 2006. He later authored the majority opinion in the decision that overturned Roe v. Wade.

In a 2022 Supreme Court decision, Samuel Alito wrote the majority opinion overturning Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey. The ruling held that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion; what was the case?
answer: Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization

question: Held in Chicago in August 1968, this gathering of a major U.S. political party became a focal point for anti–Vietnam War demonstrations and televised clashes between protesters and police. Senator Abraham Ribicoff condemned the police response in a speech using the phrase “Gestapo tactics”; what event was it?

At the 1968 Democratic National Convention, which Connecticut senator denounced the police response to antiwar demonstrations as “Gestapo tactics” while seconding Eugene McCarthy’s nomination? His speech drew a furious reaction from Chicago mayor Richard J. Daley.

Thousands of nineteenth-century emigrants left the Missouri River region and crossed the plains and Rocky Mountains toward the fertile Willamette Valley on this route. Its use grew during the westward expansion of the United States, including the large migration of 1843. What historic overland route was it?

Along the Oregon Trail, many emigrants began their westward journey at this river town east of Kansas City, an early outfitting point before later wagon traffic increasingly departed from St. Joseph. What town was it?

A career U.S. naval officer born in Newport, Rhode Island, he led the American squadron that arrived in Edo Bay in 1853 and returned the following year to negotiate with Japan’s Tokugawa government. His mission was carried out under President Millard Fillmore. Who was this commodore?

Matthew Calbraith Perry’s return to Japan in 1854 culminated in an agreement that opened Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships and made provisions for shipwrecked sailors. What was this agreement called?

During World War II, the U.S. Marine Corps recruited speakers of an Athabaskan language native to the American Southwest to send secure battlefield messages across the Pacific using a system based on their language. What name is given to these Marines?

During a 1945 campaign to capture a volcanic island south of Japan, Navajo Code Talkers transmitted secure messages for U.S. Marines. The battle became famous for the raising of an American flag atop Mount Suribachi; what was the campaign called?

In the early eighteenth century, this pirate blockaded Charles Town, South Carolina, and received medical supplies in exchange for prisoners. He commanded the Queen Anne’s Revenge before later sailing aboard the Adventure; by what name is he best known?
Blackbeard captured a French slave ship in 1717 and refitted it as his flagship. The vessel later ran aground near Beaufort Inlet in 1718; what was its name?

Published anonymously under the shared pen name Publius in New York newspapers in 1787–1788, this collection of 85 essays by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay urged ratification of the proposed Constitution. What is the collection’s natural name?

Among The Federalist Papers, which numbered essay argues that a large republic can better control the effects of faction by multiplying competing interests? Written by James Madison, it is widely cited for its analysis of factions.
Which Indigenous peoples of the American Southwest built settlements at Mesa Verde and Chaco Canyon, and are ancestors of modern Pueblo peoples?
Among the major centers of the Ancestral Puebloans, what archaeological site in northwestern New Mexico is known for monumental great houses such as Pueblo Bonito and a network of ancient roads?

Beginning with clashes at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 and ending with Britain recognizing U.S. sovereignty in 1783, this conflict pitted the Thirteen Colonies against Great Britain. What conflict was it?

During the American Revolution, this 1777 American victory over British forces helped convince France that the rebels could prevail and contributed to France’s 1778 alliance with them. What battle was it?

In the American Revolution’s climactic 1781 campaign, French naval forces blocked the Chesapeake while American and French troops besieged Cornwallis’s army, prompting his surrender. What Virginia town gave its name to this decisive battle?

She became the first woman to serve in the U.S. Cabinet when Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed her Secretary of Labor in 1933. A key architect of New Deal labor and social-welfare policies, who was she?

Frances Perkins chaired Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1934 committee tasked with devising national protections against poverty and joblessness. Its proposal became this landmark federal law, which established old-age benefits and unemployment insurance.

Passed by Congress in 1890, this federal statute outlawed contracts and combinations that restrain interstate trade and made monopolization a federal offense. It became a foundation for federal efforts to dismantle trusts; what is the name of this law?

In a unanimous 2021 Supreme Court decision applying the Sherman Antitrust Act, the justices upheld an injunction limiting a national collegiate sports governing body's restrictions on education-related benefits for student-athletes. What case, brought by a former West Virginia running back who challenged those restrictions, did the Court decide?

This Massachusetts-born lawyer defended British soldiers accused after the Boston Massacre, became the first U.S. vice president, and then succeeded George Washington as the nation’s second president. Who was he?

During John Adams’s presidency, Congress passed this pair of 1798 statutes amid tensions with France. One expanded federal powers over noncitizens, while the other made certain criticisms of the national government punishable; what are these laws collectively known as?

A New York Times Magazine initiative first published in 2019, this undertaking marked the 400th anniversary of enslaved Africans’ arrival in English Virginia by examining slavery’s enduring influence on American history. What is the initiative called?
The 1619 Project was developed by this journalist, who wrote its lead essay and received the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary for her work on the project. Who is she?

This English Quaker received a royal charter in 1681 for a large tract west of the Delaware River, partly to settle a debt owed to his late father, a prominent naval officer. He called his plan for a tolerant colony a “holy experiment” and laid out the grid-patterned capital of Philadelphia; who was this proprietor?

William Penn received a 1681 royal charter to establish this colony, where he promoted Quaker ideals and religious toleration. Its capital, laid out where the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers meet, was Philadelphia; name the colony.

In 1917, British intelligence intercepted a German diplomatic message proposing that Mexico fight the United States if the Americans entered the European war. The message offered German support for Mexico’s attempt to recover territory including Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. What was the message called?

The Zimmermann Telegram was sent to this neighboring country, whose government was promised German support in recovering land lost to the United States under the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Which country was its intended recipient?
What is the commonly used name for the 1968 Vietnam War atrocity in which U.S. Army personnel, including members of Charlie Company, killed civilians in a South Vietnamese village?

During the investigation of the My Lai massacre, which then-major was assigned to review allegations of abuses described in a letter from Tom Glen? He later served as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and U.S. secretary of state.

During World War II, a U.S. farm labor shortage led to an agreement bringing temporary agricultural workers from a neighboring country into the United States. What was the name of this guest-worker arrangement, which operated from 1942 to 1964?

Under the Bracero Program, temporary farmworkers crossed north under contracts arranged between the United States and the country just south of its border. Which country was the partner that supplied these workers?

In this 1833 Supreme Court case, Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that a presidential pardon is a deed whose delivery is not complete until it is accepted. The decision held that a recipient may refuse a pardon. What case established this rule?

In United States v. Wilson, this defendant had been convicted of robbing the U.S. mail and endangering the life of its carrier. After Andrew Jackson issued him a pardon, he refused to accept it, leading the Court to consider whether clemency could be rejected. Who was the defendant?

Which president defeated Herbert Hoover in 1932, launched the New Deal during his first 100 days in office, and led the United States through most of World War II? He was the only U.S. president elected to four terms.
Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal established this federal program in 1935 to provide old-age benefits and unemployment insurance. What program became a lasting part of the American safety net?
During Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency, this reformer became the first woman appointed to a U.S. Cabinet post, serving as secretary of labor and helping shape New Deal labor policy. Who was she?

Elected in 1960 at age 43, this Democrat from Massachusetts became the youngest person elected president and the first Catholic to hold the office. His administration faced the Bay of Pigs invasion and the Cuban Missile Crisis before he was assassinated in Dallas in 1963. Who was he?

During John F. Kennedy’s 1960 campaign, the Democratic ticket paired him with a Texas senator who had served as Senate majority leader. After Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, this vice president took the presidential oath aboard Air Force One. Who was he?

In October 1962, U.S. surveillance photographs revealed Soviet nuclear launch sites in Cuba, and John F. Kennedy responded by ordering a naval quarantine. The confrontation ended after Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the weapons, averting what many consider the Cold War’s closest approach to nuclear war. What was this crisis?

This Philadelphia printer and newspaper publisher wrote under the pseudonym Silence Dogood, later served as deputy postmaster-general for the British colonies, and helped secure French support during the American Revolution. He also became famous for experiments with electricity; identify this Founding Father.
Benjamin Franklin published an annual collection of maxims, weather forecasts, and practical advice under the name of a fictional, plain-spoken New Englander. Name the work.

Benjamin Franklin helped map and spread knowledge of a warm Atlantic current after comparing the voyage times of British packet ships with those of American vessels. What current did he chart and name?

Benjamin Franklin was one of the American commissioners who negotiated and signed this 1783 agreement with Britain, formally recognizing U.S. independence and ending the Revolutionary War. Name the agreement.

Benjamin Franklin devised this safety device after investigating electrical storms: a pointed metal rod attached to a building and connected to the ground to protect it from electrical strikes. What invention is it?

In U.S. elections, what type of political action committee may raise unlimited contributions to support or oppose candidates, as long as its spending is independent and it does not coordinate with campaigns or party committees? These groups became prominent after a 2010 Supreme Court ruling.

Which 2010 U.S. Supreme Court case arose from a dispute over whether a conservative group could distribute the film *Hillary: The Movie* near the 2008 primaries? Its ruling against restrictions on independent corporate election spending helped set the stage for Super PACs.

Which lawyer, nominated by George W. Bush in 2005 after Harriet Miers withdrew from consideration, became the 17th Chief Justice of the United States? He presided over the Supreme Court during its 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade.

During John Roberts’s tenure as chief justice, a leaked draft drew attention to this 2022 Supreme Court case arising from a Mississippi law restricting most abortions after 15 weeks. The Court’s ruling overturned the federal constitutional protection for abortion established by Roe v. Wade. What was the case?
answer: Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization

question: An Alabama civil-rights and labor leader, he headed the local NAACP branch and helped bring Martin Luther King Jr. into leadership during the protest following Rosa Parks’s arrest. He also worked for decades as a Pullman porter and organized for the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. Who was he?

Edgar Daniel Nixon and other activists established this organization in December 1955 to coordinate a citywide protest against segregated buses in Alabama’s capital. Martin Luther King Jr. served as its first president. What was the organization called?

He led the FBI for nearly five decades and oversaw COINTELPRO. After Martin Luther King Jr. criticized the bureau for neglecting white supremacist violence, this director called King the “most notorious liar” in America. Who was he?
Under J. Edgar Hoover, this secret FBI initiative ran from 1956 to 1971, using surveillance and other tactics against civil rights, antiwar, and other groups. What was the initiative called?

Near present-day St. Louis, this Mississippian center grew into the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico. Its monumental landscape included a vast platform mound and a timber-circle observatory often called Woodhenge. What site is it?
At Cahokia, which four-terraced earthen rise dominates the central precinct and is recognized as the largest prehistoric earthen structure north of Mexico?

Which Boston merchant inherited his uncle’s business in 1764 and was unanimously elected president of the Second Continental Congress in May 1775? He was the Declaration of Independence’s first signer, famous for his large, flamboyant signature.
John Hancock later became the first governor under a state constitution adopted in 1780 by the commonwealth whose capital is Boston. Which state’s governorship did he hold, and return to in 1787?

In 1907, sixteen U.S. Navy battleships departed Hampton Roads for a circumnavigation that ended in 1909, with port calls around the world meant to display U.S. naval power. What name was given to this force, recognizable by its light-painted hulls and buff-colored funnels?

The Great White Fleet’s 1907–09 world cruise was ordered by which U.S. president, who sought to demonstrate the Navy’s reach and promoted the maxim “speak softly and carry a big stick”? He was the 26th president and had earlier served as governor of New York.

In 1876, Democrat Samuel J. Tilden won the popular vote, but disputed returns in several states left the result unresolved. Which U.S. contest was decided after an electoral commission awarded the contested votes to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes?

In the 1876 United States presidential election, what agreement resolved the disputed electoral returns by allowing Hayes to take office while federal troops were withdrawn from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction?

What four-day U.S. party convention, planned for Milwaukee, took place in August 2020 with a mostly virtual program amid COVID-19 and formally nominated its party’s candidates for president and vice president?

At the 2020 Democratic National Convention, which U.S. senator from California was formally nominated as Joe Biden’s running mate? Before entering the Senate, she served as California attorney general and San Francisco district attorney.

A former U.S. Marine who had once defected to the Soviet Union, this man was arrested in Dallas on November 22, 1963, after President John F. Kennedy was assassinated. He was later shot and killed by Jack Ruby while in police custody.

After Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested following Kennedy’s assassination, this Dallas nightclub owner shot him in the basement of Dallas police headquarters on November 24, 1963. The shooting was broadcast on live television as Oswald was being transferred.

Which independent Pacific monarchy was overthrown in 1893 after its queen was deposed, then annexed by the United States in 1898 under the Newlands Resolution? Its former territory later entered the Union as the 50th state.
During the final years of the Kingdom of Hawaii, which queen succeeded Kalākaua in 1891 and was deposed in 1893 by the Committee of Safety? She was also a composer associated with “Aloha ʻOe.”

After Democrats won control of the House in the 2006 midterms, this California representative succeeded Dennis Hastert and became the first woman to hold the chamber’s top leadership post. She represented San Francisco and later led House Democrats during passage of the Affordable Care Act. Who is she?

Nancy Pelosi became the first woman elected to this congressional post in 2007. Its holder is chosen by members of the lower chamber at the start of each Congress and ranks second in the presidential line of succession after the vice president. What is this office?

At the Second Continental Congress, this Virginia delegate introduced a motion on June 7, 1776, declaring that the colonies should be free and independent states. Who made the motion that became the basis for the congressional independence resolution?

Richard Henry Lee presented his independence proposal before this assembly in Philadelphia in 1776. The same body appointed the committee that drafted the Declaration of Independence and served as the colonies’ wartime national government. What was the assembly called?

An enslaved woman from Barbados was brought to colonial Massachusetts and became one of the first people accused during the 1692 witchcraft panic in Salem. Her testimony helped fuel the proceedings, and she later appeared as a character in Arthur Miller’s play about them. Who was she?

In Arthur Miller’s drama about the 1692 Salem witchcraft panic, Tituba is pressured to confess and name others after being accused of witchcraft. The play also serves as an allegory for the anti-communist investigations of the McCarthy era. What is the play’s title?

Situated in California’s Owens Valley near Independence, this wartime site began receiving Japanese American detainees in March 1942. It was one of ten federal sites where Japanese Americans were forcibly confined during World War II; what was its full name?

During a 1943 visit to Manzanar War Relocation Center, this photographer made portraits and scenes of daily life among the incarcerated Japanese Americans. He later published many of those photographs in the 1944 book *Born Free and Equal*; who was he?

Passed by Congress on March 3, 1873, this federal law restricted the mailing of obscene publications and contraceptive information or devices. What law, named for an anti-vice campaigner who later policed the mails as a postal special agent, is commonly known by this name?
The Comstock Act was named for this anti-vice campaigner, who lobbied for the law and later served as a postal special agent enforcing restrictions on mailed materials. What was his name?

What English-governed community in New England took shape in 1636 when Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield joined as a political community, later absorbing Saybrook and beginning its union with New Haven under a royal charter issued in 1662?

In the early Connecticut Colony, what written framework for government did Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield adopt in 1639, an achievement later associated with the state’s “Constitution State” nickname?

An Illinois Central engineer, he was killed in 1900 while operating the southbound passenger train known as the Cannonball near a Mississippi rail junction. Accounts credit his staying at the controls and applying the brakes with helping spare passengers; what railroad figure became the subject of a famous American ballad?

Casey Jones was killed in 1900 when his southbound Illinois Central passenger train collided with a freight train that had not cleared the main track. Which community near Canton gives its name to the site of the wreck?
Which Upper Midwest state became the focus of worldwide protests after George Floyd was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020, and is also where the Mississippi River begins?
In Minnesota, which Black man died in Minneapolis in May 2020 after Derek Chauvin pinned him to the pavement during an arrest, setting off protests against racial injustice and police violence?

She represented Wyoming’s at-large congressional district from 2017 to 2023 and chaired a major House Republican leadership body from 2019 until her colleagues removed her in 2021. She drew national attention for criticizing Donald Trump and supporting his second impeachment. Who is this Wyoming Republican?

Liz Cheney was elected by fellow members of her party in 2019 to succeed Cathy McMorris Rodgers in a congressional leadership role, becoming the party’s third-ranking member in Congress. What was the title of that position, which she held until her removal in May 2021?

A Republican from Maine, he served as Speaker of the House and later as secretary of state before winning his party’s 1884 presidential nomination. Which politician lost that election to Democrat Grover Cleveland?

James G. Blaine’s 1884 presidential campaign was defeated by a Democrat who had served as governor of New York and later became the only U.S. president to serve two nonconsecutive terms. Who was his opponent?
An English artist and colonial governor led the 1587 Roanoke settlement. After returning from England in 1590, he found the settlement abandoned, with “CROATOAN” carved nearby; who was he?
John White governed the 1587 English settlement in present-day North Carolina where Virginia Dare was born. He returned after an absence to find the colony deserted; what was its name?

At an American exhibition in Moscow in 1959, a televised exchange took place in a furnished model home as the U.S. vice president and Soviet premier argued over the merits of capitalism and communism. What is the name commonly given to this Cold War confrontation?
During the Kitchen Debate, which Soviet leader faced U.S. vice president Richard Nixon in Moscow and, as first secretary of the Communist Party, led the USSR during the Cuban Missile Crisis?

Formed in Boston in 1765 amid opposition to the Stamp Act, this network of colonial resistance groups spread to other colonies and used protests and boycotts against British policies. Rhode Island members of the movement burned the customs schooner HMS Gaspee in 1772. What was this movement called?

A founder of the Boston branch of the Sons of Liberty, this organizer helped mobilize resistance to British policies in the years before the American Revolution. He later served as clerk of the Massachusetts House of Representatives and signed the Declaration of Independence. Who was he?

A three-judge federal panel in Alabama ruled that state and local laws requiring racial segregation on Montgomery’s city buses violated the Fourteenth Amendment, and the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the decision in 1956. What federal case produced this ruling?

In Browder v. Gayle, five African American women challenged Montgomery’s segregated bus system. Which 15-year-old student, arrested in March 1955 for refusing to give up her seat on a bus, was among the plaintiffs?

A Virginia delegate at the Constitutional Convention and principal author of the Virginia Plan, he later served as Thomas Jefferson’s secretary of state. He went on to become the fourth president of the United States. Who was he?

James Madison helped draft and promote which 1787 charter, whose seven articles established the federal branches of government? He also defended its ratification in essays later collected in The Federalist Papers.

In July 1892, a lockout at Carnegie Steel’s works near Pittsburgh escalated when armed Pinkerton agents arrived by river and clashed with striking steelworkers. What was this landmark labor conflict called?
During the Homestead Strike, which Carnegie Steel executive was shot and stabbed at his Pittsburgh office by anarchist Alexander Berkman in July 1892?
Which 1824 Supreme Court decision arose from a dispute over New York’s steamboat monopoly and held that Congress could regulate interstate navigation under its commerce power?

In Gibbons v. Ogden, which former New Jersey governor operated steamboats under New York’s exclusive privilege and sued to stop a rival sailing under a federal coasting license? He was the party named after “v.” in the case caption.
A dockworker of African and Native American descent, he became the first person killed when British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street in Boston in 1770. What was the name of this man?

Crispus Attucks was the first person killed during this 1770 confrontation on King Street, in Massachusetts’s colonial capital, where British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists. By what name is the event commonly known?

At noon on September 16, 1920, a horse-drawn wagon loaded with explosives detonated outside J.P. Morgan & Co.’s headquarters in Manhattan’s financial district, killing 38 people and injuring hundreds. What notorious attack was this?

Investigators linked the Wall Street bombing of 1920 to followers of an Italian-born anarchist whose newspaper, Cronaca Sovversiva, promoted revolutionary violence. U.S. authorities deported this radical leader in 1919; who was he?

In October 1962, U.S. surveillance photographs revealed Soviet nuclear weapons sites in Cuba, triggering a 13-day confrontation in which Washington imposed a naval quarantine. What is the commonly used name for this Cold War standoff?

During the Cuban Missile Crisis, which U.S. president announced a naval “quarantine” of Cuba in a televised address on October 22, 1962, and negotiated with Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev? His younger brother served as attorney general and was a key adviser during the standoff.

This Kentucky-born frontiersman joined the Texas Revolution and defended the Alamo during its 1836 siege. Stories of his prowess with a large fixed-blade weapon helped shape his frontier reputation. Who was he?
James Bowie became nationally famous after surviving a bloody 1827 melee near Natchez involving a duel, gunfire, and knife attacks. What is the incident commonly called?

A Stanford dropout founded a Silicon Valley blood-testing startup and became its public face. She was later convicted of defrauding investors with false claims about the company’s technology. Which former chief executive is this?

Elizabeth Holmes founded this company, which claimed its Edison device could run many tests from a finger-prick blood sample and pursued a major retail-pharmacy partnership with Walgreens. What was the company’s name?

A Tlingit civil-rights activist and leader in the Alaska Native Sisterhood, she addressed Alaska’s territorial legislature in 1945 in support of a bill banning racial discrimination. Her testimony is widely credited with helping secure the bill’s passage. Who was she?
What 1945 statute did Elizabeth Peratrovich’s advocacy help secure, barring race-based exclusion from restaurants, theaters, and other businesses open to the public?
Which Saudi-born militant founded al-Qaeda and led the organization for many years? U.S. forces killed him in a raid in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in 2011.
In May 2011, U.S. Navy SEALs raided the compound where Osama bin Laden was living, killing him during the operation. In which Pakistani city did the raid take place?

During World War II, the U.S. government forcibly removed more than 100,000 people of ancestry from the nation whose military attacked Pearl Harbor, relocating many to camps such as Manzanar and Tule Lake. What was this policy called?

In cases arising from Japanese American internment, which 1944 Supreme Court decision upheld the conviction of a California-born U.S. citizen who defied a military exclusion order? Unlike earlier wartime cases involving curfews, this ruling directly reviewed an exclusion order.

This career Army officer earned the nickname “Old Rough and Ready” after victories at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma during the Mexican-American War. He later became the 12th president of the United States. Who was he?

Zachary Taylor commanded U.S. troops during this Florida conflict, winning a major battle at Lake Okeechobee in 1837. It was the second U.S. war against a Native American people who were later forced to live in the Everglades. What war was it?

This tribunal is the highest judicial body in the federal judiciary of the United States, with appellate authority over federal cases and state cases involving federal law. It consists of a chief justice and eight associate justices and meets in Washington, D.C. What is its natural name?
answer: Supreme Court of the United States

question: In 1803, the Supreme Court of the United States considered a dispute over an undelivered judicial commission and held that it could refuse to enforce a law that conflicted with the Constitution. What case established the principle of judicial review?

Article III establishes the constitutional foundation for the Supreme Court of the United States, but Congress determined the Court’s initial organization. What statute, passed by the First Congress in 1789, set the Court’s original composition and procedures?

In 1803, the Supreme Court considered whether Congress could require its justices to serve on federal circuit courts, upholding the practice despite a challenge tied to the 1801 reorganization of the judiciary. Which companion case to Marbury v. Madison addressed this issue?

In Stuart v. Laird, the Court upheld the constitutionality of requiring Supreme Court justices to travel to designated regions and serve as judges in lower federal courts. What was this practice called?
He served eight years as Dwight D. Eisenhower’s vice president before winning the 1968 election, and in 1974 became the only U.S. president to resign. Name this 37th president of the United States.

A 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee’s headquarters in a Washington hotel complex was followed by efforts to conceal the crime, ultimately leading to Richard Nixon’s resignation. What political affair was this?

In February 1972, Richard Nixon met Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai in Beijing, marking a major opening between the United States and the Asian country governed by the Communist Party since 1949. What historic diplomatic journey was this?
Richard Nixon’s administration established a federal organization in 1970 to administer and enforce national laws addressing air and water pollution. What organization was it?
After Richard Nixon resigned in August 1974, this vice president became the 38th president and later granted Nixon a pardon. Who was he?

This New York City Democratic organization, whose leaders were known as Grand Sachems, became a major force in state politics during the 19th century. Its most infamous leader was William “Boss” Tweed.

Which early national politician helped transform Tammany Hall from a social club into a political machine? He later served as vice president under Thomas Jefferson and fatally shot Alexander Hamilton in a duel.

What name has traditionally been given to a person from New England, and more broadly to someone from the northern United States, especially in contrast with a Southerner? H. L. Mencken used it as the opposing regional label in his critique of Southern culture.
Which American author wrote the novel in which Yankee Hank Morgan is transported to King Arthur’s Britain and has a child named Hello Central?

This Chicago politician served as mayor from 1955 until his death in 1976 and became a powerful figure in city and national Democratic politics. During the 1960 presidential contest, Nixon supporters accused him of manipulating votes in Illinois to help Kennedy.

Richard J. Daley faced accusations from Richard Nixon’s supporters that vote fraud in Illinois aided John F. Kennedy in this national contest for the White House. Nixon nevertheless declined to challenge the outcome.

After John Carver’s death, this Pilgrim became Plymouth Colony’s longtime governor and led the settlement through much of its early history. His account of the Pilgrims’ migration and first years in New England is a major source on the colony’s founding. Who was he?

William Bradford began composing this history in 1630, recounting the Separatists’ departure from Leiden, their Atlantic voyage, and the founding of their New England settlement. By what title is this account known?

Commissioned by Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, this classified study traced U.S. involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1967. Daniel Ellsberg leaked it, and newspapers began publishing its contents in 1971. What is the study commonly called?

In 1971, the Nixon administration sought to stop newspapers from publishing excerpts from the Pentagon Papers, arguing that national security justified prior restraint. What Supreme Court case rejected the government’s attempt to block publication?
answer: New York Times Co. v. United States

question: During Atlanta’s 1996 Summer Games, an explosive device planted in a downtown gathering space for spectators killed Alice Hawthorne and injured more than 100 people. What is the commonly used name of this attack?

The Centennial Olympic Park bombing was one of several attacks by a fugitive who hid in the Appalachian wilderness for more than five years. A police officer arrested him in Murphy, North Carolina, in 2003; who was the bomber?
Published in January 1776, this widely read pamphlet argued that the American colonies should separate from Britain and that hereditary monarchy was irrational. What was the pamphlet called?
The author of Common Sense later wrote The American Crisis, which began with the words “These are the times that try men’s souls.” Who was this English-born political writer?

Which 11th U.S. president, a Tennessee Democrat, led the country during the Mexican-American War? His expansionist agenda included settling the Oregon boundary dispute, and his campaign was associated with the slogan “Fifty-Four Forty or Fight.”

During James K. Polk’s presidency, the United States fought Mexico from 1846 to 1848. What agreement, negotiated by Nicholas Trist despite his recall, formally ended the war and transferred California and much of the present-day Southwest to the United States?

Beginning after a January 1848 discovery at a sawmill in Coloma, this migration drew hundreds of thousands of fortune seekers by land and sea, including the arrivals known as “forty-niners.” The population boom helped the region enter the Union as a state in 1850, while also bringing dispossession and violence against Native Californians; what is this event called?

During the California Gold Rush, this carpenter and sawmill worker found gold flakes in the tailrace of John Sutter’s mill at Coloma on January 24, 1848. Which man made the discovery that sparked the migration?
Which Shawnee leader built a confederacy of Native nations to resist U.S. expansion in the Old Northwest? He was killed in 1813 during the American victory that followed the Battle of Lake Erie.

Tecumseh was killed in this 1813 engagement near Moraviantown in present-day Ontario, where U.S. forces defeated a British and Indigenous alliance after Oliver Hazard Perry’s victory on Lake Erie. What battle was it?

In 1797, American envoys Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, John Marshall, and Elbridge Gerry encountered French intermediaries who demanded payments before negotiations with the French government. What diplomatic crisis did their dispatches expose, helping bring the United States and France to an undeclared naval conflict?

During the XYZ Affair, American envoys were told that a loan to France and a private payment were prerequisites for a meeting with the French foreign minister. Which diplomat, formerly a bishop and a leading figure in the French Directory, was the minister they sought to meet?

What period followed the U.S. Civil War, when the federal government reshaped Southern governments and addressed the status and rights of formerly enslaved people? It is generally dated from 1865 to 1877.
During Reconstruction, what federal agency provided relief and helped formerly enslaved people and refugees access education, legal assistance, and labor-contract support in the postwar South?

Founded in 1997 by a former Navy SEAL, this American private military company operated a major training facility in North Carolina. It drew international scrutiny after its personnel killed 17 Iraqi civilians at Baghdad’s Nisour Square in 2007. What company was it?

Which former U.S. Navy SEAL founded Blackwater in 1997 and became a prominent figure in the private military contracting industry? He is also the brother of former U.S. education secretary Betsy DeVos.

Established in 1920 after growing out of a World War I-era group that defended conscientious objectors, this U.S. nonprofit uses lawsuits and public advocacy to protect constitutional rights such as free speech and due process. What organization is it?

A founding member of the American Civil Liberties Union, this Alabama-born writer and activist lost her sight and hearing after an illness as a young child. She later described her education with Anne Sullivan in The Story of My Life. Who was she?

This major Boston transportation project moved the elevated Central Artery underground and added a harbor crossing connecting the city to Logan International Airport. What is the project commonly known as?

This Big Dig roadway connection runs beneath Boston Harbor between South Boston and Logan International Airport. Its namesake was a celebrated Boston Red Sox hitter who wore number 9. What is the name of this crossing?

This prominent 19th-century American Congregationalist minister became a leading abolitionist and served as pastor of Plymouth Church in Brooklyn. His supporters supplied John Brown with arms for the anti-slavery struggle. Who was he?
Henry Ward Beecher’s supporters furnished John Brown with these breech-loading firearms for use in the anti-slavery struggle, with some sent to Kansas. What type of firearm did they supply?

He became the 26th U.S. president after William McKinley's assassination and had already gained national fame commanding the Rough Riders in Cuba during the Spanish-American War. Who was this Progressive reformer associated with the Square Deal?

In 1907, Theodore Roosevelt sent 16 battleships on a voyage around the world, which began at Hampton Roads and concluded in 1909. Their circumnavigation demonstrated the growing reach of U.S. naval power; what was this expedition called?

Theodore Roosevelt's administration backed the 1903 breakaway of a Central American territory from Colombia, enabling U.S. construction of this passage between the Atlantic and Pacific. What waterway, whose construction included the Culebra Cut and Gatun locks, is being described?

After Theodore Roosevelt helped bring the Russo-Japanese War to an end through negotiations at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, he received this distinction in 1906. What international award made him its first American recipient?

A former Princeton president and New Jersey governor, this 28th U.S. president led the nation into World War I in 1917 after initially maintaining neutrality. At the Paris Peace Conference, he advocated an international organization to help preserve peace. Who was he?
In a January 1918 address to Congress, Woodrow Wilson outlined principles for a postwar settlement, including open diplomacy and national self-determination. By what name is this program known?

Woodrow Wilson made this proposed international organization a centerpiece of the postwar settlement and sought U.S. participation in it. The Senate did not ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States never joined this body. What was it called?
What term describes an extrajudicial killing, often carried out by a mob, that was used extensively in the United States as racial terror against African Americans?

Which Jamaican-born poet wrote about lynching in “The Lynching,” describing “little lads” who “danced round the dreadful thing in fiendish glee”? He also wrote “If We Must Die,” which begins, “If we must die, let it not be like hogs.”
This Kansas politician of Kaw, Osage, Potawatomi, and French-American ancestry became Senate majority leader before serving as vice president under Herbert Hoover. Who was he?

While serving in Congress, Charles Curtis introduced the first version of a proposed constitutional measure addressing women’s legal equality. Congress approved it in the 1970s, but the states did not ratify it; what was the measure called?

In March 1836, after Texian troops surrendered at Presidio La Bahía following the Battle of Coleto Creek, Mexican soldiers executed several hundred captives under orders from Santa Anna. What execution is remembered alongside the fall of the Alamo in the rallying cry “Remember the Alamo!”?
During the Goliad Massacre, which Texian colonel who commanded the force defeated at Coleto Creek was among the prisoners executed after surrendering?

Margaret O’Neill first married Navy purser John B. Timberlake and later became the wife of the senator Andrew Jackson appointed Secretary of War. Her treatment by Washington’s political wives helped spark a social controversy during Jackson’s presidency. Who was she?

After Peggy Eaton’s social ostracism contributed to a rupture among members of Andrew Jackson’s official administration, the president increasingly relied on an informal circle of advisers that included Francis Preston Blair and Martin Van Buren. By what name was this group known?

Founded in 1919 after a split from the Socialist Party of America, this U.S. political organization promoted Marxist-Leninist politics and faced federal investigations and prosecutions during the Red Scare. In a Philip Roth novel centered on actor Ira Ringold and his marriage to Eve Frame, Ringold belongs to this organization. What is it?

Federal prosecutors used this 1940 statute against leaders of the Communist Party USA, arguing that they conspired to advocate the violent overthrow of the U.S. government. The Supreme Court upheld convictions under it in *Dennis v. United States*. What is this law commonly called?

Which Midwestern state contains Chicago, where Jane Addams founded Hull House and the 1893 World's Fair was held? The same state saw the Haymarket Affair and Pullman Strike, and its largest city suffered the 1871 fire popularly blamed on Mrs. O’Leary’s cow.

In Illinois, what 1886 Chicago labor gathering became a violent confrontation after a bomb exploded as police moved to disperse the crowd? The resulting trial led to the execution of August Spies and several other defendants.

In May 1927, an American aviator flew alone and nonstop from New York to Paris, becoming the first person to complete that flight. His infant son was abducted from the family’s New Jersey home in 1932 in a case known as the “Crime of the Century.” Who was the aviator?
Charles Lindbergh made his 1927 solo nonstop flight from New York to Paris in a custom-built, single-engine monoplane. What was the aircraft called?

Before the Revolution, this Boston bookseller studied military history and later became chief of artillery in the Continental Army. George Washington entrusted him with moving captured guns from Fort Ticonderoga through winter conditions to the American lines outside Boston. Who was this general?

During Henry Knox’s service in the Continental Army, what elevated position overlooking Boston did American troops fortify with artillery brought from Fort Ticonderoga in March 1776, helping prompt the British evacuation of the city?

During Ulysses S. Grant’s presidency, speculators Jay Gould and James Fisk tried to corner the market in this precious metal, triggering the 1869 financial panic known as Black Friday. It is the element with symbol Au and atomic number 79. What is it?

At the 1896 Democratic National Convention, William Jennings Bryan attacked the gold standard while arguing for free silver, and his fiery address helped propel him to the party’s presidential nomination. What title is now associated with that address?

Centered in what is now New York, this Indigenous alliance united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca nations, with the Tuscarora joining later. It was governed according to an influential framework for peace and collective decision-making. What is this alliance commonly called?

The Iroquois Confederacy’s founding political tradition is associated with a white pine beneath which weapons were buried as the nations were united. What is the name of the constitution that established its governing principles?

This former bison hunter and Pony Express rider became an internationally famous showman. His traveling Wild West extravaganza presented theatrical spectacles inspired by life on the American frontier. Who was he?
Which sharpshooter became a star performer in Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show and was famed for shooting a smoking cigar from her husband Frank Butler’s mouth?

In 1832, the Supreme Court considered a state’s attempt to extend its laws into Cherokee territory, including a licensing requirement for white missionaries living there. Chief Justice John Marshall’s opinion held that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct political community and that the state’s laws had no force within its territory. What landmark case was this?

The majority opinion in Worcester v. Georgia held that Georgia could not regulate activities in Cherokee territory and recognized the Cherokee Nation as a distinct political community. Which Chief Justice wrote that opinion, after also authoring Marbury v. Madison?

A former miner, he became a prominent labor organizer in the American West and headed the Western Federation of Miners. He also helped found the Industrial Workers of the World and was tried in connection with the assassination of Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg. Who was he?

William Dudley Haywood’s Western Federation of Miners helped lead a major strike in the Cripple Creek mining district. In what state did the Ludlow Massacre later occur during coal-field labor conflicts?

Sen. Mark Kelly sponsored the Brandon Act to address mental-health access, while Jon Stewart campaigned for the 2022 toxic-exposure law that expanded burn-pit care. What population of former service members is central to this policy context?

For military veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards, a 2022 federal law broadened Department of Veterans Affairs healthcare and benefits after Jon Stewart publicly urged Congress to act. What is the law’s commonly used name?

This Indiana-born labor organizer led the American Railway Union during the Pullman Strike of 1894 and later became a prominent Socialist presidential candidate. He made his fifth presidential run from prison in 1920. Who was he?

Eugene V. Debs was a leading figure in this political organization, which repeatedly nominated him for president and elected Victor Berger as its first member of Congress. What was the organization called?

A Boston physician and revolutionary leader, he helped organize resistance to British rule and was appointed a major general shortly before the fighting outside Boston in June 1775. Instead of directing the battle from safety, he took up a musket and was killed fighting alongside the colonial soldiers. Who was he?

Joseph Warren was killed in this 1775 battle, fought mainly on the Charlestown peninsula, where colonial defenders resisted repeated British assaults overlooking Boston. What is the battle’s conventional name?

At the May 1851 Ohio Women’s Rights Convention in Akron, Sojourner Truth spoke extemporaneously, challenging claims that women were weak and connecting women’s rights with the struggle against slavery. What title is now widely given to this speech?

The title Ain’t I a Woman? is associated with an 1863 account of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech, which rendered her words in a Southern dialect despite her New York upbringing and Dutch first language. Which writer published that account?

On April 9, 1865, Robert E. Lee agreed to terms with Ulysses S. Grant at a Virginia village, bringing organized resistance by the Army of Northern Virginia to an end. What is the name of this event, widely regarded as effectively ending the Civil War?

During the Surrender at Appomattox Court House, this Union commander accepted Lee’s surrender and offered terms allowing Confederate soldiers to return home on parole. Earlier in the war, he led the Union campaign to capture Vicksburg; who was he?

What name is given to the two 1777 engagements at Freeman’s Farm and Bemis Heights, where American forces halted John Burgoyne’s advance toward Albany in upstate New York? The resulting British surrender helped persuade France to formalize an alliance with the American cause.

During the Battles of Saratoga, this American officer helped lead the assault that captured Breymann’s fortified camp on October 7, 1777. He was wounded in the left leg during the fighting, an injury that aggravated earlier wounds. Name him.

Which Southern California city experienced the 1965 Watts uprising and the 1992 unrest that followed acquittals in the videotaped beating of a Black motorist? It is the state's most populous city and a major center of its film industry.

In Los Angeles, what Black motorist was beaten by police during a 1991 traffic stop, with footage of the assault later shown worldwide and officers' acquittals helping trigger the 1992 unrest? Years later, he publicly urged people, “Can we all get along?”
This New York lawyer served as Donald Trump’s personal attorney before pleading guilty to multiple federal crimes, including lying to Congress. What is his name?
Michael Cohen pleaded guilty to lying to Congress about discussions of a proposed Trump Tower that was to include a penthouse for Vladimir Putin. In what city was the tower planned?

This British general and royal governor of Massachusetts ordered an April 1775 expedition to seize colonial military supplies at Concord, leading to clashes at Lexington and Concord. William Howe replaced him as commander after the Battle of Bunker Hill. Who was he?

During Thomas Gage’s command of British forces in Massachusetts, troops led by William Howe repeatedly attacked colonial positions on high ground in Charlestown in June 1775. What battle, conventionally named for a nearby Boston landmark, ended in a British tactical victory with heavy British casualties?
Which 2015 U.S. Supreme Court decision held that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry and required states to license their marriages and recognize marriages performed elsewhere?

The majority opinion in Obergefell v. Hodges was written by the justice who had also authored the Court’s opinions in Romer v. Evans, Lawrence v. Texas, and United States v. Windsor. Which justice wrote the 2015 majority opinion?

In 1824, no contender received more than half of the electoral votes, so the House of Representatives made the choice. It chose John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson, prompting Jackson’s supporters to denounce a “corrupt bargain.” What contest was this?

In the United States presidential election of 1824, which Kentucky politician and Speaker of the House finished fourth in electoral votes and was eliminated from the House decision? He later became Secretary of State under John Quincy Adams, a move that fueled Jacksonian accusations of a “corrupt bargain.”

A Republican lawyer who once served on the Texas Supreme Court later argued for the state in a U.S. Supreme Court case about a Ten Commandments monument at the Texas Capitol. He became Texas governor in 2015 and held office during the February 2021 winter-storm power crisis; who is he?

Greg Abbott, while serving as Texas solicitor general, defended a Ten Commandments monument on the state Capitol grounds in a 2005 U.S. Supreme Court case. Which case ended with the Court allowing the monument to remain?

An Ohio newspaper publisher from Marion, he became the nation’s 29th president and served from 1921 until his death in office in 1923. Which politician won the 1920 election after promising a “return to normalcy”?

Warren G. Harding’s administration was tarnished by a scandal in which Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased a Wyoming naval oil reserve to a private company without competitive bidding. By what name is this scandal commonly known?

After a career as a Hollywood actor and television host, this Republican served as governor of California before winning the presidency in 1980. He was the 40th U.S. president and delivered the 1964 “A Time for Choosing” address that helped launch his national political career. Who was he?

Before reaching the White House, Ronald Reagan served two terms as governor of this Pacific Coast state from 1967 to 1975. During his governorship, his response to demonstrations over People's Park in Berkeley made the state a national political flashpoint. What state was it?

During Ronald Reagan’s second term, administration officials secretly sold U.S. arms to the government in Tehran and diverted proceeds to fund Nicaraguan insurgents opposing the Sandinista government, despite congressional restrictions. What scandal, revealed in 1986, involved this operation?

Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev signed this 1987 accord, which eliminated U.S. and Soviet ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with distances of 500 to 5,500 kilometers. What agreement was the first to abolish an entire class of such weapons?

In the 1860s, thousands of immigrants from Guangdong undertook difficult work building much of the Central Pacific Railroad across the Sierra Nevada, helping complete the first transcontinental line. What U.S. community, whose members later faced laws restricting immigration and citizenship, is described?

Which 1882 federal law, signed by President Chester A. Arthur, suspended immigration of Chinese laborers and barred Chinese immigrants from naturalization, profoundly shaping the lives of Chinese Americans?

After serving as governor of Tennessee, this military leader moved to Texas and commanded Texian forces at the decisive 1836 Battle of San Jacinto. He later served twice as president of the independent Republic of Texas.
Under Sam Houston’s command, Texian forces surprised Santa Anna’s army in an afternoon attack on April 21, 1836. The capture of the Mexican leader in the aftermath helped secure Texas independence.

As a U.S. senator, Sam Houston opposed this 1854 law, which created two territories west of Missouri and Iowa and repealed the Missouri Compromise restriction on slavery in those areas. His opposition contributed to his break with the Democratic Party.

Created by Congress on March 3, 1849, this Cabinet-level federal institution brought several offices together, including the General Land Office and the Office of Indian Affairs. Its responsibilities now range from public lands and national parks to geological science and federal trust commitments to Indigenous communities. What institution is this?
answer: United States Department of the Interior

question: Within the United States Department of the Interior, which federal agency began as an office in the War Department in 1824, transferred to Interior in 1849, and formally adopted its current name in 1947? It works with federally recognized tribes on trust responsibilities, self-determination, and self-governance.

Passed in 1862 during the Civil War, this federal law made public land available to settlers who lived on and improved a claim for five years. What law offered eligible claimants up to 160 acres under those terms?
Under the Homestead Act, what was the maximum amount of public land an eligible settler could claim by living on and improving the property for five years?

On December 29, 1890, U.S. Seventh Cavalry troops opened fire on a Miniconjou Lakota camp in southwestern South Dakota while attempting to disarm its people. What event killed more than 250 Lakota, including women and children?

In the context of the Wounded Knee Massacre, what Native religious movement did many Lakota adherents regard as a source of hope, while officials’ alarm over its spread helped spur military intervention?
On April 6–7, 1862, Confederate forces surprised Union troops in southwestern Tennessee, but the Union army counterattacked the following day after reinforcements arrived. What battle was this?

During the Battle of Shiloh, Union troops held this stretch of Sunken Road against repeated Confederate assaults on April 6 before being surrounded and captured. By what nickname was this defensive position known?

What term refers to compensation or other remedial measures proposed to address historical injustices? In the United States, it is often used in calls to redress the enslavement and subsequent oppression of Black Americans.

Which journalist published the 2014 Atlantic essay “The Case for Reparations,” arguing that the United States should address harms caused by slavery and later discrimination? The essay helped bring the debate over Reparations to a wider audience.

Raised in 1898 for the war with Spain, this force went to Cuba but fought on foot because its horses were not transported. It was the only one of three U.S. formations raised for the conflict to see combat; what was its formal designation?

This physician and Army officer commanded the 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry Regiment before his second-in-command, Theodore Roosevelt, succeeded him following his promotion to brigadier general. He later served as U.S. Army chief of staff; who was he?

The 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry Regiment’s second-in-command had previously served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy and resigned that office to join the 1898 campaign in Cuba. After Leonard Wood’s promotion, this future U.S. president led the unit; name him.

Formed in the disputed New Hampshire Grants, this Vermont militia resisted New York authorities seeking to enforce land claims there. Led by Ethan Allen, it became known for seizing a British stronghold on Lake Champlain in 1775. What was the militia called?
