In May 1775, the Green Mountain Boys seized the British post at the southern end of Lake Champlain, whose artillery was later transported to help defend Boston. What was the post called?

A Mohawk leader known in his own language as Thayendanegea, he was educated at Moor’s Indian Charity School and became a British military officer during the American Revolution. After the war, he led Mohawk Loyalists to the Grand River in what is now Ontario. Who was this leader?

Joseph Brant helped establish a settlement on the Grand River after the American Revolution. What Anglican chapel, built there in 1785 and later granted royal-chapel status, is located near Brantford, Ontario?

In 1898, amid Cuba’s independence struggle, George Dewey’s fleet defeated the opposing navy at Manila Bay, while U.S. forces also fought in the Caribbean. What conflict ended with the colonial power relinquishing its claims to Cuba and ceding Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States?

The Spanish-American War formally ended with an agreement signed on December 10, 1898. Spain ceded Puerto Rico and Guam under its terms and agreed to sell the Philippines to the United States for $20 million; what was this settlement called?
This American lawyer and author served as first lady of the United States from 2009 to 2017. Amy Sherald painted her official portrait for the National Portrait Gallery. Who is she?

This contemporary American portraitist is known for painting many sitters' skin in grayscale. She created Michelle Obama's official portrait, unveiled at the National Portrait Gallery in 2018; who is she?

Following the Bay of Pigs invasion, the Kennedy administration approved a CIA-led covert campaign involving sabotage, propaganda, and intelligence efforts to destabilize Fidel Castro’s government. What was the codename of this 1961 effort to weaken and ultimately overthrow the Cuban government?

Within Operation Mongoose, the Kennedy administration selected this U.S. Air Force officer to coordinate the interagency campaign against Castro. He had earlier gained prominence for counterinsurgency work in the Philippines and later became associated with U.S. efforts in Vietnam. Who was he?

On June 2, 1863, Union forces traveled by gunboat up a South Carolina river, destroyed plantations, and helped free hundreds of enslaved people. Co-planned by Harriet Tubman, what was this operation called?

During the Combahee River Raid, this formerly enslaved abolitionist helped plan the Union operation and used her knowledge of the region to support the mission. Known as “Moses” for guiding people to freedom on the Underground Railroad, who was she?

George W. Bush and Al Gore were the major-party nominees in this U.S. race, whose outcome hinged on a disputed Florida recount of punch-card ballots. The Supreme Court’s intervention ended the recount and left Bush the Electoral College winner despite Gore’s national popular-vote plurality; what contest was it?

In the 2000 United States presidential election, the U.S. Supreme Court halted Florida’s recount in a 5–4 ruling, concluding that inconsistent ballot-counting standards violated the Equal Protection Clause. What was the name of this case?

After ascending the throne in 1891, this Hawaiian sovereign tried to replace the Bayonet Constitution but was deposed in 1893 by the Committee of Safety. She also composed “Aloha ʻOe” and was the Kingdom of Hawaii’s last reigning monarch. Who was she?

Following the 1893 overthrow, Liliʻuokalani was held under house arrest in an upper-floor room of this Honolulu royal residence. Commissioned by King Kalākaua and completed in 1882, it was the home of Hawaii’s monarchs before the kingdom ended. What building was it?
Born in 1767 in the Carolinas, this frontier lawyer and military commander served as the seventh U.S. president from 1829 to 1837. He was widely known by the nickname Old Hickory. Who was he?

Andrew Jackson commanded American forces in this January 1815 battle, fought after the Treaty of Ghent had been signed but before news of the treaty reached the combatants. The victory over the British made him a national hero. What battle was it?

Andrew Jackson signed this 1830 federal statute, which empowered the government to negotiate land cessions with Native nations east of the Mississippi and establish territory for them farther west. What law became the statutory basis for relocating those nations?

Andrew Jackson’s removal policy helped set this forced expulsion in motion, though federal troops carried out the Cherokee removal chiefly in 1838–39 under his successor. Thousands died during the journey from their southeastern homelands to Indian Territory. What is this removal commonly called?

Andrew Jackson vetoed the 1832 bill to renew the charter of this federally chartered financial corporation, whose president was Nicholas Biddle. Jackson’s opposition led federal deposits to be transferred to selected state-chartered institutions. What institution was it?
answer: Second Bank of the United States

question: After the British bombardment of Fort McHenry in September 1814, this enormous U.S. garrison flag was still flying at dawn and inspired a poem by Francis Scott Key. What flag, now preserved at the National Museum of American History, was it?

The Star-Spangled Banner inspired a poem written after its author saw the flag flying over Fort McHenry at dawn in 1814. What Maryland lawyer, then aboard a British ship while seeking the release of an American prisoner, wrote the poem?

A severe February 2021 cold spell and winter storm overwhelmed electricity generation and fuel supplies across the Lone Star State, leaving millions without service for extended periods and contributing to hundreds of deaths. What event is commonly known by this name?

During the 2021 Texas power crisis, the state’s governor faced scrutiny over oversight of ERCOT. Before becoming governor, he served as Texas attorney general and argued for the state in the Supreme Court case Van Orden v. Perry, concerning a Ten Commandments monument on public property. Who was he?
Established in 1908 under an earlier name and renamed in 1935, this agency is the Justice Department’s principal domestic law-enforcement and intelligence service. What is its current name?

The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s COINTELPRO program targeted civil-rights and antiwar activists from 1956 to 1971. After Martin Luther King Jr. criticized the agency’s response to racist violence, this longtime director called King “the most notorious liar in America.” Who was he?

The Federal Bureau of Investigation surveilled this Baptist minister and civil-rights leader, who helped lead the Montgomery bus boycott, delivered the “I Have a Dream” speech at the 1963 March on Washington, and won the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize. Who was he?
What term describes the deliberate termination of a pregnancy, a medical practice that became the focus of major U.S. legal and civil-liberties debates?

Which 1973 U.S. Supreme Court decision held that constitutional privacy protections extended to abortion and invalidated a Texas law criminalizing most procedures? Its framework remained influential until the Court overturned it in 2022.

A 1924 federal law promised World War I veterans a bonus for their military duty, but deferred payment until 1945; instead of immediate cash, each veteran received a document recording the amount owed. What was the formal name of that document?
Holders of Adjusted Service Certificates gathered in Washington, D.C., in 1932 and demanded that Congress redeem them early. What popular name was given to this group of protesting veterans?

Fought from 1846 to 1848 between the United States and its southern neighbor, this conflict ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The treaty led to major territorial cessions to the United States; what was the conflict called?

During the Mexican-American War, which U.S. president led the country and pursued an expansionist agenda? He was the first “dark horse” president and was associated with the slogan “Fifty-Four Forty or Fight” during the Oregon boundary dispute.

In 1989, a New York City prosecution wrongly convicted a group of Black and Latino teenagers in connection with the assault and rape of a woman jogging in Manhattan. Their convictions were later vacated after the actual perpetrator confessed. What is this episode commonly known as?

In 2002, which man confessed to the jogger’s attack in the Central Park Five case while imprisoned for other crimes? DNA evidence corroborated his confession, leading to the teenagers’ convictions being vacated.

A jury’s acquittal of four city police officers charged over a videotaped beating helped ignite six days of unrest beginning on April 29, 1992. The violence was concentrated in the city’s southern neighborhoods and included arson, looting, and attacks on Korean American businesses; what event is commonly known by its year and city?

The 1992 Los Angeles riots followed acquittals in a case involving a Black motorist whose 1991 beating by Los Angeles police was captured on video and broadcast nationwide. What was the name of that motorist?
Nominated by Richard Nixon, this jurist became Chief Justice of the United States in 1969 and led the Court when it decided Roe v. Wade in 1973. What was his name?

During Warren E. Burger’s tenure as Chief Justice, this 1986 Supreme Court case reviewed Pennsylvania’s Abortion Control Act and struck down several provisions, including a spousal-notification requirement. What case was it?
answer: Thornburgh v. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

question: Which Union campaign of 1862–1863 crossed the Mississippi River south of a strategically important Confederate city, then besieged and captured it on July 4, 1863? Its success gave the Union control of the Mississippi River.
During the Vicksburg Campaign, which Union general led the forces that compelled Confederate General John Pemberton to surrender? He later accepted Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox.
What 1801–1805 conflict pitted the United States against Tripoli amid disputes over piracy and tribute in North African waters?

During the First Barbary War, a U.S.-led force marched across the desert from Egypt and captured this Tripolitan city in 1805. The victory helped pressure the pasha of Tripoli to negotiate. What city was captured?

He became president after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination and clashed with congressional Republicans over Reconstruction. The House impeached this seventeenth U.S. president in 1868, though the Senate fell one vote short of removing him. Who was he?

During Reconstruction, Andrew Johnson’s attempt to dismiss this Secretary of War led the official to barricade himself in his office. His refusal to leave became a central episode in the conflict that prompted Johnson’s impeachment. Who was the secretary?

A congressional investigative panel established in 1938 and initially led by Martin Dies Jr. examined alleged domestic subversion before becoming known for Cold War investigations into Hollywood and suspected communist influence. What was its official name?

At the House Un-American Activities Committee’s 1947 hearings on the film industry, ten screenwriters and directors refused to answer questions about their alleged Communist Party ties. Congress later cited them for contempt, and studios placed them on a blacklist; by what collective name did these witnesses become known?

A Nebraska congressman and Democratic presidential nominee in 1896, 1900, and 1908, he became famous for a convention speech declaring that ordinary people should not be “crucified” on a “cross of gold.” Who was this orator, who later served as Woodrow Wilson’s secretary of state?

In 1925, Tennessee prosecuted an educator under a state law banning the teaching of evolution, and William Jennings Bryan joined the prosecution before Clarence Darrow questioned him about the Bible. What is the commonly used name for this celebrated court case?

She turned opposition to ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment into a national grassroots campaign called STOP ERA and founded Eagle Forum. Which conservative activist used the slogan “I am for Mom and apple pie”?

In 1972, Phyllis Schlafly founded a conservative organization that mobilized grassroots opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment and advocated family-centered policies. What was the name of this organization?

In April 2010, an offshore drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico suffered a deadly explosion, and a blowout at the Macondo prospect released oil for 87 days. What 2010 disaster became the largest marine petroleum release in U.S. history?
During the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, BP's Prospect 252 beneath the Gulf of Mexico was named after a fictional town in a novel by Gabriel García Márquez. What was the source called?

Founded in 2003 by Elizabeth Holmes, this health-technology company claimed its devices could run extensive medical tests using only tiny blood samples. After reaching a reported $9 billion valuation, it dissolved in 2018. What was the company called?

In 2015, this Wall Street Journal reporter investigated Theranos and helped reveal that it used conventional laboratory machines and that its Edison devices might produce inaccurate results. Who was the reporter?

A Republican who served as governor of Texas before becoming the 43rd U.S. president, he held office from 2001 to 2009. His presidency included the September 11 attacks and the U.S. invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq. Who was this president?

George W. Bush’s 2000 victory over his Democratic opponent, the sitting vice president, depended on the outcome of a Florida recount. What Supreme Court case ended the recount dispute and effectively settled the presidential election?

George W. Bush signed a major education law that expanded standardized testing and accountability requirements for public schools. By what commonly used title is the 2001 law reauthorizing the Elementary and Secondary Education Act known?
George W. Bush announced this initiative in 2003 to fund the prevention and treatment of HIV/AIDS, with a major focus on countries in Africa. What is the program’s widely used acronym?
In September 1739, enslaved people in colonial South Carolina seized weapons and began an armed march near the river that gives this uprising its name. What major revolt was this?
During the Stono Rebellion, an enslaved man helped lead the group that seized firearms from a store and marched south. By what name is this leader commonly known?

Added as part of the Education Amendments of 1972, this federal provision bars sex discrimination in education programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. It is frequently invoked in disputes over equal access to school athletics. What is the provision commonly known as?

During debate on Title IX, this Indiana senator was its principal Senate sponsor and argued for extending the sex-discrimination ban to federally funded education programs. A former college football player, he later chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee. Who was he?

Founded in Oakland in 1966, this revolutionary African American political organization advocated community self-defense and established neighborhood programs such as free breakfast for children. What organization was it?

A prominent leader in the Black Panther Party, this Illinois chapter chairman helped organize neighborhood programs and became a target of FBI COINTELPRO. He was killed during a Chicago police raid on his apartment in December 1969. Who was he?

What historic Washington, D.C., theater opened in 1863 and became the site of Abraham Lincoln’s fatal shooting on April 14, 1865? The shooting occurred during a performance of a comedy attended by the president and first lady.
At Ford’s Theatre, what play was being performed when Abraham Lincoln was shot in the presidential box on April 14, 1865? This British comedy by Tom Taylor features the character Asa Trenchard.

In May 2020, a man died in Minneapolis after officer Derek Chauvin held a knee on his neck during an arrest over an alleged counterfeit $20 bill. Bystander video of the killing helped spark worldwide protests against racism and police violence; what event was this?

After the Murder of George Floyd, protesters and community members established a lasting memorial at the Minneapolis intersection of 38th Street and Chicago Avenue, near Cup Foods. What is this intersection and memorial site commonly called?

What collective term identifies the diverse nations and communities with ancestral ties to the present-day United States, including the Cherokee, Ojibwe, Lakota, Spokane, and Coeur d’Alene? It refers to many communities and sovereign tribal nations, not one single nation.
answer: Indigenous peoples of the United States

question: Within the history of Indigenous peoples of the United States, what 1924 federal law conferred federal political membership on Native Americans born in the country who had not previously received that status? Some states continued to deny them voting rights for decades afterward.

In the history of Indigenous peoples of the United States, which 1871 federal law ended the practice of recognizing Native nations as independent nations for treaty-making purposes? It did not erase existing treaties or eliminate tribal sovereignty.

This Massachusetts Democrat has represented her state in the U.S. Senate since 2013. Before entering elected office, she taught law and researched bankruptcy and the financial pressures facing middle-class households. Who is she?

After the 2008 economic crisis, Elizabeth Warren served as a Treasury special adviser helping establish this federal bureau. Created by the Dodd-Frank Act, it consolidated federal oversight of mortgages, credit cards, and other household lending products. What is the bureau?

In 1803, France offered the United States far more than the Mississippi River port of New Orleans, which President Thomas Jefferson had initially sought. The United States agreed to pay $15 million for the vast region west of the Mississippi; what is the conventional name of this acquisition?

During the Louisiana Purchase negotiations, U.S. envoys James Monroe and Robert R. Livingston dealt with Napoleon’s treasury minister, who presented France’s offer to sell the entire territory rather than only New Orleans. Which French official was their principal counterpart?

The Louisiana Purchase expanded U.S. claims westward, but the western boundary with Spain remained disputed. What 1819 treaty settled that boundary and arranged Spain’s cession of Florida to the United States?

Which 1735 New York proceeding ended with a jury acquitting a printer charged with seditious libel for publishing criticism of royal governor William Cosby, and later became celebrated as an early landmark for freedom of the press?

At the John Peter Zenger trial, which Philadelphia barrister served as the printer’s defense counsel and urged jurors to consider the truth of his criticism of Governor William Cosby, helping secure the acquittal?

This powerful New York Republican senator became the leading figure among Republicans who called themselves Stalwarts and defended patronage appointments. He mocked civil-service reform as “snivel service reform” and failed to win the Republican presidential nomination in 1876.
Roscoe Conkling led a Republican faction that defended the spoils system and opposed civil-service reform during the Gilded Age. By what nickname were members of this faction known?
From 1789 until the post–World War II reorganization in 1947, this Cabinet office headed the War Department and oversaw the nation’s military administration. What was the title of the office?

The first person to serve as Secretary of War under George Washington had commanded Continental Army artillery and organized the transport of cannon from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston in 1775–76. Who was he?

In the final months of the War of 1812, New England Federalists met secretly in Connecticut’s capital from December 1814 to January 1815 and recommended constitutional changes, including requiring a two-thirds vote in Congress to declare war. What was this gathering called?

While the Hartford Convention was still meeting, negotiators signed this agreement on December 24, 1814, to end hostilities between the United States and Britain. News of it reached the United States in January 1815, before the convention’s report appeared. What was the agreement called?

In 1957, this Arkansas governor used the state National Guard to prevent nine Black students from entering Little Rock Central High School. President Dwight D. Eisenhower later sent the 101st Airborne Division to enforce their admission. Who was the governor?

Orval Faubus’s resistance to integrating Little Rock Central High School defied a landmark Supreme Court ruling. Which 1954 decision held that racial segregation in public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause?

A former Union general and longtime Ohio congressman, this Republican became the twentieth president of the United States in March 1881. He was shot by Charles Guiteau that July and died several months later; who was he?

After James A. Garfield was assassinated by a disappointed office seeker, pressure grew to replace political patronage with merit-based federal hiring. What 1883 law, signed by President Chester A. Arthur, established competitive examinations for some government jobs?

During this decade, wartime labor needs led to a U.S.-Mexico agreement bringing Mexican workers to the United States, while Executive Order 9066 authorized the forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans, including at Manzanar. What decade links these developments?

During the 1940s, a documentary photographer working for the War Relocation Authority photographed Japanese American residents confined at Manzanar. Her images were largely withheld from public view during the war; who was she?

On April 3, 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. addressed striking sanitation workers at a Memphis church, describing a vision of reaching the promised land even though he might not get there with them. What was the name of this final public speech?
I've Been to the Mountaintop was delivered at a Memphis church that also served as the international headquarters of the Church of God in Christ. What was the church called?

Emerging as one of the first organized political factions in the early 1790s, this party backed commercial interests, a national bank, and a strong central government. Associated with Alexander Hamilton and John Adams, it opposed the Democratic-Republicans. What was this party called?

As the Federalist Party’s leading advocate for a strong national government, which first U.S. Treasury secretary promoted a national bank and argued for broad implied powers under the Constitution? His financial program helped align commercial interests behind the party.

This pre-Columbian Indigenous tradition flourished across much of the southeastern and midwestern United States, relying on intensive agriculture and building large earthen platforms. Which archaeological tradition is associated with monumental settlements such as Cahokia?

Cahokia was a major urban center of the Mississippian Culture, and one of its largest earthen structures still dominates the site. Which flat-topped earthwork rises about 100 feet and covers roughly 14 acres, making it the largest prehistoric earthwork in North America?

Enacted in 1906 during the Progressive Era, this federal statute restricted interstate commerce in adulterated or falsely labeled provisions and medicines. It marked an early expansion of national consumer-protection oversight; what act was it?

Upton Sinclair’s 1906 novel helped draw public attention to dangerous conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking industry and became associated with the reform momentum surrounding the Pure Food and Drug Act. It follows Lithuanian immigrant Jurgis Rudkus; what is the novel’s title?

In 1781, American and French forces under George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau besieged Charles Cornwallis’s British army at a Virginia town. Cornwallis’s troops surrendered there on October 19, bringing large-scale fighting in the Revolution to a close; what campaign was this?

During the Battle of Yorktown, whose French fleet controlled Chesapeake Bay and helped prevent British reinforcements from reaching Cornwallis? This admiral’s naval success helped the allied armies maintain their siege.

In August 1831, an enslaved preacher led a violent uprising in Southampton County, Virginia, in which dozens of white people were killed before state forces crushed it. What is this revolt commonly called?

Nat Turner's Rebellion began in August 1831 in southeastern Virginia, and its first attacks unfolded around the town then called Jerusalem, now Courtland. In which Virginia county did the revolt take place?

A post-Civil War land-redistribution proposal for formerly enslaved Black families became a lasting symbol of Reconstruction’s unfulfilled promises and later reparations debates. Associated with a January 1865 Union order setting aside coastal land from South Carolina toward Florida, what familiar name is given to this proposal?

The proposal known as “Forty acres and a mule” is often linked to a directive issued by Union general William T. Sherman on January 16, 1865. What was the formal designation of the document that reserved coastal land and islands for settlement by formerly enslaved people?

In this 1819 Supreme Court case, a state attempted to tax a branch of the Second Bank of the United States. The Court rejected the tax and affirmed that Congress could exercise implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause. What case was it?

In McCulloch v. Maryland, the Supreme Court upheld Congress's authority to establish a national bank and ruled that a state could not tax a federal institution. Which Chief Justice wrote the Court's opinion?

Which Massachusetts senator, famous for his reply to Robert Y. Hayne that concluded “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable,” joined Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun in the Great Triumvirate?
Which 1842 agreement did Daniel Webster negotiate with a British envoy to settle a boundary dispute between Maine and New Brunswick?

For roughly 18 months in 1860–61, a relay service used mounted riders and stations to carry mail between Missouri and California, aiming to make the journey in under two weeks. What was this service called?

After the Pony Express ended, which stagecoach company acquired its assets, including its distinctive logo, and later became a major U.S. banking company? Its later history included a 2016 scandal over unauthorized customer accounts and fees.

Formed in 1863 as one of the first units of Black soldiers raised in the North, this Union Army force became famous for its assault on Fort Wagner in South Carolina. What unit, led in that attack by a colonel who was killed, became a landmark in African American military service during the Civil War?

During the 54th Massachusetts Regiment’s July 1863 assault on Fort Wagner, this colonel led the regiment and was killed in the attack. A member of a prominent Boston abolitionist family, he was buried in a mass grave with his men; who was he?

What term describes law-enforcement officers’ use of force beyond what is necessary? The issue drew national attention after a traffic-stop beating in Los Angeles was captured on video and helped spark unrest in 1992.

In discussions of police brutality and the unrest that followed the 1992 Los Angeles verdicts, which Black motorist was beaten by LAPD officers during a traffic stop? The incident was captured on video, and he later appealed for people to “get along.”

Founded in Washington, D.C., in 1867, this historically Black research university was named for the Union general who led the Freedmen’s Bureau. Its alumni include Kamala Harris and Thurgood Marshall.

At Howard University, this journalist holds the Knight Chair in Race and Journalism. Her work on the 1619 Project earned her the Pulitzer Prize for Commentary, and she declined a tenured position at the University of North Carolina.
On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd outside the Custom House on King Street, killing five people and wounding six. What name is commonly given to this confrontation?

Among the five people killed in the Boston Massacre was a sailor of mixed African and Indigenous ancestry, identified as the first victim. His death later made him a prominent symbol of Black participation in the struggle for liberty. Who was he?

What name is given to the 1919 baseball controversy in which members of the Chicago White Sox were accused of conspiring with gamblers to lose the World Series? The controversy led to eight players being banned from professional baseball for life.
After the Black Sox Scandal, which federal judge became baseball’s first commissioner and imposed lifetime bans on the eight players? He barred them even after they were acquitted in court.

Which 1969 Supreme Court case arose after Iowa students were suspended for wearing black armbands to oppose U.S. involvement in Vietnam? The Court ruled 7–2 that their quiet, non-disruptive protest was protected by the First Amendment.
answer: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District

question: In Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, which justice dissented, arguing that the armbands could distract students and weaken school officials’ ability to maintain discipline?

A British Army officer in the American Revolution, he met secretly with an American general who planned to surrender West Point. Captured while traveling behind American lines with papers that exposed the plot, he was tried as a spy and hanged. Who was he?

John André’s secret contact was a senior Continental Army officer who negotiated with the British to surrender West Point, a key fortress on the Hudson River, in 1780. Which American general’s scheme was exposed when André was captured?
Fought in Charlestown in June 1775 during the Siege of Boston, this engagement saw British troops capture an American-fortified position after three assaults and heavy casualties. What battle was it?
At the Battle of Bunker Hill, which Boston physician and president of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress fought as a volunteer and was killed during the final British assault?

Commissioned in 1752 for Pennsylvania’s colonial State House, this Philadelphia artifact bears a biblical inscription calling for freedom throughout the land and is displayed across from Independence Hall. What is its familiar name?
The Liberty Bell cracked soon after arriving in Philadelphia and was recast twice by two local founders. Which founder’s surname comes first alphabetically?
The Liberty Bell was commissioned in 1752 for Pennsylvania’s colonial legislature and was then known by a name based on the government building where lawmakers gathered. What was its original name?

This Connecticut-born Continental Army officer helped capture Fort Ticonderoga in 1775 and fought at Saratoga, where he was wounded. While commanding West Point in 1780, he plotted to hand the post over to the British; who was he?

Benedict Arnold's plan to surrender West Point was exposed after a British officer was captured carrying documents that implicated him. The officer was later executed by the Americans; what was his name?

Passed by the Confederation Congress in 1787, this measure organized U.S. territory north of the Ohio River and west of Pennsylvania. It established a path from territorial government to statehood and prohibited slavery in the region, with an exception for fugitive slaves. What was this measure called?

The Northwest Ordinance created an appointed governorship for the territory, and its first governor was a former Continental Army officer from Pennsylvania. In 1791, he commanded U.S. forces in a disastrous defeat by the Western Confederacy at the Battle of the Wabash. Who was this governor?
Created from New York’s 15th National Guard, this African American unit served on the Western Front during World War I under French command. What was its U.S. Army designation?

A soldier in the 369th Infantry Regiment, he and Needham Roberts fought off a German raiding party in the Argonne sector in May 1918. He later received the Medal of Honor for his World War I service; who was he?

After the Baltimore & Ohio imposed another wage cut, workers walked off the job in Martinsburg, West Virginia, and the unrest spread to rail centers across the country. What nationwide labor uprising of 1877 was marked by clashes and federal troop deployments?
During the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, which U.S. president sent federal troops to Martinsburg after West Virginia governor Henry Mathews requested help restoring rail service?
Which Indigenous Algonquian-speaking people of southern New England fought Massachusetts Bay and its allies in a namesake war during the 1630s?

In 1638, colonial leaders in Connecticut signed an agreement that formally ended the Pequot War and imposed terms on the surviving Pequot people, including their dispersal among neighboring peoples. What is this agreement commonly called?

A Massachusetts delegate to the Continental Congress, he signed the Declaration of Independence. He later served as governor of Massachusetts and as the fifth vice president of the United States, under James Madison. Who was he?

During Elbridge Gerry’s governorship of Massachusetts, a state senate district was derided in an 1812 newspaper cartoon for its unusual outline. What term names the practice of drawing electoral district boundaries to give a political party an advantage?

First elected to represent Kentucky in the U.S. Senate in 1984, this Republican became Senate Majority Leader in 2015 and held the post through 2020. In 2017, he invoked the so-called nuclear option to lower the cloture threshold for Supreme Court nominations, helping confirm Neil Gorsuch. Who is this senator?

Mitch McConnell used the phrase “Nevertheless, she persisted” after this Massachusetts senator was blocked from reading a letter by Coretta Scott King during Jeff Sessions’s 2017 confirmation debate. She later drew controversy over claims of Native American ancestry. Who is she?

In 1804, this U.S. naval officer led the night raid that destroyed the captured USS Philadelphia in Tripoli Harbor. During the War of 1812, he later captured the British frigate HMS Macedonian. Who was he?
Stephen Decatur commanded USS United States when it defeated a British frigate off Madeira in October 1812. What was the name of the captured vessel, which was later taken into the U.S. Navy?

In April 1961, U.S.-backed Cuban exiles landed on Cuba’s southern coast in an attempt to overthrow its revolutionary government. The landing force was defeated within days. What was this failed operation called?

The Bay of Pigs invasion was repelled by Cuba’s revolutionary government, led by the man who had overthrown Fulgencio Batista in 1959 and later served as Cuba’s longtime prime minister and president. Who was this leader?

Which New York-born antislavery politician served as secretary of state under both Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson? He helped defuse the Trent Affair and negotiated the 1867 acquisition of Alaska from Russia.
Which 1867 diplomatic transaction did William H. Seward negotiate with Russia for $7.2 million, transferring Russia’s North American territory to the United States?

At the 1787 Constitutional Convention, delegates resolved a dispute between large and small states by creating a two-house Congress: seats in the House would reflect population, while every state would have equal representation in the Senate. What agreement established this arrangement?

The Connecticut Compromise is commonly credited to which Connecticut delegate, a signer of both the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution? He had represented Connecticut in the Continental Congress before attending the 1787 convention.

On December 7, 1941, Japanese aircraft launched in two waves from six carriers struck the U.S. Pacific Fleet at its base on Oahu while the United States was still formally neutral in World War II. The raid killed 2,403 Americans and prompted Congress to declare war on Japan the following day. What event was this?

In planning the Attack on Pearl Harbor, this Japanese admiral envisioned a preemptive strike to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from obstructing Japan’s planned actions in Southeast Asia. He was later killed when U.S. forces intercepted his flight over Bougainville in 1943 during Operation Vengeance. Who was he?

After the Attack on Pearl Harbor, this U.S. president asked Congress for a declaration of war on Japan on December 8, 1941. In his address, he described the previous day as “a date which will live in infamy.” Who delivered the address?
During Reconstruction, what faction of Congress pressed for broad civil and political rights for formerly enslaved people and opposed Andrew Johnson’s lenient policies toward the former Confederacy?
A Pennsylvania congressman among the Radical Republicans became a leading House advocate for impeaching Andrew Johnson and for extending rights to formerly enslaved people. What was his name?
In April 1861, Confederate forces bombarded a Union-held military position in Charleston Harbor, prompting its surrender and beginning the American Civil War. What battle was this?
During the Battle of Fort Sumter, this Union major commanded the garrison after moving his troops from nearby Fort Moultrie. He surrendered the fort after the Confederate bombardment. Who was he?

Which decade saw Bill Clinton win the presidency, the Senate confirmation hearings for Clarence Thomas become a national controversy, and a U.S. president impeached for the first time in more than a century?

In the 1990s, during the Senate Judiciary Committee’s hearings on a Supreme Court nominee, which law professor testified that he had sexually harassed her while they worked together at the Department of Education?
Amos Kendall held this office under Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren, and it oversaw the federal postal system when the role was a Cabinet-level position. What was the office called?
The first United States Postmaster General was appointed under the Continental Congress and later became the primary author of *Poor Richard’s Almanack*. Which Founding Father was he?

This organized-crime network grew among immigrants from Sicily and their descendants, becoming prominent in U.S. cities such as New York and Chicago. After the Castellammarese War, its New York branch was dominated by five major families. What is this network commonly called?

During the 1920s, the Italian-American Mafia profited from illegal liquor sales under a nationwide policy that prohibited the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating beverages. What was this constitutional ban commonly called?
Founded by César Chávez and Dolores Huerta, this union organized agricultural laborers and became nationally known for its efforts in California’s grape industry. What is the name of the labor union?
The United Farm Workers’ co-founder led a 25-day fast in 1968 to emphasize nonviolence during the Delano grape strike. What Mexican-American labor activist was he?

After serving as attorney general and treasury secretary under Andrew Jackson, this Maryland-born jurist became the fifth Chief Justice of the United States in 1836. He held the post until his death in 1864; who was he?

Roger Brooke Taney wrote the Court’s majority opinion in an 1857 dispute brought by an enslaved man who argued that living in free territory made him free. The ruling denied Black people U.S. citizenship and declared Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories; what case was it?

Founded by Spanish Franciscans in 1718 and later converted into a military post, this San Antonio compound endured a 13-day siege by Mexican troops in 1836. What site became a rallying symbol after its defenders were killed?
Among the defenders of the Alamo was this Kentucky-born frontiersman, whose name became attached to a large fixed-blade knife after his celebrated 1827 Sandbar Fight in Louisiana. Who was he?

This Boston political organizer opposed Parliament’s authority to tax the colonies, promoting resistance through newspaper writing and boycotts. He chaired a December 1773 meeting over the Tea Act, later signed the Declaration of Independence, and became governor of Massachusetts. Who was he?

Samuel Adams helped organize these local groups to share information and coordinate colonial resistance to British policies. What were these groups, which connected communities across the colonies, called?

This Detroit-based industrialist incorporated an automaker in 1903 and helped make the Model T affordable through standardized production. In 1914, he drew national attention by announcing a five-dollar daily wage for many factory workers. Who was he?
Henry Ford owned a weekly newspaper that printed a series of antisemitic articles later collected as The International Jew. What was the full title of that newspaper?

Henry Ford’s industrial model linked moving-assembly-line mass production of standardized goods with higher wages and broad consumer access. What term names this system of mass production and consumption?

At a Chicago labor rally on May 4, 1886, a bomb exploded as police moved to disperse the crowd, killing officers and civilians. The violence led to a controversial trial of anarchists and the execution of several defendants; what is this episode known as?
In the aftermath of the Haymarket affair, which German-born anarchist edited Chicago’s Arbeiter-Zeitung and was among the defendants executed in 1887?

Which event began on April 14, 1865, when a Confederate sympathizer shot the sitting U.S. president during a performance of *Our American Cousin* at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C., and ended with the president’s death the following morning at the Petersen Boarding House?
During the assassination of Abraham Lincoln, which actor and Confederate sympathizer fired the fatal shot from a theatre box, escaped into Virginia, and was tracked down and killed on April 26, 1865?
This politician represented Delaware in the U.S. Senate from 1973 to 2009, then served as vice president under Barack Obama before becoming the 46th president of the United States. Who is he?
Joe Biden made two guest appearances as himself during the 2010s on what satirical NBC sitcom? The show follows Amy Poehler’s Leslie Knope as she works in the local government of Pawnee, Indiana.

Which three-day Civil War battle was fought in southern Pennsylvania from July 1–3, 1863, after Robert E. Lee advanced into the North and Union forces under George G. Meade met his army? The Union victory ended Lee’s invasion campaign, and Abraham Lincoln later delivered a cemetery dedication address at the site.

During the Battle of Gettysburg, what is the conventional name for the Confederate assault launched on July 3 against the Union center on Cemetery Ridge? The attack crossed open ground and failed under concentrated Union fire, after which Lee began his retreat the following day.

This influential American publishing family built a newspaper empire that included the New York Journal, and one of its later heirs, Patty, became infamous after a 1970s kidnapping and bank robbery case. What family is it?
Within the Hearst family, which publisher took over the San Francisco Examiner from his father, later acquired the New York Journal, and built a national media empire?

In November 1959, a prosperous farming couple and two of their children were killed in their home in Holcomb, Kansas. What crime later became the subject of a landmark work of nonfiction by Truman Capote?
Which nonfiction novel by Truman Capote reconstructs the Clutter family murders through interviews and a detailed account of the investigation and its aftermath?

Enacted in 2002, this federal campaign-finance statute restricted national party committees from raising and spending certain unregulated “soft money” and regulated electioneering communications funded by corporations and unions shortly before elections. What is its natural title?

In 2010, which Supreme Court decision held that the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act could not constitutionally bar corporations and unions from making independent political expenditures, following a challenge involving a film about Hillary Clinton? The ruling reversed Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce and helped spur the rise of super PACs.

Held July 19–20, 1848, at a chapel in western New York, this landmark meeting was the first U.S. gathering devoted to women’s rights. Its attendees debated resolutions and issued a declaration modeled on the Declaration of Independence. What was this event called?

At the Seneca Falls Convention, delegates adopted a document that began by asserting that “all men and women are created equal” and catalogued grievances about women’s legal and social status. What was this document called?

At the Seneca Falls Convention, this abolitionist was the only African American attendee and argued forcefully for retaining its voting-rights resolution. He had also published *The North Star* and delivered the speech known as “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” Who was he?

A former Nation of Islam spokesman, this Black nationalist later made the Hajj, adopted a new Arabic name, and founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity after breaking with the movement. Who was the activist assassinated in New York City in 1965?

Malcolm X rose to prominence as the Nation of Islam’s chief public spokesman under this leader, who headed the movement during the 1950s and early 1960s. Their relationship ruptured in 1964 when Malcolm X left the organization; who was this leader?

Published in 1965 after Malcolm X’s assassination, this book-length account of his life was produced in collaboration with Alex Haley and drew on extensive interviews between them. What is the title of the work?

Founded by English colonists in 1607 on an island in the James River, this settlement became England’s first permanent settlement in North America. It hosted the colony’s first representative legislative assembly in 1619. What was it called?
In 1676, a colonial uprising driven by political and economic grievances culminated in rebels burning much of Jamestown, Virginia. What was this uprising called?
This investigative journalist developed The 1619 Project, examining the legacy of slavery in the United States, and won the Pulitzer Prize for Commentary for her work on it. Who is she?

Nikole Hannah-Jones holds the Knight Chair in Race and Journalism at a historically Black institution in Washington, D.C. Kamala Harris earned her undergraduate degree there, and Thurgood Marshall graduated from its law school. Name the institution.

Drafted in Philadelphia in 1787, this document replaced the Articles of Confederation when the new federal framework took effect in 1789. Its seven articles establish Congress, the presidency, and the federal judiciary, and it has been amended 27 times. What is this document?

Delegates who drafted the United States Constitution met in this Philadelphia building from May 25 to September 17, 1787. The same building had hosted the signing of the 1776 Declaration. What is it called?

Which agreement reached at the 1787 Constitutional Convention and written into Article I, Section 2 of the United States Constitution governed how enslaved people were counted when allocating House seats and direct taxes? The Fourteenth Amendment later changed the constitutional apportionment rule.

This U.S. economic sector builds, operates, and regulates networks of steel track, using locomotives and coupled cars to carry passengers and freight. Its nineteenth-century expansion helped create national markets and made western farming, ranching, and mining more profitable. What sector is described?

Before becoming a major power in the railroad industry, this New York entrepreneur worked for Thomas Gibbons in his fight against Aaron Ogden’s steamboat monopoly. Nicknamed “the Commodore,” he later consolidated rail lines into the New York Central system. Who was he?

In 1869, the railroad industry reached a landmark when Central Pacific crews building eastward from California met Union Pacific crews building westward from Omaha at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory. What completed route, celebrated with the driving of a golden spike, linked the nation’s eastern and western rail networks?

In 1963, a coordinated direct-action effort in Alabama’s largest city challenged segregation through marches, sit-ins, and boycotts. Its televised confrontations, including police dogs and fire hoses used against demonstrators, helped build support for federal civil-rights legislation. What was this effort called?

During the Birmingham Campaign, this Southern Christian Leadership Conference leader helped guide the 1963 demonstrations. He later delivered the “I Have a Dream” speech in Washington and the “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” speech in Memphis. Who was he?

Passed in 1933 amid widespread bank failures, this U.S. law separated deposit-taking commercial banking from securities underwriting. Its key separation provisions were substantially repealed in 1999. What legislation was it?

Signed by President Bill Clinton in 1999, which federal law allowed commercial banks, securities firms, and insurance companies to affiliate, substantially dismantling key provisions of the Glass–Steagall Act?

In August 1921, West Virginia coal miners seeking union recognition and better working conditions fought government authorities in a week-long armed conflict centered on Logan County. What conflict became one of the largest labor uprisings in U.S. history?

The Battle of Blair Mountain unfolded in 1921, during the administration of the president who campaigned on a “return to normalcy” and defeated Democrat James M. Cox. Which U.S. president was in office?

This mid-19th-century American firearm used a breech-loading mechanism, allowing it to be loaded from the rear rather than down the muzzle. Antislavery settlers in Kansas received it, and it became known by the nickname “Beecher’s Bibles.” What was this firearm called?
The Sharps rifle bears the surname of this American inventor, who received an 1848 patent for a breech-loading rifle design. What was his full name?
Which Spanish explorer and conquistador led the first recorded European expedition to Florida in 1513 and later became linked in legend to a search for a spring said to restore youth?

Juan Ponce de León is associated with an early Spanish expedition to Florida, but decades later Spanish settlers established this northeastern Florida city in 1565. What city is commonly described as the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in the continental United States?

In 1833, the Jackson administration redirected federal deposits away from Nicholas Biddle’s federally chartered financial institution and into selected state-chartered institutions. What name came to be used for those recipients?
The president whose administration established the Pet Banks ordered federal deposits withdrawn from the Second Bank in 1833; the Senate later formally censured him over that removal. Who was he?
Which Indigenous people of the Great Plains developed Northern and Southern branches that played major roles in the history of the American West? Their name is also borne by Wyoming’s capital.
Which Southern Cheyenne peace chief signed the 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise, survived the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre, and was killed during the 1868 attack on his village at the Washita River?

Opened in Chicago on May 1, 1893, this major fair commemorated the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s arrival in the Americas. Its grounds included Jackson Park and the Midway Plaisance. What was the fair called?

At the World’s Columbian Exposition, organizers wanted a landmark attraction that could rival Paris’s Eiffel Tower. The fair’s 264-foot passenger-carrying wheel was conceived and designed by which American civil engineer?

Born near Yuma, Arizona, in 1927, this Mexican American organizer experienced migrant farm labor after leaving school following eighth grade. He later left the Community Service Organization to focus on organizing agricultural workers and co-founded a major farmworker association with Dolores Huerta. Who was he?

In 1962, César Chávez and Dolores Huerta established this association for agricultural laborers. It joined Filipino organizers in the 1965 Delano Grape Strike and later helped form the union now known by the initials UFW. What was the association called?

This pharmaceutical company marketed OxyContin aggressively and pleaded guilty in 2007 to misleading the public about the drug’s risk of addiction. Which company became a major corporate actor in the U.S. opioid crisis?

Purdue Pharma’s marketing and distribution of OxyContin helped fuel a U.S. public-health crisis that spread beyond prescription pain medicines to include heroin and fentanyl. What is this nationwide crisis commonly called?

Born in Brooklyn in 1933, this lawyer became the second woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court after President Bill Clinton nominated her in 1993. Before her appointment, she argued landmark cases against sex discrimination and helped reshape constitutional protections for women. Who was she?

Ruth Bader Ginsburg co-founded and directed this litigation project for a national civil-liberties organization beginning in 1972, using carefully selected cases to challenge sex-based discrimination under the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause. What was the project called?

Fought near Boston on April 19, 1775, these opening engagements of the American Revolutionary War began with a confrontation on a village green and continued at a nearby town where colonial military supplies were targeted. What is this pair collectively called?

During the Battles of Lexington and Concord, this Boston silversmith and member of the Sons of Liberty rode out on the night of April 18, 1775, to warn colonial leaders that British troops were moving toward Concord. Who was he?
An evangelical abolitionist who rejected pacifism, this man led a failed 1859 attempt to seize a federal armory and was later hanged for treason. Who was he?
After pro-slavery forces sacked Lawrence in May 1856, John Brown and his followers killed five pro-slavery men at cabins in eastern Kansas. By what name is this reprisal commonly known?
In October 1859, John Brown’s small band seized a federal arsenal in this town, hoping to arm enslaved people and spark a wider revolt. U.S. Marines soon ended the occupation. What town was the site?
John Brown’s anti-slavery fighters in Kansas used Sharps rifles funded by a prominent Brooklyn preacher, the younger brother of the author of *Uncle Tom’s Cabin*. What was the preacher’s name?
A Massachusetts publisher and radical abolitionist, he founded and edited the Boston newspaper *The Liberator*, whose first issue in 1831 declared that he would not retreat an inch. Who was he?

William Lloyd Garrison publicly burned a copy of this nation’s governing charter in 1854, condemning it as a “Covenant with Death” and an “Agreement with Hell” because it did not outlaw slavery. What document did he burn?

Which Chiricahua Apache leader resisted Mexican and United States expansion in the Southwest before surrendering to U.S. forces in 1886? His years of resistance made him one of the most prominent leaders of the Apache Wars.

Which paratrooper is credited with starting the airborne practice of shouting “Geronimo” after leaping from a cliff near Fort Sill to prove his nerve? His shout connected the Apache leader’s name to a cry later used by U.S. paratroopers.

Abraham Lincoln was shot at Ford’s Theatre in 1865, and John F. Kennedy was shot while riding in a motorcade in Dallas in 1963. What historical crime category is represented by both attacks on sitting U.S. presidents?

During the Assassination of a U.S. President in 1865, the attacker was an actor who shot Abraham Lincoln in the presidential box at Ford’s Theatre, then leapt onto the stage and shouted a Latin slogan meaning “Thus always to tyrants.” Who was he?

Which 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision arose from a nonprofit group’s challenge to restrictions on distributing a film about Hillary Clinton? It held that limits on corporate and union independent expenditures in political campaigns violated the First Amendment.
answer: Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission

question: In Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, the Court invalidated part of a 2002 federal statute that restricted electioneering communications and addressed national-party soft-money fundraising. What statute, co-sponsored by Senators John McCain and Russ Feingold, was at issue?

This crude-oil transport project was built to carry Bakken Formation crude to a terminal in Patoka, Illinois. Its route beneath Lake Oahe near the Standing Rock Reservation became a focus of Indigenous-led demonstrations in 2016, and it began operating in 2017. What is the project called?

During the 2016 protests against the Dakota Access Pipeline, this large water-protector gathering site near Cannon Ball, North Dakota, became a central organizing hub for Indigenous activists and allies. Located near the confluence of the Cannonball and Missouri rivers, it was the largest protest gathering at Standing Rock. What was the site called?
What 1791–1794 uprising in western Pennsylvania began when farmers resisted a federal excise tax on distilled spirits? President George Washington ultimately sent troops to suppress it.
During the Whiskey Rebellion, which first secretary of the treasury advised George Washington and had helped establish the federal excise tax on whiskey as a source of revenue?

Its capital is Jefferson City, and its history includes the conflict triggered by Governor Lilburn Boggs’s 1838 Executive Order 44 against Mormon settlers. Independence, a key early starting point for the Oregon Trail, is also within this state. What state is it?

In 1820, this congressional settlement admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, while restricting slavery in much of the remaining Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′. What was this agreement called?

This 1947 federal labor law amended the Wagner Act, restricted union practices, and allowed states to prohibit union-security agreements. President Harry S. Truman vetoed it, but Congress overrode his veto; what was the law called?

The Taft–Hartley Act became law in 1947 after Congress overrode this president’s veto. This same president issued Executive Order 9981, ordering the desegregation of the U.S. armed forces; who was he?

Enacted in 1935 as a central New Deal response to the Great Depression, this federal law established old-age benefits and unemployment insurance, laying the groundwork for a national safety net. What statute was it?

The Social Security Act drew on recommendations from the Committee on Economic Security, chaired by this U.S. Secretary of Labor, who was the first woman to serve in a presidential Cabinet. Who was she?

What term describes U.S. institutions that separated Indigenous children from their families and communities, often restricting their ancestral languages and customs while imposing English-language instruction and Christian religious teaching?

Among Native American boarding schools, what institution did Army officer Richard Henry Pratt establish in 1879 at former military barracks in Pennsylvania, creating a model for off-reservation education aimed at assimilation?
This U.S. social and political movement sought to reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption. Its advocacy helped bring about the 18th Amendment and the Volstead Act.
A prominent Kansas activist associated with the Temperance Movement became notorious for entering saloons and smashing kegs and bar fixtures with a hatchet. Who was she?

Local revivals beginning in the 1730s grew into a Protestant movement across the American colonies, emphasizing personal conversion and emotionally forceful preaching. Its disputes over itinerant ministers and emotional worship divided some congregations into supporters called New Lights and opponents called Old Lights. What was this movement called?
During the First Great Awakening, which itinerant minister carried revival preaching across colonial regions on a tour from 1739 to 1741? When churches would not admit him, he preached outdoors.

After English settlers found themselves outside the jurisdiction of Virginia’s government in 1620, they agreed to form a self-governing community for their new Plymouth settlement. What agreement did the passengers sign aboard their ship to establish a shared basis for making rules and maintaining order?

The original Mayflower Compact has not survived, so its text is known from a copy in a manuscript history of Plymouth. Which Plymouth governor wrote that history, now held by the State Library of Massachusetts?

Before becoming the 48th vice president, this politician served as governor of Indiana and represented the state’s 6th congressional district in the U.S. House. He served under Donald Trump from 2017 to 2021. Who is he?

While Mike Pence presided over Congress’s electoral-vote count confirming Joe Biden’s 2020 victory, rioters breached the U.S. Capitol and tried to halt the proceeding. What attack is this event commonly called?

After passage of the Indian Removal Act of 1830, the U.S. government forced Cherokee, Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole peoples from their Southeastern homelands to lands west of the Mississippi River. Thousands died from exposure, disease, and starvation during or soon after the journeys. By what name is this displacement chiefly remembered?
Which U.S. president, often associated with the policies behind the Trail of Tears, signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830? He was also known by the nickname “Old Hickory.”

Which 1835 agreement, signed by a small faction of Cherokee representatives over the opposition of principal chief John Ross, was used by the U.S. government to justify Cherokee removal during the Trail of Tears?

On October 8, 1871, a wind-driven blaze swept through a Wisconsin lumber town and killed more people than any other wildfire in recorded U.S. history. It took place the same night as the disaster that devastated Chicago; what is this event called?

The Peshtigo Fire occurred the same night that a major conflagration began near DeKoven Street and devastated a large Illinois city, destroying thousands of wooden buildings. By what name is that 1871 disaster known?

Chartered in 1681, this British proprietary colony was envisioned as a Quaker “holy experiment.” Philadelphia became its principal city, and the 1737 Walking Purchase was a major land dispute within its borders. What colony was it?

The Province of Pennsylvania was granted to this English Quaker proprietor by Charles II in 1681. He promoted religious toleration in the colony and planned Philadelphia around a regular street grid. Who was he?
What Confederate submarine became the first underwater vessel to sink an enemy warship in combat when it attacked USS Housatonic off Charleston Harbor in 1864, before being lost with its crew?
Which Union sloop-of-war became the first warship sunk by a submarine when H. L. Hunley attacked it off Charleston Harbor in February 1864?

Which former Minneapolis police officer was convicted in April 2021 of second-degree unintentional murder and second-degree manslaughter after using a knee restraint during a May 2020 arrest? The incident was captured on video and became a central flashpoint in nationwide protests against police violence.

During the Minneapolis arrest for which Derek Chauvin was convicted of murder, what 46-year-old Black man died after being restrained by officers outside a convenience store in May 2020? Bystander video of the restraint helped spark protests around the world.

In Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, this bar was raided by police in the early hours of June 28, 1969, prompting several nights of resistance that became a landmark in LGBTQ history. What was the name of the bar?

Formed in New York City in 1969 after the uprising at the Stonewall Inn, this radical activist group later protested at the offices of the Village Voice over its coverage of LGBTQ people. What was the group called?

What is the name for the state-organized citizen military forces that supplied much of George Washington’s army during the 1794 campaign in western Pennsylvania against resistance to the whiskey excise?

The American militia is echoed in a Bill of Rights provision whose opening clause describes a well-regulated force as necessary to the security of a free state. Which numbered entry in the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, also protects the right to keep and bear arms?

During the Great Depression, unemployed Americans built informal settlements from salvaged lumber, tin, and other materials. Their name mocked President Herbert Hoover, whom many blamed for the economic crisis. What were these shantytowns called?

Among Hoovervilles, one of the largest and longest-lasting stood on tidal flats near the mouth of the Duwamish River and remained there until 1941. In what Pacific Northwest city was this settlement located?

Beginning in 1956, the FBI used a covert domestic program to infiltrate and disrupt political organizations. It targeted groups such as the American Indian Movement and surveilled a prominent civil rights leader; what was the program called?

Under COINTELPRO, the FBI secretly surveilled this Baptist minister, who led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. In 1964, the Bureau sent him an anonymous letter intended to pressure him to end his activism; who was he?

Founded in 1909 in the aftermath of racial violence and the Springfield race riot, this organization used litigation, public advocacy, local branches, and journalism to oppose discrimination and defend rights guaranteed by the Reconstruction Amendments. What organization is it?
answer: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People

question: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People launched this magazine in 1910, with W. E. B. Du Bois as its editor. Its pages covered civil rights, politics, and Black culture. What was the magazine called?

Born on Staten Island in 1794, this American entrepreneur first built his fortune operating ferries and steamboats around New York Harbor before turning to railroads. Nicknamed “the Commodore,” he later gave $1 million to establish and endow a university in Nashville.
In 1873, Cornelius Vanderbilt made a $1 million gift that helped establish and endow this Nashville institution. What institution received his major philanthropic gift?

A Houston-raised African American man died in Minneapolis on May 25, 2020, after police officer Derek Chauvin knelt on his neck during an arrest. His killing sparked major protests across the United States and around the world. Who was he?

George Floyd was killed in this Midwestern state, whose largest city is Minneapolis and whose capital is St. Paul. The state was also the site of the 2016 killing of Philando Castile. What state is it?

This African American scholar helped found the NAACP and wrote *The Souls of Black Folk*, a work exploring the experiences of Black Americans in the United States. He rejected Booker T. Washington’s accommodationist approach and argued for pressing for civil and political rights. Who was he?

In W. E. B. Du Bois’s *The Souls of Black Folk*, what term describes the divided self-awareness he attributed to Black Americans who must understand themselves both through their own experience and through the perspective of a racist society? He connected this condition to the metaphorical veil separating Black Americans from the wider world.

Born enslaved in Maryland, this abolitionist escaped in 1849 and later returned repeatedly to guide family members and others to freedom. During the Civil War, she served the Union as a nurse, scout, and spy, and helped guide a raid that freed more than 700 enslaved people. Who was this Underground Railroad conductor known as “Moses”?

Harriet Tubman helped guide a Union expedition in June 1863 through South Carolina plantations along a river west of Beaufort. The operation used gunboats and liberated more than 700 enslaved people; what was this Union operation called?

After this 1850 federal law strengthened penalties against people who helped enslaved people escape and required officials in free states to assist in their capture, Harriet Tubman increasingly led escapees farther north into British North America. What law was this?
Fernando Wood was elected to this municipal executive office in 1854 and 1856, and Fiorello La Guardia later served in it from 1934 to 1945. What position is this?

Fernando Wood’s election as Mayor of New York City was supported by this Democratic political organization, whose leaders were called Grand Sachems and whose later infamy was closely associated with “Boss” Tweed. What organization was it?

In 1995, a nationally televised Los Angeles criminal proceeding concerned a former football star accused of killing Nicole Brown and Ronald Goldman. The defense disputed a leather glove found at the scene, and the jury acquitted him; what was this proceeding commonly called?
In the O. J. Simpson murder trial, which California Superior Court judge presided over the televised proceedings and ruled on courtroom procedure throughout the case?

This Oglala Lakota war leader resisted U.S. expansion into the northern Plains and helped lead the Native victory over George Armstrong Custer’s 7th Cavalry in 1876. His legacy is also commemorated by an enormous, still-unfinished mountain sculpture in South Dakota’s Black Hills. Who was he?

Which 1876 battle in Montana Territory, fought along a river of the same name, ended in the defeat of George Armstrong Custer’s 7th Cavalry by Lakota and Northern Cheyenne forces, with Crazy Horse among the Lakota leaders?

What founding document, approved by the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, announced that the thirteen colonies were no longer under British rule and listed grievances against King George III?

The United States Declaration of Independence was drafted by a five-member committee, but its initial text was primarily composed by which Virginia delegate, who later became the nation’s third president?

This Quaker suffragist helped organize the 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington and later founded the National Woman’s Party, whose members picketed outside the White House. She also drafted the constitutional proposal later known as the Equal Rights Amendment. Who was she?

Alice Paul authored this proposed change to the U.S. Constitution, first introduced in Congress in 1923 with Crystal Eastman. Congress approved it in 1972, but it fell three states short of the 38 needed before the extended ratification deadline in 1982. What is it called?

Which Rocky Mountain state saw the Ludlow Massacre and a major Western Federation of Miners strike in the Cripple Creek district? Its capital became the site of a U.S. Mint established to process gold from western rushes.

During Colorado’s labor conflicts, which Western Federation of Miners leader became known as “Big Bill” and helped found the Industrial Workers of the World? He was also tried for the murder of Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg.

What domestic terrorist attack on April 19, 1995, destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in the state capital and killed 168 people? Timothy McVeigh was convicted of carrying it out, and Terry Nichols was also involved.

During the Oklahoma City bombing investigation, which former U.S. Army serviceman was convicted for helping Timothy McVeigh plan the attack and acquire materials for the truck bomb? He was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

A Washington boardinghouse owner was accused of aiding John Wilkes Booth’s circle by making her establishment available to conspirators. A military commission convicted her, and she was hanged in 1865, becoming the first woman executed by the U.S. federal government. Who was she?

Mary Surratt was tried for her alleged role in a conspiracy whose principal act took place at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865, during a performance of *Our American Cousin*. What event did John Wilkes Booth carry out there against the sitting U.S. president?

These government-funded institutions educate children at the elementary, middle, and high school levels. They were the setting for landmark disputes over racial segregation in education and students’ rights to wear political armbands. What are these institutions?

In 1954, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racial segregation in public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause. The case began with a challenge to segregated schools in Topeka, Kansas. What was this decision?
Born in Tuscumbia, Alabama, this author and disability-rights advocate became deaf-blind after an illness in infancy. In 1887, Anne Sullivan began teaching her by spelling words into her hand.
Helen Keller became the first deaf-blind person to earn a degree when she graduated cum laude in 1904 from which women’s institution in Cambridge, Massachusetts?
In March 1862, a Confederate ironclad rebuilt from the former USS Merrimack fought a Union ironclad with a rotating gun turret. What engagement marked the first major clash between ironclad warships?
At the Battle of Hampton Roads, which Union ironclad designed by John Ericsson used a revolving turret and a low-profile hull? It fought the CSS Virginia in the historic 1862 duel.

On June 20, 2020, the Republican presidential candidate held his first in-person campaign appearance in months in Oklahoma’s second-largest city. The event drew attention for unexpectedly sparse attendance, amid reports that some TikTok users had reserved tickets they did not intend to use. What event was this?
At the June 2020 Trump campaign rally in Tulsa, attendees gathered in a downtown arena opened in 2008 and named for an Oklahoma-based financial company. What was the venue?

During the Korean War, President Harry S. Truman ordered the federal seizure of steel mills to forestall a nationwide strike, and the companies challenged the action. What 1952 Supreme Court decision held that the seizure exceeded presidential authority?
answer: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer

question: In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, which justice wrote the Court’s majority opinion rejecting Truman’s seizure of the steel mills? He had joined the Supreme Court in 1937 after serving as a U.S. senator from Alabama.

Born in Harlem to Jamaican immigrant parents, this Army officer entered military service through ROTC at City College of New York and became chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in 1989. Appointed by George W. Bush, he later became the first African American to serve as U.S. secretary of state. Who was he?

In Colin Powell’s February 5, 2003 address to this international body, he presented U.S. intelligence alleging that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction. Later reviews found that some of the intelligence behind his presentation was erroneous. Which body heard the address?

This New York-born real-estate businessman took over his family’s company in 1971 and later became nationally known as the host of a reality television show. He won the 2016 presidential election and served as the 45th president of the United States. Who is he?

Donald Trump hosted a reality-competition series that premiered in 2004, in which contestants competed for a position in his organization and weekly eliminations often ended with his catchphrase, “You’re fired!” What was the series called?
Which Philadelphia upholsterer, born Elizabeth Griscom, became the subject of a famous but historically uncertain account claiming she sewed the first U.S. flag?
Betsy Ross is traditionally said to have sewn a U.S. emblem with thirteen red and white stripes and thirteen stars arranged in a circle on a blue field. What emblem was it?

Which former U.S. Navy SEAL served four deployments in Iraq and became known for having the most confirmed sniper kills in U.S. military history? His memoir was adapted into a 2014 film starring Bradley Cooper.
Which memoir did Chris Kyle write with Scott McEwen and Jim DeFelice about his military service and experiences in Iraq? It later inspired the 2014 film directed by Clint Eastwood.

In 1793, the U.S. Supreme Court considered a suit by the executor of South Carolina merchant Robert Farquhar, who sought payment from a state for wartime goods. The Court held that a citizen of one state could sue another state in federal court, prompting a constitutional amendment. What case was this?
Ratified in 1795 in response to Chisholm v. Georgia, which constitutional provision limits federal jurisdiction over suits against a state brought by citizens of another state or a foreign nation?

In 1970, President Richard Nixon’s Reorganization Plan No. 3 consolidated federal responsibilities for air, water, and land pollution. What newly created independent federal body was charged with protecting public health and enforcing pollution-control laws?

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency traditionally treats December 2, 1970, as its birthday because the Senate confirmed its first administrator that day. This former deputy attorney general became the agency’s inaugural head; who was he?

Which Elizabethan courtier received a royal patent from Queen Elizabeth I to explore and establish English settlements in North America? He sponsored the expeditions that attempted to plant a colony on an island off present-day North Carolina, and the region was named Virginia in the queen’s honor.

Sir Walter Raleigh sponsored an English settlement on this island in present-day North Carolina, where John White served as governor. After White returned from England, the colony was found deserted, with the letters “CRO” carved at the site; what settlement became known as the “Lost Colony”?

This Mexican general and political leader served as president on multiple occasions and commanded the army that defeated the Texian defenders at the Alamo in 1836. He later lost the Texas Revolution and fought the United States in the Mexican-American War. Who was he?

In March 1836, during Antonio López de Santa Anna’s campaign in Texas, Mexican troops killed Davy Crockett, James Bowie, and roughly 200 Texian defenders at this former mission in San Antonio. What site became famous for this siege and last stand?

This Union commander won a decisive victory at Vicksburg, was appointed general-in-chief of Union armies in 1864, and accepted Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House in 1865. He later served as the 18th U.S. president from 1869 to 1877. Who was he?

In 1863, Ulysses S. Grant led Union forces through Mississippi to capture a major Confederate stronghold after a lengthy siege. The victory gave the Union control of the Mississippi River. What was this military operation called?
