Ulysses S. Grant supported ratification of this change to the Constitution, adopted in 1870, which prohibited denying the right to vote on the basis of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. What was this constitutional provision called?
In 1870, Ulysses S. Grant signed legislation establishing this federal agency, which his administration used to prosecute members of the Ku Klux Klan. What was this agency called?
While dying of throat cancer, Ulysses S. Grant completed a two-volume account of his life, which Mark Twain helped publish after Grant’s death in 1885. What is the work’s title?
answer: Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant

question: This Boston-born silversmith and engraver joined the Sons of Liberty and helped organize a network to monitor British troop movements. On April 18, 1775, he rode through Massachusetts to alert nearby communities before the battles of Lexington and Concord. Who was he?
In 1861, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published a narrative poem that dramatizes Paul Revere’s journey to warn Massachusetts communities of approaching British troops. What is the poem’s title?
Which American poet wrote the 1861 poem about Paul Revere’s ride, as well as the narrative poems “Evangeline” and “The Song of Hiawatha”?
Paul Revere made a widely circulated engraving of this 1770 confrontation on King Street, in which British soldiers fired into a crowd and five colonists died. What event was depicted?

Enacted by Congress in 1882 and signed by President Chester A. Arthur, this federal law barred laborers from cities such as Canton and Shanghai from immigrating to the United States for ten years. It is often described as the first major federal immigration restriction based on nationality or ethnicity. What was the law called?

The Chinese Exclusion Act suspended immigration for ten years for this class of Chinese workers, while allowing certain other groups, including students and merchants, to enter under exceptions. What class of workers did it target?

A 1937 shift in Justice Owen Roberts’s voting alignment toward the Supreme Court’s liberal bloc weakened the rationale for Franklin D. Roosevelt’s court-expansion proposal. What humorous phrase, popularized by radio comedian Cal Tinney, became the nickname for this perceived turn?
answer: The switch in time that saved nine

question: The episode nicknamed “the switch in time that saved nine” is linked to the Court’s 1937 decision upholding Washington State’s minimum-wage law in *West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish*. Which associate justice’s vote helped form the five-justice majority in that case?

Which U.S. president was a mining engineer and humanitarian administrator before serving as secretary of commerce under Warren G. Harding and Calvin Coolidge? He became the 31st president and lost his 1932 reelection bid to Franklin D. Roosevelt.

During Herbert Hoover’s presidency, what was the name commonly given to the thousands of World War I veterans who camped in Washington, D.C., in 1932 to demand immediate redemption of their government-issued service certificates? Federal troops later cleared their encampment.
Which southeastern U.S. state includes Birmingham, Selma, and Montgomery, and was the setting for the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing as well as the 1965 Selma voting-rights campaign?
In Alabama, what Selma crossing became associated with voting-rights protests after state troopers assaulted marchers on March 7, 1965, in an episode remembered as Bloody Sunday?
On September 2, 1885, white miners attacked Chinese coal miners in a southwestern Wyoming mining town, killing many and driving survivors from their homes. What is this event known as?
The Rock Springs massacre took place in a coal-mining town that was part of a U.S. territory at the time. What present-day state was the site of the attack?

The disputed 1876 U.S. presidential election was resolved by the Compromise of 1877, after which federal Reconstruction ended. Which Republican became the nation’s 19th president under that settlement?
Rutherford B. Hayes’s wife became the first presidential spouse to earn a college degree, graduating from Wesleyan Female College in 1850. What was her name?

In 1838 Missouri, armed clashes pitted Latter-day Saints against their opponents amid escalating local tensions. The conflict culminated in Governor Lilburn Boggs's directive to drive the Saints from the state; what conflict is this?

During the 1838 Mormon War, Missouri governor Lilburn Boggs issued a numbered state directive declaring Latter-day Saints enemies and commanding their expulsion. What formal title is associated with this infamous measure?

On July 3, 1863, during the final day at Gettysburg, Confederate infantry advanced across open fields from Seminary Ridge toward the Union center on Cemetery Ridge, where the assault was repulsed. What is the name commonly given to this failed attack?
During Pickett’s Charge, the Union II Corps defended a key stretch of Cemetery Ridge against the assault. Which Union major general commanded that corps and was wounded during the fighting?

Amid the Vietnam War and widespread domestic unrest, Republican Richard Nixon defeated Democrat Hubert Humphrey, while George Wallace ran a major third-party campaign. What 1968 contest for the White House does this describe?

During the 1968 United States presidential election, the Democratic convention was held in a city where clashes between antiwar protesters and police became a major televised controversy. Hubert Humphrey was nominated there despite not having competed in the primaries. Which city hosted the convention?

An English soldier and explorer, he helped lead the Jamestown colony and charted much of Chesapeake Bay. His strict leadership is associated with the maxim, “He that will not work shall not eat.” Who was this colonial leader?

In an account of early Jamestown, this Powhatan woman is said to have intervened when John Smith faced danger. She later married the English colonist John Rolfe and traveled to England using the name Rebecca Rolfe. Who was she?

In early 17th-century Virginia, this cultivated leaf became the colony’s leading export crop after John Rolfe established a commercially successful way to grow it at Jamestown. What crop helped shape the region’s economy?
Tobacco became a profitable export at Jamestown in the early 1610s through the efforts of which English colonist, who later married Pocahontas, baptized Rebecca?

This American geologist and Union Army officer led an 1869 descent of the Green and Colorado rivers that included the Grand Canyon, then later served as the second director of the U.S. Geological Survey. What explorer, born in 1834, is described?
John Wesley Powell returned to active service and eventually became a major after a wound in this 1862 Civil War battle cost him his right arm. At which battle was he wounded?

Founded in 1957 after the Montgomery bus boycott, this civil rights organization united Black church leaders across the South and named Martin Luther King Jr. its first president. What organization helped lead major campaigns in Birmingham and Selma?

The Southern Christian Leadership Conference helped organize this 1968 initiative for economic justice, which brought demonstrators to Washington, D.C., and established the Resurrection City encampment on the National Mall. What was this effort called?

This severe global economic downturn began in the late 2000s amid the collapse of the U.S. housing bubble and the subprime mortgage crisis. The failure of Lehman Brothers became one of its defining events. What was this downturn called?

During the Great Recession, this economist chaired the Federal Reserve and promoted quantitative easing. Under his leadership, the Fed bought hundreds of billions of dollars in mortgage-backed securities. Who was he?
Proposed in a 1947 address at Harvard, this American initiative provided economic assistance to help rebuild Western Europe after World War II. What was the program called?
As West Germany’s first chancellor from 1949 to 1963, this Christian Democratic leader oversaw the country’s postwar economic recovery, aided in part by the Marshall Plan. Who was he?

This British North American colony encompassed much of the Hudson and Mohawk river valleys, and its Hudson River corridor became strategically important during the American Revolution. John Burgoyne’s campaign to gain control of that corridor ended in defeat there. What was this colony called?
In the Province of New York, what 1777 battle near the upper Hudson River ended John Burgoyne’s campaign and helped persuade France to ally openly with the American rebels?

Established in 1620 by English religious separatists who arrived aboard the Mayflower, this English settlement was centered in what is now Massachusetts. It remained institutionally distinct from Massachusetts Bay until both were brought under a royal government in 1691. What was this settlement?

Before the settlers chose the site that became Plymouth, they signed this agreement at Cape Cod on November 11, 1620, to establish rules for self-government. What document helped organize the settlers of Plymouth Colony as a political community?

After serving with Cherokee warriors in the Creek War, this self-taught Cherokee developed a writing system that made his people’s language readable and helped make Cherokee-language publishing possible. What was the name of this polymath?

Sequoyah created a system in which most characters represented a spoken syllable rather than a single letter sound, allowing his people’s language to be written and printed. What is this writing system called?

In May 1954, a unanimous U.S. Supreme Court ruling held that state-mandated racial segregation in public schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause, rejecting the application of “separate but equal” to school systems. What landmark case was this?
answer: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka

question: In Brown v. Board of Education, the families challenging Topeka’s segregated school policy were represented before the Supreme Court by the NAACP’s chief counsel, who later became the first African American justice on that Court. Which lawyer was this?

The opinion in Brown v. Board of Education was announced on May 17, 1954, in a 9–0 decision, and the Chief Justice who wrote it emphasized that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Which Chief Justice authored the opinion?

Brown v. Board of Education established that segregated public schools were unconstitutional, but its 1954 ruling did not set out a detailed timetable for implementation. In 1955, the Court issued a follow-up decision directing lower courts to oversee desegregation “with all deliberate speed”; what is this second decision commonly called?

What 1813–1814 conflict in the southeastern United States grew out of civil strife among the Muscogee and saw U.S. forces defeat the Red Stick faction? Andrew Jackson’s victory at Horseshoe Bend brought the fighting to a close.
During the Creek War, what March 1814 engagement on a loop of the Tallapoosa River saw Andrew Jackson’s forces defeat the Red Stick stronghold, helping end the conflict?

What English New England jurisdiction, established as a haven for religious dissenters under Roger Williams and granted a royal charter by Charles II in 1663, was the site of the Great Swamp Fight during King Philip’s War?
answer: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

question: At the Great Swamp Fight in December 1675, English forces attacked a fortified winter village of which Indigenous nation in the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations? The assault took place during King Philip’s War.

The Continental Congress adopted a declaration of separation from Britain on July 4, 1776, and the federal government established by the new nation’s Constitution began operating in 1789. What country comprises 50 states and the District of Columbia for Census Bureau purposes?

In the history of the United States of America, delegates signed this document on September 17, 1787. It established the federal government and replaced the Articles of Confederation; what was it called?

This Atlantic Coast state’s 1832 convention declared federal tariff laws null and void within its borders. It was also the first state to secede from the Union and the site of the 1861 bombardment that began the Civil War. What state is it?

In South Carolina, a state convention’s attempt to nullify federal tariff laws brought a confrontation with President Andrew Jackson in 1832–33. Congress answered with a compromise tariff and a law authorizing the use of force to enforce federal law; what was this crisis called?

At 19, this French aristocrat arrived in America in 1777, accepted a Continental Army major general’s commission, and formed a close relationship with George Washington. In 1781, his troops kept Cornwallis under pressure in Virginia as Washington and Rochambeau prepared the campaign that culminated at Yorktown. Who was he?

The Marquis de Lafayette advocated a written charter setting out individual liberties and civic principles during the French Revolution, but the National Assembly developed its wording collectively and adopted it in August 1789. By what title is this foundational text known?
answer: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

question: Beginning in the United States after the 1929 Wall Street crash and lasting through much of the 1930s, this worldwide crisis brought mass unemployment, bank failures, falling prices, and sharply reduced trade. What was this economic downturn called?

As the Great Depression intensified, this U.S. president defeated Herbert Hoover in 1932 and began the New Deal after taking office in 1933. Shortly after his inauguration, he declared a nationwide bank holiday to help stabilize the banking system. Who was he?

During the Great Depression, drought and severe soil erosion across the southern Great Plains produced “black blizzards” that drove many farm families westward, including migrants labeled “Okies.” What was this environmental disaster of the 1930s called?

This 1939 novel set amid the Great Depression follows the Joad family, tenant farmers driven from Oklahoma who travel west to seek work in California. Its author also wrote Of Mice and Men. What is the novel’s title?

A U.S. Navy pilot shot down over North Vietnam in 1967, he spent more than five years as a prisoner of war before entering politics in Arizona. Which senator later became the 2008 Republican presidential nominee and died in 2018?
During John McCain’s 2008 Republican presidential campaign, which Alaska governor did he choose as his running mate? She became the first woman nominated for vice president by the Republican Party.

This Democrat served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017 and became the first African American to hold the office. He defeated John McCain in 2008 and Mitt Romney in 2012. Who was he?

Barack Obama signed a 2009 federal law that overturned a Supreme Court interpretation of the 180-day filing deadline for pay-discrimination claims, allowing each discriminatory paycheck to trigger a fresh deadline. What was this law called?

During Barack Obama's first year in office, he nominated this federal appeals judge to the Supreme Court, where she became the first Hispanic American justice. She succeeded David Souter. Who was she?

This Confederate cavalry commander rose from private to lieutenant general during the Civil War and led the attack at Fort Pillow. After the war, he became the first Grand Wizard of the original Ku Klux Klan. Who was he?

In April 1864, Nathan Bedford Forrest’s Confederate cavalry overran a Union-held riverside installation in Tennessee, where many Black Union soldiers were killed after the defenders surrendered. What atrocity is named for that installation?

In 1977, this activist won election to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, becoming California’s first openly gay elected official. He was assassinated at City Hall the following year. Who was he?
Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone were killed at San Francisco City Hall in 1978 by this former city supervisor, whose trial centered on a diminished-capacity defense. Who was the assailant?

This 1675–1678 conflict in New England involved Wampanoag and other Native forces, English colonies, and Native allies of the English—not simply two uniform sides. Its December 1675 fighting included an attack on a Narragansett winter settlement in present-day Rhode Island. What conflict was this?

During King Philip’s War, colonial forces attacked this Narragansett winter settlement in December 1675, in what is now Rhode Island. The assault killed many people and helped bring the Narragansett into the conflict; by what name is the battle commonly known?

Formed in Montgomery, Alabama, before Abraham Lincoln’s inauguration, this secessionist government began with seven states and grew to eleven after the attack on Fort Sumter. It fought the Union until its defeat in 1865. What was this breakaway government called?
The Confederate States of America chose this former U.S. senator from Mississippi as its president in 1861. He had earlier served as secretary of war under President Franklin Pierce. Who was he?

This U.S. cabinet-level body oversees the Census Bureau and promotes trade, economic development, and technological innovation. It became independent from the federal labor administration in 1913. What is its name?

During the 1920s, this future U.S. president served as secretary of the Department of Commerce, promoting business standardization and helping expand federal involvement in aviation and radio. Who was he?

In November 1979, students seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and detained American personnel for 444 days. What diplomatic crisis concluded with their release on January 20, 1981, the day Ronald Reagan was inaugurated?

During the Iran hostage crisis, President Carter authorized a U.S. rescue attempt that reached the staging site known as Desert One in April 1980. Mechanical problems forced the mission to be aborted, and a collision there killed eight U.S. servicemen; what was the operation called?

During the Civil War, this Georgia rail and supply hub was captured by Union forces in September 1864, prompting the Confederate evacuation of the city. It later became the state’s capital and largest city; what is its name?

During the 1864 campaign to capture Atlanta, this Union commander led the forces that took the city and later marched from there toward Savannah. In 1865, he also issued Special Field Orders No. 15; who was he?
Issued in 1823 as part of a U.S. president’s annual message to Congress, this U.S. policy opposed new European colonization and political intervention in the Americas. What is this policy called?

While serving as secretary of state, this diplomat opposed a proposed joint U.S.–British declaration and helped shape the Monroe Doctrine as a separate American statement. He later negotiated the 1819 treaty that transferred Florida from Spain to the United States and became the sixth U.S. president. Who was he?

The first woman to run for U.S. president, she was an Ohio-born suffrage advocate and reformer who, with her sister Tennessee Claflin, operated a brokerage firm on Wall Street. Who was this candidate, nominated in 1872?
Victoria Woodhull ran in the 1872 presidential election on a third-party ticket that also named Frederick Douglass as its vice-presidential nominee. What was the party called?
Which African American journalist and anti-lynching campaigner published *Southern Horrors* and *The Red Record*, documenting racial violence in the United States? She also helped found the NAACP.

Ida B. Wells co-owned and edited the newspaper *Free Speech and Headlight* in which Tennessee city? The city was also the setting for the 1968 sanitation workers’ strike during which Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” speech.

Conducted by the U.S. Public Health Service in partnership with a historically Black college in Macon County, Alabama, from 1932 to 1972, this project followed 399 Black men who had a bacterial sexually transmitted infection and 201 who did not. Researchers neither obtained informed consent nor offered available treatment; what was this notorious research project called?

The Tuskegee syphilis study helped spur federal action on protections for human research participants. Published in 1979, this document set out three guiding principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice; what is its name?

Born Phoebe Ann Moses in Darke County, Ohio, this performer hunted and sold game as a child to help support her family. She later became a celebrated trick shooter after joining a famous Wild West show in 1885; who was she?

Annie Oakley became a featured star after joining this touring spectacle in 1885, which presented frontier-themed performances and sharpshooting before large audiences. What was the name of the production?

After the Supreme Court’s 1954 ruling in *Brown v. Board of Education* rejected state-mandated racial separation in public schools, federal courts and civil-rights advocates pressed districts to dismantle that system. What process did Senator Harry Byrd’s “Massive Resistance” campaign seek to obstruct?
Which 1954 Supreme Court decision became a landmark in school desegregation after families in Topeka, Kansas, challenged segregated public schools?

This officer presides over the Supreme Court of the United States and leads its judicial branch. When the Senate tries a president for impeachment, this officer presides over the trial. What is this office called?
answer: Chief Justice of the United States

question: The longest-serving Chief Justice of the United States, this Virginian led the Court from 1801 to 1835. He wrote the opinion in *Marbury v. Madison*, which established the principle of judicial review. Who was he?
Article II vests federal executive power in this four-year office, whose holder also serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. What office is this?
In the constitutional process for choosing the President of the United States, voters select electors who then cast the formal votes for president. What is this system called?

As Abraham Lincoln’s secretary of war, he led the department through the Civil War and became central to a postwar clash when he refused to surrender his office after Andrew Johnson tried to dismiss him. What cabinet official’s resistance helped precipitate Johnson’s impeachment crisis?

Edwin McMasters Stanton’s refusal to leave the War Department after Andrew Johnson attempted to remove him in 1868 became a test of presidential authority. What federal law, enacted in 1867, was at the center of the dispute and later figured in Johnson’s impeachment?

Before entering electoral politics, this cardiothoracic surgeon became a regular guest on The Oprah Winfrey Show and later hosted a daytime health program. In 2022, he was the Republican nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Pennsylvania, losing the general election to John Fetterman; who was he?

Mehmet Oz's 2022 Republican Senate campaign took place in this state, whose capital is Harrisburg and whose Democratic nominee, John Fetterman, defeated him in the general election. What state was it?

What 1797 publication did Alexander Hamilton issue as a public defense after allegations about his private life became entangled with accusations of financial misconduct? It disclosed his relationship with a married woman and argued that payments to her husband were meant to conceal the affair, not to cover up political corruption.
In The Reynolds Pamphlet, Alexander Hamilton admitted to a relationship with this woman while insisting that her husband, James, had blackmailed him. Who was she?

Andrew Jackson relied on an informal circle of political advisers who operated beyond the formally appointed heads of executive departments. What name is commonly given to this group, which included Francis Preston Blair and Martin Van Buren?
A prominent member of the Kitchen Cabinet edited the pro-Jackson Washington Globe and later helped establish the Congressional Globe. Who was this journalist and political adviser?

What U.S. cultural ideal holds that opportunity and individual effort can lead to prosperity and upward social mobility, often symbolized by owning a home? Historian James Truslow Adams gave the ideal a famous formulation in a 1931 book.
The American Dream became widely associated with a historian’s 1931 book arguing that the nation’s promise meant more than material wealth. Who wrote that book, titled *The Epic of America*?

A former Notre Dame law professor and judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, she was nominated by Donald Trump in September 2020 and confirmed the following month to fill the vacancy left by Ruth Bader Ginsburg. Who is she?
Amy Coney Barrett joined this nine-member tribunal in October 2020, becoming its fifth woman justice. What is the nation's highest federal judicial body?
answer: Supreme Court of the United States

question: This former FBI official rose to the bureau’s second-highest post and secretly supplied information to Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward during an investigation of a presidential break-in and cover-up. His family publicly identified him in 2005 after decades of speculation about the source known by a two-word codename. Who was he?

W. Mark Felt’s anonymous information helped Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein trace the 1972 break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters and the administration’s efforts to conceal it. What political crisis led to Richard Nixon’s resignation in 1974?

In Virginia’s Tidewater, a network of Algonquian-speaking communities formed a paramount chiefdom whose leader’s principal village was Werowocomoco. It traded and fought with the Jamestown settlers after their 1607 arrival; what was this Indigenous alliance known as?

The Powhatan Confederacy was headed during the founding of Jamestown by a paramount chief whose daughter Pocahontas became known for her contacts with the English. Often called Chief Powhatan by the colonists, what was this leader’s personal name?

A Massachusetts writer who educated herself from her father’s books, she wrote to her husband in March 1776 urging him to consider women when making new laws. She later became the wife of the second U.S. president and the mother of the sixth. Who was she?
Abigail Adams’s son served as secretary of state under James Monroe before becoming the sixth U.S. president in 1825. What was his name?

He became FBI director in September 2001, just days before the September 11 attacks, and later served as special counsel investigating Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Who is this former federal prosecutor whose investigation produced a 2019 report?

In March 2019, this attorney general sent Congress a letter summarizing the findings of Robert Mueller’s investigation before the full report was released. Which U.S. attorney general issued that summary?
Which American newspaper publisher took control of the San Francisco Examiner in 1887 and later built a coast-to-coast media empire that included the New York Journal?

In a 1903 newspaper story, William Randolph Hearst’s New York Journal falsely portrayed this sharpshooter and Buffalo Bill’s Wild West performer as a cocaine addict who stole money to support her habit. Born Phoebe Ann Mosey, who was the woman targeted in the story?

A six-day wave of wartime violence erupted in Los Angeles when servicemen and others attacked young people wearing conspicuously wide-legged, fabric-heavy outfits. What is the name of this 1943 unrest?

The Zoot Suit Riots followed a notorious 1942 Los Angeles prosecution after the killing of José Díaz, in which Mexican American youths faced accusations widely criticized as racially biased. By what name is that case commonly known?
The Zoot Suit Riots took place in Los Angeles during the summer of 1943 and lasted six days. What dates mark their duration?

This 34th U.S. president served from 1953 to 1961 after commanding Allied forces in World War II, including the D-Day invasion. Before entering the White House, he also became NATO’s first supreme commander. Who was he?

Dwight D. Eisenhower signed Executive Order 10450, which expanded federal employee security screening and led to the dismissal of thousands of LGBTQ+ government workers. What name is given to this campaign of purges during the Cold War?

Dwight D. Eisenhower backed a nationwide, limited-access route network authorized by a 1956 federal law. Its routes were numbered, and its construction was partly inspired by his wartime experience with Germany’s Autobahn. What is this network called?

On September 5, 1975, a member of the Manson Family pointed a pistol at the sitting U.S. president outside the state capitol in Sacramento, but the weapon did not fire. What is this incident known as?
answer: Attempted assassination of Gerald Ford by Squeaky Fromme

question: During the attempted assassination of Gerald Ford by Squeaky Fromme, the encounter took place at the seat of the state government, near the state capitol building. Which city was the scene?

What name is given to the 1920s African American cultural flowering centered in a New York City neighborhood that became a major center of Black artistic life after World War I? Its writers, musicians, performers, and visual artists explored Black identity and life across poetry, jazz, theater, and the visual arts.
During the Harlem Renaissance, which Jamaican-born poet published *Harlem Shadows* and wrote the sonnet “If We Must Die,” whose speaker urges a threatened people to resist rather than submit?

In 1876, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces defeated and annihilated a U.S. Army cavalry regiment commanded by a Civil War general in present-day Montana. What battle is named for the nearby river?

At the Battle of the Little Bighorn, this U.S. Army lieutenant colonel led the 7th Cavalry Regiment against Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces. His death in the defeat made him the battle’s most famous U.S. casualty. Who was he?
What secret audio recordings captured conversations in the president’s executive offices during Nixon’s administration and became key evidence in the Watergate scandal and United States v. Nixon?
In the dispute over the White House tapes, what 1974 Supreme Court case rejected a president’s broad claim of executive privilege and required him to turn over subpoenaed recordings?

Enacted by Parliament in 1774 after the Boston Tea Party, this punitive package included laws that curtailed Massachusetts self-government and shut Boston Harbor until compensation for the destroyed tea was made. What name did colonial opponents give the package?

One measure within the Intolerable Acts took effect on June 1, 1774, halting commercial traffic through the principal harbor of Massachusetts until the colony met British conditions, including restitution for the tea destroyed in the protest. What was this law called?

This four-year conflict began after Southern states seceded from the United States, and its opening bombardment targeted a federal fort in Charleston Harbor in April 1861. It ended with the Confederacy’s collapse and the abolition of slavery; what conflict was it?

Issued by Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, this wartime order declared enslaved people in areas still in rebellion to be free, while leaving slavery untouched in loyal border states. During the American Civil War, what document helped make ending slavery an explicit Union war goal?

During the American Civil War, a Union campaign culminated in the surrender of a major Confederate stronghold on the Mississippi River on July 4, 1863. The victory gave the Union control of the river and split the Confederacy; what city was captured?

What post-Civil War interpretation portrays the Southern rebellion as a noble defense against Northern aggression while minimizing slavery’s role in the war? It gained influence through monuments, memoirs, and histories that romanticized the secessionist South.

Which 1864 Union campaign crossed Georgia from Atlanta to Savannah, where the captured city was presented to Abraham Lincoln as a Christmas gift? Supporters of the Lost Cause cited its destruction as an example of Northern aggression.

By the time English settlers reached Jamestown in 1607, this leader headed Tsenacomoco, a Tidewater Virginia confederacy that had grown from an inherited core of six tribes. He was Pocahontas’s father, and his death was reported in 1618; who was this paramount chief, often identified by the personal name Wahunsenacawh?

Powhatan held this title as the paramount chief of Tsenacomoco when the English arrived in 1607. It designated his position above a confederacy whose local chiefs and councils also retained political roles; what was the title?
On April 18, 1942, sixteen B-25 Mitchell bombers took off from a U.S. Navy carrier to strike targets on the Japanese home islands. What is this American air operation commonly called?

During the Doolittle Raid, the B-25 bombers launched from the carrier that had sailed from San Francisco carrying the aircraft and joined Vice Admiral William Halsey’s task force. What was the carrier’s name?
Which American con artist and serial killer became associated with a Chicago hotel he owned during the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition? His crimes made him one of the era's most notorious figures.

H. H. Holmes was associated with Chicago when the city hosted a major international fair in 1893, commemorating the 400th anniversary of Columbus's first voyage. The fair's grounds became known for their striking white buildings; what was the fair officially called?

After serving as San Francisco district attorney, California attorney general, and a U.S. senator from California, this politician became vice president in 2021 alongside President Joe Biden. She was the first woman, African American, and Asian American to hold the vice presidency. Who is she?

Kamala Harris earned her bachelor’s degree at this historically Black institution in Washington, D.C., before studying law at UC Hastings. Founded in 1867, it is also the alma mater of Thurgood Marshall. What is the institution’s name?

A World War II bomber pilot and longtime South Dakota Democrat, he represented the state in the Senate and became the Democratic nominee for president in 1972 on an anti-Vietnam War platform. Who was this candidate, whom Richard Nixon defeated in a landslide?

After George McGovern’s original vice-presidential nominee, Thomas Eagleton, withdrew from the 1972 Democratic ticket, whom did McGovern choose as his replacement? The new running mate had directed the Peace Corps and served as U.S. ambassador to France.

In 1969, federal prosecutors charged antiwar activists with conspiring to incite riots and crossing state lines for that purpose, following protests around the 1968 Democratic National Convention. What is this proceeding commonly called?

At the Chicago Seven trial, which prominent defense attorney represented several defendants and repeatedly challenged Judge Julius Hoffman’s courtroom rulings, earning multiple contempt citations during the proceedings?

A South Carolina statesman became Andrew Jackson’s vice president in 1829 and later broke with him over federal authority and tariff policy. He resigned the vice presidency in 1832 amid political tensions that included the controversy surrounding Peggy Eaton; who was he?

As John C. Calhoun’s break with Andrew Jackson deepened during the conflict surrounding Peggy Eaton, Jackson increasingly consulted trusted advisers outside the official group of department secretaries. What nickname was given to the informal circle that included Francis Preston Blair and Martin Van Buren?

After the Continental Army withdrew following the battles of Brandywine and Germantown, it spent the winter of 1777–1778 in this Pennsylvania encampment. What was the site where Washington’s troops endured severe hardship while receiving military training?

At Valley Forge, which Prussian-born military officer, formerly in the service of Frederick the Great, trained Continental soldiers in disciplined drill and bayonet tactics during the winter of 1777–1778?

Created under the National Security Act of 1947 and formally established on September 18 of that year, this civilian executive-branch body gathers and analyzes information about foreign countries for U.S. national-security officials. It may conduct covert action when directed by the president, but it does not set policy or serve as a domestic law-enforcement organization. What is it?

Before the Central Intelligence Agency was established, this World War II organization, led by William J. Donovan, gathered intelligence and supported resistance groups and covert operations abroad. What was its full name?

She became the first woman to win a major U.S. party’s presidential nomination as the Democratic nominee in 2016, after serving as a U.S. senator from New York and as secretary of state. Identify this American politician.

During Hillary Clinton’s tenure as U.S. secretary of state, a September 2012 attack on a U.S. diplomatic compound in eastern Libya killed Ambassador Chris Stevens. What city gives this attack its commonly used name?

Hillary Clinton graduated in 1969 from this Massachusetts women’s school, after serving as president of its student government; she also became the first student to deliver the school’s commencement address. Name the school.

During the Eisenhower administration, federal agencies investigated and dismissed thousands of employees suspected of being gay, often treating their sexuality as a security risk. What name is given to this mid-20th-century campaign?

The Lavender Scare intensified after this 1953 federal directive broadened security investigations of federal employees and allowed dismissals on security grounds. Dwight D. Eisenhower signed it. What was its number?

This Illinois Democrat, nicknamed the “Little Giant,” championed popular sovereignty and faced Abraham Lincoln in the seven 1858 debates over an Illinois Senate seat. He later ran as the Northern Democratic candidate in the 1860 presidential election. Who was he?

Stephen A. Douglas helped shape an 1854 federal law that organized two territories west of Missouri and Iowa and let their settlers decide whether to permit slavery, overturning the Missouri Compromise’s restriction in the region. What was this law called?
Ratified in 1920 after decades of organizing, this addition to the nation's founding charter barred denying citizens the vote on account of sex. What is its commonly used name?
answer: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

question: Although the Nineteenth Amendment established nationwide constitutional protection in 1920, women had already gained voting rights in the territory that later became this state. It is also home to Yellowstone, the first U.S. national park. Which state is it?

This American family built its prominence from New York real estate and later became central to national politics. Its most prominent member served as both the 45th and 47th U.S. president in nonconsecutive terms, and the family includes a Slovenia-born former first lady. What family is it?
Within the Trump family, which Slovenia-born former model became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2006 and served as first lady during both of her husband's presidential administrations?

First introduced in Congress in December 1923 after being drafted by Alice Paul and Crystal Eastman, this proposed constitutional change would prohibit the denial or abridgment of equality on account of sex. Congress approved it in the 1970s, but it did not meet its ratification deadline.

This Michigan representative reintroduced the Equal Rights Amendment in 1971, helping move it toward congressional passage. In 1963, she had used a discharge petition to bring the Equal Pay Act to a vote in the House.

The Equal Rights Amendment was coauthored by this lawyer and journalist, who helped organize the Women's Peace Party in 1915. She also helped establish the National Civil Liberties Bureau, a precursor to the ACLU.

This conservative activist organized opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment through the STOP ERA campaign, arguing that it could undermine legal protections for women. She founded the Eagle Forum, a political organization that continues to advocate conservative causes.

Which Confederate state did William Tecumseh Sherman cross during his 1864 March to the Sea, after capturing its railroad hub at Atlanta? His troops tore up rails and twisted them into loops known as “Sherman’s neckties.”
At which coastal Georgia city did Sherman’s March to the Sea conclude? The city was also the site of the 1779 siege where Casimir Pulaski was mortally wounded while leading a cavalry charge.

Adopted by delegates at Washington-on-the-Brazos on March 2, 1836, this independent country emerged from the revolution against Mexico and was recognized by the United States the following year. Congress approved its annexation in 1845, after which it became the Union’s twenty-eighth state. What was this nation called?

During the Republic of Texas’s fight for independence, this commander led the Texian army to victory at San Jacinto in April 1836, where Santa Anna was captured. He later served as the republic’s first president, and its largest city bears his surname. Who was he?

Between about 1916 and 1970, millions of African Americans left the rural South for cities in the North, Midwest, and West, seeking greater opportunity and escape from Jim Crow discrimination. What is the name of this large-scale movement?

During the Great Migration, this civil-rights organization encouraged African Americans to seek opportunity beyond the Jim Crow South. W. E. B. Du Bois was among its leading figures, and its magazine was called The Crisis. What organization was it?

In May 1937, Ford security guards attacked United Auto Workers organizers and supporters outside the River Rouge Plant, near an elevated pedestrian crossing. What is this labor confrontation commonly called?

The Battle of the Overpass took place at the River Rouge complex of a Detroit automaker whose founder instituted the $5-a-day wage and helped popularize assembly-line production of the Model T. Which industrialist founded the company?

At the 1896 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, a former Nebraska congressman delivered a forceful address urging bimetallism and warning that working people should not be “crucified” by the nation’s monetary policy. What was the address called?

In the Cross of Gold Speech, William Jennings Bryan argued that the U.S. Mint should coin a precious metal at a 16-to-1 ratio with gold, expanding the currency rather than restricting it to gold alone. What monetary policy did he advocate?

On March 25, 1911, 146 people, mostly young immigrant garment workers, died at a clothing business occupying the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors of Manhattan’s Asch Building. The tragedy became a landmark in campaigns for workplace safety. What event was it?
After the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire, state lawmakers established a special body to investigate industrial working conditions and recommend workplace protections. What was this body called?
answer: New York State Factory Investigating Commission

question: This Black emergency medical worker was fatally shot by police in her Louisville apartment in 2020. Her death helped spark nationwide protests against police violence. Who was she?
A contemporary American painter portrayed Breonna Taylor with grayscale skin tones against an aqua background. The same artist painted the official portrait of Michelle Obama. Who is this painter?

Each spring, Washington, D.C., hosts an annual gathering organized by journalists who cover the president and the executive branch. Its program traditionally mixes political figures, a comedian’s satirical remarks, and a presidential routine; what event is it?

At the 2017 White House Correspondents' Dinner, which comedian was the featured speaker, delivering a satirical roast of the Trump administration? He served as a correspondent on The Daily Show during both Jon Stewart’s and Trevor Noah’s tenures and later hosted the weekly Netflix series Patriot Act.

During Andrew Jackson’s presidency, Washington society women ostracized the wife of his Secretary of War, turning a dispute over her social acceptance into a national political controversy. What was this scandal called?
During the Peggy Eaton Affair, which widowed member of Jackson’s cabinet publicly supported the Eatons and later became Jackson’s vice president?

Which 1857 Supreme Court case arose from an enslaved man’s claim to freedom after living in free territory? Its ruling denied African Americans constitutional citizenship and invalidated the Missouri Compromise.
In Dred Scott v. Sandford, the majority opinion was written by the Chief Justice who had taken office in 1836 after John Marshall. Identify that jurist.

Founded in Alabama in 1881 by Booker T. Washington, this historically Black institution trained teachers and became an influential center of agricultural education and research under George Washington Carver. What institution is it?

At Tuskegee University, this agricultural scientist led research and promoted crop rotation to help restore Southern farmland. Which researcher became known for practical work involving crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes?

In July 1925, a Tennessee public-school teacher was prosecuted in Dayton for teaching evolution in violation of a state law. The case became a national spectacle after defense lawyer Clarence Darrow and prosecutor William Jennings Bryan faced off in court; what is the case commonly called?

In the Scopes trial, prosecutors relied on a Tennessee statute that barred public-school teachers from teaching accounts of human origins that contradicted the Bible’s account of divine creation. What was this law called?

He became president after John F. Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963, having served as Kennedy’s vice president. A Texas Democrat, he promoted the Great Society and signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Who was this 36th U.S. president?

In 1964, Lyndon B. Johnson asked Congress to respond after reports of clashes involving U.S. and North Vietnamese forces in this body of water off North Vietnam. The resulting congressional measure gave him broad authority to take military action in Southeast Asia and later became a central justification for expanding the Vietnam War. What was this measure called?

Lyndon B. Johnson signed this landmark federal law on August 6, 1965, after urging Congress to protect Black Americans’ access to the ballot. It outlawed literacy tests and authorized federal examiners and oversight in areas with histories of voter discrimination. What was this law called?

Delivered from the Lincoln Memorial steps during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on August 28, 1963, this address called for a future in which people would be judged by their character rather than their skin color. What speech became one of the best-known addresses of the civil rights movement?
The address I Have a Dream was delivered by this Baptist minister, who led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and helped organize the 1963 March on Washington. Who was the speaker?

During the Vietnam War, opponents of conscription sometimes set fire to documents issued to men who registered for compulsory military service, making the papers a visible symbol of protest. What were these documents called?
Draft cards were issued as proof of registration through the U.S. federal agency that maintained records of eligible men and administered the military draft. What was the agency called?

This Arizona Republican served multiple terms in the U.S. Senate and won the GOP presidential nomination in 1964 after a contest with Nelson Rockefeller. Running on a staunchly conservative platform, he lost the general election to Lyndon B. Johnson in a landslide; who was he?

In a nationally televised 1964 address, Ronald Reagan made a case for Barry Goldwater’s presidential bid by warning that an expanding federal government endangered individual liberty. The broadcast helped establish Reagan as a national political figure; what was the address called?

Cato’s 1739 rising near South Carolina’s Stono River and Nat Turner’s 1831 action in Virginia are two well-known examples of the same kind of resistance. What is the general term for an organized effort by enslaved people to overthrow their enslavers?

A notorious slave revolt in Virginia began in Southampton County in 1831 after its leader, a preacher, interpreted a solar eclipse as a sign. What event, named for that leader, was suppressed after killing dozens of white residents?

Fearing that Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb first, the United States organized this secret wartime research and engineering program under Army General Leslie Groves. Its work linked Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, and Hanford, and culminated in the Trinity test. What was the program called?
Within the Manhattan Project, this Tennessee site became the center for enriching uranium, while Hanford produced plutonium and Los Alamos designed the bombs. What was the site known as?

Born in St. Ann’s Bay, Jamaica, this Black nationalist founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association and promoted Pan-Africanism and a return to Africa. Which activist also launched the Black Star Line?
In 1914, Marcus Garvey founded a mass-membership organization in Jamaica that promoted Black unity and the uplift of people of African descent. What was this organization called?

A Georgia Republican elected secretary of state in 2018, this official oversaw the state’s election administration during the 2020 presidential contest. In a January 2021 phone call, Donald Trump urged him to find enough votes to change Georgia’s result. Who was the official?

A recording of the January 2021 phone call between Brad Raffensperger and Donald Trump was published by this national newspaper. Its report brought the conversation—during which Trump pressed Georgia’s secretary of state to change the election result—to widespread attention. What newspaper published it?

In 1978, the Supreme Court reviewed a public medical school's policy reserving 16 of 100 seats for applicants from disadvantaged groups. The Court struck down that set-aside but allowed race to be considered as one factor in admissions. What case was this?
answer: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke

question: In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, what medical school operated the admissions program that reserved 16 seats in each entering class for applicants from disadvantaged groups? The institution was the public medical school where the applicant sought admission.

Which Cold War-era conflict, fought from 1955 to 1975, pitted a communist northern government and its allies against a U.S.-backed southern government and other anti-communist forces? The capture of Saigon in 1975 brought the fighting to a close.
During the Vietnam War, what was the name of the classified U.S. Defense Department study on American involvement in Vietnam that Daniel Ellsberg leaked to The New York Times in 1971?
This Cabinet office heads the Department of State and directs U.S. diplomacy and foreign policy. What is the title of the position?

During Hillary Clinton’s tenure as United States Secretary of State, a 2012 attack on a U.S. diplomatic compound in Libya killed Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens. In which Libyan city did the attack take place?

This Cuban revolutionary led the 26th of July Movement in the overthrow of Fulgencio Batista and established Cuba’s communist government. He ruled the country for decades before transferring power to his brother Raúl in 2008. Who was he?
During the revolution that brought Fidel Castro to power, rebels attacked the Presidential Palace in the city that remains Cuba’s capital. What is the city?
In 1807, amid maritime tensions between Britain and France, the United States enacted a law barring American trade with foreign nations in hopes of avoiding conflict. What was the law called?
The Embargo Act of 1807 was signed by the third U.S. president, a Virginian who drafted the Declaration of Independence and lived at Monticello. Who was that president?

As Indiana's Grand Dragon of the Ku Klux Klan, this political boss wielded enormous influence over state politics before his 1925 conviction for murder helped bring down the Klan's power in Indiana. Who was he?
D. C. Stephenson's 1925 murder trial centered on the death of this Indianapolis woman, whose statement shortly before she died described her abduction and assault. What was her name?

Which American military analyst, formerly employed by the RAND Corporation, gave the press a classified history of U.S. involvement in Vietnam in 1971? His disclosure led to a major legal battle over the government’s power to stop newspaper publication.

Daniel Ellsberg leaked a classified, multivolume history of U.S. decision-making in Vietnam that had been commissioned by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. By what familiar name did this study become known?

Born Amonute and also known as Matoaka, this Powhatan woman was captured by English colonists in 1613, baptized with a Christian name, and married tobacco planter John Rolfe in 1614. By what name is she best known?
In 1616, Pocahontas and John Rolfe crossed the Atlantic and appeared before English society in an effort to promote investment in the Jamestown colony. Which English capital did they visit?
Born in January 1615, this was the son of Pocahontas and the English colonist she married the year before. What was his name?

Beginning with accusations in a Massachusetts village now called Danvers in 1692 and continuing into 1693, this colonial episode led to more than 200 accusations and 19 hangings. What is the name of this series of prosecutions?

In the Salem witch trials, this 1953 Arthur Miller drama recast the proceedings as an allegory for anti-communist investigations of the McCarthy era. What play features John Proctor and Abigail Williams?
During the Salem witch trials, this enslaved woman from Barbados was among the first accused after girls in the household of Reverend Samuel Parris began suffering unusual fits. What was her name?
In the Salem witch trials, this accused farmer refused to enter a plea and was pressed with stones until he died. Who was he?

During the Salem witch trials, judges accepted testimony that an accused person's spirit had appeared to torment someone, even when the accused was physically elsewhere. What was this disputed type of testimony called?

This Michigan Republican represented the state’s 3rd Congressional District from 2021 to 2023, succeeding Justin Amash. After voting to impeach Donald Trump following the January 6 attack, he lost the 2022 Republican primary to John Gibbs. Who is he?

Peter Meijer was one of ten House Republicans who voted to impeach Donald Trump after his supporters stormed the building where Congress was meeting to certify the 2020 electoral votes. What attack prompted that vote?
answer: January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol

question: Which British monarch issued the 1763 proclamation restricting colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains and remained on the throne during the American Revolution?
During George III’s reign, what 1780 London uprising opposing the Catholic Relief Act involved the Protestant Association and partially destroyed Newgate Prison?

On December 16, 1773, colonists disguised as Native Americans boarded East India Company ships in the harbor of Massachusetts’s colonial capital and destroyed hundreds of chests of tea to protest British tax and trade policies. What was this protest called?

The Boston Tea Party targeted a 1773 law that let the East India Company sell tea directly to the colonies while preserving a tax many colonists rejected as taxation without representation. What was the name of that law?
During the Boston Tea Party, protesters boarded three East India Company ships in Boston Harbor. Which ship was the first to arrive carrying tea, reaching Boston in late November 1773?

In response to the Boston Tea Party, Parliament passed a package of punitive measures in 1774, including closing Boston’s port and restricting Massachusetts self-government. What collective name did colonists give these measures?
The Boston Tea Party was organized by a protest network that had opposed the Stamp Act and staged demonstrations against British policies. What was this group called?

Ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, this provision bars Congress from establishing a religion and protects the free exercise of religion, speech, press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. Which provision is this?

Under the First Amendment, this category of expression is generally outside constitutional protection, unlike pornography in general. In Roth v. United States, the Supreme Court described it as material that appeals to the prurient interest; Miller v. California later established a three-part test for it. What is this category?

This Missouri-born politician became the 33rd U.S. president on April 12, 1945, after serving only 82 days as vice president under Franklin D. Roosevelt. He won a surprise reelection in 1948 despite widespread predictions of defeat; who was he?

During Harry S. Truman’s administration, the secretary of state proposed a 1947 initiative that provided U.S. aid to help rebuild Western European economies after World War II. By what commonly used name is this recovery program known?
Born in Novo Mesto, Slovenia, and raised in Sevnica, this former fashion model became First Lady of the United States when her husband took office in 2017. Who is she?
Melania Trump introduced a White House initiative in 2018 that promoted children's well-being, with an emphasis on online safety, opioid abuse, and kindness. What was the initiative's name?

As the Great Depression deepened, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Congress launched a wide-ranging federal policy effort beginning in 1933, pursuing relief, economic recovery, and financial reform. What is the familiar name for this package of programs and laws?

As part of the New Deal’s Second New Deal expansion, this federal agency hired unemployed people for public construction and also sponsored theater, arts, music, dance, and writers’ projects. What agency was it?

An English square-rigged merchant vessel carried 102 passengers across the Atlantic in 1620 after a second ship proved unseaworthy. After a voyage of about ten weeks, it anchored near Cape Cod, where its passengers signed an agreement to establish a basic government before going ashore. What ship was it?

Before the Mayflower sailed alone in 1620, the Pilgrim families planned to cross the Atlantic aboard a second vessel. It proved unseaworthy and was left in England, and its passengers transferred to the ship that continued the voyage. What was the abandoned vessel called?

While aboard the Mayflower before landing in New England, passengers signed a written agreement to form a civil body politic and follow laws made for the settlement’s common good. What is this foundational agreement called?

Which labor organization became one of the largest unions in the United States, built its identity around representing truck drivers and other transport workers, and was led by Jimmy Hoffa during its best-known mid-20th-century period?

During Senate investigations into labor racketeering involving the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, this committee counsel gained national attention by questioning Jimmy Hoffa. He later won California’s 1968 Democratic presidential primary before being shot at Los Angeles’s Ambassador Hotel; who was he?

A self-educated frontier lawyer born in Kentucky rose through Illinois politics to become the 16th president of the United States. He led the Union during the Civil War and was assassinated in Washington, D.C., in April 1865. Who was he?

Abraham Lincoln issued this wartime order on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in areas still rebelling against the United States to be free. It did not immediately abolish slavery throughout the entire country. What was this order called?

Abraham Lincoln delivered this speech at the dedication of a cemetery in Pennsylvania on November 19, 1863, months after a major battle there. In it, he called for a “new birth of freedom” and described government “of the people, by the people, for the people.” What speech was it?

Abraham Lincoln supported this addition to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in December 1865, which abolished slavery throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime. What was this addition called?
Abraham Lincoln was shot at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865, by this actor and Confederate sympathizer, who escaped into Virginia before being found and killed. Who was the assassin?

This Mid-Atlantic commonwealth has Harrisburg as its capital and became the second of the original 13 states to ratify the U.S. Constitution, doing so on December 12, 1787. Its largest city hosted both the adoption of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitutional Convention; what state is it?
Within Pennsylvania, what historic Philadelphia building hosted the 1787 Constitutional Convention and served as the meeting place where delegates adopted the Declaration in 1776?

Which Virginia lawyer, Revolutionary War officer, and former Secretary of State became the fourth Chief Justice in 1801 and served until his death in 1835? He wrote the Supreme Court’s opinion in the 1803 dispute over William Marbury’s undelivered commission.

In John Marshall’s 1803 opinion in Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court refused to issue William Marbury’s requested writ because a provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789 conflicted with the Constitution. What principle did this ruling help establish, allowing courts to assess whether laws are constitutional?

Born enslaved in Maryland, he escaped in 1838 by traveling north disguised as a sailor and became one of the country’s leading abolitionist orators. He wrote a widely read 1845 autobiography and later challenged the nation’s celebration of liberty in a speech delivered on July 5, 1852; who was he?
Frederick Douglass founded and edited this antislavery newspaper in 1847, using its pages to press for abolition and equality. Which publication was it?

A 1777 resolution of the Continental Congress called for thirteen alternating stripes and thirteen stars on a blue field. Its current design has fifty stars and thirteen stripes. What is the name of this national emblem?

During the 1814 British attack on Fort McHenry, a large Flag of the United States remained visible after the bombardment. Seeing it inspired Francis Scott Key to write verses first titled “Defence of Fort M’Henry”; what famous work did those verses become?

What are federally recognized areas of land set aside for Native American tribes, where tribal governments exercise authority alongside the federal government? Their boundaries and legal status are shaped by treaties, statutes, and federal recognition.

Which 1887 federal law authorized dividing communal tribal lands into individual allotments and allowed remaining land to be opened to non-Native settlement, reshaping Indian reservations in the United States?

One change overturned the Supreme Court’s ruling in *Chisholm v. Georgia*, another repealed national Prohibition, and the proposal Gregory Watson helped revive became the last ratified change in 1992. What is the natural name for the full set of formal changes to the nation’s founding charter that includes these measures?
answer: Amendments to the United States Constitution

question: Among the Amendments to the United States Constitution, which proposal approved by Congress in 1972 sought to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex but failed to gain ratification from enough states, even after a deadline extension?

Alice Paul’s National Woman’s Party organized these activists, who began picketing the White House on January 10, 1917, with banners urging President Woodrow Wilson to support women’s suffrage. Their arrests and treatment in prison drew national attention to their campaign; what were these protesters called?

The Silent Sentinels’ campaign led to arrests and imprisonment during World War I. On November 14, 1917, suffragists jailed at Virginia’s Occoquan Workhouse were beaten by guards in an episode that helped build public sympathy for their cause; what is this event known as?

Born on the Caribbean island of Nevis, he served as an artillery officer and George Washington’s aide-de-camp during the Revolutionary War. He later became the first U.S. secretary of the treasury and wrote 51 of the 85 Federalist Papers; who was this Founding Father?

Alexander Hamilton argued that the Constitution’s implied powers allowed the federal government to charter this institution, established in 1791 to support national credit and serve as a fiscal agent. What was it called?
answer: First Bank of the United States

question: After a bitter political feud, Alexander Hamilton faced this former U.S. vice president in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, on July 11, 1804. Who was his opponent?

Which Pacific Coast state, still part of Mexico in 1846, saw settlers proclaim the short-lived Bear Flag Republic at Sonoma before it was ceded to the United States in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo?
Which 1846–1848 conflict between the United States and Mexico ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, through which California and other territories passed to the United States?

A Republican from Jacksonville, he represented Florida in the U.S. House from 2013 to 2018 before becoming the state’s 46th governor in January 2019. In 2022, he signed House Bill 7, commonly known as the Stop WOKE Act. Who is he?

In 2022, Ron DeSantis signed Florida House Bill 7, which restricted specified concepts in some school instruction and workplace training. What was the law’s formal title, distinct from its widely used “Stop WOKE Act” shorthand?

A Maryland banker appointed as a justice of the peace by outgoing President John Adams never received his commission before the Jefferson administration took office. Which man became the named plaintiff in the Supreme Court case that grew out of the dispute?

William Marbury asked the Supreme Court to compel delivery of his withheld justice-of-the-peace commission. What 1803 case, decided by Chief Justice John Marshall, held part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 unconstitutional and established judicial review?

Established under 1956 legislation signed by Dwight D. Eisenhower, this federally supported U.S. network was planned for both national defense and civilian travel. Its controlled-access routes follow uniform standards and connect regions across the country; what is this network called?
A 1956 law supporting the Interstate Highway System directed federal motor-vehicle tax receipts into a pool reserved for construction of the national routes. What was this pool called?

Passed by Congress in 1887, this federal law divided communally held Native American lands into individual allotments and made remaining lands available for government acquisition and non-Native settlement. What was the law called?
The Dawes Act is named for this Massachusetts senator, a Republican who introduced the allotment bill that became the 1887 law. What was his name?

This Union general graduated from West Point in 1840 and served with Ulysses S. Grant during the campaign to capture Vicksburg. In late 1864, he led about 60,000 troops from Atlanta across Georgia to Savannah, cutting their communications and relying on supplies gathered from the land. Who was he?
William Tecumseh Sherman’s 1864 March to the Sea ended on December 21 in a major Georgia port on the Atlantic coast. Which city was the destination of his army’s march from Atlanta?

Which Indigenous people formed communities in Florida from the 1700s onward, drawing on Lower Creek migrants and other Native peoples, with some communities also including people of African ancestry? They became known for resisting U.S. efforts to remove them from their lands.

During the Second Seminole War, this U.S. Army officer commanded troops at the 1837 Battle of Lake Okeechobee. He later became the 12th U.S. president and was nicknamed “Old Rough and Ready” for his military career, which included fighting the Seminole people.

In 1832–1833, South Carolina challenged federal tariff laws and claimed it could prevent them from being enforced within the state. What is this confrontation between the state and the federal government called?

During the Nullification Crisis, which South Carolina politician resigned as vice president in December 1832 after being elected to the U.S. Senate, where he continued to champion the doctrine of nullification?

A 1776 appeal written as the colonies were preparing a new government asked its recipient to ensure women were not overlooked and warned against placing unlimited power in husbands’ hands. What is this letter commonly called?

The “Remember the Ladies” letter was sent in 1776 to a man who was helping shape the new nation’s political future and would later become the second U.S. president. Which woman wrote this appeal to her husband?

What 1894 labor conflict began when factory workers in Chicago protested wage cuts during a severe depression? Led by a union boycott of trains carrying the company’s passenger cars, it was eventually broken after a federal injunction and the deployment of U.S. troops.

During the Pullman Strike, which labor leader headed the American Railway Union and was imprisoned for violating a federal court injunction? He led the union’s nationwide boycott of trains carrying the company’s passenger cars.

During the Pullman Strike, what labor organization led the boycott of trains carrying passenger cars made by the company at the center of the dispute? Under Debs’s leadership, it attracted about 250,000 workers at its peak.

During the Pullman Strike, which U.S. president sent federal troops to Chicago after a court injunction failed to end the boycott? His administration argued that the disruption interfered with delivery of the mail.

This mid-20th-century campaign challenged Jim Crow segregation and sought equal treatment under law and greater political participation for African Americans. Its milestones included the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Freedom Rides, and campaigns to expand Black voter access. What was this movement called?

During the Civil Rights Movement, John Lewis was injured by police on the Edmund Pettus Bridge during the Selma voting-rights campaign, and Martin Luther King Jr. wrote his famous jail letter in Birmingham. In which state did both events occur?

Born in Greene County, Tennessee, in 1786, this frontiersman and former U.S. congressman joined the Alamo’s defenders after losing his 1835 reelection bid. He died during the fort’s fall on March 6, 1836. What is he best known as?

While serving in the U.S. House, Davy Crockett opposed this president’s policies on Indian removal and public lands. The president was a fellow Tennessean who had commanded U.S. forces at the Battle of New Orleans. Who was he?

Born in Litchfield, Connecticut, in 1738, this Vermont leader became one of the organizers of the Green Mountain Boys amid disputes over land grants. He shared leadership with Benedict Arnold in the May 1775 capture of a British-held fort on Lake Champlain. Who was he?

On May 10, 1775, Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold led colonial forces in capturing this British-held position at the southern end of Lake Champlain. Afterward, Henry Knox organized the transport of its artillery to Boston. What was the name of this installation?

Decided on June 24, 2022, this Supreme Court case arose from a challenge to Mississippi’s Gestational Age Act, which generally barred abortion after 15 weeks of pregnancy. Its broader majority ruling overturned Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey; what case was it?
answer: Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization

question: In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which associate justice authored the majority opinion holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion? Appointed to the Supreme Court by George W. Bush, he had previously served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

Emerging in the late nineteenth century amid agrarian discontent, this American political party advocated bimetallism and reforms intended to benefit farmers and working people. What was the party commonly called?
The Populist Party nominated this former Union general and Iowa congressman for president in 1892. He won 22 electoral votes, carrying several western states. Who was he?

A West Point graduate and former U.S. senator from Mississippi, this politician led the Confederacy as its only president during the Civil War. Union troops captured him in 1865, and he spent two years imprisoned before treason charges were never brought to trial. Who was he?
