In 2005, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a Ten Commandments monument on the grounds of the Texas State Capitol could remain, rejecting an Establishment Clause challenge. What case is this?

In Van Orden v. Perry, which Texas attorney general argued before the Supreme Court in defense of the monument? He later became governor and held that office during Texas’s February 2021 winter power crisis.

What civil-rights struggle sought to dismantle legally enforced racial separation in American schools? It became a major Supreme Court issue when the Court ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional.
answer: School desegregation in the United States

question: In the context of School desegregation in the United States, what 1954 unanimous Supreme Court decision arose from a case in Topeka, Kansas, and held that segregated public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause?
This U.S. Army officer served with the 10th Cavalry, led a military expedition into Mexico, and commanded the American Expeditionary Forces during World War I. What was his name?
In 1916, John J. Pershing led U.S. troops across the Mexican border in an unsuccessful effort to capture this revolutionary, whose forces had raided Columbus, New Mexico. Who was the target?

After managing his older brother’s 1960 presidential campaign, this Massachusetts-born Democrat served as U.S. attorney general and later represented New York in the Senate. He ran for the 1968 Democratic presidential nomination and was shot after winning the California primary.
In the late 1950s, Robert F. Kennedy served as chief counsel to a Senate committee investigating labor racketeering and publicly challenged its president, Jimmy Hoffa. What union did Hoffa lead?
Robert F. Kennedy took part in his brother’s administration during the 1962 confrontation over Soviet missiles in Cuba. What title did he give his account of that crisis?

Issued in November 1775 by Virginia’s royal governor during the American Revolution, this decree offered freedom to enslaved people held by rebels if they escaped and served the Crown. By what name is the decree known?

Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation helped recruit formerly enslaved men into what named body of Black Loyalist troops serving the British, which fought in the Virginia campaign and used the motto “Liberty to Slaves”?

At a November 1863 dedication of a national cemetery for Union dead, a president spoke for only about two minutes after a celebrated orator delivered the principal speech. The brief remarks urged the living to continue the dead’s “unfinished work”; what speech was it?

At the ceremony associated with the Gettysburg Address, this former U.S. representative and Massachusetts governor delivered the principal oration for roughly two hours before Lincoln’s brief remarks. Who was the orator?

In June 1972, burglars were caught inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters at a Washington, D.C., office complex, and investigators later traced the operation to President Nixon’s reelection campaign. The effort to conceal the administration’s ties to the break-in led to Nixon’s resignation in August 1974. What name is commonly given to this U.S. political affair?

During the Watergate scandal, Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward met an anonymous source in an underground parking garage in Rosslyn, Virginia. The source’s identity was publicly confirmed in 2005 as former FBI associate director W. Mark Felt. What nickname had the source used?

During the Watergate scandal, President Nixon ordered Attorney General Elliot Richardson to dismiss special prosecutor Archibald Cox after Cox sought access to White House recordings. Richardson and Deputy Attorney General William Ruckelshaus resigned rather than carry out the order, and Solicitor General Robert Bork ultimately fired Cox. What name was given to this episode?

During the Watergate scandal, a June 23, 1972, Oval Office recording captured Nixon telling H. R. Haldeman to have the CIA urge the FBI to stop pursuing the investigation into the break-in. This recording helped establish that Nixon had joined the cover-up. What is this recording commonly called?

Which American lawyer and poet represented Sam Houston before the House of Representatives after Houston caned Ohio congressman William Stanbery? He also wrote the lyrics of the patriotic song that became the U.S. national anthem.

Francis Scott Key watched the British bombardment of Fort McHenry in 1814 from a truce ship and was inspired by the sight of the American flag still flying at dawn. What poem, first published as “Defence of Fort M’Henry,” later became the U.S. national anthem?
On January 28, 1986, a NASA orbiter broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew members, including teacher Christa McAuliffe. What is the name of this fatal shuttle breakup?
During the investigation of the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster, this physicist used a piece of O-ring material in an ice-water demonstration to show how cold could affect the seal. Who was he?

Observed each year with fireworks, parades, and other patriotic celebrations, this U.S. federal holiday commemorates Congress's adoption on July 4, 1776, of the founding document announcing the thirteen colonies' separation from Great Britain. What is the holiday called?
William Carlos Williams wrote a poem that depicts two robins crying. Its title refers to the calendar date on which Independence Day is celebrated; what is the poem's title?
Which major U.S. political party took shape around Andrew Jackson’s supporters during the 1820s? Its organized campaign in 1828 helped turn that movement into a durable force in national politics.

During the Democratic Party’s 1860 presidential split, which Illinois senator represented the Northern ticket? He had backed the Kansas-Nebraska Act and argued that settlers should decide whether slavery would be allowed in the territories.
Which Puritan minister was banished from Massachusetts Bay and went on to found the colony of Rhode Island? He advocated freedom of conscience and separation of church and state.

In 1636, Roger Williams established this settlement on Narragansett Bay after leaving Massachusetts Bay, naming it in gratitude for what he regarded as divine guidance. The settlement later became Rhode Island’s capital. What was it called?

From 1892 until 1954, this island in New York Harbor served as the principal immigration inspection station for newcomers arriving in the United States. What island became a defining gateway for millions of immigrants?

Ellis Island was the major federal inspection station on the East Coast, while an island in San Francisco Bay processed many arrivals from China and Japan. What island is often called the “Ellis Island of the West”?

In the 1930s, prolonged drought and intensive farming left Great Plains soil exposed to enormous storms that buried fields and homes. The disaster drove many farm families, including migrants known as “Okies,” westward in search of work. What is this period called?
The Dust Bowl deepened which nationwide economic crisis that began after the 1929 stock market crash and brought widespread unemployment and hardship?

In 19th-century U.S. politics, party leaders often rewarded campaign workers and loyal supporters with government jobs instead of selecting employees through merit-based procedures. What was this practice called?

The Spoils System faced growing opposition after President James A. Garfield was assassinated in 1881. What 1883 federal law established a commission to oversee government hiring and introduced competitive examinations for some federal positions?

Members of the Reagan administration secretly arranged arms sales to a Middle Eastern government and redirected part of the proceeds to aid Nicaraguan rebels, circumventing restrictions on U.S. support. What political scandal is identified by this covert arms-for-support scheme?

During the Iran-Contra affair, which National Security Council staff member and Marine lieutenant colonel helped organize arms transfers and the diversion of proceeds to the Contras, then became a prominent witness before Congress?

In U.S. history, employees use this organized tactic by collectively withholding their work rather than negotiating individually. Such stoppages can press economic, workplace, or political demands; what is this form of collective action called?

Which American Railway Union president and later Socialist Party presidential candidate was imprisoned for contempt of court after his union's 1894 boycott supported workers protesting wage reductions at a railway-car company? The dispute became one of the best-known labor strikes in U.S. history.

An American lawyer and businessman, he served on the board of a Ukrainian energy company and became a prominent subject of political controversy during the 2020 U.S. election. Identify the son of the 46th U.S. president.

A nineteenth-century American reformer, she investigated the treatment of people with mental illness in jails and almshouses and campaigned for publicly funded care. Her advocacy helped promote the establishment of state asylums. Who was she?
Dorothea Dix’s campaign helped establish a public asylum separate from prisons in this Pennsylvania city. It is also the state capital, located along the Susquehanna River. What city is it?

A Maryland-born stage actor and Confederate sympathizer became infamous after entering a Washington theater during a performance and shooting the sitting U.S. president on April 14, 1865. Who was this assassin?

John Wilkes Booth broke his leg leaping from the presidential box to the stage while escaping after a shooting at this Washington, D.C., venue during a performance of Our American Cousin. What theater was it?

An enslaved Virginian served as a spy for the Continental Army during the American Revolution, posing as a runaway to gain access to British camps and passing intelligence to American commanders. This Nebraska-born lawyer joined John F. Kennedy’s Senate staff in 1953 and became one of his closest advisers and speechwriters. He helped shape Kennedy’s inaugural address. Who was he?

Ted Sorensen helped craft the inaugural address of the Massachusetts Democrat who took office in January 1961, including its famous appeal about what citizens can do for their country. Which U.S. president delivered that address?

This American conservative served as a speechwriter and communications director in the Nixon White House, later sought the Republican presidential nomination in 1992 and 1996, and ran as the Reform Party’s presidential nominee in 2000. Who is he?

The acquittal of officers charged in the beating of Rodney King sparked days of unrest in April 1992, with violence and looting spreading from South Central into neighboring communities. What city was at the center of these riots?

In 1832, this Supreme Court case held that a southeastern state's laws had no force within the Cherokee people's territory. It arose after a missionary was convicted under that state's law for living among the Cherokee without obtaining its required license; what was the case called?

Beginning during World War II, U.S. Army codebreakers used this program to exploit Soviet messages encrypted with reused one-time-pad material, and they continued analyzing the traffic into the Cold War. question: A Massachusetts Democrat, he represented the state in the U.S. Senate for nearly five decades and challenged Jimmy Carter for the party’s presidential nomination in 1980. In 1969, Ted Kennedy drove his car off Dike Bridge on a small Massachusetts island, and passenger Mary Jo Kopechne died. What scandal, named for the island where the crash occurred, became a lasting obstacle to Kennedy’s political ambitions?

In the years after World War II, federal loyalty investigations, congressional hearings, and blacklisting in entertainment reflected a nationwide anti-communist campaign that reached its peak during the McCarthy era. What is the natural name for this period of political fear and repression?

During the Second Red Scare, which Wisconsin senator rose to national prominence by accusing alleged communists of infiltrating the federal government? Televised 1954 hearings involving his investigative subcommittee and the U.S. Army eroded his influence, and the Senate later censured him.

An American nurse and birth-control activist opened the nation’s first birth-control clinic in Brownsville, Brooklyn, in 1916 with her sister Ethel Byrne. This Prussian officer joined the Continental Army during the American Revolution and introduced standardized infantry drills at Valley Forge during the winter of 1777–78, including training in bayonet tactics. What military trainer later became a major general in the Continental Army?

Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben used this Pennsylvania encampment as the setting for his intensive training program during the winter of 1777–78. What site west of Philadelphia served as Washington’s army’s winter quarters?

Within Abolitionism in the United States, which Massachusetts publisher launched *The Liberator* in 1831 and declared in its first issue, “I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD”?
A former Arizona state legislator and appeals-court judge, she became the first woman appointed to the U.S. Supreme Court when President Ronald Reagan nominated her in 1981. Who was this justice?

In a 2003 Supreme Court case brought by a white applicant denied admission to the University of Michigan Law School, the Court upheld the school's limited use of race as one factor in a holistic admissions process. Sandra Day O'Connor wrote the majority opinion. What case was it?

At an October 2021 NASCAR race at Talladega, a reporter’s interpretation of a crowd’s profane anti-president chant turned a driver’s name into a euphemistic political slogan. What phrase became a widely recognized expression of opposition to Joe Biden?

Which two Italian-born anarchists were convicted in Massachusetts for the 1920 robbery and murders in South Braintree, despite a case that drew worldwide protests and became an emblem of perceived judicial injustice? Both men were executed in 1927.

During the Sacco and Vanzetti case, which Massachusetts Superior Court judge presided over their 1921 trial and later ruled on defense motions for a new trial? His handling of the proceedings became a central target of critics who viewed the case as biased.
After decades of organizing, this movement achieved a nationwide U.S. victory in 1920 through a constitutional change. What campaign sought to enfranchise female citizens?
Women's suffrage in the United States was secured nationally in 1920 by which numbered change to the Constitution, ratified after years of activism and barring denial of the vote on account of sex?

A landmark in the broader women's suffrage movement, this 1848 gathering in upstate New York was organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and issued the Declaration of Sentiments. What was the gathering called?

A former logistics executive and Republican fundraiser, he became the 75th U.S. Postmaster General in June 2020 after being selected by the Postal Service’s Board of Governors. Who is this businessman?

Joseph Pulitzer bought this Manhattan-based newspaper in 1883 and built it into a mass-circulation daily known for investigative campaigns and a prominent Sunday edition. Which paper was it?
Created in 1850, this U.S. administrative district encompassed the Mormon settlement centered around the Great Salt Lake before Utah became a state in 1896. What was it called?
After leading Latter-day Saints west from Nauvoo to the Great Salt Lake in 1847, this religious leader became the first governor of Utah Territory. Who was he?
Founded in 1852 as a western U.S. stagecoach and mail operation, this business later grew into one of the country's largest financial institutions. What is its name?

This short-lived mail relay used mounted couriers and relay stations to carry messages between Missouri and California in about ten days in 1860–61, before the transcontinental telegraph made it obsolete. What disaster was it?

This Republican lawyer began representing Missouri in the U.S. Senate on January 3, 2019, after serving as the state’s attorney general from 2017 to 2019. Who is this senator?
Josh Hawley earned his law degree in 2006 after graduating from Stanford University. What law school did he attend?

In 1974, Gerald Ford used this constitutional power to shield former president Richard Nixon from prosecution for federal offenses connected to Watergate. It can forgive a federal crime rather than simply shorten a sentence, and an 1833 Supreme Court case established that a recipient could refuse it. What is this action called?

Which 1833 Supreme Court case arose after a convicted person refused to accept a presidential pardon issued by Andrew Jackson? The Court ruled that the pardon was not effective without the recipient’s acceptance.

At the 1896 Democratic National Convention, William Jennings Bryan’s “Cross of Gold” speech attacked a gold-only monetary standard. What precious metal did bimetallists want recognized alongside gold?

In the U.S. silver debate of the late 1870s, which 1878 law required the Treasury to purchase between $2 million and $4 million of silver bullion each month and coin it into dollars? Congress passed it over President Rutherford B. Hayes’s veto.

A principal drafter of the Declaration of Independence, this Founding Father served as George Washington’s first secretary of state and later as John Adams’s vice president. He became the nation’s third president in 1801 and served two terms. Who was he?

During Thomas Jefferson’s presidency, Napoleon’s government sold the United States a vast territory stretching west from the Mississippi River and more than doubling the country’s area. What was this 1803 acquisition called?

In 1807, Thomas Jefferson signed a measure that barred most American exports to foreign countries in an effort to keep U.S. shipping out of conflicts between Britain and France. What was this law called?

During World War II, this group of Black pilots and support personnel trained in Alabama and became the first African American military aviators in the U.S. Army Air Forces. The aircraft of the 332nd Fighter Group, closely associated with them, were marked with distinctive red tails; what was the group known as?
The Tuskegee Airmen’s 332nd Fighter Group was commanded during World War II by this West Point graduate, who later became the first African American general in the U.S. Air Force. Who was he?

On the night of December 25–26, 1776, George Washington’s Continental Army crossed the Delaware River and launched a surprise attack on a Hessian garrison in New Jersey. What engagement ended in a Patriot victory on the day after Christmas?
At the Battle of Trenton, this Hessian colonel commanded the garrison defending the town and was mortally wounded during the American attack. Who was he?
In Boston in 1765, this circle of merchants and artisans organized demonstrations and intimidation against the Stamp Act, serving as a precursor to the Sons of Liberty. What was this group called?

The Loyal Nine helped pave the way for this later resistance organization, whose Boston branch was led by Samuel Adams. Its members organized the 1773 destruction of taxed tea aboard ships in Boston Harbor. What was this organization?

A 1927 U.S. customs dispute concerned an abstract sculpture by a Romanian-born modernist, whose import was taxed as a manufactured metal object instead of admitted under the tariff exemption for works of art. In 1928, a customs-court ruling accepted that the nonrepresentational sculpture qualified as art; what was the case?

In Brâncuși v. United States, the import at issue was a highly polished, elongated bronze sculpture that its creator described as expressing the essence of flight rather than realistically representing an animal. What was the sculpture titled?

In 1853, the United States obtained a strip of land from Mexico that now lies in southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico. The agreement was intended in part to make a southern transcontinental railroad route more feasible; what was this acquisition called?

The Gadsden Purchase was concluded while this Mexican leader was serving another term as president, and Mexico received $10 million for the territory. He had also led Mexican forces at the Alamo and San Jacinto; who was he?

Ratified in 1868 during Reconstruction, this constitutional change defined national citizenship for people born or naturalized in the United States. It also requires states to respect due process and equal protection of the laws. What numbered change to the U.S. Constitution is it?

Which 1954 Supreme Court decision held that state-mandated segregation in public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment? Its ruling rejected the claim that racially segregated schools could be constitutional merely because their facilities were nominally equal.
answer: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka

question: Born in Virginia, this military leader commanded the Continental Army through the American Revolution and presided over the Constitutional Convention. In 1789, he became the first president of the United States. Who was he?

After George Washington led his troops across the Delaware River on Christmas night in 1776, they launched a surprise attack on Hessian forces the following morning. What battle was this Patriot victory?
George Washington’s principal Virginia residence was a plantation estate overlooking the Potomac River, where he lived before and after his presidency. What was the estate called?

In 1781, George Washington and French allies surrounded British forces under Charles Cornwallis near Chesapeake Bay, bringing the Revolutionary War toward its end. What was the name of this decisive military encounter?

As he prepared to leave office in 1796, George Washington issued a public message warning against political factionalism, regional divisions, and foreign entanglements. What is this message commonly called?

Fought from 1754 to 1763 in North America as a theater of a wider imperial conflict, this struggle centered in part on control of the Ohio River Valley and ended with Britain taking Canada. British forces and colonists fought France alongside Indigenous nations, whose alliances and aims varied. What was this conflict called?

In the aftermath of the French and Indian War, this settlement was signed on February 10, 1763, and ended the conflict. It transferred most of France’s mainland territory east of the Mississippi to Britain, although Indigenous nations whose lands were affected were not parties to the agreement. What was this agreement?

Born in Dawson, New Mexico, and raised in Stockton, California, she worked as a teacher before organizing farmworkers. She co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with César Chávez and later negotiated labor agreements for California farmworkers; which activist is described?

Dolores Huerta and César Chávez launched a California labor organization in 1962; in 1966, it merged with the union organized by Filipino American labor leader Larry Itliong, and the combined group adopted its present name in 1972. What union, known for its California grape strikes and boycotts, is it?

In February 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight consist carrying hazardous materials left the tracks in an Ohio community near the Pennsylvania line, prompting a controlled burn of tank-car contents. What widely known incident is identified by this combination of date, operator, and cleanup response?

In accounts of the 2023 East Palestine train derailment, officials conducted a controlled burn after several tank cars carrying a hazardous industrial chemical threatened to rupture. Which flammable gas, used as a building block for common plastic pipes and cable insulation, was deliberately burned?

This Israeli political family includes a Likud leader who served multiple terms as prime minister and his brother, an Israeli officer killed while commanding a 1976 hostage-rescue raid at an airport in Uganda. What family is described?

A member of the Netanyahu family led Israeli commandos in a 1976 rescue at Uganda’s airport near Kampala, where hostages from Air France Flight 139 had been held after a hijacking. What is the operation commonly called?

Beginning in April 1989 after the death of former CCP general secretary Hu Yaobang, student- and worker-led demonstrations in Beijing demanded greater political participation and press freedoms. What event was violently suppressed by troops entering the capital on June 4?
Which former Chinese Communist Party general secretary’s death in April 1989 helped spark the Tiananmen Square protests and massacre? Many students viewed him as sympathetic to political reform.

The best-known image associated with the Tiananmen Square protests and massacre shows an unidentified figure standing alone in the road directly in front of a column of military vehicles in 1989. What name is commonly given to this figure?

An Egyptian army officer and member of the Free Officers Movement, this leader helped overthrow the monarchy in 1952 and became president in 1956. He promoted Arab nationalism and ordered a major canal to be nationalized, precipitating an international crisis.

In 1956, Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized this strategic waterway linking the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea. Its seizure prompted military intervention by Britain, France, and Israel in the crisis named after it.

Gamal Abdel Nasser became president of this short-lived political union formed by Egypt and Syria in 1958. Syria withdrew from the union in 1961, though Egypt continued using its name for several years afterward.

Gamal Abdel Nasser sponsored construction of this major Nile River project, completed in the 1970s after his death. Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, led to the relocation of the Abu Simbel temples to higher ground.

After Iraq occupied Kuwait in August 1990, coalition forces assembled in the region during a defensive buildup. The subsequent 1991 combat campaign opened with air attacks in mid-January and began its rapid ground offensive on February 24. What was this campaign called?

During Operation Desert Storm, which U.S. Army general commanded the coalition forces? He also led U.S. Central Command during the Gulf War and oversaw the campaign that drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait.

From 1864 to 1870, Paraguay fought a coalition of Argentina, the Empire of Brazil, and Uruguay in this conflict, the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history. Also known as the Paraguayan War, what is its other established name?
During the War of the Triple Alliance, Paraguayan president Francisco Solano López was killed by Brazilian forces on March 1, 1870, in the conflict’s final battle. What was the name of that battle?

During the War of the Triple Alliance, which member of the alliance against Paraguay was still an empire under Pedro II and had Rio de Janeiro as its capital? Its troops also occupied Paraguay with Argentine forces after the fighting ended.

Which Central African state maintained diplomatic ties with Portugal after Portuguese visitors arrived in the late 15th century? Its ruler Afonso I adopted Christianity and later objected to Portuguese involvement in the enslavement of people from his realm.
The Kingdom of Kongo had its royal seat on a plateau in what is now northern Angola. Portuguese sources later called this city São Salvador; what was its local name?

This British political strategist directed the Vote Leave campaign during the 2016 EU referendum. He later became the chief adviser to the prime minister who entered office in 2019, and drew widespread attention for a 2020 trip to Barnard Castle during the COVID-19 lockdown. Who was he?

Dominic Cummings served as chief adviser during the early period of this Conservative politician’s premiership. Before entering 10 Downing Street in 2019, he had been Mayor of London. Who was this politician?

In September 1914, French and British forces halted the German advance toward Paris in a major engagement in France. The battle disrupted Germany’s plan for a rapid victory in the west and helped usher in trench warfare; what was it called?

At the First Battle of the Marne, the Allied counterattack forced German troops to retreat and derailed Germany’s strategy for defeating France quickly before turning its forces east against Russia. By what name was that strategy known?

Which Spanish-speaking Caribbean country occupies the eastern portion of Hispaniola, sharing the island with Haiti? It declared independence from Haiti in 1844, then restored its independence in 1865 after Spain regained control.
In the Dominican Republic, what capital city began as an early Spanish colonial settlement on Hispaniola’s south coast? Its historic colonial district is designated a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Fought in Thessaly in 48 BCE, this decisive clash of the Roman Civil War ended with Julius Caesar defeating Pompey the Great and sending him fleeing after his army broke. What battle was it?
At the Battle of Pharsalus, Caesar anticipated that Pompey’s larger cavalry force would attack his flank. What part of his own army did Caesar keep back to counter that attack?

The South Slav state formed in December 1918 as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes adopted a new name in 1929. After World War II, a socialist federation of six republics also used that name. What was the state commonly called?

After the socialist federation of Yugoslavia broke apart, a smaller two-republic state retained the Yugoslavia name. In 2003, that state adopted a new name and dissolved three years later; what was its 2003 name?

Which British peer and major-general commanded the Light Brigade during its ill-fated 1854 charge at Balaclava in the Crimean War? The assault was later commemorated in a famous poem by Alfred, Lord Tennyson.
James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan, led the British Light Brigade during its disastrous assault on Russian positions at which October 1854 Crimean War battle near Sevastopol?
This Ugandan army officer seized power from Milton Obote in a January 1971 coup and ruled until Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles overthrew him in 1979. What ruler is described?

In August 1972, Idi Amin Dada gave holders of British passports from a community with roots in the Indian subcontinent 90 days to leave his East African country, then extended the order to others from that community. What mass flight of families and business owners followed?

This landlocked country in the Horn of Africa has Addis Ababa as its capital and a history that includes the Aksumite kingdom, the Solomonic monarchy, and the later Derg period. Its forces defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, making it a major example of African resistance to colonial expansion. Name the country.

In Ethiopia’s ancient predecessor kingdom of Aksum, this ruler’s reign in the early fourth century saw Christianity become the state religion. His name is also recorded on Aksumite inscriptions and coins. Who was this ruler?

In 1896, Ethiopia’s forces under Menelik II decisively defeated an invading Italian army near a town in the country’s north. The victory helped preserve Ethiopian independence and became a major symbol of African resistance to imperialism. What was the battle called?

In Ethiopia, this military council took power in 1974 and deposed Haile Selassie. It later established a Marxist-Leninist regime under Mengistu Haile Mariam, which was overthrown in 1991. What was the council known as?

Which Anglo-Saxon kingdom, centered in the English Midlands, became a powerful rival of Wessex and was ruled by kings including Penda and Offa? Its eighth-century ruler Offa is also associated with a major earthwork along the Welsh border.

In the Kingdom of Mercia, what long earthwork, conventionally attributed to an eighth-century Mercian king, runs along much of the boundary between England and Wales? It is considered one of the most substantial early medieval frontier works in Britain.

This third Roman emperor succeeded Tiberius in 37 CE, after being brought up among the soldiers of his father, Germanicus. His reign ended when members of the Praetorian Guard assassinated him in 41 CE. Who was he?
Caligula reportedly gave his favorite horse a marble stable and an ivory manger, and was said to have considered elevating it to the consulship. What was the horse’s name?

An Agiad king of Sparta, he commanded the Greek defense at a narrow coastal pass in 480 BCE against Xerxes I’s invasion. His rearguard included the famed 300 Spartans as well as allied troops from other Greek city-states. Who was this king?

Leonidas I led the Greek defense in this 480 BCE battle, where the defenders held a narrow pass for several days before Persian forces used a mountain route to outflank them. What was this battle called?

Launched after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187, this 1189–1192 campaign brought Richard I of England, Philip II of France, and Frederick Barbarossa to the eastern Mediterranean. Its forces captured Acre but failed to retake Jerusalem; what crusading campaign was it?
During the Third Crusade, Richard I conquered this eastern Mediterranean island from the Byzantine ruler Isaac Komnenos in 1191. He then sold it to the Knights Templar; what island was it?

An English Catholic conspirator was discovered on 5 November 1605 in a cellar beneath the House of Lords, guarding gunpowder intended to destroy Parliament during its state opening. He had served with Spanish forces in the Low Countries and used the name Guido there; who was he?

Guy Fawkes took part in a 1605 conspiracy to destroy the House of Lords during the opening of Parliament and kill King James I, with the aim of restoring Catholic rule. A warning letter to Lord Monteagle helped authorities uncover the explosives; what was the conspiracy called?

On February 27, 1933, Germany’s parliamentary building in Berlin was engulfed in flames, just weeks after Hitler became chancellor. Nazi leaders blamed Communists and used the crisis to help justify repression, although its origins remain disputed. What event was this?

Following the Reichstag fire, President Paul von Hindenburg approved an emergency measure on February 28, 1933, that suspended protections for speech, press, and assembly and enabled arrests of political opponents. What was this measure called?

Which conflict, fought chiefly between England and France from 1337 to 1453, grew from disputes over Aquitaine and the French crown? Its intermittent campaigns were repeatedly interrupted by truces and the Black Death.

During the Hundred Years’ War, which young woman from Domrémy said divine voices urged her to aid the dauphin, helped lift the English siege of Orléans in 1429, and accompanied him to his coronation at Reims? Captured by Burgundian forces, she was tried at Rouen and executed in 1431.

In the Hundred Years’ War, which 1415 victory of Henry V’s English army on St. Crispin’s Day became famous for French knights struggling in muddy ground against English archers? The battle followed Henry’s campaign in Normandy and is dramatized in Shakespeare’s *Henry V*.

During the Hundred Years’ War, which English king claimed the French crown through his mother Isabella, daughter of Philip IV, and styled himself king of France in 1340? His seizure of Guyenne from the French crown helped trigger open hostilities.

During the Hundred Years’ War, what 1420 pact between Henry V of England and Charles VI of France arranged Henry’s marriage to Catherine of Valois and named him, and his heirs, successor to the French crown instead of the dauphin? The settlement left Henry’s infant son as the English claimant after both monarchs died in 1422.

On June 28, 1914, a visit by the Austro-Hungarian heir and his wife to Sarajevo ended when a South Slav nationalist fatally shot them. What event is commonly identified as the immediate spark of the July Crisis and the outbreak of World War I?

The Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand set off a diplomatic confrontation in 1914, involving Austria-Hungary’s ultimatum to Serbia and its declaration of war on the 28th day of the same month. What is the conventional name for this escalation?

Britain established a penal settlement at Sydney Cove in 1788 and used its inhabitants as labor for colonial officials and settlers; similar settlements later operated on Van Diemen’s Land and Norfolk Island. What was the name of this system, which ended after a final vessel reached Fremantle in 1868?
In accounts of convict transportation to Australia, what vessel brought the final group of transported prisoners to Fremantle on January 9, 1868?

From 1855 to 1867, a series of armed clashes in Guangdong pitted long-established local communities against migrant groups whose distinctive language and customs set them apart, amid disputes over land, resources, and local power. What is the commonly used name for this conflict?

During the Punti–Hakka Clan Wars, many displaced people from Guangdong crossed the sea to a British colony where Chinese gold miners were targeted in the Lambing Flat riots in New South Wales. The colony became a federation in 1901; what was this major destination?
In Islamic political usage, this title denotes a sovereign with temporal authority and became the customary style of the Ottoman dynasty’s monarchs. What is the title?

Sultan was the sovereign title prominently used by rulers of this empire, founded by Osman I in Anatolia. Under Mehmed II, its forces captured Constantinople in 1453, and the empire was dissolved after World War I. What was the empire?

What umbrella historical designation describes successive Iranian imperial states—not one uninterrupted polity—including the Achaemenid state associated with Cyrus, the Safavid state that made Shiʿa Islam official, and the Afsharid realm founded by Nader Shah in 1736?

Within the Achaemenid phase of the Persian Empire, this sixth-century-BCE ruler defeated the Median king Astyages and established his rule around 550 BCE. His forces later captured Babylon in 539 BCE. Which ruler is this?

After Rome's monarchy was overthrown, this state was governed by annually elected magistrates, including two consuls, alongside a powerful Senate. It fought Carthage in the Punic Wars and eventually conquered Hispania before the imperial system was established.
During the Roman Republic, which conflict began in 218 BCE when Hannibal crossed the Alps into Italy and ended after Rome defeated Carthage at the Battle of Zama?

This capital of modern Italy lies along the Tiber River and successively served as the capital of the Roman Kingdom, Republic, and Empire. It is also known by the historic title “Eternal City.” What city is it?
Which river flows through Rome and, according to legend, carried the abandoned twins Romulus and Remus before they were rescued? It is Italy’s third-longest river.
Within Rome’s municipal boundaries is an independent sovereign state that serves as the headquarters of the Catholic Church and the residence of the pope. What is this state called?
Which Bourbon monarch ascended the throne in 1643, began ruling in his own right after Cardinal Mazarin’s death in 1661, and reigned until 1715? He was associated with the epithet “the Sun King.”
Louis XIV transformed this former hunting lodge outside Paris into a grand royal residence, featuring the Hall of Mirrors and expansive formal gardens. What site became the center of his court?
Louis XIV issued this measure in 1685, reversing the 1598 settlement that had granted legal protections to French Huguenots. What was the measure called?
Louis XIV relied on this finance minister, who promoted mercantilist policies, expanded manufacturing, and helped establish the French Academy of Sciences. Who was the minister?

Louis XIV’s support for his grandson Philip V’s claim to the throne based in Madrid helped spark this major European conflict, which concluded with treaties including Utrecht. What was the conflict called?

This 13th-century prince of Novgorod and Vladimir defeated Swedish forces on the Neva and later repelled Teutonic-Livonian forces at Lake Peipus, while maintaining political ties with the Mongol Golden Horde. What ruler is known by an epithet meaning “of the Neva”?
Alexander Nevsky’s forces fought Livonian-Teutonic troops on frozen Lake Peipus in 1242, halting the crusaders’ advance into Novgorodian territory. What is this engagement commonly called?

Which western European state emerged from the southern provinces of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after an uprising in Brussels, with its provisional government declaring independence on October 4, 1830? Its National Congress adopted a constitution the following February and selected Leopold of Saxe-Coburg as its first monarch.
Before it became a colony of Belgium in 1908, this Central African territory was personally controlled by Leopold II and became notorious for coercive rubber extraction. What was it called?

Artillery fragments caused many head wounds in the trenches, prompting armies to replace soft caps with protective designs. What category of headgear included the French design introduced in 1915 and the British model adopted that September?

Among World War I military helmets, which German steel design entered service in 1916, replacing the spiked leather headgear used earlier in the war? Its distinctive coal-scuttle shape covered more of the head and neck than the British design with a broad brim.
This 55-member continental organization was launched in 2002 to replace the OAU, following a process traced to the Sirte Declaration. What organization is headquartered in Addis Ababa?
The African Union is headquartered in this Ethiopian capital, which also hosted the 1963 summit that established the Organization of African Unity. What city is it?

Ancient Greek infantrymen formed this close-packed battle line, advancing in ranks with large shields overlapping so that each soldier helped protect a neighbor. Its strength depended on maintaining cohesion, since a break in the line left the troops exposed. What was this formation called?

In Philip II of Macedon’s version of the phalanx, infantry carried a pike much longer than the traditional hoplite spear, allowing its length to project several spearpoints beyond the front ranks. What was this Macedonian weapon called?

Which Spanish explorer crossed the Isthmus of Panama in 1513 and became the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas? He was later tried and beheaded in Panama by a rival colonial administrator.
After Vasco Núñez de Balboa’s crossing of the Isthmus and sighting of the Pacific, which Spanish colonial governor in Darién had him tried and executed in 1519?

In 1827, a British, French, and Russian fleet defeated an Egyptian-Ottoman fleet in a major naval clash during the Greek War of Independence. The victory helped secure Greek independence; what was the battle called?
At the Battle of Navarino, the allied fleet’s senior British commander directed the fighting from his flagship, HMS Asia. Which admiral was he?

This post–World War I German republic took its name from the city where its constituent assembly met to draft a new constitution in 1919. Its years in power included the Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation, and it ended with the Nazi seizure of power in 1933. What was this republic called?

During the Weimar Republic, this 1924 reparations arrangement rescheduled Germany’s payments and provided for U.S.-backed loans after the Ruhr crisis. It helped pave the way for French and Belgian troops to withdraw from the Ruhr. What was this framework called?
Which Australian Liberal Party politician became prime minister in 2018, served until 2022, and lost that year’s federal election to Anthony Albanese?
In which country did the May 2022 federal election, marked by a “teal wave” and a crossbench of 16 seats, end Scott Morrison’s prime ministership?

In early 19th-century Britain, these protectionist measures placed duties and restrictions on imported grain to shield domestic producers from foreign competition. Robert Peel repealed them in 1846, marking a major shift toward free trade. What were they called?

Founded in Manchester in 1838 by Richard Cobden and John Bright, this pressure group organized mass campaigning against the Corn Laws and helped build support for their repeal. What was the organization called?

This historical process ended legal systems that treated people as property, though it was distinct from simply banning the trade in enslaved people. It was achieved in the United States through the Thirteenth Amendment, in Brazil through an 1888 law, and across much of the British Empire through legislation passed in 1833; what is this process called?
In Brazil’s Abolition of Slavery, a law signed by Regent Princess Isabel on May 13, 1888 declared slavery extinct. By what name is this law known?

This eighteenth-century BCE king of Babylon expanded his realm through conquest and is commemorated on a dark stone stela. Its relief shows him before a deity associated with justice, and the monument preserves 282 judgments on subjects including family, property, trade, and labor. Who was this ruler?
On the surviving stela associated with Hammurabi, a relief depicts the Babylonian king before a seated Mesopotamian deity associated with the sun and justice. Which deity is shown?

In the late eighth and ninth centuries, Frankish rulers promoted schools for clergy, more accurate Latin texts, and renewed study of classical and Christian writings. This court-supported revival also encouraged illuminated manuscripts and reforms to worship, and its name distinguishes it from the much later Italian movement.

A leading scholar associated with the Carolingian Renaissance, this Northumbrian cleric left his teaching post in northern England after Charlemagne recruited him, then became a prominent teacher at the royal court in Aachen. He advised on grammar and biblical study, helping shape the Frankish court’s educational program.

A former socialist journalist, he founded Italy’s Fascist movement in 1919 and became prime minister after a paramilitary march in 1922. He later ruled as a dictator and was known by a title meaning “the leader.” Who was he?

Benito Mussolini became prime minister after his Blackshirts converged on this Italian capital in October 1922, pressuring King Victor Emmanuel III to appoint him. Which city was the destination of the march?

Benito Mussolini’s forces invaded this African country in 1935, and League of Nations sanctions over the conquest contributed to Italy’s diplomatic isolation before its closer alignment with Nazi Germany. Which country was invaded?

After Benito Mussolini was removed from power in 1943, German forces rescued him and installed him as head of a collaborationist government in German-occupied northern Italy. What was this short-lived regime called?
What reformist Ottoman political movement helped compel Sultan Abdülhamid II to restore the constitution during the 1908 revolution, after years of autocratic rule?
Within the Young Turks movement, what Ottoman political organization consolidated dictatorial power in 1913? The government under its control carried out the Armenian genocide in 1915–1916.
Formed after the Greek War of Independence against Ottoman rule, this monarchy began in 1832 with Otto of Bavaria as its first king. What was the name of this state?
During the Kingdom of Greece, what Athens uprising, backed by army commander Dimitrios Kallergis and veteran Ioannis Makriyannis, forced Otto to accept a constitution and led to the 1844 charter?

This Hohenzollern-ruled German kingdom defeated Austria in the Seven Weeks’ War of 1866 and France in the Franco-Prussian War. Its king was proclaimed German emperor at Versailles in 1871, completing the unification it had led. What kingdom is described?

As minister-president of the Kingdom of Prussia from 1862, this statesman pursued a policy famously summarized as “blood and iron.” He used wars against Denmark, Austria, and France to advance German unification. Who was he?
Fought between Rome and Carthage from 264 to 146 BCE, these three conflicts were waged for dominance in the western Mediterranean. What is the collective name for them?

Among the commanders of the Punic Wars, this Carthaginian general led an invasion of Italy by crossing the Alps with an army that included war elephants. He was defeated by Scipio Africanus at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE. Who was he?
In Mexico, a 1926–1929 armed conflict pitted government forces against largely Catholic rebels who opposed the enforcement of anticlerical policies. What was this conflict called?
During the Cristero War, which Mexican president, in office from 1924 to 1928, enforced anticlerical restrictions that helped trigger the rebellion?

Which Peruvian Maoist insurgent organization waged a violent campaign during the country’s internal conflict? Its attacks included the 1983 killing of 69 people at Lucanamarca and the 1992 bombing on Tarata Street in Lima.
The Shining Path was founded and led for decades by which philosophy professor, who was captured by Peruvian authorities in Lima in 1992? He was also known by the nom de guerre “Presidente Gonzalo.”
Which Persian ruler rose from Persis, defeated the Medes, conquered Lydia after defeating Croesus, and captured Babylon, founding the Achaemenid Empire?

Which royal center did Cyrus the Great establish in Persis, where a palace-and-garden complex stood and a tomb is traditionally identified as his? The site served as an early Achaemenid capital in present-day Iran.

Which Achaemenid king succeeded Cyrus the Great and led the Persian conquest of Egypt in 525 BCE, becoming pharaoh after taking Memphis? Ancient accounts also associate his reign with campaigns toward Nubia and Cyrenaica.

On 23 May 1618, Bohemian Protestant nobles at the kingdom’s principal royal castle confronted imperial officials over religious rights and threw two governors and a secretary from a window; all three survived. What incident helped launch the Bohemian Revolt and is commonly treated as the opening of the Thirty Years’ War?

During the Second Defenestration of Prague, this imperial secretary survived a fall from Prague Castle alongside two governors. He was later ennobled with the name “von Hohenfall,” a reference to his fall. What was his original name?

In 1917, this uprising in Petrograd brought the Bolsheviks to power and displaced the Provisional Government that had followed the tsar’s abdication. Its success established the revolutionary regime that became Soviet Russia. What event was it?

During the October Revolution, which Bolshevik leader returned from Swiss exile earlier that year, issued the April Theses calling for “all power to the Soviets,” and led the seizure of power in Petrograd?

A coup in September 1969 brought this Libyan officer to power, and he ruled for more than four decades before being captured near Sirte during the 2011 civil war. He also authored a work presenting his political ideas. Who was this leader?
Muammar Gaddafi presented this political manifesto as the basis for his proposed alternative to representative democracy, known as the Jamahiriya. What was the manifesto called?

After Japanese forces captured China’s Nationalist capital on December 13, 1937, weeks of mass killing, sexual violence, and looting unfolded in and around the city. What atrocity is named for this former Chinese capital?
During the Nanjing Massacre, this German businessman helped organize the international Safety Zone that sheltered civilians and kept a diary documenting events. What was his name?
What was the name of the imperial state that King Gojong proclaimed in 1897, elevating himself to emperor, and that Japan formally annexed in 1910?
During the Korean Empire, which ruler sent secret representatives to the 1907 Hague Peace Conference to challenge Japan’s protectorate over Korea, an act that helped prompt his forced abdication?

This king of Pontus fought three wars against Rome and sent forces that sacked the Aegean island of Delos in 88 BCE. Ancient accounts also associate him with taking small doses of poison to build resistance to poisoning; identify the ruler.

In 88 BCE, during the conflict between Rome and Mithridates VI Eupator, forces aligned with the Pontic king attacked this Cycladic island, a major sanctuary of Apollo and an important commercial port. Its destruction helped undermine its prominence as a trading center; which island was it?
In the Roman cursus honorum, this office ranked after the quaestorship and involved overseeing public buildings, urban administration, festivals, and games. What was this office called?
After prosecuting Gaius Verres for abuses as governor of Sicily, which Roman orator was elected to the aedileship? His successful case helped advance his political career.
Which Southeast Asian country was known internationally as Siam until 1939? Its 1932 revolution ended absolute monarchy and established a constitutional monarchy.
In Thailand’s history, which kingdom became the second Siamese capital after Sukhothai, developed into a major center of trade and diplomacy, and was destroyed by Burmese forces in 1767?

After succeeding her half-brother Edward VI, this Tudor queen sought to restore Roman Catholicism throughout her realm and brought Reginald Pole back from exile to become Archbishop of Canterbury. Her reign also saw the executions of Protestant bishops Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley. Who was this monarch?
Mary I of England’s proposed marriage to Philip of Spain prompted a 1554 uprising led by a Kentish landowner who gathered forces at Rochester and advanced toward London. What is this revolt known as?

In 1688, a Dutch ruler landed in England after receiving an invitation from a group later known as the Immortal Seven, and James II fled the country. What name is given to the upheaval that brought William and Mary to the throne and led to the English Bill of Rights?
During the Glorious Revolution, which Catholic monarch was driven from the English throne in 1688 and later, with French support, tried unsuccessfully to recover it in Ireland?
Founded in 1961 as the African National Congress’s armed wing, this organization began a sabotage campaign against apartheid government targets. What was this liberation movement called?

In 1963, a police raid on this rural property outside Johannesburg exposed a secret ANC headquarters and helped lead to the Rivonia Trial. Umkhonto we Sizwe members and other ANC leaders used the property as a clandestine base; what was it called?
A Bosnian Serb nationalist associated with Young Bosnia carried out the fatal shooting in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, killing Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie. What was the assassin’s name?

After Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Austria-Hungary issued Serbia an ultimatum in 1914, escalating tensions among the European powers. What name is given to this chain of diplomatic events?

Which Augsburg merchant-banking dynasty became one of Europe’s wealthiest families during the Renaissance, lending heavily to Habsburg rulers and influencing early modern finance? Its fortunes grew especially under a patriarch who built a major mining and metal-trading empire.

Within the Fugger family, which Augsburg financier known as “the Rich” expanded the family’s mining and metal-trading interests and helped finance the Habsburgs, including Charles V’s imperial election?
Elevated to crown prince of Saudi Arabia in 2017, this royal became the kingdom’s de facto ruler and was closely associated with its intervention in Yemen. Who is he?

Mohammed bin Salman is associated with a 2016 Saudi economic-diversification program intended to reduce dependence on oil and expand sectors such as tourism and entertainment. What is this program called?

What is the name of the organized-crime network rooted in Sicily, whose local groups have historically exercised territorial control and engaged in activities such as extortion and money laundering? Its best-known organization uses an Italian phrase meaning “Our Thing.”

A transatlantic heroin-smuggling network connected to the Sicilian Mafia was exposed in a major U.S. investigation and prosecution in the 1980s. The case became known by a name referring to the type of businesses used as fronts. What was it called?
Which Chinese imperial dynasty ruled from 1368 to 1644 between the Yuan and Qing dynasties and sponsored Zheng He’s seven maritime voyages? Its era is also renowned for blue-and-white porcelain.

Within the Ming dynasty, which emperor moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing and commissioned the palace complex later known as the Forbidden City? His reign also saw the launch of Zheng He’s first maritime expedition.

This ancient Maya city in present-day Guatemala was a major power whose rivalry with Calakmul shaped centuries of regional conflict. Its monumental architecture includes the Lost World complex. What city is it?

At Tikal, this funerary pyramid stands on the east side of the Great Plaza and was built for the ruler Jasaw Chan K’awiil I. In the site's conventional numbering of major structures, what designation does it bear?
What term collectively names maritime disasters in which ships sink, run aground, or are otherwise lost, including the catastrophe that inspired poems about the Titanic?

Among works about shipwrecks, which English poet wrote “The Convergence of the Twain” about the Titanic disaster? He also wrote the novel *Far from the Madding Crowd*, whose title was adapted from a line in Gray’s “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.”
What was the name of Portugal’s authoritarian corporatist regime, established in 1933 under António de Oliveira Salazar? It remained in power until its overthrow in 1974.
What 1974 uprising ended Portugal’s Estado Novo? A largely bloodless military revolt led by the Armed Forces Movement began on April 25 and restored democracy.

In early Chinese political thought, what doctrine held that a dynasty’s right to rule depended on divine favor, which could be withdrawn from unjust or incompetent rulers? It was used to explain why a ruling house might be overthrown and replaced by another.

The Mandate of Heaven was invoked by this ruling house to justify its overthrow of the Shang, arguing that the Shang ruler’s wrongdoing had cost him divine support. Founded by King Wu after the Battle of Muye, which Chinese ruling house held power for centuries?

Formed in 1871 after Prussia united numerous Central European states, this federation was dominated by Prussia and ruled by Hohenzollern emperors. It ended with the November Revolution of 1918, when Germany became a republic. What was this state called?
In the German Empire, this statesman became the first chancellor under Wilhelm I and helped achieve unification through wars and diplomacy. Wilhelm II dismissed him in 1890. Who was he?
The German Empire’s final emperor pursued Weltpolitik and oversaw the country during World War I. He abdicated in November 1918 as revolution swept Germany. Who was he?

This Canadian Liberal leader won the 1968 federal election amid a phenomenon dubbed “Trudeaumania.” During the October Crisis, he invoked the War Measures Act and later advanced the Just Society and National Energy Program. Who was he?

Introduced by Pierre Trudeau’s government in 1980, this policy sought greater Canadian control of the petroleum industry and redirected a larger share of oil revenues to the federal government. Its design provoked strong opposition in Alberta and became a symbol of western alienation. What was this policy called?

Born in Dublin in 1769, this British soldier built his reputation fighting Napoleon’s forces in Portugal and Spain before commanding allied troops at Waterloo. He later served as prime minister of the United Kingdom. Which military and political figure is described?

Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, commanded a multinational allied army in this battle fought on June 18, 1815, in present-day Belgium. The arrival of Prussian forces under Gebhard von Blücher helped secure Napoleon’s defeat there. What battle was it?

An Anglo-Saxon kingdom in southern England became the nucleus of a unified English state under Alfred the Great and his successors. Alfred also negotiated a peace treaty with the Viking leader Guthrum while ruling this kingdom; name it.

The Kingdom of Wessex contested power with this neighboring Anglo-Saxon kingdom, whose seventh-century ruler Penda fought numerous rival kings. Its later ruler Offa is associated with the earthwork border known as Offa’s Dyke; what kingdom was it?
Since 2013, he has served as both general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and president of the People's Republic of China. Who is this Chinese political leader?

Introduced by Xi Jinping in 2013, this program seeks to expand trade and infrastructure links through overland economic corridors across Eurasia and maritime routes connecting regions including Africa and Europe. What is it called?

The third ruler of the Mauryan dynasty governed an empire centered at Magadha and is remembered for inscriptions promoting dhamma after a devastating eastern conquest. Which emperor’s reign is closely associated with the Kalinga War and the spread of Buddhist influence?

In the eighth regnal year of Ashoka the Great, around 260 BCE, a campaign against a kingdom on the eastern coast caused mass deaths and deportations that the emperor later lamented in an inscription. What was this conflict?
Ashoka the Great governed his vast Mauryan realm from an ancient city in present-day Bihar, which had also served as the capital under Chandragupta Maurya. What was this capital called?

The historical identity of Ashoka the Great became clearer in the nineteenth century as scholars learned to read his inscriptions. Which English antiquarian is especially credited with deciphering the Brahmi script in 1837?

This Habsburg ruler became king of Spain in 1516 and was elected Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. His reign included wars with Francis I of France and the upheaval of the Protestant Reformation; he relinquished his crowns in 1556. Who was he?
During the reign of Charles V, what 1555 settlement allowed rulers within the Holy Roman Empire to choose whether their territories would be Catholic or Lutheran?
In 1980, Cuba authorized a mass departure by sea from a port west of Havana to the United States. What name is given to this migration episode?
During the Mariel Boatlift, many private boats crossed the Florida Straits to this southernmost Florida city, which served as a first U.S. landfall for many arrivals. Which city was it?
In 480 BCE, a Greek alliance used a narrow pass to delay the second Persian invasion, with a Spartan-led rearguard making a famous last stand. What battle was fought there?
At the Battle of Thermopylae, which Spartan king led the Greek defense and remained with the rearguard after most of the allied force withdrew?
At the Battle of Thermopylae, a Greek man disclosed a mountain path that let the Persians get behind the main Greek position. What was this man’s name?

The Battle of Thermopylae was paired in Greek strategy with the naval defense at Artemisium, as planners sought to block Persian movement by both land and sea. Which Athenian statesman championed this strategy and later played a major role at Salamis?
At the Battle of Thermopylae, which Achaemenid Persian king commanded the invading army? He was the son of Darius I, and his fleet was defeated at Salamis later in the invasion.

When the United States closed its airspace after the September 11 attacks, Canada coordinated the landing of hundreds of inbound international flights at airports across the country. What was the name of this Canadian emergency air-traffic operation?
During Operation Yellow Ribbon, this town in Newfoundland and Labrador welcomed thousands of stranded passengers after dozens of aircraft were diverted to its airport. Which town was it?

At the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in February 1956, an address delivered in a closed session criticized a cult of personality and crimes associated with the Soviet leader who had died three years earlier. By what name is this landmark address commonly known?

In Khrushchev's Secret Speech, the speaker attacked the cult of personality surrounding the Soviet leader who had died in 1953 and condemned the repression carried out under his rule. Which leader was being denounced?

This monarch acceded to the British throne in 1837 at age 18 and reigned until 1901. Parliament granted her the title Empress of India in 1876, and her 63-year reign gave its name to an era. Identify her.

Queen Victoria married this German-born first cousin in 1840, and their nine children married into royal and noble houses across Europe. After he died in 1861, she entered a prolonged period of mourning; name her husband.
In 1876, Parliament conferred on Queen Victoria an imperial title tied to Britain's rule over the Indian subcontinent. What title did she receive?
Queen Victoria's long reign lends its name to this era, associated in Britain with rapid industrial change, scientific advances, and strict public morality. What historical period is it?

Queen Victoria was the final British sovereign from this royal dynasty, which had held the throne since George I's accession in 1714. Her son Edward VII succeeded her in 1901, beginning a different dynastic line; name the dynasty.

Fought from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918, this global conflict pitted the Allied Powers against the Central Powers and featured trench warfare on the Western Front. By what name is this war commonly known?
During World War I, the assassination in Sarajevo of this Austro-Hungarian heir in June 1914 set off the July Crisis that led Austria-Hungary to declare war on Serbia. Who was the murdered heir?

During World War I, Germany's invasion of this neutral country in August 1914 helped bring Britain into the conflict under its treaty commitments. What country, whose capital is Brussels, was invaded?

During World War I, this 1916 battle on the Western Front became one of the bloodiest of the conflict; British forces introduced tanks in battle during its later stages. What battle, fought along a river in northern France, is described?
At the close of World War I, the 1919 peace settlement with Germany required territorial concessions, military restrictions, and reparations. What agreement was this?

A major rupture between the People’s Republic of China and the Soviet Union grew from disputes over de-Stalinization, peaceful coexistence with the West, and leadership of the communist world. What is this Cold War break commonly called?
During the Sino-Soviet Split, which Soviet leader’s 1956 denunciation of Stalin and advocacy of peaceful coexistence with the West sharpened Mao’s ideological opposition?

Australian policies and practices forcibly separated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families, placing many in institutions or non-Indigenous homes and disrupting cultural ties. What collective term describes the people affected by these removals, which were investigated in the 1997 Bringing Them Home inquiry?

On February 13, 2008, Australia’s prime minister addressed Parliament to apologize to the Stolen Generations for the forced removal of Indigenous children. Which prime minister delivered that apology?

In 1978, demonstrations and strikes weakened the Pahlavi monarchy. After Mohammad Reza Shah left the country in January 1979, Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile, and the monarchy collapsed later that month. What upheaval led to a March referendum approving an Islamic republic?

During the Iranian Revolution of 1979, this cleric returned to Tehran on 1 February after years in exile, including time in Najaf. The new constitution later placed major authority in the office of supreme leader, which he held. Who was he?

This Spanish general became the Nationalist leader during the 1936 uprising against the Second Spanish Republic and ruled Spain from the end of the Civil War in 1939 until his death in 1975. He rose rapidly through the army while serving in Spanish Morocco; name this dictator.

During the later decades of Francisco Franco’s rule, Spain moved away from autarky toward economic reforms that helped fuel rapid growth in the 1950s and 1960s. What common term names this period of economic expansion?

Francisco Franco kept Spain officially neutral during World War II, but in 1941 he sent a volunteer formation of Spanish soldiers to fight alongside Germany against the Soviet Union. By what color-based name was this unit known?

Beginning in the sixteenth century, this religious movement challenged Roman Catholic authority and practices such as the sale of indulgences, leading to the formation of new Christian churches. What is the name of this movement?

During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther circulated a document in 1517 that challenged the sale of indulgences and called for debate over church practices. What is this document commonly called?

In 787, bishops assembled to address the Byzantine Iconoclast Controversy, affirming that religious images could be venerated but not worshipped. What gathering, held in the city whose name appears in its title, made this ruling?

At the Second Council of Nicaea, the Byzantine regent who had served as empress consort supported the restoration of icon veneration and helped summon the bishops in 787. Which ruler, the mother of Constantine VI, was this?
Which West African empire rose to dominance after Mali, made Gao its capital, and was defeated by Moroccan forces at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591?
The Songhai Empire profited from trade in gold as well as a mineral extracted at Taghaza. What mineral was valued across the region for preserving and seasoning food?

Ancient Indian armies trained these animals for battle, and their use later spread to Hellenistic and Carthaginian forces. Alexander’s army faced them at the Hydaspes, while Hannibal famously took them across the Alps; what is the name for their military use?

During the Second Punic War, Scipio Africanus ordered his Roman infantry to leave lanes open so a Carthaginian charge involving war elephants could pass through. What 202 BCE battle ended in Hannibal’s defeat?

Formed in 1922 after the Bolsheviks won the Russian Civil War, this multinational federation stretched across Eurasia and was governed by the Communist Party from Moscow. It dissolved in 1991 after years of reform and rising nationalist movements; what state was it?
The Soviet Union’s space program sent this cosmonaut aboard Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961. His flight lasted about 108 minutes and made him the first human to travel into space; who was he?

In 1943, the Soviet Union repelled Germany’s Operation Citadel, a major offensive against a salient on the Eastern Front. The campaign included the armored clash near Prokhorovka; what battle is commonly regarded as the largest tank battle in history?
Which landlocked country in southern Africa, with Lusaka as its capital, became the first African country to default on foreign debt during the COVID-19 pandemic?

In Zambia, which mined metal accounted for about 64% of export earnings and figured in debates over the country’s debt burden, after critics argued that IMF agreements restricted tax increases on it? Chile is the world’s largest producer of this metal.

Argentina’s military junta seized power on 24 March 1976, and security forces abducted suspected opponents, tortured detainees in secret detention centers, and caused thousands to disappear before civilian rule returned in 1983. What name is given to this campaign of state terror?

In the aftermath of the Dirty War, President Raúl Alfonsín established a national commission in 1983 to investigate forced disappearances. It collected testimony from survivors and relatives and published the report *Nunca Más*; by what acronym was the commission known?

Traditionally associated with the Eastern Zhou period, this Chinese strategist is credited with authoring *The Art of War* and is said to have served King Helü of Wu. By what name is he commonly known?
Traditional histories say Sun Tzu served as a minister to this ruler of the state of Wu, who reigned from 514 to 496 BCE. Identify this king.

Classical texts sometimes applied “Sun Tzu” to this military thinker as well as to Sun Tzu himself; the 1972 discovery of a separate treatise attributed to him helped scholars distinguish the two. Who was this strategist, traditionally described as a descendant of Sun Wu?

This long-lived maritime state was governed by elected leaders whose authority was constrained by councils, and its trading network reached Crete and the eastern Mediterranean. Napoleon’s forces entered its lagoon capital in 1797, bringing the state to an end; what republic was it?

In the Republic of Venice, this Gothic waterfront complex housed government offices and major councils. It stands beside St Mark’s Basilica and is connected to the former prison by the Bridge of Sighs; what building is it?

This British Conservative politician served as mayor of the UK capital from 2008 to 2016, then led the national government from 2019 until resigning in 2022. He was also a prominent campaigner for leaving the European Union in the 2016 referendum. Who is he?

Boris Johnson was a prominent campaigner for this outcome in the 2016 referendum and, as prime minister, oversaw the UK’s formal departure from the European Union in January 2020. What is that departure commonly called?

Boris Johnson served as mayor of this city from 2008 to 2016, during which a public bicycle-hire scheme became popularly known by a nickname pairing his first name with “Bikes.” Which city was he mayor of?
While Boris Johnson was prime minister, lockdown gatherings at 10 Downing Street led to police fines and a major political controversy. By what widely used nickname did this scandal become known?

This Great Lakes African people has long been present in Rwanda and Burundi and was the principal target of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. The flight of many of its members into eastern Zaire helped catalyze later regional conflicts. Which people is described?

The displacement of Tutsi people into what was then Zaire after Hutu extremist violence helped set the stage for these interconnected conflicts. The first began in 1996 and toppled Mobutu Sese Seko, while the second drew in numerous African countries. What are these conflicts collectively called?

This British civil servant oversaw government relief during the Irish famine of the 1840s. He was widely criticized for treating the disaster as an expression of divine providence and for supporting limits on aid. Who was he?

Charles Trevelyan oversaw relief during this late-1840s Irish crisis, when repeated blight destroyed the island’s principal food crop and drove many people to emigrate on so-called coffin ships. What was this catastrophe?

This British White Star Line liner left Southampton on 10 April 1912, called at Cherbourg and Queenstown, and sank in the North Atlantic five days later after striking an iceberg. What was the name of this Olympic-class ship on its maiden voyage to New York?

In 1985, an expedition found the Titanic’s wreck in the North Atlantic using the towed camera sled Argo. Which American oceanographer was chief scientist for the Woods Hole team that helped locate it?
Their name derives from gladius, the Latin word for sword. In ancient Rome, these combatants fought staged public contests, often after training in specialized schools.
Roman gladiators trained at several schools in the capital. What was the largest of these imperial training complexes, located beside the Colosseum?
Among Roman gladiators, which lightly armored fighter carried a weighted net, a trident, and a dagger, and often faced a heavily armored secutor?

In the final years of Stalin’s rule, Soviet authorities accused a group of predominantly Jewish physicians of conspiring to poison senior leaders, including Andrey Zhdanov. What name is given to this 1952–53 campaign, which was discredited and abandoned after Stalin’s death?
In accusations connected with the Doctors’ Plot, which senior Soviet party official’s 1948 death from heart disease was cited as evidence that doctors had deliberately caused a leader’s death?
Established by Nazi Germany near Oświęcim in occupied Poland in 1940, this camp complex included a later section that became the principal site of mass murder. What was the name of the complex?
Within Auschwitz-Birkenau, the inscription “Arbeit macht frei” stood above the gate of the camp that opened in 1940 and initially held many Polish political prisoners. Which camp was it?

In September 2007, Israeli aircraft carried out a covert strike against a facility in Syria’s Deir ez-Zor region that intelligence agencies suspected was a nuclear reactor under construction. What was the operation’s codename?
Operation Orchard was the Israeli airstrike that destroyed a secret Syrian facility in 2007. Situated near the Euphrates in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, what was the site called?

This late-twelfth-century Japanese civil war pitted the Taira clan against the Minamoto clan. Its outcome established Minamoto dominance and paved the way for the Kamakura shogunate; what conflict was it?

During the Genpei War, a decisive 1185 naval battle in the strait between Honshu and Kyushu ended in a Minamoto victory, and the child emperor Antoku drowned during the Taira defeat. What battle was this?

Developing in colonial Latin America from the encomienda, this large agricultural estate combined landownership with a labor system that could keep workers tied to the land through debt. What was this type of estate called?

Within the hacienda system, workers sometimes received advances from landowners and remained bound to the estate as their account balances grew, restricting their ability to leave. What was this labor arrangement called?
The Manchu Aisin Gioro house established this imperial state after taking Beijing in 1644. It followed the Ming and ended when the Xuantong Emperor abdicated in 1912; what was the state called?
In the Qing dynasty’s founding generation, this ruler proclaimed the Great Qing in 1636 and was the father of the Shunzhi Emperor. Who was he?
The Qing dynasty used this color-coded military and administrative system, established by Nurhaci before the conquest of Beijing. What was the system called?
During the Qing dynasty, this major civil war began in 1850 under Hong Xiuquan, whose followers established a rival Heavenly Kingdom centered on Nanjing. What was this uprising called?

Beginning in 1967 after leaders in southeastern Nigeria declared independence, this conflict pitted Nigeria’s federal government against a breakaway region and ended in January 1970. What is the conflict commonly known as?
During the Nigerian Civil War, the secessionist government in southeastern Nigeria proclaimed an independent state in 1967, led by Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu. What was the breakaway state called?
