An Irish nationalist who served as Minister for Finance and Director of Intelligence for the IRA during the War of Independence, he negotiated the 1921 agreement that created the Irish Free State. He was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth in County Cork during the Irish Civil War. Who was this revolutionary leader?

Michael Collins signed this December 1921 agreement with British representatives, accepting dominion status and an oath to the Crown for the southern twenty-six counties. Its provisions established a self-governing dominion, while opposition to its terms helped precipitate the ensuing civil war. What was this agreement called?

Which Italian Renaissance nobleman, the son of Pope Alexander VI, was made duke of Valentinois and led campaigns to consolidate papal territories in Romagna? Niccolò Machiavelli treated his rise and political methods as a notable example when analyzing princely power.

Which political treatise by Niccolò Machiavelli uses Cesare Borgia’s career as a case study in princely rule, including the claim that a ruler unable to be both loved and feared should choose fear? It also compares effective rulers to a fox and a lion.

France’s modern history includes the Revolution of 1789 and the establishment of successive republics. Its republic describes itself as indivisible, secular, democratic, and social; what national community, defined by citizenship as well as cultural traditions, is associated with the country?

During the 1789 French Revolution, members of the French people advanced a political text that placed sovereignty in the nation and affirmed equality before the law. What document is identified by those principles?
answer: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

question: Formed by Cuban revolutionaries after a failed 1953 assault on the Moncada Barracks, this organization later directed the insurgency that overthrew Fulgencio Batista. What was the organization called?
The Twenty-sixth of July Movement was led by this Cuban revolutionary, whose courtroom defense after the Moncada attack became known as “History Will Absolve Me.” Who was he?

Announced by Canada’s federal government in 1980, this petroleum policy sought greater Canadian ownership, a larger federal role in the industry, and a greater share of oil revenues. Its provisions provoked strong opposition in Western Canada. What was the policy called?
The National Energy Program was introduced in 1980 by a Liberal prime minister who promoted a “Just Society” and invoked the War Measures Act during the October Crisis. Who was this prime minister?

Historically known as Persia, this country lies in Western Asia and has Tehran as its modern capital. Its monarchy ended in a revolution in 1979 that established an Islamic republic. What country is it?
In Iran, this dynasty reunited the country in 1501 and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, setting a lasting religious direction for the country. What dynasty was it?
In Iran, this elected prime minister was ousted in a 1953 coup backed by Britain and the United States after his government nationalized the oil industry. Who was he?

Ancient Greek tradition credits this semi-legendary lawgiver with reorganizing the institutions of a southern Greek polis famed for its dual kingship and rigid communal discipline. Accounts link him to the Great Rhetra, a foundational constitutional pronouncement associated with Delphi; who was this figure?

Lycurgus of Sparta is traditionally credited with instituting a civic upbringing in which Spartan boys entered communal training around age seven and endured rigorous physical and military instruction. What was this system of education and training called?

From 1950 to 1953, forces from North and South Korea and their allies fought over the divided peninsula in a major Cold War confrontation. The armistice that halted the fighting established a demilitarized zone. What was this conflict called?
During the Korean War, what September 1950 amphibious operation, led by General Douglas MacArthur behind North Korean lines, helped recapture Seoul?

This historical monarchy emerged from earlier English kingdoms during the Viking period and remained a separate realm until its union with Scotland took effect on May 1, 1707. What was the name of this kingdom?

In the Kingdom of England, what 1215 charter did King John agree to at Runnymede after a baronial rebellion? It addressed grievances against royal power and primarily protected baronial interests rather than establishing universal rights.

Fought in northern France on 25 October 1415, this Hundred Years’ War battle saw Henry V’s smaller English army defeat a larger French force. English longbowmen and defensive stakes helped exploit the muddy field. What was the battle called?
At the Battle of Agincourt, this English king commanded the army that defeated the larger French force. His 1415 campaign in France strengthened his reputation as a military leader. Who was he?

A Siberian-born religious wanderer gained unusual access to the Romanov court, where his perceived ability to help the heir’s hemophilia strengthened his influence over Nicholas II’s family. Aristocratic conspirators murdered him in Petrograd in 1916.
This German-born empress of Russia relied on Grigori Rasputin’s counsel, especially amid concerns about her son Alexei’s hemophilia. Born Alix of Hesse and by Rhine, she was the wife of Nicholas II.

Before the monarchy’s abolition during the French Revolution, what title was borne by the heir apparent to the French throne? It took its name from Dauphiné, transferred to the French crown in 1349 under an agreement linking the territory to the king’s eldest son.

Which son of Marie Antoinette and the French king executed during the Revolution became Dauphin of France after his elder brother died in 1789? Royalists recognized him as king after his father’s execution, though he never ruled; by what name is he commonly known?

In Caribbean plantation economies, this tropical grass was processed into a major export, while its byproducts could be stored as molasses or distilled into rum. Eduardo Galeano argued that returns on investment in this crop helped fuel the growth of European capital. What crop is it?

Sugarcane farming on this Caribbean island grew alongside a class of colono farmers after its first sugar mill opened in 1873. Juan Ponce de León was its first governor, and the harbor of its capital is guarded by the fort El Morro. Name the island.
At the Gulf of Patras in 1571, a Catholic alliance called the Holy League defeated the Ottoman fleet in a major naval engagement. What battle was this?

Fernand Braudel argued that the Battle of Lepanto did not transform Mediterranean maritime power as dramatically as some accounts claimed. Which Spanish monarch, who reigned during the era at the center of Braudel’s study and sent the 1588 Armada against England, was on the throne?
Anne Bonny and Mary Read were convicted of this maritime crime, whose so-called Golden Age in the late 1600s and early 1700s included widespread raiding in the Caribbean. What crime is it?
During the Golden Age of piracy, this island off Haiti’s north coast became a haven for buccaneers. Its shape is often compared to a turtle shell; what is the island called?
Published in 1724, this book collected accounts of notorious pirates and helped shape later popular portrayals of piracy. What work is it?
answer: A General History of the Pyrates

question: A teacher and nationalist leader, he became the first president of Tanganyika after independence and then led the new union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar. He promoted an African socialist program based on self-reliance and communal rural development; who was he?
Julius Nyerere used this Swahili-named program to shape Tanzania’s version of African socialism, emphasizing self-reliance and communal village life. What was this program?

This Dominican friar traveled through German lands preaching and selling indulgences, claiming that a contribution could shorten a soul’s time in purgatory. His campaign became a prominent target of Martin Luther’s early criticism.

Johann Tetzel’s aggressive sale of indulgences became a major controversy during the Reformation. What Catholic assembly, convened by Pope Paul III beginning in 1545, reaffirmed the doctrine of purgatory and addressed abuses connected with indulgences?

In April and May 1943, Jewish resistance fighters took up arms when Nazi forces entered a walled district of Poland’s capital to resume mass deportations. What is the name of the revolt, which ended after the district was razed?
During the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which SS and police leader commanded the German operation to crush the resistance and later submitted a report titled “The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!”?

This early-eighteenth-century pirate captured the French ship La Concorde and renamed it as his flagship, then blockaded Charleston in 1718. He was killed by Royal Navy lieutenant Robert Maynard’s force at Ocracoke Inlet later that year. Who was he?

Blackbeard captured this French ship in 1717 and renamed it to serve as his flagship. After taking part in the blockade of Charleston, it ran aground near Beaufort, North Carolina, in 1718. What was the ship called?
Which landlocked country in the African Great Lakes region borders Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo? Its capital is Kigali, and it became independent in 1962.

During Rwanda’s 1994 genocide, which political-military movement captured Kigali and overthrew the extremist-led government, bringing the killings to an end? Paul Kagame led the movement and later became the country’s president.

Founded in 1892 as a clandestine Filipino society, it sought freedom from Spanish colonial rule and helped launch the 1896 revolution. Andrés Bonifacio was among its founders; what was this organization called?

A founder of the Katipunan, this revolutionary became one of its central leaders as the movement turned against Spanish rule. After the Tejeros Convention, he was arrested and executed in 1897; who was he?

Before entering Afghan politics, this economist worked at the World Bank and taught at Johns Hopkins University. He became president of Afghanistan in 2014 and left Kabul as the Taliban retook the capital in August 2021. Who was he?

During Ashraf Ghani’s presidency, the movement that ruled Kabul from 1996 to 2001 recaptured the capital in August 2021, prompting a large international airlift from Hamid Karzai International Airport. What event marked its return to national power?

In 371 BCE, Theban forces defeated a Spartan-led army near Thebes, and Spartan king Cleombrotus died in the fighting. Xenophon described the Theban hoplites as arrayed at least fifty shields deep, far deeper than the opposing Spartan line; what battle was this?

At the Battle of Leuctra, this Theban commander massed his hoplites in an unusually deep formation on the left, facing the Spartan king Cleombrotus. Who led the forces whose victory weakened Sparta’s dominance in Greece?

As prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, this statesman used the kingdom’s entry into the Crimean War to secure a place in European diplomacy. He later met Napoleon III in 1858 to negotiate French support against Austria; who was he?
In 1858, Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, met Napoleon III at a French spa town to discuss an alliance against Austrian power in northern Italy. What town hosted the meeting?

Centered in what is now New York, this Indigenous alliance originally united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca nations. Its shared political system was guided by the Great Law of Peace. What confederation was it?
Within the Iroquois Confederacy, which nation joined the original five in 1722, bringing the alliance to six nations? Its addition is reflected in the confederation’s other name, the Six Nations.

Before World War I, governments called up reservists and assembled troops, equipment, and supplies to prepare for war. What was this process called, and why did its rapid start in 1914 alarm European powers?

During the summer of 1914, fears about mobilization featured in a series of roughly ten brief communications exchanged by Tsar Nicholas II of Russia and his cousin, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany. By what name are these communications commonly known?

The Classis Misenensis and Classis Ravennas were major fleets of the ancient empire, and naumachiae staged naval battles using the same class of craft. During the First Punic War, some vessels of this kind carried a boarding bridge called the corvus. What is the natural collective name for these combat vessels?

Among Roman warships, what hinged boarding bridge with a spike could be dropped onto an enemy deck, securing the vessels so Roman infantry could cross? Its use is associated with Rome’s naval fighting against Carthage in the First Punic War.
This kingdom occupies most of the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, and its capital is Madrid. It includes autonomous communities such as Catalonia and the Basque Country. What country is it?
In 1588, Philip II sent this enormous fleet from Spain to support an invasion of England, but storms and English resistance helped ruin the campaign. By what name is the fleet commonly known?
The 1808–1814 conflict in Spain began after Napoleon’s forces intervened and provoked a popular uprising; British and Portuguese forces also fought against the French. What is this war called?

This Habsburg ruler was both king of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor. He issued the New Laws of 1542 to restrain abuses against Indigenous people in the Americas and was succeeded on the Spanish throne by Philip II. Which ruler is described?

Born Ma He, this Ming court official served as an admiral and led seven state-sponsored maritime expeditions across the Indian Ocean in the early fifteenth century. By what name is this eunuch best known?
Zheng He’s treasure voyages were sponsored by the Ming ruler who moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing and commissioned the Forbidden City. Which emperor was this?

From 1958 through 1976, Iceland and the United Kingdom repeatedly clashed over British trawlers’ access to North Atlantic fishing grounds. Iceland extended its fishing limits in stages, while its coast guard cut trawl gear and British vessels escorted fishing boats. What name is given to these maritime disputes?
During the Cod Wars, Iceland extended its fishing limit in 1975 to a distance that Britain ultimately accepted the following year. How far offshore did the claimed limit reach?

A major uprising began in 755 when a powerful northern frontier commander rebelled against the Tang court; after eight years of warfare, it had badly weakened the dynasty and reshaped its military and political order. What is this conflict known as?

During the An Lushan Rebellion, this renowned consort of Emperor Xuanzong was killed at Mawei after soldiers in the emperor’s retreating party demanded her death. She was celebrated as a great beauty and was the subject of Bai Juyi’s poem “The Song of Everlasting Sorrow.” Who was she?
Imposed in South Africa from 1948, this system enforced racial segregation and white-minority rule through laws governing residence, public life, and political rights. What was this system called?

A key legal foundation of apartheid, this 1950 South African statute classified people as Black, White, Coloured, or Indian, with their assigned categories shaping their legal treatment. What was the statute called?

This African National Congress leader spent 27 years in prison for his opposition to apartheid and was released in 1990. He became South Africa’s first Black president after the country’s first non-racial national election in 1994. Who was he?
Passed in 1950, this apartheid law assigned separate residential and commercial zones according to racial classification, causing widespread forced removals. What was this law called?

This Tang court figure formally took the imperial title in her own right, ruling from 690 to 705 CE and interrupting the Tang dynasty. Unlike an empress who governed on behalf of a male ruler, she was the only woman to rule China as emperor. Who was she?
Wu Zetian interrupted the Tang line when she ruled from 690 to 705 CE, proclaiming a restored regime whose name echoed an earlier Chinese royal house. What name did she use for her regime?

In the medieval polity that grew from the East Frankish realm, its monarch was traditionally chosen by German prince-electors, and famous holders included Otto the Great and Frederick Barbarossa. What was this imperial title?
The Holy Roman Emperor crowned in Rome by Pope John XII in 962, after defeating Berengar II of Italy, was a Saxon ruler whose reign conventionally marks the beginning of the empire. Who was he?

Born in 1901 as the youngest daughter of Nicholas II, this member of Russia’s imperial family became the focus of decades of claims by women who said they had survived the 1918 execution of the imperial family. What is her natural name?
answer: Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia

question: The execution of Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia and her family took place in July 1918 in a basement room of a residence in Yekaterinburg. Named for its former owner, what was the residence called?

Rising to power around 1816, this early-19th-century ruler strengthened age-based amabutho regiments and expanded his kingdom through conquest and the incorporation of neighboring communities. He was assassinated in 1828; identify this ruler.
Following Shaka Zulu’s assassination in 1828, which half-brother became ruler of the Zulu Kingdom? During his reign, Zulu forces fought the Voortrekkers at the Battle of Blood River in 1838.

Campaigners sought to overturn sex-based restrictions on voting in the United Kingdom, using both constitutional lobbying and, in some organizations, militant protest. The Representation of the People Act 1918 delivered a major breakthrough by granting the parliamentary vote to qualifying adults aged 30 and over who had previously been excluded; what was this movement called?

Within the British women's suffrage movement, this activist founded the Women's Social and Political Union in Manchester in 1903, an organization known for militant direct action. Which leader was repeatedly imprisoned for her campaign for votes for women?

This French churchman served as chief minister to Louis XIII and strengthened royal authority by curbing the political power of the nobility. He directed French policy during much of the Thirty Years’ War, backing Protestant powers against the Habsburgs despite his own Catholic office. Who was this statesman?
Under Cardinal Richelieu’s direction, French forces besieged this Atlantic port city, capturing it in 1628 and ending its status as a major Huguenot political stronghold. What city was it?

What Bronze Age society flourished on the Aegean islands around Delos, with settlements dating to the third and second millennia BCE? It is especially known for abstract marble human figures with arms crossed over the torso.

In the Cycladic civilization, artists made a characteristic type of upright marble sculpture depicting nude human figures with elongated bodies and hands resting across the abdomen. Most examples have little facial modeling beyond the nose; what is this figure type commonly called?

John A. Macdonald was its first holder, resigning amid the Pacific Scandal, and later occupants included William Lyon Mackenzie King and Pierre Trudeau. What is the title of the office at the head of the federal government based in Ottawa?

During the 1926 King–Byng affair, which Conservative leader did Governor General Lord Byng appoint as Prime Minister of Canada after Mackenzie King resigned? His short-lived ministry lost a confidence vote before an election returned King to office.

On 26 April 1986, a test of a nuclear unit’s electrical supply during a loss of external power ended in an explosion and fire at a reactor in Soviet Ukraine, releasing radioactive material across several countries. What event prompted the evacuation of nearby settlements and became a landmark in nuclear safety?
During the Chernobyl disaster, this purpose-built city near the power plant—home to many plant employees and founded in 1970—was evacuated after radioactive material was released. Which city was it?

Founded in 1911 by Serbian army officers, this secret nationalist society sought to unite Serbs living outside Serbia, especially those under Habsburg rule. Its members or associates helped arm and train conspirators involved in the 1914 Sarajevo assassination. What was the society called?
The Black Hand’s leading figure was Serbian army officer Dragutin Dimitrijević, who used a short nickname drawn from the name of an ancient Egyptian bull deity. What was his nickname?

Which fifteenth-century ruler, the son of John Hunyadi, was elected king of Hungary and became known for his Renaissance court and military reforms? His name is associated with a raven, a symbol on his coat of arms.
During Matthias Corvinus’s reign, what was the name of Hungary’s professional force, famous for its disciplined soldiers and campaigns across Central Europe?

In December 1805, Napoleon drew Russian and Austrian forces into a costly advance before striking through their center. This decisive French victory helped bring the War of the Third Coalition to a close. What was the battle?

At the Battle of Austerlitz, Napoleon appeared to weaken his right flank as coalition troops moved down from this elevated central position. French forces then retook it, splitting the opposing line. What was this position called?

Between 1772 and 1795, Russia, Prussia, and Austria successively seized territory from the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth until it disappeared as an independent state. What is the collective name for these three territorial divisions?
Within the Partitions of Poland, which 1793 episode was carried out by Russia and Prussia without Austria, further reducing the Commonwealth after the 1772 settlement?

Established after the 1953 armistice, this heavily fortified buffer runs between North and South Korea near—but not exactly along—the 38th parallel. Each side withdrew about two kilometers from the military demarcation line, creating a strip roughly four kilometers wide. What is this area called?

The Korean Demilitarized Zone took shape after representatives signed terms at Panmunjom on July 27, 1953. Those terms halted large-scale fighting in the Korean War without resolving Korea’s political division; what was the document called?
What is the common name for the 1449 Ming military disaster in which Oirat forces defeated the Ming army and captured Emperor Yingzong during a campaign in northern China?
During the Tumu Crisis, which Oirat leader commanded the forces that defeated the Ming expeditionary army and captured Emperor Yingzong in 1449?

What collective term refers to diverse hunter-gatherer communities of the Congo Basin, including the Mbenga, Mbuti, and Twa, whose populations were heavily affected by migrations from elsewhere in the region?

Many communities collectively known as African Pygmy peoples encountered this major prehistoric migration, which carried farming and ironworking from the Cameroon-Nigeria border region across central, eastern, and southern Africa. What is this long-term demographic and linguistic spread called?
In Roman tradition, the seven rulers from Romulus through Tarquinius Superbus held this royal title during the period before the Republic. What was the title?
The last traditional King of Rome was overthrown, according to Roman accounts, by Lucius Junius Brutus, an event associated with the founding of the Republic. What was this ruler’s name?

This Chilean army commander took power after the September 11, 1973 coup that ousted Salvador Allende and later headed a military government known for repressing political dissidents. After voters rejected continuing his rule in 1988, he handed the presidency to Patricio Aylwin in March 1990. Who was this ruler?

In 1988, voters decided whether Augusto Pinochet would continue in the presidency, and the “No” option defeated the proposal to extend his rule. What was this national vote, which was followed by elections in 1989?

In the valley between the Capitoline and Palatine hills, this ancient complex contained the Rostra, the Curia Julia, and the Temple of Saturn. Its Via Sacra carried religious processions and triumphal parades. What central civic space of ancient Rome was this?

A three-bayed monument on the northwest edge of the Roman Forum was dedicated in 203 CE to commemorate campaigns against the Parthian Empire. Its inscription originally honored an emperor and his sons Caracalla and Geta, though Caracalla later had Geta’s name erased. What monument is it?

This Neo-Babylonian king captured Jerusalem and deported many of its inhabitants to Babylon, an episode remembered as the Babylonian Captivity. He also sponsored extensive building projects in his capital, including work on its processional way and major temples. Which ruler is described?

Nebuchadnezzar II embellished this ceremonial gateway to Babylon with glazed bricks bearing reliefs of bulls and mušḫuššu dragons. A reconstructed portion of the monument is displayed at Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. What gateway is it?
This southern European republic is centered on a boot-shaped peninsula and has Rome as its capital. Its modern state emerged when a kingdom was proclaimed in 1861. What country is it?

On 12 December 1969, an explosion at a Milan bank killed 17 people and injured 88, becoming an early major episode in Italy’s Years of Lead. What attack is known by the name of the square where the bank stood?

In July 1943, German forces launched an offensive to pinch off a large Soviet salient on the Eastern Front, hoping to regain the initiative after Stalingrad. The fighting included a major armored clash near Prokhorovka; what battle was this?

In the Battle of Kursk, what was the German codename for the July 1943 offensive intended to eliminate the Soviet salient? The plan called for coordinated attacks from the north and south by Army Group Center and Army Group South.

A native of Arpinum who rose to the consulship despite lacking patrician ancestry, he exposed Catiline’s conspiracy in a series of speeches and later wrote works on rhetoric and philosophy. After his proscription in 43 BCE, his head and hands were displayed on the Rostra. Who was he?
In this dialogue by Cicero, set in 91 BCE at the villa of Lucius Licinius Crassus, Crassus and Marcus Antonius discuss the education and abilities required of an ideal orator. What work is it?

These Old Kingdom royal funerary monuments developed from Djoser’s six-tier, mastaba-like structure at Saqqara into smooth-sided tombs, including Khufu’s largest example at Giza. What royal funerary structures are being described?
In the history of Ancient Egyptian pyramids, which high official is traditionally credited with designing Djoser’s six-tier monument at Saqqara? He was later remembered as a physician and sage.

Launched by Brazilian federal prosecutors in March 2014, this wide-ranging inquiry began with corruption and money-laundering networks investigated in Curitiba before expanding across the country. Its evidence exposed bribery tied to contractors, politicians, and Brazil’s state-controlled oil sector; by what commonly used English name is this investigation known?

In Operation Car Wash, which state-controlled Brazilian oil company became a central focus of bribery allegations involving company executives, politicians, and political parties? The company later acknowledged corrupt payments and false accounting in a U.S. resolution.

A mnemonic for these six royal consorts ends with “Divorced, beheaded, died; Divorced, beheaded, survived.” They were the women who married the Tudor king whose break with Rome reshaped England. Who were they?
Among the Wives of Henry VIII, which Spanish-born princess was his first wife and the mother of Mary I? Her marriage to the king was annulled after a long dispute over its validity.

From 1885 until 1908, this vast Central African territory was treated as the personal possession of Belgium’s King Leopold II rather than initially as a colony of the Belgian state. Reports of forced labor to extract rubber and ivory and of severe abuses made it notorious; what was the territory called?
In the Congo Free State, which colonial military and police organization enforced rubber quotas and became associated with violence against workers, including mutilation for failing to meet demands?

This Venetian merchant began an overland journey through Asia in 1271 with his father and uncle, later reaching the court of the Mongol ruler of Yuan China. His descriptions of Asian lands and customs became a widely circulated account for medieval European readers. Who was this traveler?

Marco Polo’s account of his travels was put into literary form by this Pisan writer of romances, whom he met while the two were imprisoned in Genoa after a conflict between Venice and Genoa. Who was the writer?

Signed on 10 April 1998, this accord established a devolved assembly at Stormont and a North-South Ministerial Council to support cooperation between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. What settlement, intended to help end the Troubles, was it?
A former U.S. Senate majority leader from Maine, he chaired the multiparty negotiations that produced the Good Friday Agreement as an independent mediator. Who was this American politician?

This Argentine political family included Juan, a military officer who served as president three times, his second wife, a celebrated first lady and political activist, and his third wife, who later became president. What family is identified by these members?

Within the Perón family, which actress-turned-first lady used her public influence to advocate for workers and women’s suffrage in Argentina? She founded a namesake charitable foundation and died in 1952, before her husband’s later return to the presidency.

Born in 1491 as the second son of the first Tudor king, he became heir after his older brother Arthur died and began his reign in 1509. His dispute over an annulment helped sever England’s obedience to Rome. Who was this Tudor king?
During Henry VIII’s effort to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, this Archbishop of Canterbury declared the marriage void in 1533. Which churchman issued that judgment?
Under Henry VIII, legislation declared the monarch supreme head of the Church of England and ended the realm’s submission to papal authority. What were these measures collectively called?
Henry VIII’s dissolution of monasteries helped provoke a large 1536 uprising led by Robert Aske that began in Yorkshire and spread across northern England. What was this revolt called?
Which heraldic floral emblem represented the Plantagenet branch whose last king was Richard III, during its struggle against the House of Lancaster?
The White Rose of York identified the Yorkist side in what English dynastic conflict, fought against the House of Lancaster and named for the rival sides’ floral emblems?
This ruling dynasty produced the kings of Prussia and all three emperors of the German Empire, including the monarch proclaimed emperor at Versailles in 1871. What was the family called?

The House of Hohenzollern supplied this monarch, who had ruled Prussia since 1861 and was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in 1871 after the Franco-Prussian War. Which king became the first emperor of the newly unified German Empire?

She inherited the Habsburg hereditary lands from her father, Charles VI, in 1740, and her succession helped spark the War of the Austrian Succession. She ruled until 1780 but was never Holy Roman emperor; who was this Habsburg ruler?
Maria Theresa’s son became her co-ruler in 1765 and succeeded her as ruler of the Habsburg lands in 1780. What was his name?

What is the familiar name for an international exposition where nations and host cities present advances in technology, industry, culture, and art? London’s 1851 edition occupied the Crystal Palace, and Seattle’s 1962 edition is remembered for the Space Needle.
At the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, organizers erected a 264-foot rotating amusement structure with 36 passenger cars as a dramatic American response to Paris's Eiffel Tower. What attraction was it?

A legendary, irrigated complex of elevated terraces was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Ancient accounts place it in the Mesopotamian city famed for the Ishtar Gate and Hammurabi’s law code. What is this wonder commonly called?

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are traditionally linked to a sixth-century BCE ruler who expanded Babylon and is said to have commissioned the terraces to evoke his Median wife’s homeland. Which Neo-Babylonian king is named in that account?

This Mexican army general seized the presidency after overthrowing Francisco I. Madero during the Ten Tragic Days of February 1913. His government was not recognized by the United States, and he resigned and fled Mexico in 1914. Who was he?

Victoriano Huerta’s 1913 coup during the Ten Tragic Days ended the presidency of this leader, who had defeated Porfirio Díaz in Mexico’s 1911 election after campaigning on the slogan “Effective suffrage, no reelection.” Who was he?

What dual monarchy was established by the 1867 Ausgleich, joining the Habsburg-ruled Austrian lands and the lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen under a shared ruler? It was dissolved at the end of World War I.

Which heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary was assassinated in Sarajevo in June 1914 while visiting with his wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg? His killing triggered the crisis that escalated into World War I.
Which Khmer monarch ruled in the early twelfth century, commissioned the great temple complex at Angkor Wat, and expanded the empire through military campaigns?
Suryavarman II commissioned a vast temple complex near the Khmer capital, originally dedicated to Vishnu and later used as a Buddhist pilgrimage site. What is this monumental complex called?

This Iraqi Ba'athist official, a cousin of Saddam Hussein, directed the 1988 military campaign against Kurdish communities in northern Iraq and held senior posts including defense minister. He was later convicted and executed for crimes connected to mass killings and chemical attacks. Who was he?

Ali Hassan al-Majid directed this 1988 Iraqi offensive against Kurdish populations, which involved village destruction, forced deportations, and chemical attacks. By what name is this operation known?

Beginning in 218 BCE and ending in 201 BCE, this conflict saw Hannibal lead Carthaginian forces across the Alps and win major victories at Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae before Rome ultimately prevailed. What war was it?
During the Second Punic War, Rome passed a law restricting women from displaying wealth through gold jewelry, costly clothing, and certain carriage use. What was this law called?

Meeting in several sessions from 1545 to 1563 amid the Protestant Reformation, this Roman Catholic ecumenical assembly issued decrees on Scripture, justification, and the sacraments while also reforming church discipline. What gathering became a defining institutional response to the Reformation?
At the Council of Trent, a decree adopted in 1563 required dioceses to establish institutions to educate future priests. What type of institution did this reform mandate?
Which ancient Roman seaside city near Naples was buried during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE? Hot volcanic surges there preserved timber and upper stories unusually well.
At Herculaneum, what lavish Roman residence was excavated with a large collection of carbonized papyrus scrolls, including philosophical writings associated with Philodemus?

Compiled in 1676 during Japan’s Edo period, this manual preserves ninjutsu knowledge associated with the Iga and Kōka traditions, covering training, tools, tactics, and practitioners’ conduct. What is this work, which the National Diet Library lists among three major ninjutsu books?

The Bansenshūkai, a 1676 compilation of ninjutsu knowledge, is traditionally credited to which person? The attribution is uncertain because the surviving copy names a family lineage but does not explicitly identify an individual compiler.

On September 25, 1066, King Harold Godwinson’s army hurried north to meet an invading Norwegian force near York, killing its king and his English ally Tostig. What battle was this English victory, fought shortly before the clash at Hastings?
At the Battle of Stamford Bridge, which Norwegian king had allied with Tostig Godwinson and was killed when Harold Godwinson’s forces defeated the invaders in 1066?

Founded in Jerusalem around 1119 to protect Christian pilgrims, this Catholic military order took its name from its headquarters near the Temple Mount. Its members became major landholders and financiers before Pope Clement V suppressed the order in 1312. What was the order called?

The Knights Templar emerged amid this series of military expeditions launched by western Christian powers to seize or defend Jerusalem and other holy sites. Its Third campaign included the efforts of Richard I and Philip II against Saladin after Jerusalem fell in 1187. What is the name of this broader series?

What name is given to the eighth- and ninth-century controversy in the Eastern Roman Empire over whether religious images could be venerated without committing idolatry? Its policies shifted over time, including renewed opposition beginning in 815 and the restoration of icon use in 843.

During Byzantine Iconoclasm, which synod in 787 affirmed the veneration of icons, opposing the position endorsed by Constantine V’s gathering at Hieria in 754? It was held in a city whose name appears in the synod’s title.

What name is given to the maritime raiders associated with Cilicia, on the southern coast of modern Turkey, who seized captives for ransom or sale and disrupted Mediterranean trade in the late Roman Republic? Plutarch also recounts that members of this group held a young Julius Caesar for ransom.

In 67 BCE, which Roman commander received an unusually broad command to suppress the Cilician pirates and brought their major forces to defeat near Coracesium? His campaign sharply curtailed their power, though piracy did not disappear.

Born in Vienna in 1755 as a daughter of Maria Theresa, she married the future Louis XVI in 1770 and became queen of France four years later. Who was this queen, later tried and executed during the French Revolution?

Marie Antoinette sought privacy from the formal court at Versailles at this smaller royal residence on the palace grounds. What was the name of this retreat, where she supported a quieter, more private way of life?
Which ancient Greek historian wrote the Histories, an account of the Greco-Persian Wars, and earned the title “Father of History”?
Herodotus recounts that 300 Spartans died defending a narrow mountain pass against the invading Persians in 480 BCE. What battle was this?

What prolonged British labor conflict ran from March 1984 to March 1985, pitting the National Union of Mineworkers against Margaret Thatcher’s government amid plans for coal-pit closures? It became one of the defining industrial disputes of modern British history.
During the 1984–1985 United Kingdom miners’ strike, which National Union of Mineworkers president led the union’s opposition to the Thatcher government? He had held the union’s presidency since 1982.

Founded by Genghis Khan in the 13th century, this empire became the largest contiguous land empire in history. Its successor states included the Yuan dynasty in China, the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, and the Ilkhanate. What empire was it?
A grandson of Genghis Khan, this ruler established the Yuan dynasty and completed the conquest of the Southern Song, bringing all of China under his rule. Which leader of the Mongol Empire was he?

After Nebuchadnezzar II’s sixth-century BCE campaigns, many Judeans were deported from Jerusalem, and a later campaign ended with the destruction of the First Temple. What is the name of this period of exile, from which Judeans were later permitted to return?
During the Babylonian Captivity, a Persian ruler conquered Babylon in 539 BCE and allowed Judean exiles to return to Jerusalem. What was this ruler’s name?

What term describes the deliberate killing of a prominent public figure when the person’s public role, the attacker’s motive, or consequences for government and public affairs give the act wider significance? It also applies to a failed attack when described as an attempt.

This actor and Confederate sympathizer carried out the political assassination of Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre during a performance of *Our American Cousin* on April 14, 1865; Lincoln died the following morning. Who was the attacker?
In 1453, an Ottoman siege brought the Byzantine capital under Mehmed II’s rule and ended the Byzantine Empire. What name is given to this pivotal event?
During the Fall of Constantinople, the Ottoman commander was a 21-year-old sultan who later became known by an epithet meaning “the Conqueror.” What was the name of this ruler?

Before British settlement began in 1788, the continent was home to hundreds of distinct nations and roughly 250 languages among its Indigenous inhabitants. What collective name is commonly used for these diverse peoples, whose ancestors arrived tens of thousands of years ago?

A 1992 High Court ruling rejected terra nullius and recognized that Indigenous native-title rights existed in Australian common law. What was the landmark case called that brought this change for Aboriginal peoples of Australia?

From the nineteenth century through the mid-twentieth century, government policies removed many children of mixed heritage from Aboriginal families and communities to assimilate them into white society. What collective name is used for these children and this history among Aboriginal peoples of Australia?

Founded by Shaka in southeastern Africa, this 19th-century state became a powerful kingdom with a formidable military system. Its forces famously defeated the British at Isandlwana, but the kingdom was later defeated at Ulundi in 1879. What kingdom was it?

During the Anglo-Zulu War, the Zulu Kingdom won a major victory on 22 January 1879 by overrunning a British camp after Lord Chelmsford split his column. What battle, fought near a prominent hill in present-day KwaZulu-Natal, was this?

At a major Indus civilization city in present-day Sindh, archaeologists found a brick-lined rectangular tank about 12 by 7 meters and 2.4 meters deep, with steps at both ends and water-resistant sealing. Often interpreted as a setting for communal or ritual ceremonies, what landmark is it?

The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro was part of an ancient city whose water management and urban planning were closely associated with this major South Asian river. What river gives its name to the civilization that built the city?

Which Joseon Korean warship had a covered upper deck designed to prevent enemy sailors from boarding, with openings that allowed its crew to fire cannon in several directions? It was used during the Japanese invasions of Korea in the 1590s.
Turtle ships are associated with the Joseon naval commander who led Korea’s naval resistance during the Imjin War against invasions ordered by Toyotomi Hideyoshi. What was this commander’s name?

From 1721, after Peter the Great adopted the title of emperor, this Romanov-ruled state stretched across northern Eurasia. Its monarchy collapsed in 1917 after Nicholas II abdicated during the February Revolution; what was this state called?
Within the Russian Empire, which nineteenth-century ruler issued the 1861 reform that emancipated the serfs? His reign also brought major changes to the empire’s legal and military systems.

Under Atlantic chattel slavery, the law treated these human beings as property that could be bought and sold, while enslavers compelled their labor and tried to control their movement and family lives. Many were forcibly transported from Africa and resisted through escape, work slowdowns, and revolt. What is the natural name for the people described?
Enslaved people captured in Africa were forced across the Atlantic in crowded ships, with many taken to Brazil and Caribbean plantations. What is the established name for this transatlantic voyage?
For centuries, Japan’s hereditary military ruler governed the country formally in the emperor’s name. What title did this officeholder bear before the Meiji Restoration of 1868?

After the last Shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, relinquished power, Emperor Meiji transferred Japan’s imperial capital to Tokyo. Which former capital had served as the seat of the imperial court for nearly a thousand years?
Which Hohenzollern ruler led Prussia during the Franco-Prussian War and was proclaimed the first German emperor at Versailles in January 1871?

Wilhelm I relied on this Prussian statesman, who became minister-president in 1862 and helped unify Germany through diplomacy and victories over Denmark, Austria, and France. After the empire was proclaimed in 1871, he became its first chancellor.

On 21 November 1920, during the Irish War of Independence, an IRA operation targeted suspected British intelligence personnel in the morning. That afternoon, British forces fired into spectators at a Gaelic football match at Croke Park in Dublin; what name is given to this day of violence?
During Bloody Sunday, British forces opened fire at Croke Park while Dublin and Tipperary were playing Gaelic football. Which Tipperary player was among the 14 people killed at the stadium?

This far-right German political party was officially known as the National Socialist German Workers’ Party, abbreviated NSDAP. Led by Adolf Hitler, it ruled Germany from 1933 until the end of World War II in 1945. What was the party commonly called?
The Nazi Party grew out of a precursor that existed from 1919 to 1920. Adolf Hitler joined this predecessor before it adopted the NSDAP name; what was it called?
The Nazi Party was led from 1921 by the man who became German chancellor in 1933. Who was this leader?
After the Reichstag fire, the Nazi Party consolidated its power through a law passed in March 1933 that allowed Hitler’s government to enact laws without parliament. What was this law called?
The Nazi Party established a totalitarian regime in Germany that claimed to embody a racially defined national community. What name is commonly given to this regime?

From 1568 to 1648, the Dutch provinces fought the Spanish Habsburg monarchy in a long struggle that ended with recognition of the Dutch Republic’s independence. What is the conventional name of this conflict?

During the Eighty Years’ War, this Prince of Orange became a leading political organizer of the Dutch revolt against Philip II, despite having earlier served at the Spanish court. He was assassinated at the Prinsenhof in Delft in 1584; who was he?

What is the name of the longstanding intelligence-sharing partnership among the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand? Its cooperation includes sharing intercepted communications, codebreaking, and analysis, and it grew out of wartime British-American intelligence work.
What 1946 pact formalized a communications-intelligence framework between the United States and the United Kingdom, later serving as a foundation for Five Eyes cooperation?

Founded by Phoenician settlers, this ancient city became the capital of a powerful Punic state and a major Mediterranean trading center. Rome destroyed it in 146 BC, and its ruins are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. What city is it?

In Carthage’s struggle with Rome during the Second Punic War, this commander led an army across the Alps with war elephants. At Cannae, he defeated a much larger Roman force using a double-envelopment maneuver. Who was he?

According to the traditional founding story of Carthage, this exiled royal woman from Tyre obtained land by cutting an oxhide into narrow strips and using them to mark a boundary. What was her commonly used name?
Rome’s nearly three-year siege of Carthage ended in 146 BC with the city’s destruction. What was the name of the final conflict in the series of wars between Rome and Carthage?
The archaeological ruins of Carthage lie near Lake Tunis in this modern North African country, which borders Algeria and Libya and has a Mediterranean coastline. What is the country?

Fought on 2 September 31 BCE in the Ionian Sea near western Greece, this naval engagement pitted Octavian’s forces, commanded by Marcus Agrippa, against the combined fleets of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII. What battle’s outcome cleared Octavian’s path to sole rule in Rome?

At the Battle of Actium, this Roman commander led Octavian’s victorious fleet. Before the battle, he weakened Antony’s position by disrupting communications between Greece and Egypt through operations in the Peloponnese. Who was this general and statesman?

At the Battle of Actium, this queen’s forces fought alongside Mark Antony’s, and she later returned to Alexandria after the defeat. She was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt before it became a Roman province in 30 BCE. Who was she?

In 313 CE, emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed to end the persecution of Christians, restore confiscated property, and permit religious worship throughout the Roman Empire. What agreement is known by the name of the city where it was issued?

The Edict of Milan was issued during the reign of a Roman ruler who reportedly saw a sign before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge and later convened the Council of Nicaea. Which ruler also founded Constantinople?

In 1922, this British archaeologist led the excavation in the Valley of the Kings that uncovered Tutankhamun’s tomb. A stairway was found on 4 November, and later that month he peered into the antechamber with Lord Carnarvon present; who was he?

Howard Carter’s search for Tutankhamun’s tomb was financed by this English earl, who was present when Carter looked into the antechamber on 26 November 1922. The aristocrat died in Egypt the following April; who was this patron?

What pre-Columbian civilization flourished in central Mexico, especially among Nahuatl-speaking peoples, and built a powerful state centered on an island city in Lake Texcoco? Its imperial power ended when its capital fell to Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies in 1521.
Which island city served as the Mexica capital and the leading center of the Aztec civilization? It stood in Lake Texcoco, and after its conquest in 1521, Mexico City was built over its ruins.

In the political history of the Aztec civilization, what 1427 pact united Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan to defeat Azcapotzalco? The partnership later became the foundation of a powerful central Mexican empire.

What 16th-century source on the Aztec civilization was compiled under Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and preserves parallel accounts in Spanish and Nahuatl? Its twelve books document Indigenous history, beliefs, customs, and daily life.

During Carnival in 1497, Florentines cast books, paintings, musical instruments, and other objects considered sinful into a public fire as part of a campaign to change the city’s customs. What is the name of this famous episode?

The Bonfire of the Vanities took place during this Dominican friar’s brief period of strong influence in Florence. His sermons urged residents to reject worldly display, and he also used illustrated printed pamphlets to spread his message. Who was this preacher?
Which Russian ruler succeeded Alexander III in 1894 and became the final sovereign of the Romanov dynasty? He abdicated during the 1917 revolution and was executed with his family the following year.
After Nicholas II was overthrown, he and his family were held at the Ipatiev House before being executed in July 1918. In which Ural city was the house located?

A revolt by Bohemian Protestant estates against Habsburg rule began after imperial officials were thrown from a castle window in Prague in 1618. The conflict spread across Central Europe, drew in powers with dynastic and strategic aims as well as religious ones, and ended in 1648. What was this war called?

The Thirty Years’ War ended in 1648 through agreements negotiated separately in Münster and Osnabrück. Their settlement reshaped political arrangements within the Holy Roman Empire and recognized Reformed Christianity alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism; by what name is it collectively known?

For the Asante, this sacred royal throne represented the soul and unity of the nation and was not meant for anyone to sit on. In 1900, British governor Frederick Hodgson's demand to sit upon it helped spark the conflict led by Yaa Asantewaa; what is the throne called?
During the 1900 crisis over the Golden Stool, this Asante queen mother from Ejisu mobilized resistance and became a leading commander against British forces. What was her name?

From 1648 to 1653, a succession of rebellions in France began with a dispute between the crown and the Parlement of Paris, then drew princes and nobles into a wider struggle during Louis XIV’s minority. What is this series of conflicts called?
During the Fronde, this queen mother governed France as regent while her son Louis XIV was still a child, with Cardinal Mazarin serving as a leading minister. Which ruler held the regency?

Near Xi’an, an enormous burial complex was built for the ruler who unified China in 221 BCE. Historical accounts describe rivers of mercury in its still-unopened central tomb, while nearby pits yielded thousands of life-size clay soldiers; what is this burial complex called?
answer: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

question: At the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor, farmers digging a well in 1974 uncovered pits containing thousands of life-size, individually modeled soldiers and horses, buried to guard the ruler in the afterlife. What is this famous assemblage called?

Born in Płońsk in 1886, this Zionist labor leader became chairman of the Jewish Agency during the final years of the British Mandate. He announced the creation of the new state in Tel Aviv in May 1948 and became its first prime minister; who was he?
David Ben-Gurion read the declaration establishing this country in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948, and then served as its first prime minister. What state later made the Knesset its national parliament?

A barrister who served as Director of Public Prosecutions from 2008 to 2013, he was elected leader of Britain's Labour Party in 2020. He led the party into the July 2024 general election and became the UK's prime minister afterward; who is this politician?
Keir Starmer became leader of this British political party in April 2020, succeeding Jeremy Corbyn. He led it to a parliamentary majority in the 2024 UK general election; what party was it?

Born Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili, this Soviet revolutionary became the USSR’s de facto dictator in the 1930s and led the country during World War II. He remained in power until his death in 1953. Who was he?

Under Joseph Stalin, a sweeping campaign of political repression targeted party officials, military leaders, and others accused of being enemies of the state. Thousands were executed, while many more were imprisoned, especially during the late 1930s. What was this campaign called?

Joseph Stalin’s government introduced these centralized economic programs in 1928 as it moved away from Lenin’s New Economic Policy. They set production targets and sought to rapidly industrialize the Soviet Union. What were these programs called?

Found at Babylon in 1879, this clay foundation inscription is written in Akkadian cuneiform and presents the Persian king’s conquest of Babylon as favored by Marduk. It also claims that temples were restored and displaced divine images and people were returned; what is this artifact?
The Cyrus Cylinder portrays this Babylonian deity as having chosen Cyrus to take the city, contrasting his favor with its criticism of Nabonidus. As the patron god of Babylon, who is this deity?

What conflict began after the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 and pitted the Red Army against anti-Bolshevik forces known as the Whites? Fighting spread across Russia, and major White armies were defeated by 1920.
During the Russian Civil War, which former Imperial Russian Navy admiral became a leading White commander in Siberia and was declared Supreme Ruler of Russia in 1918?

This southwestern European kingdom completed its conquest of the Algarve in 1249, and Lisbon became its capital in 1255. Which country later built a far-reaching overseas empire during the Age of Discovery?
In 1578, Portugal suffered a catastrophic defeat in Morocco in which King Sebastian died and much of the nobility was captured. Which battle was this?
After decades of rule under Portugal’s Estado Novo, a 1974 military-led uprising set off democratic reforms and the rapid end of the country’s African empire. What is the uprising known as?

Beginning in 1803, this series of conflicts saw France fight successive coalitions of European powers and concluded in 1815 after the French defeat at Waterloo. What is the common name for this era of conflict?

During the Napoleonic Wars, which 1805 naval engagement off the southwestern coast of Spain ended Napoleon’s plans to invade Britain after Admiral Horatio Nelson’s fleet defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets?

Promulgated in 1598 by a French king who had converted from Calvinism to Catholicism, this royal settlement granted the Huguenots defined worship rights and civil protections after decades of religious conflict. What decree is it?

The Edict of Nantes was issued in 1598 by this Bourbon monarch, who had been raised Protestant, converted to Catholicism, and became the first Bourbon king after the Valois dynasty ended. What king's name is associated with its promulgation?

At the Council of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II called for an armed expedition to aid Eastern Christians and recover the Holy Land. Which campaign captured Jerusalem in 1099 and helped establish the Kingdom of Jerusalem?

As Byzantine emperor from 1081 to 1118, he sought Western military assistance against the Seljuk Turks, and his appeal helped prompt the First Crusade. Which ruler negotiated with crusading leaders as they crossed imperial territory?

What 1587–1589 conflict within the French Wars of Religion pitted the reigning French king against the Catholic Duke of Guise and the Protestant claimant from Navarre in a struggle over succession to the crown?

During the War of the Three Henrys, Henry of Navarre’s Protestant faith made his succession to Henry III contentious. What collective name was used for French Protestants, especially those of the Reformed tradition?

Signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939 by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, this agreement publicly pledged that the two countries would not attack each other. Its secret protocols assigned parts of Eastern Europe to their respective spheres of influence and planned a partition of Poland. What was the agreement called?

Under the secret protocols of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, which country was slated for division between German and Soviet spheres? Germany invaded it on 1 September 1939, and Soviet forces entered from the east later that month; its capital is Warsaw.

In 1896, a valuable-metal discovery near Bonanza Creek in Canada’s Yukon drew an international influx of prospectors after news spread in 1897. What late-19th-century migration of prospectors headed toward Dawson City?

During the Klondike Gold Rush, many travelers who entered through Skagway or Dyea crossed this steep mountain passage into the Yukon before continuing toward Dawson City. Near its summit, climbers ascended a staircase of cut steps known as the “Golden Stairs”; what was this crossing called?
Which medieval empire, whose inhabitants called themselves Romans and whose capital was Constantinople, continued the Roman imperial state in the East after the Western Roman Empire collapsed?

The Byzantine Empire briefly regained much of Italy and the western Mediterranean during this emperor’s reign in the sixth century. He also commissioned the Corpus Juris Civilis, a major compilation of Roman law. Who was this ruler?
In 1204, forces on this campaign diverted from their route to the Holy Land and sacked Constantinople, severely fragmenting the Byzantine Empire. What was the name of this expedition?

Built in the fifth century under Theodosius II, this defensive system protected the landward side of the Byzantine Empire’s capital for centuries. Ottoman artillery breached it during the conquest of Constantinople in 1453. What was it called?
Serving as the Byzantine Empire’s emperor’s personal protection force, this elite military unit included Norse warriors and later many Anglo-Saxons. What was this force called?

In January 532, rival Blue and Green chariot-racing factions in Constantinople united against Justinian I, and imperial forces ultimately crushed the rebellion in the Hippodrome. What is this uprising commonly called?
During the Nika riots, fire destroyed an earlier church in Constantinople; Justinian commissioned a much larger replacement, dedicated in 537. What church was rebuilt?

Traditionally established in 930, this Icelandic assembly met at Þingvellir, where chieftains gathered to make laws and settle disputes. Its modern successor is Iceland’s national legislature. What is the institution called?

The Alþingi held its early annual meetings at this rift-valley site in southwestern Iceland, where the Law Rock served as a focal point. Today the site is a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. What place is it?

At the 1929 Lahore session of the Indian National Congress, this leader presided as complete independence became the movement’s goal. After British rule ended in 1947, he became independent India’s first prime minister and served until 1964. Who was he?

In 1942, Jawaharlal Nehru was imprisoned after a major Indian National Congress resolution called on Britain to end its colonial rule over the subcontinent. What mass nationalist campaign followed the resolution and faced a sweeping crackdown?

After Alexander the Great died without an adult successor in 323 BCE, his former commanders and other dynasts fought wars that divided his empire into Hellenistic kingdoms. By what collective name are these rival successors known?
Among the Diadochi, which former Macedonian general established control of Egypt, brought Alexander’s body to Alexandria, and founded the dynasty that ruled until Cleopatra VII?
During the French Revolution, what radical lower-class political movement was distinguished in popular imagery from aristocrats by its members’ long trousers rather than knee-breeches?

The Sans-culottes were often represented wearing what soft, forward-pointed red cap that became a wider emblem of revolutionary liberty in France? Its style was also associated with emancipated people in ancient Rome.
Alfonso X granted privileges to this powerful Castilian association of sheep owners and transhumant shepherds, helping protect their flocks’ seasonal migrations. What was this organization called?
In 1273, which Castilian king granted formal privileges to the Honrado Concejo de la Mesta, strengthening the rights of transhumant sheep herders?

This Roman emperor ruled from AD 306 to 337 and emerged from the Tetrarchic civil wars as sole ruler in 324. His reign marked a major shift in Christianity’s public status and saw Byzantium developed into a new imperial capital. Who was he?
In 313, Constantine the Great and Licinius issued a proclamation that permitted Christians to worship openly and ordered the return of confiscated church property. What was this proclamation called?

Constantine the Great developed Byzantium into an imperial capital and dedicated the refounded city in AD 330. What city, named after him and later known as Istanbul, became the capital of the eastern Roman Empire?

This Greek politician led a left-wing party to victory in the January 2015 election and became prime minister amid negotiations over the country’s international bailout. That July, he called a referendum on creditor-proposed bailout terms. Who was he?
Alexis Tsipras led this Greek left-wing political coalition, which won the January 2015 parliamentary election on an anti-austerity platform. What was the coalition called?

What Dravidian ethnolinguistic community shares a language with a major literary center in southern India, has long-established populations in Sri Lanka’s north and east, and also has communities across Southeast Asia? Its members have varied histories shaped by regional residence, colonial labor migration, trade, and diaspora.

The Tamil people have diverse histories, and no single political organization speaks for all of them. Which separatist organization, led by Velupillai Prabhakaran, fought the Sri Lankan government and sought an independent Tamil state before its defeat in 2009?

Which ancient Greek city occupied the narrow land bridge between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, giving it access to trade routes between two seas? It administered a festival honoring Poseidon and gave its name to one of the classical Greek architectural orders.

Near Corinth, a major Panhellenic festival took place at a sanctuary dedicated to Poseidon. Held every two years, it featured athletic contests and ranked among ancient Greece’s four major Panhellenic festivals; what was it called?

From Germany’s invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 to Japan’s surrender in September 1945, this global conflict pitted the Allied powers against the Axis and spread across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Pacific. What war is described?

During World War II, Allied troops landed on five beaches in Normandy, France, on 6 June 1944, beginning a major campaign to liberate western Europe. What is the commonly used name for that day of the landings?

During World War II, Germany’s advance into the Soviet Union led to a prolonged battle for a city on the Volga River. The fighting ended with the surrender of the German Sixth Army in February 1943; what battle was it?

During World War II, this Jewish teenager wrote a diary while hiding with her family and others in a concealed annex in Amsterdam. After they were discovered, she was deported and died at Bergen-Belsen; who was she?

In June 1942, during World War II, U.S. codebreakers learned Japan planned an assault on a central Pacific atoll. In the ensuing naval battle, American forces sank four Japanese fleet carriers; what battle was it?

Beginning in 1958, Mao Zedong’s government tried to transform China rapidly through collectivization and ambitious industrial production, including village steelmaking. The campaign drew labor and resources away from agriculture and was followed by a devastating famine; what was it called?

Dated 1959–1961, this catastrophe followed the Great Leap Forward and killed millions as agricultural production and food distribution deteriorated amid policy-driven resource diversion. What is this famine commonly called?
Founded in 1949 by the United States, Canada, and Western European countries, this military alliance states in Article 5 that an attack on one member is an attack on all. What is its formal name?

The creation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization prompted the Soviet Union to organize a rival military alliance in 1955 with communist governments in Eastern Europe. What was this alliance, named for the capital of Poland?

These narrow Scandinavian vessels used from roughly the late eighth through eleventh centuries had shallow-draft hulls made from overlapping planks, and crews could propel them with oars or a square sail. What are they called?

Among reconstructions of Viking longships, this full-scale vessel recreates Skuldelev 2, a large warship built in Dublin around 1042. What established name was given to the reconstruction built by the Viking Ship Museum at Roskilde?

Which Bolshevik revolutionary joined the party in 1917, organized the Red Army as war commissar during the Russian Civil War, and was assassinated in exile in Mexico in 1940 after becoming a prominent opponent of Joseph Stalin?
In 1938, Leon Trotsky helped establish a socialist organization as an alternative to the Stalin-dominated Comintern. What was this organization called?

On the early modern steppe frontier north of the Black Sea, self-governing armed communities guarded borderlands and sometimes served neighboring states as cavalry. Their name derives from a Turkic term associated with a person living freely; what people were these?
Among Cossacks in present-day Ukraine, a major military organization developed beyond the Dnieper River’s rapids and became associated with a fortified Sich. What was this organization called?

A lawyer and royal administrator who became one of Henry VIII’s most powerful ministers, he helped implement the English break with Rome and direct the dissolution of the monasteries. Which English statesman is described?

Thomas Cromwell served this Tudor king and helped implement the crown’s break with Rome. After Pope Clement VII refused to annul the king’s marriage to Catherine of Aragon, the king asserted royal supremacy over the English Church; who was he?

She was queen of the Iceni in eastern Britain, and her husband, Prasutagus, had ruled as a Roman ally. After his death, she led an uprising that sacked Colchester, London, and St Albans around AD 60–61. Who was she?

Near the end of Boudicca’s revolt around AD 60–61, the Roman governor Suetonius Paulinus defeated the rebel forces in a battle named after an important Roman road in Britain. What was this battle called?

Established in 1949 in the former Soviet occupation zone, this socialist German state was dominated by the Socialist Unity Party. It ceased to exist as a separate state when it joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. What was it called?
In East Germany, the Ministry for State Security monitored and repressed people considered opponents of the government. By what short name was this secret-police agency commonly known?

By conventional numbering, this period ran from 1701 through 1800. It encompassed Enlightenment debates about reason and political authority, the independence of Britain’s American colonies, and revolutions beginning in France and Saint-Domingue; what historical period is described?
During the 18th century, delegates from Britain’s thirteen North American colonies adopted a document in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, announcing their separation from the Crown. What document is it?
What World War II alliance, centered on Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, and imperial Japan, was formalized by a September 1940 pact and fought against the Allied coalition?
The Axis Powers never operated under a single unified military command, but Germany, Italy, and Japan formalized their partnership in September 1940 through what named agreement?

In 1588, Philip II sent a fleet to escort an army from the Netherlands across the English Channel and overthrow Elizabeth I. English attacks and severe weather scattered the expedition, including during its retreat around Scotland and Ireland; what was this campaign called?

During the Spanish Armada’s approach in 1588, this English vice admiral helped lead the fleet that harried it. Later accounts famously associate him with finishing a game of bowls at Plymouth before sailing out; who was he?

A former Indian Airlines pilot became India’s prime minister after his mother was assassinated in 1984, serving until 1989. He was later killed during an election campaign in Sriperumbudur by an LTTE-linked suicide bomber; which politician was he?

On July 29, 1987, Rajiv Gandhi and president J. R. Jayewardene signed an agreement intended to address the ethnic conflict in the island nation and provide for political changes there. It also contemplated Indian military assistance if the country requested it; what was the agreement called?
Which Mughal emperor ruled from 1628 to 1658 before his son Aurangzeb forcibly displaced him? After his wife Mumtaz Mahal died, he commissioned a monumental tomb for her at Agra.
Shah Jahan established a new Mughal capital in Delhi, with the Red Fort as its palace complex. What planned city became the empire’s imperial seat?
What was the name of the former colonial possession that encompassed much of present-day Indonesia and was administered from Batavia?
The Dutch East Indies was administered from a port city on Java that became the center of Dutch colonial rule in the archipelago. What was this city called during the colonial period?

Founded in 1392 by Yi Seonggye after the fall of Goryeo, this Korean royal house adopted Neo-Confucianism as a guiding state ideology. Its rule ended when the Korean Empire was proclaimed in 1897, though the royal order continued until Japanese annexation in 1910; what was its name?

During the Joseon Dynasty, King Sejong sponsored the creation of a phonetic writing system designed to make written Korean more accessible. Introduced in 1446 alongside an explanation of its design, what is this writing system called?

Adopted at a United Nations climate conference on 12 December 2015 and entering into force the following year, this treaty aims to keep global warming well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. What is this landmark climate accord?

Under the Paris Agreement, each country communicates its own climate action plan covering emissions and adaptation measures. Countries are expected to submit new or updated plans on a five-year cycle; what is the formal term for one of these plans?

In 490 BCE, a Persian expedition commanded by Datis and Artaphernes landed near a plain in Attica after capturing Eretria. An Athenian-led force joined by Plataeans defeated it after Miltiades strengthened the Greek flanks; what engagement was this?

At the Battle of Marathon, this Athenian general strengthened the Greek flanks, which wheeled inward and helped rout the Persian army. His leadership was central to the victory over Datis and Artaphernes in 490 BCE; who was he?
The Battle of Marathon thwarted this Achaemenid king’s first effort to subjugate Greece in 490 BCE. He later began preparing another expedition, but an Egyptian revolt delayed it; which ruler was he?

Which imperial state formally annexed Korea in 1910, occupied Manchuria beginning in 1931, and launched a wider war against China in 1937? Its attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the United States into the Pacific war.
The Empire of Japan formally surrendered on September 2, 1945, aboard an American battleship in Tokyo Bay. What was the name of that ship?

Developed by Britain during World War I to cross trenches and confront machine-gun positions, this tracked armored vehicle first entered combat on 15 September 1916. What is this type of weapon called?
The first Tank to see combat was a British model sent into battle on 15 September 1916, during fighting on the Somme. What was this model called?

Emerging from a northwestern Anatolian principality associated with Osman I near the end of the thirteenth century, this transcontinental Islamic state captured Constantinople in 1453 and made it its capital. It ruled large portions of southeastern Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa before its dissolution after World War I. What empire is described?
In the Ottoman Empire, this ruler led the 1453 siege that captured Constantinople and brought the Byzantine Empire to an end. Known by an epithet meaning “the Conqueror,” who was this sultan?

During the Ottoman Empire’s sixteenth-century expansion, this sultan reigned from 1520 to 1566, presiding over campaigns into central Europe and a major flowering of imperial arts and law. Which ruler is identified by that reign?

The Ottoman Empire undertook this nineteenth-century reform program to centralize administration and reorganize military and legal institutions. Beginning in 1839 and associated with the Imperial Edict of Gülhane, what reform era was it?
In the Ottoman Empire, this 1908 movement, organized by the Committee of Union and Progress, restored constitutional monarchy after decades of suspension. What political event was it?

A 16th-century adviser to Henry VIII helped bring about England’s break with Rome, while a later relative commanded Parliament’s forces in the English Civil Wars and became Lord Protector. What English political family is represented by these two figures?

Within the Cromwell family, which lawyer-statesman became Henry VIII’s chief minister, helped secure the king’s annulment from Catherine of Aragon, and directed the dissolution of England’s monasteries?

In October 1962, U-2 photographs exposed Soviet nuclear launch sites under construction on a Caribbean island, prompting a U.S. cordon and a tense superpower standoff. The confrontation ended after Moscow agreed to remove the weapons in exchange for U.S. assurances, including a public pledge not to invade the island. What is this crisis known as?

During the Cuban Missile Crisis, what term did President John F. Kennedy use for the maritime cordon he announced on October 22, 1962, choosing language intended to avoid the legal and diplomatic implications of declaring a blockade? This measure aimed to stop further Soviet weapons shipments from reaching the island.

On June 20, 1973, gunfire broke out among rival political factions at an international airport in Buenos Aires as thousands gathered for the return of a leader ending nearly 18 years in exile. What is this violent episode known as?

The Ezeiza massacre occurred as a crowd awaited the return of an Argentine leader who had been overthrown in 1955 and spent much of his exile in Spain. Which former president was returning to Argentina?
A Roman senator repeatedly ended his speeches with this Latin formula, urging the destruction of Carthage even when it was unrelated to the debate. What was the phrase?
The phrase “Carthago delenda est” is traditionally associated with which Roman statesman, a former censor whose repeated calls for war against Carthage preceded the Third Punic War?
Which 1215 charter issued by King John included Clause 61, a provision that allowed a group of barons to enforce the king’s compliance with its terms?
The Magna Carta was issued by King John for which kingdom, later united with Scotland in 1707 to form the Kingdom of Great Britain?

Launched by China in 2013, this global infrastructure and investment program links plans for an overland economic corridor with maritime routes connecting ports. Its projects can include railways, pipelines, and port construction, with potential trade gains accompanied by concerns about debt and governance. What is this program?

China launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013 under this leader, who became Chinese Communist Party general secretary in 2012 and president of China in 2013. His political doctrine was incorporated into the party constitution in 2017 under a title ending in “Thought.” Who is this leader?
