A late-19th-century Argentine military campaign expanded state control over Indigenous territories toward Patagonia, with a major offensive beginning in 1879 under Julio Argentino Roca. Its official name described the region as empty despite the Indigenous communities who lived there and suffered killing, captivity, and displacement. What was this campaign called?

During the Conquest of the Desert, which official expedition photographer recorded Argentine troops and Indigenous captives in photographs? His images documented the campaign alongside its military records.

After Australian federation, this system sought to limit non-European settlement and became associated with a test in which officials could require applicants to write a passage in a European language they selected. What was this system called?
Under the White Australia policy, which 1901 federal statute gave officials authority to administer a dictation test using a language chosen from among European tongues?
Founded by Osama bin Laden in the late 1980s, this transnational Islamist terrorist organization carried out the 1998 bombings of U.S. embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam. What organization is it?

Al-Qaeda claimed responsibility for the 2000 bombing of the USS Cole while the ship was refueling in this port city on Yemen’s southern coast, near the entrance to the Red Sea. What is the city’s name?

Established as an imperial capital in 330 CE on the site of Byzantium, this city stood on the Bosporus, linking routes between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Its Theodosian land walls and Hagia Sophia became landmarks of Byzantine power before Ottoman forces captured it in 1453. What was this city called?
Which Ottoman sultan captured Constantinople in 1453, made it his imperial capital, and became known by the title “the Conqueror”?

Ronald Reagan served as U.S. president for most of this decade, and communist governments across Eastern Europe fell as the Cold War neared its end. What decade saw the Berlin Wall open in its closing months?
In the 1980s, this would-be assassin wounded President Ronald Reagan outside the Washington Hilton in March 1981. A copy of *The Catcher in the Rye* was found among his belongings; who was he?

Which country in northwestern Europe emerged as a kingdom in 1815 after an earlier era as a federation of seven provinces? Its seventeenth-century maritime wealth supported artists such as Rembrandt and Vermeer.
In the history of the Netherlands, what chartered trading enterprise established a colonial system centered in Indonesia and used force to secure a nutmeg monopoly on the Banda Islands?

In 1992, Australia's highest court recognized native title for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and rejected the claim that Australia was legally unowned before British settlement. What landmark case made this ruling?
Mabo v Queensland rejected a colonial legal doctrine that treated Australia as legally unowned at the time of British acquisition, denying prior Indigenous land rights. What was this doctrine called?

This ancient Greek polis occupied Laconia in the southeastern Peloponnese and became renowned as Greece’s foremost land military power. Its citizen warriors underwent a demanding system of military training, while a much larger dependent population worked the land. What city-state is described?

In 371 BCE, Sparta’s dominance was shattered when Theban forces under Epaminondas won a decisive victory, beginning a period of Theban hegemony and helping free Messenia from Spartan control. What battle was this?

In Sparta, boys underwent a state-supervised system of upbringing and military discipline traditionally associated with Lycurgus. Training began in childhood and prepared them for service as citizens. What was this system called?

After Sparta organized its allies into a coalition against Athens, the resulting protracted conflict ended in 404 BCE with Athens’ surrender, following a Spartan naval victory at Aegospotami. What war was this?
In Sparta, much of the agricultural labor was imposed on a subjugated population of state-controlled serfs, especially in Laconia and Messenia. What was the name for members of this population?

Established in 1603 by the warlord who defeated Ishida Mitsunari at Sekigahara, this military government ruled Japan from Edo until the Meiji Restoration in 1868. It imposed controls on regional lords and sharply restricted foreign contact. What was this regime called?

During the Tokugawa Shogunate, this policy required daimyo to spend alternating periods in their domains and in Edo, while their families generally remained in the capital. The system helped the government monitor regional lords and placed a heavy burden on their resources. What was this policy called?

After his father died in 2011, this hereditary ruler assumed North Korea’s top leadership and later met a sitting U.S. president at the 2018 Singapore summit. He is the grandson of North Korea’s founder, Kim Il Sung; who is he?

Kim Jong-un’s government promoted an approach calling for nuclear-weapons development and economic growth in parallel, rather than making military affairs the overriding priority as under the earlier Songun approach. What was this approach called?
Kim Jong-un’s North Korea and South Korea are separated by a heavily guarded strip created under the 1953 armistice, running close to the 38th parallel. What is this boundary area called?

Beginning in 1648, this revolt brought Cossacks and other groups into conflict with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and lasted until 1657. It helped lay the foundations for a Cossack-led state in Ukrainian lands; what is the revolt known as?
The Khmelnytsky Uprising helped establish a polity in present-day Ukraine whose political center was Chyhyryn during Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s leadership. What was this polity commonly called?

This Russian ruler traveled through Western Europe on a diplomatic mission known as the Grand Embassy, where he studied shipbuilding and other practices he later introduced at home. He founded a new capital on the Neva River and moved the government there in 1712. Who was he?
In 1722, Peter the Great introduced a fourteen-grade hierarchy for military, civil, and court service, making advancement depend on service in the state. What was this system called?
Peter the Great fought this conflict against Sweden from 1700 to 1721. It ended with the Treaty of Nystad, which secured Russian territory on the eastern Baltic. What was the war called?
This historic nation occupies the northern part of Great Britain, and its capital is Edinburgh. After joining with England in 1707, it retained distinctive legal and educational institutions.

In medieval history, Scotland and France repeatedly cooperated against England, with their rulers making treaties and offering military support. What traditional name is given to this centuries-long relationship?

He became Chancellor of the Exchequer in February 2020, having entered the House of Commons as the MP for Richmond (Yorks) in 2015. After Liz Truss left office, he became prime minister of the United Kingdom in October 2022; which Conservative politician is this?

Rishi Sunak entered the House of Commons in 2015 for this predominantly rural constituency in North Yorkshire, which former Conservative leader William Hague represented for decades before him. What was the constituency?

In ancient tradition, Greek forces besieged a city in Anatolia after its prince took Helen from Sparta, prompting her husband and other Greek leaders to launch an expedition. The conflict’s famous episodes include Achilles’ quarrel and the death of the city’s champion, Hector. What legendary war is this?

Homer’s epic about the Trojan War focuses on a short period near the conflict’s end, centering on Achilles’ anger and the death of Hector. It concludes with the Trojans mourning their champion, rather than recounting the wooden horse’s entry into the city. What is the poem called?

A Thracian gladiator escaped from a training school near Capua in 73 BCE with about 70 fellow gladiators, then became a leading figure in a major uprising against the Roman Republic. By what name is this rebel leader known?
Spartacus’s uprising from 73 to 71 BCE became one of the most serious slave revolts in Roman history. What is the name historians give to this conflict?

Spartacus’s revolt was ultimately defeated in 71 BCE by a Roman commander who later became a member of the First Triumvirate. After the rebellion, he ordered 6,000 captured rebels to be crucified along the Appian Way; who was he?
Spartacus and the other gladiators escaped from a training school near this Campanian city, which lies south of Rome and near Naples. What was the city’s name?

In June 1967, Israel fought Egypt, Jordan, and Syria in this brief Arab-Israeli conflict and captured the Sinai Peninsula, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. What is the conflict commonly called?

During the Six-Day War, Israel captured this large region from Egypt. It lies between the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea and was later returned to Egypt under the 1979 peace treaty. What is this territory?

This Hohenzollern monarch ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786, seized Silesia from the Habsburgs, and led his state through the Seven Years’ War. Which ruler’s survival in that conflict became associated with the “Miracle of the House of Brandenburg”?

During the Seven Years’ War, Russia’s Empress Elizabeth died in 1762, and her successor Peter III soon made peace with Frederick the Great’s Prussia, easing the danger to the kingdom. What name is given to this unexpected turn that helped preserve Prussia?
answer: Miracle of the House of Brandenburg

question: An Australian Labor politician, he represented Sydney’s Grayndler electorate in federal parliament from 1996 and became prime minister in May 2022 after his party defeated Scott Morrison’s government. Who is he?

Anthony Albanese became prime minister in 2022, but this Australian wage-subsidy program was introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020 to help employers keep workers on their payrolls. What was the program called?

Eighteen monarchs of France used the same name as their regnal name, including the ruler known as the Sun King who revoked the Edict of Nantes and the king executed during the French Revolution. What name did they share?
Among the French kings named Louis, which monarch ruled from 1643 to 1715, became known as the Sun King, and issued the Edict of Fontainebleau revoking the Edict of Nantes?

In 221 BCE, after defeating rival Warring States, this Qin ruler adopted the new imperial title huangdi rather than merely calling himself king. He is also remembered for commissioning a vast mausoleum complex guarded by thousands of clay soldiers. Who was he?

Qin Shi Huang relied on this influential Qin official as chancellor during the standardization of script, weights and measures, and road widths across the newly unified empire. The official was later implicated in the court intrigue that installed Qin Er Shi as successor. Who was this minister?

Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum near modern Xi'an was built with a vast underground force of life-sized infantrymen, archers, and charioteers whose faces vary from figure to figure. What archaeological assemblage was brought to international attention after local well diggers discovered it in 1974?

After Joseph Stalin died in 1953, this Soviet politician emerged victorious from the ensuing leadership struggle and headed the USSR during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis. In 1956, he denounced Stalin’s purges and cult of personality in an address to the Communist Party’s Twentieth Congress. Who was this Soviet leader?

Nikita Khrushchev delivered this landmark address in a closed session of the Communist Party’s Twentieth Congress in February 1956, condemning Stalin’s purges and cult of personality. What address helped inaugurate de-Stalinization?
Before the northern and southern monarchies emerged, this ancient Israelite realm was ruled from Jerusalem first by David and then by Solomon. What was this polity called?

In accounts of the United Kingdom of Israel, this Phoenician ruler maintained an alliance with Solomon and supplied cedar timber and skilled workers for construction projects in Jerusalem. Who was he?

This Macedonian king became ruler in 336 BC after his father was assassinated, and Aristotle had tutored him in his youth. He led campaigns that conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and extended his realm from Greece to northwestern India. Who was he?
In 331 BC, Alexander the Great confronted Darius III near Arbela in a decisive battle that broke Persian power and opened the way to Babylon. What was this battle called?
Alexander the Great’s famous warhorse died after the campaign against King Porus at the Hydaspes, and a city founded in the region was named in the animal’s memory. What was the horse’s name?

After Alexander the Great died in Babylon in 323 BC, his generals and other successors fought over his empire, eventually establishing rival kingdoms such as the Seleucid and Ptolemaic realms. By what collective name are these successors known?

Born Sophie Friederike Auguste in Stettin, this German-born ruler took Russia’s throne in a 1762 coup that removed her husband, Peter III, and reigned until 1796. Her patronage of Enlightenment thinkers and expansion of the empire made her one of Russia’s most prominent empresses. Who was she?
During Catherine the Great’s reign, Russia annexed this Black Sea peninsula in 1783, extending its influence in a region contested by the Ottoman Empire. What peninsula was annexed?
Which Scandinavian country adopted a constitution at Eidsvoll on 17 May 1814 and ended its union with Sweden in 1905? Its capital is Oslo, and its western coastline is renowned for fjords.

In April 1940, Nazi Germany launched a coordinated invasion of Denmark and Norway under a codename, seeking to secure strategic ports and access to iron ore shipments through Narvik. What was the name of this operation?

In April 1912, a British passenger liner on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic, and more than 1,500 people died after it sank. What is the name of this maritime disaster?

During the sinking of the RMS Titanic, a Cunard liner changed course after receiving a distress signal and reached the lifeboats several hours after the ship sank. It rescued more than 700 survivors and carried them to New York; what was the ship’s name?

This Bourbon monarch inherited France’s throne in 1774 and summoned the Estates-General to Versailles in May 1789 as a financial crisis deepened. After the monarchy was abolished, the National Convention tried him, and he was guillotined on January 21, 1793. Who was he?

During Louis XVI’s reign, what October 1789 uprising began when a large crowd left the capital amid a bread crisis, marched to the royal palace, and compelled the royal family to relocate to the capital?

Which British Conservative politician became prime minister on 6 September 2022 after defeating Rishi Sunak in the party leadership contest? Her government introduced an Energy Price Guarantee, and she resigned after 50 days in office, the shortest tenure of any British prime minister.

As a PPE student at the centuries-old collegiate institution where she was active in student politics, Liz Truss became president of the campus branch of the party formed in 1988 by the merger of the SDP and the party led by David Steel. What was that student branch called?

Soon after Liz Truss took office, Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng unveiled a fiscal package that paired sweeping tax cuts with increased borrowing, prompting turmoil in UK markets and the later reversal of most of its measures. What was this package commonly called?
Which Philippine political figure served as first lady during her husband’s presidency and authoritarian rule, and became known for lavish spending and patronage of monumental architecture?
Under Imelda Marcos’s patronage, what Manila performing-arts venue, designed by Leandro Locsin, opened in 1969 as the first major building in an arts complex on Roxas Boulevard?

A Norwegian polar explorer led the first recorded party to reach the geographic South Pole, arriving on December 14, 1911, more than a month before Robert Falcon Scott’s team. His expedition sailed aboard the Fram and established its Antarctic base at the Bay of Whales. Who was this explorer?

Before his Antarctic expedition, Roald Amundsen commanded the Gjøa on a 1903–1906 voyage through a sea route north of mainland Canada connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. What long-sought route did his expedition complete?

In late January 1968, North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched a coordinated surprise campaign across South Vietnam during the lunar New Year holiday, striking Saigon and Huế and even breaching the outer walls of the U.S. Embassy compound. Although U.S. and South Vietnamese forces eventually retook the territory, the campaign’s scale undercut claims that victory was near. What was this campaign called?

During the Tet Offensive, Communist forces captured much of this central Vietnamese city, including its historic Citadel, and U.S. and South Vietnamese troops fought a costly battle to retake it over several weeks. Which city was this?

Which postwar Balkan federation comprised six republics, including Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, and Montenegro? Led by a communist government, it broke from Soviet control in 1948 and dissolved amid conflict in the early 1990s.

Who led the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for decades after World War II, having commanded the Partisans during the war? He defied Stalin in the 1948 split with the Soviet Union and remained the country’s leader until his death in 1980.

In late October 1922, armed Italian Fascist Blackshirts mobilized after demanding Prime Minister Luigi Facta’s resignation, while their leader remained in Milan. The crisis ended not with a battlefield conquest of the capital but when King Victor Emmanuel III rejected emergency military measures and invited that leader to form a government; what was this event?

During the March on Rome, this Italian monarch refused to approve Luigi Facta’s proposed martial-law order and instead invited Benito Mussolini to form a government. A member of the House of Savoy, he later also held the title of Emperor of Ethiopia; who was he?
Which fifth-century Hunnic ruler led campaigns into both halves of the Roman Empire, crossed the Rhine into Gaul, and became known by the epithet “Scourge of God”?
During Attila the Hun’s Italian campaign in 452, which bishop of Rome met him near the Mincio River in a delegation later credited with persuading him to withdraw from Italy?

In the Andean empire centered at Cusco, this hereditary office stood at the top of the political hierarchy and was held by rulers such as Atahualpa before the Spanish conquest. What was the traditional title for this supreme monarch?
Which ruler holding the office of Sapa Inca offered Francisco Pizarro a room filled with gold in 1532, hoping to secure his release after being captured at Cajamarca?

In 1969, John Lennon and Yoko Ono spent a week at Amsterdam’s Hilton Hotel speaking with journalists as part of a protest against the Vietnam War, then repeated the action in Montreal. What name was given to these demonstrations?
During the Bed-ins for Peace, Lennon and Ono held their Montreal protest in a hotel room in late May 1969. The gathering there included the recording of “Give Peace a Chance”; what hotel hosted it?
A ruler of Egypt’s Nineteenth Dynasty, he reigned for roughly 66 years and fought the Hittites at Kadesh. He also commissioned the rock-cut Great Temple at Abu Simbel. Which pharaoh was he?

After the inconclusive fighting at Kadesh, Ramesses II and King Hattusili III formalized relations in the pharaoh’s twenty-first regnal year. Versions of the resulting diplomatic document survive in hieroglyphic inscriptions and cuneiform tablets. What agreement was it?

A lawyer from Arras who became a leading Jacobin, this revolutionary was nicknamed “the Incorruptible.” After his role in the Reign of Terror, he was arrested on 9 Thermidor and executed by guillotine the next day. Who was he?
In July 1793, Maximilien Robespierre joined this executive body, which directed France’s wartime government and became closely associated with the Reign of Terror. What was this body called?

Maximilien Robespierre was arrested during this July 1794 coup, named for the month in the revolutionary calendar when it occurred. The event marked his downfall and the end of the radical phase of the Reign of Terror. What was the coup called?

This East Asian island country was governed for centuries by shōguns and daimyō, with samurai serving as its warrior class. After foreign naval pressure opened its ports in 1853, the Boshin War and the 1868 restoration reshaped its government. What country is it?
During Japan’s Heian period, a court lady composed this long prose narrative following the romantic and political fortunes of a gifted imperial son at the Japanese court. What work is it?
In 1600, this decisive battle in Japan pitted Tokugawa Ieyasu’s eastern army against forces led by Ishida Mitsunari, helping clear the way for Tokugawa rule. What battle was it?

Introduced into widespread German service in early 1916, this steel helmet replaced the less protective leather Pickelhaube and used deep sides to shield a soldier’s ears and neck. It became a widely used image in German wartime propaganda. What was this helmet called?
The Stahlhelm’s distinctive, curved profile prompted British soldiers to compare it to a familiar household container. What nickname did they give its shape?

A Roman senator from a family associated with the founding of the Republic, he became one of the leading conspirators in the 44 BCE plot against Julius Caesar. After Caesar’s death, he and Cassius led republican forces against Octavian and Mark Antony at Philippi. Who was he?

Marcus Junius Brutus joined senators who killed this Roman dictator on the Ides of March in 44 BCE during a meeting at the Theatre of Pompey. His death was followed by Mark Antony’s famous funeral oration and a renewed struggle for control of Rome. Who was the dictator?

A 2014 pro-democracy campaign in Hong Kong grew from student-led demonstrations into a 79-day occupation of major roads and public spaces. It challenged Beijing’s proposed process for screening candidates for the city’s chief executive election. What was this movement called?

The Umbrella Movement was sparked in part by a measure adopted in 2014 by China’s National People’s Congress Standing Committee. It set an election framework for Hong Kong’s chief executive that allowed a nominating committee to screen candidates; what was this measure commonly called?

After Japanese colonial rule ended in 1945, Soviet and American forces occupied different zones of the Korean Peninsula, and rival governments later emerged. A June 25, 1950 invasion began a war that ended with a 1953 armistice but did not reunify the peninsula; what two sovereign states are meant?

In the immediate aftermath of Japan’s 1945 surrender, Soviet forces administered territory to the north and American forces territory to the south along a line of latitude. In the history of North Korea and South Korea, what was this initial occupation boundary, distinct from the later armistice demarcation line?

What 1988 series of Iraqi government operations in northern Iraq combined village destruction, forced displacement, mass detention, and chemical attacks against Kurdish communities during the final year of the Iran–Iraq War?

Which Iraqi Ba'athist official, nicknamed “Chemical Ali,” directed the al-Anfal campaign under Saddam Hussein’s government? He oversaw operations that targeted Kurdish communities in northern Iraq in 1988.

This global outbreak began in 1918, spread through 1920, and was caused by an H1N1 strain. It killed tens of millions and became widely known by a nickname linked to wartime reporting from a neutral country; what was this historic outbreak?

During the 1918 influenza pandemic, one of the first widely reported U.S. outbreaks in 1918 was recorded among soldiers at this Army training installation in Kansas, a post within Fort Riley. What was the installation called?

During the Dutch Republic’s 1636–1637 frenzy, buyers traded contracts for future delivery of rare flower bulbs that were still underground, and prices fell sharply in 1637. What is the name of this speculative episode?

Tulip Mania later became famous through a dramatic account that portrayed the episode as causing widespread ruin, though modern historians caution that it relied on satire and exaggeration. Which nineteenth-century author helped popularize this portrayal in *Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds*?

In Suffolk, England, this early medieval burial ground became famous when excavators uncovered the outline of a buried ship and a chamber filled with weapons, metalwork, and an elaborate helmet in 1939. Coins from the burial date it to around 625 CE; what is the site’s name?

At Sutton Hoo, the lavish ship burial and its valuable grave goods suggest that the unknown occupant was a person of exceptional rank with connections beyond East Anglia. Which early seventh-century East Anglian king is the leading proposed identification?

Founded in northeastern Nigeria in 2002 by Mohammed Yusuf, this jihadist movement began an insurgency in 2009 and abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in April 2014. What is the organization’s natural name?
Boko Haram drew global attention in April 2014 after abducting 276 schoolgirls from this town in Borno State, northeastern Nigeria. What town was the site of the mass abduction?
This commander led Boko Haram from 2009 until his death in 2021 during fighting in Sambisa Forest. He pledged allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant in March 2015. Who was he?

Born Gaius Octavius, he inherited Julius Caesar’s estate and name before defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra after the Battle of Actium. The Senate later granted him a title meaning “revered,” and he became Rome’s first emperor. Who was this ruler?

In 31 BCE, Augustus’s forces under Marcus Agrippa defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra in a naval engagement off western Greece. The victory cleared the way for Rome’s takeover of Egypt. What battle was this?

Augustus’s settlement of 27 BCE established a system in which he held dominant authority while maintaining republican forms and leaving the Senate in place. What name is given to this early imperial system of government?
Augustus established this elite military force to protect the ruler and his household. It later became a powerful institution in Roman imperial politics. What was this force called?
This future emperor was Augustus’s stepson and adopted son. After Augustus died in 14 CE, he succeeded him as the second Roman emperor. Who was he?

Founded in the fourth century BCE by Chandragupta and expanded across much of the Indian subcontinent, this state had its capital at Pataliputra. Its later ruler Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War and promulgated inscriptions on rocks and pillars. What was this empire called?

During the Maurya Empire, which Greek ambassador visited the court at Pataliputra and described Indian society in an account known as the Indica? His observations survive chiefly through quotations by later classical writers.

Born in the German duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, he married his first cousin in 1840 and became her trusted political adviser. In 1857, he received formal recognition as the queen’s consort. Who was he?
Prince Albert married this British monarch, whose reign from 1837 to 1901 gave its name to the Victorian era. In 1876, she was proclaimed Empress of India. Who was she?

After returning to India from a civil-rights campaign in South Africa, this lawyer organized mass resistance to British rule and led the Indian National Congress. He became known for the 1930 Salt March and the 1942 Quit India campaign; who was this leader?

Mahatma Gandhi used this term for a method of resistance grounded in truth and nonviolence. It combined civil disobedience and non-cooperation with a willingness to endure suffering rather than use physical force; what was this philosophy called?
In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi and his followers completed a march from Ahmedabad to this coastal village, where they made salt in defiance of British laws. What was their destination?
This narcotic is obtained from the milky sap of Papaver somniferum and was a major commodity in Britain’s nineteenth-century trade with China. What is its natural name?

During the First Opium War, an 1842 agreement signed aboard HMS Cornwallis ended hostilities, ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, and opened five Chinese ports to foreign trade. What was this agreement called?

This modern Jewish nationalist movement took shape in late-nineteenth-century Europe, partly in response to antisemitism. It advocated establishing and supporting a Jewish homeland in the historic Land of Israel. What is the movement called?
In 1897, Theodor Herzl convened the first congress of Zionism to seek international recognition for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. In what Swiss city did the delegates meet?

From 1858 to 1861, liberal and conservative forces fought a Mexican civil war over the Catholic Church’s political role, property ownership, and the structure of the state. What is this conflict commonly called?
The Reform War was preceded by a liberal statute requiring religious and civil corporations to sell much of the land they held collectively. What was this 1856 measure called?

This Central European country’s Basic Law establishes a parliamentary system in which the Bundestag elects the federal chancellor, and its federal system comprises sixteen Länder. Reunification of its former eastern and western states took effect on 3 October 1990; what is the country’s natural name?

Germany’s federal system gives state governments a role in national legislation through a constitutional body whose members are delegated by the Länder rather than chosen in a nationwide direct election. What is this body called?

This Russian Marxist revolutionary led the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917 and headed the government of Soviet Russia before becoming the founding leader of the Soviet Union. By what name is he best known?

Vladimir Lenin's government ended Russia's participation in World War I in March 1918, ceding Ukraine and other territories to the Central Powers. What was the name of the document that formalized this withdrawal?

In 1921, Vladimir Lenin backed a temporary shift that allowed limited private trade and small businesses to revive an economy damaged by war, famine, and uprisings. What was this economic program called?

Enacted in 1918, this British electoral law expanded the male franchise and enfranchised women aged 30 and older who met property qualifications, without giving women and men equal voting ages. What law was it?

The Representation of the People Act 1918 marked a major gain for the cause this leader had pursued through constitutional methods. She headed the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies from 1897 to 1919 and received an honorary degree from Cambridge in 1920; who was she?

Signed in 1648 after negotiations at Münster and Osnabrück, this settlement ended the Thirty Years’ War within the Holy Roman Empire. It also recognized the Reformed faith alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism; what is the settlement commonly called?
Under the Peace of Westphalia, a particular date served as the benchmark for resolving many disputes over ecclesiastical property. What date was used?
In 1987, Chadian forces used fast, lightly armed mobile columns to drive Libyan forces from much of northern Chad. What commonly used name identifies this final phase of the Chadian–Libyan conflict?
During the Toyota War, Chadian forces under Hassan Djamous surprised and defeated a Libyan garrison at this oasis town in northern Chad in January 1987. What town was the site of this battle?

In Japanese tradition, the sovereign’s hereditary office is associated with descent from Amaterasu, the Shinto sun goddess. In *The Tale of Genji*, Genji’s father holds this office; what is its natural name?

In *The Tale of Genji*, this ruler’s son Genji is born to a favored but comparatively low-ranking consort and is later removed from the line of succession. What is the traditional name of this Emperor of Japan?

This constitutional office is held by the sovereign who serves as the United Kingdom’s head of state and is also sovereign of several Commonwealth realms. Its powers are largely exercised according to constitutional convention and ministerial advice. What is this office called?

The Monarch of the United Kingdom who succeeded Elizabeth II in September 2022 had previously held the title Prince of Wales for more than six decades, the longest tenure in that title’s history. What is his regnal name?

A Roman commander who supported Julius Caesar at Pharsalus later joined Octavian and Lepidus in a three-man governing alliance after Caesar’s assassination. He allied with Cleopatra VII and was defeated by Octavian’s forces in a major naval engagement in 31 BCE. Who was this politician and general?

Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII faced Octavian’s forces in a decisive naval confrontation off the coast of western Greece in 31 BCE. Their defeat helped leave Egypt exposed to Roman conquest the following year. What battle was this?

He rose amid upheaval following Alexander’s campaigns in the northwest, defeated the Nanda dynasty, and founded the empire later named for his dynasty. After abdicating, tradition says he became a Jain monk; identify this first Mauryan emperor.

Chandragupta Maurya’s westward expansion brought him into conflict with this successor of Alexander, who ruled the Seleucid Empire. Their settlement is associated with a marriage alliance and the transfer of 500 war elephants; name the Seleucid ruler.

Chandragupta Maurya founded the dynasty under which this later emperor ruled, and this ruler’s reign is associated with the empire’s greatest extent. After the Kalinga War, he embraced Buddhism and promulgated messages through rock and pillar edicts; identify him.

After Tsar Fedor died without an heir in 1598, Russia experienced famine, rebellion, foreign intervention, and competing claims to the throne. What period of Russian history ended with the election of a new tsar in 1613?
During the Time of Troubles, a zemsky sobor elected this 16-year-old to the Russian throne in 1613. His accession began the dynasty that ruled Russia until 1917; who was he?

Which present-day Ukrainian city was the political and religious center of the medieval Rus polity and the site of Prince Volodymyr’s landmark adoption of Christianity in 988? It remains the capital of Ukraine today.
In Kyiv, which prominent religious monument was built under Yaroslav the Wise in the early eleventh century and is known for preserving mosaics and frescoes from that period?
An Abadan movie theater was set ablaze on August 19, 1978, killing hundreds and becoming a flashpoint in the growing opposition to Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. What was the theater’s name?

At a special tribunal held after the 1979 revolution, which man acknowledged participating in the arson at Cinema Rex? Later accounts identified him as one of the participants, while the role of any wider organizers remained contested.

This British-born mining magnate built his fortune from Kimberley diamonds and founded De Beers Consolidated Mines in 1888. He served as prime minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896. Who was he?

Cecil Rhodes resigned as prime minister of the Cape Colony after backing a failed late-1895 armed incursion into the South African Republic, intended to spark an uprising among British workers in the Transvaal. What was this episode called?

France began its conquest of Algiers in 1830, and more than a century later an eight-year independence war led by the FLN ended with a transition to sovereignty in 1962. Which North African country became independent after voters approved independence that July?
During Algeria’s war for independence, negotiators signed an agreement on March 18, 1962, establishing a ceasefire and a transition toward sovereignty. What was this agreement called?

Held from November 1884 to February 1885, this gathering of European powers was chaired by Otto von Bismarck and established rules for asserting claims over African territory, including the principle of effective occupation. What was this meeting, convened during the Scramble for Africa?
At the Berlin Conference, which German chancellor chaired the proceedings and hosted delegates from European powers as they negotiated rules concerning territorial claims in Africa?

During the Reformation, rural communities in Swabia, Franconia, and Thuringia rose in 1524–1525 against labor obligations and limits on customary rights such as hunting and forest use. What is the conventional name for this major uprising across the Holy Roman Empire?
During the German Peasants' War, rebels circulated a 1525 program that called for an end to serfdom and the right of communities to choose their local pastors. What was this program called?
Which sovereign state in northwestern Europe comprises England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland? Its territory includes Northern Ireland, unlike the island of Great Britain.

In the history of the United Kingdom, what 1707 settlement joined England and Scotland into a single kingdom and parliament? It followed their sharing a monarch from 1603 and created the Kingdom of Great Britain.

What 1707–1708 uprising grew among Don Cossacks and peasants in southern Russia after the tsarist government sought to census settlements and return fugitive serfs to their landlords? Its rebels captured Cherkassk, the Don Cossacks’ political center, before government forces suppressed the revolt during Peter the Great’s reign.

During the Bulavin Rebellion, which Don Cossack leader organized resistance to the government’s efforts to seize fugitive serfs? His followers captured Cherkassk, and he was killed by Cossack opponents in July 1708.

From 1933 to 1945, Germany’s dictatorship and its collaborators operated this network of detention sites in Germany and occupied territories, initially imprisoning political opponents outside ordinary judicial protections. During World War II, many sites also exploited forced labor and held people persecuted by the regime; what is the natural name for this system?
Among the Nazi concentration camps, which site opened near Munich in March 1933 to imprison political opponents and later served as a model for the SS-run camp system?
At an imperial assembly in a German city in 1521, a decree outlawed a prominent reformer and condemned him as a heretic after he refused to withdraw his writings. What was this decree called?
The Edict of Worms was issued in 1521 after Martin Luther refused to recant his teachings. Which Holy Roman Emperor promulgated the decree?

Established after World War I under the Treaty of Versailles, this organization sought to promote collective security and international cooperation. Woodrow Wilson advocated its creation, but the U.S. Senate rejected American membership. What was the organization called?
At a 1936 session of the League of Nations in Geneva, which Ethiopian emperor condemned Italy’s invasion of his country and the use of poison gas against Ethiopian forces?

This anti-apartheid activist rose through senior roles in the African National Congress and served as South Africa’s deputy president before taking the national presidency in May 2009. He resigned in February 2018 after nearly nine years in office; who was he?

After Jacob Zuma left office, a South African judicial inquiry investigated allegations that public institutions had been improperly influenced for private gain. It ordered him to testify, and his refusal to comply with a Constitutional Court order led to a 2021 contempt sentence; what was this inquiry called?

What ancient city in northwestern Anatolia, near the Dardanelles, is identified with the multilayer fortified mound of Hisarlık? It became the setting for the Greek-Trojan War in Homer’s Iliad and was later known to Greeks and Romans as Ilion.

Which German archaeologist, following Frank Calvert’s earlier work at Hisarlık, excavated Troy and became associated with removing the so-called Treasure of Priam from the site? He also conducted excavations at Mycenae and Tiryns.

A Spanish general appointed governor-general of Cuba in 1896, he tried to crush the independence rebellion by forcing rural civilians into fortified towns. Spanish-American newspapers branded him “The Butcher.” Who was he?

During the Cuban rebellion, Valeriano Weyler ordered rural residents into guarded settlements to separate them from insurgents, a system that contributed to widespread hunger and disease. What was this forced civilian relocation called?

This decentralized Central European polity’s imperial title was revived when Otto I was crowned in 962, and its rulers depended on powerful territorial princes rather than a strong central government. It ended in 1806 when its last emperor dissolved it during the Napoleonic Wars. What polity is described?

Within the Holy Roman Empire, Charles IV issued a 1356 constitutional charter that established seven prince-electors and set rules for choosing the king. By what conventional name is this document known?
The final emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, this ruler dissolved the polity on August 6, 1806, after Napoleon formed the Confederation of the Rhine. What was this emperor’s name?

After years without a monarch and with much of its territory mortgaged, this medieval kingdom was rebuilt by a ruler who took the throne in 1340, sold an eastern province in 1346, and seized Gotland in 1361. What kingdom later made peace at Stralsund with the Hanseatic League?

During the Kingdom of Denmark under Valdemar IV, a 1370 settlement with the Hanseatic League gave the confederation control of the Skåne fairs for fifteen years. What agreement, named for the Baltic port where it was concluded, set these terms?

This medieval institution in the capital of Emilia-Romagna uses 1088 as its conventional founding year and developed from a community of scholars rather than a single founding decree. Its early reputation rested especially on the study of Roman law; what is its name?
At the University of Bologna, which eighteenth-century physicist helped popularize Newtonian mechanics in Italy and became a professor there in 1732?
Which landlocked Central European country has Vienna as its capital, comprises nine federal states, and shares borders with eight countries?

In the run-up to the Seven Years’ War, Austria’s Habsburg court shifted toward France, overturning a longstanding pattern of alliances and reshaping the European balance against Prussia. What is the name of this prewar realignment?

In colonial South America, especially Paraguay, missionaries established settlements that paired Catholic evangelization with churches, workshops, farmland, and livestock enterprises. What were these mission communities, whose economies could also rely on yerba mate, called?

In Jesuit reductions, Indigenous residents participated in local councils even as priests retained authority over daily life. Antonio Ruiz de Montoya wrote an early grammar of the language spoken by many residents of these missions; which Indigenous people were they?

This Greek diplomat was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya and resided at Pataliputra. His observations of India became known through a lost account later cited by classical authors; who was the envoy?

Megasthenes’s account of India described the Mauryan capital Pataliputra and the customs of the people he encountered. Though the original text survives only in fragments quoted by later writers, what was this work called?

Serving as South Africa’s state president from 1989 to 1994, this leader announced in February 1990 that the African National Congress and other banned organizations would be legalized. He shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with Nelson Mandela for their roles in negotiating the end of apartheid. Who was he?

In February 1990, F. W. de Klerk announced that a formerly banned liberation movement could operate legally again. Nelson Mandela, a leading figure in that movement, was released from prison days later. Which organization was legalized?

At a July–August 1945 meeting near Berlin, the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain discussed the occupation and political reconstruction of defeated Germany while the war against Japan continued. By what name is this Allied meeting known?
During the Potsdam Conference, which British Labour leader replaced Winston Churchill at the negotiating table after the results of Britain’s 1945 general election became known?

After France’s defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, a radical government ruled the French capital from March to May 1871 and was driven from power by Versailles troops during the Bloody Week. What was this government called?
During the Paris Commune, this revolutionary schoolteacher fought at the barricades and was later sentenced to deportation to New Caledonia. What was her name?

Founded by Batu Khan on lands originally assigned to Jochi, this Mongol successor state dominated the Russian principalities and ruled much of the western Eurasian steppe. What was this khanate, also known as the Ulus of Jochi?
The Golden Horde reached its military peak during this ruler’s reign from 1312 to 1341, when he also adopted Islam. What was his name?

The Golden Horde’s authority over the Russian principalities is traditionally said to have ended after this 1480 standoff, in which Moscow’s forces and Akhmat Khan’s army faced each other across a river without a decisive battle. What event was this?
answer: Great Stand on the Ugra River

question: During the French Revolution, this political club met in a former Dominican convent on Rue Saint-Honoré and developed a network of affiliated societies across France. It became a dominant force under Maximilien Robespierre and was associated with the Reign of Terror. What group was it?
In the National Convention, the Jacobins’ most radical deputies sat on the highest tiers of the chamber, opposite the more moderate Girondins. What geographic nickname was given to this faction?
Which early Mesoamerican culture flourished along the Gulf Coast of what is now Mexico, established major centers at San Lorenzo and La Venta, and is renowned for its colossal stone heads?
Within the Olmec civilization, which later ceremonial center in present-day Tabasco is known for four colossal heads, greenstone offerings, and a large earthen pyramid?

This ruler was the ninth sovereign of the Mali Empire, which reached its territorial peak during his reign. On his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, his entourage carried vast quantities of gold, and his lavish gifts in Cairo were said to lower gold’s value there; who was he?
Mansa Musa’s reign is associated with the construction of a portion of a celebrated mosque in Timbuktu, a landmark known for its distinctive mud-brick architecture. What is the name of this mosque?
Mansa Musa recruited scholars from across the Muslim world, including an Andalusian poet who helped foster Timbuktu’s intellectual life. What was this poet’s name?

Conventionally dated from 220 to 280 CE, this era followed the collapse of the Han dynasty and saw Wei, Shu Han, and Wu compete for control of China. What period of Chinese history ended when the Jin dynasty completed reunification?

After the Three Kingdoms period, Sima Yan established a new ruling house that defeated Wu and completed China’s reunification in 280 CE, though the restored unity did not last long. What was this regime called?
In the biblical story of Judith and Holofernes, Judith kills the Assyrian general by separating his head from his body. What execution method is also associated with the death of John the Baptist?
Artemisia Gentileschi’s dramatic Baroque canvas depicts a Jewish heroine and her maidservant killing an Assyrian general by beheading him. What is this painting commonly titled?

This Northumbrian scholar studied at the principal cathedral school of his native region and became master of the palace school at Aachen after meeting a Frankish ruler in Parma in 781. He helped shape the Carolingian educational revival and later served as abbot of St Martin’s at Tours. Name this English cleric.
Alcuin of York became a leading scholar and adviser at the court of this Frankish ruler, who made Aachen his principal residence. Pope Leo III crowned him emperor in Rome in 800. Who was this ruler?

What Mesoamerican imperial state was formed in 1428 by the alliance of Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco, and Tlacopan? Centered in the Valley of Mexico, it was conquered by forces led by Hernán Cortés in 1521.
In the Aztec Empire, what island capital stood in Lake Texcoco and connected to the mainland by causeways? The city’s ruins lie beneath much of present-day Mexico City.
Which deity was the Mexica patron god at the heart of the Aztec Empire’s imperial cult? Conquered communities were often expected to add this god to their own pantheons.
Which city-state joined Mexico-Tenochtitlan and Tetzcoco to form the Aztec Empire’s Triple Alliance in 1428? It was the alliance’s third member, alongside those two more prominent powers.
In Japanese history, what term was applied to the typhoons that twice wrecked fleets sent by Kublai Khan to invade Japan, in 1274 and 1281?
The term Kamikaze is associated with storms that destroyed two invasion fleets sent to Japan in the 13th century. Which Mongol ruler, who founded China’s Yuan dynasty, ordered those expeditions?

Which British political party, historically rooted in the Tory tradition, has long been one of the country’s two major parties alongside Labour? It governed under Winston Churchill during much of World War II and under Margaret Thatcher from 1979 to 1990.

Which politician led the Conservative Party and became Britain’s first woman prime minister after her party won the 1979 general election? She remained in office until 1990, and her government fought a prolonged confrontation with the National Union of Mineworkers during the 1984–85 miners’ strike.
In 218 BCE, this Carthaginian commander led an army that included war elephants across the Alps into Italy. He won a major victory at Cannae before Scipio Africanus defeated him at Zama.
Hannibal Barca was defeated by a Roman army at this North African battle in 202 BCE, a decisive clash that ended the Second Punic War. Which battle was it?

Beginning in 1256, this prolonged medieval conflict pitted Genoa against Venice over commercial privileges and influence in the eastern Mediterranean. Fighting in Acre followed a dispute over control of a religious compound in the city. What was the conflict called?

During the War of Saint Sabas, this port city in the Kingdom of Jerusalem became a major arena for fighting between Genoese and Venetian residents. Both maritime powers had commercial quarters there, and the conflict involved privileges tied to its harbor. What city was it?
This British commander surrendered his army at Yorktown in 1781, helping bring the American Revolutionary War to a close. He later served as Governor-General of India; who was he?

During Charles Cornwallis’s campaigns against Tipu Sultan’s South Indian kingdom, British forces encountered iron-cased weapons. William Congreve later studied these weapons when developing a British military system of the same kind; what were they?

What is the general term for a structure or coordinated system designed to make a settlement or territory harder to capture? It can include walls, towers, ditches, gates, and defenses adapted for artillery.
In a castle fortification, what surrounding obstacle could be dry or filled with water, forcing attackers to cross it before reaching the walls?

On April 18, 1943, U.S. codebreakers used decoded Japanese communications to learn the itinerary of a high-ranking naval commander. Army Air Forces P-38 fighters then flew a long-range interception over Bougainville that destroyed his aircraft and killed him; what was the operation’s name?

During Operation Vengeance, U.S. P-38 fighters intercepted the Japanese commander’s aircraft over Bougainville after codebreakers discovered his travel schedule. He was the commander in chief of Japan’s Combined Fleet; who was he?

This distant member of the Achaemenid dynasty became king in 336 BCE and ruled during Alexander the Great’s invasion of Persia. The last Achaemenid King of Kings, he was killed by his relative Bessus in 330 BCE. Who was this ruler?
The satrap of Bactria and a relative of Darius III, this Persian noble mortally wounded the king while fleeing Alexander’s advance. What was his name?
In 331 BCE, Darius III led a large Persian army onto a plain near Arbela, where Alexander won a decisive victory that shattered organized Achaemenid resistance. What was the name of this battle?

After David Cameron resigned following the 2016 referendum, this Conservative politician became UK prime minister on July 13, 2016. She led the government through the 2017 general election and left office in 2019, immediately before Boris Johnson took over; who was she?

During Theresa May’s premiership, the UK formally began its withdrawal from the European Union in March 2017 by notifying the European Council. What numbered provision of the Treaty on European Union did her government invoke to start that process?

A medieval East Slavic polity centered on Kyiv was ruled by princes, including one who reportedly chose Christianity over Islam after hearing that Islam forbade alcohol. Its history is recorded in an early chronicle traditionally associated with Nestor. What was this polity called?

In the history of Kievan Rus’, this prince is remembered for embracing Byzantine Christianity and ordering the baptism of his people in 988. The son of Sviatoslav I, he helped shape the polity’s religious identity. Which ruler was he?

Which Norwegian Arctic explorer and scientist led an 1893 expedition aboard the Fram, later served as a League of Nations humanitarian, and became associated with internationally recognized travel documents for stateless refugees?

Fridtjof Nansen used this Norwegian-built vessel on his 1893 Arctic expedition, where it was deliberately allowed to drift while trapped in sea ice. Roald Amundsen later took the same ship on an expedition to Antarctica. What was the vessel called?
Launched on June 22, 1941, this Nazi German invasion of the Soviet Union opened the Eastern Front of World War II. What was the operation’s code name?

During Operation Barbarossa, the Soviet Union was led by a ruler whose regime caused the devastating famine in Ukraine in the early 1930s. He later promoted the antisemitic Doctors’ Plot. Who was this Soviet leader?

This ethnic group forms the majority of Cambodia’s population and speaks the country’s official language. Its medieval empire built Angkor Wat under the rule of Suryavarman II. What is this people called?
The Khmer people are associated with a vast temple complex commissioned by Suryavarman II and dedicated initially to Vishnu. This landmark appears on Cambodia’s national flag; what is it called?

Founded around 550 BCE on the Iranian plateau, this empire defeated the Medes, Lydians, and Neo-Babylonians before stretching from the Balkans to the Indus Valley. Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BCE, ending the dynasty that had ruled it. What empire was it?
In the Achaemenid Empire, this maintained overland route connected Susa with Sardis and featured relay stations for state messengers. What was this celebrated network called?

The Achaemenid Empire was founded by this Persian ruler, who captured Babylon in 539 BCE. According to the biblical book of Ezra, he allowed Judean exiles to return and rebuild their temple. Who was he?

The eldest son of Pepin the Short, this Frankish ruler expanded Carolingian power through campaigns against the Lombards and Saxons. Pope Leo III crowned him in Rome on Christmas Day in 800, giving him an imperial title. Who was this ruler?
In Rome on Christmas Day 800, this bishop of Rome placed an imperial crown on Charlemagne, linking the Frankish ruler’s authority to the papacy. Which pope performed the coronation?
Charlemagne made this city the center of his court and empire, and he was buried there in the Palatine Chapel after his death in 814. What present-day German city was this Carolingian capital?

Charlemagne sponsored a revival of learning that encouraged schools, manuscript copying, and reforms in education and writing. What is the period of intellectual and cultural renewal associated with his dynasty called?

At Charlemagne’s invitation, this Northumbrian scholar joined the royal court and helped shape its palace school and educational reforms. Before that move, he had led a celebrated cathedral school in his homeland. Who was this influential teacher and writer?

This commercial Roman town near the Gulf of Naples was buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, preserving streets, houses, shops, and wall paintings. What city was uncovered through excavations that began in the eighteenth century?

Pompeii and this nearby Roman town were buried in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. Its ruins include the Villa of the Papyri, a lavish residence containing a library of ancient scrolls; what town is it?

Which medieval kingdom in southern Italy occupied the mainland territory that became distinct from the island realm of Sicily after the War of the Sicilian Vespers? Its name is also shared by the city at the foot of Mount Vesuvius.
The Kingdom of Naples emerged after a revolt that began in Palermo on Easter Monday in 1282 and helped drive Angevin rule from the island of Sicily. What was this uprising called?

A 1954 international settlement left a Southeast Asian country temporarily divided near the 17th parallel, and the ensuing conflict drew in large U.S. combat deployments before the southern capital fell in 1975. What conflict, generally dated from 1955 to 1975, does this describe?
During the Vietnam War, what name is given to the 1954 agreements that temporarily divided the country near the 17th parallel and called for nationwide elections to be held later?
During the Vietnam War, what was the name of the clandestine supply network that ran through Laos and Cambodia to carry troops and matériel from the north to communist forces in the south?

During the Vietnam War, communist forces launched a coordinated campaign beginning during the 1968 Lunar New Year, striking cities and military targets across South Vietnam. Though they suffered major battlefield losses, the attacks sharply undermined U.S. claims that victory was near; what was this campaign called?
After a June 2016 referendum in which a majority of UK voters chose to leave the European Union, this term came to name the country’s withdrawal, completed in January 2020. What is the term?

During Brexit, the UK government formally notified the European Union in March 2017 that it was invoking this provision of the Treaty on European Union, beginning the withdrawal process. What provision was it?

The modern form of this political and economic partnership was established when the Maastricht Treaty entered into force on November 1, 1993, building on earlier coal-and-steel and common-market institutions. Its single market is based on the free movement of goods, services, people, and capital; what is the name of this organization?

In the history of the European Union, what 1992 agreement, signed on February 7 and entering into force on November 1, 1993, formally established the union and expanded cooperation into foreign policy and justice?

This landlocked Central European country occupies much of the Carpathian Basin, and its capital lies on the Danube. In 1956, Soviet troops crushed a popular uprising against Communist rule there. What country is it?
During Hungary’s 1944 German occupation, this Swedish diplomat issued protective documents and established safe houses in Budapest, helping rescue thousands of Jews from deportation. Who was he?

What formal writing system of the civilization ruled by pharaohs used signs that could represent sounds, whole words, or meaning cues rather than serving only as pictures? It was often carved on monuments and became readable again through modern decipherment.

Which inscribed slab helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs by presenting the same decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek scripts? French soldiers rediscovered it during Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt in 1799.
Which English king reigned from 1272 to 1307, extended royal control over Wales, and defeated William Wallace’s forces at Falkirk in 1298? He was also known by a nickname referring to his height.

During Edward I’s reign, what name is commonly given to the broad assembly summoned in 1295, which included barons and clergy as well as knights and townspeople? It is often cited as an important landmark in the development of representative government.

In 1517, a Wittenberg theologian circulated propositions challenging the sale and theological basis of indulgences. They argued that repentance should shape a Christian’s whole life, and their rapid circulation helped spark the Protestant Reformation. What document is this?
In the Ninety-Five Theses, one proposition rejects the claim that a coin entering an indulgence chest releases a soul from purgatory. Which number identifies that proposition?

Held on 12 December after Parliament called an early poll amid deadlock over the withdrawal agreement, this contest gave Boris Johnson’s Conservatives an 80-seat majority. Labour fell to its smallest number of Commons seats since 1935. Name this 2019 British political contest.
In the 2019 United Kingdom general election, which party, led nationally by Jeremy Corbyn, won 202 seats—its lowest total since 1935—as the Conservatives secured a large majority?

In October 1993, U.S. forces conducting a raid in Somalia became trapped in prolonged urban fighting with militia loyal to Mohamed Farrah Aidid. The battle became especially notorious after two American Black Hawk helicopters were shot down. What battle was this?
During the Battle of Mogadishu, a U.S. raid sought to capture two senior aides of this Somali faction leader, whose forces were the focus of U.S. and UN operations. Who was the leader?

This nineteenth-century national movement brought the peninsula’s divided states together through diplomacy, war, and popular campaigns. It led to the proclamation of a kingdom in 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II, although Venetia and Rome joined later. What movement was this?

During Italian Unification, which nationalist commander led the 1860 Expedition of the Thousand in red shirts, overthrowing Bourbon rule in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies before handing his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II at Teano?

What name was given to the political scandal over gatherings held at Downing Street and other UK government buildings during COVID-19 lockdown restrictions, including an event for which Boris Johnson later received a fine?

During the Partygate fallout in July 2022, which then-Chancellor resigned from Boris Johnson’s cabinet alongside Health Secretary Sajid Javid, helping trigger Johnson’s departure? He later became prime minister after Liz Truss resigned.

This Indigenous Mesoamerican civilization built city-states such as Tikal and Chichén Itzá, developed hieroglyphic writing, and used an elaborate Long Count calendar. What is the natural name of this civilization and its related peoples?
In the Maya lowlands, this city-state in present-day Campeche became Tikal’s major rival during the Classic period. Its monumental core includes Structure II, a towering pyramid. Which city was this?
The K’iche’ Maya preserved this narrative in a colonial-era manuscript that recounts the Hero Twins’ trials against the lords of the underworld. What is the name of this foundational work?
On an island in Lake Petén Itzá, this capital of the Itza Maya was captured by Spanish forces in 1697, marking the final conquest of an independent Maya kingdom. What was the city called?
A Maya noblewoman from Dos Pilas arrived in Naranjo in 682 CE and exercised royal authority while her son K’ak’ Tiliw Chan Chaak was young. What name is commonly used for this ruler?

This Bronze Age urban civilization flourished across parts of present-day Pakistan and northwestern India, with major cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. Its settlements are noted for planned streets, standardized weights, and an undeciphered writing system. What civilization was it?

At Mohenjo-daro, a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization, archaeologists uncovered a large brick-lined pool with steps at either end and construction designed to keep it watertight. What name do archaeologists give to this distinctive structure?
In early June 1942, U.S. carrier aircraft sank four Japanese fleet carriers—Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū, and Hiryū—in a decisive Pacific naval engagement that checked Japan’s expansion. What battle was this?

At the Battle of Midway, this U.S. aircraft carrier was struck by Japanese dive-bombers and torpedo aircraft, abandoned by its crew, and later sunk by torpedoes from the Japanese submarine I-168. What ship was it?

The first ran from 1839 to 1842, and a second conflict followed in 1856–1860, involving Qing China, Britain, and later France. Together, they are named for the addictive imported drug whose trade and suppression helped precipitate them. What is the collective name for these conflicts?
Before the Opium Wars, merchants at Canton had to pay for Chinese goods with a precious metal; large quantities of it reached China from Acapulco aboard Manila galleons. What commodity was it?

The only surviving child of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, this Tudor monarch succeeded Mary I in 1558 and ruled until 1603. Her long reign is associated with the flourishing of English drama and the defeat of a major Spanish invasion fleet. Who was she?

During Elizabeth I’s reign, this statesman became her principal secretary soon after her accession and remained one of her most influential advisers for decades. He later served as Lord High Treasurer. Who was this administrator?

During Elizabeth I’s reign, Philip II launched a vast fleet in 1588 to overthrow her and restore Catholic rule in England. English resistance, fireships, and severe storms helped frustrate the campaign. What was the fleet’s famous name?

Fought in Leicestershire on 22 August 1485, this engagement pitted the last Yorkist king against a challenger whose victory helped establish a new royal dynasty. The Stanley forces joined the challenger’s side during the fighting, and the king was killed.

Archaeological investigations of the Battle of Bosworth Field revised the traditional location of the battlefield, placing its core southwest of this Leicestershire landmark. What landmark had long been identified as the battle’s central point?

In April 1961, a U.S.-backed force of Cuban exiles landed on Cuba’s southern coast in an attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro, but government forces defeated it within two days. What failed operation became a major setback for President John F. Kennedy’s administration?
During the Bay of Pigs invasion, the CIA trained and funded a Cuban exile force that landed on 17 April 1961 and was defeated by Castro’s forces. What designation distinguished this exile formation?

This Cuban revolutionary was a wealthy sugar planter in eastern Cuba who freed his enslaved workers and called for independence in 1868, beginning the Ten Years’ War. He later became the first president of the Cuban Republic in Arms. What was his name?

Carlos Manuel de Céspedes began the Cuban uprising at his La Demajagua plantation on October 10, 1868, freeing enslaved people and calling for independence. What name is given to this opening declaration of revolt?

This sixth-century Byzantine empress was the wife of Justinian I and urged him to stay in Constantinople during the 532 revolt, reportedly declaring that royal purple made the finest burial shroud. Who was she?

Theodora showed her resolve during this 532 uprising in Constantinople, which began with clashes between the Blue and Green factions at the Hippodrome and nearly toppled Justinian I. What was the revolt called?

Which Soviet statesman became general secretary in 1985, pursued the reforms of glasnost and perestroika, and resigned as president on December 25, 1991, as the Soviet Union dissolved? He was the country’s final leader and its first and only president.

Mikhail Gorbachev used this Russian term for his program to restructure Soviet society and revitalize its economy and political system. It was commonly paired with glasnost, his policy of greater openness. What was this reform program called?

This country occupies northeastern Africa, while its Sinai Peninsula extends into Asia. Most of its population lives along the Nile Valley and Delta, and the Suez Canal crosses its territory between the Mediterranean and Red seas. What country is described?

In ancient Egyptian religion, this jackal-headed god was associated with mummification and death. In the Hall of Two Truths, he weighed the deceased’s heart against Ma’at’s feather; which deity is this from Egypt’s mythology?

What was the name of the Catholic polity established in Constantinople after Western crusaders captured the Byzantine capital in 1204? It was formed to rule the city and other former Byzantine territories.
The Latin Empire’s first monarch was a count from Flanders who received an imperial coronation in Hagia Sophia in 1204. What was his name?

This ancient region came under imperial control chiefly through campaigns in the 50s BCE and was later reorganized into provinces under Augustus. Its territory covered much of present-day France and parts of neighboring western Europe, without matching France’s modern borders.

In Roman Gaul, which settlement founded as Lugdunum in 43 BCE stood at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône rivers and became a major administrative center for the Three Gauls? Give its modern French name.

In ancient Greece, privately owned enslaved people in Athens differed from Sparta’s helots, while in Rome manumission could change an enslaved person’s legal status without erasing social distinctions. What broad historical subject encompasses these varied systems of unfree labor across the ancient Mediterranean?

Within Slavery in Classical Antiquity, Roman law and inscriptions used this Latin term for a freed male who had formerly been enslaved; epitaphs could also identify him through a former owner’s name and a status abbreviation such as LIB. What was he called?

Which South Asian country became independent in August 1947 during the partition of British India and has Islamabad as its capital? It borders India, Afghanistan, Iran, and China, and has a coast on the Arabian Sea.
Pakistan's eastern wing was separated from its western wing by Indian territory. After the 1971 war, that eastern territory became what independent state?

Born in Figeac in 1790, this French scholar mastered Coptic and used it alongside the parallel texts on the Rosetta Stone to establish how Egyptian hieroglyphs worked. Who announced his breakthrough in a 1822 letter to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres?

Jean-François Champollion compared the matching passages on this inscribed granodiorite stele, which gives a decree for Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Ancient Greek. Found by French soldiers near Rashid in 1799, what artifact became central to deciphering hieroglyphs?

What is the name of the August 15, 1945 radio address in which Emperor Hirohito announced that Japan had accepted the Potsdam Declaration? It was the first radio speech by a Japanese emperor to the public.

The Jewel Voice Broadcast delivered Japan’s surrender announcement in an unusually formal, classical Japanese register. Which reigning emperor spoke in the address on August 15, 1945, and gave his name to the era known as Shōwa?

What name is given to the minted currency used throughout the Republic and Empire, with denominations such as silver pieces used for soldiers’ pay and bronze issues used in commerce? Its portraits and reverse designs also carried messages about rulers and public power.

Within Roman coinage, what bronze denomination is identified by a surviving issue of Trajan that pairs his portrait on one side with a bridge on the other? This large coin type was also used in everyday transactions.

Founded under an English royal charter in 1600, this joint-stock enterprise initially pursued Indian Ocean commerce in goods such as cotton, silk, spices, and tea. It later built its own armies and assumed tax-collecting and governing powers across much of the Indian subcontinent. Which company is described?

After the British East India Company defeated Mir Qasim and his allies at the Battle of Buxar, Shah Alam II granted it the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa through a 1765 agreement. What was this agreement called?

During British East India Company rule, drought and extractive revenue pressures helped fuel a catastrophic food crisis in the lower Ganges delta, with peak mortality in 1770. By some estimates, millions died; what is this disaster commonly called?

Ivan IV’s coronation in 1547 marked the first formal use of this sovereign’s title in Russia, distinguishing him from earlier Muscovite grand princes. Though Peter the Great later adopted “emperor” as his formal style, what familiar title continued to identify Russia’s monarchs until Nicholas II abdicated in 1917?

As a young ruler, this future Russian sovereign initially shared the throne with his half-brother Ivan V, then ruled alone and later adopted the imperial title. Which figure’s career illustrates the transition from the traditional Tsar of Russia title to emperor?

This major 1773–1775 uprising against the Russian Empire was led by a Don Cossack who claimed to be the deposed Peter III. It drew Cossacks, peasants, and factory workers into revolt. What was the uprising called?
During Pugachev's Rebellion, which Russian empress ruled the empire? She came to power in 1762 after the deposition of her husband, Peter III.

A British Conservative leader held the premiership in 1923–24, 1924–29, and 1935–37, serving three separate terms. He was in office during the 1936 royal crisis that ended with a monarch giving up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson. Who was he?

During Stanley Baldwin’s final premiership, the reigning monarch gave up the throne in December 1936 rather than abandon plans to marry Wallis Simpson; his younger brother succeeded him as George VI. What constitutional event was this?
What is the broad practice of cultivating crops and raising domesticated animals for useful products? Its spread helped early communities produce food and sustain permanent settlements.
In the history of agriculture in Mesopotamia, two rivers helped enrich the Fertile Crescent. Which river runs through Baghdad, distinguishing it from the Euphrates?

This Ottoman sultan reigned from 1512 to 1520 and defeated Shah Ismail I’s Safavid forces at Chaldiran in 1514. He later led campaigns that brought Syria and Egypt under Ottoman rule, ending the Mamluk sultanate. Who was this ruler?
During Selim I’s campaign against the Safavids, which 1514 battle in eastern Anatolia ended in an Ottoman victory over Shah Ismail I’s forces?

Which sovereign country in Oceania was led by John Curtin for most of the Second World War and suffered Japanese air raids on Darwin in 1942? Its federal Commonwealth was formed on 1 January 1901 when six British colonies federated.

At the 1942 Battle of the Coral Sea, fought in the campaign to defend Australia, what type of warship saw the first combat engagement between opposing forces? The USS Abraham Lincoln is a later Nimitz-class example.

In 1963–1964, South African authorities prosecuted anti-apartheid activists for sabotage after a police raid on Liliesleaf Farm uncovered plans for armed resistance. What is this famous proceeding known as?

At the Rivonia Trial, which anti-apartheid leader concluded his statement from the dock by saying he was prepared to die for a democratic and free society? He was sentenced to life imprisonment and later shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk.

Which Israeli politician first became prime minister in June 1996, later served continuously from 2009 to 2021, and returned to the office after the 2022 election? In 2019, Israel’s attorney general announced charges against him in three cases, including a bribery charge.

Benjamin Netanyahu has long led this Israeli party, which formed in 1973 from an alliance of Herut and the Liberal Party and first won national power in 1977. Its Hebrew name is commonly translated as “consolidation.”

Following Columbus’s 1492 voyages, crops, animals, diseases, people, and technologies moved between the Americas and the Old World, transforming societies and environments on both sides of the Atlantic. What term, popularized by historian Alfred Crosby, names this broad post-contact transfer?

Within the Columbian Exchange, which domesticated animal brought by Spanish colonizers spread among Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains and reshaped hunting, travel, and warfare? Native to Eurasia, it had been absent from the Americas for thousands of years before European contact.

He joined the ANC as a young man, spent 27 years in prison, and shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk before becoming South Africa’s first Black president in 1994. Who was this anti-apartheid leader?
Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 imprisoned years at this island prison off Cape Town, where inmates were assigned hard labor in a quarry. What was the name of the island?

Nelson Mandela made his famous declaration that he was prepared to die during this 1963–64 legal proceeding, which resulted in life sentences for him and other anti-apartheid activists convicted of sabotage. Named for a Johannesburg suburb, what was this case called?
Nelson Mandela was often addressed in South Africa by this Xhosa clan name, which became an affectionate term of respect. What was the name?

During Nelson Mandela’s presidency, this body held public hearings into apartheid-era human-rights abuses and considered conditional amnesty for people who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes. What was the name of this body?

What is the name of the dense, corrosion-resistant element that occupies atomic number 79 and whose chemical symbol comes from its Latin name? West African states such as Ghana and Mali gained wealth by exchanging it for salt across the Sahara.

Gold’s role in trans-Saharan trade and pilgrimage is illustrated by which 14th-century ruler of Mali? During his 1324–25 journey to Mecca, he brought so much of the metal to Cairo that its market value fell.
