Centered on the Netherlands and especially influential during the seventeenth-century Golden Age, this overseas network linked trading posts, colonies, and territories across Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Its commercial reach depended on chartered companies, while its profits came from goods such as spices and sugar and were tied to conquest, coerced labor, and enslavement. What empire is described?

Within the Dutch Empire, this chartered company was established in 1602 to conduct Asian trade and had authority to negotiate treaties, wage war, and administer territories. In 1619, it built Batavia on the site of Jayakarta as its Asian headquarters; name the company.

Fought in 216 BCE during the Second Punic War near the Aufidus River, this battle saw a much larger Roman army led by Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro surrounded by Carthaginian forces. The Carthaginian center yielded before the flanks and cavalry closed around the Romans; what was the battle called?
At the Battle of Cannae, the Carthaginian commander used a yielding center and coordinated cavalry and infantry movements to encircle the Roman army. Who led the Carthaginian forces?

What name is given to the period of rapid economic and technological change that began in Britain in the late eighteenth century, as mechanized production, steam power, and factory systems greatly increased output?
During the Industrial Revolution, this Scottish inventor patented a major improvement to the steam engine in 1769: a separate condenser that helped make steam power more efficient. Who was he?

In the early 19th century, warfare and political upheaval across southern Africa drove the forced migration of many communities, a process intensified by the rise of the Zulu Kingdom. What is the name of this period?
During the Mfecane, this early-19th-century ruler of a southern African kingdom reorganized its army around short stabbing spears and the “buffalo horns” battle formation. Who was he?
What ancient society flourished in the fertile alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia? Its independent city-states included Ur, and it developed one of the earliest known writing systems.
In Sumerian civilization, what writing system used wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay with a stylus? It was used for early record keeping in Mesopotamia.

Crowned in 1547 as the first tsar, this ruler expanded Muscovite power by conquering the Volga khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan. His reign also saw the creation of the oprichnina. Which monarch was this?

During Ivan IV of Russia’s reign, he established a separate domain under his personal authority and used its agents to seize noble estates and punish perceived enemies. The system’s violence included the 1570 assault on Novgorod; what was this arrangement called?

Ivan IV of Russia captured this city in 1552, a victory that extended Muscovite control along the Volga and was commemorated by the construction of St. Basil’s Cathedral in Moscow. Which former Tatar khanate capital was taken?

During the Second Jewish Revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE, this leader commanded rebel forces in Judaea. Some of his contemporaries hailed him as the Messiah, but Emperor Hadrian’s forces ultimately crushed the uprising. Who was this leader?
Simon bar Kokhba led a Jewish uprising against Roman rule in Judaea that began in 132 CE and ended in 135 CE after Hadrian’s forces defeated the rebels. What is this conflict commonly called?

What changing worldwide colonial network consisted of colonies, settler dominions, and other territories across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and beyond? Its imperial rule was progressively dismantled as independence movements spread, including the independence of India and Pakistan in 1947.

During the British Empire’s expansion in southern Africa, what 1879 war began with an invasion of the independent kingdom ruled by King Cetshwayo and concluded after British forces defeated his army at Ulundi?

Beginning in 1977, women whose children had vanished under Argentina’s military regime began gathering every Thursday around the central monument in Buenos Aires, wearing white headscarves as they demanded information. What human-rights organization did they form?
answer: Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo

question: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo sought the fate of people seized during Argentina’s military dictatorship, many of whom were never found or officially accounted for. What Spanish plural term is commonly used for these forcibly disappeared people?

This royal line first ruled Scotland and later supplied monarchs to England after Elizabeth I died without an heir. Its final sovereign, Anne, died in 1714 without surviving heirs, bringing the dynasty’s rule to an end. What was the dynasty called?
The House of Stuart’s first king of England succeeded Elizabeth I in 1603, having already ruled Scotland since infancy. By what dual-numbered name is this monarch known?

The eldest son and heir of the English monarch who ruled from 1327 to 1377, this commander fought at Crécy in 1346 and led the Anglo-Gascon victory at Poitiers in 1356, where the French king was captured. Known by a nickname that became familiar after his lifetime, who was this heir who died in 1376 before his father?
At the 1356 Battle of Poitiers, which French monarch was captured by the forces commanded by Edward the Black Prince after the Anglo-Gascon victory?

This Bronze Age Aegean society flourished on Crete, where major palace centers included Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia. Its administrative writing systems included Cretan Hieroglyphic and another script that remains undeciphered. What society was it?
Among the writing systems used in the Minoan civilization, this script appears on clay tablets and other administrative records but remains undeciphered. What is the script called?
Between 1932 and 1933, a catastrophic famine struck Soviet Ukraine amid collectivization and grain requisitions, causing millions of deaths. What is the commonly used name for this famine?
The Holodomor was concentrated in this Soviet republic, whose grain quotas were especially high. Which present-day country was the famine’s principal setting?

The Holodomor unfolded under the rule of this Soviet leader, whose drive for collectivization and rapid industrialization was accompanied by grain requisitions. Name the dictator who headed the USSR during the famine.
Adopted in 1982 and entering into force in 1994, what global treaty establishes rules for maritime zones, navigation, deep-seabed resources, marine research, and ocean environmental protection?
answer: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

question: Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, coastal states hold rights to explore and manage fisheries and seabed minerals in a maritime area measured from coastal baselines. Other states retain navigation and overflight freedoms there; what is this area, which may extend up to 200 nautical miles?

After hyperinflation and the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr, this 1924 agreement restructured Germany’s reparations payments and helped bring the occupation to an end. What was the agreement called?

The Dawes Plan was devised by a committee of experts addressing Germany’s reparations after the Ruhr crisis. Which American banker chaired the committee, later served as vice president under Calvin Coolidge, and shared the 1925 Nobel Peace Prize?

This Turco-Mongol conqueror founded the Timurid Empire and ruled from Samarkand in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. After defeating the Ottoman army at Ankara in 1402, he captured Sultan Bayezid I. Who was he?
Timur made this Central Asian city his capital, and it became the political heart of his empire and a center of monumental building under his successors. Which city was it?
A former Pakistani prime minister was killed at a campaign rally in Rawalpindi on December 27, 2007, in an attack involving gunfire and a shrapnel bomb. What event is identified by these clues?

During the assassination of Benazir Bhutto, the attack took place after she addressed a campaign rally at a public park in Rawalpindi. What was the park called, in a name honoring Pakistan’s first prime minister?

A German hospital for crusaders at Acre became this Catholic military organization, formally recognized by the pope in 1198. It later ruled a Prussian state centered at Marienburg and campaigned in the Baltic region. What was this organization called?

In 1242, Alexander Nevsky led Novgorodian forces against a crusading army associated with the Teutonic Order. The celebrated winter engagement took place on which lake between present-day Estonia and Russia?

In the early 13th century BCE, Ramesses II led Egyptian forces against the Hittite army of Muwatalli II near the Orontes River in what is now Syria. The clash became famous for its large-scale chariot combat and its later association with an early peace treaty. What was this battle called?
At the Battle of Kadesh, the Hittite forces were commanded by a ruler who faced Ramesses II near the Orontes River. What was this Hittite king’s name?
What is the name for the account of the fifth-century BCE Greek philosopher’s final act, which was said to be intended to convince his followers that he was immortal?
In the account of Empedocles’ legendary death, into which active volcano in Sicily was the philosopher said to have leapt?

A U.S.- and British-led coalition began this military campaign on March 20, 2003, and captured Baghdad on April 9. It overthrew Saddam Hussein’s government, after which the occupation was followed by insurgency and civil unrest. What campaign was it?

After the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the Coalition Provisional Authority served as the interim civil administration beginning in May 2003. Which American diplomat and former ambassador to the Netherlands was appointed its administrator?

Born in Havana in 1853, this Cuban poet and journalist became a leading organizer of the struggle for independence from Spain, founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party, and edited its newspaper, Patria. He was killed at the Battle of Dos Ríos in 1895; who was he?
José Martí founded and edited a Spanish-language newspaper in New York beginning in 1892 to rally support for Cuba’s independence from Spain. What was the newspaper called?

This early-fifteenth-century Czech theologian preached in Czech at Prague’s Bethlehem Chapel from 1402 and wrote religious works in both Czech and Latin. After being excommunicated, he went to defend his views at a church council, where he was condemned and burned at the stake in 1415. Who was this reformer whose death helped energize the Hussite movement in Bohemia?
Jan Hus began preaching in Czech in 1402 at a Prague chapel established specifically for Czech-language sermons. What was the name of this chapel?

This pre-Columbian Andean empire was centered at Cuzco and ruled much of western South America before Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century. Which empire was known in its own language as Tawantinsuyu, or “Realm of the Four Parts”?

The Inca Empire’s political, administrative, and military capital stood in the Peruvian highlands and later became a major Spanish colonial city. Which city was the center from which the empire expanded?
Administrators of the Inca Empire used bundles of cords with knots arranged along them to keep records and convey information. What were these knotted-string devices called?

The Inca Empire linked distant Andean provinces with an extensive network that helped officials, armies, and relay messengers travel across difficult terrain. What was this imperial road system called?
Communities in the Inca Empire owed organized periods of labor to the state, which used the work for projects such as roads, farming, and construction. What was this labor obligation called?

Which Roman scholar compiled a 37-book survey of subjects ranging from plants and animals to minerals and art, then commanded the fleet at Misenum? His nephew’s letters to Tacitus recount how he died after sailing toward the coast during the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius.

Pliny the Elder’s surviving major work is arranged in 37 books and gathers information on topics including botany, animals, minerals, and art. What influential compilation helped establish a model for later encyclopedias?

Which institution was ancient Rome’s principal aristocratic governing and deliberative assembly, advising magistrates and later emperors while debating public affairs? Its political influence shifted dramatically from the monarchy through the Republic and into the Empire.

Which emperor’s late-third-century reforms made the Roman Senate politically irrelevant while reorganizing imperial government under the Tetrarchy? His rule is also associated with a major restructuring of the empire’s administration.

Which city received a second senate when Constantine established one there, giving the Roman Senate a counterpart in the empire’s eastern capital? The city was formerly known as Byzantium and later became Istanbul.

In April 1916, Irish republicans seized Dublin’s General Post Office and proclaimed an independent Irish Republic while Britain was fighting in the First World War. What name is given to their six-day insurrection?
During the Easter Rising, this central Dublin building served as rebel headquarters, and Patrick Pearse read the proclamation of the Irish Republic outside it. What building was it?
During the Easter Rising, this schoolmaster and republican leader accepted the rebels’ unconditional surrender on 29 April 1916. Who was he?

Elizabeth I held this title of England, and Victoria used the same title as sovereign of the United Kingdom. It can also describe a king’s wife, even when she is not the reigning monarch; what royal title is it?

During the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, this English poet portrayed an idealized sovereign named Gloriana in an allegorical epic whose first installment appeared in 1590. He also wrote *The Shepheardes Calender*; who was he?

This medieval Southeast Asian empire made Angkor its political and religious center and built a vast landscape of temples and reservoirs in what is now Cambodia. It declined amid attacks by the neighboring Ayutthaya Kingdom; what empire was it?

During the Khmer Empire’s early 12th-century height, one king sponsored the construction of Angkor Wat, a vast temple complex originally dedicated to Vishnu. Which ruler is associated with this building project?

What is the name given to the World War I-era Ottoman campaign of mass deportation and killing that caused approximately 1.5 million deaths among a people whose historic homeland lay in eastern Anatolia and the southern Caucasus?

During World War I, the government responsible for the Armenian genocide ordered mass deportations and killings of Armenians across its territories. Which empire, ruled from Constantinople and dissolved after the war, was responsible?
Founded in 1950, this East German agency served the ruling Socialist Unity Party as both domestic secret police and a foreign intelligence service. What was it commonly called?

The Stasi cultivated a far-reaching network of secret sources who reported on colleagues, friends, and opposition groups, including people in workplaces and schools. What German designation was given to these recruited informants?

On August 7, 1998, coordinated al-Qaeda truck bombs targeted U.S. diplomatic missions in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, killing hundreds overall. What event is identified by these attacks?
One blast in the 1998 United States Embassy Bombings struck Nairobi, while the other struck the U.S. mission in Tanzania and killed 11 people. What Tanzanian city was the site of that attack?

This Filipino nationalist was a physician and multilingual writer whose novels *Noli Me Tangere* and *El Filibusterismo* criticized Spanish colonial rule. After helping found La Liga Filipina, he was executed by Spanish authorities in Manila in 1896.

José Rizal established this reformist civic association in Manila in 1892 to promote unity and peaceful political change in the Philippines. Spanish authorities dissolved it soon afterward, and its emergence helped spur the Katipunan.

During the Hundred Years’ War, this young woman from Domrémy said that visions of three saints guided her mission to support the dauphin Charles. Her arrival at Orléans in 1429 helped French forces break an English siege. Who was she?
Joan of Arc arrived at this Loire city in 1429 to rally French forces during an English siege, and the besiegers withdrew nine days later. Which city was this pivotal turning point named for?
Joan of Arc accompanied the dauphin to this Champagne city in 1429, where he was crowned Charles VII in the cathedral. Which city hosted the coronation?

Beginning in Paris in August 1572 and spreading to other French cities, this wave of violence targeted Huguenots and other Protestants during the French Wars of Religion. What event is known by the name of the saint whose feast day fell on August 24?

During the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, which prominent Huguenot admiral was attacked in Paris shortly before the wider killings began? He was a leading military figure in the French Wars of Religion and was killed during the violence.
Which battle around 60 or 61 CE ended Boudica’s uprising against Roman rule in Britain, when a Roman army defeated the forces of the Iceni queen?
At the Battle of Watling Street, which Roman governor of Britain commanded the forces that defeated Boudica’s much larger rebel army around 60 or 61 CE?

What was the name of the colonial army and gendarmerie established under Leopold II’s Congo Free State and later maintained by Belgium? Its units enforced rubber-collection quotas in the Congo Basin through coercion and violence.

The Force Publique enforced rubber-collection demands in a territory Leopold II governed as his personal possession before Belgium annexed it in 1908. What was this colony commonly called during that period?

What name is given to the roughly three-decade period of political and sectarian conflict centered on Northern Ireland that began in the late 1960s and was brought toward an end by the 1998 peace settlement?

During The Troubles, which settlement, signed on 10 April 1998, established a power-sharing Assembly and Executive in Northern Ireland and stipulated that a change in its constitutional status required majority consent?

Found by French troops near Rashid in 1799 during Napoleon’s Egyptian expedition, this granodiorite slab preserves a decree issued in 196 BCE in three scripts. Its parallel Greek text helped Jean-François Champollion decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs. What is the artifact?

Following the French capitulation in Egypt in 1801, the Rosetta Stone was transported to London and placed in a major national collection the following year. Which London institution has housed it since 1802?

A fourth-century BCE king of a northern Greek kingdom strengthened his army with the sarissa and brought much of Greece under his influence. He was assassinated by Pausanias at Aegae during the wedding celebrations of his daughter Cleopatra; who was he?

Following the Macedonian victory at Chaeronea, Philip II of Macedon organized a federation whose member states swore to uphold a common peace and appointed him commander for a planned invasion of Persia. What was this federation called?

Which Comorian politician, a businessman and Muslim religious figure from Anjouan, won about 58 percent of the 2006 presidential vote and served as the country’s president from 2006 to 2011? His election came under a power-sharing arrangement that rotated the presidency among the islands.
Ahmed Abdallah Mohamed Sambi came from which Comorian island, which was entitled to supply the federal president under the rotating power-sharing arrangement in 2006?

A leading figure in the Risorgimento, this revolutionary commanded the Red Shirts during their 1860 campaign against Bourbon rule in Sicily and Naples. After entering Naples, he supported Victor Emmanuel II rather than founding a separate southern state; who was he?

In May 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi sailed from Quarto with a volunteer force to challenge Bourbon rule in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. What name is commonly given to this 1860 campaign, which began with a crossing to western Sicily and helped bring the south into a united Italy?

This East German Communist official led the Socialist Unity Party from 1971 until he was forced from power in 1989. He also served as chairman of the country’s Council of State from 1976 to 1989. Who was this longtime leader?

A famous Berlin Wall mural depicts Erich Honecker sharing the ritual “fraternal kiss” with a Soviet leader. The image commemorates an embrace between the two leaders in 1979. Which Soviet leader appears with Honecker?

Fought in Boeotia in 479 BCE, this battle saw a Greek coalition rout the Persian invasion force commanded by Mardonius. Its outcome helped bring Xerxes I’s invasion of Greece to an end. What battle was this?

At the Battle of Plataea, overall command of the Greek coalition rested with the Spartan regent who served as guardian to the young King Pleistarchus. Name this commander, whose forces defeated Mardonius’s Persian army.
In 44 BCE, a group of Roman senators attacked the Roman dictator for life during a Senate meeting on the Ides of March. What is this event commonly called?

During the Assassination of Julius Caesar, the Senate met in a hall attached to a monumental theater complex on the Campus Martius, rather than in Rome’s regular Senate house. What was that hall called?

Which Indian stateswoman served as prime minister from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination in 1984? She was the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, and the mother of a later prime minister.

During Indira Gandhi’s premiership, what name is given to the 21-month period that began in 1975? Her government ruled by decree during it, suspended basic civil liberties, and imprisoned political opponents and journalists.

In 1984, Indira Gandhi ordered what military operation at the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar, aimed at Sikh separatists who had fortified the site? The action was followed months later by her assassination by two of her bodyguards.
This Japanese warlord rose to power after serving Oda Nobunaga and had effectively unified Japan by 1591. He also ordered non-samurai to surrender their weapons; who was he?
Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered invasions of Joseon Korea in 1592 and 1597, with ambitions that extended toward Ming China. What is the conflict formed by these invasions commonly called?

In 1071, a Seljuk army defeated the Byzantine forces in eastern Anatolia and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes. The defeat became a turning point that helped open Anatolia to Turkish conquest; what battle was this?
At the Battle of Manzikert, which Seljuk sultan commanded the victorious army and took Romanos IV Diogenes prisoner? His victory in 1071 is remembered as a major blow to Byzantine power in Anatolia.

Elected president of Peru in 1990 after defeating novelist Mario Vargas Llosa, this leader governed during the capture of Shining Path chief Abimael Guzmán. His administration also authorized the Grupo Colina death squad; who was this president?
Under Alberto Fujimori, Peruvian authorities arrested this founder and principal leader of the Shining Path in Lima in 1992, after years of insurgency. Who was he?
What name is given to the vast assemblage of life-size ceramic soldiers, horses, and chariots buried in pits beside the mausoleum of China’s first emperor to serve as his funerary guard?

The Terracotta Army came to public attention in 1974, when local farmers digging a well found fragments near which modern Chinese city? The excavation site is in Shaanxi Province, east of the city’s historic center.

After World War II, this U.S.-sponsored aid initiative helped rebuild Western European economies and revive industrial production, while also reflecting fears that economic hardship could encourage communist movements. Proposed in a June 1947 Harvard address and authorized by Congress the following year, what program became a major early Cold War foreign-aid effort?

The Marshall Plan bears the name of this U.S. Army general and secretary of state, who called for broad European recovery assistance in a Harvard address on June 5, 1947. Which official, serving under President Truman, gave the program its familiar name?

In 184 CE, a religiously inspired peasant uprising challenged the Eastern Han Dynasty under the leadership of Zhang Jue. Its rebels became known for wearing distinctive colored headwraps; by what name is the revolt known?

The Yellow Turban Rebellion drew support from a religious movement led by Zhang Jiao, whose followers believed the existing order was nearing its end and a new age could begin. What was this movement called?

This English monarch inherited the throne at age ten in 1377 from his grandfather Edward III and personally negotiated with rebels during the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381. Henry Bolingbroke deposed him in 1399; what was this king’s regnal name?

In the late 14th century, Richard II oversaw the rebuilding of a vast ceremonial structure in his London palace, later renowned for its exceptionally wide medieval hammerbeam roof. What building was it?

Appointed dictator of Rome in 217 BCE during the Second Punic War, this commander faced Hannibal after the Carthaginian victories in Italy. Rather than risk a decisive pitched battle, he shadowed Hannibal’s army, harassed detachments, and sought to restrict its supplies; who was he?

Quintus Fabius Maximus used a cautious approach against Hannibal, avoiding a major pitched battle while harassing his forces and limiting their access to supplies. What term, later applied to strategies of calculated delay, describes this approach?

Serving Louis XIV as controller general of finances, this French minister used state policy to encourage domestic manufactures, shipping, and trade. He also initiated work on the colonial ordinance later known as the Code Noir, which was issued after his death. Who was he?

Jean-Baptiste Colbert supported royal patronage of scientific research, helping establish a learned institution in 1666. Its first members met that December in the king’s library in Paris. What was the institution?
Between 1346 and 1353, this plague pandemic caused by *Yersinia pestis* killed a huge share of Europe’s population, with estimates often ranging from 30% to 60%. What is the pandemic commonly called?
In Giovanni Boccaccio’s frame narrative, ten young Florentines retreat from the city during the Black Death and entertain one another with stories over ten days. What is the title of this collection?
The Black Death followed a severe food shortage in Europe marked by crop failures, soaring grain prices, and widespread hunger from 1315 to 1317. What is that earlier crisis commonly called?

What name is given to the connected series of ethnic and nationalist conflicts that erupted during the 1990s as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia disintegrated, including fighting in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina?
During the Yugoslav Wars, what peace accord negotiated at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in November 1995 ended the Bosnian War and established Bosnia and Herzegovina's two entities?

Camel caravans crossed this network of desert routes linking West African trading centers with North Africa and the Mediterranean world. It carried gold northward and salt and other goods in several directions, connecting states such as Ghana, Mali, and Songhai. What is this network called?

In accounts of Trans-Saharan trade, this settlement in present-day northern Mali was a major salt-producing center. Camel caravans carried slabs of salt from its deposits toward Sahelian markets, including Timbuktu. What was the settlement called?

This natural animal fiber is obtained chiefly by shearing sheep and spun into yarn for textiles. Its natural crimp helps trap insulating air, while its overlapping surface scales allow it to bind together when felted. What is this material?
In 1378, Florence’s disenfranchised wool workers rose against guild-dominated rule and briefly won political representation for lower-status laborers. What is the name of this uprising?
Soviet Russia experienced a catastrophic food crisis from 1921 to 1922, with the Volga region among the hardest-hit areas. What is this disaster commonly called?

During the Russian famine of 1921–1922, international relief efforts were led by this Norwegian explorer, diplomat, and humanitarian. He received the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize for his work aiding famine victims; who was he?

What Roman frontier fortification, built under the emperor whose name it bears, stretched roughly 73 miles across northern Britain from the Solway Firth to the River Tyne? It later became associated with the boundary between England and Scotland.
At the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, in modern Wallsend, stood a Roman fort whose name is now used for the archaeological museum and visitor site there. What was the fort called?

In ancient Rome, what prestigious public procession honored a victorious general after a major military conquest? The ceremony could feature captured enemies, spoils of war, and the general riding through the city in a decorated chariot.
During Julius Caesar’s Roman triumph in 46 BCE, which captured Gallic chieftain, who had led a major revolt against Roman rule, was paraded through Rome and later executed?

Which precolonial Edo kingdom in present-day southern Nigeria was ruled by an oba and became renowned for its court art, including cast-metal plaques and commemorative heads? British forces invaded its capital in 1897 and removed many artworks.
During the 1897 British invasion of the Kingdom of Benin, which oba was captured after the fall of Benin City and later exiled to Calabar?

What conflict began in 395 BCE after Sparta’s growing interference prompted Athens, Thebes, and Argos to form an anti-Spartan coalition? It ended in 387/386 BCE with a Persian-backed settlement that placed Greek cities in Asia Minor under Persian rule.
During the Corinthian War, which 394 BCE naval engagement off the southwestern coast of Asia Minor dealt Sparta a major blow in the Aegean? The opposing fleet received Persian support.

In March 1921, sailors and civilians at a fortified Baltic naval base on Kotlin Island rose against the Bolshevik government, calling for political reforms and greater civil liberties. What uprising was suppressed by Red Army forces shortly before Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy?
During the Kronstadt Rebellion, which sailor chaired the rebels’ Provisional Revolutionary Committee? After the Red Army retook the island, he escaped to Finland.

On the Western Front, armies dug these protected defensive positions into the ground and used them as the main line of battle. They were often muddy, crowded, and vulnerable to artillery fire. What were these defensive works called?

Soldiers who remained in cold, waterlogged World War I trenches for long periods could develop this non-freezing injury, marked by numbness, swelling, and damaged tissue in the feet. What was the condition called?
Which southeastern European country is centered on Bucharest and includes historic regions such as Moldavia and Transylvania? Its communist regime fell during a revolution in December 1989.

In Romania, the deposed communist ruler was executed on this holiday in December 1989. The same holiday is associated with the 1914 truce in which British and German troops briefly stopped fighting and played soccer.

After incoming prime minister George Papandreou disclosed in 2009 that Greece’s budget deficit had been seriously underreported, the country entered a prolonged financial emergency marked by euro-area and IMF bailouts, austerity, and protests. What 2010s crisis is identified by this sequence of events?

During the Greek government-debt crisis, which left-wing party won Greece’s January 2015 election on a platform opposing bailout-era austerity and then led the government that held a July referendum on creditors’ terms?

This medieval Islamic state on the East African coast rose to prominence through its control of Indian Ocean commerce and extended its influence southward to the gold-trading port of Sofala. Centered on an island off present-day Tanzania, it became one of the wealthiest Swahili polities. Which polity was it?

The Kilwa Sultanate's southern commercial reach included this coastal port in present-day Mozambique, which served as an outlet for gold arriving from the African interior into Indian Ocean trade. What port was it?
Which Achaemenid king, son of Darius I, led the 480 BCE invasion of Greece that overcame the defenders at Thermopylae but ended with major Persian defeats at Salamis and Plataea?

During Xerxes I’s invasion of Greece, which naval engagement saw the Greek fleet defeat the Persian navy in the narrow waters near Athens, despite the Persians’ numerical advantage? Xerxes watched the fighting from Mount Aigaleo.

During the 1524–1525 uprising across the Holy Roman Empire, this rural population challenged serfdom, labor services, rents, and restrictions on communal land. Their grievances found influential written expression in a 1525 program from Memmingen that also invoked scripture. What social group is meant?

The German Peasants’ demands in 1525 included choosing local pastors and challenging serfdom through arguments based on scripture. What document, drafted in Memmingen by Sebastian Lotzer, set out these demands?

Enacted in Italy in 1923, this electoral law awarded two-thirds of the seats in the Chamber of Deputies to the list that won at least 25 percent of the vote. Its formula helped magnify the Fascists’ victory in the 1924 election. What was the law called?
The Acerbo Law bears the surname of this Abruzzese deputy who introduced the 1923 electoral bill. He later served as Italy’s minister of agriculture. Who was he?

Launched by Mao Zedong in 1966 and conventionally dated through 1976, this Chinese political campaign mobilized young people against supposed bourgeois and counterrevolutionary elements. It disrupted schools and institutions and subjected party officials, teachers, and intellectuals to public criticism and persecution. What campaign was this?

During the Cultural Revolution, Mao mobilized groups made up largely of students and other young people to denounce teachers, party officials, and symbols they considered old or counterrevolutionary. What were these youth groups called?

The Weimar Republic faced severe hyperinflation and political unrest during this decade, including the 1923 occupation of the Ruhr and the failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich. The 1924 Dawes Plan later helped reorganize Germany’s reparations payments; what decade is described?

During the 1920s, which reparations arrangement adopted in 1924 restructured Germany’s payment schedule, encouraged American loans, and was tied to the withdrawal of French and Belgian troops from the Ruhr?

A mid-19th-century constitutional and dynastic dispute concerned two duchies south of Denmark: one belonged to the German Confederation, while its northern neighbor did not, though both were tied to the Danish crown. The controversy helped lead to Prussia and Austria’s 1864 war against Denmark; what was it conventionally called?
The Schleswig-Holstein Question intensified after Denmark’s 1863 constitution tied Schleswig more closely to the kingdom. What 1864 conflict began when Prussia and Austria jointly invaded Denmark?

Born in Caracas to a wealthy criollo family, this military leader helped liberate Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador, and Peru from Spanish rule. He became known by a Spanish title meaning “the Liberator”; what was his name?
Simón Bolívar became president of this federation, proclaimed in 1819 and ultimately joining Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador, and Panama. What was the name of this short-lived state?

After exile in Jamaica, Simón Bolívar received weapons and other aid from the leader of this Caribbean republic, after pledging to abolish slavery in Spanish America. Which republic’s president, Alexandre Pétion, supported his expedition?

This medieval and early modern commercial and defensive alliance grew from associations of northern European merchants and linked trading towns around the North and Baltic Seas. Its trading posts, known as kontors, operated in places such as Novgorod, Bruges, London, and Bergen. Name the alliance.
Within the Hanseatic League, the trading post at Bergen was closely associated with a preserved fish product made by air-drying cod. What was this product called?

Which Eighteenth-Dynasty pharaoh ruled Egypt after Akhenaten, helped restore traditional worship of Amun and other gods, and died as a teenager? His richly furnished tomb was found in the Valley of the Kings in 1922, making him one of ancient Egypt’s most famous rulers.

In 1922, this British archaeologist’s team uncovered Tutankhamun’s tomb in the Valley of the Kings after finding steps beneath debris near the tomb of Ramesses VI. He had searched for years with Lord Carnarvon’s backing.

During Tutankhamun’s reign, this Egyptian city again became a major religious center as the cult of Amun regained prominence. Its vast Karnak temple complex and nearby Luxor Temple distinguish it from the Greek city that shares its ancient name.
Tutankhamun’s birth name honored this solar deity, whose disk was central to Akhenaten’s religious program. After taking the throne, the young ruler changed his own name to honor Amun instead.
Which former vizier succeeded Tutankhamun as pharaoh and was later followed on the throne by Horemheb? His short reign came between that of the young king and the former commander-in-chief.

Issued by Ferdinand and Isabella at Granada on 31 March 1492, this royal measure required Jews in Castile and Aragon to leave by the end of July or convert to Christianity, and barred their return. What is its established name?

The Alhambra Decree was issued in the names of Ferdinand of Aragon and his wife, the queen who succeeded her half-brother Henry IV and later co-led the conquest of Granada. She also sponsored Christopher Columbus’s 1492 voyage. Which queen was this?

A former Japanese prime minister was fatally shot on 8 July 2022 while speaking at a campaign event in Nara Prefecture in support of a candidate for the upper house of parliament. By what commonly used name is this attack known?

In the investigation of the Assassination of Shinzo Abe, security officers detained a suspect at the scene in Nara, and reports identified him as the man who used a homemade weapon. What was the suspect’s name?

Germany opened this 1940 campaign on 10 May, sending its main armored thrust through the Ardennes while Allied forces moved into Belgium. Paris fell on 14 June, and an armistice was signed eight days later. What was the campaign called?
After the Battle of France ended in June 1940, the French government based in Vichy cooperated with Germany. Which French marshal led that government?

This Swiss reformer led the Reformation in Zurich and rejected the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence in the Eucharist. At the Marburg Colloquy, he defended his view in a debate with Martin Luther.

At what 1529 meeting did Huldrych Zwingli debate Martin Luther over whether Christ was physically present in the Eucharist? The two reformers agreed on many points but could not resolve their disagreement over the sacrament.

What fortified border system did East Germany begin erecting around the western-controlled enclave of a divided German capital on 13 August 1961 to stop departures to the West? Its crossings opened on 9 November 1989 after a confused announcement about new travel rules.

At the Berlin Wall, which crossing on Friedrichstraße served as the best-known Allied-controlled passage between East and West Berlin? It became a focal point of Cold War tensions, including a 1961 tank standoff.

Following the fall of the Qing dynasty, regional commanders and their armies held power across a fragmented China, defining the period before Nationalist unification. What are these military strongmen collectively known as?

Among the Chinese warlords, which Shandong-based commander used armored trains staffed by refugees from the Russian Civil War who had settled in Harbin? His forces were eventually crushed by the National Revolutionary Army during the Northern Expedition.

Which ancient city in central Mexico became one of the largest urban centers of the pre-Columbian Americas, with the Avenue of the Dead running between its monumental pyramids? Its name is commonly translated as “the place where the gods were created.”

At Teotihuacan, which monumental structure rises at the northern end of the Avenue of the Dead beside a large ceremonial plaza? It is the city’s second-largest monument, built in several stages and topped by a temple complex.
Which southeastern European country occupies the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula and includes a mainland as well as islands in both the Aegean and Ionian seas? Its capital is Athens.
In Greece, which Aegean island group takes its name from the Greek word for “circle,” with its islands traditionally arranged around Delos? Naxos and Paros are among its islands.

Which Germanic people entered Italy in 568 under King Alboin and established a kingdom across much of the north and center of the peninsula? Their rule ended with Charlemagne’s conquest of their kingdom in 774.
The Lombards’ invasion of Italy began in 568, and their first king there captured Milan the following year before making Pavia the kingdom’s capital. Which ruler led that invasion?

Born in 1157 to Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine, this English king inherited the throne after the deaths of his older brothers. He became famous for his military leadership in the Holy Land and was nicknamed “the Lionheart.” What was his name?

Richard I of England led this campaign after reaching the eastern Mediterranean, cooperating with Philip II of France and defeating Saladin’s forces at Arsuf. It captured Acre but ended without retaking Jerusalem. What was this campaign called?
After Richard I of England began his journey home from the Holy Land in 1192, this Austrian ruler seized him near Vienna and held him until he was transferred to Emperor Henry VI. Who was the captor?

In 1358, amid the turmoil of the Hundred Years’ War and the captivity of John II, peasants in northern France attacked aristocratic estates and challenged noble authority. What is the name of this major French uprising?

During the Jacquerie Rebellion, Guillaume Cale’s peasant forces were decisively defeated in June 1358 by an army commanded by Charles II of Navarre. Which town near Beauvais is associated with this battle?

A set of four hues—red, white, black, and green—recurs in several national banners and is associated with a shared identity spanning the Middle East and North Africa. Its modern symbolism is commonly linked to the banner raised during the World War I revolt against Ottoman rule. What is this four-part palette called?

The Pan-Arab colors appear in a World War I-era banner with black, green, and white horizontal stripes beneath a red triangle at the hoist. Forces rebelling against Ottoman rule used this design. What is this banner commonly called?

Established in Madrid in 1933 by a Spanish aristocrat, this movement used a yoke-and-arrows emblem and advocated national syndicalism. It later supplied the ideological and organizational core of the party that ruled under Franco. What was this movement called?

A lawyer and politician from an aristocratic family, he founded Falange Española in Madrid in 1933. Republicans executed him in Alicante in November 1936, and he later became a symbolic martyr for the movement. Who was he?

Which Iranian Shi'a cleric became the leading figure opposing the shah, returned to Tehran from exile on February 1, 1979, and became the Islamic Republic’s first Supreme Leader? He held that office until his death in 1989.

Ruhollah Khomeini’s political theory, incorporated into the Islamic Republic’s constitutional order, holds that a qualified Islamic jurist should exercise guardianship over the state. What is this doctrine commonly called?
This English king took the throne in 1483 after his brother Edward IV’s death, displacing his young nephew Edward V, and was killed by Henry Tudor at Bosworth in 1485. Who was the last Yorkist king?
Richard III was killed on August 22, 1485, in the clash where Henry Tudor defeated his forces, ending the Wars of the Roses and clearing the way for Tudor rule. What was this battle called?

In May 1991, Israeli aircraft evacuated more than 14,000 members of the Beta Israel community from Ethiopia to Israel in a massive airlift completed in roughly 36 hours. What was this Israeli operation called?

Operation Solomon carried thousands of Ethiopian Jews to Israel in May 1991, with the evacuation departing from the airport in Ethiopia’s capital. What city served as the airlift’s main staging point?

Founded by Liu Bang after the fall of the Qin, this Chinese imperial house ruled from 202 BCE until 220 CE, apart from a brief interruption by Wang Mang’s Xin regime. Its cultural legacy is reflected in the name used for China’s majority ethnic group. Which imperial house was it?

During the Han dynasty, which ruler shifted policy toward sustained military campaigns against the Xiongnu, beginning in 133 BCE? His reign also saw Confucian learning become central to official education and government.
The Han dynasty governed some areas directly through units under central government control, in contrast to semi-autonomous kingdoms. What were these centrally administered units called?

Which constituent country of the United Kingdom occupies the central and southern parts of Great Britain, rather than referring to the whole island or the UK as a whole? Its crown was contested by Lancaster and York during the Wars of the Roses.
Which Norman duke led the 1066 invasion of England and defeated King Harold's forces at the Battle of Hastings? His victory reshaped the country's ruling dynasty and institutions.
In feudal Japan, these covert agents gathered intelligence and carried out infiltration, sabotage, and sometimes assassination. What name is commonly given to them?

Which 17th-century Japanese compendium on ninja lore, completed in 1676, preserves information about the espionage traditions of Iga and Kōka? It is regarded as one of the most important surviving manuals on these agents.

This Chinese communist revolutionary helped found the Chinese Communist Party in 1921 and proclaimed the establishment of the People’s Republic of China in 1949. He led the country through the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. Who was he?

Mao Zedong launched this late-1950s campaign to rapidly collectivize agriculture and boost industrial output through rural communes and backyard furnaces. Its disastrous policies and disruption of food production preceded a catastrophic famine. What was the campaign called?

During the Chinese Civil War, Mao Zedong and the Communist Red Army undertook this 1934–35 strategic retreat to escape Nationalist encirclement, eventually reaching a base in Shaanxi. The journey became a foundational episode in Chinese Communist Party history and helped consolidate Mao’s leadership. What was it called?

Mao Zedong’s sayings and political writings were assembled in this anthology, which was widely distributed during the Cultural Revolution and carried by many Red Guards. What is the work commonly called in English, referring to its color and compact format?

Which 13th-century Mandinka leader is remembered as the founder of the Mali Empire? He led an alliance that defeated the Sosso ruler Sumanguru, and his story became the subject of a celebrated West African epic.
In the account of Sundiata Keita’s rise, what decisive battle saw his forces defeat the Sosso ruler Sumanguru and help establish Mali’s power?

This Hohenzollern monarch ruled as German emperor and king of Prussia from 1888 until his abdication in November 1918. During the July Crisis, he exchanged personal telegrams with Russia’s tsar in an attempt to avert a wider European war. Who was he?

During the July Crisis of 1914, Wilhelm II exchanged personal telegrams with this ruler of Russia, his cousin, in an effort to avert a wider European war. He was the last emperor of Russia and abdicated in 1917. Who was he?

Born in 1952 in Leningrad, this former KGB officer served in East Germany and later headed Russia’s Federal Security Service. Boris Yeltsin appointed him prime minister in 1999, and he became acting president when Yeltsin resigned later that year. Who is this Russian politician?
Vladimir Putin was born in 1952 in the Soviet city now known as Saint Petersburg. What was the city’s name at the time of his birth?

In 1968, Czechoslovakia's Communist leadership loosened censorship and pursued political reforms described as “socialism with a human face.” The period ended when Warsaw Pact forces invaded the country. What is this period of liberalization called?
During the Prague Spring, this Slovak Communist reformer became first secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia in January 1968 and promoted “socialism with a human face.” Who was he?
What Afghan Islamist political and military movement emerged in 1994 during the Second Afghan Civil War, captured Kabul in 1996, and returned to power in August 2021?
Which leader guided the Taliban’s advance that culminated in capturing Kabul in 1996 and led its first government until the U.S.-led invasion toppled it in 2001?
What coalition, also known as the United Front, fought the Taliban after Kabul fell in 1996 and retained international recognition as Afghanistan’s government during the movement’s first rule?
After the Taliban government was toppled in 2001, what council formed by exiled leaders in Pakistan in 2002 became a central body for directing the insurgency?
Which 2020 accord, negotiated in Qatar between the United States and the Taliban, set a framework for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Afghanistan and subsequent intra-Afghan talks?

What name is given to the broad prehistoric and ancient phase in which an alloy made chiefly from copper and tin became important across many societies, often alongside early civilizations and writing, before iron gradually gained importance? Since technologies and timelines varied by region, it has no single worldwide start or end date.

During the Bronze Age, Old Assyrian merchants at this Anatolian trade center recorded business transactions on cuneiform tablets; one tablet from the site dates to the twentieth–nineteenth centuries BCE. What was the center called?

In 1948, Soviet authorities cut road, rail, and water access to the western sectors of a divided German capital. The United States and Britain responded by flying food and fuel into the city until the blockade ended in May 1949; what was this operation called?
During the Berlin Airlift, the United States gave its supply-flying effort a codename distinct from the British operation called Plainfare. What was the American effort called?

Which southeastern African country became independent from Portugal on 25 June 1975 after FRELIMO negotiated the transition? Its FRELIMO-led government later fought RENAMO in a civil war that ended with a peace agreement signed in Rome.
In Mozambique, what accord did government and RENAMO leaders sign in Rome on 4 October 1992? The accord paved the way for a ceasefire, demobilization, and a UN-monitored transition to elections.

This Cold War-era organization brought together states seeking to avoid formal alignment with either the U.S.-led Western bloc or the Soviet-led Eastern bloc. Its first summit took place in Belgrade in 1961, following the 1955 Bandung Conference. What organization was it?
The Non-Aligned Movement held its first summit in 1961 in the capital of Yugoslavia, whose president Josip Broz Tito was among the movement’s leading founders. What city hosted the summit?
This city on the Volkhov River was the political center of a powerful medieval republic and a major Hanseatic trading hub. Moscow brought the republic under its rule in 1478. What is the city’s name?
In Veliky Novgorod, a bell summoned this public assembly, which debated civic matters and chose officials such as the posadnik. What was this institution called?

Which West Asian country encompasses much of ancient Mesopotamia, the region associated with the Tigris and Euphrates rivers? Its forces invaded Kuwait in 1990, prompting a U.S.-led coalition to drive them out the following year.
During Saddam Hussein’s rule, Iraq fought an eight-year war with its eastern neighbor, beginning in 1980 and ending in 1988. What is the name of this conflict?

Fought on 14 October 1066 near present-day Battle in East Sussex, this clash pitted King Harold Godwinson’s English army against William, Duke of Normandy. Its outcome opened the way for Norman rule of England. What battle was it?

The Battle of Hastings was fought by an invading duke whose claim to the English throne rested partly on alleged promises from Edward the Confessor. What northwestern French duchy was William’s homeland and the base of his army?

At the Battle of Hastings, unsuccessful frontal attacks led Norman units to briefly break off contact. English soldiers who left their shield wall to pursue them were then met by a counterattack. What battlefield maneuver did the Normans use?

Born in 1894 as the eldest son of George V, he became king in January 1936. Before the end of that year, he gave up the throne amid a constitutional crisis over his wish to marry Wallis Simpson. Who was he?

During Edward VIII’s 1936 abdication crisis, this Conservative prime minister opposed the king’s marriage to Wallis Simpson and left office the following year, when Neville Chamberlain succeeded him. Who was he?

What name is commonly given to the 2022 Canadian protest movement that began with trucker-led opposition to COVID-19 vaccine requirements for cross-border freight drivers, expanded into demonstrations against public-health restrictions, and centered on a prolonged blockade in downtown Ottawa?

During the Freedom Convoy standoff in February 2022, what federal statute did Justin Trudeau’s government invoke to gain temporary powers to respond to blockades? It was the first use of the statute since it replaced the War Measures Act in 1988.

It is organized armed conflict involving states or other organized groups, and it may occur between countries or within a country. Under international humanitarian law, its classification does not depend on whether either side formally declares it. What is this kind of conflict called?

In the context of War, this group of four treaties forms a central part of international humanitarian law and establishes protections for wounded and captured people, as well as civilians. What is this set of treaties called?

A Saudi-born militant, he raised money and built connections among foreign volunteers during the Soviet-Afghan War. He helped found al-Qaeda in 1988 and led it until U.S. forces killed him in Pakistan in 2011; who was he?
The U.S. raid that killed Osama bin Laden in May 2011 took place in this Pakistani city, where he had been living in a compound. What city was it?

Which ruler of ancient Mesopotamia conquered rival Sumerian city-states and founded one of the ancient world’s earliest territorial empires? His daughter Enheduanna served as a high priestess and is often credited as the earliest known author identified by name.

Sargon of Akkad’s empire later reached its apogee under his grandson, who was deified during his lifetime and commemorated in a victory stele depicting his campaign against the Lullubi. Which Akkadian king was this?

On the night of June 30, 1520, after the Mexica uprising in Tenochtitlan, Hernán Cortés’s Spanish and Indigenous allied forces tried to flee the city and suffered heavy losses. By what Spanish name is this retreat and defeat commonly known?

During La Noche Triste, Cortés’s forces attempted to escape Tenochtitlan by the raised roadway leading toward Tlacopan, while Mexica fighters attacked from both the shore and the lake. What was this route called?

Its early civilization developed in the Yellow and Yangtze river basins, and its long history includes the Shang oracle-bone inscriptions and the Qin unification of 221 BCE. Name this East Asian country.

In China, this ruler defeated rival states and proclaimed himself First Emperor after unification in 221 BCE. His burial complex near modern Xi’an is famous for its thousands of terracotta warriors. Who was he?

In China, the oldest surviving Chinese writing appears on divination bones and turtle shells linked to this Bronze Age royal house. Archaeologists have identified its capital at Anyang. Which ruling house is described?
This era of Chinese rule lasted from 618 to 907, with Chang’an as its capital and a flourishing of poetry and cosmopolitan trade. Which ruling house was in power?

In China, which leader is closely associated with the 1978 launch of “reform and opening up” and the establishment of Shenzhen as a Special Economic Zone? He championed market-oriented changes while retaining Communist Party rule. Name him.

Established under the Ptolemaic dynasty in the third century BCE in the Egyptian city founded by Alexander the Great, this renowned center gathered Greek writings. Its scholars compared versions of Homer’s poems in efforts to establish reliable texts. What institution is this?

The Library of Alexandria was associated with a scholarly institution where resident thinkers pursued research and textual study. Its name referred to a sanctuary of the Muses. What was this connected institution called?
Which 18th-century British naval officer led three major Pacific voyages, charted New Zealand, and mapped the eastern coast of Australia in 1770?
On his first Pacific voyage, James Cook sailed aboard a converted collier that reached Tahiti in 1769 and the eastern coast of Australia in 1770. What was the name of the ship?
Promulgated by Emperor Meiji in 1868 as Japan began a new era of imperial rule, this declaration set out guiding principles for modernization and government. What was it called?

The Charter Oath was issued during the political transition that restored imperial rule in 1868. Before Emperor Meiji moved the imperial capital to Tokyo, which city had served as Japan’s capital for nearly a millennium?
This Roman emperor ruled from 117 to 138 CE after succeeding Trajan. During a visit to Britain in 122, he ordered a major fortification built along the northern frontier of the province.
During Hadrian’s reign, a major uprising against Roman rule in Judaea lasted from 132 to 135 CE. Roman forces suppressed the revolt, bringing severe harm to Jewish communities.

After defeating his half-brother Huascar in the Inca civil war in 1532, this ruler was captured by Francisco Pizarro at Cajamarca. The Spaniards received a vast gold-and-silver ransom but executed him in 1533; who was this ruler?
During the Spanish conquest, Atahualpa was captured by Francisco Pizarro at this Andean city in 1532. What city became the site of this pivotal seizure?

Which British statesman became prime minister in May 1940 after Neville Chamberlain resigned and led the United Kingdom through much of World War II? He delivered the 1940 speech declaring, “We shall fight on the beaches.”

In Winston Churchill’s career, he resigned as First Lord of the Admiralty in 1915 after the failure of this World War I operation in the Dardanelles. It included landings at Cape Helles and Anzac Cove, whose anniversary is commemorated in Australia and New Zealand.
In 1953, Winston Churchill received an internationally recognized prize for his historical and biographical writing, as well as his speeches. What named prize category was awarded?

Which Indigenous Polynesian people of Aotearoa New Zealand trace their ancestry to East Polynesian voyagers who settled the islands by about 1300 CE? Their communities are traditionally organized into iwi and hapū.
In 1840, many Māori people signed this agreement with representatives of the British Crown. Its Māori and English texts differ over governance and chiefly authority.
What name is given to the 1905–1907 uprising by African peoples in German East Africa against German colonial rule, which was ultimately suppressed amid forced displacement and famine?
A spirit medium from Ngarambe became a leading inspiration for the Maji Maji Rebellion after preaching that consecrated water would protect fighters from German bullets. What was his name?

Which early Islamic polity began after Muhammad’s death and was governed in succession by Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali? Its armies expanded beyond Arabia into the Levant, Egypt, and Persia before civil conflict brought this period of rule to an end.
During the Rashidun Caliphate’s campaigns, Muslim forces conquered Syria and the Levant from a Christian empire whose ruler Heraclius governed from Constantinople. What was this rival empire called?

This Old Kingdom royal official and architect served under Third Dynasty ruler Djoser and is traditionally credited with designing the king’s stepped funerary complex at Saqqara. Centuries later, Egyptians revered him as a deity associated with wisdom and healing; who was he?

Imhotep is traditionally credited with designing this six-tiered stone funerary monument at Saqqara for the Third Dynasty ruler who commissioned Egypt’s earliest monumental pyramid complex. What is this monument commonly called?
Used by Joseon Korea, this multiple-rocket launcher fired volleys of rocket-propelled arrows and other projectiles. What was this weapon called?
Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s ships used Hwacha devices alongside their cannons. What familiar projectile, normally shot from a bow, could these devices launch using rockets?

Associated with the Abbasid court in Baghdad, this institution is best supported by surviving evidence as a royal library. Older accounts sometimes portrayed it as a single grand academy, but the translation and scholarship of the period extended across a much wider network; what institution is it?

The House of Wisdom was associated with the Abbasid court in this city, where translators and scholars also worked in networks beyond any one institution. Its famous Round City design made it a major Abbasid capital, and it is now the capital of Iraq; what city is it?

This southern Mesopotamian city on the Euphrates became a major capital under Hammurabi and later served as the seat of an empire that ruled from 626 to 539 BCE. Its monumental blue-glazed entrance, decorated with bulls and dragon-like creatures, is now partly reconstructed in Berlin. What city was it?
This Amorite king made Babylon a major power in the 18th century BCE. His famous law stele depicts him receiving symbols of authority from the sun god Shamash. Who was this king?

In Babylon, this monumental blue-glazed brick structure stood on the Processional Way and was built under Nebuchadnezzar II. It was decorated with rows of bulls and dragon-like mušḫuššu. What was this structure called?

Ancient writers associated this celebrated wonder with Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar II, describing terraces irrigated with water from the Euphrates. No surviving Babylonian text mentions it, and its historical existence remains uncertain. What was this wonder called?
Traditionally attributed to Henry of Navarre, this phrase summed up his conversion from Protestantism to Catholicism as he sought to secure the French throne. What was the remark?
answer: Paris is well worth a mass

question: The remark “Paris is well worth a mass” is traditionally linked to a Bourbon ruler who converted to Catholicism in 1593 to strengthen his claim to the French throne. What regnal name did this former Protestant claimant take when he became king of France?

What ancient writing system, first developed in southern Mesopotamia, was made by pressing a cut reed into clay to produce characteristic wedge-shaped marks? It began as a way to record Sumerian and was later adapted to languages including Akkadian.

Cuneiform was first used to write this language of southern Mesopotamia, whose surviving texts include administrative records from Uruk and compositions such as the Epic of Gilgamesh. What language is meant?

Which monumental royal text helped scholars decipher cuneiform after early-19th-century copies were made? Carved under Darius I at a cliffside site in western Iran, it repeats a royal text in Old Persian, Elamite, and Akkadian.

Which Babylonian merchant was the addressee of Nanni’s well-known complaint tablet in cuneiform, which protests that copper ingots were below the promised quality? The tablet also rebukes him for the rude treatment of Nanni’s messenger at his house in Ur.

In 1932, Australian authorities sent a small Army detachment equipped with machine guns into Western Australia after large flocks of flightless birds damaged wheat fields and fences. The effort failed to stop the crop losses and became known by a humorous name suggesting a military conflict. What was this campaign called?

During the Great Emu War, three Royal Australian Artillery soldiers were sent to this Western Australian farming area, where fast-moving flocks made machine-gun fire difficult and one gun jammed during an early encounter. Which place was the operation centered on?

Beginning in 1934, the Chinese Communist Red Army broke through Nationalist encirclement and undertook a vast retreat, ultimately reaching northern Shaanxi in 1935. What is the name of this campaign, which helped the Communists survive?
At the 1935 Zunyi Conference during the Long March, this Communist leader’s influence within the movement grew. He later became the founding chairman of the People’s Republic of China; who was he?

What was the name of the imperial system that selected government officials through competitive written tests rather than hereditary appointment? Expanded over successive dynasties, it gave educated men outside the old aristocratic lineages a route into state service.

Within the Chinese imperial examinations under the Ming and Qing, what title was awarded to candidates who passed the final palace examination? Its recipients had attained the system’s highest examination rank and could enter the elite ranks of government.
In 1536, rebels in northern England rose against Henry VIII’s religious reforms and the dissolution of the monasteries. Led by Robert Aske, what was this uprising called?
The Pilgrimage of Grace was led by this Yorkshire lawyer, who represented the northern rebels in negotiations with the Crown and was later executed at York in 1537. Who was he?

During the 1916 Easter Rising, he commanded the Boland’s Mills garrison and later opposed the Anglo-Irish Treaty during the Irish Civil War. He became the first Taoiseach and later served three terms as president of Ireland; name this Irish revolutionary and statesman.

Éamon de Valera’s government submitted a new constitution to referendum in 1937, replacing the Irish Free State’s 1922 constitution. What is the Irish-language title of this document, which established the presidency and designated the state’s name as Éire?

Led westward into the Carpathian Basin under Árpád, this people established the population from which the medieval Kingdom of Hungary emerged. Their ruler Stephen I was crowned by Pope Sylvester II on Christmas Day in 1000. What people are they?

The Magyars’ westward expansion was checked at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955 by this ruler, the son of Henry the Fowler. Crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962, he is also known by an epithet meaning “the Great.” Who was he?

This faction of Chinese Communist Party officials, including Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao, reached the height of its influence during the Cultural Revolution. Its arrest in October 1976, one month after Mao Zedong’s death, marked the end of its political power. What was the faction called?
Among the Gang of Four was Mao Zedong’s widow, a former actress who became a powerful political figure and advocate of revolutionary cultural policy during the Cultural Revolution. What was her name?

In 1866, forces of the Habsburg monarchy and a northern German kingdom fought a short conflict that culminated in a decisive victory at Königgrätz and ended Austria’s leadership in German affairs. What war is also commonly known as the Seven Weeks’ War?
During the Austro-Prussian War, which July 1866 battle in Bohemia—also known as Sadowa—ended in a decisive Prussian victory over Austrian forces and is often regarded as the war’s turning point?

In 2022, dwindling foreign-exchange reserves and mounting debt left an Indian Ocean island nation struggling to import fuel, food, and medicine; it suspended external debt payments in April. Shortages helped spark mass protests and the occupation of the presidential residence before the president fled and resigned in July. What crisis is described?

During the 2022 Sri Lankan Economic Crisis, this president fled the country in July after protesters occupied his official residence, then submitted his resignation while in Singapore. A former defense secretary, he had become president in 2019 and belonged to a family prominent in the country’s politics. Who was he?

Which Indigenous peoples have Arctic homelands spanning Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, and Chukotka? Their communities have distinct local languages and histories while sharing ties across the circumpolar region.
Founded in 1977, which organization brings Inuit from four regions together to advocate for their rights, cultural continuity, and protection of the Arctic environment?

This Roman emperor ruled from 161 to 180 CE, first sharing power with Lucius Verus, and is remembered as the last of the Five Good Emperors. Which ruler wrote Stoic reflections that became one of antiquity’s best-known philosophical works?

Marcus Aurelius composed a series of personal reflections, much of it while campaigning along the Danube frontier. Divided into twelve books, this work became a major text of Stoic philosophy; what is its title?

A British political organization grew out of efforts by trade unionists and socialists to secure working-class representation in Parliament. Its roots trace to a committee established in 1900, and its elected members adopted its present name after the 1906 election. What is the organization?
In 1924, the Labour Party formed its first government, which lacked a majority in the House of Commons. Which leader became prime minister at the head of that administration?
Which Central Asian people of the Mongolian steppe founded a vast empire under Genghis Khan? Their descendants later established the Ilkhanate in the Middle East.
The Mongols’ western campaigns brought their forces to Baghdad in 1258. Which grandson of Genghis led the siege and established the Persian branch of the Mongol Empire?

During the late 13th and early 14th centuries, this people defended the northern kingdom of Scotland against English invasions. William Wallace and Robert the Bruce became leading figures in their resistance. Which people are meant?
The Scots faced an English king nicknamed “Longshanks,” who defeated William Wallace at Falkirk in 1298 and later earned an epithet for his wars north of the border. Which king was this?

Which 12th-century Holy Roman Emperor convened the Diet of Roncaglia to assert imperial authority in northern Italy and drowned in the Saleph River while traveling with crusading forces? His Italian epithet referred to his reddish beard.

Which late-12th-century campaign to the eastern Mediterranean did Frederick Barbarossa join after taking the cross at Mainz? It also saw Richard the Lionheart and Philip II of France fight Saladin, and Barbarossa drowned while traveling east with its forces.

This 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman was detained in Tehran by the morality police on September 13, 2022, over an alleged violation of compulsory hijab rules. After she fell into a coma, she died in a hospital three days later, sparking nationwide protests. Who was she?

After Mahsa Amini died in custody in September 2022, demonstrations across Iran joined objections to compulsory veiling with broader demands for women’s rights and political change. What three-part slogan became a rallying cry for the movement?

Which Turkic people formed a steppe khaganate centered at Ordu-Baliq that ended after a Kirghiz attack in 840? Afterward, communities of this people established a kingdom in the Tarim Basin, where Buddhist cave art flourished.
What traditional performance practice of the Uyghurs brings together suites of vocal and instrumental music and dance, and has been recognized by UNESCO as cultural heritage?
Which French politician served twice as prime minister before becoming president from 1995 to 2007? He also helped found the UMP party.

In 2002, Jacques Chirac survived an assassination attempt during which French national holiday? The celebration on July 14 commemorates the 1789 storming of a Parisian prison that helped launch the French Revolution.
This Korean polity ruled from 918 to 1392, between Unified Silla and Joseon, and had its capital at Songdo, now called Gaeseong. Which historical state was it?
The Goryeo Dynasty sponsored this Buddhist canon, completed in 1251 and carved onto more than 80,000 woodblocks. What is this collection known as?

Chosen in 1879 to rule Bulgaria while it remained nominally under Ottoman suzerainty, this prince accepted the union with Eastern Rumelia in 1885. A pro-Russian coup forced him to abdicate the following year. Who was he?
In 1885, Alexander of Battenberg accepted Bulgaria’s union with a separately administered Ottoman province, helping prompt Serbia to invade. Centered on Plovdiv, what was this province called?

Which Chinese leader became the country’s dominant political figure in the late 1970s without serving as president, while promoting market-oriented economic reforms? During the 1989 Tiananmen protests, he was among the party elders who supported martial law and the military crackdown.

Deng Xiaoping and other party elders backed a military crackdown after demonstrators gathered at this central Beijing plaza in spring 1989. The plaza is also associated with the famous photograph of a lone man facing a line of tanks.

This Roman commander and statesman helped Octavian defeat Sextus Pompey and later commanded his fleet against Mark Antony and Cleopatra. He also oversaw construction of Rome’s original Pantheon. Who was he?

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa commanded Octavian’s fleet in this 31 BCE naval battle off the western coast of Greece against Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Its outcome secured Octavian’s path to sole rule of Rome. What battle was it?

An ancient Indian political strategist, he is closely associated with Chandragupta Maurya’s rise to power and is traditionally credited with a Sanskrit work on government and statecraft. By what name is this adviser commonly known?
Kautilya is traditionally credited with this Sanskrit treatise, which discusses kingship, administration, taxation, diplomacy, and espionage. What is the work’s title?

Formed in 1955 by the Soviet Union and seven Eastern European communist states, this collective-defense alliance formalized military cooperation in the Eastern Bloc after West Germany joined NATO. What was this alliance called?
The Warsaw Pact took its name from this Polish capital, where the alliance’s founding treaty was signed in 1955. What city was it?

This emperor was adopted by Claudius as his heir and ruled from 54 to 68 CE, becoming the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Ancient accounts say he blamed Christians for the Great Fire of Rome, though claims that he deliberately started the fire are not established. Who was he?
During Nero’s early reign, this woman—his mother and a powerful adviser—helped guide his rule. Nero later arranged her murder in 59 CE; who was she?

Nero forced this Stoic philosopher and former tutor to take his own life after accusing him of involvement in the Pisonian Conspiracy. The philosopher wrote *Letters from a Stoic* and *On the Shortness of Life*. Who was he?

During Nero’s reign, this queen of the Iceni led a major uprising against Roman rule in Britain. Her forces attacked Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium before Roman forces suppressed the revolt. Who was she?
Nero’s suicide in 68 CE was followed by this period of civil war, during which Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian successively claimed the imperial throne. What is this period called?

In the Portuguese colony that later became South America's largest country, this system of forced labor relied heavily on enslaved Africans and their descendants. It remained legal until the Golden Law declared it extinct on 13 May 1888. What was this institution?

During Slavery in Brazil, what 1871 law established that children born to enslaved women after its passage would not inherit their mothers’ legal status, while permitting owners to retain custody or labor under specified terms until adulthood?

After consolidating the rival Mongol tribes, this steppe leader was proclaimed ruler at a kurultai in 1206 and reorganized his followers into a unified imperial force. By what name is the founder and first leader of the Mongol Empire best known?

The Mongol ruler known as Genghis Khan was born into the Borjigin clan and spent his early life amid the rivalries of the steppe before uniting Mongol tribes. What personal name did he bear before adopting his 1206 title?

In 1219, Genghis Khan launched a major western campaign after his envoys were killed during a diplomatic crisis at the frontier city of Otrar. Which Central Asian empire did his forces bring down, devastating Transoxiana and Khorasan?
Which ruling house governed the Franks from the fifth century until Pepin the Short deposed its final king, and counted Clovis I among its rulers?

Which king of the Merovingian dynasty, according to Gregory of Tours, vowed to embrace Christianity during the Battle of Tolbiac and was later baptized at Reims by Bishop Remigius? His conversion helped establish the Frankish kingdom’s lasting alliance with the Roman Church.

Near Changsha, this archaeological site contains Han-dynasty tombs, including the burial of a noblewoman whose exceptionally preserved remains became famous. Excavations there also uncovered a renowned painted silk funerary banner. What is the name of the site?

A painted silk funerary banner discovered at Mawangdui depicts this noblewoman and her attendants. Her remarkably preserved body was found in one of the site’s Han-dynasty tombs. By what title is she commonly known?

This Prussian statesman engineered German unification through wars against Denmark, Austria, and France, then served as the new empire’s first chancellor from 1871 to 1890. Who was this architect of unification?

In 1862, Otto von Bismarck argued before the Prussian budget commission that parliamentary majorities alone would not settle the German question, urging military preparedness instead. What familiar English title is given to this address?
