Otto von Bismarck’s campaign against the Catholic Church in the German Empire included the 1873 May Laws, which tightened state oversight of clerical education and appointments. By what name is this conflict commonly known?
After unification in 1871, Otto von Bismarck became the first chancellor of a new federal monarchy ruled by Wilhelm I and governed from Berlin. What was the name of this state?

Otto von Bismarck’s statecraft emphasized practical national interests and attainable goals over ideological principle, using shifting alliances and calculated force to pursue them. What term names this approach to politics?

Beginning in 1095 after a papal appeal, these medieval campaigns were primarily aimed at seizing or defending Jerusalem and the Holy Land. What name is given to this broader religiously framed military movement?

During the Crusades, Pope Urban II urged western Christians to take up arms at a major church meeting held in November 1095 in the French city of Clermont. What was the name of this meeting, associated with the launch of the First Crusade?
During the Crusades, which Ayyubid sultan defeated the crusader army at Hattin in 1187 and then recaptured Jerusalem, prompting the Third Crusade?

During the Crusades, the Fourth Crusade abandoned its intended campaign against Egypt and attacked the Byzantine capital in April 1204. What event ended with the city being looted and the Latin Empire established?
During the Crusades, what 1229 agreement negotiated between Emperor Frederick II and Ayyubid ruler al-Kamil restored Jerusalem to Christian rule for ten years without a major siege?

Which Greek city-state led the Delian League after the Persian Wars, and whose Acropolis became the site of a monumental temple dedicated to Athena? Reforms associated with Cleisthenes in this city helped lay the foundations for democracy.

In Ancient Athens, which fifth-century statesman was the city’s leading political figure during much of its imperial peak and is closely associated with the building program that raised the Parthenon on the Acropolis? Thucydides also records his funeral oration during the Peloponnesian War.

After France signed an armistice with Germany in June 1940, a new French regime established its seat in a central French spa town and governed the initially unoccupied zone. Led by Marshal Philippe Pétain, it enacted antisemitic laws and collaborated in the persecution and deportation of Jews; what was this regime called?

In November 1942, following the Allied landings in North Africa, German-led forces occupied the previously unoccupied southern zone of France, ending its separate status under the Vichy government. What was this military operation called?

This Stuart monarch became king of Scotland as an infant in 1567 and inherited England’s crown after Elizabeth I died in 1603, joining the crowns without fully uniting the governments. He also commissioned the English Bible translation later known by his name. Who was this ruler?

During the reign of James VI and I, a group of English Catholic conspirators planned to destroy the Palace of Westminster when the king and Parliament met. The scheme was uncovered in 1605 after Guy Fawkes was found guarding explosives beneath the House of Lords; what is this event commonly called?

Which Canadian prime minister and diplomat received the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize after helping resolve the Suez Crisis? His diplomacy during that international confrontation made him a prominent figure in postwar peacekeeping.

During Lester B. Pearson’s premiership, he publicly questioned U.S. policy in a Southeast Asian conflict, even though Canada did not officially participate in the fighting. The conflict also prompted many U.S. draft resisters to move to Canada; which war was it?

Beginning in 58 BCE, this series of campaigns under Julius Caesar saw Roman forces fight the Helvetii and other peoples across a broad region of western Europe. Its late phase included Vercingetorix’s surrender in 52 BCE, bringing much of the region under Roman control. What is the name of this conflict?

During the Gallic Wars in 52 BCE, Caesar’s forces besieged a hilltop stronghold and built inner fortifications facing its defenders and outer fortifications against a relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered there after the relief force failed to break the encirclement. What was the stronghold called?

He succeeded his father, Murad I, as Ottoman sultan in 1389 and rapidly expanded the empire across the Balkans. Known by an epithet meaning “the Thunderbolt,” which ruler was defeated and captured by Timur in 1402?

Bayezid I’s forces won a major victory in 1396 against a crusading army led by Sigismund of Luxembourg and other European nobles. Fought beside the Danube in what is now Bulgaria, what was this battle called?
On July 7, 2021, Haiti’s sitting president was fatally attacked inside his private residence in the capital region, intensifying the country’s political crisis. What is this event commonly known as?

The Assassination of Jovenel Moïse took place at the president’s residence in Pèlerin 5, a neighborhood within this hillside commune adjoining Port-au-Prince. Which commune contains that neighborhood?
Which Filipino president declared martial law in September 1972, faced a disputed snap election in February 1986, and fled to Hawaii after mass demonstrations and military defections ended his rule?

During Ferdinand Marcos’s rule, which senator and prominent opposition leader was assassinated at Manila International Airport in August 1983 after returning from exile, a killing that helped elevate his widow Corazon as an opposition figure?
Which Mongol-founded Chinese dynasty is conventionally dated from 1271 to 1368 and was displaced in China by the Ming dynasty? Its capital, Dadu, was also known as Khanbaliq.
Which Venetian traveler was associated with the court of Kublai Khan during the Yuan dynasty? While imprisoned in Genoa, he dictated an account of his travels to Rustichello da Pisa.
This Norse explorer, a son of Erik the Red, is traditionally credited with sailing from Greenland to North America around the year 1000. Who was he?
Norse sagas say that Leif Erikson explored a North American region known for wild grapes and plentiful timber. What name did he give the region?
Which ancient Sumerian city in present-day Iraq stood near the Euphrates and became renowned for its monumental stepped temple and elaborate royal graves?
At Ur, King Ur-Nammu began a great stepped temple platform around 2100 BCE. Which Sumerian moon god was the ziggurat dedicated to?

In archaic Athens, this lawgiver is traditionally credited with putting the city’s laws into writing near the end of the seventh century BCE. His code was remembered for imposing severe penalties, even for some relatively minor offenses. Who was he?

Solon repealed most of Draco’s laws, but Athenian tradition held that one area of his code remained in force. What area of law, concerning cases of intentional and unintentional killing, was preserved?

In 1480, the forces of Ivan III of Moscow and the Horde’s ruler faced each other along a tributary of the Oka, but the confrontation ended without a decisive pitched battle. What standoff is commonly treated as a marker of Moscow’s escape from Horde overlordship?
answer: Great Stand on the Ugra River

question: During the Great Stand on the Ugra River, this ruler led the Great Horde against Ivan III and waited unsuccessfully for support from the Polish-Lithuanian side before withdrawing. Who was this leader?
Sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella, this 1492–1493 Atlantic expedition sailed aboard the Niña, Pinta, and Santa María and reached the Caribbean at Guanahani. What is this expedition commonly called?

On the First voyage of Christopher Columbus, the expedition made its first landfall on an island in the present-day Bahamas, where it encountered Taíno people; the leader renamed the island San Salvador. What was the island’s name before that renaming?

In 1926, a Canadian prime minister whose minority government was under pressure asked the Crown’s representative to dissolve Parliament. The representative refused and instead invited the opposition leader to form a government, triggering a constitutional dispute that ended in a federal election; what is this event known as?

During the King–Byng Affair, which Conservative leader was asked by Governor General Lord Byng to form a government after the sitting prime minister’s request for dissolution was denied? His brief ministry fell within days when it failed to retain the confidence of the House of Commons.

What period of the French Revolution, usually dated from 1793 to July 1794, saw political repression, mass executions, and trials by a revolutionary tribunal? Its most intense phase ended after the arrest and execution of Maximilien Robespierre.

During the Reign of Terror, the National Convention established this emergency governing body in April 1793 to direct France’s response to foreign war and internal rebellion. Maximilien Robespierre later served on it, but it was an institution rather than a tribunal.

Founded in 1602, this chartered enterprise received a monopoly over the Netherlands’ commerce across Asia and unusual authority to sign treaties, build forts, hire soldiers, and wage war. It traded spices and other goods while also advancing the Netherlands’ colonial power; what organization was it?

The Dutch East India Company established its Asian headquarters on Java in 1619, after destroying the town that had stood at the site. What name did it give this settlement, which is now Indonesia’s capital, Jakarta?

Name the Egyptian coastal locality on the Mediterranean route west of Alexandria that became the site of two major 1942 battles. The first checked Axis forces advancing toward the Nile Delta, while the second helped drive them westward across North Africa.
During the Second Battle of El Alamein in 1942, which British commander led the Eighth Army and directed Operation Supercharge against Axis positions?

A grandson of Genghis, this Mongol ruler proclaimed a new Chinese dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of the Song by 1279. He also ordered two failed invasions of Japan, whose fleets were devastated by storms remembered in Japanese tradition as kamikaze. Who was this first emperor of the Yuan dynasty?

In 1271, Kublai Khan proclaimed a new ruling house for his Mongol-led realm in China, and his armies completed the defeat of the Song eight years later. What was the name of this Chinese ruling house?
In 1279, Kublai Khan’s forces crushed the last major Song resistance in a decisive naval engagement near the mouth of the Pearl River. What was this battle called?
Formed by the Bolshevik government in 1918, this military force fought the White armies in the Russian Civil War and later served as the armed forces of the Soviet Union. What was this force called?

As the Bolshevik commissar for military and naval affairs, this revolutionary organized the Red Army during the Russian Civil War and traveled by armored train to rally troops at the front. Who was he?

This pair of conflicts in and around the Democratic Republic of the Congo saw Mobutu Sese Seko toppled in the first and Laurent-Désiré Kabila assassinated during the second. More than nine countries participated in the later conflict. What are these conflicts collectively known as?

During the Congo Wars, members of this ethnic group fled neighboring Rwanda for the Democratic Republic of the Congo amid persecution by Hutu extremists. Their presence and protection became part of the crisis that drew regional powers into the conflicts. Which group was it?

Born Tafari Makonnen, this Ethiopian ruler became emperor in 1930 and held the throne until a military coup removed him in 1974. Adherents of the Jamaican movement Rastafari regard him as a sacred or messianic figure; who was he?
During Haile Selassie I’s reign, Addis Ababa became the headquarters of this body, established in 1963 to promote cooperation among the continent’s independent states. What was it called?

A longtime Socialist Party leader, he won Chile’s presidency in 1970 as the candidate of a left-wing coalition and promoted a democratic route to socialism. He died during the military assault on the presidential palace on September 11, 1973. Who was this president?
During Salvador Allende’s presidency, this long, narrow South American country sought to nationalize major industries, including its copper sector. Its capital is Santiago. What country was it?
Salvador Allende won Chile’s 1970 presidential election as the candidate of this left-wing coalition. Its name is commonly translated into English as two words. What was the coalition called?

An Ottoman general, he led the Turkish nationalist movement during the Turkish War of Independence and became the first president of the republic proclaimed in 1923. His government abolished the sultanate and introduced sweeping secularizing reforms. Who was he?

In 1923, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk’s government signed this peace accord with the Allied powers, replacing the settlement imposed at Sèvres and securing international recognition of the new Turkish Republic’s sovereignty. What was it called?

What Chinese student-led anti-imperialist movement began in Beijing in 1919 after demonstrators opposed the postwar decision to place Germany’s former holdings in Shandong under Japanese control? It later grew to include boycotts and strikes and became a landmark in modern Chinese nationalism.

The May Fourth Movement was sparked by anger over the Allied decision not to return Qingdao and other former German concessions in Shandong to China after World War I. What 1919 peace document did Chinese delegates refuse to sign after the movement intensified public pressure?

What separatist movement seeks an independent Sikh homeland centered on Punjab, became especially prominent during the 1980s and 1990s, and included both political advocacy and armed factions, although many Sikhs did not support militancy?

In June 1984, as the Khalistan movement was gaining force, Indian Army forces entered the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar to dislodge militants who had taken positions there. What is the name commonly given to this military operation?
Which Germanic people established a kingdom in Gaul under the Merovingians and Carolingians and later formed the political foundation of Charlemagne’s empire?
Among the Franks, which Merovingian ruler defeated the Gallo-Roman leader Syagrius at Soissons in 486 and later converted to Nicene Christianity, strengthening his control over much of Gaul?
Ancient smiths made this bladed weapon from a copper-and-tin alloy, giving it a longer reach than early daggers and knives. What is the natural name for this weapon?

In a bronze sword, the blade’s alloy generally contained a much larger share of its reddish base metal than tin, which was added in a smaller amount to improve hardness. Which metal typically formed the larger share?
In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, what was the name of the parliament that debated and enacted laws? The same name is used for the lower house of Poland’s modern parliament.

At this 1793 session of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth’s Sejm, Russian influence led delegates to accept the Second Partition and nullify the May 3rd Constitution. Held in a city now in Belarus, what is this session known as?
This Islamic ruling house replaced the Umayyad dynasty in 750, shifting the center of political power eastward. It established Baghdad as its capital in 762; what was it called?
During the Abbasid Caliphate, al-Mansur founded this planned city on the Tigris in 762, with an original circular design known as the Round City. What modern Iraqi capital was it?
Which Chinese imperial regime began in 960, fostered major advances such as movable-type printing and the compass, and ended in 1279 after Mongol conquest established Yuan rule?

During the Song dynasty, what brewed drink became central to refined social life and was often prepared by whisking powdered leaves into hot water, a practice that influenced Japanese traditions surrounding the drink?

In 2018, footage emerged of a French presidential aide wearing a police helmet and assaulting a protester during a May Day demonstration, despite not being a police officer. What scandal followed the revelations and prompted scrutiny of security practices at the Élysée Palace?
In the Benalla affair, which presidential aide was identified in footage from a May Day demonstration wearing a police helmet and assaulting a protester?

What name is given to Italy’s prolonged period of political violence, especially from the late 1960s through the 1980s, when far-left and far-right militant groups carried out bombings, kidnappings, and assassinations?
During the Years of Lead, an explosion at Milan’s National Agricultural Bank on December 12, 1969, killed 17 people. What event became one of the period’s defining attacks?

This Polish capital on the Vistula was the site of a Jewish revolt against Nazi deportations in April 1943 and, in a separate event beginning in August 1944, an uprising by the Polish Home Army. Its historic center was largely destroyed during World War II and later rebuilt. Which city is described?
Signed in Warsaw in May 1955, this Soviet-led military alliance united the USSR with several Eastern European communist states and served as a counterweight to NATO. What was this alliance called?

On 27 July 1794, opponents in the National Convention arrested Robespierre and Saint-Just, and Robespierre was guillotined the following day. What name is given to this political reversal that ended radical Jacobin ascendancy and the Reign of Terror?

The Thermidorian Reaction began on 9 Thermidor, Year II, in the French Revolutionary calendar, when the National Convention turned against Robespierre and Saint-Just. What Gregorian date corresponds to that revolutionary-calendar day?

In sixteenth-century Russia, Ivan IV formed this corps of loyal armed servitors to enforce his separate domain through confiscations and political violence. Accounts describe its members wearing black and carrying symbols of a dog's head and broom. What were these men called?

The Oprichniki took part in a brutal 1570 assault on this major northwestern Russian city, where residents and merchants were targeted during Ivan IV's campaign against suspected treason. Which city was attacked?

After Claudius’s successful invasion in AD 43, this province was governed by imperial officials and later saw Boudica’s revolt end at Watling Street during Nero’s reign. What is the common English name for this territory?
In Roman Britain under Nero, this queen of the Iceni led a revolt that destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium before Roman forces defeated her at Watling Street. Who was this leader?

Which Cuban revolutionary led guerrillas from the Sierra Maestra to overthrow Fulgencio Batista and then governed Cuba for decades? He transferred power to his brother Raúl and remained first secretary of the Communist Party until 2011.

During Fidel Castro’s alignment of Cuba with the Soviet Union, U.S. reconnaissance photographs revealed Soviet nuclear launch sites on the island, triggering a 13-day confrontation with the United States in 1962. What Cold War event brought the superpowers close to nuclear war?

After Fidel Castro’s failed 1953 assault on the Moncada Barracks, he helped organize a revolutionary movement in Mexico with Raúl Castro and Che Guevara. What movement took its name from the date of that attack?
This ancient region lay along the Nile south of Egypt and later encompassed the lands of the powerful Kushite state. What was the region called?
In Nubia, this powerful kingdom had major centers at Napata and Meroë and conquered Egypt, establishing its rulers as Egypt’s 25th Dynasty. What was this kingdom called?

This Romanian communist leader became general secretary of the Romanian Communist Party in 1965 and president in 1974. After condemning the 1968 Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, he ruled until he and his wife Elena were executed during the 1989 revolution. Who was he?

After visits to China and North Korea in 1971, Nicolae Ceaușescu announced proposals calling for tighter ideological control, stronger party influence over culture, and renewed political education. What name is given to this program?

In June 1780, London was gripped by several days of anti-Catholic violence after the Protestant Association mobilized opposition to the Catholic Relief Act. The disturbances included attacks on prisons and public buildings; what are they known as?
During the Gordon riots, which Scottish nobleman led the Protestant Association’s campaign against the Catholic Relief Act and presented its petition to Parliament in 1780?

This Saudi journalist wrote for The Washington Post and used his columns to criticize restrictions on expression in his home country. Saudi agents killed him inside the Saudi consulate in Turkey on 2 October 2018; what was his name?
Jamal Khashoggi was killed on 2 October 2018 inside the Saudi consulate in a Turkish metropolis that straddles the Bosporus and connects Europe and Asia. What city was it?
Beginning with the 1789 Estates General and ending with the 1799 coup that brought Napoleon Bonaparte to power, what upheaval overthrew France’s monarchy and established a republic?
During the French Revolution, Paris crowds seized a royal fortress-prison on July 14, 1789, and freed its few remaining inmates. What event became a powerful symbol of the uprising?

During the French Revolution, this 1789 text proclaimed that men are born and remain free and equal in status, and that sovereignty rests in the nation; it followed the abolition of feudal privileges. What landmark document became a foundation of the new political order?
answer: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

question: During the French Revolution’s Reign of Terror, this Jacobin leader dominated the Committee of Public Safety before his fall in the Thermidorian Reaction of July 1794. Who was he?

As the French Revolution approached its end, this seizure of power on November 9, 1799, displaced the Directory and established a Consulate in which Napoleon became First Consul. By what name, using the revolutionary calendar date, is this event known?

The nationalist Chetnik forces involved in Yugoslav resistance during World War II were associated with this Balkan country. After the breakup of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milošević led it during the conflict over Kosovo. Which country is it?

In the 1990s, the Republic of Serbia, under Slobodan Milošević, fought an armed conflict with ethnic Albanian forces in its southern province that ended after NATO’s 1999 air campaign and international intervention. What is this conflict commonly called?

Beginning in 2003 with a U.S.-led invasion, this conflict continued after Saddam Hussein’s government was overthrown, encompassing an insurgency and escalating sectarian violence. It lasted through the withdrawal of U.S. forces in December 2011. What war was this?
During the Iraq War, the United States announced this strategy in January 2007, deploying additional forces to help improve security amid worsening violence. What was this deployment commonly called?

This Iraqi Ba'ath Party leader became president in 1979 after serving as vice president under Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr. His rule ended during the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, and he was captured near Tikrit that December. Who was he?

After Saddam Hussein's forces occupied Kuwait in 1990, a U.S.-led coalition began a major air campaign in January 1991 and followed it with a ground offensive that drove Iraqi forces out. What was the codename of this military operation?

After an assassination attempt against Saddam Hussein in 1982, Iraqi authorities retaliated against residents of a town north of Baghdad. The Iraqi High Tribunal later convicted him over the killing of 148 Shi'a residents in this event. What was it called?

Saddam Hussein's government invaded its eastern neighbor in September 1980, beginning an eight-year conflict that ended with a 1988 ceasefire. What war, named for the two countries involved, was this?

At Balaclava on 25 October 1854, during the Crimean War, a British cavalry force rode through artillery fire toward a heavily defended Russian battery after confused orders sent it toward the wrong guns. What was this attack, later commemorated in a famous poem?

At Balaclava, this senior British commander wanted cavalry to stop Russian troops from carrying away captured guns, but a confusing message helped send the riders toward a different battery in the Charge of the Light Brigade. Who was he?

At Mawangdui in China, a painted silk banner associated with Lady Dai was found in one, while ancient Egyptian royal examples ranged from pyramids to hidden rock-cut chambers. What broad term covers structures made to hold the dead, from simple graves to monumental complexes?

In Bahrain, thousands of these tombs, chiefly dating to about 2200–1750 BCE, form a landscape that includes tower-like royal examples. What is the commonly used name for this extensive archaeological landscape?
What 1919 diplomatic gathering negotiated the post–World War I settlement and controversially transferred Germany’s former rights in Qingdao to Japan rather than China?

At the Paris Peace Conference, the decision to transfer Germany’s former rights in Shandong to Japan helped spark student demonstrations in Beijing on May 4, 1919. What movement, named for the date those protests began, grew out of this unrest?

During China’s Cultural Revolution, Mao Zedong encouraged student-led groups to challenge party officials and attack the “Four Olds.” In 1966, members of these groups gathered in mass rallies in Beijing wearing distinctive armbands. What were these groups called?

The Red Guards were urged to study this collection of Mao Zedong’s quotations, which was published in a small red-covered volume and widely distributed by the People’s Liberation Army. By what common English name is the book known?

Established in 661 after Ali’s assassination, this first dynastic Islamic empire made Damascus its capital and expanded from the Atlantic region toward the Indus before Abbasid forces overthrew it in 750. What was this Islamic empire called?
During the Umayyad Caliphate, which ruler commissioned the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 691, and made Arabic the language of government across the empire?

During the Great Depression, a municipality in Tyrol issued local notes that lost value unless holders periodically bought stamps, helping fund public works. What is the name of this 1932 Austrian currency initiative?

In the Wörgl Experiment, holders of local notes had to pay for a stamp periodically to prevent the notes from losing value. What is the economic term for this intentional depreciation, designed to encourage circulation?

Which Indigenous people of the Great Plains are also known historically as the Teton and, together with the Dakota, form the Sioux peoples? Their traditions include the spider-shaped trickster figure Iktomi.
In Lakota tradition, which trickster figure is commonly associated with the form of a spider and with a tale about the origin of protective hoops woven with nets for children?
A Spanish conquistador entered the Andes during the civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar, then captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532. He later founded Lima in 1535; who was he?

In November 1532, Francisco Pizarro’s Spanish force captured Atahualpa at this city in northern Peru, after the ruler arrived following his victory in the Inca succession war. What city was the site of the capture?

On 28 October 312 CE, Constantine defeated Maxentius near Rome in a clash that secured his control of the empire’s western territories. The defeated rival drowned while retreating across the Tiber, and later Christian accounts linked the campaign to a divine sign; what was this battle?

In later Christian traditions about the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, which bishop and historian supplied the elaborate account of Constantine seeing a cross of light above the sun and hearing the words “By this, conquer”? He recorded the story in his *Life of Constantine*, whereas Lactantius described a dream before the battle.

In January 1917, Germany sent a coded diplomatic message proposing an alliance with Mexico if the United States entered the war, and offering support for Mexico to recover Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. British Room 40 intercepted and deciphered it; what message’s disclosure helped turn American opinion against Germany?

The Zimmermann Telegram proposed that Mexico join Germany if the United States entered the war, and named Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona as territories Mexico might seek to recover. Which Mexican president rejected the proposal after evaluating it?

Which mid-eighteenth-century European conflict began after Charles VI’s death prompted challenges to Maria Theresa’s inheritance of the Habsburg lands, drew Prussia into conflict with Austria, and concluded in 1748?
In the War of the Austrian Succession, which 1748 peace agreement ended the fighting, recognized Maria Theresa’s rule, and allowed Prussia to retain Silesia?

This American automaker was founded in 1903 by its namesake industrialist and several partners; it introduced the Model T in 1908. In 1913, its Highland Park plant began using a moving assembly line to build automobiles more quickly. Which automaker is it?
In the late 1920s, Ford Motor Company established a settlement along Brazil’s Tapajós River to grow rubber for automobile tires and reduce reliance on outside suppliers. What was this project called?

In English-language histories of Thailand, what regnal designation is followed by a Roman numeral to distinguish Chakri monarchs? The sequence begins with the king who founded the dynasty and established Bangkok as the capital in 1782, and includes Bhumibol Adulyadej as number IX.
In the Rama sequence of Chakri kings, which monarch ruled Siam from 1851 to 1868 as number IV, after spending years as a Buddhist monk before his accession?

A Joseon naval commander during the Japanese invasions of Korea in the 1590s, he became renowned for defeating Japanese fleets despite facing overwhelming odds. His fleet included armored “turtle ships,” and he won a major victory at Hansan Island. Who was this commander?

In 1597, Yi Sun-sin returned to command and led a Joseon force of just 13 warships against a much larger Japanese fleet, using powerful tidal currents to secure a celebrated naval victory. What battle was this?
Established in 1912, this political organization became a leading liberation movement opposing apartheid and later won the first multiracial election held in the country in 1994. What is its name?
During the years when the African National Congress was banned in South Africa, this leader headed the movement from exile as its president from 1967 to 1991. Who was he?

Which decisive engagement of 208–209 CE took place along the Yangtze River, where forces allied under Sun Quan and Liu Bei used a fire attack to defeat a much larger invading army and halt its advance south?
During the Battle of the Red Cliffs, which northern warlord commanded the much larger force defeated by the alliance of Sun Quan and Liu Bei as he sought to bring the south under his control?

This kingdom lies in northwestern Africa and has coastlines on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. France established a protectorate over much of it in 1912, and it regained independence in 1956; what is the country?

Morocco and the United States signed this agreement in 1786, making it a foundational document in their diplomatic relations. Its title names the two principles it established between the countries; what is it called?

What name is given to the decades-long period of political repression, arrests, and executions under martial law in Taiwan, chiefly after the Kuomintang government retreated there in 1949? It remains a major episode of state repression in modern Taiwanese history.

The White Terror unfolded under a Kuomintang government that imposed martial law on Taiwan after losing the Chinese Civil War. Which Nationalist leader relocated the Republic of China government to the island in 1949 and remained its dominant ruler until his death in 1975?
Which Norman duke defeated Harold Godwinson near Hastings on 14 October 1066, then secured the English crown with a coronation at Westminster Abbey that Christmas?
During William the Conqueror’s reign, royal commissioners compiled a landmark survey of English landholdings, wealth, and resources. What was the survey, completed in 1086, called?

Ancient depictions show this light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle in settings ranging from Egyptian warfare to royal ceremony and racing. Egyptian war crews could pair a driver with a warrior, while some other examples were too light for battle. What is this vehicle called?
In Athens, four-horse races using chariots formed part of an athletic festival held in honor of Athena, alongside athletic contests and ceremonial processions. What was this festival called?

In the Andes, Inca administrators used a device made from a main cord and hanging strands to record census totals, storehouse inventories, and labor obligations. Knots and colors on its cords conveyed information. What was this recording system called?

In the Inca road network, specially trained relay runners carried quipu records and verbal messages between way stations, helping information travel across the empire. What were these couriers called?

This ninth Mexica emperor ruled from about 1502 until 1520, when Spanish forces led by Hernán Cortés arrived in the region. Who was the ruler whose reign coincided with the opening of the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire?
During Moctezuma II’s reign, this Spanish conquistador led an expedition into central Mexico, seized Tenochtitlan, and took the emperor captive. Who was he?

After Moctezuma II’s death, Spanish forces attempted to escape Tenochtitlan under cover of darkness, and many soldiers were killed during their flight across the city’s causeways. What is this retreat commonly called?

In Canada during the First World War, dwindling voluntary enlistment led the federal government to impose compulsory military service for overseas duty. The dispute became the central issue of the December 1917 election and exposed especially sharp divisions between many English-speaking supporters and French-speaking opponents in Quebec; what event was this?
During the Canadian Conscription Crisis of 1917, what federal law passed in late August made men aged 20 to 45 liable for compulsory enlistment if called?
In Mexico, this communal landholding system leaves ownership of land with the state while granting peasants rights to use it. What is this system called?
In Mexico’s 1917 Constitution, which numbered provision gave the state authority to redistribute land and provided a legal foundation for the ejido system?

From 1936 to 1939, Spain’s Republican government fought Nationalist forces led by a general who received support from Hitler’s Germany and Mussolini’s Italy. The conflict ended with a Nationalist victory and the establishment of Franco’s dictatorship; by what name is this war known?

During the Spanish Civil War, German Condor Legion aircraft and Italian aviation units attacked a Basque town in Republican-held territory on April 26, 1937, during its market day. What was the name of the town whose destruction became a major symbol of attacks on civilians?

What name is given to the armed struggle led by Fidel Castro and the Twenty-sixth of July Movement that culminated in the overthrow of Fulgencio Batista in 1959? It transformed Cuba’s government and became a defining episode of Cold War history.
During the Cuban Revolution, which Cuban ruler fled the country on December 31, 1958, after his forces lost control? His dictatorship had begun with a military coup in 1952.

From June 1975 to March 1977, India’s prime minister invoked extraordinary constitutional powers amid claims of internal instability, leading to newspaper censorship, detention of political opponents, suspension of civil liberties, and coercive sterilization campaigns. What period in Indian history is described?
Following the Emergency, this Indian government inquiry examined allegations of excesses, including unlawful detentions and other abuses of power. What was it called?
Built by ancient Egyptians as royal funerary monuments and by Mesoamerican societies for ceremonial purposes, these monumental structures have sloping or stepped sides. What are they called?
Among the pyramids at Giza, one is the largest of the three principal royal monuments in the necropolis. Which pharaoh was it built for?

The earliest examples are associated with Lydia and were struck from a naturally occurring metal alloy, and the practice later spread to city-states and empires around the Mediterranean. What broad class of artifacts served as minted metal currency in these societies?
Among ancient coins, what naturally occurring mixture of gold and silver was used for early Lydian issues before Croesus established separate standards for the two metals?

Proclaimed by David Ben-Gurion on May 14, 1948, this eastern Mediterranean state was admitted to the United Nations the following year. The war that followed its establishment ended in armistice agreements rather than a comprehensive peace treaty. What country is it?

In 1947, as Britain prepared to end its mandate over Palestine, which UN proposal recommended separate Jewish and Arab states and proposed an international regime for Jerusalem, ahead of Israel’s declaration the following year?
He took the Swedish throne in 1697 at age fifteen and ruled during the Great Northern War. His 1718 campaign in Norway ended when he was killed while besieging a fortress; who was this monarch?
In 1700, Charles XII led Swedish forces against a much larger Russian army near an Estonian town and won a celebrated early victory in the Great Northern War. What battle was this?

During Charles XII’s 1709 campaign in Russia, a wound left him unable to command actively as Swedish forces suffered a decisive defeat. What battle was followed by the Swedish surrender at Perevolochna?

Which historic English legislature developed from medieval royal councils and assemblies, eventually taking a two-house form with the Lords and Commons and helping shape the legislature of the United Kingdom?
During the Second Barons’ War, which English nobleman summoned the 1265 Parliament of England, bringing borough representatives into an assembly that also included knights of the shires?

Which Hungarian communist leader became head of government after Soviet forces suppressed the 1956 uprising and then dominated the country’s politics for decades? His comparatively permissive economic policies later acquired a nickname drawn from a popular Hungarian stew.

János Kádár’s rise followed a revolt that began with demonstrations in Budapest in October 1956 and was ultimately defeated by Soviet military intervention. What is the name commonly given to this uprising?

A Venezuelan opposition legislator became president of the National Assembly in January 2019, as Nicolás Maduro began a disputed second term. Which politician invoked constitutional succession procedures and declared himself interim president during the crisis?
In 2019, Juan Guaidó called for a nationwide campaign to end Nicolás Maduro’s rule, which culminated in an unsuccessful uprising attempt on April 30. What was the campaign called?

This Portuguese navigator commanded the fleet that departed from Lisbon in 1497, rounded southern Africa, and reached India the following year on the first recorded European sea voyage along that route. He later became Count of Vidigueira and was appointed viceroy in 1524.

Vasco da Gama’s fleet reached this Malabar Coast port in 1498 after sailing around Africa. Its ruler, the Zamorin, was the intended partner in King Manuel I’s effort to establish Portuguese trade and diplomatic ties in India.

In 1982, Argentina landed forces on islands it called the Islas Malvinas, prompting the United Kingdom to send a naval task force. The 74-day conflict ended when Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June; what is this war commonly called?

During the Falklands War, British troops advanced toward this settlement on East Falkland, where Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982. The surrender ended the fighting and restored British administration; what settlement was the site?

After marrying Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469, she became queen of the largest Iberian crown in 1474. Her forces completed the conquest of Granada in 1492, the same year her court backed Christopher Columbus’s first Atlantic voyage; who was this monarch?
During Isabella I of Castile’s reign, this 1492 royal edict ordered Jews in the monarchs’ realms to convert to Christianity or leave. What was the name of this edict?

Between 1845 and 1852, a disease repeatedly destroyed Ireland’s potato crop, a staple food for many poor rural families. The resulting hunger, disease, and mass emigration transformed the island’s population; what is this catastrophe commonly called?

During the Great Famine, this government body gathered appeals for assistance and coordinated aid in Ireland. Its surviving records include “Distress Papers” that document urgent local needs; what was the body called?

Which Dutch navigator in the service of the Dutch East India Company led a 1642 voyage that made the first recorded European sighting of New Zealand? He also charted the coast of the island then known to Europeans as Van Diemen’s Land.

In 1642, Abel Tasman’s expedition made the first recorded European sighting of this island country and anchored near present-day Golden Bay, where a violent encounter with Māori occurred. Its capital today is Wellington.

This nomadic people of the Eurasian steppe formed a powerful empire under a leader who united them in the late second century BCE. Their name is sometimes linked linguistically to the Huns. What people are they?

Chinese histories credit this Xiongnu leader with training his men to shoot at any target he indicated using whistling arrows. He seized power around 209 BCE by overthrowing his father, Touman, and taking the supreme title. Who was he?

Heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne and nephew of its reigning emperor, he was assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. His death precipitated the July Crisis that led to World War I. Who was he?
Franz Ferdinand married this Bohemian aristocrat and lady-in-waiting in a morganatic union. Their children were excluded from succession to the Habsburg throne. Who was she?

This Portuguese navigator sailed from Lisbon in 1487 with three ships in search of a sea passage toward Asia. In 1488, his fleet rounded Africa’s southern end, but he turned back without reaching India. Who was he?
Bartolomeu Dias called the southern African landmark his fleet rounded the “Cape of Storms.” What name did King João II later give it?

A former comedian and co-founder of Kvartal 95, he played a fictional Ukrainian president in a television series before winning the real presidency in 2019. Who is this leader who remained in Kyiv after Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022?

The political rise of Volodymyr Zelenskyy echoed his role in this Ukrainian television comedy, in which he played Vasyl Holoborodko, a teacher whose anti-corruption rant unexpectedly propelled him to the presidency. What is the series’ title, which later lent its name to his political party?

In 2019, Volodymyr Zelenskyy defeated this incumbent Ukrainian president in the runoff, winning roughly 73 percent of the vote to his opponent’s 24 percent. Name the confectionery magnate who had held office since 2014.

This Chinese imperial dynasty ruled from 618 to 907 CE, succeeding the Sui and governing from a cosmopolitan capital that attracted merchants, religious travelers, and envoys from across Asia. Its cultural legacy is especially associated with poets Li Bai and Du Fu; what dynasty was it?
Under the Tang dynasty, what system of competitive tests offered educated men a route into government service beyond inherited aristocratic networks?

On 14 July 1789 in Paris, a crowd that had obtained firearms elsewhere in the city attacked a royal fortress to seize its stored gunpowder. The defenders surrendered, seven prisoners were freed, and the event became a symbol of resistance to arbitrary royal power. What event was this?
The Storming of the Bastille took place in 1789, but France’s 14 July commemoration also recalls a separate gathering held on the same date the following year. What was that 1790 event called?

After defeating the last rival Warring States in 221 BCE, this short-lived regime created China’s first centralized empire and standardized writing, currency, weights, and measures. What ruling house took its name from the state of its founder, Ying Zheng, who adopted the title First Emperor?
The Qin dynasty replaced hereditary feudal domains with centrally administered territorial units, whose officials answered to the imperial government. What were these divisions called?

Founded in 1949 under a new constitutional framework, this democratic state aligned with Western institutions during the Cold War. Under Konrad Adenauer, it experienced the economic boom known as the Wirtschaftswunder; what was its common name before reunification in 1990?

In West Germany, Willy Brandt pursued a policy intended to ease tensions and improve relations with the GDR and other Eastern European states while the country remained aligned with the West. What was this policy called?

This medieval West African power grew from a Mandinka kingdom in the Manding region after its forces defeated the Sosso around 1235. Its rulers bore the title mansa, and its best-known sovereign made a celebrated pilgrimage to Mecca.

The Mali Empire rose to prominence after this Mandinka leader defeated the Sosso ruler Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina around 1235. He is remembered as the empire’s founder and as the subject of a major West African epic.

This ruler of the Mali Empire traveled to Mecca between 1324 and 1326, and his distribution of gold during the journey contributed to inflation in Egypt. He took power around 1312 and became renowned for the scale of his wealth.

The Mali Empire is associated with this charter, identified in historical accounts as its constitution. Its name refers to a gathering place in the Manding region, where traditions connected with Sundiata’s rule were preserved.

Which sovereign country occupies the continent’s southern tip, has nine provinces, and completely surrounds the kingdom of Lesotho? Its national functions are divided among Pretoria, Cape Town, and Bloemfontein.
In South Africa, this anti-apartheid leader became the country’s first Black president after the 1994 nonracial democratic elections and was inaugurated on 10 May that year. Who was he?

Fought near Basra in 656 CE after Caliph Uthman’s killing, this clash pitted the forces of the newly installed caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib against a coalition associated with Aisha, Talha, and al-Zubayr. What is this early conflict of the First Fitna called?
During the Battle of the Camel, the opposing coalition was associated with this wife of Muhammad, who was present on a camel at the center of the fighting. Which figure is described?

Which 16th-century Dominican friar became Bishop of Chiapas and was named the first Protector of the Indians by the Spanish crown? His account of Spanish abuses against Indigenous peoples helped make him a prominent advocate for their protection.
Bartolomé de las Casas published this 1552 polemic describing Spanish atrocities in the Americas and arguing against colonial abuses. What is the title of this work?
answer: A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies

question: This Florentine dynasty rose from merchant and banking wealth to dominate the city’s politics during the fifteenth century, initially exercising power without a hereditary title. Its later rulers became dukes and grand dukes, while its patronage helped make Florence a center of Renaissance art and humanist learning. What family was it?

The Medici family commissioned this Florentine complex under Cosimo I in the sixteenth century to house government offices. It later became one of the world’s best-known art museums, with collections closely tied to the family’s legacy. What is it?
During World War I, what was the name of the failed 1915–1916 Allied operation to force the Dardanelles and seize a peninsula from the Ottoman Empire?
The Gallipoli campaign’s Allied landings began on April 25, 1915, a date commemorated annually in Australia and New Zealand as what day of remembrance for their service personnel?
After disputes over citizenship and political rights, Rome’s Italian allies rose in revolt from 91 to 87 BC. What is the conventional name for this conflict?

During the Social War, which 89 BC law allowed residents of allied Italian communities to gain Roman citizenship if they registered with a praetor within 60 days? The measure is named for the two tribunes who proposed it.

Which seventeenth-century Ming loyalist crossed to Taiwan during the Ming–Qing transition, besieged Dutch East India Company positions near present-day Tainan in 1661, and established a Ming-loyalist government there after the Dutch surrendered?
During Koxinga’s 1661 campaign against Dutch rule in Taiwan, what Dutch East India Company stronghold near present-day Tainan became the focal point of the siege before the Dutch surrendered in 1662?

Established in 1397, this political arrangement placed Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a shared monarch, with Denmark holding the leading role. It ended in 1523 when Sweden broke away. What was this union called?
Within the Kalmar Union, which Danish-born ruler was the daughter of Valdemar IV and arranged for her adopted son, Eric of Pomerania, to be crowned at Kalmar in 1397?

This son of Xanthippus led Athens through much of its fifth-century Golden Age and was repeatedly elected strategos. Thucydides portrays him delivering a celebrated address honoring those killed early in the Peloponnesian War. Who was this Athenian statesman?

The account of Pericles’ address early in the Peloponnesian War appears in this Athenian historian’s work. An eyewitness to the conflict, he was exiled after failing to prevent the Spartan capture of Amphipolis. Who was he?

France observes this national holiday each July 14, a date tied to a crowd’s 1789 seizure of a Paris fortress that had become a symbol of royal authority. The holiday was formally established in 1880; what is its common English name?
Bastille Day also evokes a July 14, 1790 gathering on the Champ de Mars in Paris, held on the first anniversary of the fortress’s fall to celebrate national unity. What was this event called?
This Ayyubid ruler recaptured Jerusalem in October 1187, helping prompt the Third Crusade. He later faced Richard I’s forces, and the two leaders reached an agreement in 1192. Who was this ruler?
During the Third Crusade, Richard I campaigned against Saladin, but a 1192 agreement left this city under Saladin’s control while allowing European pilgrims access. What city was it?

What is the name for a form of protest in which a person deliberately sets their own body on fire? It became internationally associated with Mohamed Bouazizi’s 2010 act in Tunisia and a 1963 protest by a Vietnamese Buddhist monk in Saigon.

During the 1963 Buddhist crisis in South Vietnam, this monk performed a self-immolation at a Saigon intersection to protest the Diem government’s repression of Buddhists. Photographs of his act drew worldwide attention. Who was he?

He is the son of a Canadian prime minister who served in two separate periods, and he became Canada’s head of government after his Liberal Party won the 2015 federal election. He led the country during the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 trucker protests; identify this politician.

In February 2022, Justin Trudeau’s government invoked this 1988 federal law for the first time, granting temporary powers to address blockades associated with the Freedom Convoy. What was the name of this statute?

Established in April 1992 by Serbia and Montenegro after the breakup of the communist-era Yugoslav federation, this state was targeted by NATO’s 1999 air campaign during the Kosovo War. What was the name of this state?
During the Kosovo War, which military alliance conducted a 78-day air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1999? The bombing began on March 24 and ended on June 10.

This partisan leader headed Yugoslavia’s postwar communist federation and broke with Stalin in 1948, keeping the country outside Moscow’s control. His government also promoted workers’ self-management. Who was this leader?

Josip Broz Tito joined India’s Jawaharlal Nehru and Egypt’s Gamal Abdel Nasser in promoting an international grouping for countries that sought cooperation outside either Cold War superpower bloc. What movement did they help establish?

Between 1941 and 1945, Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered about six million European Jews, following years of escalating persecution. What is the commonly used name for this genocide?
In the history of the Holocaust, what January 1942 meeting brought senior Nazi officials together at a lakeside villa in Berlin to discuss the coordination of the so-called “Final Solution”?

During the Holocaust, what Nazi camp complex in occupied Poland was the largest of its kind and included mass-killing facilities at a site near Oświęcim? Deportees from across Europe were transported there, and many were murdered in gas chambers.

During the Holocaust, what 1943 revolt began when Jewish fighters in German-occupied Poland resisted the Nazis’ attempt to liquidate the Jewish quarter of the country’s capital? The fighters held out for nearly a month before German forces suppressed the resistance.
Which German-Jewish political theorist reported on Adolf Eichmann’s 1961 trial in Jerusalem and popularized the phrase “the banality of evil” in a book examining the Holocaust and its perpetrators?

This bicameral legislature consists of the House of Commons and the House of Lords, and meets at the Palace of Westminster in London. Its Conservative members held a no-confidence vote on Boris Johnson in June 2022. What is its natural name?

During the political crisis unfolding around the Parliament of the United Kingdom, this Chancellor of the Exchequer resigned from Boris Johnson’s cabinet in July 2022, shortly before Johnson announced he would step down. He later succeeded Liz Truss as prime minister in October 2022. Who was he?

Representatives from 50 countries signed this postwar organization’s founding charter in San Francisco on June 26, 1945, and the charter entered into force that October. Its Security Council has five permanent members with veto power. What organization is this?
The United Nations maintains its headquarters on First Avenue in Manhattan, where the General Assembly and Security Council meet. What city is home to this headquarters?

After Charles X was overthrown in the 1830 July Revolution, this member of the House of Orléans became France’s constitutional monarch and was often called the “Citizen King.” He abdicated during the revolution of 1848; who was he?

During Louis Philippe I’s rule, what name is given to the French political regime established after the 1830 revolution, in which the king governed under a charter and voting rights were restricted by property qualifications? It ended with the revolution of 1848.

Centered in northern Mesopotamia, this first-millennium BCE power grew from the city of Ashur and eventually extended its control as far as Egypt. A Babylonian-Median coalition sacked its capital, Nineveh, in 612 BCE. What empire was it?

At Nineveh, during the height of the Assyrian Empire, this ruler assembled a major collection of cuneiform tablets. The collection became one of the ancient world’s most important libraries. Who was this king?
In 1976, Israeli forces carried out a daring raid at an airport to rescue more than 100 hostages taken from Air France Flight 139. What was the name of this military operation?
Operation Entebbe took place at an airport near Kampala, and the hostage-takers had the backing of the country’s ruler, Idi Amin. Which country was the site of the raid?

This name refers to related Bantu-speaking communities, rather than one uniform culture, centered chiefly in present-day Zimbabwe and neighboring regions. Their ancestors built Great Zimbabwe and established the later Kingdom of Mutapa; what is this ethnolinguistic group called?

Shona heritage includes a major stone-built center that flourished chiefly between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Its distinct sections include the Hill Ruins, a massive circular stone enclosure, and the Valley Ruins, and excavations uncovered imported glass beads and porcelain; what is the name of this site?

During the 1950s, fighters associated with the Kenya Land and Freedom Army waged an armed anti-colonial campaign against British rule, drawing especially from Gikuyu, Embu, and Meru communities. What was this campaign called?
A prominent forest fighter in the Mau Mau uprising was captured in 1956, weakening organized resistance. Who was he?

Which name is given to the recurring seventeenth-century conflicts across northeastern North America in which the Haudenosaunee Five Nations fought neighboring Indigenous nations and French allies amid competition over the fur trade, diplomacy, and regional influence?

During the Beaver Wars, attacks in the late 1640s shattered the communities of this Indigenous people in Huronia, and many survivors fled or joined other nations. Which people, also known as the Huron in many historical sources, were displaced from that homeland?

Approved by France in May 1915, this steel piece of protective headgear was designed by a quartermaster after French troops suffered many head wounds. Its shell had a conspicuous ridge running along the crown; what was this French World War I item called?
The Adrian helmet had a shell assembled from several pieces, with a raised feature running along its crown. What was this distinctive feature called?

This familiar ionic seasoning occurs naturally as halite. Before refrigeration, its role in preserving meat and fish made it a valuable commodity in trans-Saharan trade. What is its standard chemical name?

During the Mali Empire’s trans-Saharan trade in sodium chloride, caravans carried salt blocks from this Saharan mining center toward Timbuktu. The settlement later became associated with salt production under the Songhai Empire. What was this center called?
Which Brazilian statute, promulgated on May 13, 1888, ended legal slavery throughout the country? It was enacted during the regency of the heir to Dom Pedro II.
The Golden Law was signed on May 13, 1888, by Brazil’s regent while Dom Pedro II was abroad. The regent was his eldest daughter and heir to the throne; who signed it?
This British Conservative politician led her party from 1975 and became the first woman to serve as prime minister of the United Kingdom in 1979. What is her name?
After Margaret Thatcher resigned as prime minister and Conservative leader in 1990 following a leadership challenge, which politician succeeded her as prime minister?

During Margaret Thatcher’s premiership, Argentina occupied a British-administered South Atlantic archipelago in 1982, prompting a conflict that ended with British forces retaking the islands after about ten weeks. What was this conflict called?

Six British kings shared this regnal name, beginning with the Hanoverian ruler who arrived in Britain in 1714 and ending with the wartime monarch whose broadcasts helped sustain public morale. A third bearer reigned during the American Revolution and the loss of Britain’s mainland colonies in North America. What was the name?

Within the history of the British monarchs named George, which minister became the leading figure in government under the first two Hanoverian kings? He managed the political fallout of the South Sea Bubble and is widely regarded as Britain’s first prime minister.

In 9 CE, a Germanic coalition led by a former Roman military ally ambushed and destroyed three legions commanded by Publius Quinctilius Varus. What battle disrupted Rome’s efforts to extend its control east of the Rhine?
The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest was led by a Cheruscan noble who had served in the Roman army and used his knowledge of Roman tactics to coordinate the Germanic forces. What was his name?

This Genoese-born mariner sailed for the Spanish monarchs Isabella I and Ferdinand II, leaving Palos in August 1492 with three ships. Seeking a westward route to the East Indies, he reached an island in the Bahamas on October 12. Who was he?

On Christopher Columbus’s first transatlantic expedition, this largest of his three vessels ran aground off Hispaniola on Christmas Day in 1492. Its salvaged timbers were used to build La Navidad, the settlement left behind by the expedition. What was the ship’s name?

The voyages of Christopher Columbus helped set in motion this historical process, the large-scale movement of crops, animals, people, diseases, technology, and ideas between the Americas and the Old World. What is this process called?

This Anglo-Irish polar explorer led the Nimrod expedition, whose party reached a record southern latitude of 88°23′ in 1909. He later commanded the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, during which his ship Endurance was trapped and crushed by Antarctic ice.

In 1916, Ernest Shackleton and five companions used this small lifeboat to sail from Elephant Island to South Georgia in search of help. After reaching the island, Shackleton, Frank Worsley, and Tom Crean crossed its mountains to reach a whaling station.

Which Central European country has Warsaw as its capital and was partitioned by Russia, Prussia, and Austria in the late eighteenth century, disappearing as an independent state until its restoration in 1918?
Adopted on May 3, 1791, by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, this reform charter sought to strengthen government and later became a lasting symbol of self-rule in Poland. What is it called?

An Argentine Marxist who trained as a physician, he became a leading commander alongside Fidel Castro in the Cuban Revolution and later led a guerrilla campaign in Bolivia. Captured there in 1967, he was executed by Bolivian forces; who was he?

In 1960, this Cuban photographer captured the iconic beret-and-star portrait of Che Guevara at a Havana memorial for victims of the La Coubre explosion. The image, later titled *Guerrillero Heroico*, became one of the most reproduced political portraits in history; who took it?

This Mongol commander served Genghis Khan and later Ögedei, helping direct the empire’s westward campaigns into the Rus’ principalities and Central Europe. Earlier, alongside Jebe, he led the 1223 campaign that defeated a Rus’-Cuman coalition at the Kalka River; who was this general?

In 1241, Subutai’s Mongol forces used coordinated movements and crossings of the Sajó River to defeat the army of Hungary’s King Béla IV. What was the name of this battle, associated with a nearby settlement?

Which Roman ruling house was established in 69 CE by the commander who took power after the Year of the Four Emperors, and then passed from its founder to his sons Titus and Domitian? Its three emperors ruled in succession until the last was killed in 96 CE.

Among the rulers of the Flavian dynasty, which emperor was Vespasian’s younger son and succeeded his brother Titus? His reign ended with his assassination in 96 CE, after which the Senate condemned his memory.

This nineteenth-century German archaeologist excavated Hisarlik, Mycenae, and Tiryns. His controversial removal of artifacts he called Priam’s Treasure from Hisarlik remains central to debates about his methods. Who was he?
Heinrich Schliemann excavated this mound in northwestern Anatolia, where successive settlement layers are associated with the ancient city of Troy. What is the name of the archaeological site?

What modern collective name is used for several groups recorded in Egyptian accounts of conflicts under Merenptah and Ramesses III near the end of the Bronze Age? Their origins and relationships remain uncertain, and the accounts describe movement and fighting by both land and sea.
Which mortuary temple complex on Thebes’s west bank preserves Ramesses III’s inscriptions and reliefs depicting battles against the Sea Peoples, including fighting near the Nile Delta?
Which Habsburg monarch ruled from 1621 to 1665, supported Diego Velázquez as a court painter, and led his kingdom during its involvement in the Thirty Years’ War?

In a 1656 court painting associated with Philip IV of Spain, the Infanta Margarita stands among attendants while the king and Queen Mariana appear reflected in a mirror. What is the title of this work by Diego Velázquez?
At this 1690 engagement in Ireland, William III’s forces defeated those of James II during the Williamite War. Its outcome is commemorated by the Twelfth of July.

At the Battle of the Boyne, this veteran Huguenot commander in William III’s army was killed while leading troops across the river, despite advising against the crossing. By what title is he commonly known?

After George VI died on 6 February 1952, his daughter learned she had become sovereign while visiting Kenya. Her coronation was televised from Westminster Abbey in 1953, and her reign lasted more than seventy years, ending with her death in 2022. Who was she?
answer: Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom

question: Elizabeth II’s coronation on 2 June 1953 took place at this London Gothic church, where British coronations have been held since William the Conqueror’s ceremony in 1066. What church was the venue?

This Ottoman ruler led the 1453 conquest of the Byzantine capital and became known by an epithet meaning “the Conqueror.” Before the siege, he commissioned Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosporus to help control access to the city. Who was he?

In the campaign led by Mehmed II in 1453, this Byzantine capital fell after its Theodosian defenses were breached, bringing the Byzantine Empire to an end. The victors later converted Hagia Sophia there into a mosque; what city was captured?

During the First World War, George V replaced the German-sounding Saxe-Coburg-Gotha designation with a new dynastic name by royal proclamation in 1917. What is the name of the reigning royal dynasty of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms?
The House of Windsor takes its name from this Berkshire royal residence, located west of London and among the oldest continuously occupied royal residences in Europe. Which place is it?

This Swedish queen inherited the throne as a child after her father, Gustavus Adolphus, died at the Battle of Lützen. She later abdicated, converted to Catholicism, and lived at the court of Pope Alexander VII in Rome; who was she?

Christina of Sweden invited this French philosopher and mathematician to Stockholm, where he tutored her before dying in 1650. He is known for the phrase “Cogito, ergo sum” and the work *Meditations on First Philosophy*; who was he?
This South Asian diamond was taken to Britain after the annexation of Punjab in 1849 and presented to Queen Victoria. Recut in 1852, it became part of the British Crown Jewels; what is its name?

The Koh-i-Noor was ceded to Britain by this deposed young ruler in the settlement following the Second Anglo-Sikh War. He was the last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire and later lived in Britain; who was he?

What term describes an unidentified service member whose burial represents a nation’s war dead whose names or remains could not be recovered? The individual’s anonymity allows the grave to serve as a shared place of mourning.
Britain’s Unknown Soldier, known as the Unknown Warrior, was buried after the First World War in which London church? The church is also the traditional site of British coronations.
Born in Smyrna in 1626, this Jewish mystic was proclaimed the Messiah by his followers and converted to Islam in 1666 after appearing before Ottoman Sultan Mehmed IV. Who was he?

In 1665, this Jewish mystic became Sabbatai Zevi’s chief prophetic advocate, issuing proclamations and letters that helped spread the messianic claim through Jewish communities. By what name is this figure known?

Built chiefly between the world wars, this French system combined concrete forts, gun positions, and underground facilities along the eastern frontier. It was designed to hold a prepared defensive border, but did not form an unbroken shield around France. What was this system called?
In May 1940, German forces bypassed the strongest defenses of the Maginot Line by advancing through a heavily wooded region and toward Sedan. What was this region?

After Haiti annulled its disputed 2015 presidential election, this candidate won the 2016 rerun and took office in February 2017. A former agricultural entrepreneur associated with banana production, he was assassinated at his residence on July 7, 2021. Who was he?

During Jovenel Moïse’s presidency, this Caribbean nation experienced escalating political conflict. Its capital is Port-au-Prince, and it shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic; what is the nation?

This New Zealand mountaineer and explorer joined Tenzing Norgay on the first documented ascent of Mount Everest in 1953. He later led expeditions to the South Pole and helped establish schools and hospitals in Nepal. Who was he?
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first documented ascent of this mountain on 29 May 1953. It is the world’s highest mountain above sea level. Which mountain is it?

This Germanic people divided into western and eastern branches, later known as the Visigoths and Ostrogoths. Their history includes the sack of Rome in 410 CE and a battle against the Huns at the Catalaunian Plains. What people are described?
Which king led the Goths in the sack of Rome in 410 CE? His forces captured the city after entering Italy, marking the first sack of Rome in nearly eight centuries.

In 1877, former samurai from Kagoshima rose against the new Meiji government under a leader who had once helped establish it. After marching toward Kumamoto, the rebels were defeated at Shiroyama in September; what was this uprising called?

The Satsuma Rebellion was led by a former samurai who had helped overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate and establish the Meiji government, but later became estranged from its leaders. What was the name of this Kagoshima-born leader?

This authoritarian Haitian family regime began after its founder won the presidency in 1957, relied on a feared militia to intimidate opponents, and passed power from father to son in 1971 before ending in 1986. What name is given to this two-generation ruling order?

During the Duvalier dynasty, François Duvalier’s government relied on a paramilitary force that terrorized political opponents and was officially styled the Volunteers of National Security. What was this force commonly known as?
In ancient Greek city-states, what was the name for a heavily equipped foot soldier who carried a thrusting spear and a large round shield, and commonly wore a helmet, body armor, and shin guards?
A hoplite relied on coordination with nearby soldiers as well as on his own armor. What close-order formation arranged these infantrymen with overlapping shields to protect one another?

Linguists infer this hypothetical prehistoric population from shared vocabulary and grammar across languages such as Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, and Germanic languages, rather than from surviving contemporary records. Which population is considered the common linguistic ancestor of the peoples speaking those related languages?

In the 19th century, which German linguist was among the earliest to reconstruct the language of the Proto-Indo-Europeans using comparative philology? He also composed a short fable in the reconstructed language, often used to demonstrate its reconstructed forms.

This transcontinental country spans Eastern Europe and northern Asia, with Moscow as its capital and territory extending from plains west of the Ural Mountains across Siberian forests and tundra. What country is it?

During the 1917 upheaval in Russia, this last tsar of the Romanov dynasty abdicated, ending centuries of imperial rule. He and his family were killed in Yekaterinburg the following year. Which ruler was he?

A Spanish princess, she was the youngest daughter of Ferdinand II and Isabella I and first married Arthur, Prince of Wales. After his death, she wed his younger brother, becoming his queen consort in 1509; their only child to survive infancy later ruled as Mary I. Who was she?

In 1513, Catherine of Aragon served as regent while Henry VIII campaigned in France and England faced an invasion from Scotland. What battle near Branxton in Northumberland ended with the death of Scottish king James IV?

This Nordic kingdom occupies much of the eastern Scandinavian Peninsula, and its capital and largest city is Stockholm. Its history includes the Vasa dynasty and an empire that once controlled extensive territory around the Baltic Sea. What is the kingdom’s name?

Sweden entered this conflict in 1630 under Gustavus Adolphus, bringing a major Protestant power into the struggle. Beginning in 1618 in the Holy Roman Empire, the war ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

This Vasa monarch succeeded her father, Gustavus Adolphus, as a child and later invited René Descartes to Stockholm. She abdicated in 1654, converted to Catholicism, and settled in Rome; what was her name?
In 1397, Sweden joined this political union with Denmark and Norway, associated with Queen Margaret I. Sweden’s membership ended in 1523 under Gustav Vasa; what was the union called?

This Scandinavian constitutional monarchy occupies the Jutland Peninsula and numerous islands, including Zealand, where its capital is located. Its wider kingdom also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands. What country is it?
Denmark’s national legislature is a single-chamber parliament, separate from the political institutions of Greenland and the Faroe Islands. What is this parliament called?

A radical preacher of the German Reformation, he served the congregation at Allstedt and promoted a more militant vision of reform than Martin Luther. He supported the 1525 uprising in central Germany, was captured after the rebels’ defeat at Frankenhausen, and was executed later that year; who was he?

Thomas Müntzer was captured after the decisive 1525 clash in Thuringia that crushed the rebel army during the German Peasants’ War. Fought in the Kyffhäuser region, it pitted the insurgents against princely troops from Saxony and Brunswick; what battle was this?

In 2015 and 2016, this country held two postal ballots about whether to replace its national banner. Voters first ranked alternative designs, then chose between the finalist and the existing design, which ultimately remained in place. What is this pair of votes known as?

During the New Zealand flag referendums, this institution documented the postal voting procedures and official results for both ballots. Its published figures show that the existing flag received 56.6% of valid votes in the binding 2016 choice. Which institution was it?

After Hippias was expelled from Athens, this Alcmaeonid statesman challenged Isagoras for influence and advanced a reorganization around 508 BCE. His reforms divided citizens among ten tribes and established the Council of 500; who was he?
In the reforms of Cleisthenes, what name was given to the local civic units in which Athenian citizens were registered, weakening the old importance of descent-based groupings?
Which Julio-Claudian ruler governed Rome from AD 41 to 54, launched the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43, and later traveled there to receive the submission of part of the island?

Emperor Claudius staged a mock naval battle on this Italian lake before water was released through an outlet built to drain it, an event described by Suetonius. What lake was the site of the spectacle?

Established in 1478 after papal authorization, this tribunal system operated under Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, who exercised unusual control over the appointment of its inquisitors. Its early investigations focused especially on baptized converts suspected of secretly practicing Judaism. What was this institution called?

The Spanish Inquisition was authorized in 1478 by a papal bull issued by this pontiff, who later attempted to limit some of the monarchs’ control over the tribunals. Which pope issued that authorization?

Founded by Sun Yat-sen in 1912, this Chinese political organization launched the Northern Expedition with its National Revolutionary Army and later led the Nationalist government that retreated to Taiwan in 1949. What was the organization called?
Beginning in Guangdong in 1926, this Kuomintang-led campaign sent the National Revolutionary Army north to defeat warlord regimes and extend Nationalist rule. What was the campaign called?

In 2019, huge marches erupted over a proposed extradition measure that could have sent suspects from a Chinese special administrative region to mainland China. Demonstrators later pressed for police accountability and universal suffrage, and the movement continued into 2020, when Beijing imposed a national security law on the territory. What movement is described?

During the 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests, the city’s chief executive first suspended the controversial extradition bill before announcing in September 2019 that the government would withdraw it. Which official held that office?

This northern South American country has a Caribbean coastline, the Lake Maracaibo basin in its northwest, and petroleum resources that have strongly shaped its modern economy and politics. What country is it?

In 1960, after President Rómulo Betancourt survived a car-bomb attack that contemporary investigations linked to Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo, Venezuela brought the case before which inter-American diplomatic body, making it an international diplomatic crisis?

Between 1700 and 1721, an anti-Swedish coalition initially led by Russia, Denmark-Norway, and Saxony-Poland-Lithuania fought to end Sweden’s dominance around the Baltic. The conflict ended with Sweden surrendering Baltic provinces to Russia under the 1721 Treaty of Nystad; what war was it?
During the Great Northern War, Charles XII’s Swedish army met Peter I’s forces in Ukraine in 1709 and suffered a decisive defeat that shattered its invasion of Russia. What battle was this?

The Great Northern War formally ended with a 1721 peace agreement signed between Sweden and Russia in a Finnish town. Under it, Sweden ceded Estonia, Livonia, Ingria, and parts of Karelia to Russia; what was this agreement called?
