Independent coastal cities such as Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos formed a maritime trading network along the eastern Mediterranean. Their merchants spread an influential alphabet and founded settlements across the sea; what ancient people are described?
Within Phoenician civilization, which North African city began as a settlement founded by migrants from Tyre and later became a major rival of Rome?

Which radical communist movement captured Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975, and ruled Cambodia as Democratic Kampuchea until Vietnamese forces overthrew it in January 1979? Its policies included forcing city residents into rural agricultural labor.

During the Khmer Rouge’s rule of Democratic Kampuchea, which man served as both general secretary of the Communist Party of Kampuchea and prime minister? He led the regime that began after its forces took Phnom Penh in April 1975.

Unlike the repeating 260-day and 365-day cycles, this Mesoamerican system records elapsed time in place-value units from k’in through b’ak’tun. Its 13-b’ak’tun rollover in December 2012 was mistakenly presented as an apocalypse; what is this system called?
In discussions of the Maya Long Count calendar, what Gregorian date corresponds to the completion of 13.0.0.0.0, the cycle rollover that fueled the false 2012 doomsday claim?

After Feodor I died childless, his brother-in-law was elected tsar in 1598, ending the direct line of Rurikid rulers. He reigned until 1605, amid rumors—never established as fact—that he had arranged the death of Prince Dmitry. Who was this ruler?
The death of Boris Godunov in 1605 deepened a dynastic and political crisis marked by rival claimants to the throne. What period of upheaval ended when Michael Romanov was chosen tsar in 1613?

The first emperor of independent Brazil declared independence from Portugal in 1822, and his son later ruled until the monarchy fell in 1889. Both emperors used the same regnal name; what name was it?
During Pedro II’s reign, his daughter Princess Isabel acted as regent and sanctioned an 1888 Brazilian law that legally abolished slavery. By what short name is that law known?

This Swedish king ruled from 1611 until 1632 and brought his forces into the Thirty Years’ War in 1630. After his army’s victory at Breitenfeld in 1631, he was killed fighting imperial troops at Lützen the following year. Who was this monarch?
Gustavus Adolphus commissioned this Swedish warship in 1625 as part of an ambitious naval program. It sank on its maiden voyage in Stockholm harbor in 1628. What was the ship’s name?
What hereditary warrior class in Japan served regional lords, trained in swordsmanship, archery, and horsemanship, and later often held administrative posts under the Tokugawa shogunate?
What term names the ethical tradition often associated with samurai, emphasizing loyalty and martial conduct and drawing on influences from Zen Buddhism and Shinto?
Which 1868 political transformation began dismantling samurai privileges and preceded domain abolition and conscription as Japan centralized under imperial rule?

This Liberal Democratic Party politician first became Japan’s prime minister in 2006, left office the following year, and returned in 2012 for a tenure that lasted until 2020. His nearly nine years in office made him the country’s longest-serving prime minister before he was assassinated while campaigning in Nara in 2022. Who was he?

During Shinzō Abe’s second premiership, he promoted an economic strategy built around monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, and structural reforms—the measures commonly described as its “three arrows.” What was this policy package called?

In 2007, Shinzō Abe helped launch a strategic consultation joining Japan, the United States, Australia, and India; it later became a recurring Indo-Pacific forum. What is the formal name of this four-country grouping?
Shinzō Abe was delivering a campaign speech in this Japanese city when he was shot on July 8, 2022. Japan’s ancient capital is also known for Tōdai-ji Temple and its Great Buddha; what city was it?

An Argentine military officer and president, he was ousted in a 1955 coup and returned from exile to win the presidency in 1973. His second wife, Eva, became a major political figure before her death in 1952. Who was he?
After the 1955 coup, Juan Domingo Perón spent years in exile in the European country that had colonized Argentina and whose language is spoken there. What country was it?

This medieval kingdom formed on the western Iberian Peninsula, and its government dates its founding to 1143. It sponsored voyages that rounded the Cape of Good Hope and helped build an overseas trading empire; its monarchy ended in 1910. What was the kingdom called?

The Kingdom of Portugal sponsored this navigator’s voyage, which rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached Calicut in India in 1498. His expedition opened a direct sea route from Europe to the Indian Ocean. Who was the navigator?

During World War I, opposing armies on the Western Front fought from fortified positions facing one another, with exposed no-man’s-land between them. What was this military practice called, which contributed to a prolonged stalemate?

Trench warfare took hold on the Western Front after this 1914 battle in France, where an Allied victory halted the German advance toward Paris. Fought along a river northeast of the capital, it also marked the failure of Germany’s Schlieffen Plan.

He became Brazil’s ruler as a child after his father abdicated, was declared of age in 1840, and presided over the country’s participation in the War of the Triple Alliance. Which Brazilian emperor was deposed by a military coup in 1889?
During Dom Pedro II’s reign, Brazil joined Argentina and Uruguay in this devastating conflict against Paraguay, which lasted from 1864 to 1870. What was this war called?

What traditional sailing vessel is recognized by its distinctive fully battened sails and hulls divided by watertight bulkheads? It carried merchants on long-distance routes linking ports in China with those across the Indian Ocean.
Which Ming dynasty admiral commanded seven major maritime expeditions from 1405 to 1433, with fleets that included the Chinese junk and sailed from China across the Indian Ocean?

In late October 1956, student demonstrations in Budapest grew into a nationwide revolt against Soviet domination and Hungary’s communist government. Soviet forces returned in November and crushed the uprising; what was it called?

During the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, which reform-minded prime minister announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and seek neutrality, before being captured after the Soviet invasion and executed in 1958?

Beginning on 4 November 1979, revolutionary students seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran, and 52 Americans were ultimately held until 20 January 1981. What 444-day diplomatic standoff became a major crisis for President Jimmy Carter?

During the Iran hostage crisis, negotiations culminated in an agreement mediated by Algeria that settled U.S.-Iran claims and preceded the release of the remaining 52 captives on 20 January 1981. What agreement is named for the Algerian capital?
This Habsburg ruler became king of Spain in 1556 and reigned until 1598. He married Mary I of England in 1554, and later sent a major fleet against her successor, Elizabeth I.

During Philip II of Spain’s reign, this fleet sailed in 1588 as part of a plan to invade England. The invasion depended on the fleet linking up with an army in the Netherlands, but the crossing was never secured.

What collective name is given to the series of 15th-century English dynastic conflicts that pitted the rival Plantagenet houses of Lancaster and York and culminated in the establishment of the Tudor dynasty?

In the Wars of the Roses, Henry VII faced a Yorkist-backed force led by John de la Pole two years after defeating Richard III at Bosworth. At which 1487 battle was this final major Yorkist rising defeated?

During the Wars of the Roses, this younger brother of Edward IV became king in 1483 after his nephew Edward V was declared illegitimate. Henry Tudor defeated and killed him at Bosworth Field in 1485; who was he?

In ancient Sparta, citizen-class boys entered this state-controlled upbringing at a young age, training in age groups under public supervision. It emphasized endurance, discipline, cooperation, and preparation for warfare, and was not shared equally by helots or all residents of Sparta. What was this system called?
Ancient writers including Xenophon credited the rules of the Agoge to which lawgiver? His historical identity and dates remain uncertain.

On January 7, 2015, armed attackers stormed a French satirical magazine’s office during an editorial meeting, killing 12 people, including journalists and cartoonists. What attack prompted worldwide debate about freedom of expression after the publication had drawn controversy for its cartoons of Muhammad?

During the Charlie Hebdo shooting, gunmen attacked the magazine’s office in France’s capital on January 7, 2015. Which city, situated on the Seine and home to the Eiffel Tower, was the scene of the attack?

During a 1914 conflict between the United States and Mexico, diplomats from Argentina, Brazil, and Chile offered mediation and convened talks at Niagara Falls, Ontario. What collective name, formed from the initials of those three South American countries, was applied to this group?
The ABC Powers’ 1914 mediation effort brought U.S. and Mexican representatives together for talks that opened on May 20. In what Ontario city did the delegates meet?

This Japanese admiral commanded the Combined Fleet from 1939 until his death in 1943. He studied at Harvard, served as Japan’s naval attaché in Washington, and lost two fingers at the Battle of Tsushima. Who was he?

Isoroku Yamamoto was a principal planner of this surprise Japanese carrier-aircraft raid on December 7, 1941, which sank the USS Arizona and struck the U.S. Pacific Fleet at its Hawaiian base. What naval base was targeted?

In April 1943, U.S. codebreakers intercepted Isoroku Yamamoto’s itinerary, allowing American P-38 fighters to ambush his aircraft over Bougainville and kill him. What was the U.S. mission to intercept his flight called?
This sovereign office placed its holder at the apex of dynastic government and was traditionally associated with authority over the Yellow and Yangtze River regions. What was this ruler’s title?
An Emperor of China could invoke this Zhou-era doctrine to explain why a dynasty had divine approval—and why misrule might justify its replacement. What was this doctrine called?

Born in Frankfurt in 1929, this German-Jewish teenager kept a diary while her family hid in a concealed space behind her father’s business in Amsterdam during the Nazi occupation. Her father later arranged for the diary’s first publication in 1947. Who was she?
After Anne Frank and her sister Margot were arrested in August 1944, they were deported to this concentration camp in Germany. Both sisters died there in early 1945. What was the camp’s name?

In Spanish America, what system granted colonists control over Indigenous labor and tribute, while requiring them, at least in principle, to protect and Christianize the communities assigned to them? It was gradually supplanted by the hacienda system.

Which Habsburg ruler issued the New Laws of 1542 in an effort to curb abuses associated with the encomienda? He ruled Spain and the Holy Roman Empire and was succeeded on the Spanish throne by his son Philip II.

Lasting from 431 to 404 BCE, this conflict pitted Athens and its maritime allies against Sparta and its coalition of Greek states. It ended after Athens surrendered, leaving Sparta temporarily dominant in Greece. What war was it?

During the Peloponnesian War, this 405 BCE naval battle near the Hellespont saw Lysander’s Spartan fleet defeat the Athenians. The loss helped cut off Athens’s grain supplies and force its surrender the following year. Name the battle.
Which Argentine general led the Army of the Andes across the mountain range in 1817, helped defeat Spanish forces at Chacabuco, and later proclaimed Peru’s independence in Lima?

In 1822, José de San Martín met Simón Bolívar for a private discussion about the leadership of the remaining campaign to free Peru from Spanish rule. What is the name commonly given to this historic meeting?

An army captain turned politician, he represented Rio de Janeiro in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies from 1991 until taking office as president on January 1, 2019. His four-year presidency ended on January 1, 2023, after he lost the 2022 runoff to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Who is this Brazilian politician?
In Brazil’s 2022 presidential runoff, Jair Bolsonaro lost to a former president who had governed from 2003 to 2010 and returned to office in January 2023. Name the winner of that runoff.

Which late-Republic Roman general and statesman first became consul in 107 BCE and was elected to the office seven times? His forces later defeated the Teutones near Aquae Sextiae and the Cimbri at Vercellae.
Gaius Marius gained prominence during Rome’s war against this Numidian king. The conflict ended with the king’s capture in 105 BCE and his eventual appearance in a Roman triumph.
Which prominent Canadian political family includes Pierre, who served as Canada’s prime minister for much of the late 20th century, and his son Justin, who later became prime minister as well?

During Pierre Trudeau’s premiership, members of the FLQ kidnapped Quebec cabinet minister Pierre Laporte and British diplomat James Cross; Laporte was later murdered, and the federal government invoked the War Measures Act. What name is given to this political crisis in the history of the Trudeau family?
Fought from 1853 to 1856, this conflict pitted Russia against an alliance that included the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France, and Sardinia. The struggle centered on influence in the Black Sea region.

During the Crimean War, a British cavalry attack at the Battle of Balaclava advanced against Russian artillery despite a mistaken order. Alfred, Lord Tennyson later commemorated the disastrous advance in a poem describing 600 soldiers riding into the “valley of Death.”

In 1605, English Catholic conspirators planned to kill James I and destroy the House of Lords during the state opening of Parliament. Guy Fawkes was arrested guarding explosives in a cellar beneath the chamber on 5 November; what is the failed conspiracy commonly called?

During the Gunpowder Plot, an anonymous warning about the state opening of Parliament was delivered to a Catholic peer, who passed it to the royal government and helped prompt a search of Westminster. Which peer received the letter?

Held on June 12, 2018, this historic meeting brought Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un together for the first time, marking the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president and the leader of the government in Pyongyang. The two leaders issued a joint statement addressing bilateral relations and the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. What was this event?
At the 2018 North Korea–United States Singapore Summit, Trump and Kim Jong-un met at a resort hotel on Sentosa Island, rather than in central Singapore. What was the name of the hotel venue?

In 1685, Louis XIV used this decree to revoke Henry IV’s 1598 settlement, ending official Protestant toleration in France and prompting many French Reformed believers to flee. Named for the royal palace where it was promulgated, what decree is this?

The Edict of Fontainebleau ended the legal protections of these French Calvinists, leading many to leave for Protestant territories such as the Dutch Republic and Brandenburg-Prussia. What was this French Protestant community called?

Which Italian Christian Democratic statesman helped negotiate the Historic Compromise between his party and the Italian Communist Party? He was kidnapped and killed by the Red Brigades in 1978, during the Years of Lead.
Aldo Moro was kidnapped and killed in 1978 by an Italian far-left militant group whose name combines a color with a military formation. What was the group called?

Wilfred Owen portrays one of these men fumbling for his gas mask during a poison-gas attack, then “guttering, choking, drowning” in a recurring nightmare. In “Anthem for Doomed Youth,” he asks what bells can sound for them; what is the name for these combatants of the 1914–1918 conflict?

The World War I soldiers in this English poet’s work include the gas-stricken figure in “Dulce et Decorum Est” and the dead youths mourned in “Anthem for Doomed Youth.” He served in the British Army and was killed in action on 4 November 1918, one week before the Armistice; who was this poet?

This South African anti-apartheid activist became a highly visible figure in the struggle while her husband was imprisoned on Robben Island. After she was banished to Brandfort in 1977, she continued political organizing under severe restrictions; who was she?

In 1977, the apartheid government banished Winnie Madikizela-Mandela from Soweto to a remote town in the Orange Free State, where she remained under restrictions until 1985. What town was the site of this forced relocation?

On December 7, 1941, Japanese aircraft launched a surprise assault on the U.S. naval base at Oahu, striking warships and airfields while the two governments were still engaged in diplomacy. What event prompted the United States to enter World War II?

During the Attack on Pearl Harbor, this U.S. battleship suffered a catastrophic explosion and the greatest loss of life of any ship struck in the attack. Its wreck remains beneath a memorial at the naval base. Which ship was it?

After Nero’s death, this Roman commander defeated rival claimants during the Year of the Four Emperors and became emperor in AD 69. Alongside his son Titus, he led the campaign that suppressed the Great Jewish Revolt. Who was he?
Vespasian began building this Flavian amphitheater in Rome on the site of an artificial lake in Nero’s palace complex. His son Titus later inaugurated it. What landmark was it?
What maritime industry involved hunting whales and processing their blubber into oil that was widely used to fuel lamps before kerosene became common?

During the early U.S. whaling trade, this Massachusetts island was a leading center before the industry shifted toward mainland ports such as New Bedford. Whaling history is commemorated there by a museum bearing the island’s name. Which island is it?

In 1565, Ivan IV established a separately governed personal domain with its own administration, finances, and armed force, distinct from the rest of his realm. This system, used to strengthen the tsar’s authority and punish suspected opponents, ended in 1572. What was it called?

During the Oprichnina, Ivan IV’s forces carried out a notorious punitive expedition in 1570 against a northern Russian city once known for its powerful veche and extensive trade. Which city was attacked?

Born José Doroteo Arango Arámbula, this Mexican revolutionary joined Francisco Madero’s movement against Porfirio Díaz and later commanded the División del Norte. What leader’s 1916 raid on a New Mexico town prompted the U.S. Punitive Expedition?

In March 1916, Pancho Villa’s forces raided this U.S. border town, leading President Woodrow Wilson to send John J. Pershing on a punitive expedition across the border that failed to capture Villa. Which town was attacked?

From 1925 until 1961, what name did the Russian industrial city on the Volga River bear before it was renamed Volgograd? It is especially remembered as the site of a devastating World War II battle in 1942–1943.

In accounts of Stalingrad’s wartime defense, what colossal memorial sculpture stands atop Mamayev Kurgan in present-day Volgograd? The sword-bearing figure depicts a woman calling her people to battle.
Which conservative Austrian statesman chaired the 1814–15 diplomatic gathering that reshaped Europe after Napoleon’s defeat? He resigned from office during the Revolutions of 1848.
Klemens von Metternich famously dismissed this peninsula as a mere “geographic expression.” In the 19th century, Charles Albert of Piedmont-Sardinia pursued the unification of this country.

Which Mexican political party, established under its final name in 1946 after the PNR and PRM, dominated the presidency from 1929 to 2000? During its long rule, the outgoing president’s selection of the party’s next presidential nominee became known as the Dedazo.

After the Institutional Revolutionary Party lost Mexico’s presidency for the first time in 71 years in the 2000 election, which National Action Party candidate defeated PRI nominee Francisco Labastida and took office that December?

Adopted in France in 1792, this mechanical device uses a heavy falling blade to execute a condemned person by decapitation. It became closely associated with the French Revolution and was used to execute Louis XVI in 1793. What is this device?
The guillotine was designed by a physician, not by Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, who advocated for a uniform method of execution. Which French physician designed the instrument?

This French politician founded En Marche! on 6 April 2016, then won the presidential runoff against Marine Le Pen on 7 May 2017. Reelected in April 2022, he began a second five-year term that May. Who is he?
Emmanuel Macron founded this political movement on 6 April 2016, and it supplied the platform for his 2017 presidential campaign. What was the movement’s original name?

This Roman statesman served as consul in 195 BCE and censor in 184 BCE, and he fought in the Second Punic War. He became famous for urging the destruction of Carthage at the end of his speeches; who was he?

Cato the Elder wrote a surviving Latin prose manual offering advice on farming and estate management, often considered the oldest surviving complete work of Latin prose. What is the title of this work?

This British Cunard ocean liner was torpedoed by German submarine U-20 off southern Ireland on May 7, 1915, while sailing from New York to Liverpool. Its sinking killed nearly 1,200 people and heightened tensions between Germany and the United States. What was the ship's name?
The RMS Lusitania was sunk off Ireland by German submarine U-20 on May 7, 1915. Which German naval officer commanded U-20 during the attack?

They were an elite infantry corps of the Ottoman army, and many of their recruits were Christian boys taken through the devşirme levy, converted to Islam, and trained for imperial service. What was this corps called?

In 1826, Sultan Mahmud II ordered Ottoman forces to suppress the Janissaries after their resistance to military reforms, ending the corps and clearing the way for a new army. What is the historical name for this episode?
Which Byzantine general serving under Justinian I defeated the Vandals at Ad Decimum in 533 and later led campaigns to recover Italy from the Ostrogoths?
During the Gothic War, Belisarius captured this city in 540 after the Ostrogoths surrendered it. What former Ostrogothic capital became a key center of Byzantine rule in Italy?
Created in 1938 after Mexico nationalized its oil industry, this state-owned company became the country’s petroleum producer. What is the company’s natural name?
Pemex was established after this Mexican president nationalized the country’s oil industry in 1938. Who was the president?

Opened in July 1942 as part of a Nazi campaign in occupied Poland, this killing center received deportation trains from the Warsaw ghetto and used engine exhaust in its gas chambers. After prisoners revolted on August 2, 1943, the Germans dismantled the site and tried to conceal their crimes; what was this extermination camp?

Treblinka extermination camp opened in July 1942 as one site in a Nazi operation that also encompassed the killing centers at Bełżec and Sobibór. What was the codename for this campaign of mass murder against Jews in occupied Poland?

Which Late Bronze Age society flourished on mainland Greece from roughly 1600 to 1100 BCE? Its palace centers used a script that recorded an early form of Greek, and its fortified citadels and culture are often connected with the world portrayed in Homeric war poems.

In Mycenaean civilization, palace scribes pressed this syllabic script into clay tablets to record inventories, offerings, and personnel. Its decipherment established that the language it represented was an early form of Greek.

This 1862 address followed a dispute over Prussia’s army expansion and appropriations. It argued that military strength, rather than parliamentary debate or majority votes, would decide the central political questions of German unification. What was this address called?

In the Blood and Iron Speech, the speaker addressed a Prussian parliamentary budget committee on September 30, 1862, amid a dispute over army expansion and government appropriations. Which Prussian minister-president argued that national power would decide Germany’s major political questions?

These financial institutions operate in a country known for its neutrality and are covered by a 1934 law whose Article 47 criminalized the disclosure of client information. During World War II, some held gold looted by Nazi Germany from occupied territories. What are these institutions commonly called?

In 1997, this Swiss security guard drew international attention after taking documents from UBS that were slated for destruction and related to Holocaust-era assets. His actions became part of the controversy over secrecy at Swiss banks. Who was he?

In classical Athens, citizens recorded a fellow citizen’s name on pottery shards during a civic vote, and a successful result sent that person away for ten years. What was this democratic procedure called?

Ostracism is associated with classical Athens, where this statesman’s father, Xanthippus, was recalled from exile during the Second Persian invasion. His son later led Athens during its Golden Age and delivered the famous funeral oration described by Thucydides; who was he?

This Roman commander expanded Roman control through campaigns in Gaul, then defied the Senate by leading his army across a small northern Italian river in 49 BCE. His victory over Pompey’s forces left him dictator, but senators killed him on 15 March 44 BCE. Who was he?

Julius Caesar joined Marcus Licinius Crassus and Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus in an informal political pact formed around 60 BCE to coordinate their influence in Rome. What alliance is commonly known by its ordinal name?

During Julius Caesar’s campaigns in Gaul, this Arvernian leader united a coalition of Gallic tribes against Rome and surrendered after the siege at Alesia in 52 BCE. Who was this defeated Gallic chieftain?

Julius Caesar introduced a reformed way of reckoning dates in 45 BCE, replacing the old Roman system with a solar year of 365 days and an extra day every fourth year. What system bears the reformer’s name?

In 49 BCE, Julius Caesar’s decision to cross this river with his legion violated the Senate’s order to disband his army before entering Italy and precipitated civil war. Which river became shorthand for an irreversible point of no return?

Which Israeli military operation, carried out on June 7, 1981, sent eight F-16s with six F-15s in support to destroy Iraq’s Osirak reactor southeast of Baghdad? The strike prompted Iraq to raise the attack before the UN Security Council.
In Operation Opera, what was the name of the Iraqi nuclear reactor southeast of Baghdad that Israeli aircraft destroyed on June 7, 1981?

Founded in 2002, this Ukrainian natural-gas company became one of the country’s largest private gas producers. It drew international scrutiny after the son of a U.S. vice president joined its board in 2014. What company is it?

A Yale-trained lawyer and co-founder of Rosemont Seneca Partners, this person served on Burisma’s board from 2014 to 2019. His appointment drew controversy because his father was then serving as U.S. vice president. Who was he?

Ancient Egyptian monarchs combined civil government with religious leadership, commanded the military, collected taxes, and were expected to maintain Maat. What traditional title is used for these rulers and the institution of kingship they embodied?
The pharaoh was expected to uphold an Egyptian ideal encompassing cosmic order, balance, and justice. What was this principle called?
After Upper and Lower Egypt were united, the pharaoh’s official crown combined the White Crown of the south with the Red Crown of the north. What was this double crown called?
In 1922, Howard Carter discovered the largely intact tomb KV62 in the Valley of the Kings, belonging to a young pharaoh whose burial treasures became world-famous. Which ruler’s tomb was it?
This Eighteenth-Dynasty pharaoh established a new royal capital at Akhetaten, now known as Amarna, and elevated the worship of Aten. He was married to Nefertiti; which ruler was he?

Founded by Babur after his victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, this early modern Islamic empire ruled much of the Indian subcontinent for centuries. Its court later patronized monumental architecture such as the Taj Mahal. What empire was it?
Within the Mughal Empire, which emperor abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, promoted a policy known as sulh-i kul (“universal peace”), and established his court at Fatehpur Sikri?
During the Mughal Empire’s period of greatest territorial extent, which ruler reimposed the jizya in 1679 and led prolonged campaigns in the Deccan?

Which major armed struggle began in 1910 with Francisco I. Madero’s call for an uprising against Porfirio Díaz, then continued through rival revolutionary factions and reshaped Mexico’s political and social order?

During the Mexican Revolution, a constituent congress produced a charter promulgated on February 5, 1917. Which document’s Articles 3, 27, and 123 addressed education, land and subsoil rights, and labor, respectively?

This 1868–69 Japanese civil war pitted supporters of the new imperial government against defenders of the Tokugawa shogunate. Imperial forces won its opening battle near Kyoto, and the last shogunate supporters surrendered in Hokkaido. What conflict was it?
During the Boshin War, the first major battle took place in January 1868 near Kyoto, where imperial forces defeated troops loyal to the Tokugawa shogunate. What battle marked this opening victory?

In the fifth year of his reign, Akhenaten chose a site beside the Nile for a new royal capital dedicated to the Aten, naming the city Akhetaten. By what modern name is the archaeological site commonly known?
At Amarna, archaeologists uncovered diplomatic clay tablets exchanged between Egypt and foreign courts, many written in Akkadian. What wedge-shaped writing system was used to inscribe them?

This English queen consort was the second wife of Henry VIII and the mother of Elizabeth I. She was executed at the Tower of London in 1536, during the political and religious upheaval surrounding the king’s break with Rome. Who was she?
During Anne Boleyn’s queenship, Parliament passed a 1534 statute declaring Henry VIII the supreme head of the Church of England and rejecting papal authority in England. What was this statute called?
This Spanish conquistador led the 1519 expedition into Mexico, took Moctezuma II captive, and ultimately brought down the Aztec Empire after capturing Tenochtitlan. Who was he?
In 1520, Hernán Cortés and his forces fled Tenochtitlan at night after an uprising, suffering heavy losses during their retreat. What name is commonly given to this disastrous escape?

Which Scottish knight and resistance leader became Guardian of Scotland after helping lead the uprising against Edward I? Alongside Andrew Moray, he won a major victory at Stirling Bridge in 1297, but his forces were defeated by Edward the following year.
William Wallace's army faced Edward I at this battle in July 1298, where English forces defeated the Scottish resistance and prompted Wallace to resign as Guardian of Scotland. What battle was it?

During the twelfth-century struggle between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire, this pope resisted Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and faced a rival claimant to the papal throne. Which pontiff reigned from 1159 to 1181?

Pope Alexander III's chief imperial adversary convened the Diet of Roncaglia after subduing Milan. The Holy Roman emperor later drowned in the Saleph River while traveling to the Third Crusade; what was his name?

Centered on the Nile Valley and Delta, this civilization was traditionally divided into a southern “Upper” land and a northern “Lower” land before early rulers united them. Its pharaohs built funerary monuments ranging from Djoser’s Step Pyramid at Saqqara to Khufu’s Great Pyramid at Giza. What civilization is this?

In Ancient Egypt’s New Kingdom, this Dynasty 18 ruler commissioned a terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri. Official images sometimes show this female pharaoh wearing the traditional regalia of a king, including a false beard. Who was she?

This Ottoman sultan reigned from 1520 to 1566, captured Belgrade in 1521, and launched a siege of Vienna in 1529. His rule coincided with the empire’s political and cultural high point; who was this ruler?
During the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent, which Ottoman architect designed the Süleymaniye mosque complex in Istanbul?
An unidentified serial killer murdered at least five women in London’s Whitechapel district in 1888. What name became attached to the killer in accounts of the case?

Some theories about Jack the Ripper’s identity proposed that he was a physician serving the British monarch who reigned in 1888. Her reign was later surpassed in length by Elizabeth II; who was this queen?

After her husband Thutmose II died, this Eighteenth-Dynasty ruler first served as regent for the young Thutmose III, then adopted the title and royal imagery of a king. Her reign included a celebrated expedition to Punt and major building projects near Thebes; who was this pharaoh?
Hatshepsut’s famous terraced mortuary temple was built against cliffs on the west bank of the Nile near Thebes. What archaeological site, also home to the temple of Mentuhotep II, is its location?
Commissioned under the Flavian emperors and opened by Titus in 80 CE, this elliptical amphitheater in Rome hosted gladiatorial contests and animal hunts. What is its common name?

The Colosseum’s common name is linked to an enormous statue that once stood nearby, originally depicting the emperor associated with the Great Fire of Rome and later altered to represent the sun god. What was this statue called?
Which southern African Bantu people speak isiZulu, a language in the Nguni group, and formed a powerful nineteenth-century kingdom by bringing many chiefdoms under centralized rule?
The Zulu people’s early nineteenth-century kingdom was centralized under a ruler who reigned from 1816 until his assassination in 1828 and reorganized its military forces. Who was this monarch?
He is often regarded as the last great king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Ruling from Nineveh, he established a renowned royal library there. Who was this king?
Ashurbanipal established his renowned royal library in the Assyrian capital that also served as his seat of government. What was the name of this city?
A former member of the M-19 movement and former mayor of Bogotá, this Colombian politician won the 2022 presidential runoff as the Historic Pact candidate. Who became president that August?

Gustavo Petro pledged to halt new contracts for oil exploration as part of his climate agenda. Which 2015 international treaty calls for keeping global warming well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C?

This Indigenous people historically lived in south-central Chile and neighboring parts of Argentina, where they resisted Spanish efforts to impose colonial rule. Their language and identity endure today, alongside continuing demands concerning land and political recognition. What people is this?

The Mapuche people resisted Spanish domination in a prolonged conflict in south-central Chile, where a frontier shaped by both warfare and trade persisted for generations. By what name is this colonial-era conflict commonly known?

A Dominican friar from Valladolid, he became the first Grand Inquisitor of the Spanish Inquisition in 1483. He directed the tribunal’s early expansion under Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile; who was he?

Tomás de Torquemada was appointed the first head of this royal tribunal in 1483, and it expanded under Ferdinand and Isabella to investigate alleged heresy and enforce religious orthodoxy. What institution was this?

What clandestine Imperial Japanese Army research organization, based in occupied Manchuria during World War II, carried out lethal experiments on prisoners and researched plague and other biological weapons? Its operations were centered at a complex near Harbin.

Unit 731 was led by a Japanese army physician and microbiologist who directed its biological-warfare research and later received U.S. immunity from prosecution in exchange for experimental data. What was his name?

Beginning in 1868, this Japanese political transformation ended Tokugawa shogunal rule and established a government acting in the name of the emperor. It also set in motion sweeping reforms to centralize and modernize the country. What is this transformation called?
During the Meiji Restoration, this 1868 declaration outlined five guiding principles, including public deliberation and seeking knowledge from around the world. What was this document called?

After the 1682 Moscow uprising, this daughter of Tsar Alexis became regent while her younger half-brothers Ivan V and Peter shared the throne. Peter’s supporters removed her from power in 1689; what was her name?
Sophia Alekseyevna’s rise to the regency followed a 1682 revolt by a corps of Russian infantrymen who intervened in the succession dispute. What was this corps called?

Founded in 1905, this Irish political organization became closely associated with the campaign for Irish independence and later with Irish republicanism. Its elected members of the British Parliament have traditionally abstained from taking their seats. What is the organization?
Which Irish journalist and nationalist founded Sinn Féin in 1905 and later served as president of Dáil Éireann in 1922? He died during the Irish Civil War that same year.

In this 1942–43 Eastern Front battle, Soviet defenders held positions along the Volga while German troops fought through ruined streets and factories. A Red Army counteroffensive encircled the German Sixth Army, whose remaining troops surrendered by February 1943. What battle was this?

During the Battle of Stalingrad, the Red Army launched this codename counteroffensive on 19 November 1942, striking the Axis-held flanks and trapping Germany’s Sixth Army. What was this operation called?
A nation's permanent diplomatic mission in another country's capital is usually led by an ambassador and handles official relations with the host government. What is this mission called?

In August 1998, coordinated bombings struck the U.S. embassy in Nairobi and the U.S. embassy in Dar es Salaam, killing more than 200 people. Which jihadist organization was responsible for these attacks?
This German king was the son of Henry the Fowler and became a leading defender of the Latin Church. Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome on February 2, 962; who was he?
In 955, Otto I defeated Magyar raiders near Augsburg in a victory that helped end their westward incursions. What was this battle called?

What is the name of the colonial-era commerce in which European traders exchanged goods with Indigenous communities for animal pelts, especially beaver, reshaping alliances and economies across what is now Canada? Rivalries among trading companies in this commerce also fueled European expansion into the continent’s interior.

Within the Canadian fur trade, which English trading enterprise received a royal charter in 1670 granting it exclusive rights over Rupert’s Land, a vast drainage basin in northern North America? Its charter gave it a central role in the contest for the continent’s interior.

In early sixth-century BCE Athens, this lawgiver was traditionally credited with replacing much of Draco’s code while retaining its homicide provisions. He barred the use of Athenians as security for loans and divided citizens into four property classes. Who was he?

Solon’s reforms included a measure whose name is often translated as “shaking off of burdens.” It ended debt bondage for Athenians and prohibited using a person as security for a loan; what was this reform called?
Which Italian far-left armed organization operated during the Years of Lead and kidnapped former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978, holding him captive for 55 days before killing him?
What former Italian prime minister, a Christian Democratic leader who helped pursue the Historic Compromise with the Italian Communist Party, was abducted and killed by the Red Brigades in 1978?

A German Augustinian friar and theology professor in Wittenberg, he challenged the church’s use of indulgences in a set of 1517 theses. His protest became a catalyst for the Protestant Reformation. Who was he?
Martin Luther was summoned to this 1521 imperial assembly before Emperor Charles V to defend his writings. After he refused to recant, he was condemned as an outlaw. What was the assembly called?

Martin Luther completed this landmark German translation of the Christian scriptures in 1534, making them more accessible to lay readers and helping shape standard German. By what name is the translation commonly known?

Martin Luther’s 1517 objections targeted church certificates associated with remission of temporal punishment, which preachers such as Johann Tetzel promoted for payment. What were these certificates called?
Which Syrian political family rose to power when its patriarch seized control in 1970 and became associated with decades of Ba’athist rule?
In the history of the Assad family, what was the name given to Hafez al-Assad’s 1970 seizure of power, in which he ousted Salah Jadid and established his rule in Syria?

This civilization began as a city on the Italian peninsula, and its republican government is traditionally dated to around 509 BCE. Conquest and diplomacy later expanded its power across much of the Mediterranean. What civilization is described?
In Ancient Rome, what title did Octavian receive in 27 BCE, marking his emergence as the dominant ruler after the civil wars that followed Julius Caesar’s assassination?

Irish and Manx belong to the same Celtic language branch as the traditional language of Scotland’s Highlands, while Welsh and Breton belong to another branch. What name applies both to this branch and to cultural traditions associated with its speakers?
At the 1893 founding meeting of the Gaelic League, this scholar chaired the proceedings and later became the organization’s first president. Who was he?

After France’s 1940 armistice with Germany, this French general broadcast from London on 18 June urging continued resistance. He led Free France during World War II and later founded the republic inaugurated in 1958.

After Charles de Gaulle returned to power during the Algerian crisis, French voters approved a new constitution in a 1958 referendum. What republic did that constitution establish, under which he served as president from 1959 to 1969?

Which sixth Mughal emperor expanded the empire’s rule across much of the Indian subcontinent and fought the British East India Company in Child’s War? He secured the succession by defeating his elder brother Dara Shikoh at Samugarh.
Aurangzeb’s decisive 1658 victory over Dara Shikoh in this battle near Agra helped determine the Mughal succession after Shah Jahan became incapacitated. What was the battle called?

In one year, uprisings demanding constitutional government, national self-determination, and social reform spread from France across the German and Habsburg lands and into parts of Italy. Often called the “Springtime of the Peoples,” what is this wave of European upheavals known as?

During the Revolutions of 1848, elected delegates from the German states formed a national assembly to draft a liberal constitution and consider unification. It offered the imperial crown to Prussian King Friedrich Wilhelm IV, who refused it; what was this assembly called?
Which early Hungarian state emerged after the Magyar conquest and settlement of the Pannonian Basin in the late ninth century? It preceded the Christian kingdom established under Stephen I.

The Grand Principality of Hungary was ruled by a house descended from the son of Álmos, who is traditionally credited with leading the Magyars into the Carpathian Basin. That same family supplied Hungary’s monarchs until its male line ended in 1301; which ruling house was it?

Called by Pope Innocent III for an expedition intended to recapture Jerusalem, this 1202–1204 campaign instead became entangled in Byzantine politics and culminated in the sack of Constantinople. Give the expedition’s customary name.

During the Fourth Crusade, a shortage of funds for Venice’s transport fleet led Doge Enrico Dandolo to propose attacking this rebellious Adriatic port. It became the first Catholic city assaulted by a Catholic crusader army.

During the Fourth Crusade, which Byzantine prince, son of Isaac II, persuaded the western army to help restore his father and was crowned co-emperor in August 1203? A popular uprising deposed him the following January.

In 1970, two FLQ cells in Quebec kidnapped British trade commissioner James Cross and cabinet minister Pierre Laporte. The federal government responded by invoking emergency powers under a national statute; what is the name of this Canadian political crisis?
During the October Crisis, which Canadian statute did Pierre Trudeau’s federal government invoke on 16 October 1970, granting authorities sweeping powers of arrest and detention?

What name is given to the early modern international movement of bullion from the Americas and elsewhere into China? A major stream crossed the Pacific from New Spain and helped pay for Chinese goods.
In the Global Silver Trade, which Spanish colonial mining city in present-day Bolivia became famous for Cerro Rico, a mountain that yielded vast quantities of silver?
Which country in southern North America became independent from Spain in 1821 and adopted a constitution in 1824 establishing a federal republic?
In Mexico’s nineteenth-century history, what 1848 agreement ended the U.S.–Mexican War and transferred extensive territory, including California, to the United States?

A German industrialist initially used forced labor for his enamelware factory in Kraków, but later moved more than a thousand Jewish workers to a factory in Brünnlitz to protect them from Nazi persecution. Who was this businessman?

Oskar Schindler’s efforts to save Jewish workers during the Holocaust inspired a 1993 film directed by Steven Spielberg. This largely black-and-white drama includes the image of a girl in a red coat during the liquidation of the Kraków ghetto; what is the film’s title?
Which 1983–2009 conflict pitted Sri Lanka’s government against an insurgency seeking a separate Tamil homeland called Eelam? It ended after government forces defeated the Tamil Tigers.
During the Sri Lankan Civil War, which insurgent leader founded and headed the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam? He was killed in May 2009 during the government’s final offensive.

This Bourbon monarch succeeded his brother Louis XVIII in 1824 and was crowned at Reims the following year. His July 1830 ordinances restricting the press and changing election rules helped trigger the revolution that drove him into exile; who was he?

After Charles X was forced to abdicate during the July Revolution of 1830, the Chamber installed a ruler from the Orléans branch, later known as the “Citizen King.” Which monarch held the French throne until the revolution of 1848?

A Christian Democratic politician became the first head of government of the Federal Republic of Germany when it was founded in 1949. He remained chancellor until 1963, leading the country through postwar recovery and closer ties with Western Europe and the United States. Who was he?

Konrad Adenauer became West Germany’s first chancellor four years after this 1945 Allied meeting at a palace near Berlin. The victorious powers used it to establish postwar arrangements for Germany and Europe. What was the meeting called?

In the late 1690s, Scottish investors organized a colonial trading venture intended to connect Atlantic and Pacific commerce through a settlement on the Isthmus of Panama. Its failure cost many lives and much of Scotland’s invested wealth, becoming one factor in negotiations before the 1707 union with England. What was this project called?

During the Darien scheme, what name did the colonists give the settlement founded by the first expedition, which sailed from Leith in July 1698? The settlement was established in Panama, where inadequate supplies, disease, and Spanish opposition contributed to the venture’s failure.

In 911, a Viking leader reached a land-for-allegiance settlement with a Carolingian ruler at Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, laying the foundation for the duchy later associated with the Normans. What was the leader’s Norse name, rather than his baptismal name Robert?
Rollo received territory in northern France through the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, concluded in 911. Which Carolingian king negotiated that settlement and ruled West Francia from 898 to 922?

Founded in late 1918 by figures including Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, this German party emerged from the Spartacist movement. Ernst Thälmann led it in the 1932 elections. What was the party’s name?

On 27 February 1933, a blaze at Berlin’s parliament building became the pretext for Hitler’s emergency decree and a crackdown that included members of the Communist Party of Germany. What event was this?

In 325 CE, Constantine summoned Christian bishops to a gathering in a city in present-day Turkey to address a dispute over Christ’s relationship to God the Father. The bishops rejected a teaching about the Son and issued a creed describing him as “begotten, not made” and of the same substance as the Father; what gathering was this?

The First Council of Nicaea rejected this Alexandrian presbyter’s claim that the Son was created and was not co-eternal with the Father. What churchman gave his name to the theological dispute the council addressed?
In the Mandinka language, this royal title means “king” or “emperor.” Rulers of the Mali Empire, including Musa I, bore it; what was the title?

Under the Mali Empire, a ruler bearing the title Mansa helped make this Saharan city a leading center of trade and Islamic scholarship. Its Sankore mosque and university became famous, and it was long portrayed in Europe as a mysterious, hard-to-reach destination. Which city was it?
Born in Corsica, this French general rose to power during the Revolution, became First Consul after a 1799 coup, and crowned himself emperor in 1804. Who was he?

Near the end of the French Revolution, Napoleon Bonaparte used army support to overthrow the Directory and replace it with a three-man Consulate, in which he became First Consul. What event marked this transfer of power?
In 1804, Napoleon Bonaparte introduced a civil-law framework that standardized laws across France, protected property rights, and ended many feudal privileges. What is this legal system called?

At a 1805 battle in Moravia, Napoleon Bonaparte drew Russian and Austrian forces onto the Pratzen Heights before striking their weakened center. This victory broke the Third Coalition; what battle was it?
After Napoleon Bonaparte’s defeat at Waterloo and the end of the Hundred Days, the British exiled him to a remote South Atlantic island, where he remained until his death in 1821. What island was it?
This sovereign country in Western Europe has Paris as its capital. Its history includes the development of West Francia into a kingdom and the revolution that began in 1789. What country is it?
In France, what 1598 royal proclamation issued under Henry IV sought to end the Wars of Religion by granting Huguenots protections, before Louis XIV revoked it in 1685?
In the history of France, what 843 agreement divided the Carolingian Empire among Charlemagne’s grandsons, with its western partition later developing into West Francia?

Beginning with Iraq’s invasion and occupation of Kuwait on 2 August 1990, this conflict followed months of United Nations demands and a coalition military buildup. A January 1991 air campaign and a ground offensive beginning on 24 February expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait; what 1990–1991 conflict is described?
During the Gulf War, which small, oil-rich state between Iraq and Saudi Arabia was invaded by Iraq on 2 August 1990 and liberated by coalition forces after their ground offensive?

Emerging from Scandinavia between the late 8th and late 11th centuries, these seafarers raided, traded, and founded settlements across Europe and the North Atlantic. Their voyages reached Greenland and a place they called Vinland. What people are described?

Vikings used these shallow-draft, clinker-built vessels for coastal raids and long-distance voyages. Archaeological examples have been excavated from Norway’s Oseberg and Gokstad burial mounds. What vessels were they?
Vikings established a Norse settlement on this North Atlantic island, where the Althing was founded around 930. Reykjavik is its capital today. Which country is it?

Vikings reached a North American region they called Vinland centuries before Columbus. The explorer often credited as the first European to reach North America was a son of Erik the Red and a brother of Freydis. Who was he?

During the French Wars of Religion, this French Calvinist Protestant community was targeted in the 1572 St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre and later received limited toleration under Henry IV’s 1598 settlement. What name is given to this group?
Which 1598 settlement issued by Henry IV granted the Huguenots a measure of religious toleration and civil rights after decades of conflict, before Louis XIV revoked it in 1685?

This major Maya center on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula grew near natural sinkholes that provided water. Its main plaza is marked by El Castillo, and its monuments include a vast ball court with stone rings and carvings. Name the city.
At Chichén Itzá, a prominent natural sinkhole provided access to water and was associated with ritual activity. What is this feature known as?

This English humanist and lawyer became lord chancellor under Henry VIII in 1529 after serving as Speaker of the House of Commons. He resigned in 1532, refused to affirm the king’s supremacy over the English church, and was executed in 1535. Who was he?
Thomas More published a 1516 work describing an imagined island society, whose name later became associated with an ideal or visionary community. What is the title of this influential work?

Fought near a city in present-day Ukraine on July 8, 1709, this engagement saw Peter I’s Russian army decisively defeat Charles XII’s Swedish forces. Its outcome broke Sweden’s offensive momentum during the Great Northern War. What battle was it?
At the Battle of Poltava, this Ukrainian hetman had allied with Charles XII in hopes of escaping Russian control. After the Swedish defeat, he fled with the Swedish king. Who was he?

On 21 April 2019, coordinated suicide bombers struck three churches and three hotels in cities including Colombo, Negombo, and Batticaloa, killing more than 200 people. What is the commonly used name for this series of attacks?

During the 2019 Sri Lanka Easter bombings, which city—Sri Lanka’s commercial capital and the site of attacks on the Shangri-La, Cinnamon Grand, and Kingsbury hotels as well as St. Anthony’s Shrine—was hit?
